DNA Replication: Study Notes (Lecture 7.3)
Oct 6, 2026 · @simon
Big picture
DNA is copied using each existing strand as a template, and the core rules are the same in every organism studied.

The template idea: Watson and Crick (Nature, 1953) noted that complementary base pairing immediately suggests a copying mechanism. Each strand dictates the sequence of its new partner.
History: by the 1940s DNA was known to be the genetic molecule; the structure (1953) showed how it could be copied.
Most of what we know comes from E. coli (in vitro work with purified proteins), but the principles are conserved in all replication systems.

The three fundamental rules:

Replication is semiconservative.
Replication starts at an origin and usually proceeds bidirectionally.
Synthesis runs 5’ to 3’ and is semi-discontinuous (leading strand continuous, lagging strand in fragments).

The process itself has three phases: initiation (open the helix at the origin), elongation (build the new strands), termination (forks meet, complex released).
Rule 1: Replication is semiconservative
Each daughter molecule contains one old (parental) strand and one newly made strand.

Each parental strand serves as the template for one new strand, giving two double helices that are each half old, half new.
Proposed by Watson and Crick; proven by Meselson and Stahl in 1957.
Background you may be asked (not on the slide): Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in heavy nitrogen (15N), switched to 14N, and separated DNA by density. After one generation all DNA was hybrid density; after two, half hybrid and half light. This ruled out conservative and dispersive models.

Rule 2: Origins and bidirectional replication
Replication starts at defined origins and two replication forks move away from each origin in opposite directions, forming a “replication bubble”.
E. coli: oriC

One origin, oriC, about 245 bp, on a circular chromosome.
Contains a tandem array of three 13-mer, AT-rich repeats (easy to melt: A-T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds vs 3 for G-C) plus binding sites for DnaA (9 bp repeats).
Order of assembly: DnaA binds oriC, which recruits the helicase DnaB; exposed single strands are coated by SSB; this complex lets primase (DnaG) and DNA polymerase bind.

Eukaryotes
Same overall mechanism, but more complex because of:

























FeatureE. coliHumanGenome sizeabout 4 x 10^6 bpabout 6 x 10^9 bp (diploid)Chromosomes1, circular23 pairs, linearOrigins1 (oriC)many, about 3 x 10^5

Eukaryotic origins have no single specific consensus sequence (in humans); they tend to be AT-rich regions.
The origin recognition complex (ORC) assembles there. The lecture lists its associated parts as: a hexamer similar to bacterial DnaA; the Mcm2-7 helicase (six subunits); replication protein A (RPA), the single-strand binding protein; and DNA pol alpha and pol delta, which interact sequentially.
Yeast is the exception on sequence: its origins are defined ~150 bp sequences called ARS (autonomously replicating sequences).

Rule 3: 5’ to 3’ synthesis, semi-discontinuous
Polymerases only add nucleotides to a free 3’-OH, so every new strand grows 5’ to 3’ (reading the template 3’ to 5’). Because the two template strands are antiparallel, the two new strands must be made differently.






























Leading strandLagging strandSynthesisContinuousDiscontinuous (Okazaki fragments)Direction vs forkSame direction as fork movementOpposite to fork movementPrimers neededOne (at the origin)One per Okazaki fragmentJoiningNot neededFragments joined by DNA ligase
Okazaki fragment length:

Bacteria: about 1000 to 2000 nucleotides.
Eukaryotes: about 150 to 200 nucleotides.

Memory aid: the lagging strand template runs 5’ to 3’ in the direction the fork moves, so its new strand must be built pointing away from the fork; each time more template is exposed, a new primer and fragment are started.
DNA polymerases: requirements and mechanism
Every DNA polymerase needs a template and a primer with a free 3’-OH; none can start a chain from nothing.

Discovery: the search began in 1955. Arthur Kornberg purified the first one from E. coli, a single-polypeptide enzyme now called DNA polymerase I. E. coli was later found to have at least four others. The core reaction is conserved across species.

Two requirements

Template: base pairing dictates the sequence of the new strand.
Primer with a free 3’-OH: short RNA oligonucleotides made by an RNA polymerase called primase. (Lengths quoted in this lecture vary: about 5 nt on the polymerase slide, 10 to 60 nt for the E. coli leading-strand primer.)

Catalytic mechanism (two-metal-ion)
Reaction: (DNA)n + dNTP gives (DNA)n+1 + PPi.

The 3’-OH of the last nucleotide in the growing chain makes a nucleophilic attack on the alpha-phosphate of the incoming dNTP.
Upper Mg2+ activates that 3’-OH (helps the nucleophilic attack).
Lower Mg2+ helps the pyrophosphate (PPi) leave.
Both ions stabilize the transition state; they are held by Asp residues of the enzyme.
RNA polymerases use a similar mechanism.

Extra (not on slide, but explains direction): PPi is then hydrolyzed by pyrophosphatase, which pulls the reaction forward. Growth 5’ to 3’ means the energy for each step comes from the incoming nucleotide’s own triphosphate.
Fidelity: why replication is so accurate
Accuracy comes from three layers: base selection, proofreading, and later repair.
1. Base selection (geometry)

Selection depends on hydrogen bonding and on base-pair geometry.
Correct A-T and G-C pairs have nearly the same shape, so the active site fits both.
Mismatched pairs have the wrong geometry and are excluded from the active site.

2. Where errors come from: tautomers

A base can briefly sit in a rare tautomeric form and pair with the wrong partner.
Examples from the slide: rare imino cytosine (C)* pairs with A; rare enol thymine (T)* pairs with G; rare imino adenine (A)* pairs with C; rare enol guanine (G)* pairs with T.
In vitro, polymerase alone inserts about 1 wrong nucleotide per 10^4 to 10^5.

3. Proofreading (3’ to 5’ exonuclease)

A wrong nucleotide is added (for example C* opposite A).
The base shifts back to its normal form, so it is now mispaired.
The mispaired 3’ end blocks translocation; the polymerase slides back, placing the end in the 3’ to 5’ exonuclease site.
The wrong nucleotide is cut off.
The polymerase slides forward and resumes.

Key point: proofreading is not the reverse of polymerization (it releases a dNMP by hydrolysis, not a dNTP).
Error rates





















StageErrorsBase selection only1 in 10^4 to 10^5Selection + proofreading1 in 10^6 to 10^8Plus repair systems (e.g. mismatch repair)lower still
E. coli DNA polymerases
Pol III is the main replicase; Pol I does clean-up (primer removal) and repair; Pol II does some repair.



























































Pol IPol IIPol IIIGenepolApolBpolC (dnaE)Subunit types1710 or moreMr103,00088,000 (polymerizing subunit)791,5003’ to 5’ exo (proofreading)YesYesYes5’ to 3’ exoYesNoNoRate (nt/s)16 to 2040250 to 1000Processivity (nt before dissociating)3 to 2001500500,000 or moreMain rolePrimer removal, repair, recombinationSome DNA repairPrincipal replication enzyme

Trap: over 90% of the polymerase activity in E. coli extracts is Pol I, yet it is not the main replicase (too slow, too low processivity).
Pol II shares several subunits with Pol III (beta, gamma, delta, delta’, chi, psi).

Pol I: nick translation

Only Pol I has 5’ to 3’ exonuclease activity. It lets Pol I bind at a nick, remove the nucleotides ahead of it (RNA or DNA, released as rNMPs or dNMPs) while adding dNTPs behind, so the nick moves along the strand.
Uses: removing RNA primers in replication, repair, recombination.
When it dissociates, a nick remains for DNA ligase to seal.

Pol III: subunits


















































































SubunitCopiesGeneFunctionGroupalpha2polC (dnaE)PolymerizationCoreepsilon2dnaQ (mutD)3’ to 5’ proofreading exonucleaseCoretheta2holE(part of core)Coretau2dnaXStable template binding; core dimerizationClamp loadergamma1dnaXClamp loaderClamp loaderdelta1holAClamp openerClamp loaderdelta’1holBClamp loaderClamp loaderchi1holCInteraction with SSBClamp loaderpsi1holDInteraction with gamma and chiClamp loaderbeta4dnaNSliding clamp for processivityClamp

gamma and tau come from the same gene (dnaX); gamma is a shorter product made by translational frameshifting.
beta clamp: two beta subunits form a donut that encircles the DNA, keeping Pol III from falling off. This is the source of its huge processivity.
The clamp-loading (gamma) complex loads a new beta clamp on the lagging strand for every Okazaki fragment.
Overall layout: two cores (alpha-epsilon-theta), each on a beta clamp, linked by tau to the clamp loader and to the DnaB helicase.

The mechanism in E. coli
Phase 1: Initiation
At least nine proteins open the helix at oriC and build a prepriming complex; DnaA is the crucial one.













































ProteinFunctionDnaARecognizes ori; opens the duplex at specific sitesDnaB (helicase, 6 identical subunits)Unwinds DNADnaCNeeded to load DnaB at the originHUHistone-like DNA-binding protein; stimulates initiationPrimase (DnaG)Makes RNA primersSSB (4 identical subunits)Binds single-stranded DNARNA polymeraseFacilitates DnaA activityDNA gyrase (topoisomerase II)Relieves torsional strain from unwindingDam methylaseMethylates (5’)GATC sequences at oriC
Steps:

About 10 DnaA molecules (with ATP) bind the 9 bp repeats of oriC.
DnaA then denatures the AT-rich 13 bp repeats. Needs ATP and HU.
DnaB hexamers load onto each strand with help from DnaC (ATP). DnaB unwinds further.
SSB coats the single strands, stabilizing them and preventing re-annealing.
Priming and replication begin.

Phase 2: Elongation

Leading strand: primase (DnaG) makes one RNA primer (10 to 60 nt) at the origin; Pol III extends it continuously, keeping pace with unwinding.
DnaB moves along the lagging strand template 5’ to 3’, unwinding the fork.
DNA gyrase works ahead of the fork to relieve supercoiling.
Lagging strand: the template loops out so one Pol III dimer can make both strands at once (the “trombone” model). For each Okazaki fragment: primase lays a primer, the clamp loader adds a beta clamp, and a core extends it until it hits the previous primer.
Speed: about 1000 nt/s on both strands.
Finishing each fragment: Pol I removes the RNA primer (5’ to 3’ exo) and fills in DNA; DNA ligase seals the nick. E. coli ligase uses NAD+ (releases NMN); eukaryotic ligases use ATP (release AMP + PPi).

Phase 3: Termination

The two forks meet in a terminus region opposite oriC containing several Ter sequences (20 bp).
Ter sites bind the Tus protein (terminus utilization substance).
Ter-Tus complexes are polar: a fork can pass in one direction but not the other, creating a fork trap the fork can enter but not leave.
The replication complex is released.

Eukaryotic replication
The core machinery is conserved, but eukaryotes use many origins, an ORC tied to the cell cycle, and their own set of polymerases.

Yeast: several origins per chromosome, the ~150 bp ARS sequences.
Origins are bound by the ORC, which is regulated by cell-cycle factors (ensures each origin fires once per cycle).
Humans: bidirectional replication from many origins spaced 30,000 to 300,000 bp apart.

Eukaryotic DNA polymerases






















































PolymeraseLocation3’ to 5’ exoEssential for nuclear replicationRole (as taught)alphaNucleusNoYesPrimers during initiationbetaNucleusNoNoRepairdeltaNucleusYesYesMain elongation of both strands; uses PCNA clampepsilonNucleusYesYesOther replicative enzyme; possibly primer removal on lagging strandgammaMitochondriaYesNoReplicates mitochondrial DNA (nuclear-encoded)zetaNucleusNoNoRepair

PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen) is the eukaryotic equivalent of the beta clamp: a ring that raises processivity.
Bacteria-to-eukaryote equivalents: DnaA ~ ORC; DnaB ~ Mcm2-7; SSB ~ RPA; beta clamp ~ PCNA; Pol III ~ Pol delta/epsilon.

Review: numbers, slide inconsistencies, self-test
Numbers to memorize













































ItemValueoriC size245 bporiC repeatsthree 13 bp (AT-rich), four 9 bp (DnaA sites)Okazaki fragmentsbacteria 1000 to 2000 nt; eukaryotes 150 to 200 ntE. coli fork speedabout 1000 nt/sPol III processivity500,000 nt or moreError rate10^-4 to 10^-5 alone; 10^-6 to 10^-8 with proofreadingHuman originsabout 3 x 10^5, spaced 30 to 300 kbTer sequence20 bpMeselson and Stahl1957
Where the slides are imprecise or inconsistent (check what your exam expects)

DnaA site count: the oriC diagram shows five DnaA sites; the initiation slide says four 9 bp repeats. Lehninger editions differ on this. The slides also call DnaA a “hexamer” in one place and “about ten molecules” in another.
Primer length: about 5 nt on one slide, 10 to 60 nt on another.
Pol alpha does not itself make the RNA primer. It forms a complex with a primase subunit: primase makes the short RNA, then Pol alpha extends it with a short stretch of DNA.
Pol delta vs epsilon: the slide says delta elongates both strands. The current consensus is that Pol epsilon synthesizes the leading strand and Pol delta the lagging strand. Primer removal in eukaryotes is mainly done by FEN1 and RNase H, not Pol epsilon.
PCNA is called a “subunit” of Pol delta; it is really a separate sliding-clamp protein that Pol delta binds.
“6 x 10^9 bp” for humans is the diploid figure; the haploid genome is about 3 x 10^9 bp.

For the exam, learn the version on the slides but know the modern view in case of a conceptual question.
Self-test

 Why must the lagging strand be made discontinuously?
 What two things does every DNA polymerase need to start?
 Which Mg2+ ion does what in the polymerase active site?
 How does a tautomeric shift cause a mutation, and how is it corrected?
 Why is proofreading not the reverse of polymerization?
 Pol I is >90% of E. coli polymerase activity. Why is Pol III the replicase?
 Which activity lets Pol I remove RNA primers, and what is that process called?
 What gives Pol III its high processivity, and what is the eukaryotic equivalent?
 List the initiation steps at oriC in order, with the protein for each.
 Name the protein that seals Okazaki fragments and its cofactor in E. coli.
 How do Ter and Tus create a fork trap?
 Give three reasons eukaryotic replication is more complex than bacterial.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis: fatty acid synthesis and its regulation
Source: Audio Clip 8 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file; the recording starts just after the beginning of the lecture and seems to run to the end.
Official code Lec 5.10 (taught Thu 1 Oct). Study notes by Dr. Alberto Pérez-Mediavilla. Companion lectures: Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies, Lec 5.11 Cholesterol metabolism and lipid transport, Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation.
Resources:

Slides: 5.10 Biosíntesis de lípidos (slides)
Study material: Biosynthesis of fatty acids and TAG (lecture notes)
Previous-year notes: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 5.13. Synthesis of lipids” (PDF p. 141-143)

Marking: [Notes] = gap filled from the study-material lecture notes (A. Pérez-Mediavilla). [Lucía] = gap filled from FMCI  Lucia Reed notes. [check] = lecturer or transcript conflicts with a source in your vault (named). [verify] = possible error that the sources in your vault do not settle.
Exam flags from the lecturer

ACC regulation and malonyl-CoA: “a number of questions that I pose in the final exam are around this”. Be able to connect glucose oxidation, fatty acid oxidation and fatty acid synthesis through the regulation of ACC.
Not examined: synthesis of TAG and glycerophospholipids in depth; the step-by-step chemistry of fatty acid synthase or of desaturation.

1. Why we synthesize lipids

Mainly in the liver (also the main site of glycogen synthesis), though all cells can make lipids.
Uses:

Energy storage (TAG).
Membrane lipids: glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids (both contain fatty acids).
Lipid anchors for peripheral membrane proteins, e.g. farnesyl and palmitoyl groups. Examples: G-alpha and G-beta-gamma of heterotrimeric G proteins are anchored, not floating in the cytosol; Ras (an oncogene, at the start of signalling cascades) is held at the membrane by lipid anchors.
Signalling molecules: membrane phosphatidylinositol (PIP2) is the source of IP3, which triggers Ca2+ release.


Link to cholesterol: the more acetyl-CoA accumulates (instead of being oxidized in the Krebs cycle), the more cholesterol and fatty acid can be made. More carbohydrate, more acetyl-CoA, more fatty acid and more cholesterol synthesis.
[Notes] Other lipid roles: pigments (retinal, carotenes), cofactors (vitamin K), detergents (bile salts), hormones (vitamin D derivatives, steroids), messengers (inositols, eicosanoids), membrane anchors (myristoyl, palmitoyl). Lipid synthesis is endergonic and uses reducing power (NADPH). Most active synthesis: liver and lactating mammary gland.

2. Raw materials

Carbon source: acetyl-CoA, from glucose oxidation (glycolysis + PDH) or beta-oxidation. Excess carbohydrate that cannot be stored as glycogen becomes fatty acids, then TAG.
Reducing power: NADPH.
Energy: ATP (for ACC).

When acetyl-CoA is diverted to synthesis

High NADH/NAD+ and ATP/ADP ratios mean plenty of energy: time to store, not oxidize. These ratios are the main regulators of the Krebs cycle and partially inhibit it.
As a result citrate and acetyl-CoA accumulate and are available for synthesis.
The lecturer said citrate synthase activity falls, while his next step depends on citrate accumulating. [Lucía] When the ATP/ADP and NADH/NAD+ ratios are high the Krebs cycle slows, and acetyl-CoA and citrate accumulate in the mitochondria; citrate is then released to the cytoplasm. Lucía’s Krebs section lists citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase among the regulated enzymes.

Hormonal state (insulin vs glucagon)

[check] Transcript says “the ratio between insulin and glucose”; it is the insulin/glucagon ratio (as in Lec 5.9).
High insulin: PDH and ACC are very active, so glucose carbons go to acetyl-CoA and then to fatty acids.
High insulin also “silences” the glucagon pathway in fat tissue: low cAMP, low PKA, low HSL activity, little TAG hydrolysis.

3. Moving acetyl-CoA out of the mitochondrion
Fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis happen in the cytosol, but most acetyl-CoA is in the mitochondrial matrix, and there is no acetyl-CoA transporter in the inner membrane.
Citrate shuttle

Matrix: acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate to citrate (citrate synthase, as in Krebs).
Citrate leaves via the tricarboxylate (citrate) transporter of the inner membrane.
Cytosol: citrate lyase splits citrate into acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate (the reverse of citrate synthase).
Oxaloacetate must return, or the shuttle stops. Two routes:

Oxaloacetate is reduced to malate (malate dehydrogenase, uses NADH), and malate enters the mitochondrion through a malate transporter.
Or malate is converted by malic enzyme to pyruvate + CO2, producing NADPH. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion through its transporter and pyruvate carboxylase turns it back into oxaloacetate.




[check] The transcript places pyruvate carboxylase in the cytoplasm; the study notes and Lucía place it in the mitochondria (activated by high acetyl-CoA).
[Notes] Cost: the shuttle consumes 2 ATP per acetyl-CoA exported (one at citrate lyase, one at pyruvate carboxylase).

The NADH-to-NADPH conversion
Adding malate dehydrogenase + malic enzyme: electrons taken from NADH end up in NADPH. This is a second source of NADPH, besides the pentose phosphate pathway.
NADPH sources

Pentose phosphate pathway: main source in hepatocytes; also in mammary glands.
Malic enzyme.
[Notes] Malic enzyme supplies about half of the NADPH for fatty acid synthesis; the rest comes from the pentose phosphate pathway.

4. Lactation link: medium-chain fatty acids and MCAD deficiency

During pregnancy and lactation the mammary glands synthesize lots of fatty acids; human milk is rich in medium-chain fatty acids.
Connection to remember: babies with MCAD deficiency (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, a beta-oxidation enzyme) cannot obtain energy from medium-chain fatty acids, which is dangerous on a milk diet.
Why medium-chain: prolactin rises in pregnancy and activates the thioesterase (TE) of fatty acid synthase early, so chains are released at 12 or 14 C instead of 16. Only in mammary glands; the liver in women still makes palmitate. Men and women have the same fatty acid synthase. [Notes] Maternal milk contains fatty acids shorter than 16 C because, with the hormonal profile of pregnancy and lactation, TE acts earlier.

5. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC): the key step
“The most important part of this topic.”
Acetyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP to malonyl-CoA + ADP + Pi

Activation of acetyl-CoA by carboxylation of its methyl group, so units can be joined.
The carboxyl comes from CO2 after hydration to bicarbonate.
Cofactor: biotin (vitamin), as in other carboxylases.
[Notes] The reaction is irreversible and is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis. ACC has three activities in one multifunctional polypeptide; biotin is bound to the epsilon-amino group of a lysine (like pyruvate carboxylase).

Malonyl-CoA: the switch

Malonyl-CoA inhibits CAT I (carnitine acyltransferase I), so long-chain fatty acids cannot enter the mitochondrion: beta-oxidation stops.
CAT I activity is regulated only by malonyl-CoA.
So: more malonyl-CoA = more fatty acid synthesis and less fatty acid oxidation. Both pathways never run at full speed at the same time.

6. Regulation of ACC
Allosteric




















EffectorEffectLogicCitrateActivatesCitrate in the cytosol means the mitochondria are full of energy. [Notes] Citrate also inhibits PFK-1, slowing glycolysisPalmitoyl-CoAInhibitsFeedback: palmitate (16 C) is the main end product
Covalent (phosphorylation; very important in the liver)

Dephosphorylated = active. Phosphorylated = inactive. Same strategy as PDH.
Glucagon (low carbohydrate): GPCR, G-alpha-s, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA, which phosphorylates and inactivates ACC.

Less malonyl-CoA, so CAT I is released and more fatty acids enter the mitochondria for oxidation.
At the same time, in adipose tissue glucagon activates HSL and fatty acids are mobilized to peripheral tissues.


Insulin (after a meal, high carbohydrate): activates a phosphatase that dephosphorylates ACC, making it very active.

Acetyl-CoA from the meal (“the cake”) becomes malonyl-CoA, which inhibits CAT I and feeds fatty acid synthesis, then TAG or cholesterol.
This is why excess carbohydrate after a meal is mostly converted to fat.


[Lucía] In muscle, ACC is additionally phosphorylated and inactivated by AMPK. Epinephrine, like glucagon, activates PKA and inhibits ACC.
Clinical link: one of the connections between obesity and hypercholesterolemia (excess carbohydrate drives both fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis).

Summary of the two states








































Fed (high insulin)Fasting (high glucagon)ACCDephosphorylated, activePhosphorylated by PKA, inactiveMalonyl-CoAHighLowCAT IInhibitedActiveFatty acid synthesisOnOffBeta-oxidationOffOnHSL (adipose)OffOn
7. Fatty acid synthase (overview only)

Human type I fatty acid synthase: one large complex with seven activities. [Notes] Precisely: one multifunctional polypeptide with six active sites plus a seventh domain without catalytic function, the ACP, whose phosphopantetheine prosthetic group anchors the growing chain.






































AcronymActivityKSbeta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (condensation)MATmalonyl/acetyl-CoA-ACP transferase (loads substrates)KRbeta-ketoacyl-ACP reductaseDHbeta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydrataseERenoyl-ACP reductaseACPacyl carrier protein (carrier, not an enzyme)TEthioesterase (releases the product)

ACP carries a phosphopantetheine arm that moves the growing chain between the active sites in each cycle.
[check] Transcript calls DH a “hydrate activity” and TE “tireless trait”; the cycle includes a dehydration step (Lucía) and Lucía names the TE domain, which releases palmitate as a thioesterase.
[Lucía] The ACP “arm” is part of coenzyme A; its function is to keep the fatty acid bound during the whole process.

Each cycle: four reactions, the chemical reverse of beta-oxidation






























Fatty acid synthesisBeta-oxidation1CondensationOxidation (FAD)2Reduction (NADPH)Hydration3DehydrationOxidation (NAD+)4Reduction (NADPH)Thiolysis
[check] The recording pairs synthesis “hydration” with beta-oxidation “dehydration”. Lucía and the study notes give synthesis as condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction, and beta-oxidation uses a hydratase (enoyl-CoA hydratase, Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies). So synthesis dehydrates and beta-oxidation hydrates; the steps appear in reverse order.
First cycle in detail [Notes]

Loading: MAT transfers the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA to the KS thiol, and the malonyl group of malonyl-CoA to the ACP thiol.
Condensation (KS): malonyl is decarboxylated (the CO2 released is the one added by ACC) and its methylene attacks the acetyl on KS, giving acetoacetyl-ACP (beta-ketobutyryl-ACP).
Reduction (KR): the C3 carbonyl is reduced by NADPH, giving beta-hydroxybutyryl-ACP.
Dehydration (DH): water is removed between C2 and C3, giving trans-delta2-butenoyl-ACP.
Reduction (ER): the double bond is reduced by NADPH, giving butyryl-ACP (4 C).


Butyryl is moved to KS so ACP can take the next malonyl; cycles repeat until 16 C, when TE releases palmitate.

Products

Main product: palmitate (16:0), released as palmitate by TE (hence palmitoyl-CoA as the feedback inhibitor of ACC).
Additional enzymes elongate it to stearate (18 C), 20 C, etc. [Notes] Elongases in the smooth ER and mitochondria, with the same chemistry as fatty acid synthase.
Unsaturated fatty acids: we can introduce double bonds (do not learn the chemistry), but not beyond C9. So linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential and must come from the diet.
[Notes] Fatty acyl-CoA desaturases introduce cis double bonds by an oxidative reaction. Palmitate and stearate give palmitoleate (16:1 delta9) and oleate (18:1 delta9). Mammals can add a double bond at delta9 but not beyond C10 (the lecturer said C9), so they cannot make linoleic (18:2 delta9,12) or alpha-linolenic (18:3 delta9,12,15); plants can. These are precursors of arachidonic acid (20:4), the precursor of eicosanoids (prostaglandins, prostacyclins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes).
[check] Transcript says “essential amino acids”; Lucía’s notes: linoleic and linolenic acid are essential fatty acids, obtained from the diet.

Overall balance [Lucía]

Activation: 7 acetyl-CoA + 7 ATP + 7 CO2 to 7 malonyl-CoA + 7 ADP + 7 Pi.
Synthesis: 7 malonyl-CoA + 1 acetyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H+ to palmitate + 8 CoA + 7 CO2 + 14 NADP+.
Net: 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 ATP + 14 NADPH + 14 H+ to palmitate + 14 NADP+ + 8 CoA + 6 H2O. A high-energy process, only carried out when possible. The study notes give the same balance.

8. TAG synthesis (study notes only; “not in depth” per the lecturer)

[Notes] Fatty acids go either to TAG (storage) or to phospholipids (membranes). During growth (childhood, adolescence) much goes to phospholipids; afterwards most becomes TAG in adipose tissue.
[Notes] Highest TAG synthesis: liver and adipose tissue. We store about 15 kg of TAG against about 400 g of glycogen.
[Notes] Precursors: glycerol 3-phosphate (mostly from DHAP of glycolysis; in liver and kidney also from glycerol via glycerol kinase) and fatty acyl-CoA (made by the acyl-CoA synthetases of Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies).
[Notes] C1 and C2 of G3P are acylated, giving phosphatidic acid, precursor of both TAG and glycerophospholipids. For TAG it is dephosphorylated to DAG and acylated at C3.
[Notes] Insulin promotes conversion of glucose to fatty acids and TAG. Insulin-dependent diabetics cannot use glucose or make fatty acids from it, and have high fat oxidation and ketone body production.
[Notes] Triacylglycerol cycle: about 75% of fatty acids released by lipolysis are re-esterified to TAG (partly in adipose tissue, partly in the liver after travelling in blood), keeping a steady pool of circulating fatty acids ready for energy needs.

Final message from the lecturer: what matters most is connecting glucose oxidation, fatty acid oxidation and fatty acid biosynthesis through ACC regulation.

What the lecturer wants you to know

The overall process of synthesis (4 phases, locations), not every reaction or carbon count.
The HMG-CoA reductase reaction in detail: it is the regulated step and the target of statins.
Regulation of HMG-CoA reductase (long and short term).
Concepts over numbers: cholesterol synthesis is very costly.

1. Introduction

Cholesterol “is not bad, it is not good, it is essential”. Too much or too little is harmful; the amount must be tightly controlled.
Functions: membrane component; precursor of many molecules (bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D).
At the molecular level there is only one cholesterol molecule; there is no “good” or “bad” cholesterol.
[Lucía] Mostly hydrophobic with a very small hydrophilic area; in membranes it regulates fluidity and stability. Two sources: diet (absorbed by enterocytes) and de novo synthesis, mainly in the liver.
[Notes] Structure: four fused rings (cyclopentaneperhydrophenanthrene, “steran”), a small polar OH head and a large non-polar region. Synthesis mostly in liver and intestine; also adrenal cortex and gonads (for steroid hormones). An adult on a low-cholesterol diet can make close to 1 g/day.
[Notes] Absorption: enterocytes take up dietary cholesterol mainly through NPC1L1; ABCG5/ABCG8 pumps sterols back into the lumen. Ezetimibe inhibits NPC1L1. The ring structure cannot be metabolized, so elimination is hard: faecal excretion of bile acids and biliary cholesterol is the main route.
Importance: many Nobel Prizes of the 20th century relate to cholesterol (synthesis, metabolism, structure, steroid hormones). Statins were the most profitable drug class in history (over 10 billion dollars per year for one early statin).

2. Cholesterol synthesis (overview)
All 27 carbons come from acetyl-CoA (acetate, 2 C). Mainly in hepatocytes. Acetyl-CoA is made in mitochondria and must be exported to the cytosol (as citrate, via the citrate transporter: see Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis, section 3).



































PhaseReactionProductLocation1Condensation of 3 acetyl-CoA (3 reactions)Mevalonate (6 C)Cytosol2Phosphorylation (from ATP) and decarboxylation (loses 1 C as CO2)Activated isoprenes (5 C, with 2 phosphate groups; two types)Cytosol3Condensation of 6 isoprene units (6 x 5 C)Squalene (30 C, linear)Cytosol, then to ER4Cyclization, oxidations, loss of 3 carbons, many reactionsCholesterol (27 C)Mostly smooth ER

Phase 1 resembles ketone body synthesis (also a condensation of acetyl-CoA units).
Isoprene units: the pyrophosphate groups are released as inorganic phosphate during condensation; their hydrolysis supplies the energy for condensation.
[Notes] The two activated isoprenes are interconvertible isomers: isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate; making them uses 3 ATP per mevalonate. The last step to squalene is catalyzed by squalene synthase (ER). Squalene is converted to cholesterol in the ER by monooxygenases, cyclases, isomerases, reductases and others.
[Notes] HMG-CoA reductase is an integral membrane protein of the smooth ER and its reaction is irreversible.
[Notes] Other organisms: plants make phytosterols (sitosterol, stigmasterol), fungi make ergosterol.
Squalene: the lecturer said it is named after the animal from whose liver it was first isolated. [verify] The transcript says “stars”; probably a mistranscription (the name suggests sharks, Squalus). Not covered in the slides or notes.
The lecturer was not fully sure where squalene enters the ER; what is certain is “start in the cytosol, finish in the smooth ER”.
Steroid nucleus = the four fused rings; any molecule keeping this structure is a steroid.

Cost

Very costly: lots of ATP, lots of carbon (acetyl-CoA) and lots of reducing power (NADPH, which itself costs energy to make).
Real cost is higher than the slide numbers because acetyl-CoA must be exported from the mitochondrion.
[check] The sources disagree on cost. Slides: 18 acetyl-CoA, 18 ATP, 16 NADPH. Study notes: 18 ATP directly (activation of six mevalonates), higher estimates if acetyl-CoA supply is counted. Lucía: 18 acetyl-CoA, 36 ATP, 16 NADPH. Learn the slide numbers. Cholesterol is also not easily (or safely) eliminated, another reason for tight regulation.

3. The key reaction: HMG-CoA reductase
Last reaction of phase 1.
HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH + 2 H+ to mevalonate + CoA-SH + 2 NADP+

HMG-CoA = 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA: glutarate (5 C, two carboxyl groups, as in alpha-ketoglutarate) with a methyl and a hydroxyl on C3, one carboxyl bound to CoA as a thioester.
How to read it (compare substrate and product):

CoA is removed.
The thioester carboxyl becomes a primary alcohol: a reduction in two steps (carboxyl to aldehyde to alcohol).
The electrons come from 2 NADPH, the typical electron carrier for biosynthesis, produced mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway (important in lipid-synthesizing tissues).


Enzyme name = substrate + reaction: HMG-CoA reductase.
It is the rate-limiting, regulated step of cholesterol synthesis.

4. Statins

Statins are structurally similar to mevalonate/HMG-CoA, bind the active site of HMG-CoA reductase and act as competitive inhibitors.
Result: less cholesterol synthesis, used in patients with high cholesterol.
Discovery (Japan, 1970s): a group screened more than 6,000 fungal products for inhibitors of cholesterol synthesis and found one in a soil fungus related to the mould used for blue cheese (Penicillium). Modern statins are modified versions with better stability and specificity.
[check] The transcript gives the first statin as “Novastatin”. [Slides] In the early 1970s Akira Endo and colleagues screened 6,000 microbial strains; Penicillium citrinum (a relative of the blue-cheese fungus) yielded mevastatin, the first cholesterol-lowering compound identified.
[Lucía] / [Notes] Statins (natural fungal products and synthetic derivatives) are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase; they also reduce other mevalonate-derived compounds.
Lecturer’s message: there are not “natural” versus “pharmaceutical” medicines, only medicine that works (with evidence) and medicine that does not. The most profitable drug in history is a natural product.

5. Regulation of HMG-CoA reductase
Needed because excess cholesterol precipitates in vessels, forming plaques that impair circulation, and because synthesis is energetically expensive.
Long-term (adaptive, takes time)

Depends on dietary cholesterol. High dietary cholesterol: less synthesis. Low dietary cholesterol: the body makes more.
Mechanism: changes in transcription of the reductase gene (more mRNA, more protein) and in degradation of the enzyme.
[check] The transcript says the hepatocyte “levels of glucose” reflect the diet; from context, and as in Lucía’s notes, he means cholesterol.
[Notes] Transcription: controlled by SREBPs (ER integral proteins). When ER cholesterol falls, the SREBP-SCAP complex moves to the Golgi, SREBP is cleaved, and its DNA-binding domain goes to the nucleus and binds sterol regulatory elements (SRE) of genes such as HMG-CoA reductase.
[Notes] Degradation: the reductase has sterol-sensing regions; high sterols trigger ubiquitination and proteasome degradation.

Short-term (fast): phosphorylation

First question to ask with any phosphorylation: which form is active? There is no fixed rule.
Here: phosphorylated = inactive, dephosphorylated = active.
AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) phosphorylates and inactivates the reductase. [check] The transcript says “when the kinase is active, you have an activation of the enzyme”; it is inactivation (Lucía: the kinase phosphorylates = inhibition).
Phosphatases remove the phosphate and reactivate it.






























SignalWhenEffectCholesterol synthesisInsulinHigh glucose (after a meal)Activates phosphatases, inhibits the kinaseOn (plenty of energy)GlucagonLow glucoseInhibits phosphatasesOff (save energy for glucose production)High AMP (low ATP)Low energyActivates AMPKOff
[check] The transcript says “level of ALT” and “AFP activates the kinase”; this is AMP (Lucía: high AMP signals low energy and inhibits cholesterol synthesis).
6. Fates of cholesterol made in the liver

Bile acids: a large fraction of cholesterol.
Free cholesterol secreted in bile into the intestine: the main (and inefficient) route of elimination. Humans are very poor at eliminating cholesterol, which is why it accumulates.
Esterification: the 3-OH of cholesterol forms an ester with a fatty acid (cholesteryl ester), making it even more hydrophobic. Done for storage in the liver (lipid droplets) or export in lipoproteins (VLDL); free cholesterol is not released into blood because it is insoluble. [Slides] / [Notes] Enzyme: ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase), transferring a fatty acid from CoA to the C3 hydroxyl.
Delivery to other tissues for membranes and hormone synthesis. The liver is the main producer and distributor.

Bile acids and enterohepatic circulation

Bile acids are steroids (keep the four-ring nucleus) with extra hydroxylations; different hydroxylation patterns give different bile acids. Example: cholic acid. Be able to recognize one as a cholesterol derivative.
Circulation: made in the liver, stored in the gallbladder, released into the intestine after a fatty meal, help digest (emulsify) fat, then most are reabsorbed and return to the liver; only a small fraction is lost in faeces. Recycling matters because they are expensive to make.
[check] The transcript says bile acids are “stored in the whole blood”; Lucía’s notes: stored in the gallbladder.
Free cholesterol in bile follows the same circulation; the fraction not reabsorbed is eliminated.
Some cholesterol-lowering drugs target this step, reducing reabsorption and increasing elimination.
[Notes] Most abundant human bile acids: cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid (recognized by the carboxylic acid on the side chain). Most are conjugated with glycine or taurine to form bile salts (glycocholic, taurocholic acid).

7. Other cholesterol derivatives

Steroid hormones: sex hormones, glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids (covered later in physiology). [Notes] All derive from cholesterol via pregnenolone. Corticosteroids (adrenal cortex): mineralocorticoids (ion balance, e.g. aldosterone) and glucocorticoids (carbohydrate metabolism, immunity, inflammation, e.g. cortisol). Sex hormones (gonads, placenta): androgens (testosterone), estrogens (estradiol, which have an aromatic ring), progestogens (progesterone). Androgens and estrogens lack the C17 side chain. Only a small fraction of cholesterol is used, since hormones act at low concentrations.
Vitamin D: from 7-dehydrocholesterol (a cholesterol precursor). UV light in the skin breaks one ring (B ring), so it is technically no longer a steroid. It is then modified further to the active form, which is important for bone formation and remodelling.

It is not strictly a vitamin because we can make it, but supplementation is sometimes needed.
[check] The transcript says “B-hydrocholesterol”; Lucía and the study notes: 7-dehydrocholesterol, whose UV-broken bond gives cholecalciferol (vitamin D3).
[Notes] The ring opens between C9 and C10; strictly a prehormone, not a vitamin or a steroid. Activation by two cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases: C25 in the liver, then C1 in the kidney, giving calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol), which promotes intestinal Ca2+ and phosphate absorption. Deficiency: rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults.


[Notes] Isoprenoids from isopentenyl diphosphate: dolichol (N-glycosylation), ubiquinone (CoQ10, Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation), and prenylation of proteins, e.g. Ras anchored by a farnesyl group (Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis); drugs blocking Ras prenylation have had little success.

8. Lipid transport: lipoproteins (recording cut mid-section)
Lipids are insoluble in water, so cholesterol and triacylglycerols cannot circulate free; they travel in lipoproteins.
Structure

Surface (polar parts facing the blood): apolipoproteins, free cholesterol (OH facing out), phospholipids (phosphate heads facing out).
Core (non-polar): triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters.

Classes (by density)



































LipoproteinSizeProtein contentDensityChylomicronsLargestLowestLowestVLDLVery lowLDLLowHDLSmallestHighestHighest
Lipid is less dense than protein, so more protein means higher density.
Chylomicrons

Made in enterocytes from digested dietary fat, packaged with protein, released into circulation.
After a high-fat meal, plasma is turbid (milky) from circulating chylomicrons; a fasting sample is clear.
[check] The transcript says diacylglycerols are packed into chylomicrons. The 5.9 study notes (Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies) say fatty acids and glycerol are reconverted into TAG in the enterocyte, and TAG with dietary cholesterol and proteins form chylomicrons. [Notes, 5.9] At target tissues apoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which hydrolyzes the TAG again.

The recording ends here. [Lucía] for the rest:

Chylomicrons reach the liver or other tissues; what the body does not use arrives at the liver.
VLDL: made in the liver; releases fatty acids to other tissues and, once depleted, becomes the cholesterol-rich LDL.
LDL: the liver’s way of delivering cholesterol to other cells. ApoB-100 recognizes the LDL receptor; LDL is internalized in clathrin-coated vesicles (review endocytosis, Lec 3.4). Defects in the receptor cause familial hypercholesterolemia.
HDL: removes cholesterol from tissues and returns it to the liver. Lucía says it is produced in the intestine. [verify] origin in the lipoprotein chapter (not yet read).
[Slides] LDL uptake by clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Anderson, Brown and Goldstein, Cell 1977; Nobel Prize).

Next session: synthesis of other lipids (Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis). The transcript’s “Maria Villa” is almost certainly Dr. Pérez-Mediavilla, author of the 5.7, 5.9 and 5.12 study notes.

Exam flags from the lecturer

Overview of purine synthesis, “not step by step, only this”. Memorize the general purine structure and the origin of each ring atom.
The two branch steps IMP to AMP and IMP to GMP: “these two steps you must study”.
Regulation of ribonucleotide reductase, especially dATP as the main inhibitor: “very important”.
dTMP synthesis cycle (thymidylate synthase, DHFR) and cancer drugs: “I used to ask questions about this micro-cycle, either as a quiz or as a developing question”, e.g. “draw a diagram explaining a strategy to treat cancer using dTTP synthesis as the target”.

1. Why nucleotides matter

DNA and RNA (replication, transcription); ATP as energy currency; parts of cofactors (CoA, NAD, FAD).
All our tissues can synthesize nucleotides.
[Slides] Also: GTP as energy carrier; SAM as cofactor; activators of biosynthetic intermediates (UDP-glucose, CDP-DAG); second messengers (cAMP, cGMP).
[Notes] There are no nucleotide stores (except ATP), so cells must make them continuously. [Slides] Nucleotide pools are kept low; their synthesis may limit rates of transcription and replication.

Clinical relevance: drug targets
Pathogens and fast-dividing cancer cells need a continuous nucleotide supply, so blocking synthesis is a treatment strategy. Problem: these drugs are not specific; they hit healthy cells too.



































DrugTargetUseAzaserine, acivicin (glutamine analogs)Glutamine amidotransferases (enzymes transferring the side-chain N of glutamine)Antibiotics; [Slides] highly toxicFluorouracilThymidylate synthase (via FdUMP), so no dTTPCancerMethotrexate (and [Slides] aminopterin)Dihydrofolate reductaseCancer; also rheumatoid arthritis[Slides] TrimethoprimBacterial DHFR (binds human DHFR far less)Antibiotic[Slides] Allopurinol and relatedStudied against trypanosomes (African sleeping sickness), which lack de novo synthesisAntiparasitic

[check] The transcript gives the glutamine analogs as “a cesarean, a siliceum”; the slides name them azaserine and acivicin.
[Slides] Many parasites (e.g. malaria) lack de novo pathways and rely only on salvage, so salvage inhibitors are promising antiparasite drugs.

2. De novo purine synthesis (adenine and guanine)
Two strategies: de novo (from scratch, the main pathway) and salvage (section 5).
Ingredients

Activated ribose (PRPP), from ribose 5-phosphate of the pentose phosphate pathway.
Amino acids as N donors: glutamine, aspartate, glycine.
One-carbon units: CO2 and formyl-tetrahydrofolate.
A lot of ATP.

Origin of ring atoms (memorize the structure)

N1 from the amino group of aspartate.
C2 and C8 from two formyl-tetrahydrofolate molecules.
The other ring atoms: see the “Origin of Ring Atoms in Purines” figure on the slides (the figure did not come through in the text extraction, so it is not transcribed here).

Folic acid and pregnancy

The formyl groups come from tetrahydrofolate, made from folic acid (vitamin B9).
During embryogenesis (e.g. neural tube closure) cells divide very fast and need many nucleotides, so women are advised to take folic acid, ideally before pregnancy.
Lack of folate during neuro-embryogenesis can cause spina bifida. [Notes] Folate deficit causes anencephaly, spina bifida, premature births and megaloblastic anaemia, among others.
Folate-rich foods (from class): mainly dark green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, asparagus), lentils, avocado, oranges, liver, eggs.

Overview of the pathway (what you need to know)

Ribose 5-phosphate is activated by pyrophosphorylation at C1 to PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate). [Slides] Enzyme: PRPP synthetase, using ATP (giving AMP). PRPP is needed for both purines and pyrimidines.
Committed step: an amino group from glutamine is added to C1 of PRPP, by glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase (the target of the glutamine-analog drugs).
The ring is built on the ribose, step by step (do not learn the steps), until the first intermediate with a complete purine ring: IMP (inosine monophosphate, inosinate), whose base is hypoxanthine.


[check] The slides say synthesis begins with the reaction of PRPP “with Glu”; the lecturer and the study notes both give glutamine (Gln) as the donor.

IMP to AMP and IMP to GMP (must know)






























AMP (adenine = 6-aminopurine)GMP (guanine = 2-amino-6-oxopurine)Change neededAdd an amino group at C6Add an amino group at C2, keeping the C6 carbonylStep 1Aspartate binds C6, forming adenylosuccinateIMP dehydrogenase oxidizes C2, forming XMP (xanthosine monophosphate)Step 2The bond is broken, releasing fumarate; the amino group stays on C6An amino group from glutamine is added by another amidotransferase[Slides] Energy donorGTPATP

Then kinases: AMP to ADP (kinase), ADP to ATP mainly by oxidative phosphorylation; GMP to GDP to GTP by kinases.
Rule: kinases use ATP as the phosphate donor, which is another reason oxidative phosphorylation is so important.

3. Regulation of purine synthesis (feedback inhibition, 3 levels)

Ribose 5-phosphate to PRPP (commits ribose to nucleotides in general). Regulated by energy: more ATP, more nucleotide synthesis; low energy, less. Example: poor nutrition in fast-growth periods (infancy) impairs growth, e.g. of bone. [Notes] The reaction needs ATP, and ADP inhibits it. [Slides] PRPP synthesis is inhibited by ADP and GDP.
Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase (commits PRPP to purines): inhibited by IMP, AMP and GMP. All three high: complete inhibition (synergy). Only IMP, or only AMP or GMP, high: weaker inhibition, so the other branch can still be made.
The branch point (balance between AMP and GMP, since DNA needs similar amounts of each):

[Notes] AMP inhibits adenylosuccinate synthetase, so IMP goes to GMP; GMP inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, so IMP goes to AMP.
The lecturer phrased this as “high AMP promotes GMP synthesis and high GMP promotes AMP synthesis” (same effect).
The cross-use of energy donors (GTP for AMP, ATP for GMP) helps keep the two balanced.



4. Catabolism of purines (gap in the recording; from slides and notes)
The recording stops as the lecturer starts this pathway. [Slides] / [Notes]:

Dephosphorylation of AMP/GMP by 5’-nucleotidase.
Adenosine is deaminated to inosine by adenosine deaminase (ADA); the ribose is removed, giving hypoxanthine. Guanosine gives guanine, then xanthine.
Xanthine oxidase oxidizes hypoxanthine to xanthine, and xanthine to uric acid, the final product, excreted by the kidneys.


[Notes] Dietary nucleic acids are broken down by pancreatic nucleases and phosphodiesterases; very little of the absorbed bases is incorporated into tissue nucleic acids, since needs are met by de novo synthesis and salvage.
[Slides] Pyrimidine catabolism leads to NH4+ and urea.

Uric acid and gout

Uric acid has very low solubility; when its concentration rises it precipitates, mainly in the joints: gout (Spanish gota). It also damages the kidneys.
Lower uric acid by:

Diet: less food rich in nucleotides. Lecturer: red meat and seafood (lobster, prawns). [Slides] Seafood and liver, and avoidance of fructose. [Notes] Diet excessively rich in glandular tissue, liver and crustaceans.
Allopurinol: inhibits xanthine oxidase, at both steps (hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid). More hypoxanthine and xanthine accumulate instead; they are more soluble than uric acid. “Not the perfect strategy.”


[Slides] Painful joints (often toes) from sodium urate crystals; mainly affects males; may involve genetic under-excretion of urate and/or overconsumption of fructose.
[Notes] Uric acid accumulates in joints and kidney, causing inflammation and nephritis.

5. Salvage of purines

The lecturer’s favourite strategy: recapture free bases from degradation before they become uric acid.
Two advantages ([Notes]): less uric acid to excrete and less energy than de novo synthesis. Hence the need for a good balance between de novo and salvage.
Student question: does salvage inhibit uric acid production? No: it lowers the amount of substrate (intermediates) available to become uric acid.
Mechanism: the base condenses with PRPP.

APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase): adenine + PRPP to AMP + PPi.
HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase): hypoxanthine + PRPP to IMP + PPi; guanine + PRPP to GMP + PPi.



Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (start of this section not recorded)

[Notes] HGPRT deficiency. A genetic disease of children with extreme symptoms: intellectual deficit, hostile behaviour, self-mutilation (fingers, lips). Lost salvage causes an extreme rise in uric acid, giving gout and strong CNS toxicity.
[Notes] Purine salvage is very active in the fetal and postnatal brain, erythrocytes, platelets, bone marrow and lymphocytes.
From the recording: neurons are disrupted and cannot work properly, hence the aggressive behaviour.

6. De novo pyrimidine synthesis
Precursors (fewer than for purines)

Aspartate (4 ring atoms), glutamine (N, via carbamoyl phosphate), CO2 (one carbon).
Different strategy: first the ring is built, then ribose is added (from PRPP). [Slides] The ring is made as orotate.

Steps (outline)

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II): glutamine amide N + CO2 + ATP to carbamoyl phosphate. Like the first reaction of the urea cycle, but a cytoplasmic isoform (CPS I is mitochondrial; Lec 5.8 Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle). Pyrimidine synthesis is entirely cytoplasmic.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase) adds aspartate.
Linear process (not required step by step) to UMP (uracil = 2,4-dioxopyrimidine).
UMP to UDP to UTP by kinases; UTP is aminated to CTP (cytosine = 4-amino-2-oxopyrimidine).


[Notes] CPS II uses 2 ATP. In humans the first three enzymes (CPS II, ATCase, dihydroorotase) form one multi-enzyme complex, CAD. Dihydroorotate is oxidized to orotate, which binds PRPP to give orotidylate; decarboxylation gives UMP. UTP to CTP is catalyzed by cytidylate (CTP) synthetase, with glutamine as amino donor and ATP.

Regulation

CTP inhibits ATCase (feedback inhibition); ATP activates.
[Notes] ATP removes the inhibitory effect of CTP: energy is available and the cell is ready to replicate. During apoptosis, caspase 3 degrades the CAD complex, stopping pyrimidine synthesis.

7. Deoxyribonucleotides: ribonucleotide reductase

No need to start again: ribonucleotides are converted to deoxyribonucleotides by replacing the 2’-OH of ribose with H.
One enzyme, ribonucleotide reductase, converts every ribonucleoside diphosphate (ADP, CDP, GDP, UDP) to its deoxy form. The real mechanism is more complex; only this overall reaction is asked.
[Slides] The two H atoms come from NADPH, carried by thioredoxin or glutaredoxin (glutathione).

Regulation (very important)

Activity site: ATP activates; dATP inhibits. dATP is the main inhibitor (link to SCID, section 9).
Specificity site: the enzyme chooses which substrate to reduce, to keep balanced dNTP pools. E.g. if dGDP is low, the enzyme increases its affinity for GDP.
[Notes] ATP or dATP increase affinity for CDP and UDP; dTTP favours GDP; dGTP favours ADP. [Slides] The enzyme oligomerizes to change specificity. [Notes] Structure: alpha2-beta2 heterodimer; alpha subunits catalytic, beta subunits generate radicals.

8. Thymidine nucleotides: dTMP synthesis (likely exam question)

dTTP is needed only for DNA (thymine replaces uracil), so replicating cells need it.
Thymine = 5-methyl-2,4-dioxopyrimidine: thymine is uracil with a methyl on C5.
Path: dUMP to dTMP to dTDP to dTTP (the last two by kinases). [Slides] dUMP comes from dUTP via dUTPase (“roundabout pathway”).

The micro-cycle

Thymidylate synthase transfers a methyl group from methylene-tetrahydrofolate to dUMP, giving dTMP. The folate becomes dihydrofolate (DHF).
Folate is scarce in cells, so it must be regenerated:

Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) reduces DHF to tetrahydrofolate (THF).
THF is converted back to methylene-THF. [Notes] By serine hydroxymethyltransferase.




So folic acid is needed for purines and for dTMP, which is why it matters so much during embryogenesis.
[check] The transcript calls the donor “methyl tetrahydrofolate”; the study notes and slides give methylene-tetrahydrofolate, as the lecturer himself says later.

Cancer strategy

Blocking only dTTP synthesis is enough: no dTTP, no DNA replication, no cell division.
Fluorouracil: inhibits thymidylate synthase. [Slides] It is converted by the salvage pathway into FdUMP, which is the actual inhibitor. “A poison for cancerous cells, but also for healthy cells.” Less used today.
Methotrexate: inhibits DHFR, blocking folate regeneration. Still widely used, also in inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (immune system over-activation). [Slides] Methotrexate and aminopterin are DHF analogs (competitive inhibitors); trimethoprim targets bacterial DHFR.
[Notes] These inhibitors are not selective for tumour cells, so they have major side effects.

Folic acid deficiency

[Slides] / [Notes] Less thymidylate synthesis raises dUTP, so uracil is incorporated into DNA. Repair enzymes remove it by cutting the strand, causing breaks and mutations; associated with cancer, heart disease and neurological impairment.

9. SCID: severe combined immunodeficiency

Patients cannot mount an immune response.
Cause: mutation in adenosine deaminase (ADA).
Mechanism: adenosine nucleotides accumulate, so dATP accumulates; dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, so dNTPs are not made.
Activated lymphocytes must proliferate (clonal expansion), which needs DNA replication, so they fail: immunodeficiency.
First disease treated by gene therapy: a girl received the human gene carried by a virus at the end of the last century and is still alive. [verify] the lecturer’s “around 50 years old”.
Also called “bubble child” syndrome (there is a film with John Travolta; not exam material).

Exam flags from the lecturer

The chemiosmotic diagram (electron transport, proton pumping, ATP synthase): “could be one question in the practical part of the final examination”. If you understand it, you can answer the quiz questions.
Coupled vs uncoupled mitochondria: “I usually ask this question”, in physiological terms.
Know the chain “on average, not deeply”: complexes, coupling sites, protons pumped, ATP per NADH/FADH2, and where cyanide acts.
Shuttles: study yourself; “do not spend more than half an hour”.

1. Why oxidative phosphorylation matters

We use roughly our body weight in ATP per day but store very little (about 250 g).
This is only possible because ADP is continuously rephosphorylated to ATP using the energy of electron transport.
[Notes] Humans use about 83 kg of ATP per day against stores of about 250 g; each ATP is recycled about 300 times a day. Oxidative phosphorylation is the culmination of cellular respiration: an electron-motive force (NADH, FADH2) is converted into a proton-motive force, which drives ATP synthesis.

2. Chemiosmotic theory (Mitchell)

Electrons from NADH or FADH2 pass through carriers organized as complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane, ending at oxygen.
At some points the energy of these redox reactions is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space.
This creates a proton gradient: an electron flow is converted into a proton gradient.
Protons flow back through the “fifth component”, ATP synthase, which uses the energy of the gradient to make ATP.

[verify] The lecturer dated the theory to the 1970s; neither the slides nor the study notes give a date.
[Slides] ADP + Pi to ATP is highly unfavourable; ADP is not phosphorylated by a direct reaction with a high-energy phosphate carrier, but by the flow of protons down their electrochemical gradient. The intermembrane space has the higher H+ concentration (lower pH), the matrix the lower; cristae increase the inner membrane surface.
Requirements

Intact, impermeable inner mitochondrial membrane. If holes or channels let protons back in, the gradient dissipates without passing through ATP synthase and no ATP is made (basis of uncoupling, section 7).
Proton pumps: three complexes of the chain pump protons.
ATP synthase, which uses the gradient.

[check] The lecturer said cytochrome c is overall hydrophobic and moves in the inner membrane. [Slides] Cytochrome c is not part of a complex; it moves between complexes III and IV as a freely soluble protein (Lucía and the study notes agree). Ubiquinone is the lipid-soluble carrier inside the membrane. Both are connectors.
[Lucía] Complex I contains FMN and Fe-S centres as cofactors. Fe-S clusters are one-electron carriers; there are three cytochrome types in mitochondria (a, b, c).

Cytochromes and Fe-S clusters are one-electron carriers; ubiquinone takes two electrons and two protons to become ubiquinol.
Aside: anti-ageing creams contain coenzyme Q because it can capture free electrons and lower oxidative stress in the skin. Oxidative stress lowers the activity of prolyl hydroxylase, which adds OH groups to proline in collagen; these OH groups form hydrogen bonds that give collagen fibres their strength.

NADH comes from the Krebs cycle, PDH, beta-oxidation and other reactions.
Complex II contains succinate dehydrogenase, the only Krebs cycle enzyme bound to the inner membrane rather than free in the matrix. It oxidizes succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH2.
Coupling site = a point where electron transfer is coupled to proton pumping. Complex II is not a coupling site: “really important”.
Student question: complex I needs protons to make CoQH2, so how is that different from pumping? Protons are present everywhere for reduction; pumping is moving them against the gradient, which only happens in complexes I, III and IV.

Entry points (“doors”) for electrons

Complex I (NADH) or complex II (succinate/FADH2). Both end at CoQ.
Also directly to CoQ: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase of beta-oxidation (FADH2) and the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (section 10). [Lucía] Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase passes its electrons via the electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF).
[Lucía] Oxidative phosphorylation is mainly regulated by the availability of ADP.

5. Inhibitors (clinically relevant)

























SiteInhibitorNotesComplex IRotenone, amytal, piericidin[Notes] Rotenone is an insecticide, amytal a barbiturate, piericidin A an antibiotic. [check] The lecturer described rotenone as a herbicideComplex IIIAntimycin AAntibioticComplex IVCyanide, carbon monoxideBlock electron transport at IV, so I and III also stop

Cyanide binds components of complex IV, changes their conformation and blocks transport. A physician must know this mechanism.
CO is toxic both by binding the heme of haemoglobin with high affinity and by blocking complex IV.
Anecdote: during his PhD the lecturer swallowed a nanomolar amount of cyanide while mouth-pipetting, and went to the emergency room.
Rotenone and Parkinson’s disease: the lecturer told the story of young drug users who developed Parkinson’s after taking contaminated drugs; this led to an animal model of Parkinson’s made by blocking complex I. Neurons are very sensitive to ATP shortage and die.
[verify] The details of this story (place, drug and contaminant); not covered in the slides or study notes.

6. Oxidative stress

Main source of reactive oxygen species (ROS): the electron transport chain itself. Electron leakage forms superoxide and other ROS.
Mechanism of damage: ROS are radicals, highly reactive; they react with nearby molecules, creating more radicals in a chain:

Membrane lipids: change their properties. [verify] He said unsaturated lipids are turned into saturated ones; the study notes only say ROS damage membrane lipids.
Proteins: oxidize amino acid side chains, changing structure and enzyme activity.
[Notes] Superoxide (O2 + e- to O2.-) can generate even more reactive hydroxyl radicals (.OH), which damage enzymes, membrane lipids and nucleic acids.


Linked to ageing, cardiovascular and arterial disease, and neurodegeneration.

Defences

Enzymes that inactivate ROS. Peroxides derived from superoxide are reduced using glutathione, which becomes oxidized (a disulfide bridge between two glutathione molecules).
Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to break that disulfide bridge and regenerate reduced glutathione.
NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway.
[Notes] Sequence: superoxide dismutase (SOD): 2 O2.- + 2 H+ to H2O2 + O2; then glutathione peroxidase neutralizes H2O2 using glutathione (GSH, the tripeptide Glu-Cys-Gly), whose SH groups reduce it to water, forming GS-SG; glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate 2 GSH. GSH also keeps protein -SH groups reduced.
[Lucía] Antioxidants also help.
[Notes] / [Lucía] In hypoxia, electrons keep entering the chain but cannot reach O2, so ROS rise. Cells respond through HIF1 (hypoxia-inducible factor 1): it inhibits PDH (via PDH kinase, Lucía) and replaces complex IV with a form more effective in hypoxia (study notes); Lucía adds increased glucose transporters, glycolytic enzymes and lactate dehydrogenase.
[Notes] Also in hypoxia (heart attack, stroke) the gradient disappears and ATP synthase could run backwards as an ATPase, draining ATP. The fall in pH (lactate) makes the inhibitor protein IF1 dimerize, blocking ATP hydrolysis.

Ageing

With age, the activity of these enzymes and of the pentose phosphate pathway falls, so less NADPH and less capacity to control oxidative stress. More damage then further impairs mitochondria: a vicious circle (“pez que se muerde la cola”).
Age is a main risk factor for vascular and neurodegenerative diseases; oxidative stress is one reason, not the only one. Healthy habits reduce the risk.

7. Coupled vs uncoupled mitochondria (likely exam question)

Coupled: electron transport (respiration, O2 consumption) drives ATP synthesis.
Uncoupled: electrons are transported and O2 is consumed, but little or no ATP is made because the proton gradient is dissipated.

Experiment (isolated mitochondria, e.g. from bovine heart; O2 consumption and ATP synthesis measured)



































ConditionO2 consumptionATP synthesisInterpretationBuffer onlyNoNoNo electron donor+ Succinate (+ ADP, Pi)YesYesCoupled+ CyanideNoNoElectron transport blocked. NOT uncoupled.+ 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP)YesNoUncoupled

Cyanide result supports Mitchell’s theory: no electron transport, no proton pumping, no ATP. A common mistake is to call these mitochondria uncoupled; they are simply inhibited.
DNP: a lipid-soluble weak acid that picks up protons in the intermembrane space and carries them across the inner membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. The lecturer called it a poison (“venom”). Lucía’s notes and the study notes give the same experiment.
[Notes] The reverse also holds: blocking ATP synthase with oligomycin or venturicidin stops electron transport (no O2 consumption).

Physiological uncoupling: brown fat

Brown adipocytes express UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1, thermogenin), a proton channel in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Protons re-enter the matrix through it, so energy is released as heat instead of ATP.
Newborns have brown fat (e.g. at the back of the neck) because their hypothalamic temperature control is still immature.
Brown fat decreases with age; the lecturer said some muscle groups contain a little brown fat and that it can be trained, with a genetic component related to physical performance.
He also said cold-climate animals (he gave whales and birds as examples) have lots of brown fat.
[Slides] Brown adipose tissue mitochondria contain large amounts of UCP (thermogenin), which is activated by fatty acids.
[verify] The claims about brown fat in adult muscle and in whales and birds; not covered in the slides or study notes.

8. ATP synthase (F0F1)
“The most perfect molecular mechanism we have”, a molecular machine.
Structure

F0: in the inner membrane, works as a proton channel.
F1: the “mushroom head”, facing the matrix. Made of 3 alpha + 3 beta subunits, alternating. The beta subunits hold the active sites (bind ADP and Pi).
Gamma subunit: central shaft connecting F0 and F1. It is asymmetric, so as it turns it contacts each beta subunit differently.

Binding-change mechanism (rotational catalysis)
Each beta subunit cycles through three conformations:

























ConformationAffinityEventOpen (O)None for ADP or ATPReleases ATPLoose (L)Binds ADP + PiTakes up substratesTight (T)Very highForms the anhydride bond: ATP made

3 protons pass through F0.
The gamma subunit rotates, changing its contacts with the beta subunits.
Each beta subunit changes conformation: T to O (ATP released), O to L (substrates bound), L to T (ATP formed).
The next 3 protons repeat the cycle.


Analogy: a hydroelectric turbine. Water (protons) flows through a tube (F0) and turns a turbine (gamma) that generates electricity (ATP).
What drives rotation: the passage of protons through F0. So more gradient means more ATP. In uncoupled mitochondria, protons pass through other structures (thermogenin), not F0.
[check] The names of the middle state differ between sources: the slides say open, loose, tight; the study notes say open, light, tight (so the transcript’s “light” follows the study notes). Use “loose” as on the slides. “Time” in the transcript is “tight”. States: open = empty/low affinity, releases ATP; loose = binds ADP + Pi; tight = makes and binds ATP.
[Notes] Model proposed by Paul Boyer: rotational catalysis. F1 composition: alpha3 beta3 gamma delta epsilon. Each 120 degree turn of gamma meets a different beta subunit.
[Notes] About 4 H+ per ATP (3 through ATP synthase + 1 for transporting Pi, ADP and ATP across the inner membrane). With 10 H+ per NADH and 6 per FADH2, that gives 2.5 and 1.5 ATP. The lecturer, Lucía and the slides say 3 protons fuel one ATP synthesis; the 4 includes the transport proton.

9. Brain and ATP per glucose (link to section 10)
Brain oxidation of glucose gives about 30 ATP instead of 32, because neurons use the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle for cytosolic NADH.
[Slides] Lehninger Table 19-5, ATP per glucose: glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 cytosolic NADH (3 or 5 ATP depending on the shuttle); pyruvate oxidation 2 NADH (5); citric acid cycle 6 NADH (15), 2 FADH2 (3), 2 GTP/ATP (2). Total 30 or 32.
10. Shuttles for cytosolic NADH (self-study, not the most important part)

Most NADH is made in the matrix, but glycolysis makes some in the cytosol (at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, GAPDH in Lucía’s glycolysis notes). [check] The transcript says “glycerol-3 dehydrogenase” here; for glycolytic NADH it means GAPDH.
Without oxygen, NAD+ is regenerated by reducing pyruvate to lactate. With oxygen, the electrons are better used to make ATP, but there is no NADH transporter in the inner membrane, so a shuttle is needed.

Malate-aspartate shuttle (yields NADH in the matrix, 2.5 ATP; Lucía: liver, kidney and heart)

Cytosol: oxaloacetate + NADH to malate (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase).
Malate enters the matrix through a malate transporter.
Matrix: malate to oxaloacetate, regenerating NADH (mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase, as in Krebs). “We have tricked the system.”
Oxaloacetate must return: transaminated with glutamate to aspartate, which leaves through an aspartate transporter.
Cytosol: aspartate gives its amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate and oxaloacetate, ready for the next NADH.

Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (neurons; yields FADH2, 1.5 ATP)

Cytosol: NADH reduces dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glycerol 3-phosphate (cytosolic glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase).
On the outer face of the inner membrane, a second isoform oxidizes glycerol 3-phosphate back to DHAP using FAD (not NAD+), giving FADH2.
Electrons go straight to CoQ, bypassing complex I: 2 fewer ATP per glucose (2 cytosolic NADH x 1 ATP less each).


[check] The transcript says the electrons enter at “complex 2”; Lucía and the study notes: this shuttle reduces ubiquinone directly (via G3PDH in the inner membrane), skipping complex I and one coupling centre (1 ATP less).
[Lucía] / [Notes] This shuttle is used in skeletal muscle and brain; the malate-aspartate shuttle (the most active) in liver, kidney and heart.

11. Regulation [Notes]
Oxidative phosphorylation is regulated by ADP availability: when ATP use rises, ADP rises, which increases O2 consumption and ATP synthesis. [Slides] Mainly by substrate availability (NADH and ADP/Pi). IF1 prevents ATP hydrolysis at low O2 (active only at low pH). Blocked oxphos makes NADH accumulate, which feeds back up to PFK-1 in glycolysis.
