What the lecturer wants you to know

The overall strategy (transamination, transport of nitrogen to the liver, urea cycle, fate of carbon skeletons).
The urea cycle steps in outline; three enzymes highlighted: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (regulation), arginase (makes urea), ornithine transcarbamoylase (most common defect).
Diseases are used only as examples to understand normal physiology: “this session is not about diseases”. Do not memorize disease names or symptoms; read and understand the table of genetic disorders.
Cofactors, because their deficiencies have clinical consequences.

1. When are amino acids degraded?

We do not store proteins (or nucleic acids), probably because the body does not want free amino groups around.
Physiological:

Continuous protein turnover in cells: some amino acids are reused, the rest catabolized.
After a protein-rich meal.


Pathological:

Starvation: amino acids are a main carbon source for making glucose, so proteins are degraded fast.
Diabetes: the body has glucose, but without the insulin signal cells respond as in starvation and degrade proteins to make glucose.


[Lucía] Nitrogen compounds are not stored, so nitrogen must be supplied continuously in the diet (nitrogen balance: intake = excretion).

2. General strategy

Hydrolysis of proteins to amino acids by proteases (in the intestine for dietary protein, inside cells for endogenous protein): stage 1 of catabolism.
In most amino acids, the amino group is separated from the carbon skeleton, which becomes an alpha-keto acid (keto group on the alpha carbon).
The amino group is not released as free ammonium (toxic) but transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate (a Krebs intermediate; 5 C, carboxyl at both ends), which becomes glutamate. Glutamate collects the amino groups of all amino acids.
Amino groups are then either reused (e.g. glutamine donates amino groups for nucleotide synthesis) or eliminated as urea when not needed (e.g. after a high-protein meal).
Alpha-keto acids feed pathways around the Krebs cycle: energy, glucose, ketone bodies (section 8).

Transamination

Amino acid + alpha-ketoglutarate to alpha-keto acid + glutamate. Enzyme: aminotransferase (= transaminase).
Amino groups are constantly moving between amino acids by transamination.
Clinical: transaminases are measured in blood tests; liver or heart damage releases them into circulation.
[Lucía] Transaminations are reversible (used in both degradation and synthesis); transaminases are cytoplasmic and need pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), from vitamin B6. Named examples: AST (aspartate transaminase) and ALT (alanine aminotransferase).

3. How animals excrete nitrogen





























StrategyProductExampleWhyAmmonotelicAmmoniumFishPlenty of water to dilute itUreotelicUreaHumansNot enough water to dilute ammoniumUricotelicUric acidBirdsCannot afford to lose water

Urea: 2 nitrogen atoms per molecule, low toxicity, water-soluble. Made in the liver, released into blood, filtered by the kidneys into urine.

4. Transport of amino groups to the liver
All tissues degrade proteins, but only the liver makes urea, so nitrogen must travel to the liver.
Glutamine (most tissues)

Glutamate picks up a further amino group and becomes glutamine (two amino groups: alpha carbon and side chain).
Glutamine is the most abundant amino acid in blood.
[Lucía] Glutamine is a non-toxic carrier and also an amino donor for many biosyntheses. In liver mitochondria, glutaminase releases NH4+ from glutamine (giving glutamate), and glutamate dehydrogenase releases a second NH4+ from glutamate; the resulting alpha-ketoglutarate goes to the Krebs cycle or gluconeogenesis.

Alanine (muscle): glucose-alanine cycle

During vigorous activity muscle makes a lot of pyruvate from glycolysis.
Pyruvate is transaminated to alanine. This removes pyruvate (keeping glycolysis going) and exports amino groups at the same time.
Alanine goes to the liver, where its carbon is used to make glucose, which returns to the muscle.


Alanine is the second most abundant amino acid in blood.
[check] The transcript says “in the liver, many of the pyruvates … are transaminated into alanine”; the context and Lucía’s notes put this step in muscle (enzyme ALT), and the reverse (alanine to pyruvate) in liver cytosol.

5. The urea cycle

Discovered by Krebs (with another researcher), the same scientist as the Krebs cycle; the two cycles are connected. [Slides] Hans Krebs and Kurt Henseleit, 1932.
Almost exclusively in the liver; two compartments (mitochondria and cytosol); five steps.
Nitrogen sources: one N from ammonium (from glutamine/glutamate), the other from aspartate.

Step 0/1: carbamoyl phosphate (mitochondria)

Free NH4+ is toxic, so it reacts very fast and efficiently with CO2 (as bicarbonate) and ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate.
Enzyme: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). “I” because a CPS II appears in nucleotide metabolism.
Plenty of energy is spent so the reaction always runs forward. [Lucía] It uses 2 ATP.
Parallel with Krebs: before the cycle comes the “entry” molecule (acetyl-CoA for Krebs, carbamoyl phosphate here).
Naming rule (lecturer): enzymes called synthetase use ATP; synthase typically does not. [check] The transcript has the two words garbled at this point; this is the version consistent with the rest of the lecture and with Lucía’s names (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, N-acetylglutamate synthase).

Cycle



































StepReactionEnzymeLocation2Carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine to citrullineOrnithine transcarbamoylase (OTC)Mitochondria3Citrulline + aspartate (second N) to argininosuccinateArgininosuccinate synthetaseCytosol4Argininosuccinate to arginine + fumarateArgininosuccinate lyaseCytosol5Arginine + H2O to urea + ornithineArginaseCytosol

Ornithine and citrulline are alpha amino acids not found in proteins. The lecturer said ornithine is easy to remember because it resembles a standard amino acid, “only one carbon short”. [verify] which amino acid (the transcript says “iso”).
Citrulline leaves the mitochondria and the cycle continues in the cytosol; ornithine re-enters the mitochondria; urea crosses the membrane into blood.
Aspartate entry costs another ATP, giving AMP, “energetically like using two ATP”. [Lucía] Argininosuccinate synthetase hydrolyzes two high-energy phosphate bonds.
The lecturer left the fate of the aspartate skeleton as an exercise: it becomes fumarate (Lucía). [Lucía] Fumarate can enter the mitochondria and the Krebs cycle, regenerating oxaloacetate, the source of aspartate.
Arginine: a standard protein amino acid that is also a urea cycle metabolite (guanidinium group). Arginase hydrolysis is spontaneous, but the enzyme speeds it up.
Arginase is found mostly only in the liver, and only in the liver of ureotelic animals. [check] The transcript says only we “produce urease”; it means urea (Lucía: arginase is only in the liver of ureotelic animals).

Connections with the Krebs cycle
Fumarate and oxaloacetate (aspartate) are Krebs intermediates, and glutamate becomes alpha-ketoglutarate: the two cycles exchange intermediates.
6. Balance and regulation
Balance

Urea synthesis costs energy: about 3 high-energy molecules per urea. “This is not free”, but nitrogen must be eliminated efficiently.
[Lucía] CO2 + NH4+ + 3 ATP + aspartate + 2 H2O to urea + 2 ADP + AMP + 4 Pi + fumarate (the slides give the same balance). Because it is so expensive, dietary protein is more important as a source of precursors than of energy.

Long-term

Liver levels of urea cycle enzymes adapt to the average diet (transcription and degradation of enzymes). High-protein diet or starvation increases them. Measuring them would tell you roughly how much protein someone eats.

Short-term

Arginine allosterically activates N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS), which is not part of the cycle. More arginine means the cycle must speed up.
NAGS: glutamate + acetyl-CoA to N-acetylglutamate.
N-acetylglutamate is the main (allosteric) activator of CPS I, the main regulatory site of the pathway, which sits just before the cycle.
Logic: a lot of glutamate means a lot of nitrogen to eliminate. [Lucía] N-acetylglutamate signals both enough energy (acetyl-CoA) and nitrogen to eliminate (glutamate).

7. Hyperammonemia and urea cycle defects (examples only)

Hyperammonemia: high blood ammonium. Ammonium is toxic, especially neurotoxic, and can kill.
Causes: liver damage (less urea production) or genetic defects of the urea cycle (rare but real).
[Lucía] Symptoms: lethargy, tremors, slurred speech, blurred vision, vomiting, coma, death. Liver damage from alcohol, toxic chemicals, hepatitis. [Slides] Genetic causes: NAGS, CPS I, OTC (most frequent), ornithine translocase, argininosuccinate synthetase (citrullinemia), argininosuccinate lyase (argininosuccinic aciduria), arginase (hyperargininemia).

Case 1: OTC deficiency

Woman, 58, admitted for recurrent asthmatic bronchitis. Found: high ammonia ([Slides] 280 µmol/L), cerebral oedema on CT, very low citrulline and arginine, raised uracil in urine. She tended to avoid large protein intakes.
[check] The transcript’s “uracin” / “eulacin” is uracil (slides). The lecturer explained it rises because accumulated carbamoyl phosphate is diverted to nucleotide (pyrimidine) synthesis (Lec 5.12 Nucleotide metabolism).
Reasoning (class exercise; exclude by what accumulates):

Arginase (step 5) defect: arginine would accumulate. Excluded.
Steps 3 or 4: citrulline would accumulate. Excluded.
CPS I (step 1): carbamoyl phosphate would not accumulate. Excluded.
So step 2, OTC: carbamoyl phosphate builds up and is diverted to nucleotide synthesis, citrulline and arginine fall, ammonia rises.


OTC deficiency is the most frequent urea cycle defect. It is X-linked, so it is mostly manifest in men; she was a symptomatic carrier. [Slides] She had four male infants who died of OTC deficiency; her two adult daughters are carriers: one (healthy) lost a son, the other has mild intellectual disability and mild hyperammonemic episodes.
Why it showed now (lecturer’s speculation): infection causes tissue damage and fast protein degradation, unmasking the disease.

Case 2: NAGS deficiency (pre-class reading)

[Slides] Man in his early 30s after a four-wheeler accident and orthopaedic surgery. That night: confused, combative, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, generalized tonic-clonic seizures. History of chronic hypertension, persistent anaemia and nonspecific psychiatric problems. An “autoselective” vegetarian who systematically rejected meat.
[Slides] Labs: low blood urea nitrogen, ammonia 553 µmol/L, very high glutamine and high alanine, very low citrulline and low arginine.
[check] The transcript says “urea around 500”; the case report gives ammonia 553 µmol/L and low urea nitrogen.
First guess (class and physician): CPS I defect, since nitrogen is not entering the cycle and stays in its carriers (glutamine, alanine) while everything after step 1 is low.
Genetic test: CPS I activity was normal.
Answer: NAGS deficiency. Step 1 is blocked, not because of its enzyme, but because its activator N-acetylglutamate is missing.
Not because his low-protein diet left him unadapted: the short-term response is very fast. He avoided meat because protein raised his ammonia and made him feel ill.
[check] The transcript switches between “male” and “she”; the case report: a man.

Treatment (outline)

Restrict dietary protein, but supplement essential amino acids (about half of the amino acids are essential; next week’s lecture on amino acid synthesis). [Lucía] Also specific therapies for particular enzyme deficiencies.
[Slides] Clinical management of hyperammonemia: dietary protein restriction, haemodialysis, nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate), liver transplantation.
[Slides] Essential amino acids (Lehninger Table 18-1): histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine. Conditionally essential: arginine, cysteine, glutamine, glycine, proline, tyrosine. Nonessential: alanine, asparagine, aspartate, glutamate, serine.

8. Fate of alpha-keto acids: glucogenic vs ketogenic

Each amino acid is different; general classification by the fate of its carbon skeleton.
Glucogenic: can be used to make glucose (via pyruvate or Krebs intermediates that lead to oxaloacetate). Examples: alanine to pyruvate by transamination; glutamine to glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate to oxaloacetate to glucose.
Ketogenic: give acetyl-CoA (or acetoacetyl-CoA), so they can be used to make ketone bodies (not that they always do). Acetyl-CoA carbons cannot make glucose.
Lysine and leucine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids. Some amino acids are split into two fragments and are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
Why acetyl-CoA cannot make glucose: in the Krebs cycle two decarboxylations remove 2 C, the same number that entered as acetyl-CoA, so there is no net gain of carbon (link: this answers the open question in Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies, section 4).
Student question: how can glycine become pyruvate? “A complex process”; not answered in the recording.
The individual reactions are not required.

9. Cofactors of amino acid metabolism



































CofactorOriginRolePyridoxal phosphate (PLP)Vitamin ([Lucía] B6)Cofactor of transamination (aminotransferases) and many other reactionsBiotinVitamin ([Lucía] B7)Carboxylations (e.g. acetyl-CoA carboxylase, Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis)Folates (tetrahydrofolate)Vitamin ([Slides] folate, B9)Transfer of one-carbon units (at different oxidation states); example in nucleotide metabolism (Lec 5.12 Nucleotide metabolism). Pregnant women take folate supplementsS-adenosylmethionine (SAM, AdoMet)Adenosine + methionineMain methyl group donor (DNA, proteins, other molecules). [Lucía] Cofactor of the methyltransferases that methylate cytosine in DNATetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)Oxidation-reduction reactions, e.g. phenylalanine hydroxylase

[check] The transcript calls PLP a cofactor of “oxenocyanins”; context and Lucía’s notes: of transaminases.
[verify] The product after SAM donates its methyl group: the transcript says “homocystine”; check the slides (S-adenosylhomocysteine/homocysteine).
[Lucía] PLP also works in isomerizations, side-chain modifications and decarboxylations. BH4 carries electrons from NADPH to O2, being oxidized to dihydrobiopterin.

10. Phenylketonuria (PKU)

Most prevalent disorder in the table of genetic disorders of amino acid catabolism (read the table to understand it, not to memorize).
Defect: phenylalanine hydroxylase, which hydroxylates phenylalanine to tyrosine, the first step of phenylalanine degradation.
The enzyme is a monooxygenase (mixed-function oxidase): of the two O atoms in O2, one goes into the product and the other forms water, with electrons from tetrahydrobiopterin.
Patients accumulate phenylalanine, which forms toxic compounds. [Lucía] Seizures, brain damage and intellectual disability.
Common enough to be screened in newborns (heel-prick blood test); treatment must start from birth.
Aspartame (sweetener) contains phenylalanine. Harmless unless you have PKU, which is why diet sodas carry the mandatory label “Contiene una fuente de fenilalanina”. Patients need a specific low-phenylalanine diet plus amino acid supplements.
Other example in the table: argininemia (arginase deficit, arginine accumulation, hyperammonemia). [Lucía] Others: tyrosinemia, homocystinuria, nonketotic hyperglycinemia, maple syrup urine disease; diagnosed by measuring amino acids in body fluids.
[Slides] The table (Lehninger 18-2) also lists: albinism (tyrosinase), alkaptonuria (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase), argininosuccinic acidemia, CPS I deficiency, homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase), maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase), methylmalonic acidemia (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, the odd-chain fatty acid step in Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies). PKU is the most common (under 8 per 100,000 births).

Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies
Sources (Transcripts/FMC I; automatic transcription, errors corrected): the recording was cut, so this lecture is split across two files.

Sections 1-7: lecture 5.9 fatty acid catabolism
Sections 8-12: Audio Clip 2 (continues directly from the first file, mid beta-oxidation)

Official code Lec 5.9 (ADI files labelled “Lec 5.10”).
Resources:

Slides: 5.9 Oxidación de Ac (slides)
Study material: Fatty acid oxidation (lecture notes)
Previous-year notes: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 5.10. Fatty acids oxidation” (PDF p. 134-136)
Related: Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation, Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis, Lec 5.11 Cholesterol metabolism and lipid transport

Marking used below:

[Slides] / [Notes] = gap filled from the lecture slides / the study-material lecture notes (Alberto Pérez-Mediavilla).
[Lucía] = gap filled from FMCI  Lucia Reed notes.
[check] = the lecturer or transcript conflicts with a source in your vault (named in the line).
[verify] = possible error in the lecture or transcript that the sources in your vault do not settle.

Exam flags from the lecturer

Mobilization cascade (glucagon, GPCR, cAMP, PKA, HSL, perilipin): he said he will ask questions on it.
Carnitine shuttle: “very important”, memorize the diagram.
Three stages of cellular respiration: possible applied-exam question asking for a diagram of cellular respiration starting from carbohydrate.

1. Brown fat

White adipocytes: normal mitochondria. Brown adipocytes: uncoupled mitochondria. They transport electrons and consume O2 but make very little ATP; the energy is released as heat.
Uncoupling is due to UCP1 (thermogenin), a proton channel in the inner mitochondrial membrane (explained in Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation, section 7).
In humans, brown fat is mostly present in childhood, especially just after birth, for heat production. Adults can increase brown fat (lecturer: “train” the body to make it).

2. Why fat yields more energy than carbohydrate

Fatty acids are more reduced: more electrons per carbon to feed the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis.
Lecturer: about 9 kcal/g for fat vs 4.5 kcal/g for carbohydrate. [check] The study notes give 9 kcal/g fat vs 5 kcal/g carbohydrate. The sources disagree on the carbohydrate figure; ask which value the exam uses.
[Slides] Fat is also stored with less water (non-polar). Glucose and glycogen serve short-term needs with quick delivery; fats serve long-term needs (months). About 80% of the energy of heart and liver comes from fatty acid oxidation; about one third of our energy needs come from dietary TAG.

3. Sources of fat

Internal storage (triacylglycerols, TAG, in adipose tissue)
Diet (part oxidized immediately, part stored)
Endogenous synthesis

Clinical aside: fat around the liver and the heart is dangerous; reducing fat accumulation is the first advice for weight loss.
4. Hormonal control: insulin/glucagon ratio

More insulin: more storage, less mobilization. More glucagon: more mobilization.
Glucagon exceeds insulin in hypoglycemia (low blood glucose, fasting). High glucose: insulin up, glucagon down, and excess glucose is converted to fat.
Key rule: carbohydrate carbons can become fatty acids (all excess carbohydrate is stored as TAG), but fatty acid carbons cannot be used to make glucose.
Why: explained in Lec 5.8 Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle, section 8. The 2 C that enter the Krebs cycle as acetyl-CoA are lost in its two decarboxylations, so there is no net carbon for glucose.
Tissue preference: the heart (among others) prefers fatty acids; the brain (neurons) depends mainly on glucose. When glucose is low, it is spared for the brain and other tissues are given fatty acids.

5. Fat mobilization (lipolysis) in the adipocyte
Links to Prof. Tavira’s GPCR lecture (Lec 4.3).
Cascade

Glucagon binds the glucagon receptor, a GPCR (G protein-coupled receptor; 7 transmembrane domains).
Ligand binding causes a conformational change that reaches the intracellular domain and promotes exchange of GDP for GTP on G-alpha.
G-alpha-GTP dissociates from the G-beta-gamma dimer; both can signal.
G-alpha-s-GTP activates membrane adenylyl cyclase: ATP to cAMP. ([check] The lecturer said “GTP binds adenylate cyclase”; in Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis he says it is the alpha subunit that stimulates adenylyl cyclase.)
cAMP, a hydrophilic second messenger, binds proteins with cAMP-binding domains such as PKA (cAMP-dependent protein kinase). More cAMP, more PKA activity.
PKA phosphorylates:

Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL): hydrolyzes the ester bonds between fatty acids and glycerol in TAG of the lipid droplet.
Perilipin: protein coating the lipid droplet; phosphorylation “opens holes” in the coat so the lipase can reach the TAG.


Free fatty acids leave the adipocyte, bind serum albumin, and are carried to the liver, muscle, heart and other tissues.

[Lucía]

Epinephrine as well as glucagon triggers this cascade in hypoglycemia.
Phosphorylated perilipin attracts the cytosolic lipase to the TAG, which is hydrolyzed into glycerol and fatty acids; both are released into the bloodstream.
[Notes] Glycerol can also provide energy through glycolysis. Albumin carries fatty acids to liver, muscle, heart and adrenal cortex.

G protein review

Heterotrimer: alpha, beta, gamma. G-alpha has intrinsic GTPase activity.
Alpha subtypes: alpha-s, alpha-i, alpha-q, alpha-o, alpha-12 (details not required). Alpha-s stimulates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP up); alpha-i inhibits it (cAMP down).

Switching the signal off

Glucose rises, glucagon falls, less receptor activation.
G-alpha hydrolyzes its GTP to GDP; G-alpha-GDP changes conformation, rebinds beta-gamma and stays inactive until a new stimulus.
GAPs (GTPase-activating proteins) increase GTPase activity: more GTPase activity means a shorter, weaker signal, and vice versa.

Practical point: to burn more fat, eat less carbohydrate or raise energy expenditure. Balancing fat and carbohydrate intake plus physical activity is enough; strong carbohydrate restriction is not needed. Genetics and other factors also play a role.
6. Burning fatty acids in the target cell
Sequence: mobilization, then activation, then transport into the mitochondrion, then beta-oxidation (in the mitochondrial matrix).
6a. The transport problem

The inner mitochondrial membrane is highly restrictive; fatty acids are hydrophobic.
Short fatty acids cross freely; long ones (16, 18, 20 C, which are most fatty acids) need the carnitine shuttle.
[check] The lecturer said 14 C or fewer cross freely. Study notes and Lucía’s notes: 12 C or fewer enter the mitochondria without a transport system; 14 C or more need the carnitine shuttle (slides: fewer than 12 C diffuse freely).

6b. Activation (all fatty acids, any length)

The carboxyl group is activated by forming a high-energy thioester with coenzyme A:
fatty acid + CoA-SH + ATP to fatty acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi
Enzyme: fatty acyl-CoA synthetases, a family of isoenzymes in the outer mitochondrial membrane (study notes). [check] The transcript says “fatty acid synthetase”; the study notes and Lucía’s notes give fatty acyl-CoA synthetases. Do not confuse with fatty acid synthase (Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis).
Occurs in two steps; the lecturer said you do not need to learn them.
Not a phosphorylation. ATP goes to AMP + PPi, so both phosphoanhydride bonds are used.
Cost = 2 ATP equivalents: oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP from ADP, not from AMP, so adenylate kinase first does AMP + ATP to 2 ADP, and then both ADP are rephosphorylated.
Reversibility: asked in class; the lecturer was unsure (“I guess it is reversible”). [verify] Not addressed in the slides or study notes.

6c. Carnitine shuttle

Carnitine = 4-trimethylammonio-3-hydroxybutyrate: butyrate (4 C with carboxylate), trimethylated, positively charged N on C4, OH on C3. Known in gym culture as a “fat burner” because it is needed to bring fatty acids into the mitochondrion.
Components:

CAT I (carnitine acyltransferase I): outer side. The lecturer learned it as the outer face of the inner membrane and said the location does not matter; the study notes also place it on the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Acylcarnitine/carnitine translocase: antiporter in the inner membrane.
CAT II (carnitine acyltransferase II): matrix side of the inner membrane (study notes and Lucía: inner face of the inner membrane).


Cycle:

CAT I: acyl-CoA + carnitine to acylcarnitine + CoA-SH (transesterification onto the OH of carnitine).
Translocase: acylcarnitine in, free carnitine out (keeps free carnitine available outside).
CAT II: acylcarnitine + CoA-SH to acyl-CoA + carnitine, inside the matrix.


Net result: the same molecules on both sides. The point is only to get the long acyl chain across the inner membrane, where all the beta-oxidation enzymes are.
[Lucía] / [Notes] This transport is the rate-limiting stage of fatty acid oxidation; once in the matrix, the only fate of the fatty acid is oxidation. The main allosteric regulator of CAT I is malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase in fatty acid synthesis, so fatty acids are not made and degraded at the same time. In hypoglycemia, glucagon (cAMP, PKA) inhibits malonyl-CoA synthesis and CAT I works at full capacity (Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis).

7. Beta-oxidation: introduction
Three stages of cellular respiration

Oxidation of fuels to acetyl-CoA: glycolysis, pyruvate oxidative decarboxylation (PDH), beta-oxidation of fatty acids.
Krebs cycle.
Oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport + ATP synthase).

The lecturer taught beta-oxidation before oxphos so that oxphos can then cover the electrons from glycolysis, Krebs and beta-oxidation together.
Why “beta”

Each turn releases one acetyl-CoA (2 C) by breaking the bond between C2 (alpha) and C3 (beta). Numbering starts at C1 = the thioester carbon bound to S-CoA.
A C-C bond between two methylene groups is very stable; breaking it directly is not thermodynamically feasible.
Strategy: oxidize the beta carbon (C3) to a carbonyl (keto) group (beta-ketoacyl-CoA). This weakens the C2-C3 bond so it can be cleaved.

Acetyl-CoA yield























Fatty acidCarbonsAcetyl-CoATurnsPalmitic1687Stearic1898
Turns = (n/2) - 1, since the last turn yields two acetyl-CoA (section 8). (The class gave mixed answers for stearic; 9 is correct.)

From here on: FMC I/Audio Clip 2. The start of this file (the individual reactions of each turn) was not recorded; they are filled in below from the study notes and Lucía’s notes.
8. End of each turn: thiolysis

After the beta carbon is oxidized to a keto group, the C2-C3 bond is weaker. CoA-SH acts as nucleophile and cleaves it (thiolysis).
Products: acetyl-CoA + a fatty acyl-CoA 2 carbons shorter.
The shortened acyl-CoA goes through another turn; the acetyl-CoA goes to the Krebs cycle.
Last turn of an even-chain fatty acid: the 4 C acyl-CoA is cleaved into 2 acetyl-CoA. Nothing is wasted: all carbons end as acetyl-CoA and can be fully oxidized in the Krebs cycle.
[Notes] The reactions of each turn:

Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidizes C2 and C3, giving trans-delta2-enoyl-CoA, with FAD as acceptor (FADH2). The electrons pass straight to the respiratory chain through the electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF): 1.5 ATP. Three isozymes by chain length: VLCAD (12-18 C), MCAD (4-14 C), SCAD (4-8 C). (Lucía writes “LCAD” for the first.)
Enoyl-CoA hydratase adds H2O to the double bond, giving L-beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA.
Hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidizes C3 (the beta carbon) to beta-ketoacyl-CoA, with NAD+ as acceptor (NADH).
Thiolase (acyl-CoA acetyltransferase): thiolysis (above).


[Notes] The first three reactions turn a -CH2- into a carbonyl, making the C2-C3 bond unstable. They are analogous to succinate dehydrogenase, fumarate hydratase and malate dehydrogenase of the Krebs cycle.
[Lucía] / [Notes] Clinical: MCAD deficiency is one of the most frequent genetic defects of fatty acid catabolism: fat accumulation in the liver, low blood glucose, vomiting and coma. Other defects in fat oxidation cause serious heart and skeletal muscle disorders. Link to breast milk in Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis, section 4.

9. Energy balance: palmitoyl-CoA (16 C)















































ProductAmountATP eachATPFADH271.510.5NADH72.517.5Acetyl-CoA (via Krebs)81080Subtotal108Activation-2Net106 ATP

[check] In class the number of turns was answered as “eight”; it is 7 turns (one FADH2 and one NADH per turn) giving 8 acetyl-CoA. The arithmetic in the recording is messy but the final 106 is correct.
Fat yields more ATP per carbon than glucose because it is more reduced. Study notes, slides and Lucía give the same totals (108 gross, 106 net); the slides break the 108 down by enzyme (Table 17-1).
[Notes] Balance of beta-oxidation alone: palmitoyl-CoA + 7 CoA + 7 FAD + 7 NAD+ + 7 H2O to 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH + 7 H+.

Peroxisomal oxidation (study notes only; not in the recording)

[Notes] Peroxisomes also oxidize fatty acids, mainly very long-chain ones, to shorten them; the shortened chains go to mitochondria (peroxisomes lack Krebs enzymes). Difference: in the first step FADH2 passes electrons directly to O2, making H2O2, removed by catalase.
[Notes] Phytanic acid (branched; dairy, meat, fish) is oxidized there by alpha-oxidation.
[Notes] Diseases: Zellweger syndrome (no peroxisomes), X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (cannot oxidize very long-chain fatty acids), Refsum disease (cannot metabolize phytanic acid).

10. Unsaturated and odd-chain fatty acids
Unsaturated (not examined in detail)

Oxidized the same way, but the cis double bond needs extra steps to be converted to the trans form.
One acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step is skipped (the double bond is already there), so one FADH2 less: 1.5 ATP less per double bond at that position. Example: palmitoleoyl-CoA (16:1) gives 1.5 ATP less than palmitoyl-CoA (16:0).
Polyunsaturated fatty acids yield even less energy.

Odd-chain (lecturer: “not the most important part”)

The last turn starts with a 5 C acyl-CoA and gives acetyl-CoA + propionyl-CoA (3 C).
Propionyl-CoA also comes from bacterial fermentation of dietary fibre in the gut; it has biological activity (receptors) and is considered healthy.
Fate: converted to succinyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle. Do not learn the steps.
Sources mentioned: plant foods and meat from herbivores.

11. Regulation (to be continued in Lec 5.10)

Synthesis and oxidation of fatty acids are reciprocal: more synthesis, less oxidation, and vice versa.
Linked to carbohydrate availability: more carbohydrate, more insulin, less glucagon, less mobilization and less oxidation.
Mechanism: malonyl-CoA inhibits CAT I (section 6c and Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis).

12. Ketone bodies

Part of normal physiology: a small fraction of the acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation in the liver is diverted to ketogenesis.
Three ketone bodies:

Acetoacetate
Beta-hydroxybutyrate
Acetone: volatile, exhaled through the lungs, not useful as fuel.


Key point (lecturer: important): ketogenesis rises when there is an imbalance between carbohydrate and fatty acid oxidation.

Rationale

Acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation enters the Krebs cycle by condensing with oxaloacetate to form citrate, so acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate are needed in similar amounts.
When carbohydrate is scarce (fasting, low-carbohydrate diet, uncontrolled type 1 diabetes), the liver makes glucose by gluconeogenesis, which pulls oxaloacetate out of the mitochondrion (to PEP, then glucose).
Oxaloacetate falls, so acetyl-CoA cannot enter the Krebs cycle and accumulates.
The excess acetyl-CoA is converted into ketone bodies, which the liver exports as a transportable fuel for peripheral tissues.

[check] The recording says this happens with a “huge increase” and an “extreme increase in availability” of carbohydrates. From his own reasoning he means a lack of carbohydrate: the study notes say the route is especially intense in continuous hypoglycemia, when the liver must make glucose from oxaloacetate; the slides say ketone bodies form when oxaloacetate is depleted, which also frees CoA so beta-oxidation can continue.
Ketogenic diet

Very low carbohydrate, to raise ketone body production. Acceptable if balanced and supervised by a physician.
Lecturer: low carbohydrate with “high amounts of protein and lipids”. [verify] the protein part; not addressed in the slides or study notes.
Risk: acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are acids, so high levels lower blood pH (ketoacidosis). [Lucía] Low-carbohydrate diets can also lead to ketoacidosis.

Type 1 diabetes

Blood glucose is high, but the glucose is not available to cells, so the body behaves as if fasting: the liver makes large amounts of ketone bodies to send fuel to peripheral tissues.
[Lucía] / [Notes] In untreated diabetes the excess of ketone bodies lowers blood pH (ketoacidosis), which can lead to coma; the breath smells of acetone. [Slides] Extreme ketosis (untreated diabetes): blood ketone bodies about 90 mg/100 mL (normal under 3), urine 5,000 mg/24 h (normal under 125).
[verify] He said patients “don’t have or are insensitive to insulin”; the slides and study notes only say “untreated diabetes”.

What to know
The rationale, not each step. For reference, [Lucía] / [Notes]:

Thiolase condenses 2 acetyl-CoA into acetoacetyl-CoA.
HMG-CoA synthase adds a third acetyl-CoA, forming HMG-CoA (same intermediate as in Lec 5.11 Cholesterol metabolism and lipid transport).
HMG-CoA is split into acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. Acetoacetate is reduced to D-beta-hydroxybutyrate (D-beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase) or decarboxylated to acetone.
Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are soluble and reach peripheral tissues (skeletal and cardiac muscle, adrenal cortex; the brain for a short period when glucose is lacking) through the blood. There acetoacetate is activated to acetoacetyl-CoA by beta-ketoacyl-CoA transferase.
Thiolase cleaves acetoacetyl-CoA into 2 acetyl-CoA, which are oxidized in the Krebs cycle.

Next lecture
The lecturer asked you to review the Krebs cycle and beta-oxidation before oxidative phosphorylation.

G protein review

[check] The lecturer said 14 C or fewer cross freely. Lehninger gives 12 C or fewer; 14 C and longer need carnitine.

6b. Activation (all fatty acids, any length)

The carboxyl group is activated by forming a high-energy thioester with coenzyme A:
fatty acid + CoA-SH + ATP to fatty acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi
Enzyme: acyl-CoA synthetase (fatty acyl-CoA synthetase, thiokinase). [check] The transcript says “fatty acid synthetase”; do not confuse it with fatty acid synthase, the enzyme of fatty acid synthesis (Lec 5.10).
Occurs in two steps ([added] via an acyl-adenylate intermediate); the lecturer said you do not need to learn the two steps.
Not a phosphorylation. ATP goes to AMP + PPi, so both phosphoanhydride bonds are used.
Cost = 2 ATP equivalents: oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP from ADP, not from AMP, so adenylate kinase first does AMP + ATP to 2 ADP, and then both ADP are rephosphorylated.
[added] Long-chain activation occurs on the outer mitochondrial membrane (cytosolic side).
Reversibility (asked in class; lecturer unsure, “I guess it is reversible”). [added] The synthetase reaction itself is close to equilibrium, but inorganic pyrophosphatase hydrolyzes PPi to 2 Pi, which makes overall activation effectively irreversible.

6c. Carnitine shuttle

Carnitine = 4-trimethylammonio-3-hydroxybutyrate: butyrate (4 C with carboxylate), trimethylated, positively charged N on C4, OH on C3. Known in gym culture as a “fat burner” because it is needed to bring fatty acids into the mitochondrion.
Components:

CAT I (carnitine acyltransferase I, also CPT I): outer side. The slide places it in the outer mitochondrial membrane; the lecturer learned it as the outer face of the inner membrane and said the location does not matter. Lehninger: outer membrane.
Acylcarnitine/carnitine translocase: antiporter in the inner membrane.
CAT II (CPT II): matrix side of the inner membrane.


Cycle:

CAT I: acyl-CoA + carnitine to acylcarnitine + CoA-SH (transesterification onto the OH of carnitine).
Translocase: acylcarnitine in, free carnitine out (keeps free carnitine available outside).
CAT II: acylcarnitine + CoA-SH to acyl-CoA + carnitine, inside the matrix.


Net result: the same molecules on both sides. The point is only to get the long acyl chain across the inner membrane, where all the beta-oxidation enzymes are.
[added] Keeps cytosolic and matrix CoA pools separate. CAT I is the regulated, rate-limiting step: inhibited by malonyl-CoA (first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis), so synthesis and oxidation do not run at the same time.

7. Beta-oxidation: introduction
Three stages of cellular respiration

Oxidation of fuels to acetyl-CoA: glycolysis, pyruvate oxidative decarboxylation (PDH), beta-oxidation of fatty acids.
Krebs cycle.
Oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport + ATP synthase).

The lecturer taught beta-oxidation before oxphos so that oxphos can then cover the electrons from glycolysis, Krebs and beta-oxidation together.
Why “beta”

Each turn releases one acetyl-CoA (2 C) by breaking the bond between C2 (alpha) and C3 (beta). Numbering starts at C1 = the thioester carbon bound to S-CoA.
A C-C bond between two methylene groups is very stable; breaking it directly is not thermodynamically feasible.
Strategy: oxidize the beta carbon (C3) to a carbonyl (keto) group (beta-ketoacyl-CoA). This weakens the C2-C3 bond so it can be cleaved.

Acetyl-CoA yield























Fatty acidCarbonsAcetyl-CoATurnsPalmitic1687Stearic1898
[added] Turns = (n/2) - 1, since the last turn yields two acetyl-CoA. (The class gave mixed answers for stearic; 9 is correct.)
The transcript ends before the individual steps of beta-oxidation. Continue with the lecture slides and FMCI  Lucia Reed notes p. 134-136.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lec 7.2 Meiosis
Sources

Meiosis (automatic transcription). A 16-line fragment only: the opening minute of the lecture, ending at “This is one chromosome.” Everything after that was not recorded. Code log: Thu 15 Oct.
Coverage: section 1 comes from the transcript. Everything else is built from the Genetics class notes, the slides and Lucía, and is marked as such. Points the lecturer made about meiosis in later lectures (7.7, 7.8, 9.1) are added where they were recorded, with the lecture named.
Because the lecture itself was not recorded, there are no exam flags from the lecturer for 7.2; see “Exam-relevant points from other lectures”.

Resources

Slides: Slides Unit 7.pdf, section “Lec 7.2: Meiosis”. Mostly images; the learning goals, the gametogenesis labels (ovary, testis), the gonium-to-gamete ploidy scheme, the two oocyte arrest points and “Homologs linked only by chiasmata” came through as text. See the slides for the figures.
Study material (Unit 7 folder): “7.2 HR_Watson.mp4” and “7.2 holliday model.mp4” (videos of homologous recombination and the Holliday model).
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “LECTURE 7.2 MEIOSIS” (Figures 1 to 8, Table 1).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 7.2. Meiosis”, PDF p. 196-198.
Related notes: Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination (SPO11, homologous recombination repair, HR vs HRR table), Lec 7.7 Genetic variation (unequal crossing over, genomic disorders), Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis (nondisjunction, maternal age, Robertsonian translocations in meiosis), Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging (cohesin).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 7 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam-relevant points from other lectures

HR (meiosis) vs HRR (mitosis) table, gone through row by row in Lec 7.8: function, initiating lesion (SPO11), timing (prophase I), outcome (crossovers favoured in meiosis). See Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination.
Lec 7.8: “Remember SPO11 creates double-strand breaks to initiate meiosis”, the beginning of homologous recombination.
Lec 9.1: rare mis-joining of meiotic double-strand breaks is how translocations and inversions arise; Robertsonian translocations cause trivalents in meiosis and trisomies or monosomies in offspring.

[Slides] Learning goals:

Formation of gametes requires a special type of cell division.
Meiosis includes two segregation steps (and two cell divisions).
In order to increase genetic diversity in the offspring, meiosis includes HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION by which homologous chromosomes exchange segments of DNA.

1. Why a special division (recorded)

Meiosis is a different type of cell division. Mitosis is the standard division for all somatic cells; every dividing cell in the body uses it, except the cells that will make the gametes (eggs in women, sperm in men).
Why do gametes need a special division? (Student:) from a diploid cell we must generate haploid cells.
He began explaining that a diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, drawing one chromosome. The recording ends here.

2. Not recorded: overview (from [Notes], [Slides], [Lucía])

[Notes] Diploid primordial germ cells migrate into the embryonic gonad and divide by mitosis to give spermatogonia (males) or oogonia (females); growth and differentiation give primary spermatocytes and primary oocytes, which undergo meiosis. Many more mitotic divisions in males than in females, likely contributing to sex differences in mutation rate.
[Notes] Meiosis is a reductive division: one round of DNA replication, two cell divisions (meiosis I and II), giving four haploid cells. Each gamete is designed to be genetically unique.
[Slides] Ploidy and DNA content:


























CellPloidy / DNA contentGonium2n / 2CAfter replication (S phase): primary oocyte / spermatocyte2n / 4CAfter meiosis I: secondary oocyte / spermatocyten / 2CAfter meiosis II: gameten / 1C

[check] [Notes] Figure 3 caption calls the products of meiosis I “two diploid cells” (“diploid secondary spermatocytes”); the slide scheme and the [Notes] main text (secondary gametocytes have the haploid number, n, with two chromatids per chromosome, 2C) say n/2C.

3. Two sources of diversity

Independent assortment [Notes]: each diploid cell has two homologs of each chromosome (one paternal, one maternal; X and Y are the special case in males). For each of the 23 pairs the choice of daughter cell is independent: 2^23, about 8.4 x 10^6 (8,388,608) combinations from one meiosis (Figure 1). [Lucía] Bivalents are randomly oriented at metaphase I: 2^23 options.
Recombination in prophase I superimposes more variation: each transmitted chromosome is a mosaic of paternal and maternal sequences (Figure 2).
[Notes] The combined effect makes each gamete genetically unique.

4. Meiosis I: prophase I
[Notes] Homologs pair (synapsis) to form a bivalent; because DNA has already replicated, each bivalent has four chromatids. X and Y can also form a bivalent in male meiosis. Prophase I has five stages (Figure 4):



































StageMeaningEvents ([Notes])Leptoteneleptos = thinReplicated chromosomes begin to condense, unpaired. DSBs begin to form; their repair using the homologous chromatid starts to bring homologs together. Chromatin in loops joined at the base by cohesins.Zygotenezygos = joinThe synaptonemal complex (SC) forms between homologs: two lateral elements and a central element (proteins of the “SYPC” family, as written in the notes); lateral elements bind the cohesin axis. Homologs pair completely: synapsis into bivalents.Pachytenepachy = thickStarts when the SC is complete. Crossing over becomes evident: physical breakage of DNA in one paternal and one maternal chromatid. Each connection point is a chiasma (plural chiasmata). About 55 chiasmata per cell in male meiosis and about 90 in female, mostly at recombination hotspots.Diplotenediplos = doubleSC degraded; homologs separate slightly but stay joined at the chiasmata.Diakinesisdia = through, kinesis = moveBivalents contract; nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear; spindle begins to form, leading into metaphase I.

[Slides] Figure label: “Homologs linked only by chiasmata”.
[Lucía] Chiasmata form during pachytene but are only seen in diplotene, when the chromosomes separate a little. [check] For diakinesis she writes “chiasmata disappear… and histones begin to form”; [Notes] say the bivalents contract and the spindle begins to form.

5. Homologous recombination at the molecular level
[Notes] (Figure 7, Figure 8):

SPO11 (the main endonuclease in humans) makes a double-strand break at specific sites in one chromatid.
The MNR complex (MRE11, NBS1, RAD50), an exonuclease, digests the ends, leaving 3’ overhangs.
One 3’ overhang invades a chromatid of the homologous chromosome, forming a Holliday structure.
A polymerase extends the 3’ ends using the other chromatid as template (DNA synthesis). The complex includes replication protein A (“REPA” in the notes), RAD54 and others such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 (mutated in breast cancer).
The double Holliday junction is resolved by cutting two strands and religating to the opposite partner. Depending on how the junctions are cut: crossover (recombinant) or non-crossover (non-recombinant).


Gene conversion: some new DNA may be copied from one chromatid to the other. Four possible outcomes: crossover with or without gene conversion; non-crossover with or without gene conversion.
In meiosis the resolution complexes favour crossovers; in mitotic repair (HRR) non-crossovers are favoured.
Recorded in Lec 7.8: “SPO11 creates double-strand breaks to initiate meiosis… the beginning of the process of homologous recombination”; the same process (MNR digestion, overhangs invading the other double strand, synthesis, two Holliday junctions, resolution) is reused in HRR with partly different proteins. Videos in the study material: “7.2 HR_Watson.mp4”, “7.2 holliday model.mp4”.

6. Meiosis I (rest) and meiosis II

[Notes] Metaphase I: homologous pairs align at the equatorial plane; microtubules attach to each pair of centromeres. Anaphase I: each homolog of a pair goes to opposite poles (chiasmata separate). Telophase I and cytokinesis: two secondary gametocytes, haploid (n) with two chromatids per chromosome (2C).
[Notes] Meiosis II resembles mitosis (prophase II to telophase II) with 23 chromosomes instead of 46; sister chromatids separate at anaphase II. Unlike in mitosis, the two chromatids are usually genetically different because of recombination in meiosis I. No DNA replication before meiosis II.
[Lucía] At the end of meiosis I, the two haploid cells have duplicated material and enter the second division directly; telophase I nuclear membrane only partly forms.
[Slides] Figure label: “Meiosis I anaphase”.

7. Gametogenesis: male vs female



































MaleFemaleDivisionsBoth symmetrical: four functional spermatozoaAsymmetrical: one egg and polar bodies (discarded)Meiosis I productTwo secondary spermatocytesLarge secondary oocyte + first polar bodyMeiosis II productSpermatids, then spermMature egg + second polar bodyTimingFrom puberty, continuous to old age ([Notes], Lec 9.1 section)Starts in fetal lifeArrestsNoneProphase I (dictyotene) until ovulation; metaphase II until fertilization

[Notes] Primary oocytes enter meiosis I during fetal development and arrest in a prolonged diplotene called the dictyotene. Each menstrual cycle the dominant follicle completes meiosis I just before ovulation, giving a secondary oocyte, which arrests in metaphase II; meiosis II is completed when a sperm penetrates the oocyte. Since ovulation continues to the fifth or sixth decade, meiosis I can be arrested for decades. The notes pose the question of the implications for the embryo’s health (see maternal age effect in Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis: about 70% of Down syndrome cases from nondisjunction at maternal meiosis I).
[Slides] “Arrested in Prophase I (Dictyotene)” and “Arrested in Metaphase II”; testis labels: spermatogonium (diploid), mitotic division, primary spermatocyte (in prophase of meiosis I), first meiotic division, secondary spermatocyte (haploid), second meiotic division, spermatids (haploid), sperm cells; Sertoli cell; seminiferous tubule, epididymis.
[Lucía] Male meiosis takes 64 days in the testis. Female meiosis starts around the 5th month of gestation; oocytes arrest at diplotene of prophase I until puberty/ovulation; after fertilization the secondary oocyte divides, the second polar body is removed and the pronuclei fuse to form the zygote. Neither figure is in [Notes].

8. Mitosis vs meiosis
[Notes] Table 1:













































CharacteristicMitosisMeiosisLocationAll tissuesSpecialized germ-line cells in testis and ovaryProductsDiploid somatic cellsHaploid sperm and eggReplication and divisionOne round of replication per divisionOne round of replication per two divisionsDuration of prophaseShort (about 30 min in human cells)Can take decadesPairing of maternal and paternal homologsNoYes, during meiosis IRecombinationRare and abnormalEvery meiosis; normally at least once in each chromosome arm after pairingDaughter cellsGenetically identicalGenetically different (independent assortment and recombination)

[Lucía] Example with one pair of homologs (A, a): after replication there are 2 A and 2 a; mitosis gives two cells each with A and a; meiosis, with recombination between non-sister chromatids, gives four haploid cells with mixed maternal and paternal information.
From Lec 7.7 (recorded): misaligned homologs at repeated sequences (segmental duplications) can undergo unequal crossing over, giving duplications and deletions (genomic disorders such as DiGeorge). See Lec 7.7 Genetic variation.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging
Sources

Levels of Chromatin packing (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file only. It starts with the size problem (2 m of DNA in a 5 micrometre nucleus) and ends with the lecturer’s closing summary, so it looks complete. The very first sentence is cut (“You should know this…”).
Coverage: all sections come from the transcript. Gaps filled from the Genetics class notes (TAD and compartment sizes, CTCF binding sequence) and Lucía.

Resources

Slides: Slides Unit 7.pdf, section “Lec 7.4: Levels of chromatin packaging”. The slides are almost all images: only the learning goals and a few figure labels came through as text. For the figures, see the slides.
Study material: no separate study material for 7.4 in the vault. The lecturer refers to a video (4 to 10 minutes) in the ADI material for this lecture; the institute name is garbled in the transcript.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “LECTURE 7.4 LEVELS OF CHROMATIN PACKAGING” (Figures 1 to 4).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 7.3. Levels of chromatin packaging”, PDF p. 199-201.
Related notes: Lec 7.2 Meiosis (cohesins, previous class), Lec 8.2 Regulation of gene expression and Lec 8.3 Epigenetics (enhancers, promoters, histone modifications).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 7 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

“Close to the lamina, inactive. Far from the lamina, active.” He calls it a general rule of thumb to keep in mind (section 3).
The loop organization that brings an enhancer next to its gene is “crucial”: without it genes cannot be regulated (section 7).
On TAD insulation by CTCF boundaries: “if you understand this, then I think you have understood everything you need to understand” (section 8).
The video in the ADI material covers basic nomenclature on chromosomes and genes, which he says is important to have very clear. Watch it.
[verify] CTCF binding sequence: the transcript reads “I think you have to know the exact sequence to which CTCF binds”. It is unclear whether he said you have to know it or do not. The class notes give the sequence (section 7).

[Slides] Learning goals:

DNA in the linear genome is packaged into chromatin, and chromatin into chromosomes.
Chromosomes occupy territories in the nucleus.
Loops and compartments (formed at different levels of resolution) can be active or inactive.

1. The packaging problem

Nucleus: about 5 micrometres (depends on the cell). Inside it must fit 23 pairs of linear chromosomes.
Genome: 3,000 million nucleotides (3 x 10^9) per haploid set. Worked out, the whole genome (two copies) is about 2 metres of very thin double-stranded thread. [Notes] agrees: “two meters of DNA in a diploid cell nucleus”.
Why not just cram it in at random (his “golf ball” demonstration with a piece of cord)?

It would waste space and be hard to fit.
Mainly, chromatin is not an inert molecule: transcription, replication and other processes run all the time, so the DNA must be accessible at very specific sites and distant elements must interact. An orderly arrangement makes that possible.
[Notes] Packaging must be dynamic and reversible so that transcription factors and other molecules can reach the DNA.


Supercoiling (suggested by a student) helps: coiling his 2 m cord around a finger reduced it to about 1 cm. But it is not enough; there are higher levels.
Key message: packaging is hierarchical, with several levels of compaction, ending in long loops of chromatin, and each chromosome occupies its own territory.

2. Chromatin and chromosomes

Chromatin = DNA plus all the proteins that help package it densely in the nucleus. It is what is seen under the microscope.
Interphase (G1, S, G2): no chromosomes are visible, only a nucleus with relatively relaxed chromatin. [Lucía] During interphase, chromosomes cannot be observed under the light microscope.
Mitosis (metaphase): highest level of packaging, about 10,000-fold compaction (lecturer’s figure). Only then are chromosomes visible. [Lucía] Mitotic chromosomes are about 100 nm.
Stained metaphase chromosomes show bands (example on the slide: chromosome 2). You see the two homologs (maternal and paternal), each with two sister chromatids after replication; before replication each homolog has one chromatid.

[Notes] Every locus is present in two allelic forms (one paternal, one maternal); after S phase each chromosome is made of two identical sister chromatids.
[Lucía] G-banding: lighter bands are less compact, darker bands more compact. p = short arm, q = long arm; bands are named by number.


Cytogenetics gets its own lecture (Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis).

3. Chromosome territories

Seen in interphase with FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization), which “paints” the chromatin of each chromosome a different colour; the image is then converted to more contrasted pseudocolours. [Notes] Chromosome paints; see Figure 1 of the class notes.
The technique was perfected about 20 years ago. It showed that chromatin is not a tangle of crisscrossed chromosomes: the chromatin of each chromosome occupies its own territory in the nucleus.
Territories touch at their boundaries, so some intermingling at the edges is conceivable, but that has to be demonstrated. [Notes] Territories are “largely non-overlapping”, with contacts at the boundaries.
[Lucía] The two homologs do not necessarily occupy neighbouring areas of the nucleus.
Positions are not fixed (chromosome 2 is not always in the same place in every cell or tissue), but there are general rules:


























Rule (lecturer)PositionLarge chromosomesUsually towards the outsideSmall chromosomesUsually towards the insideChromosomes with active chromatin (expressed genes)Inside, away from the nuclear laminaChromosomes with many silenced genesNext to the nuclear lamina

Why positions vary between cell types: a skin cell and a neuron have the same genes but have activated or repressed different sets. A chromosome with many genes active in skin but not in brain might move towards the interior or towards the lamina depending on the cell type.

4. First level: nucleosomes and the 10 nm fiber

The double helix is wound around a protein complex, the nucleosome: about 145 nucleotides, one and three-quarter turns (lecturer’s figures). Then the next nucleosome, and the next.
Electron microscopy: “beads on a string” (like a pearl necklace). [Lucía] “modelo del collar de perlas”.
Nucleosome core = histone octamer = two identical tetramers, each made of H2A, H2B, H3, H4. [Notes] Two molecules of each of the four histones form the octamer (Figure 2).
Histone H1 sits outside and helps stabilize the nucleosome. [Lucía] H1 acts as a linker, giving stability between nucleosomes.
This level is the 10 nm fiber (10 nm thick).
[Lucía] Histones have tails whose amino acids undergo modifications (see Lec 8.3 Epigenetics).

5. 30 nm fiber and the solenoid

The 10 nm fiber is further bent and coiled. One of the first models was the solenoid (like copper wire wound round a cylinder to make an electromagnet), originally called the 30 nm fiber.
[check] Whether the solenoid exists in vivo:

Lecturer: more refined recent techniques suggest the solenoid is apparently not what happens in vivo; whatever the exact configuration, the fiber ends up folding into loops.
[Notes]: thanks to chromosome conformation capture techniques “we know that the 10-nm fiber is wound following the structure of a solenoid”.
[Lucía]: second level = solenoid, giving the 30 nm fiber; third level = further coiling up to mitotic chromosomes.
The slide text does not settle it. Ask or check the slide figure.


[Notes] The techniques used to study the spatial relationship of sequences are collectively called chromosome conformation capture.

6. Loops, TADs and compartments

Scales (figure from a recent review, see the slide): nucleosomal scale, supranucleosomal scale (loops), nuclear scale (chromosome territories). The middle level was a “black box” until recent research.
TADs = topologically associating domains: regions of DNA that associate in space. Inside a TAD, chromatin forms loops so distant parts can touch and interact physically. [Notes] Typically 500 kb on average, with several loops of various sizes inside each TAD.
TADs come in two “flavours”:

A compartment = active TADs (active chromatin).
B compartment = inactive TADs, close to the nuclear lamina.
Active and inactive TADs carry different chemical modifications, which helps them cluster with their own kind (“like phase separation”). In the linear genome A and B TADs may alternate, but in 3D they cluster.


Compartment = several TADs in the same functional state. Many compartments (active and inactive) make up the chromatin of one chromosome territory.
[Notes] Compartments are about 5 Mb and contain different TADs in different cell types. Compartments in the centre of the nucleus and on the outside of chromosome territories are generally active; those near the lamina or in the interior of territories are generally inactive.
[check] Hierarchy: [Lucía] calls the TAD “the largest type of compartment in the hierarchy”. The lecturer and [Notes] put compartments above TADs (a compartment contains several TADs). Follow the lecturer and the class notes.
Result: chromosomes are isolated from each other, and inside each chromosome some regions are isolated from others.
TADs vs loops (lecturer, agrees with [Notes]):





















TADsLoops inside TADsStabilityRelatively fixed and stable during the life of a cell; similar between cells and tissuesDynamic, fluid; change with gene expression[Notes]Highly conserved across cell types and speciesUsually change during the cell cycle

Example: if a gene needs a given enhancer in one cell type, loops change to bring them together; in another cell type where the gene is silent, other elements are brought together instead. [Notes] Figure 4: different loop configurations allow different promoter-enhancer contacts.
[Slides] Figure labels: metaphase chromosome 17, interaction frequency (low to high), TAD #1 and TAD #2. See the slide.

7. How TADs are made: loop extrusion (cohesin and CTCF)

Current model: loop extrusion. Analogy: folding a thread and passing the fold through the eye of a needle, then pulling, makes a long loop.
Cohesin extrudes chromatin. It is the ring complex seen in the meiosis class. It acts like a molecular motor, pulling chromatin through the ring to form a loop; smaller sub-loops form inside.

Components: SMC proteins (structural maintenance of chromosomes), e.g. SMC3, plus a protein transcribed as “Rav21”. [verify] Check the name of this cohesin subunit; no vault source gives it. “Everything is in the notes”, he says, but the class notes do not list the subunits.
Classroom demonstration with student volunteers as chromatin and a ring as cohesin.


CTCF: a protein that binds a specific DNA sequence (about 20 to 30 nucleotides by the lecturer’s estimate). Its sites are scattered throughout the genome. [verify] The expansion of the name is garbled in the transcript (“the CTCF binding factor”); no vault source gives it.

[Notes] Binding sequence: 5’-CCGCGNGGNGGC(G/A)(C/G)(T/C)-3’.


When extrusion stops: when cohesin reaches two CTCF molecules bound in opposite orientation (pointing towards each other). They clash and extrusion stops. That defines the boundaries of a TAD: CTCF, CTCF and cohesin at the base of the TAD.

CTCF sites in the same orientation do not form a TAD boundary together. This is why a diagram can show three CTCF sites in one TAD: a site can only pair with one in the opposite orientation (arrows on the slide show orientation).
So there can be smaller TADs inside larger ones (sub-TADs, meta-TADs; names on the slide).


In the linear genome the two CTCF sites are far apart; in the 3D TAD they are next to each other, with loops in between.
[Notes] CTCF can dimerize when bound to different DNA sequences, mediating long-range looping. CTCF also positions nucleosomes and delimits heterochromatin, which tends to spread.
[Lucía] CTCF behaves as an insulator; it forms a dimer that flanks compartments at the boundaries.

8. Why it matters: contacts and insulation

Bringing elements together. Example (lecturer’s): the insulin gene and an enhancer that may be a million nucleotides away. The enhancer must physically interact with the gene’s promoter for insulin to be made. Only loop folding makes that possible. “Without this we are dead.”

[Notes] Segments in the same TAD can contact each other even though they may be 1 to 2 Mb apart in the linear genome.


Insulation. Example: gene A (insulin) with enhancer A (makes it pancreas-specific) and gene B (hemoglobin) with enhancer B (red-blood-cell-specific). If enhancer A reached gene B, you would have hemoglobin in the pancreas; applied to all genes, chaos.

Each gene and its enhancer sit in their own TAD. The two CTCF molecules form a boundary element: the enhancer cannot cross it.
Contacts between TADs are very infrequent but not impossible; contacts inside a TAD are favoured.
Second example from the slides: a mouse embryo gene expressed only in brain and one only in liver, separated into different TADs by CTCF sites (see the slide).


[Notes] Insulators = the DNA sequences at TAD boundaries, which are CTCF binding sites.
[Lucía] Disrupting a TAD border can cause disease: it creates bigger TADs and therefore more (aberrant) interactions, e.g. a brain enhancer contacting a liver gene.

9. Summary of the hierarchy (lecturer’s closing recap)









































LevelStructure1DNA double helix2Nucleosomes, 10 nm fiber (“beads on a string”)330 nm fiber (solenoid model; see [check] in section 5)4Loops inside TADs (dynamic)5TADs (stable; bounded by CTCF and cohesin)6A and B compartments (clusters of TADs)7Chromosome territoriesMitosisMetaphase chromosome, highest compaction

Throughout, proteins keep accessing the chromatin; this overview is needed to understand gene regulation and “all of genetics”.
