Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lec 7.6 Protein-coding and non-coding genes
Sources

7.8 continue (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file only. The file name is misleading: the content is Lec 7.6 (genes), not 7.8. It opens with “in this lecture we are going to focus on genes” and ends with a student question after the pseudogene section, so it looks complete.
Lec 7.5 (general features of the human genome) was not recorded. The lecturer refers back to it several times (GC content of the genome, LINEs and SINEs); those points are kept as he stated them here.
Coverage: all sections come from the transcript. Gaps and conflicting numbers filled from the Genetics class notes, the slides and Lucía.

Resources

Slides: Slides Unit 7.pdf, section “Lec 7.6: Genes (protein-coding vs. non-coding)“. Mostly images; the learning goals, the lncRNA vs protein-coding statements and the expression percentages came through as text. The gene catalogue table and the summary table did not: see the slides.
Study material: none separate for 7.6 in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “LECTURE 7.6 GENES (protein-coding and non-coding)” (Tables 1 to 3, Box 1). Table 1 (gene catalogue) and the final summary table are images and did not come through as text: see the PDF.
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 7.6. Protein coding and non-coding genes”, PDF p. 209-211. Her numbers are from last year and differ in places.
Related notes: Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging (loops; lncRNAs help make them), Lec 8.1 DNA transcription, Lec 8.2 Regulation of gene expression, Lec 7.7 Genetic variation (segmental duplications).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 7 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

The protein-coding vs lncRNA comparison table (section 6). “Perhaps in the exam you would find this table empty and you would have to fill it up… perhaps it’s happened before… So you should be able to reconstruct this table from scratch.”
Number of genes: about 80,000. He said he might ask it in the second self-assessment the following week (“What should you answer? … Close to 80,000”).
“This is very important for you to understand”: the mRNA has the same sequence as the top (non-template) strand, with U instead of T (section 2).
“The first thing I’d like you to take from this lecture”: genes now come in two classes, protein-coding and non-coding (section 1).
lncRNA characteristics are “something you should understand and should have very clear in your mind” (section 5).
On gene structure: “that’s all you have to know about a gene… in terms of the structure” (exons, introns, UTRs, CDS).

[Slides] Learning goals:

Genes come in two classes: protein-coding or non-coding.
Abundance, size, characteristics and function of human genes.

1. What is a gene?

Classical definition (a student’s answer, and what he would have given about 20 years ago): a section of DNA that codes for a protein.
Largely thanks to the human genome sequence, many genes have been found that do not meet this definition. Two main classes are now recognized:

Protein-coding genes (the classical gene).
Non-coding RNA genes: they make an RNA that is not translated; the functional molecule is the RNA itself. This whole class was unknown when he was a student; “probably many more surprises” remain.


Current definition (lecturer): a gene is a stretch of DNA that makes a functional RNA. Its boundaries are the start and the end of transcription, and it includes exons and introns.
[Lucía] “A gene is a sequence of DNA that is used to make a messenger.” Enhancers do not make RNA, so they are part of the DNA but are not genes.
[Notes] Even the gene count is uncertain: some genes make both coding and non-coding transcripts, and some “lncRNA” genes turn out to have short coding sequences that make micropeptides.

2. Structure of a typical protein-coding gene

Transcription. RNA polymerase II (a protein complex) binds a region of the genome, opens the double strand and moves along, using the bottom strand as template to make an RNA complementary to it.

The RNA therefore has the same sequence as the top strand, with U instead of T. Flagged “very important”.


Start of the gene = the first nucleotide transcribed = the TSS (transcription start site), drawn as an arrow. By definition it is also the start of exon 1.
End of the gene = the last nucleotide of the RNA, where the polymerase complex disassembles and transcription stops.
Splicing. The long primary RNA is cut; some segments are degraded and the rest are joined (“spliced”) into a shorter mRNA.

Exons = the segments spliced together. Introns = the segments removed between them.
The gene in the genome = all exons + all introns.
The mRNA exits the nucleus and is translated in the cytoplasm.
[Lucía] The unspliced RNA is the primary transcript; spliceosomes cut it exactly at exon-intron boundaries; the mature mRNA has a 5’ cap.


Translation. The ribosome scans the mRNA until it finds AUG (methionine), the initiation codon; methionine is always the first amino acid. The AUG is usually somewhere in exon 1.

Stop codons are in the final exon. [Lucía] UAA, UAG, UGA (the transcript is garbled on the third).


CDS (coding sequence) = from start codon to stop codon; the only part that codes for amino acids.
UTRs (untranslated regions) = transcribed into the mRNA but not translated: 5’ UTR (before the start codon, in exon 1) and 3’ UTR (after the stop codon, in the last exon). [Notes] Shown in orange in Figure 1.

3. The gene catalogue (how many genes?)

An international consortium keeps the catalogue; it changes all the time. The slide shows the 2026 version. [Notes] Annotation: gencodegenes.org; assembly GRCh38.p14 (2026). The table itself is an image (Table 1): see the slide or the PDF.










































CategoryLecturer[Notes][Lucía] (last year)Total genesAbout 80,000About 80,000not givenProtein-codingAbout 20,000 (unchanged for years)About 20,000About 20,000Non-coding RNA genes”About twice the number of protein-coding”; later “40K” for lncRNAAlmost twice as many lncRNA genes as protein-coding (36,000 lncRNA genes)About 15,000 (long and short)PseudogenesAbout 15,000About 17,000 (as of 2024)not givenTotal transcriptsAbout 650,000 (later “600,000”)not given as text (Table 1)not given

[check] Non-coding gene number: the transcript says “about 14,000 non-coding genes, or actually twice the number of protein-coding genes”, then adds “20, 40 and 15,000, that’s 75,000”, and in the summary table gives 40K for lncRNA. “14,000” is probably a transcription error for 40,000. [Notes] says 36,000 lncRNA genes, almost twice the protein-coding number. Lucía’s 15,000 is last year’s figure.
[check] Pseudogenes: lecturer about 15,000; [Notes] about 17,000 (as of 2024).
[verify] Total transcripts: the lecturer says 650,000, then 600,000. Check Table 1 on the slide.
The “20,000 genes” figure is true for protein-coding genes. What has grown is the number of non-coding genes.
[Notes] History: the first draft (2001) suggested about 30,000 protein-coding genes; the number was inflated, as shown when mouse and dog genomes failed to show counterparts for many predicted genes.

4. Alternative splicing

Far more transcripts than genes. The only explanation is that one gene makes several transcripts, by alternative splicing: using different combinations of exons (e.g. exons 1, 2, 3 in one transcript; exons 1, 3, 4 in another).
Lecturer: on average about 10 transcripts (isoforms) per protein-coding gene, so 20,000 genes give about 200,000 RNA molecules.
Advantage (lecturer): economy of genome space. One gene per RNA would need a huge genome; this saves space and energy and is more efficient.
[Lucía] Each transcript codes for a slightly different protein.

Protein-coding gene numbers















































FeatureLecturer[Notes][Lucía]Exons per geneAbout 9 (8 to 10); “average of 8” in the class discussionAverage 7 to 9 exons; Figure 1: average of 87 to 8Internal exon sizeAbout 145 nucleotidesMean internal exon 147 nt (median 121); mean of all exons 268 nt (median 129)145 ntIntronsVery long, very variable (thousands to hundreds of thousands of nucleotides)From a few nt to over 100,000 nt; intron size generally correlates with gene lengthVery large, very variableGene size (exons + introns)About 30 kbMean 64.9 kb, median 26.0 kb20 to 30 kbmRNA (no introns)About 2 kbnot givennot givenCoding DNA in the genome1.5%not given1.5%

[check] Gene size: the lecturer’s 30 kb is close to the [Notes] median (26.0 kb), not the mean (64.9 kb).
Exon 1 and the last exon are usually longer because they contain the UTRs. Internal exons are short and fairly similar in size. [Notes] As genes get larger, exon size stays fairly constant; large genes tend to have large introns.
Only 1.5% of the genome codes for amino acids. The rest is functional but does other things, such as regulating how genes are expressed (lecturer).

Variation between genes (table on the slide; [Notes] Table 3)

Titin: the longest protein, but the gene is not so large.
Dystrophin: the longest gene, but the protein is not that large. Its average intron is about 28,000 nt ([Notes] 28,560 bp).
SRY: one exon only (mono-exonic, no splicing).
Some genes have hundreds of exons.
[check] Titin gene size: lecturer 183 kb; [Notes] Table 3: 283 kb (34,350 aa, 363 exons).
[check] Longest gene: lecturer says dystrophin, about 2 Mb. [Notes]: the longest protein-coding gene is now CNTNAP2 (2.305 Mb), which “just pips” dystrophin (2.242 Mb), the previous record holder.
[check] Dystrophin protein: transcript “only 3000-mins” (probably about 3,000 amino acids). [Notes] Table 3: 3,685 amino acids.
[Notes] Transcribing the 2.24 Mb dystrophin gene takes 16 hours; very highly expressed genes often have short or no introns. Other intronless genes besides SRY: other SOX genes, interferons, histones, many GPCRs, heat shock proteins (Table 3 footnote).

5. Non-coding RNA genes

Some examples were known long ago but thought to be exceptions; then more and more were found. “A big discovery”; very fashionable now.
Divided by size, because the functions differ. The threshold is arbitrary: 200 nucleotides.
























ClassSizeLecturer’s examples and functions[Notes] Table 2Short ncRNAUp to 200 ntMany already known. snRNAs (splicing), tRNAs (translation), microRNAs (later class). Mostly work inside the nucleussnRNA (splicing); snoRNA (rRNA maturation); scaRNA (snRNA maturation); tRNA (protein synthesis); miRNA (regulation of target genes by base pairing); piRNA and siRNA (genome defense, limiting transposons in germ cells)Long ncRNA (lncRNA)Over 200 ntThe new class nobody suspected. Transcribed in the nucleus, spliced; can stay in the nucleus or go to the cytoplasm; not translated. Usually regulate other (protein-coding) genes, activating or silencing them. Some help make chromatin loops. Important in cancer and many processesNuclear lncRNA: regulate target genes by modifying chromatin or by transcriptional regulation (includes antisense transcripts). Cytoplasmic lncRNA: some regulate translation, protein localization or activity

[Notes] The division is “extremely arbitrary”: it would split rRNAs (28S, 18S long; 5.8S, 5S short), and many important regulators are small. Many lncRNAs have a 5’ cap and poly(A) tail like mRNAs, but others do not.

6. Protein-coding vs lncRNA genes (exam table)
Box plot on the slide: compare the number of introns (median and interquartile range). See the slide.
[Slides] text:

lncRNA genes are shorter than protein-coding genes.
lncRNA genes have fewer exons.
lncRNA genes are NOT GC-rich.
Expression of lncRNAs is very restricted: tissue-specific differences.
Protein-coding: 7% expressed only in one cell line; 50% expressed in all cell lines.
lncRNAs: 30% expressed only in one cell line; 10% expressed in all cell lines.

The table as reconstructed in class (fill it from memory):


















































FeatureProtein-coding geneslncRNA genesNumber of genesAbout 20,000About 40,000 (about double) [check] [Notes]: 36,000Gene sizeAbout 30 kbSlightly smaller; “I could put 20 there” (about 20 kb)Exons per geneAbout 8 to 10Fewer: “about 4” (transcript garbled as “4%“)GC contentHigher than the genome average: about 53%About the genome average: about 45% (genome average 42%)Alternative transcripts per geneMore than 10Fewer: about 5Expression levelHigh, strong (many mRNA copies)Low, weakExpression profileBroad (several tissues)Narrow, restricted, tissue-specific (usually one tissue)Main repeat type insideSINEs (Alus)Retroviral elements

If you find a gene that is not GC-rich, it is probably a non-coding gene. Why protein-coding genes are GC-rich he could not explain then; “that’s a fact”.
Repeat types: “people really don’t know what’s the meaning of all this.”
[check] Sources on the lncRNA column:

[Notes]: lncRNA genes have an average of five transcripts (190,000 transcripts from 36,000 lncRNA genes), but later: “Today, we recognize a similar number of alternative transcripts per gene in protein-coding and lncRNA genes.” The class notes contradict themselves; the lecturer gave >10 vs about 5.
[Notes]: protein-coding genes are longer, with more exons and higher GC% than lncRNA genes; lncRNAs are expressed at lower levels and more tissue-restricted. Agrees with the lecturer. The summary table in the class notes (“as of 2024”) is an image: see the PDF.
[Lucía] (last year): lncRNA 2 to 4 exons, 10 to 15 kb, about 43% GC, 2 alternative transcripts; protein-coding at least 4 alternative transcripts.
[Notes]: lncRNA exons have a mean length of 683 nt (median 129 nt).



The tissue-expression experiment

Cell lines representing 14 tissues (brain, liver, lung, spleen, pancreas, stomach…). For each gene, count in how many of the 14 it is expressed; plot how many genes are expressed in 1, 2, … 14 cell types.
Red = protein-coding; green and blue (including “intergenic novel”) = lncRNA.
Result: most protein-coding genes are expressed in all cell types, very few in only one. lncRNA genes are the opposite: most are expressed in just one cell type.
Take-home message (lecturer): lncRNA genes are very tissue-specific; protein-coding genes are usually expressed in several tissues. lncRNAs are also expressed at much lower levels.
Background: a neuron and a skin cell differ because, during differentiation, they activated and silenced different sets of genes.

7. Pseudogenes

“False genes”: copies of genes that have been inactivated (degraded by mutations, mostly inactive). Symbol: Greek letter psi.
The catalogue lists three types: unitary, processed and non-processed. About 10,000 processed and about 4,000 to 5,000 non-processed (lecturer). [Notes] Processed account for nearly three-quarters, non-processed for nearly one-quarter.





















TypeOrigin (lecturer)[Notes]Non-processedDuplication of a stretch of DNA during evolution. A copy of the gene, usually close to the original, inactivated by mutationsDirect copies made at the DNA level (e.g. tandem duplication). A full-length one keeps introns and nearby regulatory sequences such as the promoterProcessedCopy of the mRNA (already spliced) inserted elsewhere in the genome by the proteins encoded by LINEs (retrotransposons), which sometimes take the wrong mRNA from the cytoplasm. Then inactivated by mutation or simply not expressed”Retropseudogenes”: copies of processed transcripts converted into cDNA by the LINE-1 machinery. Lack the promoter, regulatory sequences and introns, so usually silent

Why the names: “processed” because they come from a processed (matured, spliced) mRNA; the others are therefore “non-processed”.
The retrotransposon mechanism was the answer a student gave from the previous class (7.5, not recorded).
Pseudogenes matter because some are expressed or have other functions; to be discussed later.
[Notes] Not all pseudogenes are functionless; some are transcribed. A cDNA copy that acquires regulatory sequences and is useful can be kept by selection as a functional retrogene (Box 1 Figure 1).
[Notes] Olfactory receptor family: close to 1,000 genes, the majority of the sequences inactive.

8. Student question at the end

Q: If RNA polymerase makes a mistake when synthesizing the mRNA, would that be a mutation?
[verify] The answer is garbled in the transcript (“Yes, the RNA polymerase does describe it. Like sometimes DNA polymerase 3 can make a mistake”). It is unclear what he concluded. Ask or check.

9. In the class notes but not covered in the lecture

[Notes] Segmental duplications: over 5% of the euchromatic genome, about 400 large blocks with very high identity (often over 95%), from duplications in the past 40 million years of primate evolution; intra- and interchromosomal. They contribute to copy number variation and rearrangements causing disease (see Lec 7.7 Genetic variation). The slide also has a segmental duplication figure (chromosome 7p).
[Notes] Tandem duplication by unequal crossover between misaligned chromatids (unequal crossover on homologs, or unequal sister chromatid exchange), possibly stabilized by Alu repeats (Figure 3).

Study material: none separate for 7.7 in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “LECTURE 7.7 GENETIC VARIATION” (Table 1, Figures 1, 2, 6). Microsatellite sizes are in “LECTURE 7.5 GENERAL FEATURES OF THE HUMAN GENOME”.

Related notes: Lec 7.6 Protein-coding and non-coding genes (segmental duplications), TBL 7.3 Forensic DNA analysis (microsatellites, Hardy-Weinberg), Lec 7.2 Meiosis (crossing over), Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis (microdeletions).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 7 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Self-assessment: “the microsatellites and the polymorphisms of these microsatellites” will be included in the self-assessment. TBL 7.3 (forensic DNA analysis) will not, because it is on the same day.
Learning goal he states: be able to explain how individual genomes differ, at small scale and large scale (structural variants), and how these variants affect predisposition to common diseases. In-depth application comes next year.
Genomic disorders: “You have learned in the notes more about that. There are some types, names, and the scale” (section 8).
Admin: TBL 7.3 (Thursday) was moved to this lecture room; its preparation materials (two links and a short reading) were already visible on ADI.

[Slides] Learning goals:

Individual genomes differ in single-nucleotide polymorphisms and in larger structural variants.
These variants have profound implications for predisposition to disease.

1. Why study genetic variation

Once the reference genome exists, the next question is where individual genomes differ.
For medicine: these differences underlie different susceptibility to disease. Not only single-gene genetic diseases, but common diseases with a genetic predisposition (diabetes, Alzheimer’s at 65, heart disease, cancer). This has been the focus of genetic research for about the last 20 years; covered in a future class and next year.

2. Classifying variants: small scale vs structural

The threshold is arbitrary: 50 nucleotides.





















Small-scale variationStructural variation (SV)SizeUnder 50 ntOver 50 ntExamplesSingle nucleotide variants (SNVs), small insertions/deletions, indels, microsatellitesMobile element insertions, large deletions, inversions, copy number variants (CNVs)

Some variants change the total amount of DNA, some do not:

No change in DNA content: a single nucleotide substitution (one person has T, another C); an inversion (a segment in opposite orientation), which may still affect how genes in the area work.
Change in DNA content: insertions (e.g. T vs CT), deletions, mobile element insertions, CNVs.


[Notes] The two broad categories are changes that do not affect DNA content and changes in copy number. In the 1000 Genomes Project, 1 to 50 nucleotides = small-scale; over 50 bp = structural variation (because short-read sequencing could not detect larger indels well). In the past, SV meant 1 kb or longer.

3. Types of small-scale variant
Reference genome on top, “my genome” below (examples on the slide; [Notes] Figure 1).

Deletion polymorphism: a segment missing. A deletion is not necessarily a disease mutation; it depends where it is (it may be outside a gene).
Insertion polymorphism: the reverse.
Indel: a deletion and an insertion at the same site (lecturer’s example: a stretch replaced by GCA). [Notes] Figure 1C: deletion of GGTTC plus insertion of CA. [Notes] “Indel” is also used broadly for any small insertion, duplication or deletion (1 to 50 nt in the 1000 Genomes Project).
Microsatellite (short tandem repeat): e.g. a CA dinucleotide repeated in tandem (“CACACA”), with 12, 15 or 20 repeats in different people. [Notes] Microsatellites vary in copy number but are classified as indels; Figure 1D: 12 vs 11 copies of CA.

Polymorphism and allele frequency

Polymorphism = a genetic element that appears in many different forms in the population.
Worked example (lecturer): 50 people in the room, chromosome 1, two alleles each = 100 alleles. Sequencing finds 96 alleles with the gene and 4 with a deletion: deletion frequency 4%. So it is a population polymorphism, not a unique mutation causing disease.

There is always a frequent allele (here: having the gene) and a rare allele (the variant). What matters is the frequency of the rare allele.
If 20% carry it, it is probably not very bad for health. If only two people carry it, it might be one reason they develop, for instance, diabetes. “So rare that it approaches the definition of a mutation.”


[Notes] Traditionally, a variant with population frequency over 0.01 (1%) was a polymorphism, below 0.01 a rare variant (arbitrary cut-off). The term is declining. Current classes: common (over 5%), low frequency (1 to 5%), rare (under 1%). In medicine, “polymorphism” often means a variant that does not cause disease and “mutation” a disease-causing one.

Microsatellites and copy number polymorphism

Recall from 7.5 (not recorded): satellite, minisatellite and microsatellite DNA, tandem repeats.
New point: in some tandem repeats the number of repeats differs between people (e.g. 3 in one person, 5 in another, 2 in another). That number is the polymorphism.
Microsatellite size (class Q&A): a student said “less than 100 base pairs”; he corrected that this is the total array; the repeat unit is small. He first thought 1 to 6; a student said 1 to 4 bp and he accepted it. [Notes] (Lecture 7.5 table): microsatellite arrays under 100 bp; repeat unit often 1 to 4 bp; widely dispersed throughout all chromosomes.
Typical example he gives: CAG repeated in tandem (a trinucleotide). Many microsatellites are polymorphic (10, 8, 12 copies…).
Uses: very useful for forensic DNA analysis (TBL 7.3). Some are implicated in cancer (“you will study that throughout your degree”).
Large repeats: an element of about 100 nt repeated in tandem whose number of repeats differs between people is also a copy number variant. The term CNV is usually reserved for the large ones, which are structural variation. [verify] The transcript calls these “segmental mutations”; probably “segmental duplications”, but the transcript is garbled.

4. How much variation? Numbers

Genome: 3 x 10^9 nucleotides.
SNVs per genome: about 4 to 5 million compared with any other person (the transcript’s “5 trillion” is a transcription error; he says 4 to 5 million several times).
Genomes are about 99.85% identical: roughly one difference every 700 nucleotides (elsewhere in the lecture he says one every 500 to 1,000, and 700 to 800).
Small-scale variation involves about 5 Mb of DNA, mostly SNVs.
Structural variants: about 2,000 per genome (textbook figure), much fewer than SNVs but much larger, so they involve more DNA: about 10 to 20 Mb. Latest studies claim about 20,000 SVs per genome.
















































MeasureLecturer[Notes] Table 1 (1000 Genomes)[Lucía]Small-scale variants per individual4 to 5 million4,076,000 to 4,935,000 (99.95% of all changes); about 4.9 Mb4 to 5 million variants vs reference; elsewhere “3 million” when comparing two genomesSNVsMost of the above3.53 to 4.31 million; 3.92 MbIndels546,000 to 625,000; 1 MbSVs per individualAbout 2,000; latest studies about 20,0002,114 to 2,507 (0.05% of changes)About 2,000DNA in SVs10 to 20 MbAbout 18.4 Mb raw; median 8.9 Mb when collapsed onto the haploid reference (footnote c). Elsewhere: about 20 Mb, average SV 10 kb20 MbSNP spacingOne every 700 (also 500 to 1,000)Differences at 4 to 5 per 1,000 sites between two haploid genomesOne every 500

[Notes] SV breakdown per individual: mobile element insertions 1,012 to 1,225 (90% Alu or L1); large deletions 939 to 1,100 (5.6 Mb); CNVs 153 to 170 (11.3 Mb); inversions 9 to 12.
[Notes] Structural variation is more correlated with functional sequences than small-scale variation and contributes significantly to altered gene expression and disease. Most SNVs and short indels fall outside coding DNA and are thought to be neutral.
[Lucía] A total of 68,000 SVs have been described in humans. About 100 million positions vary among all humans on the planet.

5. SNPs / SNVs

Historically called SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms), pronounced “snip”. Because “polymorphism” suggests something benign and some SNPs increase disease risk, the more neutral single nucleotide variant (SNV) is now preferred: a variant may be bad, good, or do nothing.
Each allele is double-stranded, but only one strand is written for clarity. At a given position one chromosome may have T and the homologous one C: a C/T polymorphism.
Heterozygote = the two alleles differ (TC or CT, which count as the same). Homozygote = identical (TT or CC).

Hardy-Weinberg (introduced here; detail in TBL 7.3)

Genotype frequencies: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p and q are the frequencies of the two alleles.
Lecturer’s example: T frequency p = 0.8, C frequency q = 0.2. Predicted: TT = p² = 64%, CC = q² = 4%, heterozygotes 2pq = 32%. (The transcript says “6.4%” for TT; 64% is the value that makes the three add up to 100%.)
Not in the class notes text for 7.7; to be covered in TBL 7.3 Forensic DNA analysis.

Reading SNVs on a sequencing trace

The sequencer gives a trace of coloured peaks, one per nucleotide (example on the slide).
One peak (e.g. only A) = both alleles the same, homozygous.
Two overlapping peaks (e.g. blue and red, C and T) at the same position = heterozygous. It is a polymorphism if it also appears in other people.
[Lucía] Single peaks = homozygous; smaller double peaks = two different nucleotides (maternal and paternal).
Asked if the class had seen sequencing techniques: no.

What the SNVs do

Of the 4 to 5 million SNVs in a typical genome:

About 10,000 are potentially dangerous because they lie inside genes and change an amino acid.
Others in genes are silent: the genetic code is degenerate (two different codons can code for the same amino acid), so the amino acid does not change. (The class had the genetic code lecture later that day.)
About 25 to 30 have previously been associated with disease in other people (“30”, then “25” in the transcript). Whether you will develop that disease is an open question.
Many do not overlap genes but overlap regulatory regions (promoters, regions dictating how genes are expressed).


[Lucía] 25 to 30 disease-associated SNPs per person; about 500,000 overlap regulatory regions.

6. Geographic distribution of variation

Data from a project that sequenced millions of SNVs in many people from many parts of the world. [verify] The transcript calls it “a map project”. [Notes] Figure 2 is from the 1000 Genomes Project (2,504 individuals, 26 populations); [Notes] also mentions the HapMap project. Check which one the slide figure is.
Populations on the figure (lecturer): European (Italy, Caucasians living in Utah, Great Britain, Finland); East Asian (Chinese, Japanese, Vietnam); South Asian (Bangladesh, Punjab…); Central and South American (Mexico, Puerto Rico, Colombia, Peru); African (Yoruba from Ibadan in Nigeria, Sierra Leone, African Americans).
Finding: far more genetic variation in Africa than in the rest of the world.
Student suggestions discussed: sun exposure (no: about the same across the equatorial region), retroviruses (no: these are SNVs), large continent with varied climates, environment, more people.
Explanation (lecturer): out-of-Africa and the bottleneck effect.

Anatomically modern humans originated in Africa (earlier species: heidelbergensis, erectus). All humans were in Africa until about 100,000 years ago; only a few thousand.
Our species left Africa in several waves: first to South Asia, then the Far East, the last into Europe (then under glaciation), and eventually across the Bering Strait.
Only a few groups of a few hundred people left, carrying only some of the variants present in Africa: a bottleneck effect. New variants arose later, but never matched the variability inside Africa, which kept accumulating its own.
So two people living 100 km apart in Africa are genetically more different than the lecturer and a Chinese person.


Why Central and South America show a wider spread: admixture. Present-day populations mix native genomes with genomes that arrived from Europe and Africa (colonization by Spaniards, Vikings before, and migration from Africa; a student suggested slavery) in the 15th to 17th centuries: introgression of new variants. Modern migration is also changing global variation.
[Notes] Individuals show 3.90 to 5.05 million variant sites per genome. African populations show considerably greater diversity, consistent with out-of-Africa; Central and South American populations show elevated diversity that roughly correlates with the degree of recent African ancestry (Figure 2).
[Lucía] Two people from the same African city differ more than two individuals from different parts of the world.

7. Structural variants and homozygous gene loss

SV types: inversions, deletions, mobile element insertions, CNVs (summary figure from the textbook on the slide).
Mobile element insertions: some people carry insertions of retrotransposons that others lack; a child may carry a new insertion not present in the parents. A very common type of SV that increases DNA content (e.g. a 200 to 300 nt element copied to a new location). [Slides] “One AluY new germ-line insertion per 20 births” (Lec 7.5 section).
Large deletions often contain one or two genes. A heterozygous carrier has one copy instead of two; a homozygote has no copy of that gene.
Each of us has on average about 100 genes homozygously deleted, and these are healthy people.
Why are we healthy?

The obvious answer (student): the genes may be redundant; other genes do the same thing.
The other way round (lecturer): perhaps we are not so healthy after all. These deletions might be what gives Alzheimer’s or diabetes in 10 to 20 years. Not a congenital syndrome, but something subtle that increases the risk of common diseases.


[Notes] About 100 protein-coding genes are homozygously deleted in healthy individuals, suggesting they are non-essential; they usually belong to large gene families and may be redundant or have late-onset effects that do not substantially reduce fitness. It was unexpected that a “normal” genome has about 2,000 SVs; large gains or losses had been assumed to be pathogenic.
[Notes] Balanced SVs (same DNA content): inversions (a fragment rotated 180 degrees between two double-strand breaks) and balanced translocations. Inversions can still cause disease: hemophilia A, 45% of cases due to an inversion in the factor VIII gene on the X chromosome. Unbalanced SVs: mostly CNVs (copy number of a sequence over 50 nt, arising by tandem duplication; often multiallelic) plus large insertions and deletions (1 or 0 copies). Also called copy number polymorphisms (CNPs) or low-copy repeats (LCRs).

8. Unequal crossing over and genomic disorders

In meiosis, homologous chromosomes align and recombine. Repeated sequences such as segmental duplications (nearly identical copies) can cause misalignment of the chromatids.
A crossover in the misaligned region = unequal crossing over: one chromatid ends up with a duplication, the other with a deletion of the region.
These cause syndromes called genomic disorders. Example in the notes: DiGeorge syndrome, a deletion syndrome caused by unequal crossing over between segmental duplications.
People with such a deletion have the disease, so it is not a polymorphism.
[Notes] Structural variants (a few kb to a few Mb) are too small to see under the microscope; a 3 Mb deletion or duplication is invisible on a standard karyotype but can alter the dosage of dozens of genes. Example: microdeletion syndromes such as DiGeorge (chromosome 22).
[Slides] Genomic disorder examples (figures; see the slides for the mechanisms):


























Disorder (slide label)Detail on slideDiGeorge (22q11DS)Deletion of 3 Mb (90%); deletion of 1.5 Mb (5 to 10%)Charcot-Marie-Tooth / HNPPShown against “normal” (figure)Hemophilia AF8 (Xq28), 500 kbMicrodeletion 17q21.31Sporadic mental retardation (1% of cases); labels H1 (80%), H2 (20%), 900 kb, 700 kb (which size goes with which is not clear from the text)

The figures (which disorder is a duplication, deletion or inversion) did not come through as text: see the slides.

Exam flags from the lecturer

“It’s pretty important then that you understand the different types of lesions and how they are repaired, because all these impact health in a very important way.”
The “basic message”: damage that is not repaired, in a cell that does not commit apoptosis, is the recipe for cancer. “You will hear about this a lot throughout your degree” (section 4).
HR (meiosis) vs HRR (mitosis) comparison table (section 12): he went through it row by row in class and asked whether it was in the notes. [Notes] only say “In class we will summarize the differences”, so the table in this note comes from the lecture.

[Slides] Learning goals:

How is DNA variation created? Mistakes happen.
Mismatch repair (MMR) is the mechanism that repairs loops and mismatches between normal nucleotides, arising from errors during replication.
Base excision repair (BER) and types of DNA lesions repaired by BER.
DNA lesions that distort the double helix are usually repaired by nucleotide excision repair (NER). A similar repair pathway works during transcription.
Recombination not only creates new variants during meiosis, it also repairs double-strand breaks (DSBs) during mitosis.

1. Why DNA changes: variation and the damage/repair balance

Where does genetic variation come from? Usually from mutations in the DNA. Why does our species need so much variation? (Student: sexual reproduction.)
If we were all clones, a single virus or disease could kill us all and the species would be eradicated. Variation helps evolution.
Bacteria are clones and survive by numbers (millions of them). Sexual reproduction introduces variation between individuals, so smaller populations can survive.
Variation is possible because DNA is an unstable molecule, prone to change. But too much change is lethal.
So there must be a balance between damage and repair: the balance determines how many new variants are created (“not too much, not too little”).
Questions for the lecture: why does DNA change, what damages it, what lesions result, and what mechanisms repair them.
[Notes] Mutation as event vs outcome; most mutations are neutral, so “DNA variant” is preferred, while variants with an altered phenotype are still called mutations. The great majority of DNA changes arise from endogenous sources (errors in chromosome segregation, recombination, replication and repair, plus spontaneous chemical damage), only occasionally from radiation and environmental chemicals.

2. Sources of DNA damage
DNA is relatively stable but under constant attack, physical and chemical, endogenous and exogenous (“You have in the notes this diagram”: [Notes] Figure 3, see the PDF).

























SourceLecturer’s examplesIntrinsicInstability of DNA itself; DNA replication: polymerases have proofreading but still leave mistakes. Replication is the main source of new changes.Chemical, endogenousCell respiration: oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria releases reactive oxygen species (ROS), which react with DNA. “The fact that your cells have to breathe… damages the DNA.”Chemical, exogenousSmoking (attacks DNA in lung cells); toxins in the dietPhysicalCosmic rays (mostly filtered by the atmosphere); ionizing radiation (X-rays); UV radiation (skin cells, sun exposure)

Radiotherapy kills tumour cells because ionizing radiation damages their DNA. We are all exposed to some ionizing radiation.
[Notes] Polymerase proofreading: an intrinsic 3’ to 5’ exonuclease removes the wrong nucleotide and a short stretch before it; if the mispair escapes, MMR is activated. About 20,000 to 100,000 lesions arise each day in the DNA of each nucleated cell, mostly spontaneously.
[Notes] Third endogenous type not mentioned in the recording: aberrant DNA methylation by S-adenosylmethionine (SAM); about 300 to 600 adenosines per cell per day become 3-methyladenosine, a cytotoxic base that distorts the helix.

3. Types of DNA lesion

Mismatches: e.g. an A on one strand opposite a C instead of a T. The bases do not hydrogen-bond properly, so the helix bulges; replication and transcription cannot work across it. Typical result of replication errors (the polymerase put in the wrong base and proofreading missed it). [verify] The transcript has a student asking “since they are both purines, do they still make hydrogen bonds?”; A and C are not both purines, so the question is garbled.
Base modifications: a base chemically altered by radiation or a chemical agent.
Adducts and cross-links: bulkier lesions that distort the topology of the helix, e.g. pyrimidine dimers.
Abasic sites: a position where the base has been removed.
Strand breaks: single-strand or double-strand.
[Notes] Figure 4: four classes of chemical damage: strand breakage, base deletion, base modification, base cross-linking (intrastrand or interstrand). Cisplatin (anticancer) makes interstrand cross-links between guanines; alkylating agents cause cross-linking, which is why they are used in chemotherapy.

4. What the cell does with damage

Cells have a sensing mechanism: when a lesion is detected during the cell cycle, the cycle stops (checkpoints) to let repair work; once repaired, the cycle continues. (Checkpoints, apoptosis and p53 already studied: see TBL 7.1.)
If repair is not correct, the cell should commit apoptosis.
If mutations prevent apoptosis and the cell keeps cycling while accumulating DNA damage, the usual result is cancer. Most cancer cells arise from some form of genomic instability: they acquired damage, did not repair it, and did not commit suicide.
[Lucía] Same sequence: checkpoints, repair, or apoptosis; surviving damaged cells propagate mutations and give tumours.

5. Chemistry of the damage
Figure on the slide: one DNA strand (phosphate, sugar, base) with the susceptible sites ([Notes] Figure 5). The sugar and several positions on the bases can be attacked.



































TypeMechanismResultHydrolytic: depurination / depyrimidinationWater breaks the bond between sugar and base (spontaneous; DNA is in aqueous solution)Abasic site (gap where a base should be)Hydrolytic: deaminationAn amino group (NH2) is removedCytosine to uracil (uracil belongs in RNA, not DNA); adenine to hypoxanthineOxidativeROS from oxidative phosphorylation (superoxide, peroxide, hydroxyl) oxidize basese.g. 8-oxoguanine, an abnormal nucleotide that must be repairedAdductBenzo(a)pyrene (tobacco smoke) bonds to a baseLarge group that completely distorts the helix; powerful mutagen; lung cancerUV cross-linkTwo adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand become covalently linked (cyclobutane structure)Pyrimidine dimer in skin cells; why doctors advise sunscreen

Lecturer on UV: “Far ultraviolet is more dangerous.” [verify] No vault source mentions UV subtypes.
[Notes] Each day every nucleated cell loses 5,000 or more purines and about 300 pyrimidines by hydrolysis (depurination is particularly common), and 100 to 500 cytosines become uracil. Hypoxanthine pairs with C (behaves like G); uracil pairs with A.
[Notes] 8-oxoguanine (7,8-dihydro-8-oxoguanine) pairs with adenine, so it is highly mutagenic. Thymidine glycol is not a mutagen but blocks DNA polymerase. ROS attack especially purines, and also sugars (strand breaks). Benzo(a)pyrene bonds to N7 of guanine. Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (carbons 4 and 5 of adjacent pyrimidines linked) are the most prevalent UV damage.
[Lucía] O6-methylguanine (from alkylating agents in the diet or toxic substances) pairs with thymine instead of cytosine.

Why C to T changes are the most frequent

[Slides] Figure: 5-methylcytosine (5-meC) is deaminated to thymine (T) (labels only; see the slide).
[Notes] Deamination of cytosine gives uracil, which is recognized as foreign (uracil DNA glycosylase, BER). But many cytosines are methylated at carbon 5, and deamination of 5-methylcytosine gives thymine, a normal DNA base. The resulting T-G mismatch often escapes detection; at the next replication T pairs with A, producing a C to T mutation. So C to T substitutions are the most frequent single-nucleotide change in our DNA. The main source of mismatches is still polymerase error during replication.

6. Replication slippage at microsatellites

Example: a CA microsatellite (CACACA on one strand, TGTGTG on the other).
During replication the polymerase copies the template strand; in the repeat region the newly made strand, not yet stable, can slip back, form a loop, and replication continues. The result is a longer tract of CA repeats. “That’s how these CACACA repeats grow, changing number.”
These insertion loops or deletion loops are lesions and must be repaired.
Summary from the lecturer: replication is the main source of DNA damage, through single-nucleotide mismatches and loops when replication fails.
[Notes] Figure 7: looping of the growing strand gives an insertion (e.g. (CA)12 to (CA)13); looping of the template strand gives a deletion ((CA)11). These errors are often repaired by MMR.
[Lucía] Slippage happens specifically during the formation of Okazaki fragments, leaving a protruding loop.

7. Lesion to repair pathway
“The name says it all.” These pathways cover most DNA lesions.

























LesionPathwayMismatches, insertion/deletion loops (replication errors, slippage)Mismatch repair (MMR)Modified bases, abasic sitesBase excision repair (BER)Pyrimidine dimers, bulky adducts (helix-distorting)Nucleotide excision repair (NER)Double-strand breaksDouble-strand break repair (NHEJ or HRR)

[Notes] Table 1 adds: transcription-coupled repair (TCR) for helix-distorting lesions that stall RNA polymerase (similar to NER, different detection, uses CSA and CSB). NHEJ does not need a template and is available throughout the cell cycle but is less accurate; HR-mediated repair is accurate but needs an intact homologous strand (post-replication, S phase or occasionally G2).
[Notes] Direct reversal of damage is rare in human cells: O-6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase reverses methylation of guanine at O6; DNA ligase seals nicks.

8. Mismatch repair (MMR)
Recorded

Carried out by complexes from two protein families: MutS and MutL. “h” = human (hMutS, hMutL).
Also found in bacteria, where they were discovered; the names come from bacteria.
MutS comes in two versions, alpha and beta; they are dimers (transcript garbled; [Notes] confirms protein dimers).
The recording ends here.

Not recorded: from [Notes] and [Lucía]

[Notes] Three types of protein dimer do most of the work (Figure 8A):


























DimerSubunitsFunctionhMutSαMSH2 + MSH6Recognizes base-base mismatches and single-nucleotide insertions/deletionshMutSβMSH2 + MSH3Recognizes short insertions/deletions from replication slippagehMutLαMLH1 + PMS2Forms a complex with MutS and DNA; PMS2 is the nicking endonuclease

[Notes] Strand discrimination: MMR must repair the new (wrong) strand, not the template. Freshly replicated strands carry nicks not yet sealed by ligase; a nearby nick identifies the new strand.
[Notes] Steps: MutSα or MutSβ recognizes the mismatch (MutS acts as a sliding clamp that scans the DNA); MLH1-PMS2 binds; Pol δ, RPA, PCNA and RFC activate PMS2 to nick the new strand on the 3’ side of the error; EXO1 digests that strand 5’ to 3’, producing a gap containing the mismatch; RPA stabilizes the single strand; Pol δ (with PCNA and RFC) resynthesizes; ligase I seals. MMR can also occur without EXO1 (less understood).
[Notes] Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer), “discussed next year”: germ-line mutation in one allele of an MMR gene (mostly MLH1, MSH2 or MSH6); when a somatic cell loses the other allele, MMR fails, mismatches accumulate and the cell shows microsatellite instability (MSI).
[Lucía] Describes the complex as a tetramer: the hMLH1-hPMS2 dimer binds either hMSH2-hMSH6 or hMSH2-hMSH3. She attributes replication mismatches to insertion of wrong tautomeric forms of the bases.

9. Base excision repair (BER) (not recorded: from [Notes] and [Lucía])

[Notes] For a single base that is modified or has been lost by hydrolysis (abasic site; about 20,000 such events per nucleated cell per day). Removes the base, not the whole nucleotide ([Lucía]).
[Notes] Steps (Figure 9A):

A specific DNA glycosylase cleaves the sugar-base bond, removing the modified base and leaving an abasic site. Different glycosylases for different bases (e.g. uracil DNA glycosylase, 8-oxoguanine DNA glycosylase, N-methylpurine DNA glycosylase).
At any abasic site, the remaining sugar-phosphate is removed by a dedicated endonuclease and phosphodiesterase.
DNA polymerase inserts the correct nucleotide (template = undamaged strand).
DNA ligase seals the nick.


[Notes] Occasionally a long-patch repair replaces more than one base.

10. Nucleotide excision repair (NER) and transcription-coupled repair (TCR) (not recorded: from [Notes] and [Lucía])

[Notes] For bulky, helix-distorting lesions (adducts, pyrimidine dimers). The lesion is on one strand, so the other strand is the template.
[Notes] Steps (Figure 9B, Figure 10):

Damage sensing: XPC-Rad23B recognizes the distortion; DDB1 and DDB2 (DDB2 = XPE) recognize some UV damage; XPA also has a role in recognition, not fully understood.
TFIIH (includes XPB and XPD) unwinds the helix, opening 25 to 35 nucleotides, stabilized by RPA.
Nucleases XPF (5’ incision) and XPG (3’ incision) cut on either side.
The single-stranded fragment of about 30 nucleotides is removed and degraded.
DNA polymerase (epsilon/delta) fills the gap; ligase 1 seals.


[Lucía] Same steps: XPC with XPA recognize the damage; RPA binds one strand; XPF and XPG cut; oligonucleotide of about 30 nt.
TCR [Notes]: priority is to repair bulky lesions in actively transcribed DNA. Starts when RNA polymerase stalls at a lesion: the stalled polymerase is the recognition signal, so XPC and DDB are not needed; CSA and CSB are used instead of XPC-Rad23B. Otherwise the global-genome NER pathway is used.
[Notes] Failure of NER: hypersensitivity to sunlight and cancer predisposition, e.g. xeroderma pigmentosum (XPA, XPB, XPC…). Failure of TCR (CSA or CSB mutations): Cockayne syndrome (short stature, premature ageing, eye disorders, photosensitivity).
Ligase in NER (recorded, end-of-class question): see section 13.

11. Xeroderma pigmentosum (recorded)

Name: Greek xero = dry, derma = skin (the class worked it out); pigmentosum (Latin) = pigmented, with colour.
Slide photo: a girl with the disease after only a few minutes of sun exposure.
She has a mutation in one of the genes for the XP proteins, so NER does not work correctly (mutation in XPA or XPC, per the lecturer).
A few minutes of sun cause serious damage in her skin cells; many of these lesions are pre-tumoural.
Normally sun exposure does nothing to us because our NER pathway works; a defect leads to serious genetic disease.
The gene names come from the disease: patients were studied, the mutated gene was called XPA; patients with a mutation in a different gene gave the next name, and so on. [verify] Transcript: “they called it XPE or FPC, XPA”; which letter he named is unclear.

12. Double-strand break (DSB) repair (recorded)

DSBs are “terrible”: the cell may commit suicide.
Caused mostly by ionizing radiation; sometimes by oxidative damage.
A physiological process starts with a DSB: meiosis, where SPO11 creates DSBs to start homologous recombination (see Lec 7.2 Meiosis). Here the DSBs are not physiological: created by radiation in somatic cells (skin, liver…), not gametes.
[Notes] DSBs also occur naturally in developing B and T cells (rearrangements for immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor diversity) ([Lucía] same). Unrepaired DSBs can inactivate genes or cause chromosome rearrangements; incomplete repair usually triggers apoptosis.
Two ways to repair: the easy way (NHEJ) and the more complex way (HRR).

Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)

Just join the two ends back together, without a homologous template.
Not accurate: a few nucleotides are usually lost when the break forms, so the joined sequence has a small deletion. “Good enough, but not perfect”; at least the DSB, which is very bad for the cell, is removed.
Proteins (lecturer): the MNR complex (“you remember MNR from homologous recombination”); the Ku80/Ku70 proteins bind the free ends and recruit the catalytic subunit of DNA-PK (a kinase); this consumes energy, involves phosphorylation, and brings the ends together; the ends are then sealed by a ligase.
[check] MNR in NHEJ: the lecturer names it; [Notes] Figure 11 lists only Ku70/80, DNA-PKcs, polymerases μ and λ and the ligase IV complex, and [Notes] describe MNR (MRE11, NBS1, RAD50) only in meiotic recombination.
[Notes] Ku70/80 heterodimer recognizes and stabilizes the ends; DNA-PKcs processes them; polymerases μ and λ resynthesize as needed; ligase IV complex (ligase IV, XRCC4, XLF) ligates. The transcript’s “ligates forum of the totium” is presumably this ligase IV complex.
[Notes] NHEJ is in principle always available, but most important in quiescent differentiated cells and in G1 before replication. Hallmark: small deletions (sometimes insertions) at the breakpoint. NHEJ causes small-scale indels, not large SVs, except when a stalled replication fork gives a single-ended DSB that is joined to another broken end: this can produce translocations and other major structural variants.

Homologous recombination repair (HRR)

Needs an available homologous double strand as template. In somatic (mitotic) cells this exists after S phase, once DNA has replicated.
Same process as homologous recombination in meiosis; some proteins differ. MNR digests one strand leaving overhangs; the overhang invades the homologous double strand; new DNA is synthesized; a double Holliday junction forms and is resolved; the result is a perfectly repaired double strand.
Much more accurate than NHEJ, but requires a homologous template.
Resolution differs: in meiosis it usually gives recombinants; in repair the proteins of the final steps favour non-recombinant products, because the goal is repair, not recombination.
[Notes] The template is the undamaged sister chromatid; HRR works after replication and before mitosis (particularly S phase), and is very important in early embryogenesis. Cells deficient in HRR show excess sister-chromatid exchanges in mitosis.
[Lucía] KU80, KU70 and DNA-PKcs bring the strands together for NHEJ; HRR uses the meiotic recombination machinery, one strand used as template to repair the other.

HR (meiosis) vs HRR (mitosis)

13. Question at the end of class

Student: is there a DNA ligase at the end of NER? Yes: “at the end it’s always ligase”. DNA polymerase (delta/epsilon) fills the gap; after the last nucleotide is added a nick remains, which ligase seals. He did not think the ligase step was shown on the slide.
[verify] Which ligase: transcript “the same [ligase] as one that is used during the formation…“. [Notes]: ligase 1 in NER and in MMR.

Exam flags from the lecturer

No explicit “this will be in the exam” in the recording.
Marked as “very important”: the RNA polymerase’s ability to identify the start of transcription (the promoter). Also stressed as important: detecting termination signals.
Question asked in class: why RNA polymerases do not need proofreading while DNA polymerases do (answer in section 3). Typical reasoning question.
Strand nomenclature (template vs non-template/coding strand) and promoter numbering (+1, -1, upstream/downstream): he called these conventions and explained them carefully.

1. Transcription and the types of RNA

DNA is the repository of genetic information; it replicates (Lec 7.3), but its information must be expressed. The first step is transcription: DNA serves as template for the synthesis of RNA. mRNAs are then the template for translation. Part of the central dogma of molecular biology.


























RNA classLecturermRNA (messenger)Polynucleotides carrying the information for protein synthesistRNA (transfer)Short molecules with a characteristic secondary structure; intermediary between mRNA and the translation machineryrRNA (ribosomal)Structural and functional components of the ribosomal subunits; participate in protein synthesisncRNA (non-coding)Growing family of different lengths: small ncRNAs (< 200 nucleotides) and long ncRNAs (> 200 nucleotides)

Transcriptome: the whole collection of RNA molecules present in a cell (or tissue) under specific conditions, at a given time. [Slides] “The complement of RNA molecules produced in a cell under specific conditions”.

2. Non-coding RNAs and “junk DNA”

Only about 3% of the nuclear genome is coding. Until recently most of the genome was thought never to be expressed: “junk DNA”.
About 10-15 years ago, better transcriptome techniques showed that about 80% of the genome is expressed (transcribed into RNA), but most of these RNAs are not mRNA, rRNA or tRNA: they are non-coding RNAs.
[Lucía] Less than 3% of the genome are coding genes; 80% corresponds to non-coding genes transcribed into RNA but not translated.
Functions: key roles in the control of gene expression, at several levels:

gene transcription at the level of chromatin;
interaction with the translational machinery (control of protein synthesis);
mRNA turnover (inducing degradation or stabilizing).


Many functions are still uncharacterized. They have physiological roles (cell-specific expression, responses to extracellular signals).
Disease: deregulated (altered) ncRNA expression is involved in disease, including cancer. They can serve as biomarkers (changing levels may signal a pathological process).
[Lucía] They are starting to be used as new pharmacological targets.

3. RNA synthesis: the reaction

A polymerization reaction catalyzed by RNA polymerases.
[Slides] DNA template + n(NTP) → pppN(pN)n + (n-1) PPi + DNA template; NTPs = ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP.


































FeatureDetailTemplateRequired: RNA polymerases cannot make RNA without a DNA template. The template is unchangedSubstratesNucleoside triphosphatesBy-productPyrophosphate (PPi) released for each nucleotide addedDirection5’ to 3’ (of the new RNA)DNAMust be locally denatured (strands separated) to expose the templateWhich strandFor different genes, either strand can serve as template

[Lucía] The DNA template is read 3’ to 5’.

Catalytic mechanism (same as DNA polymerases)

Catalytic pocket with two Mg2+ ions coordinated by aspartate residues.
The incoming NTP is selected by Watson-Crick base pairing with the template.
The 3’-OH of the last nucleotide in the chain is ionized and makes a nucleophilic attack on the alpha phosphate of the incoming NTP (phosphates named alpha, beta, gamma from the one attached to C5’).
The alpha-beta phosphoanhydride bond breaks; PPi is released and a new phosphodiester bond forms.


Role of the two Mg2+ (lecturer): one assists the nucleophilic attack; the other helps break the anhydride bond between the alpha and beta phosphates.
[check] Lucía: one Mg2+ “helps in the nucleophilic attack and the breakage of the phospho bond”, the other “helps in the removal of the PPi”. The lecturer assigned bond breakage to the second ion. Slides show it only as a figure (see the slide).
Thermodynamics: favourable, partly because the released PPi is degraded by pyrophosphatases; removing a product pushes the reaction forward.
Mechanism worked out first in bacteria (E. coli) but well conserved up to mammals.

Functions of RNA polymerase



































#FunctionNotes1Identify the DNA sequence marking the start of transcription”Very important”; transcription cannot start anywhere in the genome2Separate the two DNA strands to expose the template3Select the correct nucleotide and catalyze bond formation, 5’ to 3’, processivelyProcessive: once bound, does not detach until the transcript is complete (same concept as DNA polymerases)4Detect termination signalsTranscription cannot go on indefinitely5Interact with regulatory proteinsModulate recruitment, speed and termination. [Slides] “activating and repressing proteins that modulate transcription’s speed”
Why no proofreading? (question asked in class)

Unlike DNA polymerases, RNA polymerases have no well-recognized proofreading activity ([Slides]: “does not have proofreading activity”).
Reason (student’s answer, confirmed by the lecturer):

An error in DNA synthesis risks a permanent mutation.
An expressed gene is transcribed into many copies of RNA; one wrong mRNA gives a wrong product that is “one among millions”.
Faulty RNAs may also be less stable and degraded faster.
So the impact on cell function is small.



4. Prokaryotic RNA polymerase

Bacteria have a single RNA polymerase that makes mRNA, rRNA and tRNA. Multi-subunit complex.
[Slides] Molecular weight about 390 kD.


























SubunitRole (lecturer)betaCatalytic: carries out the polymerization reactionbeta primeImportant for DNA bindingalphaInteracts with regulatory proteins that help initiationsigmaFamily of proteins essential for promoter recognition

[Lucía] beta subunits also interact with the template and carry out elongation.

5. Gene structure, nomenclature and the three steps

Three sequential steps (as in DNA synthesis): initiation (binding, identification of the start site at the promoter), elongation (synthesis), termination (end of gene or regulators mark the end).

Numbering and orientation (conventions)

+1: first transcribed nucleotide (transcription start site). Transcribed region: +1, +2, +3…
Promoter: the nucleotide just before +1 is -1; then -2, -3… All promoter positions are negative.
Promoter region = upstream = 5’ region. Transcribed (coding) region = downstream = 3’ region.
Termination signals at the other end of the gene.

Template vs coding strand




















StrandAlso calledRelation to the RNATemplate strandComplementary to the RNANon-template strandCoding strandSame sequence as the RNA, with T instead of U

Why “coding” for the strand that is not copied: seen from the RNA, the RNA has the same sequence (“code”) as the non-template strand. A convention; “may be counterintuitive”.

6. Prokaryotic transcription step by step
6.1 Initiation

RNA polymerase recognizes the promoter (the sigma subunit is key) and binds: closed complex.
Structural changes open the double helix: the transcription bubble (template exposed). [Lucía] This is the open complex.
First nucleotides are incorporated; the polymerase starts moving into the coding sequence.
Once the promoter is recognized and the polymerase enters the coding sequence, sigma dissociates (no longer needed).

6.2 The bacterial promoter (consensus sequence)

Consensus = prototype obtained by comparing the promoters of many bacterial genes and keeping the conserved features.


































Region (moving upstream from +1)Lecturer+1Transcription start siteAbout 6-8 nucleotides just upstream of +1Not conserved-10 region = Pribnow box (around -9/-10)Conserved; rich in T and ASpacerNot conserved between genes. [verify] length garbled (“60 to 18 nucleotides”); see the slide-35 boxConservedUP elementFurther upstream; present in some genes only. [verify] distance garbled (“several hundreds of thousands of nucleotides”); check the slide

RNA polymerase binds over a region of about 70-100 nucleotides, mainly over the Pribnow box and the -35 box.
Experiments: artificial genes in which the distance between the -35 box and the Pribnow box, or between the boxes and the start site, was lengthened or shortened: transcription no longer started correctly. This shows the structure is meaningful.
The boxes are asymmetric, so they orient the polymerase: it cannot bind backwards and transcribe in the wrong direction. They tell the polymerase where to bind and in which orientation.
[Lucía] The UP element also shows similarities between genes; the conserved sequences are recognized by RNA polymerase and help position it in the right orientation.

6.3 Elongation

Sigma has dissociated; the core enzyme moves along the coding region.
The transcription bubble moves with the polymerase.
The newly made RNA stays temporarily base-paired with the template: RNA-DNA hybrid of about 8 base pairs.
Opening the helix and moving along it creates supercoiling ahead and behind (lecturer’s analogy: a twisted telephone cord that coils elsewhere to release tension). Released by topoisomerases (as in DNA replication).

6.4 Termination: two mechanisms

























Rho-independentRho-dependentNeedsSequence features of the gene onlyThe protein RhoSignalTemplate region rich in adenines at the end of the gene, so uracils go into the RNA; the RNA also has self-complementary sequences that fold into a hairpinRho binds specific sequences in the new RNAHow it destabilizesA-U pairs (2 hydrogen bonds) are weaker than G-C (3); the hairpin, bound by a protein, plus the weak A-U hybrid, weaken the polymerase-template interaction; the RNA detachesRho is a hexamer (6 subunits) forming a ring around the RNA; ATPase activity powers its movement along the RNA (“like climbing a rope”) until it collides with RNA polymerase and destabilizes it from the template

[verify] The name of the protein that binds the hairpin is garbled (“Moose A” / “loose A”); check the slide figure.
[verify] The RNA sequences Rho recognizes are garbled (“in C’s and A’s”); check the slide.
[Lucía] In the rho-independent mechanism, G- and C-rich sequences form the hairpin, followed by the adenine-rich region. (The lecturer explained the hairpin by self-complementarity and did not mention G/C content.)

7. Lecturer’s analogies and remarks

Telephone cord for supercoiling (section 6.3).
Rho “climbing a rope” (section 6.4).
Junk DNA story: a decade of transcriptome research overturned the idea that most of the genome is never expressed.

8. [Slides] Part II: transcription in eukaryotes and RNA processing (not in this recording)
Everything in this section is from the slides unless marked [Lucía]. Figures did not come through in the PDF text: see the slides.
8.1 Fundamental differences with prokaryotes





























#Difference1In eukaryotes, transcription and translation take place in separate subcellular compartments2In eukaryotes, DNA is tightly associated with proteins forming chromatin3In prokaryotes there is no post-transcriptional processing of mRNA, while tRNAs and rRNAs are processed in both types of cells4Eukaryotic nuclear genes are transcribed by three RNA polymerases; additional ones in mitochondria (and chloroplasts in plants)5Eukaryotic polymerases do not contact DNA directly: they need transcription factors

[Lucía] In prokaryotes (no nucleus) transcription and translation can be almost simultaneous; in eukaryotes RNAs mature in the nucleus before export, which adds regulatory points.
[check] Lucía writes that in prokaryotes “there are no post transcriptional processes for RNA”. The slides limit this to mRNA: tRNAs and rRNAs are processed in both.

8.2 The three eukaryotic RNA polymerases

























PolymeraseGene classProducts ([Slides])RNA Pol IClass ILarge pre-rRNA, giving 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNAsRNA Pol IIClass IImRNAs and most snRNAsRNA Pol IIIClass IIItRNAs, 5S rRNA

[check] Lucía lists Pol II as making “most sncRNAs” and Pol III “5’-rRNA”. The slides say snRNAs and 5S rRNA.

8.3 RNA Pol II: transcription factors and initiation

Requires general transcription factors (GTFs) common to all genes, plus gene-specific factors: activators (trans-activators) and coactivators.
Eukaryotic promoter with a core promoter (see slide).
[Lucía] Many genes have a TATA box around -30 (not all genes); regulatory sequences lie further upstream. Expression of each gene depends on which factors (activated by hormones and signals) bind its regulatory regions. Chromatin must be relaxed for transcription.
Initiation: sequential binding of GTFs and RNA Pol II to the promoter, starting with TFIID and/or TFIIA. The pre-initiation complex (PIC) has 60-70 proteins, about 3 MDa.






























FactorRole ([Slides])TFIIDInteracts with positive and negative regulatory proteinsTFIIBBinds TBP and recruits the RNA Pol-TFIIF complexTFIIFBinds RNA Pol and TFIIB; prevents binding of RNA Pol to non-specific DNATFIIEHelicase activity (as listed on the slide)TFIIHHelicase activity; kinase activity on the RNA Pol CTD

[Lucía] TBP = TATA box binding protein. Phosphorylation of the CTD (carboxyl-terminal domain) causes a conformational change that activates the polymerase. Initiation is the most regulated phase, the main control point.
Slides then show formation of the PIC, initiation and elongation by Pol II, and termination for Pol I, II and III: figures only, see the slides.

8.4 RNA processing

In both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, RNAs are chemically modified to reach their mature, functional forms. Reactions: nucleotide elimination, modification of nucleobases, nucleotide addition, splicing.

8.5 mRNA processing in eukaryotes

About 3/4 of mRNA primary transcripts are eliminated during maturation in the nucleus.
Three steps: 1. cap synthesis, 2. intron splicing, 3. polyadenylation.


























Step[Slides][Lucía] additions5’ capProtects mRNA from 5’ exonucleases; participates in nucleus-to-cytoplasm transport; anchors mRNA to the ribosomeAdded by the cap-synthesizing complex; stabilizes the strandSplicing90% of pre-mRNA is introns; average exon 100-200 nt; introns up to 20 kb. Done by the spliceosome: snRNPs, about 150 proteins and 5 snRNAsSpliceosome breaks phosphodiester bonds and forms new ones between exons. 8.6 Alternative splicing

Alternative patterns of intron removal give several mRNAs from one gene, encoding different proteins with potentially different functions.
Expands the information in the genome (protein variants) and adds regulatory possibilities.
Affects most human genes.
Mutations or altered expression of splicing regulatory factors can contribute to disease.
