Lec 8.2 Regulation of gene expression
Sources

8.3 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file only. The file name follows Lucía’s numbering (her “Lecture 8.3”); the official code is Lec 8.2 (code log). The class notes also head this section “Lec 8.3”.
It opens with “you have had a lecture about DNA transcription” and ends with “remember this for tomorrow… which is epigenetics”, so it looks complete. He mentions it was his fourth hour of teaching that day and he was losing his voice.
Coverage: all sections come from the transcript. Gaps filled from the Genetics class notes and Lucía.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault (the Unit 8 slides folder has 8.1, 8.4, 8.5, 8.6 and 8.8 only). Figures he describes (cis/trans diagram, PAX6 locus, TAD disruption, microRNA processing, sponge) are reproduced in the class notes as Figures 1, 4, 6, 7, 8.
Study material: none for this lecture in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “Lec 8.3. Regulation of gene expression” (Box 1, Box 2, Figures 1 to 8, Table 1).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 8.3. Regulation of gene expression”, PDF p. 232-235.
Related notes: Lec 8.1 DNA transcription (promoters, transcription factors), Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging (loops, TADs, CTCF, cohesin), Lec 7.6 Protein-coding and non-coding genes (microRNAs, lncRNAs, pseudogenes), Lec 8.3 Epigenetics (histone modifications, next lecture).

Marking: [Slides] = from the slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

No explicit exam statements in the recording.
“The first idea that you should understand” is the cis vs trans distinction (section 2).
His summary of the lecture: regulation has many layers (core promoter, enhancers, chromatin opening, loops and TADs, then microRNAs destroying mRNAs and ceRNAs “destroying the destroyers”) because expression must be kept within very narrow limits (section 9).
“Remember this for tomorrow”: lncRNAs recruiting chromatin-modifying complexes leads into Lec 8.3 Epigenetics.

1. Why gene expression must be regulated

Humans and other mammals and birds have a very complex system for regulating gene expression, first because we are multicellular with different tissues.
A neuron is a neuron and not a skin cell because, from the same genome, different sets of genes have been activated or repressed; that leads to differentiation.
In the embryo (from one cell to all tissues), at specific times (e.g. day 21) and in specific parts, some genes are turned on and others off. The same happens in the stem cells of adult organs.
Main sequences regulating expression: promoters. But chromatin is tightly packed and transcription factors need access, so chromatin configuration also influences expression.
Plan of the lecture: opening and closing chromatin (histone acetylation); enhancers, which give tissue-specific and time-specific expression (promoters are usually general); the chromatin conformation needed for enhancer-promoter contact; newer mechanisms: microRNAs (“a Nobel Prize about two or three years ago”) and long non-coding RNAs (“probably a Nobel Prize in five to ten years”).
[Notes] Radio metaphor: the basal transcription apparatus is the ON switch (ubiquitous factors on the core promoter); additional circuits act as the volume control (non-ubiquitous factors on other cis elements, co-activators and co-repressors, lncRNAs and microRNAs). Post-transcriptional control and chromatin domains also matter.

2. Cis vs trans regulation

Terms borrowed from chemistry (cis and trans configurations of molecules).
Cis: the regulatory element is on the same DNA molecule as the gene it regulates. Example: genes A and B with their promoters, and a long-distance element (e.g. an enhancer) on the same DNA that interacts with the promoter.
Trans: the regulator comes from a different molecule, e.g. a gene on another chromosome. Example (anticipating microRNAs): another gene makes an RNA that binds the mRNA of gene A and destroys it, so no protein is made. It regulates A not at the promoter but by breaking down its mRNA.
Transcription factors are also trans-regulatory elements: proteins made elsewhere that bind specific DNA sequences.
[Notes] Box 1: a cis-acting DNA element acts only on the DNA molecule it sits on (the promoter of the paternal insulin gene on chromosome 11 regulates only the paternal allele). A cis-acting RNA sequence regulates the transcript it is on (often in UTRs). A trans-acting regulator (protein or RNA) diffuses and regulates both alleles of distant genes, often many genes. Transcription factors, lncRNAs and microRNAs are encoded away from their targets, so they are trans-acting.

3. The core promoter (recap of transcription)

The transcription start site (TSS) marks the beginning of the first exon. Upstream is the core promoter, about 100 to 200 nucleotides, where RNA polymerase II and a whole complex of proteins (transcription factors) bind.
TATA box, bound by TATA-box binding protein (TBP).
Another regulatory element whose name is garbled in the transcript (“brain, whatever”). [verify] Possibly the BRE: [Notes] Figure 2 lists BRE, TATA box, Inr and DPE as core promoter elements.
GC box: very rich in G and C, usually about 100 nucleotides upstream of the TSS; bound by the transcription factor SP1.
These sequences bound by transcription factors make up the core promoter: “this is what really turns on this gene”.
Covered in detail in the transcription lecture by Dr. “Matthias Avila” (transcript spelling). [verify] name.
Transcription factor families: some bind the double helix through a motif garbled in the transcript; others are leucine zippers (“like zippers, with many leucines”). [Notes] Figure 5: zinc fingers and leucine zippers; a factor recognizes a short sequence of 4 to 9 nucleotides; only a tiny fraction of potential binding sites are used, because the site must be accessible and binding is combinatorial.
[Lucía] TBP binds the TATA box, SP1 binds GC boxes; when the factors assemble, RNA polymerase is phosphorylated, binds and initiates transcription.

4. Enhancers and the mediator complex

New point: long-distance regulation. Far upstream (kilobases or even megabases away) are enhancers, which bind transcription factors.
The mediator complex (“the name says it all”: it brings two things together) binds the transcription factors on the enhancer and those on the promoter: protein-protein interactions.
Often the core promoter alone is not enough: it is “ready, waiting for the final push”. The push comes when the enhancer binds its transcription factors, recruits mediator, and the final configuration triggers expression.
Problem: an enhancer up to a million nucleotides away can only reach the promoter if chromatin forms loops (cohesin, see Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging).
[Notes] Enhancers amplify transcription, silencers repress it; both are often far from the promoter, even inside introns of the same or other genes. The intervening DNA must loop out (Figure 4B). Boundary elements (insulators) block inappropriate enhancer-promoter interactions; CTCF acts as insulator at loop domains and TADs.
[Lucía] Enhancers about 100 kb upstream; activators bound to enhancers form enhanceosomes, which bend DNA by looping and interact with co-activators such as HATs; contact with the promoter through Mediator triggers assembly of RNA polymerase and general transcription factors.

5. Opening chromatin: histone acetylation

For transcription factors to bind, compacted chromatin (nucleosomes, solenoid…) must be opened, relaxed at that point. The most important modification for opening or closing chromatin is histone acetylation.
Histone octamers have N-terminal tails that protrude; they contain several lysines.
Lysine can be acetylated by histone acetylases or deacetylated by histone deacetylases.
Mechanism: DNA is negatively charged, lysines positively charged; the attraction draws DNA and histones of neighbouring nucleosomes together. Acetylation removes the positive charge, releasing the interaction: open chromatin.
Open, relaxed regions = acetylated histones (he mentions “lysine 27”, to be seen in the next lecture); compact regions = deacetylated histones.
“This is the first thing you need”: without access to the DNA there is no way to regulate anything.
[Notes] Chromatin packaging imposes a basic level of repression. Open chromatin regions are detected as DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHS) (DNase I can only cut accessible DNA). Accessible sites include all gene promoters (about 70,000) plus millions of regulatory elements (enhancers, silencers), which explain cell-type-specific expression.
[Lucía] HATs (histone acetyltransferases) and HDACs (histone deacetylases). DHS: 3,000,000 found; very tissue-specific (50% active in one cell line, about 1% (4,000) in all). [check] She gives each DHS as “100-200 Mb” and about 18.7% of the genome devoted to regulation; “Mb” is likely a slip for bp, and the class notes do not give these figures.

6. Example: PAX6 and its remote enhancers

PAX6 is very important for eye formation in humans and most animals (“since octopus” in the transcript [verify]); during development it organizes the whole eye and must be expressed in the eye-forming structures. “I think we have this in the notes.”
PAX6 lies next to ELP4, an unrelated gene with many exons and a long intron.
Inside the long intron of ELP4 are two elements regulating PAX6:

promoter of PAX6 contacts one element: expression specifically in the lens (crystalline);
contacts the other: expression specifically in the retina.


So tissue-specific regulatory elements can be far away, even inside an intron of another gene. Contact needs proteins on the enhancer (transcription factors), the RNA polymerase II complex on the promoter (dozens of factors), and the mediator complex.
[check] The transcript says PAX6 “only has one exon”; [Notes] Figure 4A says PAX6 is drawn as a single box including exons and introns only for clarity (30 kb gene).
[Notes] Figure 4A: about 260 kb region; PAX6 is mutated in aniridia.

7. TADs and CTCF boundaries

Enhancer-promoter contact is possible only if the conformation allows it, e.g. both in the same TAD. Across a boundary the interaction is not possible.
Recall from the chromatin lecture: the TAD boundaries (yellow arrows on the slide) are CTCF binding sites.
Example (slide figure): two TADs, each with a gene and its enhancers; one gene expressed in the kidney, the other in the brain.
If a mutation prevents CTCF binding at the boundary, the two TADs merge into one large TAD; sequences can now interact across it, and a gene can be driven by the other gene’s enhancer: wrong expression (e.g. in the brain).
Promoters and enhancers are fine; only the chromatin conformation is wrong, yet expression changes in important ways.
[Lucía] Same example with brain and liver; flanked TADs do not contact each other; CTCF disruption gives a large TAD where enhancers activate additional genes, with physiological consequences.

8. MicroRNAs: post-transcriptional silencing

Very short RNAs (miRNAs), part of the short non-coding RNA genes (see Lec 7.6 Protein-coding and non-coding genes).
Known first in plants; nobody suspected them in humans until the human genome was sequenced and short genes making non-protein RNAs were found.

Biogenesis

A short gene (single exon) is transcribed into an RNA of about 100 to 150 nucleotides (“100 million parts” in the transcript).
The RNA folds on itself (complementary bases, some mismatches, a bubble) into a hairpin.
In the nucleus, the Drosha complex trims it into the pre-microRNA.
Exported to the cytoplasm, where Dicer (“because it dices”) cuts it further, releasing the loop and leaving a microRNA duplex: two strands, not perfectly complementary but stable.
One strand is degraded; the remaining single strand is the active microRNA.


[Notes] Mature miRNAs are typically 20 to 22 nucleotides; Dicer cleaves asymmetrically leaving overhanging 3’ ends; the degraded strand is the passenger strand, the remaining one the guide strand.

Action

The active miRNA binds the 3’ UTR of target mRNAs (the transcribed region after the stop codon), by partial complementarity: not 100%, but enough bases to bind despite mismatches.
Binding prevents translation or leads to degradation of the mRNA: less protein. MicroRNAs are inhibitory.
One miRNA can act on several genes, and one mRNA can carry sites for several different miRNAs. We have hundreds to thousands of miRNA genes.
Another layer: even with a perfect promoter, if the mRNAs are degraded there is no protein.
[Notes] Pairing of the seed sequence (about the first 8 nucleotides from the 5’ end) is important; mismatches are tolerated elsewhere. Several hundred miRNA genes, often tissue-specific; at least 50% of protein-coding genes are thought to be regulated by miRNAs. Example: PTEN mRNA has binding sites in its 3’ UTR for seven miRNA families.
[Notes] Box 2: related RNA interference (Dicer, siRNA, Argonaute, RISC) protects cells against viruses and transposons. [Lucía] RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex) performs the silencing once the miRNA finds its target.

9. Competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs): “sponges”

Pseudogenes (copies of real genes that do not work) are sometimes transcribed into an mRNA that makes no protein. lncRNAs are transcribed, spliced, exported to the cytoplasm, but not translated.
One function: acting as sponges for microRNAs. A lncRNA may contain short regions perfectly complementary to a miRNA; several miRNA molecules bind it and are removed from the cytoplasm. They can no longer reach their target gene (e.g. insulin), which is then not inactivated and is expressed.
“You have the inhibitor and you have inhibitors of the inhibitor.”
Called ceRNAs: competing (they compete with the mRNAs for miRNA binding) endogenous (made by the cell itself) RNAs.
Summary: gene expression must be regulated within very narrow limits, hence so many layers: core promoter, enhancers, chromatin configuration, then destroying mRNAs and “destroying the destroyers”. Networks refined over millions of years give the right levels of our 20,000 protein-coding genes.
[Notes] Example: PTEN (10q23, a tightly controlled tyrosine phosphatase; aberrant expression common in cancers) is regulated by the processed pseudogene PTENP1 (9p21), whose non-coding RNA keeps many PTEN 3’ UTR miRNA sites and sequesters those miRNAs (Figure 7). ceRNAs include pseudogene RNAs, lncRNAs and circular RNAs (human fibroblasts make more than 25,000 different circular RNAs).
[Lucía] lncRNAs, pseudogenes and circular RNAs (from alternative splicing of exons or from introns) all act as sponges.

10. lncRNAs recruit chromatin-modifying complexes (lead-in to epigenetics)

Another lncRNA function: binding a region of the genome with one domain and, with another domain, binding chromatin-remodelling (chromatin-modifying) complexes.
These complexes are enzymes that add or remove chemical groups on histone tails. Brought to a promoter by the lncRNA, they can add groups that prevent transcription; other modifiers remove them and allow transcription.
Next lecture: all the histone modifications (acetylation already seen) that affect transcription.
[Notes] Long ncRNAs recruit chromatin-modifying complexes to defined loci, often repressive ones, without needing base pairing (Figure 8). Most act in cis; some in trans, e.g. HOTAIR (from the HOXC cluster at 12q13) silences genes in the HOXD cluster on chromosome 2. Table 1 (examples): Airn, Kcnq1ot1 (imprinted domains), Xist (almost all genes on the inactive X, via PRC2 and H3K27me3), HOTAIR (PRC2, LSD1).

Lec 8.3 Epigenetics
Sources

lec 8 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file only. It opens with “lecture 8.3, this is about epigenetics, which I introduced yesterday” and ends with “I’ll give you 15 minutes until the next class”, so it looks complete. The first two sentences are garbled.
Coverage: all sections come from the transcript. Gaps and conflicts checked against the Genetics class notes and Lucía. The figures he describes (CpG lollipop map, methylation cycle, TET pathway, methylation through development, histone maps) are reproduced in the class notes.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault (the Unit 8 slides folder has no epigenetics file). He mentions a learning-goals slide; its content did not come through in the transcript.
Study material: none for this lecture in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “Lec 8.4. Epigenetics: DNA methylation and histone modifications” (class-notes numbering; Box 1, Figures 1 to 6, Table 2).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 8.4. Epigenetics: DNA methylation and histone modifications”, PDF p. 236-238.
Related notes: Lec 8.2 Regulation of gene expression (histone acetylation, enhancers, lncRNAs recruiting chromatin modifiers), Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination (BER, 5-methylcytosine deamination), Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging (euchromatin, heterochromatin), Lec 7.2 Meiosis (gametogenesis).

Marking: [Slides] = from the slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

No explicit exam statements in the recording.
He frames points as ideas to keep: “First idea” (methylation only at CpG, section 2), “Second idea” (CpG distribution and CpG islands, section 3), “another concept that you should keep in mind” (dynamic silencing by CGI methylation, section 3), “this is the first message” (lysines are the modified residues, section 7).
On the histone maps (sections 8 and 9): “You can draw these things at home if you like to do the practice of this.” “It sounds a bit complex, but once you read about it, it will be like second nature to you.”
“You have a table in the notes of the main players”: [Notes] Table 2 (section 9).

1. What epigenetics is

Changes to chromatin that do not change the nucleotide sequence: chemical modifications of the DNA molecule or of the histones that impact gene function while the sequence stays the same.
Two levels: DNA (methylation) and histones (chemical modifications).
[Notes] Epigenetic changes are sometimes the cause of changes in gene expression and sometimes the consequence. Heritable patterns of DNA methylation and histone modification are called epigenetic marks (settings); writers add chemical groups, erasers remove them, readers bind them and recruit other factors.

2. DNA methylation: 5-methylcytosine at CpG

The main epigenetic change in DNA is methylation (adding a methyl group). In humans (unlike bacteria and other species) it takes place on cytosine, at carbon 5: 5-methylcytosine. Very common, with important functional implications.
First idea: cytosines are methylated only when followed by a G on the same strand: the CG dinucleotide, also written CpG (p = phosphate, to show the C and G are on the same strand, linked by a phosphodiester bond). Not the C-G base pair across strands.
Not every CpG is methylated, but any methylated C is in that context.
[Notes] 5-meC still pairs normally with G (the methyl group faces outward). In a somatic cell about 70 to 80% of CG dinucleotides carry a methylated C. Because 5-meC deaminates spontaneously to thymine, CG dinucleotides have been eroded during evolution: expected frequency 4.2%, observed under 1%.
[Lucía] Same: methylation at the C of CpG, carbon 5, by DNA methylases.

3. CpG islands (CGIs)

Second idea: with 3,000 million nucleotides you would expect millions of CpGs by chance. They are distributed more or less uniformly, except in short regions where they are particularly rich: CpG islands.
Old representation: lollipops, one per CpG; empty = unmethylated, solid (here yellow) = methylated. Today methylation can be mapped across the whole genome.
Figure (gene with three exons, E): CpGs uniform except in a short region near the transcription start, the island.
Criteria for a CGI (attributed in the transcript to “Mackay and Jones” [verify] names):






















CriterionValue (lecturer)G+C contentOver 55% (genome average about 42%, given by a student and accepted)CpG frequencyMuch higher than expected by chanceLengthOver 500 bp (transcript “500 days a month”) [verify]

Why CGIs matter: they can be methylated or unmethylated, which changes the functional state of the gene. They usually overlap promoters and behave as the promoter of those genes.

Unmethylated island: gene expressed.
Methylated island (not necessarily all CpGs, about 80%): gene silenced.


About 70% of human genes have a CGI; the other ~30% are regulated by the typical TATA box etc.
Dynamic: methylate to silence, demethylate to re-express. During differentiation (e.g. a liver cell), a gene no longer needed can be silenced by methylation; a gene that must stay active (e.g. in a brain cell) keeps an unmethylated island.
[Notes] Box 1: nearly 30,000 CGIs, often 1 kb or less; about 50% near transcription start sites, a further 25% in gene bodies. Heterochromatin and intergenic regions are highly methylated (pericentromeric hypermethylation matters for genome stability).
[check] Methylation of the island itself: the lecturer says a methylated CGI silences the gene. [Notes] Box 1 says TSS-associated CGIs stay unmethylated even when the gene is not transcribed, and that silencing relates more to CpGs in the CGI “shores” (up to 2 kb from the TSS); only genes permanently repressed in development, or in diseases such as cancer, have heavily methylated CGIs.
[check] Genome GC content: 42% (class) vs 41% ([Notes] Box 1).
[Lucía] Unmethylated CpGs concentrate around the promoter of most genes and act as the promoter (“unmethylated CpG islands”); not all genes are regulated by CGIs.

4. Who methylates: maintenance and de novo

Enzymes: DNA methylases (DNA methyltransferases). There are no DNA demethylases (“we’ve been searching for decades”).
The problem of replication: a fully methylated CpG has methyl-C on both strands (CG on one, CG on the complementary). Replication is semi-conservative; the polymerase inserts ordinary C in the new strand, so each daughter cell gets hemimethylated DNA.
If the cell keeps dividing without remethylation, methylation decreases with each division until very little remains.
DNMT1 (DNA methyltransferase 1): remethylates hemimethylated DNA after replication, restoring full methylation (maintenance).
De novo methyltransferases (“de novo” = from scratch): DNMT3 family (transcript “DNMT3A, B, L”); they methylate DNA that is unmethylated on both strands.
Cycle (“you have this in the notes”): fully methylated, then replication gives hemimethylated, then DNMT1 remethylates; without DNMT1, repeated divisions give unmethylated DNA (passive demethylation, no enzymes involved); DNMT3s methylate it again.
[Notes] Figure 1: DNMT1 is usually at the replication fork and methylates only CGs paired with a methylated CG on the parental strand, so symmetric patterns are transmitted to daughter cells. DNMT3A and DNMT3B are the de novo enzymes, important in epigenetic reprogramming. [verify] “DNMT3L”: not in [Notes] or [Lucía].
[Lucía] DNMT1 keeps strands methylated after division; de novo methylases methylate CpGs not methylated before; both needed.

5. Active demethylation: TET + BER

Passive demethylation takes time (many divisions), but cells sometimes need to demethylate quickly (e.g. to express a gene whose CGI is methylated). No demethylase exists; the pathway was worked out only a few years ago (“this is what you have explained in the notes”).
It relies on two things: oxidation of DNA and base excision repair (BER) (see Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination).
TET enzymes (DNA oxidases specialized in oxidizing methylated C) act in three successive oxidation steps:






























StepProductStart5-methylcytosine (made by DNMT1 or de novo methylases)1st oxidation (TET)5-hydroxymethylcytosine2nd oxidation (TET)5-formylcytosine3rd oxidation (TET)5-carboxylcytosineBERFormyl and carboxyl forms recognized as abnormal, removed, replaced by a normal unmethylated C

He compares the BER recognition to the uracil DNA glycosylase (UDG) from the DNA repair lecture.
This solved the puzzle of how cells demethylate quickly.
[Notes] TET = ten-eleven translocation family; the 5-carboxy-cytosine is excised by thymine-DNA glycosylase (a BER enzyme); Figure 2 also shows α-ketoglutarate.
[Lucía] “There is no active demethylase, but there is an active demethylation pathway”: the modified C becomes so different that the cell replaces it by BER.

6. Methylation through development
Figure: DNA methylation levels from oocyte and zygote to adult ([Notes] Figure 3).

In the zygote, the paternal and maternal genomes have different methylation levels.
First wave of demethylation in the very early embryo: one parental genome is demethylated passively by cell division, the other very fast (actively). [verify] The transcript says “maternal” for both and then “the sperm cells… the DNA is more methylated”. [Notes]: egg and especially sperm DNA are extensively methylated; after fertilization the sperm genome undergoes active demethylation, then global demethylation of the zygote continues to the early blastula stage.
At the blastocyst stage the DNA is remethylated (somatic cells: normal methylation; the placenta is different). [verify] Timing “two weeks, three weeks” in the transcript.
In the gonad, primordial germ cells (future gametes) undergo another fast demethylation during gametogenesis, particularly at some regions.
So there are two peaks of active demethylation; that is how we knew active demethylation had to exist.
[Notes] Remethylation coincides with the first differentiation steps; extensive in somatic lineages, moderate in trophoblast lineages (placenta, yolk sac). PGCs are initially heavily methylated, are demethylated as they enter the genital ridge (erasing parental settings), then de novo methylation resets the marks (including imprinting marks). Animals deficient in DNA methyltransferase die during development; mice unable to methylate sperm DNA are infertile.

7. DNA methylation and cancer

When methylation goes wrong, diseases follow; one of the most common is cancer.
CpG dinucleotides are mutation hotspots: the C very frequently mutates to T (see 5-methylcytosine deamination in Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination).
Pattern in cancer cells:

Global hypomethylation of the genome.
Hypermethylation of the CGIs of some promoters, mostly of tumour suppressor genes, which silences them and increases the chance of a tumour.


Example: p53 does not have a CGI, but p16 does; other tumour suppressors are regulated by CGIs. “Very frequent in cancer.”
[check] [Lucía] writes “global hypermethylation of the promoters of CpG islands”; the lecturer says global hypomethylation plus CGI hypermethylation of tumour suppressors. [Notes] Box 1 only says heavily methylated CGIs occur in diseases such as cancer.

8. Histone modifications

Recap: acetylation opens chromatin (needed for expression), via HATs (histone acetyltransferases) and HDACs (histone deacetylases).
Modifications occur on the N-terminal tails that protrude from the globular histones.
Examples on histone 3 and histone 4 (“forget about histone 4 if you like, and just focus on histone 3”). H3 tail from the amino terminus: alanine, arginine, threonine, lysine 4…
“First message”: the modified residues are mostly lysines. Types: methylation and acetylation of lysines; some serines can be phosphorylated.
Key H3 lysines: K4, K9, K27, and K36 (36 not on the slide).
Acetylated lysine loses its positive charge. Lysine can instead be mono-, di- or trimethylated; methylated lysine is different from acetylated. [verify] The transcript’s statement about which methylated forms keep the charge is garbled. [Notes]: with one, two or three methyl groups the positive charge is retained; a given lysine (e.g. H3K9) can be methylated or acetylated but never both.
Nomenclature: H3K4me3 = histone 3, lysine 4, trimethylated.
[Notes] Acetylation occurs only on lysines; phosphorylation mostly on serines; methylation on lysines and arginines; also ubiquitination. Enzymes: HATs, HDACs, histone lysine methyltransferases (KMTs) and demethylases (KDMs). Bromodomain proteins read acetyl-lysines; chromodomain proteins read methyl-lysines.
[Lucía] K4, K9, K27, K36 of H3 determine whether a gene is active.

9. The histone code

Certain combinations of modifications correlate with gene activity, others with silence: the histone code (“some people don’t like the term”).
How the maps are made (no technical detail required): monoclonal antibodies against a given modification pull down the nucleosomes carrying it; the DNA around them is purified, sequenced and mapped to the genome. A peak = high levels of that mark.

Silent gene (promoter nucleosomes)

H3K4me3: flat, very low (it is an activating mark).
H3K9 methylation: high (repression). [check] Lecturer: “monomethylation of lysine 9”; [Notes] Table 2 and [Lucía]: H3K9me2/me3 in inactive regions.
H3K27me3: high. If K27 is methylated it is not acetylated: closed chromatin (K27 acetylation is basic for opening).
If there is a CGI, it is methylated. “Everything works together.”

Active gene

Peak of RNA polymerase II at the promoter (nucleosome gap).
H3K4me3 high at the promoter nucleosomes.
K9 and K27 acetylated (H3K9ac, H3K27ac): open region; repressive marks absent.
H3K36me3 in the gene body, not at the promoter: found only on nucleosomes where RNA polymerase has already passed, so it marks active transcription (transcript says “lysine 26” once; 36 is meant).
A CGI would be unmethylated.
Crosstalk: DNA methylation and histone modification talk to each other; the enzyme complexes sometimes interact.










































MarkSilent promoterActive promoterActive gene bodyH3K4me3AbsentHighH3K9MethylatedAcetylatedH3K27TrimethylatedAcetylatedH3K36me3HighCGI (if present)MethylatedUnmethylated
Chromatin states and enhancers

Heterochromatin (repressed): H3K9me3 and H3K27me3.
Euchromatin, active promoters: H3K27ac and H3K4me3; inactive genes: H3K27me3.
Enhancers have their own code: an active enhancer has H3K4me1 (mono, rather than tri) and H3K27ac (open, to bind transcription factors).
Active enhancer looping to its active promoter:


























MarkActive enhancerActive promoterH3K27acHighHighH3K4me1HighLowH3K4me3LowHigh

[Notes] Table 2 (examples by chromatin state): active promoters H3K4me3, H3K9ac, H3K27ac; inactive promoters H3K9me3, H3K27me3; active enhancers H3K4me1/me2, H3K27ac; inactive gene bodies H3K9me2/me3; facultative heterochromatin H3K9me2, H3K27me3; constitutive heterochromatin H3K9me3. Figure 6: active promoters also show lower H3K4me2.
[Lucía] Promoters and enhancers are both acetylated and nucleosome-depleted at the centre (transcription factors bind there); promoters high H3K4me3 and low me1/me2, enhancers the opposite. “We can know if a promoter or an enhancer is being activated just by looking at the methylation ratio.”
[Notes] Interactions: methyl-DNA-binding proteins recruit histone methyltransferases or deacetylases; methylated histones recruit DNMTs; transcription factor binding inhibits DNA methylation; some lncRNAs guide these enzymes. Whether the marks are cause or consequence is debated (pioneer transcription factors may come first).

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lec 8.6 Protein folding, targeting and degradation
Sources

lec 8.6 targeting and protein degradation. (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file.
Sections 1 to 4 come from the transcript. Gap: the recording stops mid-sentence at the start of protein targeting (“the mitochondrion must move from…”). Everything from section 5 on (signal sequences, ER targeting, glycosylation, lysosomal, mitochondrial and nuclear targeting, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation) is filled from the slides and study material only.
Not continued by “8.7 protein degradation.txt”: that file is a separate lecture (lysosomes, different lecturer). See Lec 8.7 Protein degradation and lysosomes.
Lecturer identified from the study-material authorship (Alberto Pérez-Mediavilla).

Resources

Slides: 8.6 Protein targeting and degradation (FtMtC I) Diapos.pdf
Study material: 8.6 Targeting and protein degradation (lecture notes).pdf (Alberto Pérez-Mediavilla)
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 8.7. Protein maturation, folding and targeting” (PDF p. 246-249).
Related notes: Lec 8.7 Protein degradation and lysosomes, Lec 8.1 DNA transcription.

Marking: [Slides] = filled from the 8.6 slides. [Notes] = filled from the 8.6 study material (Pérez-Mediavilla). [Lucía] = filled from Lucía’s notes. [check] = transcript conflicts with a vault source, or sources disagree (both versions given). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Do not memorize the Levinthal numbers (10 conformations per amino acid, etc.): “this is not necessary to study… to memorize”. Understand the argument instead.
“This is important”: protein folding is stepwise and cooperative.
What “you must know” about Hsp chaperones: they bind mainly to the intermediate states and prevent aggregation.
He stressed that these processes underlie many human diseases (“I’m explaining this to you because these processes are related at the base of many human diseases”).

1. Why this topic matters: proteinopathies

Last step of gene expression: the protein must fold, be modified (post-translational modifications), reach its destination and eventually be degraded.
Many diseases are linked to failures of folding, maturation, targeting and degradation.
Neurodegenerative diseases are now grouped as proteinopathies: a common feature is protein aggregates inside neurons or in the brain tissue.
Newest therapies try to block aggregate formation. For Alzheimer’s, treatment used to be only symptomatic; now there are antibodies against the aberrantly aggregated proteins (beta-amyloid, tau; alpha-synuclein in Parkinson’s).
[verify] He named one disease as a specific “-opathy” example (“the Kyrgyzakos is a protein apathie… a pectinopathy”); garbled. Check the slide table.






























ProteinDisease ([Slides])CFTRCystic fibrosisbeta-amyloidAlzheimer’sTauAlzheimer’s, Pick’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, progressive supranuclear palsyalpha-synucleinParkinson’s diseaseHuntingtinHuntington’s disease
Clinical example: cystic fibrosis (not neurological)

Caused by a mutation in one codon that eliminates one phenylalanine in the primary structure of the chloride channel CFTR. That is enough to cause degradation of the channel, so lung cells lack it. A disease caused by aberrant degradation.
[check] He then said the cells “don’t produce enough surfactant, which is a mucus that allows absorption of oxygen”. Lucía (Lecture 3.4 Microtransport, PDF p. 47-49) describes it differently: CFTR expels Cl-; when it fails, Cl- is not transported out, water is drawn in by osmosis, the mucus layer becomes thicker, cilia cannot move and infections follow.

2. Protein folding

A protein is not just its primary structure: it needs folding to reach its three-dimensional native conformation and be active. (Lecturer’s image: insulin-like growth factor; “this is not the insulin”.)
Question asked in class: how long does an average 100-amino-acid protein take to fold? Milliseconds (less than a second).
Folding starts during translation. For proteins made on ER-bound ribosomes, translation, folding and post-translational modifications happen at the same time.

The Levinthal paradox (understand, do not memorize)





























StepValueConformations per amino acidabout 10 (because rotation around the phi and psi angles is almost free; side chains add possibilities)Conformations for 100 aa10^100Time to sample one conformation10^-13 sRandom search for 100 aa10^87 s = 3.17 x 10^79 years [Slides]Age of the universeabout 1.38 x 10^10 years

Conclusion: folding cannot be a random search; other forces drive it. [Slides] “If protein folding were a purely random search, no protein in your body would ever fold.”
Main driving force: hydrophobic interactions (also hydrogen bonds and others).
Biological sense: a gene is expressed because its product is needed as soon as possible.

Stepwise and cooperative (“this is important”)

Analogy with hemoglobin cooperativity: when one region adopts its secondary structure, the rotation possibilities of nearby amino acids decrease, so folding accelerates as it proceeds.
In parallel: glycosylation, needed by many proteins to reach their final conformation.
[Notes] As some regions acquire their secondary conformation, it is easier for others; certain sequences fold into helices or sheets driven by the backbone rotation restrictions.

3. Aggregation risk and chaperones

Hydrophobic forces and modifications are sometimes not enough: some proteins cannot fold by themselves. Chaperones help them fold and also drive them to their destination.
Why intermediates are dangerous: in intermediate folding states, regions of the protein are exposed; hydrophobic segments (e.g. sheets) tend to stick to hydrophobic parts of other molecules of the same protein, so aggregation is likely. Hence folding must finish fast.
Chaperones prevent misfolding and aggregation, and can fix aggregation problems: the cell activates signaling that induces chaperones.
If chaperones cannot fix it, a secondary pathway drives the cell to apoptosis.

Lecturer’s example: neurons of the hippocampus (memory acquisition). If a protein aggregates, the neuron tries to fix it (chaperone expression); if that fails, the neuron dies by apoptosis.


Folding with chaperones consumes a lot of ATP: ATP hydrolysis changes the chaperone’s conformation and lets it move along the protein from one segment to another.
























FamilyStructure (lecturer)How it works[Notes]Hsp70 (heat shock proteins)Usually monomericBinds mainly to intermediate states, prevents aggregation, helps foldingExpression induced by heat stress; creates a favourable microenvironment; can bind poorly folded regions and unfold them so they refold correctly; also keeps proteins unfolded during transport into organellesChaperoninsMultimericForm a cavity (tube) with a chemical environment in which the unfolded protein foldsMultiprotein complexes for proteins that do not fold spontaneously; prokaryotic GroEL/GroES, eukaryotic analog Hsp60; rings forming two chambers; the protein is trapped by hydrophobic interactions and folds before the ring’s ATP is hydrolyzed; ATP hydrolysis changes GroES conformation and releases the folded protein

[check] The transcript gives the Hsp as “HSP-17”. The slides and study material say Hsp70.
[Lucía] Hsp were discovered after a heat shock (many proteins had been denatured). Chaperones avoid long exposure of hydrophobic regions, bind them and unfold them to refold correctly; some take part in targeting and transport.
[Notes] When glycosylation in the ER is disrupted, ER stress triggers the UPR (unfolded protein response), aimed at reactivating the process or, if not achieved, at apoptosis. (Lucía: incorrect glycosylation causes many proteinopathies.)

4. Protein targeting: the problem (recording ends here)

Thought experiment: a newly made chloride channel must end up in the plasma membrane. How does it get there, since proteins have no “legs”?
The cytoplasm is very dense (many solutes), “like jam”, yet proteins and organelles must move inside it.
Neuron example: mitochondria are mostly in the soma, but when a dendrite forms a synapse, energy is needed there, so mitochondria must move. Recording ends here.

5. [Slides]/[Notes] Signal sequences

Proteins move from their site of synthesis to exit the cell, become part of a membrane, or enter a subcellular compartment [Slides]. This compartmentalization is a feature of eukaryotic cells.
The destination is encoded in the protein itself as a short signal sequence, usually at or near the N-terminus, 13-36 amino acids long [Slides, Notes].
[Notes] Proof: chimeric proteins in which the N-terminal region is replaced by that of a lysosomal protein end up in the lysosome.
[Notes] Except those made in mitochondria, most proteins are synthesized on membrane-associated ribosomes (RER) and must be targeted. Degradation selectivity is also encoded in the sequence.

ER signal sequence (consensus)

























Feature[Slides][Notes]CoreRich in hydrophobic aaHydrophobic aa abundantN-terminusA positively charged aaA positively charged aaC-terminusaa with short side chains (Ala, Gly)Short sequence of polar aa with small side chains (Ala); contains the proteolysis point that removes the signal peptide in the ER

[Lucía] The C-terminal feature refers to the signal peptide, not the whole protein.

6. [Notes] Translation at the ER (SRP pathway)

Synthesis starts on free ribosomes.
The N-terminal signal sequence emerges from the ribosome.
It binds the signal recognition particle (SRP), a ribonucleoprotein; translation stops.
SRP binds GTP; SRP-GTP brings the ribosome to the SRP receptor on the ER membrane; the signal peptide crosses the membrane through the peptide translocation complex.
GTP is hydrolyzed, SRP dissociates, translation restarts.
Translation continues to completion.
A peptidase cleaves the signal peptide.
The ribosome dissociates from the ER and is recycled.


[Slides] After the ER (where some modification such as glycosylation occurs), transport vesicles take proteins to the Golgi: the biosynthetic/secretory pathway.

7. [Slides]/[Notes] Glycosylation

























N-linkedO-linkedAttached to[Slides] nitrogen of Asn or Arg; [Notes] side chain of AsnOxygen of Ser, Thr, Tyr [Slides]WhereBegins in the RERTypically Golgi (or cytosol for proteins not entering the ER) [Slides]; [Notes] in the Golgi via O-glycosidic bondsConsensusN-x-S/TP-x-S/T-x-x-P

[check] The slides list Asn or Arg for N-linked glycosylation; the study material and Lucía mention Asn only. Neither settles the Arg part.
[Notes] The oligosaccharide differs between proteins but shares a common core made and attached in the ER. Glycosylation is essential for maturation to the final conformation; disruption triggers the UPR (section 3). Proteins go from ER to Golgi in vesicles, are sorted in the Golgi and sent to their destinations (mechanism not well known).

8. [Notes] Lysosomal targeting: mannose 6-phosphate

Lysosomal hydrolases reach the Golgi carrying a “tag” recognized by a phosphotransferase, which phosphorylates a terminal mannose of the oligosaccharide.
Mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) is the signal for lysosomes.
An M6P receptor in the Golgi membrane binds it at pH 6-6.5.
Hydrolase-receptor complexes are coated by clathrin, forming vesicles sent to the lysosome.
Lysosomal pH is acidic (3-4) (continuous proton pumping into the lumen); low pH dissociates the hydrolase from the receptor.
A phosphatase removes the M6P tag and the receptor is recycled to the Golgi. Both events stop the hydrolase from returning to the Golgi.


Failure of this transport: waste accumulates in lysosomes, leading to diseases such as sphingolipidoses, glycogenoses, mucopolysaccharidoses ([Lucía]: “lysosomal storage diseases”).
See Lec 8.7 Protein degradation and lysosomes for the lysosome lecture.

9. [Slides]/[Notes] Mitochondrial targeting

Directed by specific N-terminal sequences. The protein binds chaperones in the cytosol that bring it to receptors on the outside of the mitochondrion, which promote its translocation inside.

10. [Slides]/[Notes] Nuclear targeting

Many nuclear proteins (RNA and DNA polymerases, histones, topoisomerases, transcription factors) are made on cytoplasmic ribosomes and imported [Notes].
NLS (nuclear localization sequence): 4-8 aa, rich in basic residues (Arg, Lys); stays in the protein after transport [Slides, Notes].
[check] Lucía describes the NLS as “rich in hydrophobic regions”. The slides and study material say basic amino acids.
Mechanism [Notes]:

Importins alpha and beta bind the protein in the cytoplasm and take it to the nuclear pore complex; it is translocated inside.
In the nucleus, Ran (GTPase; Ras-related nuclear protein) binds importin beta and separates it.
The nuclear protein-importin alpha complex binds Ran and CAS (cellular apoptosis susceptibility protein), releasing the nuclear protein.
Importins return to the cytoplasm, where Ran hydrolyzes GTP and releases them.
Ran-GDP returns to the nucleus via NTF2; in the nucleus Ran-GEF exchanges GDP for GTP.


[Slides] Ribosomal proteins are made in the cytosol, imported into the nucleus, assembled into subunits in the nucleolus, then exported to the cytosol.

11. [Slides]/[Notes] Protein degradation

Inevitable; maintains protein homeostasis, prevents accumulation of aberrant proteins, recycles amino acids [Notes].
Half-lives: from seconds to days or even months [Slides]; [Notes] about 30 s to several days; hemoglobin lives about as long as the erythrocyte (about 110 days). Short-lived: damaged or erroneous proteins, and critical regulatory proteins.
Two systems in eukaryotes [Notes]:

Lysosomal: membrane proteins, extracellular proteins, long-lived proteins.
ATP-dependent ubiquitin-proteasome system.



Ubiquitin-proteasome system





























ElementDetailUbiquitin76 aa, highly conserved (identical in most organisms) [Notes, Slides]AttachmentCovalently to lysine of the target, ATP-dependent, by E1 (activating), E2 (conjugating), E3 (ligating) [Slides, Notes]PolyubiquitinRepeated ubiquitination forms polyubiquitin tails [Notes]Proteasome26S proteasome cleaves ubiquitinated proteins [Slides]; [Notes] two copies of a complex with 32 different subunits; proteolysis insideSignalsNot exactly known; some sequences make proteins more prone to ubiquitination [Notes]

[Lucía] The more ubiquitin, the more likely degradation. Cyclins carry a sequence that favours ubiquitination, hence a short life.

[Slides] N-terminal residue and half-life (Bachmair et al. 1986, measured in yeast)

































N-terminal residueHalf-lifeAla, Gly, Met, Ser, Thr, Val (stabilizing)> 20 hGln, Ileabout 30 minGlu, Tyrabout 10 minProabout 7 minAsp, Leu, Lys, Pheabout 3 minArgabout 2 min
[Notes] Diseases of degradation

Altered degradation of cell-cycle proteins (oncogene products) leads to tumors.
Neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer, Parkinson, Huntington): aberrant aggregates accumulate partly because cells cannot get rid of them (links back to section 1).

Lec 8.7 Protein degradation and lysosomes
Sources

8.7 protein degradation (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file, complete from the start of the lecture to the end (“two more minutes… see you next time”).
Separate lecture from 8.6, not a continuation: it starts fresh (“we have to study today the discovery of lysosomes”). Some overlap in content with 8.6 (M6P tagging): the 8.7 lecturer says Alberto (Dr. Pérez-Mediavilla) showed the same tagging scheme but left the explanation to him.
Lecturer: probable, not confirmed. In 8.6, Dr. Pérez-Mediavilla said the next lesson would be given by a “Dr. Calvin” (garbled) and addressed someone in the room as “Alfonso”. The 3.6 and 8.5 study materials list Alfonso Calvo as an author. No slide or document names the 8.7 lecturer.
No gaps in the recording. Section numbers follow the lecture.

Resources

Slides: Lec 8.8. Lysosomes.pdf (file named 8.8; official code 8.7).
Study material: none specific in the vault. The 8.6 study material covers lysosomal targeting: 8.6 Targeting and protein degradation (lecture notes).pdf.
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 8.8. Protein degradation: lysosomes” (PDF p. 250-253). Her section also covers types of digestion (heterophagy, autophagy, extracellular digestion), which were not in this year’s lecture or slides.
Related notes: Lec 8.6 Protein folding, targeting and degradation (M6P targeting, ubiquitin-proteasome), Lec 5.11 Cholesterol metabolism and lipid transport (LDL endocytosis), TBL 7.2 CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (gene therapy, vectors).

Marking: [Slides] = filled from the lysosome slides. [Notes] = filled from the 8.6 study material (Pérez-Mediavilla). [Lucía] = filled from Lucía’s notes. [check] = transcript conflicts with a vault source, or sources disagree (both versions given). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Acid phosphatase = universal marker of lysosomes: “a typical question for the exam… many times I ask this”.
Mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) as the lysosomal tag: “another possible question”.
Ultracentrifugation: “you don’t have to learn or memorize anything except” that lysosomes (and peroxisomes) are found in the mitochondrial fraction. Understand the process; the rest is informative.
EM identification: he will not ask you to identify a primary lysosome. If an EM image of lysosomes appears, it will be a clearly identifiable one. Review lysosome morphology from the first TBL (TBL 1.1).
Tagging system: “very important”, because I-cell disease depends on it.
Gaucher disease: was a MIR question “a couple of years ago”.
Enzyme replacement therapy mechanism: “you don’t need to know this”, only understand the concept.

1. Discovery: Christian de Duve and ultracentrifugation

Christian de Duve, a medical doctor, discovered both lysosomes and peroxisomes while studying liver enzymes in cell fractions. Nobel Prize in Medicine 1974 [Slides].
[verify] His country is garbled in the transcript (“Ventium”); not on the slides.
[Slides] Discovery by ultracentrifugation and TEM.
Goal of the technique: isolate specific organelles to study their function (more than their morphology).










































StepSpin (lecturer)Pellet (sediment)Supernatant goes to0Homogenize the tissue (mortar and pestle, buffer) to break the cellsCentrifuge tube1800 g, 10 minNuclei (densest, sediment fastest)Step 2215,000 g, 10 minMitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes (“mitochondrial fraction”; similar density)Step 33100,000 g, 60 minMembranes (plasma membrane, RER, SER)Step 44Further spinRibosomesSupernatant = cytosolic fraction

[verify] He first read “200,000 g for 3 hours” for step 3, then corrected himself (“sorry, it is this tube”); it seems to belong to the final ribosome spin. Check the figure on the slide.
[check] Lucía gives the second spin as 15 minutes; the lecturer said 10 minutes.

2. Structure of lysosomes

Function: digest (destroy) molecules: proteins, lipids, nucleotides, etc.
[Slides] Size 0.2-0.5 um. Name: lysis (decompose) + soma (body).

Membrane

























ComponentRole (lecturer)Lipid bilayerCarrier proteinsExport useful products out of the lysosome. Example: after LDL endocytosis, the protein part is destroyed but cholesterol is exported for the cell’s membranes. Not everything is fully destroyedComplex glycans on the inner face ([Slides]: glycosylated proteins)Protect the membrane from self-digestion: no lysosomal enzyme can digest themProton pumpsPump H+ in against the gradient to keep pH about 5, needed for digestion

[Lucía] The pump is an ATPase that imports H+.

Interior

Acid hydrolases: about 40 types (slides: lipases, nucleases…). Not every lysosome has all 40; they can be specialized (30, 15…) for specific substrates.
All lysosomes contain acid phosphatase: the universal marker of lysosomes. A round organelle containing acid phosphatase is a lysosome.

3. Endocytosis review and primary vs secondary lysosomes

LDL binds its receptor in the plasma membrane and enters in clathrin-coated vesicles.
Vesicles fuse with the early endosome, which has proton pumps: low pH separates receptor and ligand.
The receptor is recycled to the plasma membrane; LDL moves to the late endosome, where digestion will happen.
Lysosomal enzymes are made on RER ribosomes, N-glycosylated in the RER, then go to the Golgi (N- and O-glycosylation there) for modification and stability.
They leave the trans-Golgi in vesicles: hydrolytic vesicles = primary lysosomes (“bags full of enzymes”).
Primary lysosomes fuse with late endosomes: now substrate and enzymes meet = secondary lysosome = endolysosome.































Primary lysosome (hydrolytic vesicle)Secondary lysosome (endolysosome)ContentEnzymes only, no substrateEnzymes + substratespHAbout 7About 5 (proton pumps)DigestionNoYesEMSmall round vesicles near the Golgi; to be sure, immunohistochemistry for acid phosphataseVery variable morphology (some with concentric membranes)

Student question in class: the early endosome contains no enzymes; enzymes reach the late endosome deeper in the cell. A primary lysosome holds many enzymes, bound to the receptor on its membrane.

4. Tagging and sorting lysosomal enzymes (M6P)
Lecturer’s sequence:

Enzyme synthesized on the RER and N-glycosylated; one of the sugars in the branch is mannose.
Vesicles carry it to the cis-Golgi, where a phosphotransferase adds a phosphate to carbon 6 of the terminal mannose: mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) = the tag (“barcode”).
The enzyme moves through the Golgi stacks to the trans-Golgi network, where M6P receptors bind it and drive the formation of vesicles (primary lysosomes) towards the late endosome.
In the late endosome, acid phosphatase removes the phosphate so the enzyme is free and fully functional; it then digests the substrates (e.g. LDL).


[check] Number of enzymes adding the phosphate: the lecturer named one phosphotransferase; the slides and Lucía say mannose is phosphorylated “by sequential activity of two enzymes”. The 8.6 study material names a phosphotransferase.
[check] How the enzyme is released from the receptor: the lecturer said acid phosphatase removes the phosphate “because otherwise the enzyme gets attached to this receptor”. The slides and Lucía say low pH in the late endosome causes dissociation of enzyme and receptor; the 8.6 study material says low pH dissociates them and then a phosphatase removes the M6P, and the receptor is recycled to the Golgi. The slides list “Receptor is recycled”.
[check] Lysosomal pH: lecturer, slides and Lucía say 5; the 8.6 study material says 3-4. The 8.6 study material also gives the receptor-binding pH in the Golgi as 6-6.5.

Default pathway

Every compartment needs its own tag (Golgi-resident, RER-resident, lysosomal…). A protein made in the RER with no tag goes out of the cell by default (secretion).

5. I-cell disease (inclusion-cell disease, mucolipidosis type II)





































FeatureDetailInheritanceAutosomal recessiveCauseMutations in the phosphotransferase: no M6P on lysosomal enzymesConsequence 1Untagged enzymes are secreted out of the cell. They need pH about 5, so outside they work suboptimally, but may still have some activity. [Lucía] This extracellular activity contributes to defectsConsequence 2Lysosomes devoid of enzymes: undigested substrates accumulate as inclusions (hence the name)Why so severeLacks essentially all lysosomal enzymes (not just one)PatientsDeformities, malformations, mental retardation; life expectancy about 5 years. [Slides] abnormal development, dwarfismCellsExample: peripheral blood lymphocytes filled with lysosomes of undigested material; cytosol occupied, cells stressed

Lecturer’s analogy: a person who hoards garbage at home (photo of a car full of rubbish). [verify] He named a syndrome for this (“Diabetes Syndrome” in the transcript); garbled, and it is not on the slides.

6. Lysosomal storage disorders (LSD): general features

Storage of undigested substrates, cell stress and malfunction, developmental and metabolic problems [Slides].
Two kinds of cause: lack of all enzymes (tagging defect, I-cell) or mutation of one specific enzyme (e.g. Gaucher).
More than 50 LSDs; incidence 1:5,000 to 1:8,000 newborns: rare diseases [Slides].
Inheritance: autosomal recessive, except some X-linked (example: Fabry) [Slides].
High incidence in endogamic populations, e.g. Ashkenazi Jews: carriers marrying carriers within a closed community propagate the disease. Hence their traditional use in genetic studies of rare diseases.

Lecturer’s remarks

Rare diseases and the pharmaceutical industry: industry traditionally did not invest (hard to treat genetic diseases; not profitable for few patients). Developing a drug is very expensive: of about 1,000 candidates, with luck one reaches a clinical trial. This has changed; there are now drugs for some LSDs.
Story: a rabbi in Brooklyn lost two children to such a disease (they died at 5-6) and founded an organization offering genetic counseling to young Jewish couples. [Slides] Dor Yeshorim, founded by Rabbi Josef Ekstein, 1983, Brooklyn (doryeshorim.org); premarital counseling to prevent LSDs in Jewish communities.

7. Gaucher disease

























FeatureDetailCauseMutation in one enzyme, glucocerebrosidase (tagging is normal)AccumulatesGlucosylceramideKey cellMacrophage (all cells carry the mutation). Affected macrophages = Gaucher cells; bone marrow biopsy shows macrophages full of bluish undigested materialClinicalSkeletal and neurological defects; hepatosplenomegaly (enlarged liver and spleen); bone loss is a typical finding

[Lucía] Macrophages are abundant in bone, liver and spleen, which is why the manifestations affect those organs.

Treatment






























OptionLecturerStatusSymptomaticTreat pain and other symptomsBone marrow transplantMacrophages come from the bone marrow. High-dose irradiation kills the patient’s marrow to make room; donor marrow repopulates it and produces normal macrophagesApprovedEnzyme replacement therapySee belowApprovedGene therapyE.g. bone marrow stem cells infected with a virus carrying the normal gene, replacing the defective oneClinical trials ([Slides]: “in trials”)
Enzyme replacement therapy (understand the concept only; “you don’t need to know this”)

Recombinant glucocerebrosidase is produced in bacteria.
It is covered with glycans typical of bacteria.
The Gaucher macrophage “thinks” it is a bacterium and phagocytoses it.
Through the endosome pathway it reaches the endosomes/lysosomes holding the undigested substrate, which can now be digested.


“A very smart way of fooling” the macrophage.
[Lucía] The enzyme is covered with mannose to favour its endocytosis.

Exam flags from the lecturer

Reading assignment at the end of the second file is garbled (see Sources). Final words: “Do the exercise.”

1. Cytogenetics and the karyotype

Unit 9 is about classical genetics: transmission of genetic traits and diseases (autosomal dominant, etc.). This first lesson: cytogenetics, the analysis of genetics with the microscope, plus some molecular techniques.
Goals he states: what a normal karyotype is and how it is made; what abnormalities (numerical or structural) can be found; how they arise.
Karyotype: an ordered representation of all the chromosomes of a cell at mitosis. Cells are made to divide and stopped at a particular phase of mitosis; DNA is stained with Giemsa, which colours some parts darker: the bands.
Band meaning (lecturer): dark bands = usually inactive, compact chromatin; clear bands = relaxed chromatin. [verify] He names the clear ones “R bands” and the dark ones “G bands”, then says “the dark ones are called R bands”; the transcript is inconsistent.
[Notes] G-banding: trypsin then Giemsa, which binds preferentially AT-rich regions: dark bands = Giemsa-positive, AT-rich, gene-poor; light bands = GC-rich, gene-rich. Preparations from peripheral blood white cells stimulated to divide (phytohaemagglutinin) and arrested with colcemid; metaphase or prometaphase.
[check] [Lucía] writes that “darker G bands correspond to more gene dense regions” and then that darker bands are compacted and repressed; the first statement contradicts [Notes] and the lecturer.

Ordering the chromosomes (1 to 22, then the sex chromosomes)

Size, from largest (chromosome 1) to smallest. The smallest is actually chromosome 21; people originally thought 22 was smaller.
Banding pattern (distinguishes chromosomes of similar size).
Position of the centromere: metacentric (two arms of the same size) or submetacentric; most chromosomes have a short arm on top and a long arm below. Short arm = p (“petit”, small in French); long arm = q.
[Lucía] Also lists telocentric; ideogram = map of a single chromosome.

2. Acrocentric chromosomes

(Answering Pedro.) Acrocentric = the short arm is very tiny, “just like a blob of DNA” (satellite and ribosomal DNA).
Group D: 13, 14, 15; group G: 21, 22. The Y is sometimes considered acrocentric.
Important because they undergo Robertsonian translocations (section 7).
[Notes] Each short arm has about 30 to 40 large tandem repeats encoding the 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNAs; the five rDNA regions congregate at the nucleolus, which favours Robertsonian translocation.

3. ISCN nomenclature

Needed to communicate findings (you cannot email “a little region somewhere in chromosome 9”): the International System for Human Cytogenetic Nomenclature (ISCN). “You have in the notes how it works.”
[Slides] Format: total number (of centromeres), sex chromosomes (comma, no space). The total is counted by centromeres because it can be hard to tell how many chromosomes there are. Normal female 46,XX; normal male 46,XY.


















































SymbolMeaning (lecturer / [Slides]);Separates chromosomes or bands (inside brackets) when two chromosomes are involved/Mosaicism: two cell populations with different karyotypes in one individual+ / -Extra / missing chromosomedelDeletiondupDuplicationinsInsertioninvInversiontTranslocation (“like transposing a matrix”)derDerivative chromosome (section 7)iIsochromosome

“There are many more; this is a book with recommendations.”

Bands and sub-bands

Each arm is divided into regions defined by the banding pattern, numbered individually: q21 is read “q two-one”, not “q twenty-one” (saying “twenty-one” is a mistake): long arm, 2, then 1. The lecturer calls these band 2, sub-band 1.
[Notes] Box 1: arm, region, band, sub-band, sub-sub-band, numbered by proximity to the centromere (region 1 closest). 4q21 = long arm of 4, region 2, band 1; 4q21.22 = “two-one-point-two-two”. Proximal = closer to the centromere, distal = closer to the telomere. [check] terminology: the lecturer’s “band and sub-band” for q21 corresponds to [Notes] “region and band”.
Resolution: depends on when mitosis is stopped. Earlier = less compacted chromosomes = more bands = more resolution; with about 500 bands per karyotype you can define sub-bands (e.g. q21.1). Very high resolution is difficult and rare. Figure: the same chromosome at three resolutions.
[Notes] Figure 1b: about 400, 550 and 850 bands per haploid set.
Ideograms: the drawings in books and papers; not the real thing but the ideal banding pattern of each chromosome.

Worked examples ([Slides] karyotype list, lecturer’s reading)

































KaryotypeMeaning69,XXXWoman with three sets of chromosomes: triploidy (he adds that not all her cells would be like this [verify])47,XY,+21/46,XYMosaic: some cells with trisomy 21, some normal; probably Down syndrome; the percentage of trisomic cells matters; common in Down syndrome45,XY,-13,-14,t(13q;14q)45 chromosomes: lost normal 13 and normal 14, gained a translocation fusing the long arms of 13 and 14 (both acrocentric): a Robertsonian translocation46,XY,dup(5p)Normal male, part of the short arm of 5 duplicated46,XX,del(4)(p14;pter)Normal female, chromosome 4 lost from p14 to the terminal end (pter = telomere)46,X,i(Xq)One normal X plus an isochromosome of the long arm of X: the short arm was lost and the long arm duplicated, so both arms are identical

[Slides] list also includes 46,XX,t(4;12)(q12;p13) and 46,XY,del(5p) (not discussed in the recording).
[check] Band notation: the slides and lecturer separate the two bands of one chromosome with a semicolon, e.g. del(4)(p14;pter), dup(7)(q21;q23); [Notes] Table 1 writes them without separator, e.g. del(5)(q13q33), dup(1)(q22q25), and keeps the semicolon for two chromosomes, e.g. t(2;6)(q35;p21.3).
[Notes] Table 1 further examples: 46,XX,ins(2)(p13q21q31); 46,XY,r(7)(p22q36); 47,XX,+mar (unidentified marker chromosome); 45,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10) balanced Robertsonian carrier (q10 indicates the centromere); 46,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21 Down syndrome from a Robertsonian translocation.

4. Classifying abnormalities

Two types: numerical and structural.
[Notes] Also by distribution: constitutional (all nucleated cells, present from very early development: abnormal gamete, fertilization or early embryo) vs somatic/acquired (only some cells: a mosaic). Structural abnormalities come from chromosome breaks that are not repaired; numerical ones often from segregation errors.
[Notes] Chromosomal aberrations are the main cause of embryo loss in the first three months; up to 20 to 30% of spontaneous abortions until week 20 show one, around 5% later.

5. Numerical abnormalities (recorded part)

Aneuploidy: “euploidy” = the right number; an- (Greek negative) = not the right number of chromosomes.
Polyploidy: whole sets, e.g. triploidy (3n), tetraploidy (4n). More common is one chromosome extra or missing.
Trisomy and monosomy are the most common aneuploidies:






























ConditionKaryotypeDown syndromeTrisomy 21Edwards syndromeTrisomy 18Patau syndromeTrisomy 13Turner syndromeMonosomy X (women with one X)Klinefelter syndromeMales with two X instead of one (XXY)

Trisomy 21 is the most common because 21 is the smallest chromosome, so an extra copy “is not so bad”; you could not have a trisomy of chromosome 1 (the largest: excess of genes). Trisomies 18 and 13 are less common.
The first recording ends here.

6. Not recorded: rest of numerical abnormalities (from [Slides], [Notes], [Lucía])

[Slides] Sex chromosome aneuploidies: Klinefelter 47,XXY (males with an extra X), triple X 47,XXX (females with an extra X). Turner 45,X: missing or incomplete X in females.
[Slides] Prevalence per 1,000 live newborns:


































KaryotypePer 1,00047,+211.547,+180.1247,+130.0745,X0.447,XXY1.547,XYY1.5

[Slides] Chromosomal aberrations in spontaneous abortions and stillbirths: until week 7, 20%; weeks 7 to 20, 35%; weeks 20 to 40, 4% ([Lucía] same). [check] [Notes] text: 20 to 30% until week 20, around 5% later.
[Slides] Down syndrome risk by maternal age: 15 y 1:1578; 20 y 1:1528; 25 y 1:1351; 30 y 1:909; 35 y 1:384; 40 y 1:112. [check] [Notes]: about 1 in 1,500 at 20 and about 1 in 25 at 45.
[Notes] Nondisjunction: homologues fail to separate at meiosis I, or sister chromatids at meiosis II or mitosis; meiotic nondisjunction gives gametes with 22 or 24 chromosomes (nullisomy or disomy), hence monosomic or trisomic zygotes; mitotic nondisjunction gives mosaics. Anaphase lag also causes aneuploidy. About 70% of Down syndrome cases arise at maternal meiosis I, explained by the very long arrest of female meiosis I (decades); hence the maternal age effect.
[Notes] Polyploidy: triploidy in about 3% of recognized pregnancies, mostly dispermy (66%), or a diploid egg (10%) or diploid sperm (24%); almost never born alive (diploid/triploid mosaics can survive). Tetraploidy is rarer, always lethal, from failure of the first zygotic division (endomitosis).
[Notes] Table 2: autosomal monosomies and nullisomies lethal very early; trisomy 13 and 18 may survive to term, trisomy 21 beyond 40; 47,XXX, 47,XXY, 47,XYY relatively minor problems; 45,Y never viable; about 99% of 45,X conceptions abort, survivors of normal intelligence but infertile. Cancer cells often show extreme aneuploidy.
[Notes] Mixoploidy: mosaicism (cell lines from one zygote) or chimerism (from different zygotes).

7. Structural abnormalities (second recording)
Types listed (start lost): … and translocations, reciprocal or Robertsonian.
Isochromosomes

Two identical arms: one arm lost, the other duplicated. [verify] The transcript then says “the most frequent one is the same”; probably i(Xq), as in [Notes].
[Notes] Rare except i(Xq) and i(21q) (an occasional cause of Down syndrome).

Deletions

Terminal: a break and everything beyond it is lost.
Interstitial: the lost part is inside an arm (e.g. one band).
The microdeletions of the genomic disorders (e.g. DiGeorge) belong here; often not visible on the karyotype, needing more sophisticated techniques (Lec 7.7 Genetic variation).
Example: cri du chat (French, “cry of the cat”): terminal deletion of the end of the short arm of chromosome 5 (del(5p)); the pitch of the babies’ cry resembles a cat’s. It takes a trained cytogeneticist, who has seen thousands of karyotypes, to see it.
[Slides] TERMINAL DELETION del(7)(p22;pter).

Duplications

One segment duplicated: the same banding pattern appears twice.
Example: dup(7)(q21;q23) ([Slides]): duplication of chromosome 7 in brackets, then in brackets the regions involved separated by a semicolon. (Transcript reads “from Q1 to Q3”.)
Aside: as doctors you may ask an AI to explain such lab reports, “but it’s nice to know whether AI got it wrong, which usually gets it wrong.”

[Gap in the recording here.]
Inversions

Need two breaks; the segment between them is inverted.
Both breaks on the same arm (same side of the centromere): paracentric.
One break in each arm (either side of the centromere): pericentric. Pericentric ones are usually larger than paracentric.
If the segment is lost instead of inverted: interstitial deletion.

Ring chromosomes

Both terminal segments lost and the broken ends of the long and short arms fused: a ring with one centromere.
[Notes] Figure 4: ring chromosomes with a centromere are stable in mitosis; the acentric distal fragments are lost.

Reciprocal translocations

A piece of one chromosome passes to another and vice versa: a break in each chromosome.
Stable when the exchanged pieces are the fragments without centromere, so each product keeps one centromere.
Naming: each product contains parts of both chromosomes; it is named by the centromere it carries. E.g. chromosomes 2 and 13: the product with the centromere of 2 is der(2) (derivative 2), “not a chromosome 2”; the other is der(13).
If the exchange gives one chromosome with two centromeres (dicentric) and one with none (acentric), these are unstable and lost in mitosis.
[Notes] Translocation needs the two breaks in close proximity; chromosome territories matter (e.g. 4, 13 and 18 at the nuclear periphery often translocate with each other). Specific translocations are common in certain cancers.

Robertsonian translocations (centric fusion)

Only the acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22). They fuse by their centromeres (centric fusion).
The short arms are only satellite and ribosomal DNA, so losing them is no problem.
Products: a dicentric chromosome with both centromeres together, stable (works as a single centromere); and an acentric fragment (short arms, rDNA) lost in mitosis.
Meiosis problem: e.g. a 14;15 fusion pairs with the normal 14 and the normal 15, forming a trivalent; segregation can give offspring with trisomies or monosomies (“complex… I don’t have time to explain that”).
[Notes] Figure 5B; Table 1: 45,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10) balanced carrier; a carrier’s child may have Down syndrome with 46 chromosomes. [Lucía] A carrier may pass missing or extra DNA, giving monosomies or trisomies.

How structural abnormalities arise (student question)

Not mutations in the usual sense: they happen spontaneously and are very rare.
In meiosis, homologous recombination begins with double-strand breaks; normally they are processed correctly, but rarely two nearby DSBs are joined wrongly, fusing two chromosomes. “No biological process is 100% efficient.”
[Notes] Breaks come from unrepaired DNA damage or faults in recombination (mispaired homologues, unequal crossing-over, intrachromatid recombination). Breaks in G2 are chromatid breaks; breaks in G1 not repaired by S become chromosome breaks.

8. Molecular cytogenetics: FISH

Banding resolution is limited; small deletions cannot be seen. Molecular techniques give much better resolution. “The one you have to know about”: FISH, fluorescence in situ hybridization.
Hybridization: denature DNA (separate the strands) by heat (as in PCR), pH change or chemicals; then let it renature. With a probe (a short DNA fragment whose genomic origin is known; Spanish “sonda”) present, cooling slowly lets the probe strands anneal to their matching site in the genome.
Probes are fluorescently labelled. Fluorescence: the molecule absorbs light of one wavelength and emits at another (he contrasts it with phosphorescence).
On the slide: the cell’s DNA is denatured on the slide, the probe anneals to its identical region, and a coloured signal appears under a fluorescence microscope. DNA counterstained blue with DAPI.
On metaphase chromosomes each signal is a double dot (two sister chromatids).
Example, chromosome 15: two probes, one for the centromere of 15 (shows both chromosomes 15 are present) and one for a region on 15q. One chromosome 15 lacks the 15q signal: an interstitial deletion of 15q.
[Notes] FISH confirms duplications/deletions found by other methods; detects oncogene amplification (MYCN in neuroblastoma) and translocations. Figure 2: 22q11.2 deletion detected with HIRA probe (red) and ARSA control probe (green).
[Lucía] If the probe does not fluoresce, it has not bound: a microdeletion in that region.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia: t(9;22) (exam case years ago)

CML (a blood cancer): the cells carry a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22: a der(9) with part of 22 and a der(22) with part of 9.
The der(22) is the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph).
Notation t(9;22)(q34;q11) ([Slides]): the first breakpoint (q34) refers to the first chromosome (9), the second (q11) to the second (22). (Transcript reads “Q811” and “Q3134”; [Slides] has q34;q11.)
The Philadelphia chromosome carries a fusion gene of one gene from 22 and one from 9. A tyrosine kinase normally not expressed in blood stem cells is, because of the fusion, expressed at high levels in developing white blood cells, driving their proliferation: leukaemia.
[Notes] The genes are BCR (22q) and ABL1 (9q); the BCR-ABL1 hybrid gene.

Interphase FISH

Great advantage: no metaphase chromosomes needed; cells (nuclei) are put on a slide directly.
Detects aneuploidies (trisomies, monosomies) and translocations.
t(9;22): probe for 9 in green, for 22 in red; where they are fused, the signals sit together and can look yellow where they overlap (transcript “green and blue” [verify]; [Notes] Figure 3: red and green, overlap orange-yellow).
Trisomy 8 (another leukaemia): a centromere probe for chromosome 8; count dots per nucleus across hundreds of cells to see how many carry the trisomy.
“Very powerful”: molecular cytogenetics complements classical cytogenetics.
