Lec 9.2 Single gene inheritance
Sources

Lec 9.2 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Opens mid-sentence during an overview of the remaining Unit 9 sessions (“TBL issues surrounding the main genetics in the medicine”) and ends with “The next class will be about different types of diseases with many genes involved and environments.”
Gaps: the start of the Unit 9 overview is missing (the file begins mid-sentence). The lecture content itself appears complete. He skipped the practice pedigrees at the end of the slides (“I will leave that to you”).

Resources

Slides: Slides Unit 9.pdf, the part after the cytogenetics slides (variable expressivity, cystic fibrosis organs and CFTR mutations, X-inactivation, mitochondrial inheritance). Mostly images: pedigrees, Punnett squares, the Duchenne histology and dystrophin staining, the Barr body picture: see the slides.
Study material: none for 9.2 in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “Lec 9.2. Patterns of single gene inheritance” (Figure 1 pedigree symbols, Figures 2 to 7, Box 1 consanguinity and coefficient of relationship).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 9.2. Patterns of single gene inheritance”, PDF p. 265-268.
Related notes: Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis (Barr bodies in sex aneuploidies), Lec 9.3 Polygenic inheritance (next class), Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation (mtDNA-encoded OxPhos proteins), Lec 5.11 Cholesterol metabolism and lipid transport (LDL receptor), Lec 7.4 Levels of chromatin packaging (heterochromatin).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 9 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Draw and read pedigrees: “you should be able to draw these things” (section 2).
Recurrence risks: couples “will ask you… What is the risk that the child will be affected? … So you have to be able to work this out” with Punnett squares (sections 3 to 6). He insists you must explain risks clearly to families “who usually have no idea of what the probability is, what dominance is, or recessiveness”.
Compound heterozygotes: “perhaps you might read that in the exam, I don’t know. So you should know what we are talking about” (section 4).
Mitochondrial inheritance: “a completely different type of inheritance, which you have to recognize” (section 8).
Telltale signs he asks you to spot: X-linked recessive = only males affected; X-linked dominant = no father-to-son transmission (sections 5 and 6).
Practice pedigrees at the end of the slides: “I will leave that to you.”
Admin (start of the file): two TBLs left in the block, one “TBL 8 something” related to epigenetics and a final “TBL 9 something” related to Unit 9. Lec 9.2 and 9.3 cover “the classical genetic stuff” (Mendelian and non-Mendelian inheritance) applied to medicine.

1. Single gene (Mendelian) diseases vs Lec 9.3



































Lec 9.2 single geneLec 9.3 polygenicCauseOne mutation in one gene causes the diseaseMany genes plus environmentFrequencyRare in the populationVery commonSeverityUsually quite seriousFamiliesRun in families, following set patterns of inheritanceGenetic component not a single geneHis examplesHemophilia AType 1 diabetes (“you wouldn’t say it’s a genetic disease. Well, in a sense it is, but not only”)

The basic tool of medical genetics is pedigree analysis: take the family history, build the pedigree, apply Mendel’s rules (which he does not re-explain: “you’re probably filled up with… Mendel’s experiments… from your high school”). From the pattern alone you should have an idea of what is happening.
Mitochondrial DNA mutations follow a different pattern (section 8).
[Notes] A more accurate term than “Mendelian” is monogenic (covers chromosomal loci and mtDNA loci). Five basic Mendelian patterns: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, X-linked recessive, Y-linked; plus mtDNA inheritance.
[Notes] Terms: locus; allele; genotype; homozygous/heterozygous; men are hemizygous for most X and Y loci. Dominant = manifested in the heterozygote; recessive = not; co-dominant = both phenotypes shown by the heterozygote (AB blood group).

2. Pedigrees

Taking the family history: e.g. “your son has this problem with the lungs… when did this happen… is there anyone else in your family with this?” Then you construct the pedigree.
Name: from French, “the foot of the crane”, because of the shape. (Transcript: “La pied du coul”; [verify] the French phrase.)
Drawing it quickly while talking to the family gives an overview instead of writing “one son, three daughters…“.


































































Symbol / conventionMeaningSquare / circleMale / femaleHorizontal line between twoMating (“marriage”); children hang from a line belowChildren orderLeft to right, firstborn to lastbornRoman numerals (left)GenerationsArabic numeralsIndividuals in each generation, left to right; “II-4” identifies one personAgesCan be written by each symbolFilled symbolShows the disease (he first said “homozygote for the mutation”, then corrected to “the person shows the disease”)Half-filled (diagonal or vertical, “depends on your taste”)Healthy carrier of an autosomal recessive mutationDot inside the symbolFemale carrier of an X-linked diseaseTwo lines from the same pointFraternal (non-identical) twinsSame, with a line joining themIdentical twinsDouble mating lineConsanguinityDiamond with a numberChildren of unstated sex pooled together (e.g. “4” = four children)ArrowProband: the person who initiates the diagnosis

Before any molecular analysis you do not know who carries the mutation; you only see who shows the disease.
Consanguinity: genetic relatedness greater than the population average, e.g. spouses whose grandparents were siblings. “Used to be very common in rural areas” where the same families intermarried for generations. “Very important to account for.”
[Notes] Figure 1 adds: deceased, spontaneous abortion, termination of affected pregnancy, obligate carrier, carrier who may go on to manifest disease. Proband also called propositus/proposita. Relatives of first degree (parent-child, sibs), second degree (grandparent, uncle/aunt, half-sibs), third degree (first cousins).
[Notes] Box 1: proportion of genes in common = (1/2)^n per path, summed over paths: parent-child 1/2, sibs 1/2, half-sibs 1/4, uncle/aunt-nephew/niece 1/4, first cousins 1/8, second cousins 1/32. Coefficient of inbreeding = half the parents’ coefficient of relationship (first cousins: 1/16). Not covered in the lecture.

3. Autosomal dominant (AD)
Three questions to ask of the pedigree:

Are all generations affected? Yes.
Is the ratio of affected children about 50% in each mating? Roughly (his example matings: 2 of 3, 1 of 3 [transcript garbled], 2 of 4). Short generations make percentages “not very meaningful”.
Are both sexes affected? Yes.


Dominance: one mutated allele of the two is enough to show the disease. Recessiveness: both alleles must be mutated.
A healthy parent must have two normal alleles; the affected parent is probably heterozygous and passes either chromosome to each child: about 50%.
“Autosomal”: the mutated gene is on chromosomes 1 to 22, so sex does not matter.
Punnett square (Reginald Punnett, early 20th century): normal mother (AA) x affected heterozygous father (Aa, lower case = mutated): 2 of 4 normal homozygotes, 2 of 4 heterozygotes with the disease = 50% risk for each child. [Notes] Figure 2: same 1 in 2.
[Notes] Because AD disorders are rare, affected people are almost always heterozygotes.

Example: familial hypercholesterolemia (AD)

Very high LDL cholesterol in blood (“hundreds, thousands”) due to mutations in the LDL receptor in the liver. [Notes] Gene LDLR.
Lipid deposits in soft tissues (transcript “xanthelathic”; [Notes] tendon xanthomas and xanthelasmata of the eyelids). Same in the coronary arteries: coronary disease at 20 to 30 years of age.
Frequency 1 in 200 to 250 people (lecturer and [Notes] agree). Late enough onset that people reproduce before diagnosis, so the mutation is frequent and homozygotes occur.
Homozygotes: for most AD diseases two mutated alleles are lethal (the embryo dies); in FH they are born but have heart disease very young (“heart attack at 18-20 years of age”). [Notes] Homozygous form more severe, usually appears in childhood.
[Lucía] Also gives a mutation in APOB-100 (the LDL ligand for the receptor) as a cause. Not said in the lecture.

Complications in AD pedigrees








































Incomplete penetranceVariable expressivityDefinitionNot everyone with the mutation develops the diseaseThe disease presents in many different ways in different patientsTypical figure”the penetrance for this mutation is 80%” = 80% of carriers show the diseaseImaginary disease with brain, liver and skin symptoms: some patients have only some of themCause”usually unknown”, to do with how different genes cooperate (not explained, no time)Pedigree effectA healthy person who must carry the mutation (his example: II-2, with an affected mother and an affected child); can be confused with the recessive patternMildly affected relatives may be misdiagnosed and left as empty symbolsPedigree drawingQuarters of the symbol for each organ affected ([Slides] “Variable expressivity” pedigree: see the slide)LessonMolecular analysis: same mutation in all = incomplete penetrance; a new mutation arising in meiosis is “very unlikely”Be very sure the diagnosis is correct

[Lucía] Incomplete penetrance may involve additional variants (e.g. in the promoter) changing expression of the dominant allele. [Notes] (in Lec 9.3) Differences between affected relatives with the same disease allele are explained by modifier loci.

4. Autosomal recessive (AR)
Questions for the pedigree:

All generations affected? No.
50%? (garbled in the transcript; [Notes]: 25% per child of two carriers.)
Both sexes? Yes.
Consanguineous mating? Yes, in his example (first cousins; frequency varies with culture).


Many empty symbols are carriers with one mutated allele; disease only with both alleles mutated.
Parents of an affected child must both be healthy carriers (one mutated allele each). Without molecular analysis you do not know who else carries it.
Punnett square, Aa x Aa: 1/4 healthy non-carrier, 1/2 healthy carriers, 1/4 affected (homozygous mutated).
Counselling wording: risk the next child is affected = 1/4; healthy (no disease) = 3/4 (75%); of the healthy, 1/3 will not transmit the mutation and 2/3 will. Affected children always transmit it.

Consanguinity and compound heterozygotes

























True homozygoteCompound heterozygoteTypical settingConsanguineous parentsUnrelated parentsMutationsThe same mutation, inherited from a common ancestor, on both allelesTwo different mutations in the same gene (e.g. CFTR, one in one exon from the father, one in another exon from the mother)FunctionBoth copies inactivatedBoth copies inactivated; “in real terms it doesn’t matter”

Consanguinity raises the odds of two copies of a mutation “lying around” in a family meeting in one child.
[Notes] Figure 3 (A) compound heterozygotes, (B) true homozygotes via first cousins; risk stays 1 in 4 in both. For rare disorders, parental consanguinity strongly indicates AR.

Example: cystic fibrosis (AR)

One of the most common genetic diseases in European populations or people of European descent; the mutation appeared some centuries ago in Northern Europe.
The gene (CFTR) codes for a chloride channel. In epithelial cells that make mucus (bronchi, glands, pancreatic duct, liver), the salt (sodium chloride) concentration is wrong, the mucus becomes thick and blocks the lumen: in bronchi, pneumonia; in pancreas, pancreatitis. Blocked bronchioles and alveoli get infections and fibrosis, hence the name.
Carriers: about 1 in 20 people; “probably two of you in this room are carriers”.
[Slides] Organs affected: airways, lungs, pancreas, sweat glands. Distribution of CFTR mutations across the exons, with ΔF508 (transcript of slide “AF508”) the most frequent: see the slide.
[Notes] Frequency 1 in 2,500 to 3,500 newborns in Caucasian populations; meconium ileus, CF-related diabetes, congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens in most men.
[Notes] Carriers may show disease-related traits: sickle-cell trait (mild anaemia, sickling under hypoxia or exhaustion); sickle-cell disease is recessive but the trait is dominant. [Lucía] same. Not in the lecture.

5. X-linked recessive (XR)

Women have two X chromosomes, men one. A man passes his X to daughters and his Y to sons.
Pedigree: like AR (few people affected, not all generations), but only (or mostly) males are affected: this “should alert you” that it is X-linked.
Female carriers shown with a dot.


























ParentsDaughtersSonsCarrier mother x normal father1/2 normal, 1/2 healthy carriers; none affected1/2 unaffected, 1/2 affectedAffected father x normal motherAll healthy carriersAll healthy (father passes his Y)Affected father x carrier mother (“worst case”)1/2 affected1/2 affected

The third case is how women can rarely be affected (his example: a carrier who only knew of an uncle with hemophilia marries a man with hemophilia). [check] He also says “one fourth, 25% of the offspring” for this cross, then “50% of the daughters… and 50% of the sons” (which is 1/2 overall). [Notes] Figure 5B: “a 1 in 2 chance that a child would be affected, irrespective of whether it was a boy or girl”; the apparent male-to-male transmission is an illusion (the son’s mutant X came from his mother).
Examples: hemophilia A, colour blindness (“many things”).
“Work out the Punnett squares of the different situations is great fun.”

Example: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (XR)

“One of the most frequent” XR diseases. Named after the doctor who described it.
Muscle weakness and wasting from a young age; he gives about 10 years, wheelchair by 20, death by about 30 from respiratory failure. [verify] these ages in a textbook (no vault source gives them).
Mutations in dystrophin, a protein at the sarcolemma needed for communication between the muscle fibre and the extracellular matrix. Images: dystrophin staining at the sarcolemma; normal skeletal muscle cross-section vs dystrophic muscle with inflammation and fibres of different sizes (see the slide).
[Notes] About 1 in 5,000 newborn males; DMD gene; dystrophin in skeletal and cardiac muscle; female carriers have increased risk of cardiomyopathy. [Lucía] Death from respiratory failure (weak diaphragm) or heart failure (cardiomyopathy).

6. X-linked dominant (XD)

“Very, very rare”, few diseases.
Resembles AD: all generations, about 50%, both sexes.
Telltale sign: never father-to-son transmission. An affected male passes the mutation only to daughters (all of them), never to sons. “If you see that in a pedigree, you should think there’s something fishy going on… Careful.”
[Notes] More affected females than males; affected females milder and more variable (X-inactivation); in some XD disorders males die prenatally (incontinentia pigmenti, Figure 6B). [Lucía] example: X-linked hypophosphatemia (X-linked rickets). Neither example was given in the lecture.

7. X-chromosome inactivation

One of the two X chromosomes in females becomes inactive: seen cytologically as the Barr body, very densely packaged chromatin of the inactive X at the nuclear periphery. Named after “Murray Barr, Scottish doctor” ([verify] his nationality). [Slides] X-chromosome inactivation picture: see the slide.
Random: either X can be inactivated; happens early in the embryo. [check] Timing: lecturer “by the blastocyst stage, more or less, chromosome inactivation is complete”; [Notes] and [Lucía] the decision begins “at around the eight-cell stage” in the preimplantation embryo.
About 50% of a woman’s cells inactivate each X. With a mutation, if inactivation is skewed against the healthy X (e.g. 80% of cells keep the mutated X active), a heterozygous woman can show symptoms of the disease (“for some reasons that are rare”).
[Notes] These are manifesting heterozygotes; female carriers are mosaics; skewing can also protect carriers. Some genes (pseudoautosomal regions) escape inactivation. [Lucía] the inactive X is only about 60% inactivated; XIST is expressed from the X that will be inactivated.

8. Mitochondrial inheritance

Mitochondria have many copies of a short circular mtDNA; each cell has many mitochondria, each with many copies.
mtDNA codes some of the proteins of the OxPhos cascade (transcript: “some of the oxidase, and MAPH, blah, blah”, [verify] which ones he named); the rest are encoded in the nucleus. Mutations in mtDNA cause mitochondrial diseases.
All the zygote’s mitochondria come from the egg. [check] Lecturer: the sperm cell “has actually got rid of the mitochondria… there is a lot of debate about this”; [Notes]: the sperm does contribute mtDNA but paternal mtDNA is destroyed in the very early embryo after ubiquitin tagging; [Lucía]: males don’t contribute mitochondria at fertilization. All agree: no paternal mtDNA in the child.
Pattern: matrilineal. [Slides] “Males NEVER pass the disease. Females can pass the disease to sons and daughters. Some women are unaffected carriers.”
Unaffected carrier women: the number of mtDNA molecules with the mutation is very low, and not all mitochondria passed to the embryo carry it. (A garbled sentence before this, “Or not, but it has to be via a male, as it’s called”: [verify].)
[Notes] Heteroplasmy (mixed normal and mutant mtDNA) vs homoplasmy; variable heteroplasmy and the mitochondrial bottleneck explain variability within families; incomplete penetrance is common; high-energy tissues (muscle, brain) mainly affected; mtDNA 16.5 kb, 37 genes.
Student question: is all mtDNA from the mother? “Only from the mother… none from your father.” Hence the mitochondrial Eve of human evolution studies: using mtDNA, all humans living on Earth come from (coalesce into) a “mitochondrial Eve”; so mtDNA is useful for evolutionary studies too.

Lec 9.3 Polygenic inheritance
Sources

Lec 9.3 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Opens with “To deal with very, very common diseases” and ends with the announcement of Thursday’s TBL (“Okay?”).
Gaps: possibly the first sentence or two are clipped (the file starts mid-thought). No internal gaps seen. He shortened the end: “with this I will finish because my voice is starting to break”.

Resources

Slides: Slides Unit 9.pdf, the Alzheimer and heritability part (molecular characteristics of AD, ApoE Cys/Arg, AD summary slide, λs example, twin formula and concordance table with measles). Figures (APP processing, pathway diagram, regression plots, concordance values): see the slides.
Study material: none for 9.3 in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “Lecture 9.3 Polygenic inheritance and multifactorial diseases” (Box 1 liability threshold, Box 2 Alzheimer pathways, Figure 2 ApoE, Figure 3 types of study, Table 1 λs, Table 2 twin concordance, Figure 4 regression).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 9.3. Polygenic inheritance”, PDF p. 269-272.
Related notes: Lec 9.2 Single gene inheritance (previous class; pedigree twin symbols, incomplete penetrance), Lec 7.7 Genetic variation (SNPs), Lec 5.11 Cholesterol metabolism and lipid transport (apolipoproteins).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 9 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Heritability is the core concept: “If you know this, then you know a lot, more than most people around the world, because the concept of heritability is sometimes confusing” (section 2).
Twin formula h² = 2 x (CMZ - CDZ) and the point that “it’s not actually the concordance rate that matters. It’s the difference” (measles example, section 5). [Notes]: “In class we will apply this formula to some diseases in Table 2.”
The three types of study (familial aggregation, twins, adoption) plus the parent-offspring regression for quantitative traits (sections 4 to 7).
ApoE: “I think you have this slide anyway” (section 3).
Scope: estimating heritability and finding the causal variants come back next year in the second-year course Mecanismos de Enfermedad. “For this year we’ll just keep it simple.”
Multifactorial diseases “will affect 80% of the population”: very important for public health.
Admin: “So Thursday we have TBL… TBL 8-2 I think. So read whatever you have… to get ready for that TBL.” [check] The code log has no TBL 8.2; Thu 29 Oct is listed for TBL 8.1 (epigenetic diseases, Prader-Willi/Angelman) and TBL 9.2 (cell cycle dysregulation in cancer). In Lec 9.2 he said one remaining TBL is “TBL 8 something… related to epigenetics”. Check ADI for which TBL is on Thursday.

1. Polygenic, multifactorial (complex) diseases

Very common diseases affecting millions: heart disease, diabetes, neurodegenerative diseases, asthma, many autoimmune diseases, cancer.
Not usually considered genetic: not single genes, not Mendelian. But genes are involved in the predisposition: many genetic variants (SNPs, “remember the variants we talked about”), hundreds or thousands, each conferring increased susceptibility. Hence polygenic.
Plus environmental risk factors: cholesterol, dietary fat, exercise, lifestyle.
Genetic + environmental = multifactorial, “in modern days” called complex diseases.
They also appear in families, but less than single-gene diseases; they show different degrees of heritability.
[check] He says “many rare variants… SNPs”; [Notes] Box 2 describes the GWA-study loci for late-onset AD as common disease susceptibility factors with modest or weak effects, and says rare variants of strong effect occur in some subsets (heterogeneity). Possibly a transcription error for “many variants”.
[Notes] Even single-gene disorders are influenced by modifier loci. Non-genetic factors include environmental (sometimes via epigenetic modification) and chance (stochastic) factors. Affected individuals often appear as sporadic cases; some families show quasi-Mendelian transmission (early-onset AD, diabetes, Parkinson, cancers).

2. Heritability: the concept

Heritability = the contribution of genetic factors to the variation in the risk of developing a disease.
His example: if we could measure everyone’s risk of Alzheimer’s in the room, the values would form a normal (bell-shaped) distribution: few with very low risk, few with very high, most intermediate. A normal distribution is defined by mean and standard deviation; the curve can be narrower or broader with the same mean: “what is interesting here is the variance”.
Total phenotypic variance = genetic variance + environmental variance (VP = VG + VE). Environmental factors for Alzheimer’s he names: schooling (for cognitive diseases), diet, lifestyle, exercise (“quite important for the risk of developing Alzheimer’s in particular”).
Heritability measures how much of the total variance in risk is due to genetic factors.
[Notes] h² = VG/VP, from 0 (no genetic factors) to 1 (exclusively genetic). VG = additive + dominance + interaction effects. Heritability is not fixed: it describes a population in a specific environment, not an individual.
[Notes] Box 1, liability threshold: continuous susceptibility in the population, disease only above a threshold; in first-degree relatives the curve shifts to higher susceptibility, so more are affected. Thresholds can differ between sexes (pyloric stenosis about 1 in 200 newborn males vs 1 in 1000 females); environmental factors can move the threshold. (He described the shifted curve for siblings, section 4, but not the threshold.)
[Lucía] Only when risk goes beyond a certain threshold will a person manifest the disease.

3. Example: Alzheimer’s disease
Pathology

Two accumulations: amyloid plaques outside neurons and neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons (tangles made of phosphorylated tau).
Amyloid precursor protein (APP): a normal, physiological transmembrane protein, processed by β-secretase and then γ-secretase. γ-secretase can cut at different positions, releasing fragments of different sizes. Cutting at one position releases amyloid β-42 (42 amino acids), “particularly dangerous” because it aggregates into amyloid deposits (plaques).
Accumulation over years triggers an inflammatory reaction, loss of neurons, dementia. “It’s the action of γ-secretase that matters.”
[Slides] Plaques and tangles consist of amyloid fibrils with different components but similar tertiary (cross-β sheet) structure.
[Notes] Box 2: APP is 770 residues; Aβ40 is the predominant isoform, Aβ42 the most aggregation-prone; disease mutations raise the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio; APP duplication and trisomy 21 (three APP copies; APP on chromosome 21) also cause AD pathology.

Familial vs sporadic

























Familial (rare)Sporadic (typical)InheritanceLike autosomal dominant “basically, or almost”Does not run in familiesCauseMutations in presenilin (presenilin-1, -2), the gene for γ-secretase: more Aβ42; everyone who inherits the mutation develops ADNo mutations; genetic variants (SNPs) that shift the risk (“not just a black and white sort of situation”)OnsetVery aggressive; people of about 50 in these families

“Sporadic” = from time to time.
[Slides] Early onset < 65 years (β-amyloid pathway); late onset > 65 years, 95% of all patients (downstream pathways). [Notes] Dominant early-onset AD presents between 30 and 60; causative genes APP, PSEN1, PSEN2; presenilin is the catalytic subunit of γ-secretase.
[check] [Lucía] calls PSEN1 and PSEN2 “cofactors for beta-secretase”; lecturer and [Notes] both say presenilin is (the catalytic subunit of) γ-secretase.

ApoE: risk and protective variants

A risk factor known “for 20 years or more” (and “nobody really knew why”): a polymorphism in the APOE gene (apolipoprotein E).
Two variable positions: amino acid 112 and amino acid 158, each cysteine or arginine depending on the nucleotide ([Slides] “Cys Arg” figure; [Notes] Figure 2A).






























Allele112 / 158 (as he states it)Risk vs ε3/ε3 (lecturer)[Slides]ε2 (ApoE2)Cys / Cysε2/ε2: about halfε2 decreases risk to 0.6-foldε3 (ApoE3)one Cys, one Argε3/ε3 = 1, the average; most frequentε4 (ApoE4)Arg / Argone ε4: about 4 times; ε4/ε4: about 15 timesone ε4: 3-4-fold; two: 9-15-fold

He also says ε2/ε4 people have a risk “much lower than 15”.
[Slides] ε4 increases risk and lowers the age of onset of late-onset AD; ε2 seems protective. [Notes] One ε4 roughly threefold, two roughly fifteenfold; odds ratio close to 4; APOE*ε4 is the ancestral allele (great apes), also predisposes to cardiovascular disease; ApoE is also a modifier gene in presenilin families. [Lucía] one ε4 3-5 times, two up to 15 times. [check] numbers differ slightly between sources; the slides give 3-4-fold and 9-15-fold.
[check] [Lucía] says ApoE4 lowers the age of “early onset”; [Slides] and [Notes] link ApoE4 to late-onset AD.
[Lucía] gives the alleles as SNP combinations: T/T = ε2, T/C = ε3, C/C = ε4.

Why many genes: convergent pathways

The final phenotype results from several pathways working together: production of Aβ42, deposition, and clearance (macrophages or astrocytes in the brain degrade deposits). The balance decides the amount of amyloid β in plaques.
ApoE turned out to work in several of these pathways, “in subtle ways”, but strongly enough to change risk.
When a disease results from many converging pathways, you need several variants across them to raise or lower risk. The genes in yellow on his slide each raise the risk “by two times or three times” separately; combined (e.g. bad variants of “B1”, “Picarbonate” and ApoE in the transcript; probably BIN1 and PICALM, both in [Notes] Box 2 Figure 2) they explain the heritability of AD. Plus environmental factors, “always”.
[Notes] Box 2 Figure 2: early-onset genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2, blue) and GWA susceptibility loci (yellow: CR1, BIN1, CLU, SORL1, PICALM, GAB2, CH25H, ACE; APOE with a red border, moderately strong effect), grouped into production, clearance and degradation of Aβ. [Lucía] If clearance works well, even high Aβ production need not lead to disease.

4. Study type 1: familial aggregation (epidemiological) studies

Epidemiology studies how diseases are distributed in populations. Question: does the disease aggregate in families?
Siblings share half their alleles (50%), much more than two random people.
Take healthy people who have a sibling with the disease (his example: type 1 diabetes). Their risk curve is displaced to the right. Follow them 20 to 30 years and count how many develop it.
Relative risk (RR) or λ, subscript for the relationship (λS for siblings) = prevalence in relatives of affected people / prevalence in the general population.
[Slides] Worked example: general population 3/100, siblings 15/100, λS = 15/3 = 5 (“five times greater”). (He attaches this example to type 1 diabetes; it is illustrative: [Notes] Table 1 gives λS = 15 for type 1 diabetes, as he then says: “For type 1 diabetes it’s 15 times actually”.)
Problem: siblings share the family environment too, so the excess could be environmental.

[Notes] Table 1, approximate λS:









































DiseaseλSAlzheimer disease (late-onset)4Autism spectrum disorder6.5Breast cancer, female2Crohn’s disease25Multiple sclerosis20Schizophrenia9Type 1 diabetes15Type 2 diabetes3

His comments: type 1 diabetes very high (“more genetic factors involved in this because it’s an autoimmune disease”); type 2 not so high; Crohn’s and multiple sclerosis (autoimmune) very high; autism “quite a few factors”; schizophrenia: having a sibling or parent with it increases risk a lot.
Clinical aside, schizophrenia: the strongest environmental risk factor is cannabis use during adolescence, dose-dependent (“the number of joints you smoke during adolescence”) because the brain’s connections are still forming; the effect disappears in adulthood. Final risk = genetic + environmental: low genetic risk with very high environmental risk can still give disease.

5. Study type 2: twin studies

























Monozygotic (identical)Dizygotic (fraternal)OriginOne zygote that divided into two embryos very earlyTwo different fertilizations sharing the wombGeneticsIdentical (they acquire small differences over life)Share 50% of variants, like any siblingsSexSame sexCan differ

Concordance: if one twin has the disease, the other has it too (concordant pair); otherwise discordant. Measure concordance in many MZ and DZ pairs where at least one twin is affected.
Difficult: you need 100 to 200 pairs; usually collaborative between hospitals in several countries. A collection of such families “is a treasure”.
h² = 2 x (CMZ - CDZ). DZ concordance is what any pair of siblings would show; what matters is the difference, not whether the values are high or low.
His values from the slide: schizophrenia about 0.7 (“like 35 times 2”), Alzheimer’s about 0.48, type 1 diabetes about 0.7, type 2 lower, multiple sclerosis 0.4. Values above 0.4 “begin to be very, very suggestive of high heritability”.
Measles example: very contagious; twins share everything, so concordance is high in both: DZ about 0.9, MZ “very high as well”, “very similar”. h²: a difference of about 0.05, “0.05 times 2, 0.1”, very low. Same for a traffic accident: concordance may be high but genetics has no impact.

[Notes] Table 2, concordance (%), with h² worked out from it using his formula (computed here, not stated in the notes):



























































DiseaseMZDZ2 x (MZ - DZ)Type 1 diabetes42.97.40.71Type 2 diabetes34160.36Multiple sclerosis25.35.40.40Crohn’s disease37100.54Ulcerative colitis730.08Alzheimer disease32.28.70.47Parkinson disease15.511.10.09Schizophrenia40.85.30.71

[Notes] Significant discordance in MZ twins: “genetics is not everything!” Genetic factors much more important in schizophrenia than in Parkinson. Problems (Figure 3): same-sex DZ, MZ may be treated more alike; ideal (MZ separated at birth) too rare.
[Lucía] Example: if 80 of 100 co-twins of affected individuals are affected, concordance is 80%.

6. Study type 3: adoption studies

Even more difficult: someone adopted at birth (ideally) or very early into a different, distant family. Compare the biological family and the adoptive family.
If the adoptee develops a disease frequent in the adoptive family: probably environmental. If, e.g. at 25, he develops a disease present in the biological family: genetic factors.
“The only type of study that really corrects for environmental factors”; if it shows up, genetic factors must be very strong.
Logistics: workable for frequent diseases (type 1 diabetes); for rarer ones hard to find adoptees who developed the disease, and you must trace who had it in both families.
[Notes] Figure 3 problems: adoption at birth? selective placement? intrauterine influences?

7. Heritability of quantitative (continuous) traits

Variables can be continuous (height, blood pressure, blood glucose) or categorical/dichotomous (healthy vs diseased; hypertension yes/no).
For a continuous trait (his example: blood pressure), compare the mid-parent value (mean of father and mother) with the offspring value.
Plot mid-parent (x) vs child (y) and fit a regression line, y = coefficient x X. The slope = heritability.
No genetic influence: high-pressure parents with low-pressure children and vice versa, a shapeless cloud, flat line, slope near 0. Strong genetic influence: slope tends to 1.
Hard to do: you must measure the trait in parents and children.
[Notes] Figure 4: values normalized (mean = 0); slope of the regression line shows low (left) or high (right) heritability. Infectious diseases are mainly environmental, though host genetics contributes; schizophrenia, ASD, AD, type 1 diabetes, MS and Crohn’s have a strong genetic contribution; Parkinson and type 2 diabetes less.

8. Closing

These methods are how we “suss out the genetic influence of complex diseases”, an important public health issue.
Next year: how to identify which variants and genes are responsible ([Notes]: using the variability in human genomes, mostly single-nucleotide variants).

p21: “This is important also, the important exam” (garbled; probably “important for the exam”; section 3).
Oncogenic addiction: “a concept that we need to know” (section 6).
Resistance to targeted therapy and the minor resistant clone: “do you understand this, this is very important for cancer treatment” (section 6).

CML / BCR-ABL: “we are not going to ask in the final exam diseases or you don’t have to know this is related to leukemia” (garbled). [verify] what he said is not examined. Note that the Lec 9.1 lecturer said the CML t(9;22) case was the centre of a past exam.

Recurring “you have studied this” items he assumes: EGFR, HER2, p53, p21, Rb, BCR-ABL / Philadelphia chromosome, DNA methylation, FISH.

1. Overview

Cancer is a genetic disease, also influenced by external and environmental factors.
Two families of genes are responsible: oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes.
Plan: the two concepts; how oncogenes are generated and how tumour suppressor genes are mutated; drugs that target some oncogenes.
Opening image: a breast cancer specimen, immunohistochemistry for HER2: huge expression, “this is what is driving this tumour”. HER2 stimulates proliferation, so these tumours are highly aggressive.

2. Oncogenes

Oncogenes = abnormal versions of proto-oncogenes. Proto-oncogenes = genes coding for cell-cycle-promoting proteins: normal function is to stimulate the cell cycle.
Examples: EGFR (membrane receptor binding EGF, epidermal growth factor; stimulates proliferation), HER2 (membrane protein, stimulates proliferation), and all proteins that move the cell cycle forward, e.g. cyclins and CDKs (G1 to S).
Problem: gain of function: “they function too much”.
Mutation types (EGFR as the example):































Inactivating mutationHyperactivating (activating) mutationFrequencyMost mutations, for EGFR and “for the whole genome”RareEffect on proteinMesses up the protein; sometimes it disappearsProtein not destroyed; more active than normalFor EGFRNo problem for cancer: cells won’t divide, or dieReceptor sends too many signals for cell divisionSettingLung cancer: many patients with EGFR-mutated tumours

Oncogenes are dominant: a mutation in one allele is enough to hyperstimulate the cell.
[Lucía] EGFR hyperactivating mutations are present in 10-15% of lung cancers.

3. Tumour suppressor genes

The opposite concept: genes coding for proteins that slow down or stop the cell cycle. Examples: p53, p21, Rb.






















ProteinRole (lecturer)p53Apoptosis (student answer); regulates the DNA damage response: stops the cell cycle when needed so DNA can be repaired; if not repairable, apoptosisp21Regulated (induced) by p53; a CDK-cyclin inhibitor: blocks the kinase activity of e.g. CDK4-cyclin D, so the cycle stops after DNA damage; once the damage is fixed, p21 expression disappears and the cycle continuesRbBlocks E2F and controls cell proliferation; if Rb is mutated, cells proliferate (tumours)

Mutations very frequent in p53 (“the most mutated of the three”), also quite frequent in p21 and Rb.
Tumour suppressor genes are recessive: usually both alleles must be mutated to lose the activity; with one mutation, the other copy usually compensates.
[Lucía] Rb is bound to E2F; when phosphorylated it releases E2F, which acts as a transcription factor. Having one dysfunctional allele makes the other more prone to mutation and silencing.

4. How proto-oncogenes become oncogenes






























MechanismWhat happensHis examplePoint mutationHyperactive proteinEGFR (section 2)Gene amplificationInstead of two copies (two alleles), “five, six, ten, a hundred copies”; the sequence is normal, no mutation; overproduction of the protein; same effect: hyperactivity, signalling dysregulated, cells divide all the timeHER2 in breast cancer (also ovarian cancer sometimes, and others, but mainly breast)Chromosome rearrangement: viral insertion near the promoterA virus infects the cell and inserts its DNA in the promoter region of a proto-oncogene (“it’s not just an image, this happens”); expression is altered: many copies of mRNA and protein instead of normal regulated productionGene A (generic)Chromosome rearrangement: fusion proteinA translocation joins part of gene B (from another chromosome) to gene A: mixed mRNA and a fusion protein. Often abnormal and non-functional (the cell may die: “Who cares?”); the problem is when the fusion protein is hyperactiveBCR-ABL

BCR-ABL: the Philadelphia chromosome, from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (portions exchanged both ways), producing a small abnormal chromosome and a hyperactive fusion protein stimulating pathways of cell division. Very common in chronic myeloid leukaemia: the cause in a large percentage of patients. (See Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis.)
[Lucía] lists “deletions or point mutations in the coding sequence” as mechanism 1, and for the rearrangement, “relocation of a promoter region” near the gene.

5. How tumour suppressor genes are inactivated





















MechanismWhat happensPoint mutationNon-functional gene (e.g. p53)Chromosome loss (of a piece)A missing region containing many genes, e.g. including p53, which is then absentPromoter methylationDNA methylation of the promoter silences the gene: the gene is normal and present, but no protein is made

Because both alleles must be affected, combinations inactivate the two copies: two point mutations (one per chromosome), point mutation plus chromosomal deletion, promoter methylation plus point mutation. Any combination affecting both alleles transforms a normal cell into a tumour cell.
[Lucía] lists four: inactivating point mutations, chromosome deletion, chromosome loss (of a whole chromosome), silencing by DNA methylation.

6. EGFR: targeted therapy, oncogenic addiction and resistance
The video (narration of a trial summary; “you don’t have to learn anything” from it)

A point mutation in the EGFR coding region, T790M, reduces binding of EGFR-TKI therapy to the receptor: less inhibition, cancer progression.
Osimertinib: oral, irreversible EGFR-TKI, selective for both EGFR and T790M resistance variants, active against central nervous system metastases.
Trial: 419 patients with T790M-positive advanced non-small cell lung cancer who progressed after prior EGFR-TKI therapy; 144 (34%) with asymptomatic CNS metastases; randomized to osimertinib daily vs IV platinum plus “hemotrexate” chemotherapy (as transcribed) every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, then “hemotrexate” maintenance. [verify] the name of the second chemotherapy drug.
Median progression-free survival 10.1 months (osimertinib) vs 4.4 months (chemotherapy), hazard ratio 0.30. CNS metastases subgroup: 8.5 vs 4.2 months. Side effects: diarrhoea, rash, dry skin; severe myelotoxicity less common than with chemotherapy. Results at NEJM.org.
His summary: osimertinib blocks the specific mutated EGFR found in lung cancer patients; it is better than chemotherapy and is used now in patients.
[Lucía] First-line drug gefitinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI): blocks EGFR kinase activity and signalling. Up to 60% develop the T790M resistance mutation in the kinase domain, so the drug cannot bind. Osimertinib binds normal and mutated kinase domains and crosses the blood-brain barrier. Drugs ending in -ib are chemical compounds; -ab are therapeutic antibodies. (None of this is in the transcript.)

Oncogenic addiction

For some oncogenic mutations (e.g. EGFR), the tumour depends very much on the mutation: it is “addicted” to it.
Blocking the mutated receptor makes the tumour collapse: a very intense response, massive cell death. Does not apply to all oncogenes, but to many.
Response: the tumour shrinks very much, sometimes disappears; often something remains on the CT scan, but the response is “quite impressive”.

Resistance

In most patients, after several months, the tumour grows again.
In the clinic, EGFR is sequenced at the beginning for all such patients: no mutation, the therapy makes no sense; mutation, eligible for the drug.
Sequencing the relapsed tumour often shows another EGFR mutation with the same effect (signals for division) that the drug does not affect.
Origin (probably; “unknown at this point”): a small resistant clone with the second mutation already in the original tumour, while the dominant clone drove the original growth. The drug eliminates the dominant clone; the minor clone grows. Industry must then design a new drug for the resistant protein.
Very common for cancer therapies in general, more specifically for targeted therapy.





















Targeted therapyChemotherapyAimOne specific proteinAll proliferating cellsHis image”like a venom, like a poison”
7. HER2 in breast cancer (second file)

[Lucía] (gap fill) 25-30% of breast cancer patients overexpress HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2), in primary tumours and metastatic sites.

The HER2 video (narration)

HER2 membrane overexpression in cancer cells is much higher than in normal adult tissue; overexpression is found in primary tumour and metastases: rationale for anti-HER2 therapy at all disease sites.
Trastuzumab: the first HER2 inhibitor registered for HER2-overexpressing breast cancer; a recombinant monoclonal antibody against the extracellular domain of HER2 (binds domain 4). Approved in the metastatic and adjuvant settings. Proposed mechanisms: antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, preventing formation of a truncated membrane-bound HER2 fragment, receptor downregulation; main mechanism thought to be binding to HER2 and inhibition of HER2 signal transduction.
Pertuzumab: fully humanized monoclonal antibody binding domain 2 (extracellular, essential for dimerization); sterically blocks ligand-induced homodimerization and HER2-HER3 heterodimerization (which activates survival signalling, e.g. PI3K-AKT). Trastuzumab has only a minor effect in the presence of ligand.
Approved mid-2012 with trastuzumab and docetaxel for metastatic or locally recurrent unresectable HER2-positive breast cancer without prior anti-HER2 therapy or chemotherapy for metastatic disease.

His comments

Approved combination: two blocking antibodies on different domains plus docetaxel (“this taxane”, one of the drugs that block the microtubules; transcript “macrubule decolonization”, [verify] what he said about the mechanism). A trial combining them gave better response and overall survival.
Cancer therapy usually combines drugs, but there is a balance: more drugs may work better, but toxicity can rise “exponentially” and become unbearable.
Antibodies bound to chemotherapy (new drugs “combining antibodies bound to chemotherapy”; “a revolution also in oncology”, “a very hot topic”; already approved): chemotherapy molecules bound to the antibody (e.g. trastuzumab). Injected in blood, the antibody goes quickly to the tumour and binds HER2; the cell internalizes HER2 + antibody + chemotherapy by endocytosis; endosome, lysosome; the drug is released inside the cell, blocks microtubules and the tumour cell collapses. Both effects: HER2 blocking plus targeted chemotherapy, avoiding chemotherapy circulating everywhere and hitting all dividing cells.
[Lucía] The conjugated toxin is called TDM1 (with trastuzumab); causes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis by inhibiting microtubule assembly.

8. Testing HER2: immunohistochemistry and FISH

Before anti-HER2 therapy you must show the target is present.
Immunohistochemistry first (easier): strong membrane staining in the primary tumour = eligible.
FISH for gene amplification: two DNA probes, e.g. green for the centromere of the chromosome and red for HER2.

Normal cells: two green and two red signals per cell.
Some cells show only one or no signal: the tissue is a section, so part of the nucleus is not captured.
Amplification: many red dots per cell.


Practice: IHC first; if the result is unclear (“superior” in the transcript, [verify]) they do FISH. With three or four copies the result is doubtful; with 20 or 100 copies, the woman is going to respond.
[Lucía] The centromere probe labels chromosome 17, where HER2 is; cancer cells typically show one green dot followed by many red ones. [check] The lecturer expects two green signals per cell (fewer only from sectioning); Lucía describes one green dot.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Metabolic map 5: integration of fatty acid oxidation, Krebs, transamination and purine synthesis
Source: Audio Clip 16 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). A short review session (probably Dr. Pérez-Mediavilla, given the topics and style) walking through “map 5”, a metabolic map with lettered unknowns, followed by an ADI group quiz. Several minutes of the recording are noise.
Related: Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation, Lec 5.8 Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle, Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies, Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis, Lec 5.12 Nucleotide metabolism. Previous-year notes: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “TBL 5.3 Integration” (PDF p. 154-155).
Marking: [check] = lecturer or transcript conflicts with a source in your vault (named). [verify] = possible error that the sources in your vault do not settle. The map itself is not in the transcript; letters below are the ones read out in class.
Reading the map

Keys: a membrane separating two compartments = the inner mitochondrial membrane; palmitoyl-CoA in the cytoplasm; a transport system for it = the carnitine shuttle.
Palmitoyl-CoA enters the matrix and is converted into myristoyl-CoA (14 C) + L: so the process is beta-oxidation and L = acetyl-CoA.
L condenses with J to give I: J = oxaloacetate, I = citrate. Part of the citrate is oxidized in the Krebs cycle, part is exported to the cytoplasm.
In the cytoplasm citrate is split (citrate lyase) into acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate (Lec 5.10 Lipid synthesis).
Oxaloacetate is transaminated with glutamate, giving aspartate and N = alpha-ketoglutarate. The enzyme is aspartate aminotransferase.
Aspartate donates its amino group in purine synthesis: IMP (inosine monophosphate, a purine nucleotide and the precursor of AMP and GMP) to adenylosuccinate; adenylosuccinate lyase releases AMP (6-aminopurine) and fumarate, which can be oxidized in the Krebs cycle (Lec 5.12 Nucleotide metabolism).

The point of the map: parallel reactions
The two oxidations of beta-oxidation are chemically the same as two Krebs reactions:





















Beta-oxidationKrebs cycleAcyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD): acyl-CoA to trans-enoyl-CoASuccinate dehydrogenase (FAD): succinate to fumarateEnoyl-CoA hydratase: hydration to beta-hydroxyacyl-CoAFumarase: hydration of fumarate to malateBeta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (NAD+): to beta-ketoacyl-CoAMalate dehydrogenase (NAD+): malate to oxaloacetate
The 5.9 study notes say the same: the first three beta-oxidation reactions are analogous to succinate dehydrogenase, fumarate hydratase and malate dehydrogenase (Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies).
Transamination recap

Purpose: collect the amino groups of all 20 amino acids into a few (mainly glutamate, then alanine and glutamine) with one general reaction instead of 20 enzymes.
A transaminase moves the amino group of an amino acid to the carbonyl of an alpha-keto acid: with pyruvate you make alanine; with alpha-ketoglutarate you make glutamate.
Glutamate can be aminated to glutamine. Lecturer: this happens mainly in the brain, which sends ammonia to the liver as glutamine; glutamate itself is “too acidic” to be the transport form. [verify] these two claims; Lec 5.8 Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle says glutamine is used by most extrahepatic tissues.
[check] The transcript says “with alpha-ketoglutarate we will produce glutamine”; transamination of alpha-ketoglutarate gives glutamate (5.8 notes and Lucía).
Carbon skeletons: some give glucose (oxaloacetate, pyruvate, succinate, malate); those that give acetyl-CoA cannot make glucose.

Clinical names of the two main transaminases




















NameAlternative name (blood tests)ReactionAST (aspartate aminotransferase)GOT (glutamate-oxaloacetate transaminase)Aspartate + alpha-ketoglutarate to oxaloacetate + glutamateALT (alanine aminotransferase)GPT (glutamate-pyruvate transaminase)Alanine + alpha-ketoglutarate to pyruvate + glutamate
The GOT/GPT names tell you the substrates.
Quiz answers given in class

Coenzyme Q is directly reduced by electrons from both succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, FADH2) and fatty acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (via ETF) (Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation).
CAT I: inhibited by the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (malonyl-CoA); catalyzes the rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation; catalyzes a transesterification. All three statements true.
Turns to oxidize myristoyl-CoA (14 C): 6 turns, so 6 FADH2 (and 7 acetyl-CoA). [check] Someone in class said “14 carbons are 7 cuts”; by the rule in the 5.9 note (turns = n/2 - 1) it is 6.
Cofactor for transaminations: pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). “Typical question.”
Urea cycle enzyme in the question: the class debated arginase vs argininosuccinase. The lecturer clarified that arginase is the enzyme that splits arginine into urea + ornithine, while argininosuccinase (argininosuccinate lyase) releases fumarate. [verify] which option was marked correct; the recording is unclear.
Main regulator of urea synthesis: N-acetylglutamate, the allosteric activator of CPS I; without it CPS I does not work. “Typical question”, “very important”.

TBL 5.3 Integration of metabolism (review session)
Source: TBL 5 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). A review session (“we are preparing the final exam now”) by the lecturer of the 5.7-5.12 block (probably Dr. Pérez-Mediavilla; he refers to “Dr. Pío” and “Dr. Keogh” as colleagues). The recording starts mid-session and ends before the group quiz. The blank cycle diagrams are in a separate ADI file; he gives the answers afterwards.
Related: Lec 5.7 Oxidative phosphorylation, Lec 5.8 Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle, Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies, Map 5 Integration session, lecture-5-5-gluconeogenesis-and-glycogen-metabolism-notes. Previous-year notes: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “TBL 5.3. Integration of metabolism” (PDF p. 154-155).
Marking: [Lucía] = gap filled from FMCI  Lucia Reed notes. [check] = lecturer or transcript conflicts with a source in your vault (named). [verify] = possible error that the sources in your vault do not settle.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Why fatty acids cannot give net glucose (section 5): “a typical question at the exam”.
Odd-chain fatty acids as a glucose source: “another typical question”, though “not strongly important”.
Advice: draw the cycles (Cori, glucose-alanine, fasting) on a small piece of paper to fix them.

1. Cori cycle (muscle and liver)

Triggered by intense exercise: muscle energy comes from glycogen to glucose to pyruvate.
There is not enough O2 to reoxidize the NADH to NAD+, but glycolysis needs cytosolic NAD+. Escape route: pyruvate is reduced to lactate with those electrons.
Lactate still contains carbon and energy, but cannot be used in the muscle: it travels in the blood to the liver, which makes glucose by gluconeogenesis and sends it back to the muscle. This closes the cycle.
[Lucía] Lactate goes into circulation so as not to lower the pH in the muscle cell.
Blind-cycle exercise from class: the right-hand tissue (muscle) uses glucose, makes fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, splits it into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and DHAP, then to phosphoenolpyruvate, pyruvate and K = lactate.

2. Fuels of muscle

Strong exercise (start of exercise): glycogen and glucose, producing lactate (Cori cycle).
Light activity or rest: mainly fatty acids, a little glucose, and a small amount of ketone bodies (at rest, with balanced nutrition, little ketogenesis).
Phosphocreatine: a quick reserve; its phosphate rephosphorylates ADP, catalyzed by creatine kinase.
Clinical: high blood creatine kinase means tissue damage, mainly muscle (also heart, e.g. heart attack).

3. Liver in prolonged fasting and untreated type 1 diabetes

Low blood glucose is sensed by the pancreas, which releases glucagon.
In adipose tissue, glucagon binds its GPCR: G-alpha exchanges GDP for GTP and separates from beta-gamma; G-alpha-s activates adenylyl cyclase; cAMP activates PKA, which activates hormone-sensitive lipase. TAG is broken down and fatty acids are released (Lec 5.9 Fatty acid catabolism and ketone bodies).
Fatty acids reach the liver, are activated to acyl-CoA, cross the carnitine shuttle and are oxidized to acetyl-CoA.
The liver is also doing gluconeogenesis, which uses oxaloacetate. Acetyl-CoA cannot enter the Krebs cycle, so it is converted into ketone bodies, exported as fuel for peripheral tissues.


Untreated type 1 diabetes: no insulin, so high blood glucose but none inside the tissues, because insulin is needed to bring glucose transporters to the membrane. The body behaves as in fasting.
Ketone body production must be monitored: high levels lower blood pH (ketoacidosis).
[check] The lecturer called glucagon’s receptor “the beta-adrenergic glucagon receptor”; beta-adrenergic receptors bind adrenaline. In the 5.9 lecture he described it as the glucagon receptor (both are Gs-coupled GPCRs; Lucía: glucagon and epinephrine both trigger lipolysis).
[Lucía] Fatty acids travel bound to serum albumin; in the liver acetyl-CoA becomes ketone bodies (hydroxybutyrate), converted back to acetyl-CoA in the brain or other tissues. Diabetics make them because their body does not detect the glucose in the blood.

4. Fuels of the brain

Mainly glucose: on average 100-200 g per day (depends on size and activity).
Without enough glucose, the brain uses beta-hydroxybutyrate (and acetoacetate) for a short period. Brain, muscle and heart can use ketone bodies for a short time.
Ketone bodies: acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. No tissue is adapted to use acetone.
[check] The transcript lists “hair” among the tissues using ketone bodies; it is the heart.

5. Can we make glucose from these carbons? (typical exam questions)



































Carbon sourceNet glucose?WhyAlanine (keto acid: pyruvate)YesPyruvate is gluconeogenicAspartate (keto acid: oxaloacetate)YesGlutamate (keto acid: alpha-ketoglutarate)YesNot directly to PEP, but via succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate, oxaloacetateEven-chain fatty acids (acetyl-CoA)NoSee belowOdd-chain fatty acids (last turn gives propionyl-CoA)Yes, the propionyl partPropionyl-CoA becomes succinyl-CoA, which gives net oxaloacetate
Why acetyl-CoA gives no net oxaloacetate: acetyl-CoA (2 C) condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate, then isocitrate; isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase each release one CO2. So the 2 C that entered leave before oxaloacetate is regenerated: no net gain (Lec 5.8 Amino acid catabolism and the urea cycle, section 8).
Student question: “doesn’t pyruvate have the same problem?” No, because pyruvate used for gluconeogenesis does not enter the Krebs cycle: in the mitochondrion it is carboxylated and leaves as malate, which is reoxidized to oxaloacetate.

[check] The transcript says pyruvate “is carboxylated to malate”; Lucía’s gluconeogenesis notes: pyruvate carboxylase turns pyruvate into oxaloacetate in the mitochondria. Review gluconeogenesis (lecture-5-5-gluconeogenesis-and-glycogen-metabolism-notes) for the malate step.

6. Glucose-alanine cycle in fasting

In long fasting (hypoglycemia) with continued activity, muscle uses alternative fuels: fatty acids and proteins.
Protein use starts with transamination; the nitrogen goes to the liver, the only tissue that converts it into urea.
The resulting keto acids feed gluconeogenesis (section 5).

7. Receptor review (GPCRs)

Main receptor types: GPCRs, tyrosine kinase receptors, ion channels (ligand-gated), and intracellular receptors (e.g. steroid hormones).
GPCR = G protein-coupled receptor: 7 transmembrane domains, coupled to heterotrimeric G proteins (not monomeric ones such as Ras, which GPCRs can only affect indirectly).
Signalling depends on the G-alpha type:

Gs: activates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP up).
Gi: inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
Gq: activates phospholipase C, which hydrolyzes PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate), producing IP3. IP3 opens Ca2+ channels of the endoplasmic reticulum; free Ca2+ activates other proteins (e.g. PKC) and membrane channels.


cAMP is a soluble second messenger: the signal moves from the membrane into the cytoplasm. It acts on proteins with cAMP-binding domains, chiefly PKA (cAMP-dependent protein kinase).

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
TBL 7.2 CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing
Sources

TBL 7 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file only. The transcript file is named “TBL 7”; its content matches the TBL 7.2 slides (CRISPR, Dr. Serrano, 22 Oct 2026), not TBL 7.1 (apoptosis and senescence).
Coverage: sections 1 to 7 come from the transcript. Gap: the recording stops mid-sentence while listing the complications of beta thalassemia major (“kidney failure is because this also…”). Everything after that (rest of complications, treatment, fetal hemoglobin, BCL11A, the Casgevy procedure, patient results, problems) is filled from the slides only (section 8). No group quiz or iRAT questions were recorded.

Resources

Slides: TBL 7.2 CRISPR_ST.pdf
Study material: none for TBL 7.2 in the vault (“STUDY MATERIAL TBL 7.1.pdf” belongs to TBL 7.1).
Previous TBL (progeria example): TBL 7.1 Students.pdf
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “Lecture 7.8 DNA damage and repair” (NHEJ and homologous recombination repair) and “Lecture 9.5 Ethical considerations” (CRISPR and germ-line editing).
Lucía: TBL 7.2 is new this year and not in her notes. Related sections used: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “Lecture 3.4 Microtransport” (CFTR, PDF p. 47-49) and “Lecture 9.2 Patterns of single gene inheritance” (sickle cell, from PDF p. 265).
Related notes: DNA Replication Study Notes (Lecture 7.3).

Marking: [Slides] = filled from the TBL 7.2 slides. [Notes] = filled from the FMC I Genetics class notes. [Lucía] = filled from Lucía’s notes. [check] = transcript conflicts with a vault source (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

None stated in the recorded part. He did not say what would be examined or what to skip.
The slides’ first content slide is a list of key components (CRISPR sequences, spacers, Cas9, guide RNA, tracrRNA) with one-line definitions; these are the obvious definitions to know (section 1 table).

1. What CRISPR/Cas9 is

In evolution, CRISPR/Cas9 originated as an adaptive immune system of bacteria.
Discovered by the Spanish researcher Francisco Mojica, in 1993 (lecturer’s date; not on the slides).




































ComponentLecturer[Slides] definitionCRISPR sequencesShort, palindromic, repeated sequences; they gave the technique its nameClustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic RepeatsSpacersSit between the repeats; correspond to DNA sequences of viruses that infected the bacteriumDNA sequences derived from viruses that attacked the bacteriumtracrRNA”Trans-activating CRISPR RNA”; a scaffolding RNA that binds the spacer-derived guideSmall scaffolding RNA that facilitates binding of gRNA to Cas9Guide RNA (gRNA, crRNA)The spacer-derived RNA that binds the tracrRNASmall RNA sequence matching a target DNA sequence, directing Cas9 to cut the DNACas9The “molecular scissors”; the enzyme that cuts the viral DNAAn enzyme that cuts DNA at specific locations

[verify] The length of the spacers is garbled in the transcript (“20-20”). See the slide figure.
[verify] The bacterial species the lecturer named is garbled (“Peptogogos”). Check which species he meant.

2. How it works in bacteria (two phases)

Acquisition (memory). A virus infects a bacterium. The system takes fragments of the viral DNA and incorporates them into the bacterium’s own DNA as spacers in the CRISPR array. The bacterium now holds a “memory” of that virus.
Defence. When the same virus attacks again (the same bacterium, or its descendants after division), the system activates:

the spacer-derived guide RNA binds the tracrRNA (scaffold);
tracrRNA + guide RNA bind Cas9, forming an active RNA-protein complex;
the complex interrogates the viral genome, searching for the sequence that matches the spacer;
when it finds it, Cas9 cuts the viral DNA, stopping the virus.




It is “primitive” but adaptive: specific for each virus, and works against as many viruses as there are spacers in the bacterium.

3. Adapting the system to human cells

The system can be transferred to eukaryotes, including humans, with minor modifications.
Main modification: tracrRNA and guide RNA are fused into a single guide RNA (sgRNA) with two segments: the scaffold (tracrRNA part) and a guide sequence designed to match a chosen region of the genome.
By choosing the guide’s nucleotides, Cas9 is targeted to a specific human gene. When it finds the sequence, it makes a double-strand break (DSB).
[verify] A garbled phrase (“and we can put plasma”) follows the sgRNA description; check the slide for what he meant.

4. How the cell repairs the Cas9 cut
The cell must fix the double-strand break. Two options:



































Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)Homology-directed repair (HDR)LecturerSimply joins the two broken endsThe cell repairs the break by homologous recombinationTemplateNoneNeeds a donor DNA (repair template)ResultSmall deletions (lost nucleotides) or insertions (added nucleotides) at the cutThe sequence of the donor is copied in: allows correction of a geneUseChanges the reading frame, so the protein is non-functional and its expression is lostGene correction (section 5)[Notes] Genetics notes, Lec 7.8No template; ends fused quickly; hallmark of NHEJ-repaired sequences is small deletions, sometimes insertions; available throughout the cell cycle; less accurateHomologous recombination repair normally uses the sister chromatid as template; highly accurate; acts after replication

Transcription correction: the transcript says “an homologous end joining”, but the pathway described (no template, ends simply joined, contrasted with homology-directed repair) is non-homologous end joining, as named in the Genetics notes.
Link to protein synthesis: he reminded the class that inserting or deleting nucleotides alters the reading frame (see Unit 8, genetic code and protein synthesis).

5. Example: correcting a disease gene

Lecturer’s example: a disease taught “a few weeks back” caused by mutations in a transporter gene.

[verify] The disease and gene names are garbled (“C-5 process”, “TRG”). The context fits cystic fibrosis / CFTR, which was taught as a transporter example in microtransport. [Lucía] CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) expels Cl-; in cystic fibrosis it is mutated and does not work (Lecture 3.4, PDF p. 47-49). Confirm this is the disease he meant.


Strategy:

Design two sgRNAs, one on each side of the mutated region.
Cas9 cuts at both sites, removing the whole region carrying the mutation from the patient’s cells.
Provide a repair template: a fixed copy of the gene without the mutation.
The cell repairs by homologous recombination using the template, giving a corrected gene.


Feasible in principle, sometimes easy, but this is where the ethical concerns begin.

6. Ethical and practical concerns

To cure a patient, the system must be delivered to all the affected cells of the organism.

Example from the previous TBL (TBL 7.1): progeria, caused by a single point mutation in the lamin A (LMNA) gene. Curing it would require modifying the genome in every cell. [Slides] TBL 7.1 lists a “gene corrector” (CRISPR-Cas9) and gene therapy among cutting-edge therapies, with improvement in transgenic progeria mice.


Modifying the human genome “by our will”: some people accept it, but bioethics committees raise major concerns.
Vectors: the CRISPR/Cas9 system has to be transferred into human cells with a vector, e.g. modified viruses that reach every cell. This can be problematic.
Feasible in theory; easy in some cases; a lot of work still needed.
[Notes] Genetics notes, Lec 9.5: approved gene therapies are somatic (the change is not inherited); germ-line editing would be transmitted to descendants and is prohibited by law in many countries. In November 2018 a researcher in China announced the birth of twin girls (and another child) from CRISPR-edited embryos, aimed at HIV resistance; experts called it unnecessary and risky.

7. Nobel Prize and Mojica

Lecturer: Mojica made the original discovery (1993); the optimization of the system for use in humans was awarded the Nobel Prize to researchers from the US and other countries. He presented it as a pity that Mojica was not included (transcript garbled; this is the clear sense of both passages).
[check] The transcript gives the prize year as “1930”. [Slides]: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuel Charpentier (spelling as on the slide).

8. First CRISPR therapy: Casgevy

[Slides] Name: Casgevy (code CTX001). Indication: beta thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD).
Lecturer: it cleared all ethical committees and is approved in the US and Europe.

[verify] The approval date is inconsistent in the transcript (“approved in 2023 … December of 2020”). The slides give no date. Check the year and month.


[verify] He said something like “this is some way of malaria” when introducing thalassemia and sickle cell disease; garbled, and no vault source in this TBL explains the link. Ask or check the slide.

8.1 Hemoglobin, sickle cell disease and thalassemia

Normal adult hemoglobin: transports oxygen and carbon dioxide; 4 subunits: 2 alpha-globins and 2 beta-globins. Red blood cells have a normal shape.
Sickle cell disease (lecturer): mutation in beta-globin. The hemoglobin works but transports oxygen less efficiently. Red blood cells take an aberrant (sickle) shape, pass badly through capillaries and can block vessels.

[Lucía] / [Notes] (single-gene inheritance): affected people are homozygous for a beta-globin mutation and make HbS; the cells become rigid and sickle-shaped, have a shorter life span (anemia) and block small vessels (hypoxic tissue damage). Carriers can have mild anemia (sickle-cell trait).


Thalassemia: alpha or beta thalassemia [Slides]. The one treated with CRISPR (Casgevy) is beta thalassemia (lecturer; slides also list SCD).
Lecturer: thalassemia is quite common in some populations. [verify] which populations; garbled (“new world”).





















Beta thalassemiaGenes affectedSeverityMinorOne geneMilderMajorBoth genesSevere
Symptoms (similar to anemia; lecturer: usually in beta thalassemia minor):





























SymptomSourceFeeling tired or weakLecturer and slidesShortness of breath[Slides]PalenessLecturer and slidesDizziness and faintingLecturer (“dizziness”) and slidesHeadachesLecturer and slides

[verify] The lecturer also said “pain is very common”; pain is not on the slide list. Check whether he said pain or fainting.

Complications (beta thalassemia major):

Blood clots (blood tends to coagulate and clog a vessel), which can lead to heart attack (lecturer and slides).
Liver and kidney failure (lecturer and slides; recording ends here).
[Slides] Dementia; diabetes.

[Slides] Treatment (major thalassemia):

Regular blood transfusions.
Iron chelation (iron overload caused by the transfusions).
Bone marrow transplant.

8.2 [Slides] How Casgevy works (not in the recording)

The slides compare fetal hemoglobin and adult hemoglobin, show gamma/beta globin gene regulation, and the CRISPR/Cas9 modification of BCL11A, targeting a “motif that binds to [the] globin promoter” (the slide spells it “goblin”). The mechanism is shown in figures that did not come through in the PDF text: see the slides.
Procedure: uses the patient’s HSPC (hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells); CTX001 = Casgevy. Steps are in a figure: see the slide.
Results: two patients (Patient 1, Patient 2) shown in figures: see the slide.

8.3 [Slides] Problems with Casgevy





























ProblemCost2,200,000 US$ (Casgevy alone)ChemotherapyRequired, with its side effectsOff-target events(term only on the slide)LymphopeniaListed as a problemFollow-upNo long-term monitoring yet
