Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
TBL 7.3 Forensic DNA analysis
Sources

tbl 7 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). One file only.
Starts mid-session: the recording opens in the middle of the history of DNA fingerprinting (“…the familiar relationships between people”). The introduction and the name of the scientist he is describing are not recorded.
Structure of what was recorded: history and theory (sections 1 to 4), individual quiz on ADI (section 5), recap of the STR method (sections 6 and 7), then the team quiz (section 8). The team part is mostly student discussion, partly in Spanish, and the lecturer rarely confirms answers; the file ends in repeated garbage lines.
Coverage: everything comes from the transcript. Method details filled from [Lucía]; the class notes have only the learning goals and the reading list for this TBL.

Resources

Slides: Slides Unit 7.pdf, end of the file: only the “Prosecutor’s fallacy” slide came through as text. The fingerprint, paternity and electropherogram figures did not: see the slides.
Study material: none in the vault. The three pre-reading items are listed in the class notes (below); the pdf “How DNA was found at killing scene” is not in the vault.
Genetics class notes: FMC I Genetics class notes 2026, “TBL 7.3 Forensic DNA analysis” (learning goals and study materials only).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “TBL 7.2. Forensic DNA analysis” (her numbering), PDF p. 223-224.
Related notes: Lec 7.7 Genetic variation (microsatellites, polymorphism, Hardy-Weinberg introduced), Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination (replication slippage changes microsatellite length).

Marking: [Slides] = from the Unit 7 slides. [Notes] = from the FMC I Genetics class notes (official source, Novo). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Key concept, stated twice: you can exclude a person with certainty, but you can never include with 100% certainty; you can only give the probability of a random match. “This is the main thing that you have to understand.” “The crucial question is to calculate the probability of a random match… That’s the whole process of forensic genetics.”
You should be able to calculate genotype and random-match probabilities from allele frequencies: “that’s what you should be able to do, hopefully”.
Prosecutor’s fallacy (section 4) is on the slides as a set of questions.
From Lec 7.7 Genetic variation: TBL 7.3 will not be in the self-assessment (same day), but microsatellites and their polymorphisms will.
He does not expect the technology in detail: “you are not biochemistry students… you are interested in the application”.
Admin: the individual quiz gave no points (self-check of the pre-reading). He shortened the TBL to about 1 hour 15 to 1 hour 30.

[Notes] Learning goals:

Short tandem repeats (microsatellites) can be used to identify individuals.
Calculating genotype probabilities from allele frequencies.
Using DNA evidence in forensic science.

[Notes] Pre-reading: the DNA Interactive animation “Today’s DNA profile” (dnalc.cshl.edu); the web page on the process of DNA analysis (forensicsciencesimplified.org); the pdf “How DNA was found at killing scene” (pitfalls of DNA analysis). In class: questions individually, then by teams, then a team exercise calculating the probability that a crime-scene sample belongs to a suspect.
1. History: DNA fingerprints

A scientist (name not in the recorded part) realized that patterns of tandem repeats reflect family relationships between people and could be used to identify individuals.
He first used the technique to help the police in the UK solve a crime. [verify] Transcript: “a case of rape or a crime. The first case was of their crime, a murder”; the type of the first case is unclear. He then helped solve other cases, and the technology became easier.
He called the patterns “fingerprints”: each person has a unique fingerprint of minisatellite repeat numbers. There are hundreds or thousands of minisatellites in the genome; for each, a person has a certain number of repeats, giving a band of a different size.
The method moved from minisatellites to microsatellites: also tandem repeats, but of very short units, 1 to 4 nucleotides.

2. Why microsatellites (STRs) and not minisatellites

Asked in class and as quiz question 1 (also: why not SNPs?). Students: “more specific”.
Lecturer: “one of the reasons is technical, basically”. Minisatellite fingerprinting is a complex technology; for microsatellites it is just a PCR. PCR is fast; the products are run in capillary electrophoresis and the different sizes appear as peaks.
Quiz answers (word cloud): PCR, faster, specific.
Calculating random-match probabilities cannot be done for minisatellites but can for microsatellites, the technology used today.
[Lucía] STRs are in non-coding regions and highly polymorphic (nine or more detectable alleles); different people carry different allele combinations. The more microsatellites analysed, the better.

3. Paternity case: exclusion vs inclusion

Figure (minisatellite fingerprints; see the slides): mother, child, two potential fathers (F1, F2).
Each band in the child must be maternal or paternal, because the child inherited one allele from each parent.
Bands not from the mother all match F1; F2 cannot have contributed them, so F2 is excluded.
Can we say with 100% certainty that F1 is the father? No.

Technical reasons (partial profile, contamination) were set aside: “just biological reasons”.
A student (Pedro) suggested we only look at part of the genome. Answer: the markers are scattered throughout the genome, so it is a fairly broad view.
The real reason: we do not know whether someone else in the world has exactly the same pattern (“you go to Australia… that Australian man could have been the father”).


So you give a probability, based on how likely the pattern is to be found again in human populations: the random-match probability. If it is, say, 1 in 3,000 million and you know the whole population, you may conclude no one else could have it; still, it is a very high probability, not a certainty.
Exclusion is certain; inclusion is always a probability.

4. The prosecutor’s fallacy

[Slides] “Prosecutor’s fallacy: Is #1 guilty? Is #1 innocent? Are #2 and #3 guilty?”
Case: a rape. A specimen found on the victim (minisatellites, old technology) and three suspects rounded up by the police. Suspect 1 matches.
The tempting conclusion: suspect 1 must be the offender. That is the prosecutor’s fallacy (a fallacy = a flawed argument).
Suppose the same profile occurs by chance in 1 in 10 males in that city. Then there may be 1,000 potential offenders in the city, so the probability that suspect 1 is the real one is 1 in 1,000: very low.
Suspects 2 and 3 can be excluded: their DNA is not in the sample.
To attribute the sample to one person you must calculate the probability of finding the same pattern by chance. Only if that probability is lower than anything plausible (he jokes: lower than the number of people even if there were life on other planets) can you say it must be him, and even then you give a probability such as 99.999%.
The pre-reading case (“How DNA was found at killing scene”) shows these limitations: people can be wrongly convicted.

5. Calculating probabilities (individual quiz)
Hardy-Weinberg underlies the calculation (“I don’t have time to explain that”; see Lec 7.7 Genetic variation).
Question 2: heterozygote

One STR marker with 5 alleles in the population: A 20%, B 20%, C 10%, D 30%, E 20% (sum 100%). The transcript says “30% have allele B”; with B already at 20%, the 30% must be D.
Probability that a random person is C/D: multiply the two frequencies and multiply by 2 “because it’s the heterozygote”: 2 x 0.1 x 0.3 = 0.06.
[verify] The transcript reads the answer as “0, 0, 0, 6” and D as “0, 0, 3”; 0.06 is what the stated frequencies give.

Question 3: homozygote

Probability of a random B/B homozygote: frequency squared, 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04 (confirmed as the right answer). For homozygotes you do not multiply by 2.


















GenotypeFormulaHomozygote (a/a)p²Heterozygote (a/b)2pq

[Lucía] Same: homozygous = (frequency of A)²; heterozygous = 2 x (frequency of A) x (frequency of B).

Question 4: random match in a city

The evidence sample from a crime scene is usually a mixture: DNA of the victim, the culprit, and people who simply passed by.
A suspect matches a profile of many markers; the random-match probability is 1 in a million (10^-6); the offender is known to come from a city, so the potential offenders are the people of that city. Which statement is more correct?
[verify] The options and the right answer are not audible. Fragments: “the 10 million is the highest”, “in every million”, “50%“. Apply the reasoning of section 4: expected number of chance matches = city population x random-match probability.

6. The STR method (recap)

Example microsatellite with a trinucleotide repeat: 3 repeats = 9 nucleotides.
PCR primers are placed on both sides of the repeat; their sequences are the same in everyone, so they bind everyone’s DNA.
Product of e.g. 199 bp with 3 repeats; someone with 5 repeats gives 205 bp (6 nt longer). Alleles are named by the number of repeats (allele 3, allele 5).
Many allele sizes exist in the population, but each person has only two alleles (one from each parent), the same or different.
Capillary electrophoresis: a thin tube filled with acrylamide, a polymer with many tiny pores. An electric current moves the DNA towards the positive electrode; shorter fragments migrate faster. The products are fluorescently labelled; a detector window records light over time: baseline, a peak when a fragment passes, baseline again.
Two peaks (alleles 3 and 5) = heterozygote 3/5. One peak (somewhat higher) = homozygote.
Timing: PCR in about 1 hour, electrophoresis about half an hour.
[Lucía] One primer of each pair is fluorescently labelled; out of 14 STRs analysed, 3 or 4 are labelled with each of four fluorescent dyes; a laser reads all four colours and displays the PCR output by size and colour. She describes a gel; the lecturer describes capillary electrophoresis.

7. Reading a real profile and the product rule

Real result (see the slide): 17 markers; for each, the person’s genotype.

e.g. a marker on chromosome 10 heterozygous 12/15.
Amelogenin: sex marker with alleles X and Y (this person showed both).
A single peak, e.g. homozygous 28 at D21S11.


In the marker names, the number after D is the chromosome: markers on chromosome 10, 16, 2… so they are scattered across all chromosomes (the answer to Pedro’s concern in section 3).
You need a table of allele frequencies for the relevant population: e.g. US tables by ethnicity (Caucasian of European descent, African-American); for a crime in Spain, Spanish frequencies. The example table was for a marker on chromosome 8.
For each marker: homozygote p², heterozygote 2pq.
Product rule: multiply the probabilities of all individual markers to get the final probability of a random match (someone who is at the same time 12/14 at one marker, 28/30 at another, 9/9, 10/10…). Example result: 1 in 26 billion (US population). [verify] the figure.
Then the probability that the suspect is the source depends on the number of people in the population. This is what the judge or jury must understand.
[Lucía] The FBI analyses 13 STRs plus a sex marker, reducing random matches. A complete profile comes with a random-match probability calculated from allele frequencies in the population.

8. Team quiz
Only one team member logs in. Mostly student discussion; points below are what can be reconstructed. The lecturer confirmed only the first (“everyone got it right”).

Hardy-Weinberg, homozygote: p² (everyone correct).
Structural feature that distinguishes a microsatellite: garbled. The lecturer’s comments mention that STR arrays are smaller than 100 bp with repeat units of 1 to 4 bp, that minisatellites (“VNTRs” in the transcript) are much longer, and something about telomeres and alpha satellite at the centromere. [verify] which option was correct.
Amelogenin with X and Y peaks of equal intensity: male (students’ answer).
Mixture at one locus with four alleles: cannot be a single donor, because one person cannot have more than two alleles at the same locus (students’ reasoning).
Exclusion vs inclusion of a suspect (students’ reasoning): a suspect is excluded if one of his alleles is missing from the evidence; if all his alleles are present he is included as a potential contributor, but you cannot conclude he is the only contributor. [verify] the exact wording of the options.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
TBL 9.1 PCR
Sources

TBL 9.1 PCR (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Opens during the individual test (“So these are different steps, different molecules…”); covers the readiness tests, the logic and steps of PCR, Taq, history, reagents, equipment, gel visualization, qPCR. Ends at the break with the qPCR question (“which one of these samples… has the most amount of DNA from the beginning?”).
TBL 9.1 PCR continued (automatic transcription). Opens on PCR applications (“…and then you can do genetic engineering”); covers RT-PCR for gene expression and the SARS-CoV-2 exercise (primer design, interpretation). Ends at the final team test: “this is the last session that you have for me.”
Gaps:

The start of the session (before the individual test): any introduction and the material the test was about.
Between the files: his answer to the qPCR question after the break, and the start of the applications list. Section 7 fills the qPCR answer from the study material; section 8 lists the applications from [Slides].
Several team discussion passages are unintelligible; student side conversation is left out.



Resources

Slides: TBL slides.pdf (“Polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The power of exponential growth”). Most text came through; figures (Thermus aquaticus, thermal cycle graph, gel, qPCR probe, qPCR curves, interpretation graphs): see the slides.
Study material: The use of PCR for clinical diagnosis.pdf (modified from The Jackson Laboratory, “The power of a test”; the Marcus case, test protocol stages 1 to 3).
Video he set for home: www.youtube.com/watch (about 8 minutes; also linked in the slides and the study material).
Online tools from the slides: SARS-CoV-2 genome at www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/NC_045512.2 and NCBI Primer-BLAST at www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/tools/primer-blast/
Genetics class notes: no TBL 9.1 section.
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “TBL 9.1. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)”, PDF p. 277-280.
Related notes: TBL 7.3 Forensic DNA analysis (forensic use of PCR), Lec 8.1 DNA transcription, Lec 9.4 Cancer genetics (same day; EGFR sequencing).

Marking: [Slides] = from the TBL slides. [Notes] = from the study material “The use of PCR for clinical diagnosis” (The Jackson Laboratory, modified). [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Goal of PCR: “what is more important is please remember… the goal of the PCR”: to generate millions of copies of a specific fragment of DNA. “There are many applications that come after the PCR, but the PCR is just that” (section 2).
Specificity comes from primer annealing / primer design: “This is critical in the PCR. The specificity comes here” (section 5). [Slides] “This step is critical for specificity.”
Interpreting real-time PCR curves: “I think this is important here” (section 7).
RT before PCR for RNA: “remember always to do first retrotranscription because you have to work with DNA” (sections 8 and 9).
Report wording: a negative result means “no virus detected in the sample”, not “the patient is not infected” (section 9).
Homework: watch the 8-minute SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR video at home and review the session with it.
[Slides] Learning goals: understand the principles and main steps of PCR; explore applications; interpret real-time PCR results.
Admin: a TBL “at the end of this week” on disease treatment based on DNA sequencing and PCR (code log: TBL 9.3 Gene mutations as therapeutic targets, Fri 30 Oct). This was his last session.

1. Readiness tests (start of the recording)

Individual test on ADI, Unit 9, “9.1 PCR”: 7 or 8 questions, 4 minutes; identify the molecules and processes numbered in a scheme of the flow of genetic information. Then the same as a team test, 20 seconds per question.
Answers he discusses: item 1 = DNA; retrotranscription (not a usual step in our information flow; organisms with an RNA genome need this enzyme to make DNA from RNA; we have this activity in our telomeres); item 7 = cDNA, C = complementary: a DNA complementary to an RNA. cDNA is used later in the session.
Last question: which process PCR uses: PCR is based on the capacity of enzymes to catalyse DNA replication. Retrotranscription is a particular application, not the PCR itself.

2. The problem and the idea

“Finding a needle in a haystack”: before PCR (about 30 years ago, he says), scientists wanted to study a tiny part of a huge genome (a sequence of about a hundred nucleotides among millions; transcript “100 to 100”, [verify]).
The idea (transcript “Gary Moores”; [Slides] Kary Mullis): replicate the needle millions of times until the haystack is almost only needle. Then it is easy to work with.
Goal: [Slides] “To generate millions of copies of a specific fragment of DNA by using an enzymatic method based on DNA replication, and the repetition of these three steps: 1. Denaturation 2. Primer annealing 3. Extension.”

3. Building the method (team questions)

Is there a tool to copy DNA? Yes, already in nature: DNA polymerase (replication: one double-stranded DNA becomes two). He wanted to do it in a test tube, so the cell’s steps must be reproduced.
Step 1, denaturation: separate the two strands. Cells use enzymes; in the tube, heat.
Step 2, primer annealing: the polymerase needs primers to start: short sequences (around 20, or 30, nucleotides) bound by complementarity to the DNA.
Step 3, extension: the polymerase synthesizes the new DNA.
The copied fraction is the one after the primer sequence: primer position decides what is copied. Repeat for many cycles: many copies of the same sequence.

The heat problem and Taq polymerase

Denaturation needs about 95 °C: the polymerase would also denature. At first the enzyme was added again in each cycle: “terrible”.
Solution: organisms living at high temperature, e.g. hot basins in Yellowstone (about 70 °C, he says): Thermus aquaticus. Its enzymes are adapted: its DNA polymerase works at about 70 °C and resists 90 °C.
Taq polymerase: heat the sample to 95-96 °C, and extension is done at 72 °C, its optimal temperature, not 37 °C. “So this is the PCR. As simple as that.” A revolution in science.
Today’s polymerases have been modified to be more stable and efficient; the original was natural Taq.
[check] [Lucía] says Taq polymerases “work optimally at temperatures even higher than 90 degrees”; lecturer and [Slides] give 72 °C for extension (lecturer: optimal temperature).

History ([Slides] timeline; he went through it briefly)





































YearEvent1983Kary Mullis develops PCR at Cetus Corporation1985First PCR publication in Science1986Purified Taq polymerase first used in PCR1988PCR with thermostable Taq published; PCR used to amplify cDNA from reverse transcription1991Roche buys the Taq and PCR patents from Cetus for $300 million (he: “because it was very profitable”)1992Fluorescent DNA-binding dye applied: foundation for qPCR1993Kary Mullis shares the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

He: the Nobel Prize “because it changed everything” in molecular biology.
Anecdote, his first PCR: during his thesis in the States, detecting particular genes in different numbers of cells: GAPDH and “an amylase” ([verify]: the slide labels them “GAPDH” and “PAM”). Even with only 10 cells you detect their DNA: “very, very powerful”. [Slides] cell numbers 10 to 10^4.

4. What you need
Information

The DNA sequence, but not the complete sequence: only the sequences flanking the target region (the ends), where the primers go. Hence PCR is useful for sequencing genes: know the flanks, copy what is inside, sequence it.

Reagents (team answers on the board)





























ReagentWhyTemplate DNAThe sequence to copy (“don’t forget to put DNA”)Two primers: forward and reverseOne at each end: forward on the left of the sequence, reverse on the rightNucleotides (“dNTPs”, N = any of the nucleotides)Added by the polymerase; deoxynucleotides, because you make DNA, not RNA. [Notes] dATP, dCTP, dTTP, dGTPTaq polymeraseSynthesis (copying)BufferSolution with the right pH and ions, e.g. magnesium, so the enzyme works in optimal conditions

DNA dye (proposed by a team) is not for the PCR but for visualizing it (section 6).
Student question: must you add nucleotides each cycle? No: you put in far more than needed at the start so they are never limiting; “just put the tube and wait”.
[Lucía] This mix is called the Master Mix.

Equipment

Micropipettes, tubes, microplates.
Something to change the temperature continuously: three water baths (e.g. 90 and 70 °C) and move the tube by hand (“very tedious”), or a thermocycler: changes temperature very fast and precisely. Each step needs a different temperature.
His lab’s old thermocycler (transcript “BTC1 100”, [verify] model): up to 96 tubes at once.

5. The cycle step by step

























StepLecturer[Slides]1. DenaturationAbout 90-95 °C; double-stranded to single-stranded DNA92-95 °C; dsDNA melts into ssDNA2. AnnealingLower to around 60 °C; each primer binds one strand at the two ends of the fragment50-60 °C; primers bind complementary sequences; critical for specificity3. ExtensionPolymerase synthesizes new DNA on both strands at once; synthesis 5’ to 3’, reading 3’ to 5’: two replications, one per strand72 °C; ssDNA is the template; polymerase extends each primer from its 3’ end, 5’ to 3’

Specificity: whatever lies between the primers is amplified, so if a primer binds somewhere unwanted, that gets amplified. Primers must be specific for the target.
Cycles: repeated typically up to 40 times; beyond about 40 the enzyme is not totally stable and degrades. He gives “between 25 or 40” (transcript “25 or 49”, [verify]). [Slides] “Typically 25-40 cycles, depending on the assay.”
Exponential growth: the chessboard story (he refers to a reading about the chessboard; “the power of the exponential”). Copies double each cycle: after 35 cycles, from two copies, billions. A PCR takes about two hours.
[Slides] “After 35 cycles…” table: starting from one molecule with 100% efficiency, 34,359,738,368 copies. [check] [Lucía] “35-40 cycles… half a million fragments are produced at the end”, contradicted by the slide table.
[Lucía] By the end of the second cycle, the short fragment flanked by both primers appears; these are the copies that increase each cycle.

6. Seeing the result: agarose gel electrophoresis

After the PCR the tube looks the same: you cannot see anything.
DNA dyes: fluorescent molecules that bind DNA, e.g. ethidium bromide, fluorescent under UV light. Adding it to the tube alone “is not very useful”.
First separate by size: electrophoresis in an electric field (smaller molecules go faster); support = agarose, “a jelly”. Then stain with ethidium bromide and illuminate with UV.
DNA ladder: fragments of known size. His example gel: an amplified band of about 200 (another about 100) nucleotides.
You already knew the expected size from primer design: the gel confirms the right fragment. The band can be cut and used for cloning or sequencing.
[Slides] “PCR products are separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, stained with a fluorescent DNA-binding dye such as ethidium bromide, and visualized under UV light.”

7. Quantitative (real-time) PCR, qPCR

Same principles; aim: a more quantitative, precise determination of how many copies you had at the beginning.
Extra element: the probe, a short sequence like a primer but not a primer, carrying a reporter (fluorescent) and a quencher; while they are close, fluorescence is blocked. Designed to bind between the forward and reverse primers.
During extension, Taq has a nuclease activity (transcript “nucleotidase”, “hydrolysis”): it degrades a strand bound in its way, i.e. the probe, separating reporter from quencher, so fluorescence appears. [Slides] “During extension, Taq polymerase cleaves the probe, separating the reporter from the quencher and increasing fluorescence.”
You follow the PCR as it runs, no gel needed. qPCR thermocyclers do the same plus read fluorescence continuously: “real-time”. 96 samples, or in some machines “364” ([verify] the number).
Reading the curves (x = cycle, e.g. 40 cycles; y = fluorescence): at the start fluorescence is zero (intact probe), early cycles still too low; with more cycles it rises. Five samples (five tubes) cross the threshold at different cycles. Above the threshold = positive, below = negative.
Question before the break: which tube started with the most DNA? Students: “the first one”. (His answer after the break is not recorded.) [Notes] “Samples containing more target RNA initially generally cross the fluorescence threshold after fewer cycles.”

8. Applications

[Slides] list: molecular identification; gene expression analysis; pathogen detection; forensic medicine; disease-risk identification; disease-treatment customization; genetic engineering.
He (start of file 2): a TBL this week on disease treatment based on DNA sequencing and PCR; genetic engineering: copy a fragment many times to clone it in a vector, e.g. for gene therapy. He explains two applications.

Gene expression analysis (RT-PCR)

Different cell types express different sets of proteins; knowing them helps understand the cell’s function. Example: macrophage, muscle cell ([Slides] smooth muscle), neuron; genes A to D: gene A in macrophages and muscle cells, gene C specific to neurons, gene B in all.
Protein methods: immunohistochemistry, Western blot, ELISA. Limits: you need a good antibody; sensitivity may be low.
Alternative: measure the mRNA: no mRNA means no protein; high mRNA, probably plenty of protein. Some technologies analyse all mRNAs at once; PCR analyses one gene per reaction.
Problem: PCR is replication and needs DNA; mRNA is RNA, so a PCR on it gives nothing.
Solution: isolate RNA, do retrotranscription with reverse transcriptase (plus primer and nucleotides) to get cDNA, keeping the proportions of the mRNAs; then (real-time) PCR.
Result: neurons no amplification (do not express gene A); macrophages express it more than muscle cells.
RT-PCR = retrotranscription PCR, two steps; here a real-time RT-PCR. Also used to compare a treated cell with an untreated one.
[Lucía] mRNA is retro-transcribed into cDNA “by using an additional primer”; example of genetic engineering: many copies of insulin genes for recombinant insulin (not in the lecture).

9. Pathogen detection: SARS-CoV-2

The virus: lipid membrane, genome = single-stranded RNA coding few proteins (it uses the infected cell’s machinery).
Antigen tests detect proteins: good, but PCR is more powerful because of its amplification; RT-PCR became the standard test.
Always RT then PCR, and always real-time to know how much virus there is.
[Notes] Protocol: Stage 1 nucleic acid extraction and purification (viral RNA plus human and other nucleic acids; remove interfering substances); Stage 2a reverse transcription to cDNA (“because the Taq polymerase requires a DNA template”, [Slides]); Stage 2b qPCR with fluorescent probes; Stage 3 data interpretation. Samples handled on 96-well microplates.

Designing the PCR (real exercise)

Sequence from the NCBI (National Library of Medicine) database, free: SARS-CoV-2 genome about 29,900 nucleotides (human about 3,000 million). The record shows the authors, the sequence (written with T: it is the cDNA of the viral RNA) and the encoded proteins.
Example protein: gene N, around positions 28,000-29,000, the nucleocapsid protein (transcript “nucleocardial capsule”, later “nucleotaphyl phosphoprotein”). First amino acid methionine, since the virus uses the cell’s machinery and the genetic code.
Any fragment of the virus works for detection; PCR runs well on short fragments (transcript “100 to 100 nucleotides”, [verify]), not the 30,000 nucleotides.
Paste the sequence into Primer-BLAST; he restricted the forward primer to positions 28,274-28,328 and the reverse to 28,330-28,360 ([verify] the numbers as transcribed), around the N gene, because these match the primers his hospital uses. Leave default settings; the program considers specificity, secondary structure, etc.; the first suggestion is typically the best.
“It takes 10 minutes to design a PCR for COVID.” Primers are cheap (about $20 each, many reactions); the polymerase a bit more expensive; PCR overall not expensive.
The real assay: forward primer, reverse primer and the probe in the middle. [Slides] CDC-N1: nCoV_N1-F GACCCCAAAATCAGCGAAAT; nCoV_N1-R TCTGGTTACTGCCAGTTGAATCTG; nCoV_N1-P FAM-ACCCCGCATTACGTTTGGTGGACC-IABkFQ. [check] He says there are “two different PCRs for two different areas” of the virus; on the [Slides] table the second assay is human RNase P (RP-F, RP-R, RP-P), not a viral region.

Interpretation (team exercise)

Controls:

Negative control: a sample known to have no virus, e.g. water. Must be negative; if positive, contamination.
Positive control: a sample known to have virus. Must be positive; if not, something went wrong.


Three patients: highest viral load = patient 2.
Another patient: not negative and not clearly positive: inconclusive, repeat (take the sample again). “This is happening, of course.”
Another: not detectable.
Final question: controls fine, no amplification: report “no virus detected in the sample”, not “the patient is not infected”, because the lab did not take the sample and does not know if it was taken correctly.
[Notes] Positive sample: high signal early in the run, like the positive control. Negative: low signal below the threshold, like the negative control, reported negative “assuming sample quality and successful processing”. Threshold of detection = fluorescence needed to distinguish true signal from background.
End: final team test to review; “this is the last session that you have for me.”

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
TBL 9.2 Cell cycle dysregulation in cancer
Sources

TBL 9.2 pt. 1 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Opens with which slides are examinable; covers cancer as a multistep disease, tobacco smoke, papillomavirus, familial adenomatous polyposis, genomic instability, BRCA1/2 and HBOC. Ends at the 10-minute break.
TBL 9.2 continued (automatic transcription). Opens with clinical case 1 (BRCA1 carrier); covers the team discussion, angiogenesis and metastasis (with a narrated video), the immune system and immunotherapy (narrated video), and clinical case 2 (HER2-positive breast cancer). Ends: “So we are done.”
Gaps:

Nothing obvious missing at the break.
The team discussions (case 1 and case 2) are partly unintelligible and partly in Spanish. Students’ answers read from internet or AI searches are kept only where the lecturer confirmed them.
The breast cancer epidemiology and histology slides were skipped for lack of time (“I’m going to skip this”); section 11 comes only from [Slides] and [Lucía].
The two videos are narrations, not the lecturer. The angiogenesis video was stopped when it moved to another topic.



Resources

Slides: TBL 9.2. Dysregulation of the cell cycle in cancer ADI.pdf. Text came through; figures (hallmarks scheme, lung histology, papillomavirus scheme, FAP sequence, karyotype, HBOC risk table, vasculature images, HER2 FISH, treatment timeline of case 2): see the slides.
Videos (from the slides): anti-angiogenesis www.youtube.com/watch ; escape from the immune system: YouTube search “immunotherapy the path to cure cancer”.
Study material: Reading material TBL 9.3.pdf (titled “Study material for TBL 9.3”, last year’s numbering for this TBL: summary of chapter 16 “Biología Celular del Cáncer”, Biología Celular Biomédica; Gil-Bazo, Baraibar, Castañón, Nistal, Bandrés, Agirre, Prósper, Calvo).
Lucía: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes, “TBL 9.3. Dysregulation of the cell-cycle in cancer”, PDF p. 285-290.
Genetics class notes: no TBL 9.2 section. Relevant passages in FMC I Genetics class notes 2026: Lec 7.2 (BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the homologous recombination complex, p. 6), Lec 7.8 (homologous recombination repair, p. 41), Lec 9.1 (extreme aneuploidy in cancer cells, p. 70).
Related notes: Lec 9.4 Cancer genetics (oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes, HER2 amplification and anti-HER2 drugs), Lec 7.8 DNA damage, repair and recombination (p53, homologous recombination), Lec 9.1 Cytogenetics and genome analysis (karyotypes, FISH), POM Clinical interview social and family history (smoking and lung cancer screening, from the clinical side).

Marking: [Slides] = from the TBL slides. [Notes] = from the study material (Gil-Bazo et al., chapter 16 summary) or, where named, the Genetics class notes. [Lucía] = from Lucía’s notes. [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no source settles it.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Rule for this TBL: “In some of the slides, you will see study this for final test.” The other slides are “just information in general… not going to be asked in the final test”, which does not mean they are not interesting to discuss.
Papillomavirus slide: “Now this is a slide that you have to study” (section 3). [Slides] labelled “Slide that you have to study”.
Angiogenesis and metastasis: [Slides] labelled “Slide that you have to study (excluding the video)” (section 9). The lecturer did not say this aloud. In the extracted text the label sits just before the angiogenesis slide; confirm in the PDF which slide carries it [verify].
BRCA1/2 in DNA repair: “I’m not going to ask this in the exam or anything. It’s just something that is needed for a clinical case” (section 6).
Format: the TBL focuses on breast cancer, with two clinical cases discussed in teams (search the internet or AI, then share).

1. Cancer: a complex, multistep disease

[Slides] “A complex and multistep disease: genetic and environmental factors”; “The hallmarks of cancer” (scheme: see the slide).
Not only proliferation of cells and inhibition of cell death: also angiogenesis, the effect of the immune system, external radiation; many factors. A step-by-step process leading to metastasis and eventually death.
Genetic basis: oncogenic transformation of proto-oncogenes and inactivation of tumour suppressor genes, due to many factors:


























FactorLecturer’s example or pointGenetic predispositionCarrying a mutation that promotes tumorigenesisCarcinogensExposureSpontaneous mutationsGarbled in the transcript; [Slides] “Spontaneous”Viruses and other pathogensHelicobacter pylori, which causes stomach cancer. [Notes] it causes chronic gastritis; inflammatory cells produce free radicals that can damage DNA

These lead to hyperproliferation and DNA damage, forming the primary tumour. If cells escape the primary tumour they enter the bloodstream and attach to organs: metastasis. Typical sites for breast cancer: the lymph nodes first, the brain, the liver, the bone. The new tumour masses are “what is eventually killing the patient”.

2. Tobacco smoke and lung cancer

Compounds: lecturer “more than 4,000 chemical compounds”, about 100 able to induce malignant transformation. [check] [Slides] “4500 chemical compounds, 100 carcinogenic”; the slides give 4,500.
[Notes] Carcinogenic components include tars, polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines.
Malignant transformation here = inactivation of tumour suppressor genes and oncogenic transformation of proto-oncogenes.
Lung cancer from tobacco is the result of two main factors ([Slides] “Effects of tobacco smoke”):


















FactorLecturer’s explanationDNA damageDaily exposure over years. Some compounds bind DNA covalently and induce mutations. Over many years a cell may acquire a mutation, e.g. KRAS (“very typical” in many tumours, including lung cancer), EGFR mutations (transcribed “EJPAR”), or loss of p53 (transcribed “loss of 50”) [verify]. [Slides] activation of oncogenes, inactivation of TSGChronic inflammationHeat burns the alveolar epithelium; tar (combustion products) gets stuck in the alveoli; macrophages come to remove it but cannot digest it all because the damage is daily; they die, more inflammation, more neutrophils and lymphocytes. “Any chronic inflammation is going to be due to cancer promotion” (wording garbled) [verify]

Why inflammation promotes cancer: inflammatory cells (macrophages, lymphocytes) produce cytokines and growth factors, meant to recruit inflammatory cells and make them proliferate. Cancer cells “learn” to express the receptors for these cytokines on their membrane and respond to the proliferative effect. “They learn how to survive in these adverse conditions.” [Lucía] the same; also ROS produced by macrophages and leukocytes damage our own cells. [Notes] chronic inflammation produces large amounts of reactive oxygen species that damage DNA, and cytokines and growth factors that stimulate tumour cell proliferation.
Histology ([Slides] healthy lung, lung from a heavy smoker, lung cancer; see the slides):

Normal: alveoli, pneumocytes in the septa.
Heavy smoker: thickened alveolar septa (“like a scar”, the tissue protecting itself) and dark macrophages digesting tar. Not cancer.
Lung cancer: many cells in mitosis, invading the lung.


Late detection: once there are symptoms (coughing blood, pain), the tumour has usually spread; most lung cancers are detected late, and cure is then very difficult. Some programmes offer heavy and past heavy smokers an annual CT scan to detect growing nodules.
[Notes] Tobacco relates to cancers by direct contact (pharynx, larynx, stomach, lungs) or indirect contact (pancreas, bladder); alcohol and tobacco act synergistically for lung and head and neck tumours. [Lucía] “Its common effects are lung and bladder cancer.”

3. Oncogenic viruses: papillomavirus (examinable slide)

The lecturer: “This was included also in this type of material” (the study material).
Papillomavirus: sexually transmitted, infects and colonizes the epithelium of the cervix; stays inside the nucleus and divides when the cells divide.
Two harmful viral proteins:





















Viral proteinTargetConsequenceE6Binds and inactivates p53Loss of p53’s protective function: more mutations ([Slides] “Cells unprotected from DNA damage”)E7Binds and inactivates RbE2F active all the time, inducing proliferation ([Slides] “E2F: Excessive proliferation”)

Not a mutation, not a problem in the gene or promoter sequence: inactivation of the protein.
Excessive proliferation plus loss of p53 = “the perfect combination for cancer development”.
p53 described by the lecturer as “the caretaker of the genome”. [check] [Notes] calls p53 “the gatekeeper of the genome”. The slides do not decide.
Infection does not mean cancer; it increases the risk. Some infected women never develop cancer; other factors contribute. “This is why the vaccine is very important.”
[Notes] HPV can cause cervical, penile, anal and head and neck cancer. Hepatitis C virus is the second example in the study material (chronic hepatocyte infection, hepatocarcinoma); not discussed in class.

4. Accumulation of mutations: familial adenomatous polyposis

Aggressive tumours usually accumulate many mutations; cancer is not a single mutation in one gene, though it usually starts with one.
Studied in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): an inherited condition; [Slides] germline mutations in the APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene.
Polyps (benign) form in the colon; as cells accumulate more mutations, an aggressive tumour penetrates the connective tissue, reaches the bloodstream and metastasizes.
Because carriers are known, researchers sequenced polyps at each stage. Order as transcribed: loss of APC, then p53, then KRAS activation through activating mutations, then loss of other tumour suppressor genes (see the slide for the exact sequence) [verify].
Images: normal colon mucosa with its infoldings versus a colon full of polyps. Polyps increase progressively; at some point removing the colon “as a whole” may be needed because of the risk of malignancy.
Message: as cancer progresses, different mutations accumulate.

5. Genomic instability

“Progression implies higher genomic instability”: more mutations, chromosome alterations, alterations of all kinds of genes.
[Slides] karyotype of a breast cancer cell from a metastatic tumour (see the slide): e.g. five copies of chromosome 1, unclassifiable chromosomes, multiple extra chromosomes. [Notes] (Genetics class notes, Lec 9.1) cancer cells often show extreme aneuploidy, with multiple chromosomal abnormalities.
Many such cells are not viable and die: this is why tumours contain many apoptotic cells. Others survive by unknown means, and these are usually the more aggressive ones, found in advanced, highly metastatic tumours; they resist chemotherapy and radiotherapy, “maybe because this is kind of a natural selection process”.
Paradox: many genetic alterations, yet survival in all kinds of adverse conditions. “This is very difficult to treat; this is the key message.”

6. BRCA1 and BRCA2 (not examined)

Not for the exam; needed for clinical case 1.
DNA damage response recap: proteins track DNA and find lesions; this activates p53, which stimulates production of DNA repair proteins. One repair mechanism is homologous recombination; BRCA1 and BRCA2 are involved in DNA repair through recombination. [Notes] (Genetics class notes, Lec 7.2) BRCA1 and BRCA2 are part of the multi-protein homologous recombination complex, “mutated in breast cancer”; the HRR complexes are largely the same as in meiotic recombination (Lec 7.8).
[Slides] “BRCA1/2 mutations and genomic instability”.
Discovery of BRCA1 credited to a woman, name transcribed “very clear king” (Mary-Claire King, outside knowledge), who the lecturer says received the Asturias prize last year [verify].

7. Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC)

Women inherit a mutated copy of BRCA1 or BRCA2 and have a high increase in risk of both cancers.
General population (no BRCA1/2 mutation): breast cancer risk about 12%, ovarian cancer risk 1 to 2% (transcribed “baby brain cancer”, ovarian). With BRCA1 or 2 mutation: a “huge increase” in both (figures in the slide table: see the slide).
Carriers need monitoring and prevention.

8. Clinical case 1: a BRCA1 carrier
Case ([Slides])

29-year-old woman, no personal history of cancer; genetic counselling for a striking family history of breast and ovarian cancer.


























RelativeHistoryMotherBreast cancer at 43, died at 46Maternal auntOvarian cancer at 50, died at 52 (transcript “15”; slide 50)Maternal grandmotherBreast cancer at 60, died at 65FatherHealthy, no personal or family history of malignancy

Multigene hereditary cancer panel (a genetic test that can be done in women with this history): BRCA1 pathogenic variant (frameshift/truncating mutation), confirming HBOC. The lecturer: the protein is altered and not functional; “the gene is gone, basically”.
Patient: “I feel perfectly healthy, but since my mom and aunt both died young, and now I carry the same BRCA1 mutation, what should I do next?”
Task: as a board of oncologists, decide your advice.

The two options

















OptionPoints from the discussionSurgery (risk-reducing removal of breasts and ovaries)She is very young; we do not know if she wants children; “if you remove the breast you have to remove the ovaries as well”. Maybe not necessary at this ageSurveillance (close monitoring)Breast: mammography. Ovary: blood tests for circulating tumour markers (“this is done for ovary cancer”) and ultrasound (ecography), so a growing tumour is detected early. Preventive drugs such as tamoxifen are possible but “not very common”

Recommendation: surveillance now; risk-reducing surgery (mastectomy and removal of the ovaries) at 35 to 40. “You don’t know exactly, this is a matter of risks”, but clinical trials found this the reasonable timing. At 35 to 40 the risk “increases exponentially” (wording garbled) [verify]; surgery then decreases the risk “very much, almost completely”.
The risk between 29 and 35 is not so high, so she can wait; removing breasts and ovaries “is kind of tough”. The recommendation is based on population studies. In the end, it is the decision of the woman and the doctors; ask whether she wants children (some women decide on surgery right away).
Fertility options raised in the discussion: freezing oocytes, preimplantation genetic options. A student’s remark that in some cases the uterus is kept and another structure removed is garbled (“coloquial ducts”) [verify].

Consequences of early removal of the ovaries

Early surgery causes hormonal dysregulation; loss of oestrogens has consequences in other diseases.
Students’ search results included premature menopause, cardiovascular risk, osteoporosis, dementia, Parkinson’s disease, infertility. The lecturer: the main two are:


















RiskLecturer’s explanationCardiovascular diseaseEarlier atherosclerosis, heart attacks: oestrogens protect the vascular bedOsteoporosisOestrogens protect bone from losing its mineral part

In men: testosterone is converted into oestrogens by the enzyme aromatase in the vascular system, bone and fat, so oestrogens also protect men against vascular events and bone demineralization.
After removing the ovaries, the woman must be treated with oestrogen therapy (also an option if she chooses early surgery).

9. Tumour angiogenesis and metastasis (examinable slide, excluding the video)

[Slides] “Without blood vessels: 1-2 mm3”; tumour angiogenesis (recruitment of vessels) allows tumour growth and cell escape into the bloodstream; tumour vessels disorganized (VEGF).
At about 1 to 2 mm3, oxygen diffusion no longer reaches the core; cells cannot keep growing.
Angiogenic switch: the tumour produces factors such as VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) that act on nearby vessels, stimulating proliferation of endothelial cells and pericytes; new vessels enter and vascularize the tumour, supplying oxygen and nutrients.
Critical point: a tumour that cannot overproduce these factors stays at 1 to 2 mm3 and does not grow.
Second consequence: tumour cells are now near vessels, so they easily enter the circulation. People with cancer may have many circulating tumour cells; the bloodstream is hostile and few survive, but some anchor in an organ (e.g. the liver) and grow: metastasis.
[Notes] the main stimuli of VEGF expression are hypoxia and hypoglycaemia; the main angiogenic factors are VEGF and FGF; without vascularization the tumour becomes necrotic or quiescent; most circulating tumour cells are destroyed by the immune system or do not survive outside the primary tumour. [Lucía] hypoxia and hypoglycaemia stimulate VEGF expression (HIF-1).
Normal versus tumour vasculature (electron micrographs; see the slide):














NormalTumourHierarchy: arterioles, capillaries, venules; normal flowNo distinguishable capillaries, arterioles or venules; deformed vessels, abnormal morphology, from hyperstimulation by VEGF and other factors

[Notes] the new vessels are aberrant, tortuous, with excessive ramifications and microhaemorrhages.
Therapy: because tumour vasculature differs, drugs can target tumour vessel cells without affecting normal vasculature: anti-VEGF antibodies or other drugs blocking excessive production of vascular factors. Used usually not alone: in combination with chemotherapy. [Notes] bevacizumab, an antiangiogenic monoclonal antibody against VEGF, indicated in combination with chemotherapy.
Video (not to study, per [Slides]): VEGF family (seven subtypes, three receptors); VEGF makes endothelial cells proliferate (extracellular kinases and MAP kinase pathways), induces proteins that break down the basement membrane (MMPs, uPA and its receptor, tPA), increases permeability, helps new endothelial cells survive; drugs: bevacizumab (Avastin, binds VEGF), sunitinib (Sutent, small-molecule inhibitor of VEGF and PDGF receptors). The video then moved to cetuximab (anti-EGFR) and the lecturer stopped it: “this was a different topic”.

10. The immune system and immunotherapy

Does the immune system defend us from cancer? Yes, an important role. Proof: people on immunosuppressors (AIDS, liver or kidney transplant recipients) have a high risk of developing cancer. [Notes] incidence is higher in congenital immunodeficiency and in immunosuppressed patients (HIV, transplants).
Cancer still develops because tumours learn to avoid the immune system.
Immunotherapy aims to re-stimulate the immune system so it recognizes and kills malignant cells. “A revolution”, “a breakthrough in oncology”: it does not benefit all patients, but some clinical trials found cures of advanced or very malignant tumours.
Video (narration; summary):


































TopicContentSurveillanceProteins are broken into peptides, presented on the cell surface by MHC (HLA); T cells scan them with the T cell receptor (TCR), “a barcode scanning machine”. Mutated proteins (e.g. from smoking) give abnormal peptides recognized as foreignEvasionTumours build defences: keep immune cells out, or weaken T cells. Checkpoints on the tumour surface bind T cells and inhibit killing: PD-1 (transcribed “ED1”) and CTLA-4. Secreted factors turn T cells into T regulatory cells that deactivate other T cellsEnhancing immunityCancer vaccines from neoantigens (mutated tumour proteins); adoptive T cell transfer (T cells grown and educated in the laboratory, or modified); cytokines (IL-2, 7, 12, 15); agonist antibodies (anti-OX40, anti-GITR, anti-4-1BB)Removing tumour defencesAntibodies neutralizing inhibitory factors (anti-IL-10, anti-TGF-beta, transcribed “PGF-beta”; inhibitors transcribed “IDL”, possibly IDO (outside knowledge) [verify]); approved by the FDA: anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4Melanoma trialUntil recently 50% of patients with advanced melanoma died within 12 months; with antibodies against both CTLA-4 and PD-1, 70% survived more than 3 yearsSide effectsNot very common but potentially life-threatening; treatable if found early: diarrhoea (intestinal inflammation), endocrine disease (thyroid dysfunction, diabetes)

Nobel Prize: the lecturer: last year’s Nobel Prize in Medicine went to the researchers who discovered T regulatory cells, which tumours manipulate to inhibit the immune system. [Slides] Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi, Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2025, for discoveries on peripheral immune tolerance; regulatory T cells are the immune system’s security guards; tumours induce T regulatory cells, which block the immune cells that fight cancer.
[Notes] tumour antigens are presented on MHC class I to CD8+ T cells and, after phagocytosis, on MHC class II to CD4+ T cells; tumours evade by decreasing MHC class I or antigen presentation, and secrete immunosuppressive factors such as TGF-beta.
[Lucía] the tumour types that respond best to immunotherapy are lung cancer and melanoma, because a high mutation load gives more antigens for T cells.

11. Focus on breast cancer (skipped in class)

From [Slides] only (“Epidemiological data in Spain”):

About 35,000 new cases every year; first in incidence among women.
5-year survival after diagnosis >90%.
1 out of 8 women in Spain will develop breast cancer in their lifetime.
If detected early, the possibility of cure is about 100%.
Histology: normal breast, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), invasive carcinoma (see the slide).


[Lucía] in DCIS the glands are enlarged with many cells, but the tumour is still within the gland; in invasive carcinoma glands and ducts can no longer be seen. Not all tumours express oestrogen receptors; tamoxifen can only treat oestrogen receptor-expressing tumours.

12. Clinical case 2: HER2-positive breast cancer

First confirm that the tumour expresses HER2: by immunohistochemistry or by FISH (“as we explained yesterday”). [Slides] FISH image: Her-2 in red, chromosome 17 centromere in green; gene amplification of Her-2 in breast cancer. [Notes] about 25 to 30% of breast tumours have multiple copies of Her-2 (amplification, not mutation).
Point of the case: real-life treatment of a HER2 tumour is not as easy as just giving anti-HER2 antibodies.
[Slides] the case:






































StepTreatmentDiagnosis (2013)41-year-old woman, T3N2M0, stage IIIA, HER2 positivePreoperative chemotherapy2 cycles of epirubicin plus cyclophosphamide, then 2 cycles of weekly paclitaxelSurgeryMastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection; pathological response to chemotherapy not completeThenTrastuzumab and tamoxifen; no post-mastectomy radiotherapyRelapse (2 years after surgery, during treatment)Lung and internal mammary lymph node metastases; paclitaxel with pertuzumab and trastuzumab; after 4 cycles, complete radiological responseThenIrradiation to the chest wall and internal mammary lymph node region; maintenance pertuzumab plus trastuzumab for about 18 months, stopped October 2017Last follow-upAugust 2018: alive 10 months after ending anti-HER2 therapy

[Slides] abbreviations in the timeline figure: Op = operation; RTx = radiotherapy; CTx = chemotherapy; ETx = endocrine therapy; cCR = clinical complete response; MBC = metastatic breast cancer.

Terms discussed





























TermDiscussionT3N2M0, stage IIIM0 = no metastasis (student, accepted). “Stage three is kind of a parallel classification. It’s more simple” (garbled) [verify]. T3 and N2 were not explained in the transcriptTamoxifenAn oestrogen receptor inhibitor: if the tumour expresses the oestrogen receptor it relies on oestrogens to grow; removing the oestrogen effect reduces the tumour. As tumours progress they lose their dependence on oestrogens (more advanced tumours); early tumours usually rely on themPaclitaxel”Something we have studied”; a student’s answer about microtubule polymerization is garbled. [Notes] taxanes (e.g. taxol) are mitotic inhibitors that interfere with microtubules during mitosisTrastuzumab, pertuzumabAnti-HER2 antibodies (“we discussed this yesterday”). [Notes] two monoclonal antibodies with slightly different mechanisms; clinical activity relies on combination with chemotherapy. [Lucía] they target different domains of HER2 (domains 2 and 4)Radiotherapy to the chest after relapseImaging may show no tumour, but remaining cells may still be there and cause relapse; chemotherapy or radiotherapy eliminates them
Sequence (timeline figure)

Chemotherapy to reduce the tumour, then surgery; then maintenance trastuzumab (to eliminate remaining HER2-positive cells) plus tamoxifen (anti-oestrogen, in green in the figure); relapse; then chemotherapy plus anti-HER2 therapy plus chest radiotherapy; then free of disease for a long period. “I don’t know exactly what happened after five years because they didn’t tell in the paper.”
The lecturer described the relapse as “lung nodules, not lung metastasis”. [check] [Slides] “lung and internal mammary lymph nodes metastases were found”.
Closing: “I think we have learned a lot about [how] cancer develops and new drugs.”

Lecture 5.4 - The Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs Cycle)
Course: From the Molecule to the Cell I (Prof. Alberto Perez-Mediavilla)
Sources: Lecture slides (Ciclo_Krebs_DMCI) + Lecture notes PDF
Big Picture: Cellular Respiration

Glycolysis alone captures only a small fraction of glucose’s energy: Delta-G’0 = -146 kJ/mol released in glycolysis vs -2,840 kJ/mol for full oxidation to 6 CO2 + 6 H2O. Glycolysis nets only 2 ATP.
Cellular respiration = the set of reactions converting biochemical energy from nutrients into ATP; cells consume O2 and produce CO2. Captures energy from glucose, lipids, AND amino acids. Evolutionarily ancient (~2.5 billion years old); used by animals, plants, many microbes.
Three stages:


Acetyl-CoA production (carbon skeletons of fuels oxidized to acetyl-CoA; carbohydrates release ~1/3 of potential CO2 here)
Acetyl-CoA oxidation (Krebs cycle: acetate’s 2 carbons oxidized to CO2; energy conserved as NADH and FADH2; 1 GTP per turn)
Oxidative phosphorylation (NADH/FADH2 reoxidized via electron transport chain, electrons end up reducing O2; vast majority of ATP generated here)


Location in eukaryotes: glycolysis in cytoplasm; Krebs cycle in mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation in inner membrane. EXCEPTION: succinate dehydrogenase is bound to the inner membrane (it IS Complex II of the ETC).
The Krebs cycle does NOT directly make much ATP; its job is to generate electrons (NADH, FADH2) that drive stage 3. It is also the central hub/gateway of aerobic metabolism: supplies precursors for amino acids, nucleotides, porphyrins, and even glucose (from oxaloacetate). Amphibolic pathway.

Production of Acetyl-CoA: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDC/PDH)

Net reaction: pyruvate + CoA-SH + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH (oxidative decarboxylation; first carbons of glucose fully oxidized).
Energy released is conserved both as a thioester bond (acetyl-CoA) and as NADH (later worth 2.5 ATP).
Large multienzyme complex (up to 10 MDa) in the mitochondria, 3 enzymes + 5 coenzymes:
E1: pyruvate dehydrogenase
E2: dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
E3: dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase
Coenzymes: TPP, lipoic acid (lipoyllysine), FAD (prosthetic groups, tightly bound); NAD+ and CoA-SH (co-substrates, associate/dissociate).
Advantage of multienzyme complexes: substrate channeling (intermediates never leave the complex), minimizes side reactions, regulation of one subunit affects the whole complex.
Cofactor/vitamin notes (exam-worthy clinical links):
TPP = coenzymatic form of vitamin B1; deficiency causes Beriberi (nervous + cardiac disorders). Severe thiamine deficiency → Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (memory loss, confusion, paralysis), common in alcoholics (poor intestinal absorption).
FAD contains riboflavin (vitamin B2).
NAD+ contains nicotinamide (vitamin B3); deficiency causes Pellagra (dermatitis, fatigue, encephalopathies).
Lipoic acid: two SH groups carry the acetyl group and electrons. Arsenic toxicity = binds lipoic acid’s SH groups, blocking PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
CoA structure: beta-mercaptoethylamine + pantothenic acid + 3’-phosphoadenosine 5’-diphosphate. Its function is to accept and carry acetyl groups.
PDH regulation (two mechanisms):


Allosteric inhibition by NADH and acetyl-CoA (they keep E2 acetylated, unable to accept the hydroxyethyl group from TPP).
Covalent modification (reversible phosphorylation of E1): PDH KINASE phosphorylates → INACTIVE; PDH PHOSPHATASE dephosphorylates → active. Kinase stimulated by ATP, acetyl-CoA, NADH; phosphatase stimulated by Ca++ and Mg++; ADP, pyruvate, NAD+ favor the active (dephosphorylated) state. High ATP → phosphorylated PDH → less acetyl-CoA. Analogous to glycogen synthase/phosphorylase regulation.

The Eight Steps of the Cycle
Overall per turn: Acetyl-CoA + 3 NAD+ + FAD + GDP + Pi + 2 H2O → 2 CO2 + 3 NADH + FADH2 + GTP + CoA-SH + 3 H+.
Each lap: 1 acetyl-CoA in, 2 CO2 out; oxaloacetate (OA) regenerated.

Citrate formation - CITRATE SYNTHASE


Condensation of acetyl-CoA (methyl carbon) with OA (carbonyl); only C-C bond forming reaction of the cycle. Intermediate citroyl-CoA stays bound; thioester hydrolysis makes it highly exergonic/irreversible. RATE-LIMITING step; activity depends strongly on [oxaloacetate]. Acid/base catalysis (OA carbonyl = electrophile; acetyl methyl must be deprotonated to become nucleophile). CoA is recycled. Regulated by substrate availability and product inhibition (also inhibited by succinyl-CoA, citrate).


Citrate → isocitrate - ACONITASE (aconitate hydratase)


Reversible isomerization by dehydration/rehydration; Fe-S center positions substrate and adds/removes water. Although citrate is symmetric, aconitase acts only on the carbons that came from OA. Inhibited by ATP and NADH (after a big meal, citrate accumulates, exits mitochondria, feeds fatty acid/TAG synthesis and inhibits PFK-1 in glycolysis). Fluoroacetate is a poison: converted to fluoroacetyl-CoA, inhibits aconitase.


Isocitrate → alpha-ketoglutarate + CO2 - ISOCITRATE DEHYDROGENASE (IDH)


First oxidative decarboxylation. Two isozymes: mitochondrial NAD+-dependent (main catabolic one) and NADP+-dependent (mito + cytosolic; main job = generate NADPH for biosynthesis). Highly favorable/irreversible; regulated by [ATP].


Alpha-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA + CO2 - ALPHA-KETOGLUTARATE DEHYDROGENASE (KDH)


Second (final) oxidative decarboxylation: after two turns all glucose carbons are released as CO2, but the CO2 released is NOT the same carbons that entered (they came from OA). Mechanistically identical to PDH: same 3 enzymes (E1 alpha-KG dehydrogenase, E2 dihydrolipoyl transuccinylase, E3 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) and same 5 coenzymes (TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD+). Energy conserved as NADH + thioester (succinyl-CoA). Highly favorable/irreversible; product inhibition.


Succinyl-CoA → succinate - SUCCINYL-COA SYNTHETASE


Substrate-level phosphorylation: thioester energy used to make GTP from GDP + Pi, via a phospho-enzyme (His) intermediate. 3 steps: succinyl-P forms (CoA released) → P transferred to His → P transferred to GDP forming GTP. GTP ←> ATP via nucleoside diphosphate kinase (GTP + ADP ←> GDP + ATP). Slightly favorable/reversible.


Succinate → fumarate - SUCCINATE DEHYDROGENASE


Oxidation of alkane to alkene. Flavoprotein (FAD covalently bound, unusual); electrons go to FAD → FADH2 (redox potential of C-H too low for NADH), then into the ETC (drives 1.5 ATP). Bound to inner mitochondrial membrane = ETC Complex II. Near equilibrium/reversible. STRONGLY inhibited by MALONATE (structural analog of succinate) - classic experiment blocking the cycle.


Fumarate → L-malate - FUMARASE


Stereospecific trans hydration across the double bond; OH- adds to fumarate, then H+ to the carbanion. Only uses the trans isomer. Slightly favorable/reversible.


Malate → oxaloacetate - MALATE DEHYDROGENASE (MDH)


Regenerates OA for citrate synthase. Equilibrium actually lies FAR LEFT (thermodynamically very unfavorable) but is pulled forward because citrate synthase keeps [OA] extremely low. Reversible under physiological conditions; when NADH accumulates the reaction reverses, dropping OA availability and slowing citrate synthase.

ATP Yield

Per turn of the cycle: 3 NADH (x2.5 = 7.5 ATP) + 1 FADH2 (x1.5) + 1 GTP → ~10 ATP per acetyl-CoA.
Per glucose (Table 16-1 logic): glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH (3 or 5 ATP depending on cytosolic NADH shuttle: 30-32 total); PDH: 2 NADH = 5; Krebs x2 turns: 6 NADH (15) + 2 FADH2 (3) + 2 GTP (2). TOTAL = 30-32 ATP per glucose (2.5 ATP/NADH, 1.5 ATP/FADH2).

Regulation of the Cycle

Regulated at the irreversible, highly favorable steps: PDH, citrate synthase, IDH, alpha-KDH.
General logic: activated by substrate availability; inhibited by product accumulation. Pathway-level products NADH and ATP inhibit; NAD+ and AMP activate. Overall cycle flux depends on NAD+ availability, which depends on NADH consumption by the respiratory chain, which depends on the cell’s ATP consumption.
Product accumulation (citrate, succinyl-CoA, ATP) inhibits the three limiting steps (CS, IDH, KDH). NADH accumulation also reverses MDH → less OA → slower CS.
PDH: allosteric (NADH, acetyl-CoA) + phosphorylation (see above).
Extra cross-talk:
Succinyl-CoA also inhibits citrate synthase (signals flux at the alpha-KG amino acid branch point back to the cycle start).
IDH inhibition → isocitrate accumulates → aconitase reverses → CITRATE accumulates → citrate leaves mitochondria and INHIBITS PFK-1 (glycolysis) and provides carbon for fatty acid synthesis.
Ca++ (muscle contraction signal) activates IDH, KDH, and PDH → matches ATP production to contraction.

Amphibolic Nature and Anaplerotic Reactions

Amphibolic = both catabolic and anabolic. Intermediates leave for biosynthesis: alpha-KG and OA → Asp/Glu → nucleotides; OA → glucose (gluconeogenesis); succinyl-CoA → porphyrins.
Because intermediates are drained, the cycle would stop (no OA to accept acetyl-CoA); anaplerotic (“filling up”) reactions replenish them. 4-carbon intermediates are formed by carboxylation of 3-carbon precursors:


Pyruvate carboxylase (liver, kidney - MOST IMPORTANT): pyruvate + HCO3- + ATP → OA + ADP + Pi. Consumes energy, requires BIOTIN (covalently bound), allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA (acetyl-CoA accumulates precisely when OA is low - elegant self-correcting signal).
PEP carboxykinase (heart, skeletal muscle): PEP + CO2 + GDP → OA + GTP.
Malic enzyme: pyruvate + HCO3- + NAD(P)H → malate + NAD(P)+.

Key exam hooks

Location exception: succinate dehydrogenase in inner membrane (Complex II).
Malonate inhibits SDH; fluoroacetate inhibits aconitase; arsenic poisons lipoic-acid enzymes (PDH, KDH).
Thiamine (B1) deficiency → Beriberi / Wernicke-Korsakoff; B3 deficiency → Pellagra.
CO2 released in a turn does not come from the acetyl-CoA that just entered - it comes from OA carbons.
MDH reaction is unfavorable but pulled forward by low [OA] maintained by citrate synthase.
Glycolysis vs Krebs: linear vs cyclic; OA regenerated each turn.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lecture 5.5 - Gluconeogenesis and Glycogen Metabolism
Course: From the Molecule to the Cell I (Prof. Alberto Perez-Mediavilla; notes author Ruben Pio)
Sources: Lecture notes PDF (2 parts) + slide deck
Reading: Lehninger Ch 14.4 (Gluconeogenesis) and Ch 15.3 (Coordinated regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis)
Why Glucose Production Is a Necessity

Body needs ~160 g glucose/day (75% consumed by the brain). Body stores: only ~20 g free glucose + ~500 g glycogen (100 g liver, 400 g muscle).
Erythrocytes rely EXCLUSIVELY on glucose; the brain uses glucose as its major fuel under normal conditions. Most tissues also need glucose for nucleotide synthesis and the carbohydrate part of glycoproteins/glycolipids.
Timeline of fasting: after a meal glucose is stored as liver glycogen → 2-3 h fasting: glycogenolysis releases glucose → as glycogen falls, adipose TAGs are degraded (fatty acids as alternative fuel, glycerol for gluconeogenesis) and muscle releases amino acids → ~30 h fasting: liver glycogen mostly depleted, gluconeogenesis becomes the major source of blood glucose.
Fasting blood glucose normally maintained at ~80-100 mg/dL.

Gluconeogenesis: Overview

Definition: synthesis of glucose from noncarbohydrate precursors (lactate, glycerol, most amino acids).
Site: mainly LIVER; renal cortex contributes (especially prolonged fasting; kidneys use amino acids as their main precursors); minor contribution from intestinal epithelium. Very low in muscle and brain.
Location within the cell: mitochondria AND cytosol.
NOT the reverse of glycolysis: pyruvate → glucose via simple reversal is thermodynamically impossible because glycolysis (glucose → pyruvate) is highly exergonic. 7 of the 10 reactions are shared (reversible ones); the 3 irreversible glycolytic steps must be BYPASSED with different enzymes:


Hexokinase: glucose + ATP → G6P (Delta-G’0 = -16.7 kJ/mol)
PFK-1: F6P + ATP → F1,6BP (Delta-G’0 = -14.2 kJ/mol)
Pyruvate kinase: PEP + ADP → pyruvate (Delta-G’0 = -31.4 kJ/mol)


Both pathways therefore run favorably and are independently (but coordinately) regulated.

Bypass 1: Pyruvate → Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)

Spans mitochondria and cytosol; costs 2 high-energy phosphates (1 ATP + 1 GTP).
Steps: pyruvate enters mitochondria → pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate + CO2 → OXALOACETATE → OA reduced to MALATE by mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase (OA has NO transporter across the inner membrane, so it leaves as malate via the malate/alpha-ketoglutarate transporter) → cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reoxidizes malate to OA → PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK) decarboxylates and phosphorylates OA → PEP.
Pyruvate carboxylase: contains BIOTIN (vitamin H/B7) covalently attached via amide bond to a Lys residue; allosteric ACTIVATION by acetyl-CoA = first regulator of the pathway (high acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation signals abundant energy → make glucose). Also has the anaplerotic role (replenish CAC intermediates).
The CO2 incorporated by pyruvate carboxylase is released by PEPCK; the carboxylation-decarboxylation sequence is a way to “activate” pyruvate.
MDH1 (cytosolic) and MDH2 (mitochondrial) are ISOZYMES: different genes, same reaction.
Bonus consequence: malate shuttle transfers reducing equivalents from mitochondria to cytosol, supplying the cytosolic NADH needed by GAPDH.
Overall: pyruvate + ATP + GTP + H2O → PEP + ADP + GDP + Pi + 2 H+. The 2 ATP-equivalent cost makes it favorable.

Bypasses 2 and 3

Bypass 2: fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase-1 (FBPase1) hydrolyzes F1,6BP → F6P + Pi.
Then phosphohexose isomerase (shared with glycolysis): F6P ←> G6P.
Bypass 3: glucose 6-phosphatase hydrolyzes G6P → glucose + Pi. Expressed mainly in LIVER and KIDNEY (less in intestine), NOT in skeletal muscle → muscle glycogen is used only locally (as G6P), liver/kidney can release free glucose to blood.
G6P enters the ER via a specific translocase; hydrolysis there; free glucose returns to cytosol via a transporter and exits the hepatocyte via GLUT2.

Shared reversible reactions (PEP back to F1,6BP)
Six reversible glycolytic reactions in reverse (enolase, phosphoglycerate mutase, phosphoglycerate kinase, GAPDH, triose phosphate isomerase, aldolase). Everything from PEP to GAP must run TWICE (two 3-carbon molecules per glucose).
Energy Balance

2 pyruvate + 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH + 2 H+ + 4 H2O → glucose + 4 ADP + 2 GDP + 6 Pi + 2 NAD+
Gluconeogenesis is expensive (6 ATP equivalents + 2 NADH per glucose); this energy expenditure is what makes it thermodynamically favorable.

Gluconeogenic Precursors

Major hepatic carbon sources: LACTATE (from erythrocytes and exercising skeletal muscle; lactate dehydrogenase → pyruvate), GLYCEROL (from adipose TAG breakdown; glycerol kinase → glycerol 3-phosphate → DHAP via glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase), and AMINO ACIDS (mainly from muscle protein degradation).
All amino acids except LEUCINE and LYSINE are glucogenic. ALANINE is the most abundant amino acid delivered to the liver (produced in muscle from other amino acids; alanine aminotransferase → pyruvate).
KEY EXAM POINT: Animals CANNOT make net glucose from fatty acids. Acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) cannot give net conversion to OA in animals - the 2 carbons it enters the cycle with are lost as 2 CO2 before OA is regenerated. Pyruvate carboxylase fixes this for PYRUVATE but there is no enzyme converting acetyl-CoA to pyruvate/OA in animals.

Regulation of Gluconeogenesis
Two main regulatory points: (1) pyruvate → PEP, (2) F1,6BP → F6P.

Pyruvate → OA: pyruvate carboxylase activated by acetyl-CoA. PEPCK inhibited by ADP (low-energy signal). So abundant energy (high acetyl-CoA, low ADP) favors gluconeogenesis. Simultaneously: pyruvate kinase is INHIBITED by PKA-mediated phosphorylation in response to GLUCAGON; pyruvate dehydrogenase is strongly inhibited by acetyl-CoA. Net: high acetyl-CoA favors gluconeogenesis and blocks pyruvate’s exit routes (glycolysis and oxidation).
F1,6BP ←> F6P futile cycle (PFK-1 vs FBPase1) is prevented by reciprocally acting regulators:
FRUCTOSE 2,6-BISPHOSPHATE: strongly activates PFK-1, inhibits FBPase1. Glucagon induces its DEGRADATION (via PKA phosphorylating PFK-2/FBPase-2, shifting toward FBPase-2) → glucagon induces gluconeogenesis, inhibits glycolysis.
AMP: activates PFK-1, inhibits FBPase1 → blocks gluconeogenesis when energy is low.

Glycogen Metabolism: Structure and Roles

Glycogen = storage form of glucose in animals: glucose units with alpha1→4 bonds, alpha1→6 branches roughly every 10 residues. Cytosolic granules; virtually all cells can make it, but synthesis matters most in liver and skeletal muscle.
Liver glycogen = glucose reserve to maintain blood glucose; muscle glycogen = G6P for LOCAL energy only (no glucose 6-phosphatase).
Synthesis and degradation are separate pathways → independently regulated.

Glycogenolysis (Breakdown)

Glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose residues from NON-REDUCING ends by phosphorolysis, releasing GLUCOSE 1-PHOSPHATE (not free glucose). Requires PYRIDOXAL PHOSPHATE (vitamin B6) as cofactor. Energetic advantage: glucose is already phosphorylated (saves 1 ATP).
Debranching enzyme has two activities: transferase (moves a short oligoglucose segment to another chain) and alpha1→6-glucosidase (hydrolyzes the branch bond, releasing FREE glucose).
Some glycogen is also degraded in lysosomes by lysosomal alpha-glucosidase (acid alpha-glucosidase).
Phosphoglucomutase: glucose 1-P ←> glucose 6-P.
Muscle: G6P enters glycolysis. Liver: G6P → ER via translocase → glucose 6-phosphatase → glucose → cytosol → GLUT2 → blood.

Glycogenesis (Synthesis)

Glycogen synthase transfers glucose from UDP-GLUCOSE (activated, high-energy glucose donor) to the non-reducing end forming alpha1→4 bonds.
Requires a PRIMER of at least 8 glucose residues, generated by GLYCOGENIN (initiates synthesis).
Branching enzyme introduces the alpha1→6 branches.

Coordinated Regulation of Glycogen Metabolism

Breakdown and synthesis are reciprocally regulated via reversible phosphorylation, so they never run simultaneously (prevents futile cycling):
Glycogen PHOSPHORYLASE: PHOSPHORYLATED = active (form a); dephosphorylated = inactive (form b).
Glycogen SYNTHASE: DEPHOSPHORYLATED = active (form a); phosphorylated = inactive (form b).
Same phosphorylation event therefore activates breakdown AND inhibits synthesis.

Hormonal Regulation

INSULIN: peptide hormone from pancreatic beta cells (islets of Langerhans), released when blood glucose is HIGH. Induces DEPHOSPHORYLATION of both enzymes → inhibits breakdown, stimulates synthesis. Lowers blood glucose. Acts on liver and muscle.
EPINEPHRINE: catecholamine from adrenal medulla, released with stress or low glucose (fight-or-flight). Induces PHOSPHORYLATION of both enzymes → stimulates breakdown (hepatic glycogenolysis to raise blood glucose; muscle glycogenolysis for ATP), inhibits synthesis. Acts on skeletal muscle AND liver.
GLUCAGON: peptide from pancreatic alpha cells, released when blood glucose is LOW. Like epinephrine: induces phosphorylation → stimulates breakdown, inhibits synthesis. Acts primarily on the LIVER.
Epinephrine/glucagon cascade: hormone receptor → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP up → PKA activated → PKA phosphorylates phosphorylase KINASE → phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase (active form a). Cascade AMPLIFIES the signal enormously. PKA also phosphorylates glycogen synthase (inactivating) and pyruvate kinase, and phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2 lowering F2,6BP → whole-liver response to low glucose: glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis + less glycolysis.
Muscle extra: phosphorylase kinase also activated by Ca++ during contraction → links glycogen degradation directly to ATP demand.

Glycogen Storage Diseases (GSDs / glycogenoses)
Genetic diseases of glycogen metabolism enzymes; glycogen accumulates mainly in liver, muscle, kidney. Frequency low; symptoms mild to fatal. Key ones:

Type 0 (glycogen synthase, liver): low blood glucose, high ketone bodies, early death.
Type Ia VON GIERKE (glucose 6-phosphatase, liver): one of the most serious - liver cannot release glucose into blood → hypoglycemia, enlarged liver, kidney failure. Case presentation: 7-month-old with doll’s face, protuberant abdomen, massive hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, high lactate, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Treatment: frequent high-carbohydrate meals. Type Ib = G6P translocase defect (also infection susceptibility); Ic = Pi transporter.
Type II POMPE (lysosomal glucosidase; skeletal + cardiac muscle): infantile form death by age 2; juvenile myopathy; adult form like muscular dystrophy.
Type III CORI/FORBES (debranching enzyme; liver + muscle): infant hepatomegaly, myopathy (IIIb = liver only).
Type IV ANDERSEN (branching enzyme; liver, skeletal muscle): hepatosplenomegaly, myoglobinuria.
Type V McARDLE (muscle phosphorylase, skeletal muscle): exercise-induced cramps/pain, myoglobinuria, elevated CK; liver unaffected. Case: 30-year-old woman with persistent CK elevation (~4000 IU/L) and post-exercise weakness; biopsy showed absence of myophosphorylase activity. Treatment: control physical activity, carb-rich diet, simple carbs 5 min before exercising.
Type VI HERS (liver phosphorylase): enlarged liver.
Type VII TARUI (muscle PFK-1; muscle + erythrocytes): like type V plus hemolytic anemia.
Phosphorylase kinase deficiency (VIb/VIII/IX): enlarged liver.
Type XI FANCONI-BICKEL (GLUT2): failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, rickets, kidney dysfunction.
Lafora disease: progressive epilepsy from mutations in genes regulating glycogen production; LAFORA BODIES in neurons contain poorly branched glycogen.

Key exam hooks

Gluconeogenesis is NOT glycolysis in reverse: 3 bypasses, 7 shared reactions.
OA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane → leaves as malate (this shuttle also delivers cytosolic NADH for GAPDH).
No net glucose from fatty acids in animals (acetyl-CoA carbons lost as CO2 in the cycle).
Leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids.
Glucose 6-phosphatase absent in muscle → muscle glycogen is for local use only.
Phosphorylase a = active; synthase a = active - opposite phosphorylation logic for the two enzymes.
Glucagon acts on liver; epinephrine on liver and muscle; insulin on both.
