Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMCI/Lectures/Lect.content:
Lecture 5.6 - Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP)
Course: From the Molecule to the Cell I (notes author Ruben Pio)
Subtitle/theme: “The balance of redox homeostasis”
Sources: Lecture notes PDF + slide deck + Pythagoras/beans reading
Reading: Lehninger Ch 14.5 (Pentose phosphate pathway of glucose oxidation)
Objectives of the PPP
Also called the phosphogluconate pathway or hexose monophosphate pathway. An ALTERNATIVE route for glucose oxidation whose main function is NOT ATP production. Its goals:

Generation of NADPH - carrier/donor of reducing equivalents for:


Biosynthesis of lipids and steroids (important in mammary gland, adipose tissue, adrenal cortex, liver)
Deoxyribonucleotide synthesis (ribonucleotides → deoxyribonucleotides for DNA), so rapidly proliferating cells (bone marrow, skin, intestinal mucosa) have high PPP activity - they need both reducing power AND ribose 5-phosphate
ANTIOXIDANT defense: NADPH powers glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from oxidized (GSSG); GSH then eliminates ROS like hydrogen peroxide. Especially critical in ERYTHROCYTES: no mitochondria, so the PPP is their ONLY source of NADPH.


Synthesis of pentoses - ribose 5-phosphate provides the ribose moiety for nucleotides and nucleotide-derived molecules (ATP, CoA, NAD+, FAD).
Recycling of pentoses - pentoses converted into hexoses and trioses for entry into glycolysis/gluconeogenesis.

Characteristics

Cytosolic; both anabolic and catabolic.
Two phases:
OXIDATIVE phase: IRREVERSIBLE; produces NADPH and ribulose 5-phosphate.
NON-OXIDATIVE phase: REVERSIBLE; interconverts pentose phosphates and glycolytic/gluconeogenic intermediates.

Oxidative Phase (3 reactions)

Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH): G6P oxidized to 6-phosphoglucono-delta-lactone; 1 NADPH formed. THIS IS THE RATE-LIMITING/REGULATED STEP.
Lactonase: hydrolyzes the lactone ring to 6-phosphogluconate.
6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase: oxidative decarboxylation to RIBULOSE 5-phosphate; releases CO2, generates a 2nd NADPH. (6C → 5C sugar.)
Optional: phosphopentose isomerase converts ribulose 5-P ←> RIBOSE 5-P.


Net balance if the cell needs BOTH NADPH and ribose 5-P (products used directly):
Glucose 6-P + 2 NADP+ + H2O → ribose 5-P + CO2 + 2 NADPH + 2 H+

Non-Oxidative Phase

Converts 3 pentoses into glycolytic intermediates: 2 xylulose 5-P + 1 ribose 5-P → 2 fructose 6-P + 1 glyceraldehyde 3-P (2x6C + 3C = 3x5C carbon balance).
Xylulose 5-P comes from ribulose 5-P via ribulose 5-phosphate EPIMERASE.
Three carbon-transfer reactions catalyzed by two enzymes:
TRANSKETOLASE: transfers TWO-carbon units; catalyzes reactions 1 and 3; requires THIAMINE PYROPHOSPHATE (TPP, from vitamin B1) - same cofactor family as PDH and alpha-KDH.
TRANSALDOLASE: transfers a THREE-carbon unit; catalyzes reaction 2.
Reversibility = metabolic flexibility: pentoses → glycolytic intermediates, OR glycolytic intermediates → pentoses WITHOUT producing NADPH.
GLOBAL BALANCE: 3 glucose 6-P + 6 NADP+ + 3 H2O → 2 fructose 6-P + glyceraldehyde 3-P + 6 NADPH + 6 H+ + 3 CO2

Regulation

Oxidative phase: controlled at G6PDH via the NADP+/NADPH ratio. NADP+ is a SUBSTRATE; NADPH INHIBITS the enzyme. When NADPH is consumed (e.g. GSSG → GSH by glutathione reductase), NADP+ rises and G6PDH activity accelerates - the key response mechanism to oxidative stress.
Non-oxidative phase: no major allosteric regulation; direction depends on substrate/product concentrations (because reversible).

Glutathione and Oxidative Stress

Glutathione = gamma-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine (a Glu-Cys-Gly tripeptide).
Glutathione PEROXIDASE uses 2 GSH to reduce peroxides (R-OOH → R-OH + H2O), producing GSSG.
Glutathione REDUCTASE uses NADPH to convert GSSG back to 2 GSH.
This cycle protects proteins and lipids from oxidative damage; in erythrocytes it protects hemoglobin.

G6PD Deficiency (favism)

The most frequent genetic alteration of the PPP and one of the most common enzyme deficiencies in the world: ~400 million affected, frequencies up to 25% in parts of Africa and the Middle East.
X-LINKED → more frequently expressed in males. Reduces enzyme activity; all variants retain SOME activity (complete loss would be lethal).
Most carriers asymptomatic normally; acute HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA triggered by high oxidative stress: infections, certain drugs/herbicides (e.g. QUININE - see below), and FAVA BEANS.
Mechanism: G6PD-deficient erythrocytes cannot produce enough NADPH → cannot keep glutathione reduced → oxidative damage to hemoglobin and cell components → red cells break down (anemia, jaundice, even heart failure).
MALARIA CONNECTION: Plasmodium parasites develop inside red blood cells and are highly susceptible to oxidative stress. G6PD deficiency creates a more oxidatively stressful erythrocyte environment → confers partial resistance to malaria → classic balanced polymorphism (deficiency concentrated exactly where malaria is endemic; geographic maps overlap).
QUININE paradox: first effective malaria drug, from cinchona tree bark; interferes with heme detoxification in Plasmodium, raising toxic stress in the parasite. But in G6PD-deficient (malaria-resistant) individuals quinine can push oxidative stress over the edge and trigger hemolytic anemia.

The Pythagoras and Fava Beans Story (fun aside from the reading)

Pythagoras’s cult avoided beans - ancient writers (Pliny) say Pythagoreans believed fava beans could contain the souls of the dead; favas were a symbol of death for Greeks, Egyptians, and Romans (priests of Jupiter couldn’t touch or mention them; favas served at Roman funerary feasts, the silicernium).
Before 1492, “bean” in European texts almost always means the FAVA (green/kidney/lima beans arrived after Columbus).
Plausible biological explanation: FAVISM, a genetic disorder most common in the Mediterranean - i.e., G6PD deficiency. Eating favas (or inhaling their pollen) triggers hemolytic anemia in susceptible people: red cells break down, causing anemia symptoms, jaundice, even heart failure. Even today about 1 in 12 affected die of favism.
Take-home: the ancient “bean = death” superstition likely reflects a real, geographically concentrated enzyme deficiency - the same G6PD deficiency that protects against malaria. Nice example of why the same allele can persist: malaria resistance advantage vs favism risk.

Alternative Uses of Glucose (flexibility of glycolysis + PPP)
Cells route glucose 6-phosphate between PPP (NADPH + ribose 5-P) and glycolysis (NADH, ATP, precursors) depending on needs - the classic four modes:

Cell needs BOTH NADPH and ribose 5-P (e.g. proliferating cells): oxidative phase runs, products used directly (G6P → ribose 5-P + CO2 + 2 NADPH).
Cell needs NADPH and ATP (e.g. red blood cell under oxidative stress): oxidative phase + non-oxidative phase recycle pentoses back to F6P/GAP → glycolysis for ATP. Full global balance above (3 G6P → 6 NADPH + 3 CO2 + glycolytic intermediates).
Cell needs only NADPH (e.g. adipose/fat synthesis): full cycle, pentoses recycled to glucose 6-P and re-run through the oxidative phase repeatedly.
Cell needs only ribose 5-P (e.g. rapidly dividing cells with abundant NADPH already): non-oxidative phase runs in REVERSE, making pentoses from glycolytic intermediates without NADPH production.

Thiamine Deficiency Link

TPP is the cofactor of transketolase, and also of PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
Severe thiamine (B1) deficiency → beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ATAXIA, abnormal eye movements, classically associated with chronic alcohol misuse (poor intake + impaired absorption). Untreated, progresses to Korsakoff syndrome: severe memory impairment and confabulation.

Key exam hooks

PPP’s main function is NADPH (not ATP) + pentoses; cytosolic; oxidative phase irreversible, non-oxidative reversible.
G6PDH is THE regulated step: inhibited by NADPH, activated by rising NADP+ (i.e., by NADPH consumption).
Transketolase = 2C units + TPP (B1); transaldolase = 3C units.
Erythrocytes: PPP is their only NADPH source (no mitochondria) → why G6PD deficiency causes hemolytic anemia.
G6PD deficiency: X-linked, ~400M people, favism, malaria resistance, quinine risk.
The transketolase/TPP link makes transketolase activity an index of thiamine status.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF ANS 2
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF ANS 2
Sources

autonomic nervous system 2 FMF (automatic transcription, heavily garbled in places). Starts mid-sentence (parasympathetic and the bladder: “…when it contracts is in order to empty the bladder”) and ends with student questions about dorsal and ventral. The first ANS lecture is the second half of FMF Embryology Spinal nerves and nervous system (Audio Clip 2), which stops at the white and grey rami; the part between the two recordings is not recorded.
Coverage: transcript first, filled from Lucía (“Autonomous nervous system”: sympathetic system, parasympathetic system, viscerosensory fibers, chromaffin cells, neurotransmitters; and the ANS TBL with the epidural case). Date not recorded.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault. Drawings from Gray’s Anatomy for Students (“look at the very end, all these beautiful drawings”); much was drawn on the board.
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “Autonomous nervous system” and “TBL. Autonomous Nervous System”. PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Embryology Spinal nerves and nervous system, FMF Physiology Smooth muscle.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

“This is a key question”: which fibres carry visceral sensory information: distension travels with the parasympathetic, pain with the sympathetic, both in the opposite direction (section 8).
Summary of neurotransmitters (section 7): all preganglionic fibres use acetylcholine; sympathetic postganglionic norepinephrine, with exceptions.
Cervical ganglia fusion: “to make it a little bit more complicated, you don’t need to know” the further fusion detail (section 3).
Function tables: “we can go through this at home.”

1. Sympathetic vs parasympathetic: functions

Bladder: the parasympathetic contracts the detrusor muscle to empty the bladder; the sympathetic inhibits that contraction, letting the bladder relax and fill, and closes the sphincters.
Generally the sympathetic closes the sphincters (anal, urethral, all of them): it goes to the sphincter, not the whole bladder or gut wall.
Sympathetic: alertness, “fight or flight”. Parasympathetic: brings things back to normal, “rest and digest”, calm; near vision (pupil constriction).
Secretions for digestion (saliva, gastric, pancreatic) are produced or enhanced by the autonomic system (transcript garbled about which division [verify]; it fits “rest and digest”, i.e. parasympathetic).
Adrenaline release in a danger situation: sympathetic.
Recap: autonomic ganglion cells (sympathetic and parasympathetic) come from the neural crest; second (motor) neurons are always in ganglia.

2. Sympathetic ganglia: two sets

Preganglionic neurons: lateral horn, T1 to L2 (intermediolateral column).
Sympathetic chain (trunk): paired ganglia on both sides of the vertebral column, at each spinal level.
Prevertebral (preaortic) ganglia: single ganglia in the abdominal (and pelvic) cavity, anterior to the vertebral bodies and the abdominal aorta and its branches; some have names.

3. How many chain ganglia?

Class exercise: spinal levels are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral (and coccygeal; the class was unsure of the count).
Cervical: instead of one per level, they fuse into three: superior, middle and inferior cervical ganglia.
The inferior cervical also fuses with the first thoracic (C7 + T1), with a different name (“you don’t need to know”; name not given [verify]).
The rest: one per level, including sacral ganglia (more ganglia lower down for the limbs); at the bottom a single unpaired ganglion where the two chains meet.
[Lucía] Above T1 and below L2 there is no lateral horn: preganglionic fibres from T1 go up the chain, those from L2 go down, to reach ganglia at those levels.

4. Sympathetic routes
To the skin (body wall)

Why are chain neurons right next to the spinal nerves? Two small bridges link each spinal nerve to its chain ganglion:

one carries preganglionic fibres from the spinal nerve into the chain;
the other carries postganglionic fibres back to the spinal nerve.


Postganglionic fibres then travel with the spinal nerves to reach small smooth-muscle “viscera” of the dermis, which is segmentally organized: arrector pili muscles (hair follicles), sweat glands, blood vessels. Towards the back via the dorsal ramus, towards the front via the ventral ramus.
Reaches skin everywhere (except palms and soles, transcript [verify]). These structures have only sympathetic innervation: fear makes hairs stand up.
[Lucía] White communicating ramus (preganglionic, myelinated) and grey communicating ramus (postganglionic, unmyelinated).

To the thoracic viscera

Preganglionic neurons at the same level exit the spinal nerve and enter the chain; for higher levels (cervical ganglia, e.g. supplying the heart, which originates from cervical levels), preganglionic fibres from T1 to T4 enter the chain and go up.
Postganglionic fibres leave the ganglia towards the midline, forming a mesh around the bronchi, lungs, heart, oesophagus.
These are the sympathetic cardiac nerves: postganglionic fibres.

To the abdominal and pelvic viscera

Preganglionic neurons are in the lateral horn (thoracic levels), but the second neurons are in the prevertebral ganglia in the abdomen and pelvis.
The preganglionic fibre leaves the spinal nerve, passes through the chain ganglion without synapsing (no neurons there for it), crosses the diaphragm, and synapses in a prevertebral ganglion near the aorta (e.g. at the superior mesenteric artery). Postganglionic fibres go to the gut, liver, etc.
These preganglionic fibres form the splanchnic nerves (thoracic splanchnic; also lumbar, going to pelvic ganglia).
Contrast: cardiac nerves = postganglionic; splanchnic nerves = preganglionic.

5. Blood vessels: sympathetic only

How does the sympathetic shut down the GI tract in fight or flight? Not by acting on gut muscle (that is the parasympathetic’s job): by reducing its blood supply.
The sympathetic is the only system innervating blood vessels, causing vasoconstriction: viscera with less blood reduce their activity. Skin too: in fight or flight you look pale (cutaneous vasoconstriction).
Muscle blood vessels dilate in fight or flight, also sympathetic: the same transmitter acts through different receptors in different tissues (pupils, bronchi, heart, skin vessels, muscle vessels). “Blood vessels of the muscle have cholinergic receptors” [check]: [Lucía] says the sympathetic postganglionic fibres to skeletal muscle vessels (and sweat glands) release acetylcholine.
Student question on brain blood flow: left open (“let’s do some research”).
[Lucía] Sympathetic nerves enter the viscera with the arteries; the vascular system, kidney and glycaemia regulation are exclusively sympathetic.

6. Parasympathetic system

Preganglionic neurons in the brainstem and at S2 to S4.
Sacral levels have no lateral horn: the preganglionic neurons are in the ventral horn region (motor), exit by the ventral root, leave the spinal nerve and go to the midline viscera (e.g. bladder).
Ganglia are in the walls of the viscera, often microscopic: long preganglionic, very short postganglionic fibres. (Sympathetic: visible postganglionic nerves.)
Pelvic splanchnic nerves: the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from S2 to S4 (transcript “Felix-Platlick”). Not to be confused with the sympathetic splanchnic nerves.
Vagus nerve (10th cranial): preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the brainstem, a very thick nerve leaving the skull; branches to thoracic viscera (heart…) and abdominal viscera: stomach, small intestine, ascending colon and the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves go up to the distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon, rectum, and to the bladder etc.
In the GI tract the parasympathetic ganglia lie within the gut layers, forming two plexuses: one between the two muscle layers, another between the mucosa and the first muscle layer (part of a very complex system, coordinating contraction along the gut). Sympathetic supply to the gut: essentially just the blood vessels.
[Lucía] Vagus leaves via the jugular foramen; slows heart rate, contracts bronchi, stimulates the GI tract. Pelvic splanchnic nerves also reach prostate/clitoris (erection) and form the inferior hypogastric plexus.

7. Neurotransmitters and the adrenal medulla

























FibreNeurotransmitterAll preganglionic (sympathetic and parasympathetic), synapse in the ganglionAcetylcholine, alwaysSympathetic postganglionic (chain and prevertebral ganglia)NorepinephrineExceptions: sympathetic fibres to sweat glands and the dilating vessels of skeletal muscleAcetylcholineParasympathetic postganglionicAcetylcholine ([Lucía]; not explicit in the transcript)

Adrenal medulla: some neural crest cells migrate into the adrenal gland and form something like a sympathetic ganglion. When they receive preganglionic fibres, they release norepinephrine and epinephrine into the bloodstream: a dual nervous and hormonal action; very fast; the whole body is activated.
[Lucía] These are chromaffin cells; the adrenal medulla secretes mostly epinephrine (80%, 20% norepinephrine). Preganglionic = cholinergic; sympathetic postganglionic = adrenergic; parasympathetic postganglionic = cholinergic.

8. Visceral sensory fibres

Sensory neurons from the viscera have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia, together with the somatosensory neurons from skin and dermis: peripheral process, cell body in the ganglion, central process ending in the dorsal horn.
Key question: with which system does sensory information travel?

Distension (awareness that the stomach, bladder or rectum is full) travels with the parasympathetic fibres, in the opposite direction. In the CNS it arrives right next to the parasympathetic motor neurons, so if it is appropriate the reflex (e.g. going to the toilet) is close at hand.
Pain travels with the sympathetic fibres, in the opposite direction (e.g. stomach pain from an ulcer enters via the chain).


[Lucía] Exception: pelvic pain travels with the pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) nerves. Pain reaches the spinal nerve via the white communicating ramus. Distension from viscera down to the distal third of the transverse colon travels with the vagus.

9. Not recorded this year: the ANS TBL case ([Lucía])

Epidural anaesthesia in labour: blood pressure drops (130/85 to 80/45 mmHg) with tachycardia (120 bpm): the anaesthetic blocked sympathetic preganglionic fibres, removing the basal sympathetic tone on vascular smooth muscle (alpha-1 receptors), so arterioles dilate.
Treatment: fluids, then alpha-1 agonists (ephedrine, phenylephrine). Possible reflex bradycardia via the baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus, glossopharyngeal nerve, solitary nucleus, dorsal vagal nucleus, vagus, M2 receptors); treat with muscarinic antagonists (atropine).
Key ideas: vessels have only sympathetic innervation and depend on basal tone; the heart has both.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF Biophysics Action potential scenarios
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Biophysics Action potential scenarios
Sources

Audio Clip 11 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Starts mid-sentence (“…action potential that you may trigger inside a neuron, for the behaviour that you have for muscles”) and ends with “we will upload this presentation to ADI”. Long stretches are students discussing in groups (some in Spanish) and a looping garbage line.
This is the membrane potential workshop announced at the end of FMF Biophysics Membrane potential: four scenarios, discussed in groups, then explained by the lecturer. Scenario 4 was left for homework.
Coverage: transcript first; filled from Lucía (“Membrane potential workshop”, same four scenarios last year). Date not recorded.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault; the scenarios presentation is on ADI (“as always”).
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “Membrane potential workshop” (scenarios 1 to 4) and “Time and length constants”. PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Biophysics Membrane potential.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Exam format (FMF): two parts.

Multiple choice, about 100 to 120 questions, four options. [verify] the “for options” fragment.
Short questions, answer space limited to about half a page. “These scenarios are the typical possibility” for one of these: “you will find something similar to this scenario.”


No calculator needed: “you don’t need to do the maths in the exam, but you need to understand the equation”, so as a doctor you can predict the effect of a change in a patient.
Correction of the Nernst equation: the right order inside the logarithm is outside concentration on top, inside concentration on the bottom. He was not sure what he wrote in the lecture; this is the correct expression.
Notation: “log” = natural logarithm; decimal logarithm is written “log10”.
“Something that you need to remember”: during an action potential the ion concentrations do not change (section 5).
“The take-home message”: the membrane potential can change through concentrations and through permeabilities (section 4).
Course end: after this, two TBLs remain (MRI with Dr. Domínguez, nuclear medicine with Dr. Sancho), then the exam.

1. Reference values




















IonExtracellular (mmol/L)Intracellular (mmol/L)Na+14515K+5150 (transcript “550”; 150 matches the lecture table [verify])

Potassium is mainly inside, sodium mainly outside, but there is always a small concentration on the other side.
Nernst potentials in a normal neuron: Na about +60 mV, K about -90 mV. Resting membrane potential about -70 mV, an equilibrium between K pulling towards -90 and Na pulling towards +60. Threshold to trigger an action potential about -50 mV, a property of the cell that does not change in these scenarios.
Boltzmann constant given in class: 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K.

2. Scenario 1: severe hyponatremia

Question: extracellular Na falls to 120 mmol/L (hyponatremia: extracellular sodium below normal; “natrium”, the Latin name, gives the symbol Na). How does this affect the Nernst potentials of Na and K?
“You’re going too far”: first answer about the Nernst potentials, before jumping to action potentials.
Do not assume the missing sodium went into the cell (it may be the kidneys extracting too much). Only extracellular sodium changes; intracellular Na and both K values stay the same.
K Nernst potential: unchanged (-90 mV), because it depends only on K concentrations outside and inside.
Na Nernst potential: decreases (below +60 mV): the top of the fraction is smaller, so the logarithm is smaller. The limits within which the membrane potential can move become narrower.
Follow-up (not on the sheet): with Na’s Nernst potential lowered (e.g. to about 40 mV), the resting membrane potential decreases (below -70 mV). The threshold stays at -50 mV, so it is harder to trigger an action potential. A small change in sodium can have large consequences, in neurons and, as will be seen, in muscle, especially the heart.
[Lucía] Same answers; less Na entry, RMP more negative.

3. Scenario 2: hypokalemia

Extracellular K falls to 3 mmol/L (normal 5).
Na Nernst potential: unchanged.
K Nernst potential: decreases: the top of the fraction is smaller, so it becomes more negative, e.g. about -95 mV instead of -90 (“you have to do the numbers to get the correct value”).
“Don’t be confused about what reduction means: reduction means more negative.”
Membrane potential decreases again, so it is more difficult to trigger an action potential. Different mechanism from scenario 1 (K’s Nernst potential vs Na’s), same consequence.
[Lucía] Same; RMP decreases towards -90 mV.

4. Scenario 3: sodium permeability halved (at rest)

Resting situation, all concentrations normal; only p(Na) is halved. Effect on the membrane potential?
(Some students thought it would only change timing, not the value; he corrected this.)
Explanation with the Goldman equation: ignore chloride (its potential, about -70 mV, is close to rest). It is a competition between a sodium term and a potassium term: if the K term were zero, Na wins (+60 mV); if the Na term were zero, K wins (-90 mV). -70 mV results because p(Na) is smaller than p(K).
Halving p(Na) reduces sodium’s influence further: the membrane potential falls below -70 mV.
Take-home message: the membrane potential changes with concentrations and with permeabilities.
If instead p(Na) doubles: the membrane potential increases.
[Lucía] Same: the decrease comes from permeability, not from a change in the Nernst potential. [check] She gives p(Na) = 0.02 p(K) here but 0.002 p(K) in her lecture notes.

5. Concentrations do not change during an action potential

During depolarization many sodium channels open and many sodium ions cross. Do the intra- and extracellular concentrations change? No.
The number crossing is tiny compared with the pools: e.g. 2,000 ions crossing against perhaps 10^10 ions outside. “This is something that you need to remember.”
The charge distribution changes only right next to the membrane.

6. Scenario 4 (left as homework): time constants

Question: how does a reduction of sodium permeability affect the depolarization and repolarization characteristic times?
Hint: with more sodium permeability, sodium crosses faster, so the time is reduced. “I leave that for you”; he would send an answer.
[Lucía] Lower p(Na): depolarization takes longer; repolarization time unchanged (depends on potassium permeability; sodium channels are closed). Time constant: time to reach 63% of the final value; depends on membrane resistance (inversely proportional to permeability) and capacitance.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF Biophysics MRI basics
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Biophysics MRI basics
Sources

US & MRI FMF, from “this is another topic… MRI” to the end. The first part (ultrasound) is in FMF Biophysics Ultrasound. Ends mid-sentence (“when you are inserted inside the magnetic field, all your protons…“): the rest of the MRI lecture (alignment, excitation, relaxation) is not recorded.
Audio Clip 12: this turned out to be the MRI TBL (with Dr. Domínguez, radiologist, and the biophysics lecturer). Its first part (parallel/antiparallel orientations, radiofrequency, proton density, precession, T1 and T2) is a physics recap by the biophysics lecturer and is used here; it starts mid-sentence. The safety part is in FMF Radiology MRI.
The TBL recap partly fills the gap left by the end of the lecture recording; T1 and T2 “were not introduced in the classroom because there was no time”.
Coverage: transcripts first, filled from Lucía (“Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)”, “MRI basics”).

Resources

Slides: none in the vault; the precession animation and the T1/T2 curves are on the TBL slides (ADI).
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)” (biophysics) and “MRI basics” (radiology). PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Radiology MRI (how MRI works clinically, safety), FMF Biophysics Ultrasound.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

What is covered is “just the fundamentals: the points that you need to understand in order to understand the risks of magnetic resonance and how the system works.”
TBL: “This is the key point”: the energy difference between parallel and antiparallel orientations, which radiofrequency of the right energy can use to reverse the dipoles (section 6).
“Please remember that you need to have a magnetic dipole”: hydrogen (a proton) can be imaged; normal oxygen cannot (section 6).
Safety is the main point of the TBL: see FMF Radiology MRI.

1. MRI among imaging techniques

For image quality, MRI is the most powerful technique; he expects it to become the first choice for many exams.
Comparison:










































UltrasoundX-raysMRICostCheapest; even one per doctor’s officeAlso cheapHugeDangerNot dangerous if you know the rulesMore dangerous; needs a large facility(safety rules: see Radiology note)Image qualityLowestMiddleBestExam timeOften over half an hour, even one hour, inside the tubePhysicsSimplest, most intuitive (forces)MiddleBy far the most complex (quantum mechanics)

Possibilities are huge: spectroscopy (which molecules are in the brain), detecting active brain regions, measuring flow velocity.
Device: a tube, a metre long or more, into which the patient is introduced, containing a huge magnetic field: forces on magnetic material are so large that nothing could be held.

2. Magnetic fields

Everyone has played with permanent magnets: north and south poles (historical names); like poles repel, opposite attract.
Explaining magnets is very complex: not until the 1930s-40s was there a correct theory, although the structure of matter was known. Unlike electricity, turning one magnet around changes attraction into repulsion.
Field lines leave the north pole and enter at the south pole. Magnetic field symbol: B.
Origin: moving electric charges. Any charge moving along a line or rotating creates a magnetic field around it.
[Lucía] Lorentz force: only moving charges feel it; it is perpendicular to velocity and field, so it changes the trajectory, not the kinetic energy. A ring of moving charges makes a magnetic dipole (N and S); poles cannot be isolated.

3. Types of magnetic materials

Everyday experience suggests three groups (no interaction, weak attraction, can be permanent magnets). The real classification:






















TypeBehaviourFerromagneticCan become permanent magnets (permanent magnetization)ParamagneticNo permanent magnetization, but are attracted (magnetization induced by a field)DiamagneticRepelled: in a field, the force is a repulsion

“No interaction” is false: diamagnetism is always present, even if very weak. The human body is diamagnetic, because water is diamagnetic.
We always interact with the Earth’s magnetic field, which is weak.
[Lucía] Ferromagnetic: iron, nickel (magnetization remains after the field is removed). Paramagnetic: O2, aluminium (disappears). Diamagnetic: living materials.

4. Spin and why matter is usually not magnetic

Matter is made of electrons, protons and neutrons. All have spin: classically, they are rotating, so each has a small magnetic field. You cannot have a proton that does not spin.
Why does a table not attract things? In normal materials the particles’ small magnetic fields point in random directions and cancel: total field zero.
In some materials neighbouring dipoles align parallel to each other: a net magnetization (quantum explanation not given).
Without an external field (his drawing): ferromagnetic materials have aligned regions; paramagnetic have random orientations, no net magnetization; diamagnetic molecules (e.g. water: protons, oxygen, electrons) have zero total, but magnetization can be excited.

5. Units and field strengths

Unit: tesla (T), very large; smaller unit the gauss (G): 1 G = 10^-4 T (transcript “into the nine-fourth”; [Lucía] 1 T = 10^4 G).
Earth’s field: transcript “roughly 1.5” gauss [check] [Lucía]: 0.5 G.
Clinical MRI: transcript “between 4.5 to 7.0” [verify]; [Lucía]: over 1 to 1.5 T, most equipment 1.5 to 3 T.
In Europe, the limit for clinical use is 3 T (research can go higher, per [Lucía]).
The strongest permanent magnet you may hold: below 0.1 T, already a very large magnet.
Idea of MRI: outside the field the body’s protons point in all directions; inside the strong field they… (recording ends here).

6. Parallel and antiparallel; resonance (TBL recap)

In a magnetic field, dipoles can adopt two orientations: parallel (lower energy) and antiparallel (higher energy). For a given field there is a fixed energy difference between them. This is the key point.
Providing exactly that energy reverses the dipoles: the device’s antennas send radiofrequency of the selected frequency to the patient.
You need a magnetic dipole: hydrogen nuclei (single protons) have one. Oxygen (normal isotope) has an even number of protons and neutrons: their fields cancel, no net dipole, so it cannot be observed in normal MRI.
Sequence:

Outside the device, protons are randomly oriented.
Inside, all protons align with the main magnetic field (starting point).
Radiofrequency reverses the orientation.
Switch the radiofrequency off; protons return to the original orientation, emitting radiofrequency that is detected. This shows where radiofrequency was absorbed.


This gives the proton density image (normal MRI focuses on hydrogen).
[Lucía] Slightly more protons are parallel, giving a net magnetization M; the emitted frequency depends on the particle and the local magnetic field (surrounding molecules); the precession frequency is the Larmor frequency, depending on a constant specific to the atom and on B. Only nuclei with an odd number of nucleons are detected (O-16 is not).

7. Precession, T1 and T2 (TBL recap)

The proton cannot simply flip back: it is spinning. Instead it makes a spiral movement around the external field direction, becoming more and more parallel: precession (a behaviour of rotating objects subjected to a force).
This spiral is slow compared with a simple flip, so its speed can be measured.
Components (animation: red arrows = external field, black arrow = proton):

Longitudinal (parallel to the field, vertical): grows.
Transverse (horizontal): decreases.


T1 = characteristic time for the longitudinal component to grow.
T2 = characteristic time for the transverse component to disappear.
T1 and T2 are very sensitive to the chemistry around the proton (in water vs in a protein): each tissue has its own relaxation times, and sequences are designed accordingly. T1- and T2-weighted sequences differentiate soft tissues in much better detail than CT. “This is why magnetic resonance is so powerful.”
[Lucía] T1 = time for the longitudinal component to reach 63% of its maximum; T2 = time for the transverse component to fall to 37% (1/e). [check] Her biophysics section writes “0.67” for T1. Water: long T1 and T2; solids: very short.
[Lucía] Gradients make the field slightly different at each point, so the signal can be located in space.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF Biophysics Membrane potential
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Biophysics Membrane potential
Sources

Audio Clip 5 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Opens with “what was the point that we were discussing the last day? …the electric behaviour of cells” and ends mid-sentence in the charge-neutrality discussion.
Audio Clip 6 (4 lines): “the membrane is impermeable… no holes… a barrier that prevents the crossing of ions”. Fits between Clips 5 and 7.
Audio Clip 7: the selectively permeable pore and diffusion; ends a session (“I’m going to stop here and we’ll continue”; weekend).
Audio Clip 8: starts mid-sentence in the next session (flux to the outside), covers Nernst, Goldman and the resting potential, and ends “we will continue on the workshop”.
So this is two sessions: Clips 5 + 6 + 7 (session 1), Clip 8 (session 2). Gaps: the part of session 1 between Clip 5 and Clip 7 (Clip 6 is only a few seconds), and the opening of session 2. The first session on electric forces (“the last day”) is not among the transcripts.
Coverage: everything from the transcripts; gaps and formulas filled from Lucía. Date not recorded.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault (FMF Lecture slides folder is empty). Ion concentration table and the voltage-versus-time diagram are on his slides (see ADI).
Study material: none in the vault.
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “Electric behaviour of a cell”, “Membrane resting potential”, “Membrane potential in a real cell”. PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Biophysics Action potential scenarios (continuation), FMF Physiology Smooth muscle.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

“An important message to retain”: whatever the situation, the centre of the cell always has charge neutrality; any excess of positive or negative charge sits on the inner side of the membrane (section 2). “This is the explanation for any neuron, for any muscular cell.”
“An important point”: the potential is created by diffusion; electric forces stop the process. “When you are faced the first time with the membrane potential, you will believe that it is due to electric forces… No” (sections 4 and 5).
Goldman equation: “pay attention to the order of outer and inner” (section 7).
At rest, permeability order K > Na (and Cl): “only at rest. That’s important because we are going to introduce the action potential.”
The action potential will be analysed in detail in the workshop.

1. Electricity in biology: ions, not electrons

Recap of the previous session: in biophysics electric current is carried by ions, not electrons. Ions are much heavier, so they are much harder to move through the water of the intracellular and extracellular media.
Membrane potentials matter for neurons and the nervous system, and for muscle cells.
Model cell: for its electric behaviour, the only relevant part is the membrane, separating intracellular and extracellular media.
Ions considered: positive (sodium, potassium), negative (chloride); also large negatively charged molecules (proteins). Calcium is relevant only for muscle.
[Lucía] Previous session’s key ideas: electric forces are conservative; field lines from positive charges (source) to negative (sink); superposition principle; electric potential decreases along the field direction.

2. Charge neutrality and shielding

One positive ion alone: no forces. Several positive ions: they repel each other and end up on the inner side of the membrane; the centre has zero charge.
Positive and negative ions together: each ion feels many small attractive and repulsive forces in all directions; if the numbers of positive and negative charges are equal, the total force on each ion is zero. The forces are always there, but cancelled.
So the only way to have ions inside a cell in equilibrium is charge neutrality: total positive balanced by total negative.
Shielding: add two extra (unbalanced) charges to a neutral cell. The effect of all the other, balanced charges cancels, so for the extra charges it is as if they were behind a shield and only the two extra charges exist. They repel each other and move to the inner side of the membrane.
Result: the centre stays neutral; any excess (positive or negative) accumulates on the inner face of the membrane. Charges move only if there is a net force; at the centre there is none.
From here on he does not draw all the ions, but there are always a huge number of positive and negative ions in equal numbers.
[Lucía] Equilibrium requires total charge Qt = 0 (resting cell).

3. Impermeable vs selectively permeable membrane

Clip 6: an impermeable membrane has no holes: a barrier that prevents ions crossing.
Now open a passive hole (no pump, no active mechanism; not the sodium-potassium pump): a discontinuity of the membrane that lets only positive ions cross.
In reality pores are selective for an element (potassium, sodium, chloride), but here it is enough that one charge type crosses.
Thermal motion: the body is at about 310 K (37 °C). Ions, like water molecules and proteins, are vibrating, colliding and moving randomly. The cause of this movement is thermal energy, not electric forces, which are cancelled.
An ion that happens to approach the hole in the right direction escapes to the outside.
The probability of crossing depends on temperature (faster vibration) and on the number of ions (more ions, more chances).
[Lucía] If the membrane is impermeable to an ion, it bounces back; if permeable, an ion hitting a pore crosses. At 0 K nothing would change.

4. Diffusion creates a charge distribution across the membrane

Start: total charge zero inside and outside. After a while, say 5 positive ions are outside.
Inside, 5 negative charges (out of perhaps 10^20 ions) are now unbalanced; they move to the inner face of the membrane. Outside, the 5 positive ions end up on the outer face.
New situation: negative charges on the inner side, positive on the outer side. Away from the membrane both media stay neutral.
The driving force is diffusion, not electrostatic force. Electric forces appear afterwards, because of the charge distribution, and they are what stops the movement: “Actually they will stop moving because of the electric forces.”
Once the hole is open, ions outside can also cross inwards: two probabilities, one in each direction. The winner is the side with higher concentration.
[Lucía] The concentrations themselves do not change: very few ions cross relative to the total, so no water flow (not osmosis).

5. Equilibrium: the Nernst potential

Assume the concentration inside is higher: net ion flux to the outside. Does it continue forever? No.
At first (charge neutrality) there is no electric force; only diffusion pushes.
After some time, positive charges outside and negative inside: an ion trying to leave is repelled by the outside positive charges and pulled back by the inside negative charges. An electric force pointing inwards appears.
While small, diffusion still wins and more charges accumulate; the electric force grows until it balances diffusion. Then crossing stops (net).
Electric force means energy can be extracted: there is an energy difference between inside and outside, i.e. a voltage across the membrane. Defined as V = V(inside) - V(outside).
In a neuron it can be about 70 mV, large for a membrane: compare the roughly 3 V of a phone battery (a factor of about 50). He mentions it being close to the limit the membrane can withstand [verify].
Two kinds of forces: diffusion (depends on number of ions and temperature) and electric (depends on the voltage and the charge of the ion). “There are no more magnitudes.”
Balancing them (derivation not given; the logarithm not demonstrated):

Nernst potential: the voltage equals k_B T / q (Boltzmann constant times temperature, divided by the ion’s charge) multiplied by the logarithm of the ratio of the concentrations outside and inside. Named after Nernst (transcript “NAPS”). The exact form is on his slide. In the workshop he corrected it: outside concentration on top, inside on the bottom (see FMF Biophysics Action potential scenarios); “log” means natural logarithm.
[Lucía] Formula only as an image; she notes that with equal concentrations the log is 0 and the Nernst potential is 0; k_B T/q about 26.7 mV.


“Ideal” value: valid only for a membrane permeable to one ion. It is never found in a real cell, because several ions act at once. The time to reach it would also be very long (“two years”; for chemistry, seconds) [verify] meaning.

6. Nernst potentials in a real neuron

His table: concentrations inside and outside of sodium, potassium, chloride and other negatively charged molecules (values for a non-human neuron, but close). Positive and negative charges balance inside and outside.
The large negative molecules cannot cross passively; only sodium, potassium and chloride have passive pores.
Sodium is high outside, potassium high inside: maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, always working.
With T = 310 K, k_B, and q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C:






















IonNernst potentialNa+about +60 mVK+about -90 mVCl-about -70 mV (transcript once “minus 7”)

Student question: should chloride’s be positive? No: its charge q is negative, which reverses the sign.
Meaning: a neuron with pores only for sodium would end at +60 mV; only for potassium, at -90 mV.
+60 and -90 mV are the limits of what diffusion alone can produce.
[Lucía] Same three values.

7. Which ion wins: permeability and the Goldman equation

The ion that controls the membrane potential is the one with the most open pores.
Permeability (p): the number of open pores for an ion (not probability). Zero when all closed; very large when many open.
At rest: p(K) > p(Na), and chloride; sodium and chloride permeabilities are small but not zero. “Only at rest.”
So the resting potential is close to K’s -90 mV, but sodium and chloride pull it: about -70 mV.
Goldman equation (for a neuron only; “you cannot apply that for muscular cells”):

Same prefactor k_B T / q (q now the positive elementary charge, 1.6 x 10^-19 C) times a logarithm of a ratio of sums, each term a permeability multiplied by a concentration (Na, K, Cl).
The transcript is garbled; he read the terms as “inside, outside, inside, outside” and then “but here this is outside”, i.e. one term has inside and outside the other way round. Together with “pay attention to the order of outer and inner”, copy the exact formula from his slide. [verify]; [Lucía] has it only as an image.
With physiology-textbook permeabilities you get about -70 mV.


[Lucía] p(Cl) is so small it can be left out; p(Na) = 0.002 p(K); result -70 mV.

8. Small perturbations vs threshold

Diagram: voltage against time, with the Na and K Nernst potentials as limits; the neuron starts at -70 mV, where it is polarized.
Input from other neurons can give (A) a small depolarization (e.g. -60 mV) or (B) a hyperpolarization (more negative).

A: electric forces are now smaller than at equilibrium, so diffusion wins, pushing potassium out; back to -70 mV.
B: electric forces are bigger, ions come in; back to -70 mV.
Small perturbations disappear (are damped). He calls it “an unstable situation” in the transcript, but describes a return to rest [verify] wording.


Crossing the threshold: many voltage-sensitive sodium channels open suddenly; p(Na) becomes much larger than p(K) and p(Cl); the membrane potential approaches the sodium Nernst potential (+60 mV).
Speed depends on permeability: many channels, very fast transition; fewer, slower.
Then the sodium channels close and the original situation returns.
Summary he gave: (1) a cell at charge neutrality has constant voltage inside and outside; (2) opening a pore for one ion creates a membrane potential, set by diffusion (temperature, concentrations), which is the limit for that ion; (3) with Na, K, Cl all active, the equilibrium depends on which wins: K at rest, Na when the sodium channels open.
[Lucía] To switch the membrane potential the cell changes permeability (opens channels); diffusion then drives the change. Close Na gates with high p(K): towards -90 mV; raise p(Na): towards +60 mV.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF Biophysics Radioprotection
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Biophysics Radioprotection
Sources

Audio Clip 10 (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Starts mid-sentence in the recap of the previous session (“…radiation is damaging for our health”) and ends “that’s all for our side”. Apart from the opening, it looks complete.
This is the second of two radiobiology/radioprotection sessions (ADI lists “L6 and 9 radiobiology/radioprotection”). The first session (natural radiation, effects, the three principles introduced on the last slide) is not among the transcripts.
Coverage: transcript only. Lucía’s notes have a radiobiology section (units, stochastic vs deterministic effects) but nothing on the protection measures, limits or regulation discussed here.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault (see ADI). Signage pictures, the CT-room monitoring map, the dose leaflet and the DRL table are on his slides.
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “Radiobiology”. PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Biophysics Ultrasound (ionizing vs non-ionizing), FMF Nuclear medicine L1 Conventional, FMF Nuclear medicine L2 PET.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

The three principles (justification, optimization, dose limitation) are “the main umbrella over any application with radiation”. For patients, dose limitation does not apply (section 7).
“That’s the main message”: ionizing radiation is useful in many applications, but we must work with it carefully.
Training in radiation protection is compulsory for every student and hospital worker who may be involved; that is why these two sessions are in first year.
“Justification is dynamic”: what is justified today may not be tomorrow, so stay updated with guidelines.

1. Context and regulation

Many doctors are exposed: radiologists, but also cardiologists, neurologists, and surgeons who use X-rays to check during surgery.
Occupational exposure: radiation received because you are doing your job.
Main Spanish regulation: published in 2022 (with roots about 20 years earlier and updates) on the protection of health against the risks derived from ionizing radiation. [verify] exact name and number. It applies to all uses of ionizing radiation, not only medical.
It divides the population into workers and public, and requires both to prevent exposure as far as possible and to monitor it.

2. Types of risk

Irradiation (external exposure): an external source (photons, particles, gamma rays, X-rays) irradiates the body from outside.
Contamination: working with unsealed radioactive material (e.g. liquid radiopharmaceuticals in nuclear medicine) that can be spread and get on or into you.
Identify which risks you are exposed to before choosing measures.

3. Protecting against irradiation: distance, time, shielding

Distance: dose falls with the square of the distance (inverse square law). Source at 1 m gives, say, 100; at 2 m: 25 (factor 4); at 3 m: about 11 (factor 9). “Really easy and really efficient.”
Time: dose is proportional to exposure time. A surgeon controlling the X-rays (often by a foot pedal) should use the minimum compatible with what is needed, for themselves, the patient and the staff. If you are not needed in the room, leave: your dose is zero.
Shielding: choose the material for the type of radiation. For X-rays, lead (efficient but heavy): lead aprons and screens. They are less effective for other radiation (e.g. in nuclear medicine). TV series show lead aprons; people forget distance and time, which are very efficient too.

4. Protecting against contamination

Distance, time and shielding are not useful: if your hand is contaminated, you carry the source with you.
Use work clothes and gloves: they do not prevent contamination but make it easy to remove (take them off, clean yourself before leaving).
Measure: detectors to check work surfaces, hands and even feet before leaving any area with contamination risk. Awareness is the best way to stop the spread.
Student question: can there be contamination risk without irradiation risk? Yes, rarely: isotopes of very low energy that cannot even penetrate gloves or clothing (laboratories handling very low activity). They are the hardest to detect because detectors are less sensitive to them.

5. Signalling of areas

International radiation trefoil symbol on the doors of areas with risk; the colour indicates the level of risk:






















ColourMeaning (as given)GreyThe lowest level: a person working there full time all year could exceed the limit for the public (so not everyone may work there)GreenUp to 6 mSv per year (he says about “two-thirds of the limit of the worker” [verify]; 6 is less than a third of 20)YellowWorking there all day for a year (about 2,000 hours) could exceed the limit for exposed workers: more care, limited stays (no desks; enter to do the job and leave)

Background of the sign: plain white = irradiation risk only; dots = contamination risk; both can be present.
Operating room example: sign on the door, lights that flash when radiation is on, and a shielded door.

6. Workers: classification and monitoring
Classification

Exposed vs non-exposed workers: those with any probability of being exposed at some time.
Exposed workers: category A (likely to receive about 6 mSv per year or more: higher control) and category B.
His hospital: transcript “we are like 200… 400 exposed… 40 category A”; earlier “more than 2,000 people”. [verify] numbers.
Category A in a hospital: interventional radiology (complex procedures with high X-ray use, staff in the room; transcript “angiography or a mathematician” [verify]); people working with sealed sources in therapy (transcript “write therapy” [verify], presumably brachytherapy); staff preparing radiopharmaceuticals in the PET department and PET technicians.

Training and procedures

Training and information (compulsory; refreshed every 2 to 4 years) and written procedures.
Example: mobile X-ray units (low power, usable anywhere, e.g. ICU): when the button is pressed only the patient and the operator stay; everyone else at least 3 m away; lead aprons.
So five preventive measures: distance, time, shielding (plus contamination measures), training, procedures.

Monitoring

Workplace monitoring: fixed detectors with alarms (e.g. lights, door locked if radiation too high), portable real-time detectors (like a Geiger counter), passive dosimeters placed around rooms. Example CT room map: outside readings at natural background, showing the shielding works; some high-intensity X-ray rooms read 2 to 3 mSv per month [verify] units.
Personal dosimeter (compulsory for exposed workers): does not protect and has no display or alarm; it records the accumulated dose, changed and read monthly; annual totals checked against limits and used to improve procedures. Records kept essentially forever.
Pregnant workers: the worker may be exposed, but the fetus is a member of the public: on (voluntary) declaration of pregnancy the limit changes from 20 to 1 mSv; an extra abdominal dosimeter estimates fetal dose, plus measures to avoid any dose.
Category A: yearly medical examination by the occupational health doctor, who receives their doses and declares them fit or not.
Limits mentioned: public 1 mSv/year, workers 20 mSv/year.

7. Patients: justification and optimization

For patients, no dose limitation (forget the 1 and 20 mSv): so special care with the other two principles.

Justification

European regulation: all medical exposures shall be justified in advance: balance potential risk against benefit; only if justified is the test done.
Risk is harder for a clinician to judge than benefit.
First level: follow guidelines from scientific societies (someone has already done the justification); stay updated.
He uses a Spanish Society of Radiology list of about 100 things not to do (the opposite of a recommendation list, with justification and references). Examples:

Trauma (e.g. car accident): do not do plain radiography; go straight to CT (higher dose, but plain films lose time and often do not give the information).
No routine preoperative chest X-ray (in the pre-anaesthesia work-up) unless there is a specific reason.


Student question (emergencies): in his hospital there is no CT dedicated to the emergency department, so the full radiology department is available; may differ in big hospitals. Contrast CT dose depends on parameters (kV, mAs) [verify].
Individual justification: outside the guidelines, for this patient today. The requesting doctor is responsible, and it must be recorded in the patient’s record. Example: an X-ray in a pregnant patient with a serious, life-threatening problem; the patient must be informed and agree. Responsibility is shared between requester and radiologist; if they disagree, the radiologist decides.
Tools to understand risk: a Spanish leaflet used at the Clínica translating each test into mSv, equivalent chest X-rays and days of natural background:

chest X-ray: about 0.02 mSv, about 3 days of background;
skull X-ray: about 3 chest X-rays; spine films more (bone needs more radiation): months of background;
CT: hundreds of radiographs, years of background.
(Not a dose limit, just a way to grasp the risk.)


Gather previous information: past tests elsewhere, CDs of images; avoid repeats.
Questions for individual justification: Has the patient already had it? Do I need it (will it change management, or am I just reassuring myself; e.g. suspected pneumonia: start antibiotics, re-evaluate in 1 to 2 weeks)? Do I need it now? Am I ordering too many tests at once instead of step by step? Have I given radiology all the information (they may suggest a better test)? Is there an alternative without radiation? (“I am not a physician”, so the clinical examples are only illustrative.)

Optimization

Mainly in the hands of radiologists, nuclear medicine physicians and radiotherapy staff: do everything with as low a dose as possible.
Hard to know if you used the minimum: good images make everyone happy regardless.
Main tool: diagnostic reference levels (DRL). Built from surveys of hospitals in a region (Spain uses European surveys): each reports its dose for a test (e.g. chest CT); the 75th percentile of the distribution is the reference level (75% of hospitals are below it). Published by the European Commission.
Each year, device by device, a representative sample of patients’ doses is compared with the DRL. Below: acceptable (still improvable). Above: investigate with physicists, radiologists and technicians (too many series, too high kV or mAs…).

8. Effects to avoid

Justification and optimization aim to minimize the probability of stochastic effects, assuming that deterministic effects are never produced.
Deterministic effects in patients from X-rays have been published in the past; machines and procedures have improved, but if a very hard case used a lot of radiation, the patient should be followed up for such effects.
[Lucía] Deterministic: death of many cells; threshold dose; severity increases with dose; after high doses. Stochastic: sublethal DNA damage in one or few cells (germ cells: hereditary disorders; somatic: cancer); no threshold; probability (not severity) increases with dose; special caution in children and women of child-bearing age. Units: absorbed dose Gy; equivalent and effective dose Sv.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF Biophysics Ultrasound
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Biophysics Ultrasound
Sources

ULTRA SOUND FMF (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Starts mid-sentence in the comparison of ionizing and non-ionizing techniques; ends announcing “the next session we will start with… why do we have grey levels”, then a video.
US & MRI FMF: the first part (grey levels, anechoic regions, thermal and mechanical index) belongs here; from “this is another topic… MRI” onwards it is in FMF Biophysics MRI basics. It starts mid-sentence, so the opening of that session is missing.
So: two sessions; the start of each is missing. Doppler was deferred to the workshop. Date not recorded.
Coverage: transcript first, filled from Lucía (“Mechanical waves”, “Medical ultrasound”, “Effect of acoustic impedance”, “Ultrasound imaging”, “Ultrasound - safety concerns”).

Resources

Slides: none in the vault. The echography image with the TI and MI numbers and a video are on his slides / ADI (“I will upload this video”).
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), sections above plus “Ultrasound workshop I”. PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Biophysics MRI basics, FMF Biophysics Radioprotection.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

“Something that you have to remember”: total reflection when the impedances are very different; transmission when they are similar (section 4). “The point is not the equation; the point is the consequences.”
Pressure units: “at least you need to know the relationship between these three units” (atm, Pa, mmHg).
Safety indices to check during an exam: thermal index below 1, mechanical index below 1.9 (section 7).
Doppler effect will be discussed in the workshop.

1. Ionizing vs non-ionizing techniques

Ionizing radiation can break chemical bonds with a small amount of energy, so even small doses can have important consequences; that is why it is more dangerous.
Non-ionizing techniques (ultrasound, MRI) cannot break chemical bonds, at least not easily; they need much more energy to cause damage. They can still cause damage if the device is used without control.

2. What an ultrasound wave is

A mechanical wave: it creates mechanical forces between parts of a material (pushing or pulling).
Model: a material made of molecules filling space, with a movable wall on one side.

Push the wall right: molecules accumulate in front of it, density increases: a force on an area, i.e. a pressure (compression).
Pull it left: molecules spread out, density decreases (pulling).


Vibrate the wall: repeated pushing and pulling = a mechanical wave (a loudspeaker does this). The wave travels from the source to the ear.
In an ultrasound probe the source is a small piezoelectric crystal: an oscillating voltage makes it expand and contract. Unlike a loudspeaker (magnetic system moving a membrane), because the frequencies are much higher.
Result: a train of compressions moving away from the crystal. Plotted against time, pressure oscillates around a central value, the atmospheric pressure: pulling lowers it, pushing raises it. Characterized by amplitude and frequency (period).
Units of pressure: 1 atm = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa (SI unit) = 760 mmHg. Centimetres of water will come with respiration.
[Lucía] In fluids only longitudinal (pressure) waves exist; in solids also transverse (shear) waves. “Negative pressure” means below ambient pressure; absolute pressure is always above 0.

3. Frequency ranges





















CategoryFrequencyInfrasoundbelow 20 HzSound20 Hz to 20 kHzUltrasoundabove 20 kHz

The transcript says “20 GHz” for the upper limit; [Lucía] gives 20 kHz.
The classification is anthropocentric: the range humans can hear.
Medical devices: 1 to 10 MHz, about three orders of magnitude above the sound/ultrasound limit. [check] [Lucía]: 1 to 20 MHz.
[Lucía] Diagnostic ultrasound analyses the reflected wave (X-rays analyse the transmitted wave). Therapeutic uses: lithotripsy, HIFU.

4. Acoustic impedance, reflection and transmission

A probe on a patient: the wave crosses skin, fat, muscle, liver, perhaps lung or ribs. Each interface separates materials with different properties. Two properties matter for a push-and-pull wave: density and how hard the material is to compress (its elasticity).
Echo analogy: shouting at a stone wall in the mountains; the sound is reflected and comes back. When two materials have very different properties, the wave “prefers” to stay in its material rather than cross: it is reflected.
Air/water example: air density about 1.4 kg/m³ (as given; [verify]), water about 1,000 kg/m³: a factor of about 1,000. Molecules in air pushing on water must move a thousand times more molecules; very hard to transmit the oscillation. (Skin, fat and muscle behave roughly like water for ultrasound.)
Pressure (N/m²) and the vibration velocity of molecules (m/s) are proportional; the constant is the acoustic impedance (Z). Impedance = resistance to being moved: large Z, hard to move; small Z, easy.
Z = density x speed of sound in the material.





















MaterialDensitySpeed of soundWaterabout 10³ kg/m³1,500 m/sAirabout 1.4 kg/m³ [verify]340 m/s

So Z of water is much larger than Z of air.
Reflected intensity = incident intensity times a factor depending on the two impedances: the difference of the impedances squared, over the sum (transcript garbled: “Z of B minus Z of A, squared, and the addition of both”). [verify] exact form; [Lucía] has the formula only as an image.
Energy is conserved: incident intensity = reflected + transmitted; knowing one, you get the other.
Consequences:

Very different impedances: everything reflected, nothing transmitted.
Similar impedances: nothing reflected, everything transmitted.


[Lucía] Same two limiting cases; continuity of velocity and pressure at the interface.

5. Consequences in the body: shadows and gel

Order of impedances: bone > soft tissue (human body) > lung > air.
Lung (air) and bone/ribs are barriers ultrasound practically cannot cross: everything behind them is in shadow (hidden).
First interface: air (lowest impedance) to skin would reflect everything; no wave would enter the patient.
Solution: gel between transducer and skin, with impedance similar to the body, so the wave enters and nothing is reflected there.
Inside: skin, fat, muscle and liver have similar but not equal impedances, so each interface reflects a small part of the wave back to the transducer.
Image formation: emit ultrasound, wait for the echoes; the time of arrival tells where each echo was produced. Echoes at each interface, a big echo at a rib, nothing behind it.
[Lucía] The transducer is both source and receiver; distance from the round-trip time; image in grey scale proportional to reflected intensity (bright = strong echo, black = none).

6. Grey levels and anechoic regions

Organs are not homogeneous: small vessels, different cells, fat inclusions. These heterogeneities are smaller than the wavelength.
Wavelength in tissue: with a typical frequency (garbled in the transcript [verify]) and 1,500 m/s, about 1.5 mm ([Lucía] also gives 1.55 mm). This is also the minimum detail visible; nothing below that size can be seen.
At heterogeneities the wave is sent in different directions: scattering (he avoids calling it reflection). In real tissue there is always scattering.
Grey level is proportional to heterogeneity: more heterogeneous, more scattering, brighter. Such material is echogenic.
Two ideas: a clear interface gives a line (echo); heterogeneity inside an organ gives small echoes, the grain of the image.
Completely black region: a homogeneous material (a liquid): no scattering. Called anechoic (no echo).
[Lucía] Fluids and air-filled cavities appear black. Low frequency for depth (less detail), high frequency for superficial structures (more detail).

7. Safety: thermal index and mechanical index

The numbers on the screen come from absorption: as the wave propagates inside the tissue (after the interface), a small part is absorbed, intensity decreases.
Absorbed energy breaks no bonds and causes no ionization: it becomes heat.

Thermal index (TI)

TI = power absorbed / power needed to raise the temperature by 1 °C.
Must be below 1; in the example image 0.3 (index for soft tissue; there is another for bone).
It is an estimate made by the device, not a measurement.
Above 1, local temperature rises of 2 °C or more are possible: maybe acceptable in a healthy patient, but in a patient with a local temperature of 39 °C it can be dangerous.

Mechanical index (MI)

Background: vapour pressure. In a closed box with water below boiling point, molecules vibrate (temperature); some have enough energy to jump into the vapour. Equilibrium when jumps liquid to vapour balance vapour to liquid: the pressure then is the vapour pressure at that temperature. A vapour phase is always present, without reaching 100 °C.
In tissue the wave oscillates around normal pressure. Increasing the power increases the amplitude; if the minimum pressure falls below the vapour pressure, the liquid (mainly water) can no longer stay liquid: bubbles form.
The mechanical index exists to prevent bubble formation. Must be below 1.9 (depends also on frequency); in the example 1.2.
[Lucía] This is cavitation; MI is proportional to the peak negative pressure.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Embryology Spinal nerves and nervous system
Sources

Audio Clip 1 FMF (8 lines): a fragment of the lecturer describing a drawing or image (a whitish staining, a central process going towards the spinal cord, somites). Too short and garbled to place; it probably belongs to the dorsal root ganglion / spinal nerve part of the same lecture series. Nothing from it is used below except section 1.
Audio Clip 2 FMF (automatic transcription, heavily garbled in the middle). Starts mid-lecture (recap of somatic spinal nerves) and ends at a break (“see you in 20…”, then student chatter). Covers the start of the autonomic nervous system: origin of the ganglia and the first part of the sympathetic pathway.
Date and lecturer: not in the transcripts; not in the code log (FMF has no codes). The ADI module list has two “NS/spinal cord” items; this is probably the second.
Coverage: sections 1 to 6 from the transcript, filled from Lucía. Everything after the break (rest of the sympathetic system, parasympathetic system, sensory part “next day”) is not recorded.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault (FMF Lecture slides folder is empty). The lecturer drew most of this on the board.
Study material: none in the vault.
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes); sections “Formation of the nervous system” (peripheral nervous system, neural crest) and “Autonomous nervous system” / “Visceromotor fibers”. PDF pages not yet in the page index.
Related notes: FMF ANS 2 (later ANS lecture), FMF Physiology Smooth muscle.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. There are no slides or official notes in the vault for FMF, so there are no [Slides] or [Notes] markers.
Exam flags from the lecturer

“We’re going to stress on this: voluntary movement, involuntary movement” (somatic vs autonomic).
“What we care about is the postganglionic fiber: we need to know the trajectory of the nerves.” What is studied is the trajectory of the preganglionic and of the postganglionic fibers.
The lateral horn exists only from T1 to L2: “not in cervical levels, not in inferior or sacral, only from T1 to L2.”

1. Recap: the somatic peripheral nervous system

Information comes from the periphery (skin, muscle…) to the spinal cord (for trunk and limbs); the CNS integrates it and sends a motor response back through the peripheral system to the target organs.
Spinal nerves innervate the somatic derivatives, which come from the somites:

striated muscle from the dorsomedial and ventrolateral myotome (transcript “metrolatic myotone”);
skin (dermis) from the dermatome.


Smooth muscle and cardiac muscle come instead from the lateral mesoderm, specifically its visceral (splanchnic) layer, which surrounds the organs; the somatic (parietal) layer lines the body wall.
Clip 1 fragment: the lecturer points out a whitish staining, a central process going towards the spinal cord, and the somites. [verify] context.
[Lucía] Dorsomedial (epaxial) myotome gives the intrinsic back muscles; ventrolateral (hypaxial) myotome gives the anterolateral body wall muscles (intercostals, rectus). Smooth muscle of the gut wall from the splanchnic layer of lateral mesoderm; the gut mucosa from endoderm.

2. Smooth and cardiac vs striated muscle

Question to the class: what do smooth and cardiac muscle have in common that differs from striated muscle? Student answer, confirmed (“that’s exactly it”): their contraction is involuntary; skeletal (striated) muscle is voluntary.
So the peripheral nervous system has two components:

somatic: spinal nerves and plexuses, innervating skin and striated muscle;
autonomic: a different series of nerves innervating smooth muscle, glands (to contract the gland and release secretions) and sensory structures in the mucosa of the viscera. “Autonomic” refers to their being involuntary.


Plan: motor fibres today; sensory information “the next day”.
[Lucía] Somatic plexuses = striated muscle; visceral plexuses = muscle in viscera and glands. The ANS has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

3. Where the neurons come from

Spinal cord recap: alar plate (sensory area) and basal plate (motor), separated by the sulcus limitans.
Neural crest cells migrate out:

some form the sensory neurons: pseudounipolar cells (in the dorsal root ganglia);
others form autonomic ganglia: these motor ganglion cells also originate from neural crest cells.


Autonomic ganglia formed by migrating neural crest cells (board drawing, e.g. fibres going to the heart):

paired ganglia at every level on both sides of the spinal cord (a chain);
single (unpaired) clusters in front, “normally in the abdomen”. [verify] wording garbled.


[Lucía] Neural crest cells (ectodermal, becoming mesenchymal; “4th germ layer”) give rise to sensory neurons (dorsal root ganglia), melanocytes, autonomic nervous system cells and Schwann cells. They give rise to both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglionic neurons. Pseudounipolar: one process leaves the body and splits into a central and a peripheral process.
[Lucía] Sympathetic ganglia: (1) sympathetic trunk/chain (paravertebral), paired at each level; (2) preaortic single ganglia (prevertebral), ventral to the aorta, in the abdominal and pelvic cavities.

4. Central control without consciousness

Autonomic does not mean independent: some ganglia work “pretty much” on their own, but there is central control; the difference is that it is not conscious.
Example: while lecturing, the lecturer needs airways dilated, muscles well irrigated, heart quite active. Sitting in the office with a coffee after class, heart rate goes down and blood goes to the digestive system. Depending on the activity, the CNS controls these neurons without conscious control.
[Lucía] Sympathetic = “fight or flight” (activates organs for a challenge: pupils dilate, heart rate up, digestion inhibited); parasympathetic = “rest and digest” (digestion stimulated, less blood to skeletal muscle, pupils constrict).

5. A two-neuron motor system

The ganglion cells are controlled by motor cells from the basal plate of the spinal cord, placed more laterally than the somatic motor neurons.
Preganglionic neuron: in the CNS; its axon goes to the ganglion and connects with the ganglion cell. It receives input from higher up in the CNS (the brain).
Postganglionic (ganglionic) neuron: in the ganglion; it is the effector, targeting the visceral cells (e.g. smooth muscle of the gut).
Compare: somatic system = one neuron in the ventral horn going directly to striated muscle; autonomic = two neurons, one in the CNS and one in a ganglion.
The preganglionic neuron is a visceral efferent (vs somatic efferent) motor neuron.
Naming: preganglionic neuron/fibre (before the ganglion), ganglion, postganglionic fibre.
[Lucía] The second neuron is always in a ganglion, outside the CNS; the first is in the spinal cord or brainstem. Its axon is the preganglionic fibre.

6. Location and route of the sympathetic preganglionic neurons

The visceral motor cell bodies cluster in the lateral horn of the spinal cord.
The lateral horn is a column of neurons from T1 to L2 (12 thoracic levels plus L1 and L2); not at cervical or sacral levels. All the sympathetic preganglionic neurons are there.
Question: how does the preganglionic axon leave the spinal cord? Being motor, by the ventral root with the other motor axons.
The sympathetic chain runs on either side of the vertebral column on the posterior wall of the thoracic and abdominal cavities. Its ganglia have nothing to do with the dorsal root ganglia.
The preganglionic fibre goes out with the spinal nerve, then leaves it and enters the chain, where it synapses on a ganglion neuron; that neuron’s axon travels to the target (e.g. the heart). The lecturer named the two connecting branches (transcript “bone-councing fiber, and the free-councing”) [verify]; [Lucía]: preganglionic fibres (myelinated, whitish) form the white communicating ramus; postganglionic fibres (unmyelinated) form the grey communicating ramus.
The recording ends here (break).
[Lucía] Because the lateral horn exists only at T1 to L2, preganglionic axons ascend or descend in the chain to reach ganglia above and below. Targets: dermis (sweat glands, arrector pili, blood vessels) only sympathetic, via chain ganglia and the dorsal or ventral ramus; thoracic viscera via chain ganglia (postganglionic cardiac nerves); abdominal and pelvic viscera via preaortic ganglia (preganglionic splanchnic nerves). Sympathetic preganglionic fibres are short, postganglionic long. Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons are in the brainstem (mainly vagus) and sacral cord (S2 to S4).
