Exam flags from the lecturer

Aim of the class: “that you understand what’s a radiopharmaceutical and what we do in nuclear medicine”; radiopharmaceuticals are “the most important thing that we should remember”.
“What I want you to know”: alpha and beta-minus emitters for therapy; beta-plus (positrons, PET) and gamma (gamma camera, SPECT) for diagnosis (section 4).
Names of radiopharmaceuticals: “I don’t want you to know all these names”, except: “something that you should know”: the most common radioisotope for the gamma camera is technetium-99m; and “you have to know” fluorine-18 FDG for PET.
Theragnosis: “that’s very important” (section 6).
The key difference with radiology: nuclear medicine studies function, radiology anatomy.

1. What nuclear medicine is

Completely different from other specialties: it studies the function of organs; radiology studies anatomy.
Uses small amounts of radioactive material, radiopharmaceuticals, for diagnosis and treatment of different diseases.
Usually combined with an anatomical image: molecular imaging fused with CT (PET-CT, SPECT-CT): hybrid imaging.

2. The radiopharmaceutical

A molecule with two parts:





















PartDeterminesNotesRadioisotopePhysical characteristics (the radiation emitted, detection)The radioactive partPharmaceuticalBiological behaviourNon-radioactive part; the vehicle that takes the isotope to the target organ (e.g. a kidney-seeking pharmaceutical to study the kidneys)

Administration: intravenous, inhalation, oral.
Many combinations of isotope and pharmaceutical, chosen for what you want to study or treat.
[Lucía] The drug targets the site; the isotope “acts as a flashlight”.

Three ways the pharmaceutical reaches its target

Binding a cellular receptor: very common in oncology. Tumour cells are more active and overexpress receptors/transporters (e.g. glucose transporters: radioactive glucose, FDG, enters through them, so tumour cells take up more than normal cells).
Normal cell channels: e.g. iodine for the thyroid, entering through the sodium-iodide transporter.
A support/carrier created for the purpose: e.g. microparticles of calcium or resin containing the isotope, placed directly in the organ. Example: treatment of intraperitoneal carcinomatosis in ovarian cancer: calcium microparticles distributed through the peritoneal cavity.


[Lucía] For thyroid scintigraphy no drug is needed: iodine is incorporated naturally (hormonogenesis). Iodine emits gamma and beta, so it serves for diagnosis and for thyroid cancer therapy.

Production of radioisotopes

Nuclear reactors, generators and cyclotrons. Her centre has a cyclotron in the nuclear medicine facility, so they produce their own radiopharmaceuticals.

3. Radioisotopes and types of radiation

Isotopes can be stable or unstable; radioisotopes are unstable and emit energy to reach stability. That energy is what the cameras detect. (She refers to the biophysics lectures by “Javier Burgette” [verify] name.)






























RadiationEnergy / damagePenetrationUseAlphaVery high energy, a lot of damageVery, very shortTherapy, e.g. treating surfaces without damaging deeper tissueBeta (beta+ and beta-)Less harmful than alphaFarther than alphaBeta-: therapy; beta+ (positrons): diagnosis (PET)GammaLess ionizingMore penetrating than betaOnly diagnostic imaging, not treatment

Neutron radiation exists but belongs to radiotherapy, not nuclear medicine.
Radiopharmaceuticals often emit a combination of radiations: a therapeutic (alpha or beta-) agent may also emit gamma, allowing post-treatment imaging. The activity given is calculated to produce the intended damage and no more.
[Lucía] Alpha stopped by paper, beta by aluminium foil, gamma by lead. For a deep (e.g. spinal) lesion a gamma emitter is chosen for its penetration.

4. Therapy vs diagnosis

Therapy: alpha and beta-minus emitters (tumour treatments).
Diagnosis: beta-plus (positrons) for PET; gamma for the gamma camera and SPECT (the gamma camera image in 3D).
[Lucía] Same division.

5. Examples of radiopharmaceuticals















































RadiopharmaceuticalIsotope / emissionTargetUse18F-FDGFluorine-18 (PET)Glucose transportersMost tumour cells; “you have to know”68Ga-DOTATOCGallium-68 (PET)Somatostatin receptorsNeuroendocrine tumours (overexpress them)99mTc-bisphosphonatesTechnetium-99m (gamma)BoneBone scan; Tc-99m is the most common gamma-camera isotope99mTc-MAG3Technetium-99mKidneysRenal studiesYttrium-90 microspheres (transcript “Y9-3S”; yttrium [verify])Beta-Deposited in the tumour via intra-arterial injection (not receptors or channels)Liver tumours (transcript “batheic” [verify])Lutetium-DOTATATE (transcript “nutrition”; lutetium [verify])Beta-Somatostatin receptorsTreatment of neuroendocrine tumours

Patients become radioactive: in X-rays the machine emits radiation; in nuclear medicine the patient is the source. Hence shielded rooms for treatment administration and measures to protect doctors and nurses.

6. Theragnosis

Before treating, confirm that the tumour still expresses the receptor: a more aggressive tumour may have lost it; the therapeutic agent would then not bind and would irradiate the body without benefit.
So: same (or similar) pharmaceutical, change only the radioisotope: first image with a positron emitter, then treat with a beta-minus emitter.

Somatostatin receptors: 68Ga-DOTATOC to see the receptors; then the lutetium ([verify]) DOTATATE to treat.
PSMA (antigen on the membrane of prostate cancer cells): 68Ga-PSMA PET to locate the tumour, then the same PSMA ligand with the therapeutic isotope (transcript “nutrition”, lutetium [verify]) to destroy it (beta-minus).


Theragnosis = combination of diagnostic imaging and therapy. “That’s very important.” (More in L2.)

7. Emission vs transmission imaging; the cameras

Transmission imaging (X-ray, CT): the machine emits radiation that crosses the patient; images from attenuation.
Emission imaging (nuclear medicine): the patient emits; devices detect it.
A PET image alone is only molecular imaging (no anatomy); fused with CT it gives both.





















CameraIsotopesConfigurationGamma camera / SPECT-CTGamma emitters; gamma rays detected directlyTwo detectors (anterior and posterior) with collimators that accept only radiation perpendicular to them; often a CT behindPET-CTPositron emitters (detection explained in L2)A whole ring of detectors, CT inside
8. Bone scintigraphy, SPECT and SPECT-CT

Planar whole-body bone scan (old camera without CT): Tc-99m bisphosphonates; anterior and posterior views; only bone is seen (functional imaging). Example: normal distribution with increased uptake in one joint (inflammation).
Planar images may not localize an uptake (e.g. which part of a vertebra, or a rib vs the vertebra): SPECT moves the detectors around the patient for a volumetric (3D) image with axial, coronal and sagittal planes; can be whole-body.
SPECT-CT fusion: the SPECT is coloured and fused over the CT, localizing the activity precisely on the anatomy.
Bisphosphonates are absorbed by the surface of hydroxyapatite crystals. Studies infection, trauma, tumours and other bone conditions.
Practice: compare a lesion (e.g. skull) with the whole body, then a dedicated planar image or SPECT of the region.
Normal distribution: kidneys and bladder visible (urinary elimination); the bladder is masked because it takes all the counts.
Dynamic study for inflammation or infection: from the vascular injection, to the tissue phase, to early bone images; then late images (about 2 to 3 hours later) once the tracer has incorporated.
Case: temporomandibular joint (SPECT): a young patient (transcript “70/75 year old” [verify]; context implies a teenager) with asymmetric mandible. Surgery only if the joint is no longer active (joints usually active until about 18 to 21); otherwise bone keeps growing and the deformity worsens. Both joints were very active: not operable yet.
[Lucía] Bisphosphonates (MDP) taken up in proportion to vascularization and osteoblastic activity; physiological uptake in joints, sternum, spine, sacroiliac joints, kidneys and bladder. Usually planar first, then SPECT/CT if an abnormal uptake needs localizing.

9. Questions answered

How long is the patient radioactive? Depends on the isotope’s half-life: Tc-99m about 6 hours, so about 24 hours. F-18: transcript “a 100 and I think that is nine minutes”; in L2 she gives 109 minutes: by the end of the day the patient no longer emits and could repeat a study the next day.
Another nuclear medicine study must wait until the first radiopharmaceutical has been eliminated, or images would mix.
Masking of organs (bladder, injection site…) with software (recording ends here).
[Lucía] Other conventional studies (not recorded this year): renal scintigraphy (Tc-MAG3, Tc-DTPA; dynamic studies with activity-time curves); myocardial perfusion (Tc-MIBI; stress vs rest: defect only in stress = ischaemia; in both = infarction); sentinel node (Tc-nanocolloidal albumin; first node draining a tumour, e.g. melanoma); thyroid (iodine; cold nodule = reduced uptake).

The rest (other protocols, clinical cases) is not recorded.

Exam flags from the lecturer

“What I want you to understand”: PET needs a positron that annihilates, producing two photons detected one in front of the other; without both signals there is no image (section 1).
“I want to call your attention on something”: function changes before anatomy; PET detects disease before anatomical change (section 3).
Nuclear medicine physicians must know the normal (physiological) distribution of each radiopharmaceutical, or they will call normal uptake pathological: “something that is very important” (section 2).
Patient preparation for FDG PET (section 5): fasting, glucose control, no exercise, warmth, drugs; PET-CT is scheduled, not an emergency test.

1. How PET detects positrons

PET = positron emission tomography, using radiopharmaceuticals that emit beta-plus particles (positrons). (Previous class: gamma emitters for gamma camera and SPECT.)
The PET ring does not detect positrons: a positron leaving the nucleus annihilates with a nearby electron within about 2 mm, producing two high-energy photons in opposite directions. (She refers to Javier’s biophysics explanation.)
The ring of detectors registers only pairs detected one in front of the other (in opposite detectors). Without both signals, no image.
Difference from the gamma camera: the gamma camera’s two detectors register whatever gamma rays reach them; PET requires the annihilation and the paired detection.
PET-CT: CT image first, then PET acquisition; the patient is the source; result: PET (function only), CT (anatomy), and the fused (hybrid) image with the PET in colour over the CT. The PET alone cannot clearly separate structures; the CT shows exactly where the uptake is.
[Lucía] Annihilation gives two 511 keV photons; PET needs attenuation correction and quantification (SUV); attenuation artefacts must be corrected in reconstruction.

2. Normal distribution depends on the radiopharmaceutical

























RadiopharmaceuticalPhysiological uptake (as shown)Use18F-FDGBrain very high (consumes mainly glucose, “99.9%”), heart (glucose, but can switch to lipids or proteins), diffuse liver and spleen, kidneys and bladder (elimination)Most tumours (many glucose transporters)68Ga-DOTATOCElimination via kidneys (cortex) and bladder, liver/biliary route; pituitary (transcript “hypothesis” = hypophysis) as internal control [verify] detailsNeuroendocrine tumoursFDOPA (transcript “Ectopan”/“endophan”, then “FDOPA” [verify])Basal ganglia (internal control)Neuroendocrine tumours; Parkinson’s disease and similar

Heart and endocarditis: to see infection in the heart, its glucose uptake must be suppressed: a diet full of lipids beforehand switches the heart from glycolytic to lipid metabolism, so cardiac uptake becomes very low and the infection becomes visible.
Normal adrenal uptake must not be called pathological: know the physiological distribution.

3. Function changes before anatomy

Before an organ’s anatomy changes, its function changes. E.g. in Alzheimer’s, before MRI shows atrophy of the temporal lobes, neurons die and function falls, visible on PET.
Oncology: most oncology patients in Spain get a PET (many PET-CTs in Spanish hospitals). A lymph node of normal size on CT but with increased uptake is pathological (tumour).

4. FDG: mechanism and uses

Tumour cells have more glucose transporters and more glycolytic enzymes. FDG enters through the transporters and is trapped inside the cell; she says it is “not detected by the hexokinase” [verify] ([Lucía]: the glycolytic enzymes incorporate FDG and it is retained). After the fluorine-18 decays, the molecule is processed by the enzymes and eliminated.
Uses of FDG PET:

staging tumours;
assessing treatment response early (uptake falls before CT changes);
detecting recurrence;
guiding biopsy to the most active part of a tumour (a big tumour may have a necrotic centre that gives no useful information);
caution: uptake is also increased in many benign conditions.


Dementia: normal brain FDG is high; frontotemporal dementia: reduced frontal and temporal uptake; Alzheimer’s: e.g. reduced parietal uptake. The pattern indicates the type of dementia.
[Lucía] FDG measures glucose metabolism, an indirect measure of proliferation; GLUT-1 and hexokinase increased (HIF-1, anaerobic conditions). Very well-differentiated tumours can have very low uptake (false negatives).

5. Patient preparation for FDG PET

PET-CT is scheduled and prepared, not an emergency test: normal cells should take up FDG normally and tumour cells more, so they can be distinguished.






















































FactorRequirement / effectFastingAt least 4 to 6 hoursBlood glucoseMust be controlled: high glucose competes with FDG for the transporters; poor distributionBreakfast (non-compliance)Insulin rises, glucose (and FDG) goes to muscles: diffuse muscle uptake, poor image (example glucose levels 200 and 140); liver looks paler; the study may have to be repeated another dayBrain studiesNo psychotropic drugs (alter brain metabolism)Medical historyReview it: many possible false positivesExerciseNone the day before: exercised muscles take up FDG (e.g. trochanteritis uptake after exercise); can hide a small pathological nodeColdKeep the patient warm: cold (winter, air conditioning) activates brown fat (more in thin women): intense uptake can make the study unreportable; in lymphoma it can prevent judging progression vs response; repeatDiabetes, insulinDiabetic patients first in the morning; no insulin on the day (maybe the day before); low-carbohydrate diet two days beforeDiabetes, metforminMetformin increases bowel (colon) uptake (glucose eliminated via the bowel): stop it two days before, which may raise glucose, hence the dietSame-day proceduresE.g. colonoscopy before PET: bowel inflammation from the preparation; also post-surgical inflammation (laparotomy) or infection: inflammatory cells consume a lot of glucoseBreastfeedingHigh breast uptake; discard milk for 24 hours, the baby cannot be breastfed

Glucose limits: Spain is stricter; in the USA the limit is 200 to perform a PET-CT. She used to give rapid insulin and wait (to avoid muscle uptake); now she injects FDG with levels around 150 and images are usually acceptable.
Uncontrollable cases: a glottic tumour patient coughing constantly showed intense neck muscle uptake, anatomically normal muscles on CT.
[check] [Lucía]‘s preparation table: “type II diabetic: 6 h fasting + metformin”; “type I diabetic: breakfast + insulin”. This year’s lecturer: stop metformin two days before; no insulin on the day, first appointment, low-carb diet. Lucía also lists hydration the day before and on the day.

6. Timing and working with radioactive patients

Half-lives: FDG (F-18) 109 minutes; Tc-99m 6 hours (“we are very calm” with technetium). Most PET radiopharmaceuticals are around 100 minutes.
Wait about one hour after injection for incorporation, then image (at 60 minutes; transcript “eight minutes after… but not three hours after” [verify], probably 80 minutes). Too late: decay gives poor images.
Hence “people running through the corridors”: schedules must be tight; if one patient’s glucose must be lowered, another patient takes their slot so activity is not wasted.
Staff exposure: personal dosimeter and ring dosimeters (they record but do not alarm), so protection relies on shielding: the radiopharmaceutical inside a shield, injected through a line without touching it; a clock records the exact injection time.

7. Recognizing variants

Quiz images: a pelvic kidney and a horseshoe kidney (both kidneys joined): normal function, abnormal position; not pathological. The truly abnormal finding was a lung nodule with high uptake on the axial CT slices: lung cancer, the reason for the study.

8. Acquisition protocols (recording ends)

What is imaged depends on the question: for e.g. ovarian cancer, not whole body (no metastases expected in the feet). Whole-body protocols for diseases that can involve any bone or the skin: melanoma, multiple myeloma (recording ends here).
[Lucía] Protocols: head and neck (arms down), body (arms up), whole body, base of skull to mid-thigh. SUV (standardized uptake value) for semiquantitative analysis. Examples: lung cancer nodes of normal size with uptake; tuberculosis; neck and oesophageal cancer.

Coverage: transcript first; slides fill the receptor locations, the prevertebral ganglia and the cranial nerves; Lucía for receptor subtypes and second messengers. Date 26 Oct 2026 (slides); a Monday 9 am class (lecturer).

Several slides are figures that did not come through as text (adrenergic receptor mechanism of action, neurotransmitter elimination, adrenal medulla, sympathetic actions, micturition, pupil, actions table, the vascular tone experiment, vasovagal syncope): see the slide.

Exam flags from the lecturer

Exceptions are typical exam material: “It’s always important to remember the exceptions because that’s the typical thing that is in an exam.” The exceptions in this lecture: sweat glands (cholinergic sympathetic postganglionic) and the adrenal medulla (sections 3 and 7).
Atropine: “one drug that you have to remember”: a vagolytic (section 4, used again in section 11).
Muscarinic and nicotinic receptors: “something that you have to barely know, at least now”; in the future simply know that they exist.
Adrenergic receptors: “very important receptors in the body”. Remember: alpha-1 = vascular smooth muscle, beta-1 = heart, beta-2 = respiratory system (bronchi). Referring to a slide with an anaesthesia (?) example, he said “in the European exams there’s always a question about this… this is not first-year medicine” (passage garbled [verify] what exam and what slide).
“Catecholamines”: “another word that you have to know”.
Table of sympathetic and parasympathetic actions: “You just need to know them… it’s just memory.” He did not go through it.
Eye (pupil contraction) and the heart: “someone else will tell you” / “we’ll talk about them when we talk about the heart.”

1. Outline [Slides]

Physiological anatomy of the ANS (sympathetic, parasympathetic)
Neurotransmitters and receptors (sympathetic, parasympathetic)
ANS actions
Sympathetic and parasympathetic tone

2. Anatomy reminder
“The anatomy is just a very good reminder.”
Sympathetic

Mainly based on the sympathetic chain: a chain of ganglia just in front of the vertebral bodies, one on the left and one on the right, except the last one: a single ganglion in the middle, the ganglion impar (“impar as in not the pair”). All the others are bilateral.
Groups of ganglia: celiac, aorticorenal, hypogastric, mesenteric. [Slides] Prevertebral ganglia: celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric, aortico-renal, hypogastric. Slides also list the splanchnic nerve and the spinal nerve (piloerector…).
Two neurons, always, in the ANS: the first leaves the spinal cord, connects with the second, and the second goes to the effector.
Short preganglionic (spinal cord to the chain or ganglia), long postganglionic (ganglia to the effector).

Parasympathetic

“A completely different system when it comes to anatomy”: cranial nerves and sacral nerves, and “in the middle there’s nothing”. The sympathetic is mainly a chain along the spine.
Above C1 the nerves that come out are the cranial nerves. [Slides] Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X (transcript garbled here).
Cranial nerve X, the vagus nerve, the most important: about 75% of the parasympathetic capacity on its own (also [Slides]).
Long preganglionic, very short postganglionic: the opposite of the sympathetic.
[Lucía] Brainstem nuclei: Edinger-Westphal (III), superior and inferior salivatory (VII), dorsal vagal (X), ambiguus (IX and X); sacral S2 to S4. The sympathetic preganglionic neurons are in the intermediolateral columns T1 to L2.

3. Neurotransmitters: acetylcholine and noradrenaline

Two completely different molecules: acetylcholine (ACh) and noradrenaline. Noradrenaline = norepinephrine, adrenaline = epinephrine: the same thing; he uses either.
Cholinergic = mediated by acetylcholine. Adrenergic = fibres whose transmitter is noradrenaline.






























FibreTransmitterAll preganglionic (sympathetic and parasympathetic)ACh, alwaysParasympathetic postganglionicACh, alwaysSympathetic postganglionicMainly noradrenalineException: sympathetic postganglionic to sweat glands (and some blood vessels)AChException: adrenal glandthe second “neuron” is not a neuron (section 7)

“Remember only sweat glands. Sweat glands are the exception.” [Slides] “S-ANS: mainly adrenergic (except sweat glands and some blood vessels).”
[check] [Lucía] lists sweat glands and piloerector muscles as the cholinergic exceptions (muscarinic M3 for sweat glands); elsewhere in the same notes she calls arrector pili muscles adrenergic. Lecturer and slides: sweat glands (and some blood vessels). The slides side with the lecturer.
[Lucía] Preganglionic co-transmitters (enkephalin, substance P, neurotensin) are modulatory.

4. Cholinergic receptors

Every transmitter, hormone or drug needs a mechanism of action: a chemical and a receptor, “like putting a key into a keyhole”. Each molecule has its specific receptor(s) (one or two in this case).































MuscarinicNicotinicNamed afterMuscarine, from some mushrooms ([Slides] “poison from toadstools”; image: Clitocybe dealbata)NicotineMechanismG protein (he did not go into it)Ligand-gated ion channelSubtypesM1 to M5N1 and N2Location [Slides]Postganglionic cholinergic, P and SAutonomic ganglia (pre-post junction), P and S; N1: skeletal muscle, N2: ganglia

[Lucía] Muscarinic subtypes: M1 CNS and stomach secretion; M2 heart; M3 smooth muscle; M4 pancreas, lungs; M5 salivary glands, pupil sphincter.
Atropine: “one drug you have to remember”. A vagolytic: it inactivates the parasympathetic nervous system. Pharmacology “will come step by step”.

5. Adrenergic receptors

Sympathetic postganglionic fibres are the only adrenergic ones; they work through adrenergic receptors.
Alpha (alpha-1, alpha-2) and beta (beta-1, beta-2, beta-3). All G protein coupled. Activated by noradrenaline (the sympathetic postganglionic transmitter) and by adrenaline.
Agonist = activates; antagonist = inactivates.
Noradrenaline: mainly alpha agonist. Adrenaline: alpha and beta, beta-2 > beta-1 > alpha (also [Slides]).
Used clinically, e.g. in hypertension and possibly asthma (passage garbled; transcript “for my ass mom” [verify]).

Locations



































ReceptorLecturer[Slides]Alpha-1Vascular smooth muscleVascular smooth muscle; GI tract and bladderAlpha-2not mentionedPresynaptic; negative feedback (inhibition)Beta-1HeartHeart; salivary glands, fat, kidneyBeta-2Respiratory system, mainly the bronchiBronchial, bladder and GI smooth muscleBeta-3not mentionedFat

[Lucía] Alpha-1: postsynaptic, IP3, Ca2+ release, smooth muscle contraction. Alpha-2: pre- and postsynaptic (autoreceptor), adenylate cyclase inhibition, inhibits noradrenaline release. Beta-1, -2, -3: postsynaptic, adenylate cyclase stimulation, increased cAMP. (Compare FMF Physiology Smooth muscle: IP3 contracts, cAMP relaxes.)
Mechanism of action of adrenergic receptors: see the slide.

Clinical example: pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine

“You all use alpha-1 agonists without even knowing it”: pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine are potent alpha agonists (“I’m sure once in your lifetime you’ve taken any of these drugs”).
Runny nose: they cause vasoconstriction in the nose, which stops the runny nose; that is why the nose feels dry. “The effect is purely alpha.”
They also act on the rest of the body: hence the warnings, e.g. be careful if you have heart disease (“cardiopathy”).

6. Elimination of the neurotransmitter

Sequence: the signal reaches the end of the axon, the transmitter is released, it activates the postganglionic (postsynaptic) receptor, which creates a new action potential; then the transmitter must be eliminated. “The elimination is completely different” for the two.


























AcetylcholineNoradrenalineEnzymeAcetylcholinesterase (“esterase” = it cuts)Catechol-O-methyltransferase (transcript “OBCGNT”, “catechol-o-mintyl transparase”)ProductsAcetate + cholineAn inactive metabolite, excretedRecyclingCholine is reabsorbed to make a new ACh moleculeNone: completely inactivated; each new molecule must be made from scratch

[verify] “Noradrenaline is simply completely inactivated” with no part reused: no vault source covers noradrenaline removal (the elimination slide is a figure, “xxx” in the text). Check the slide and a physiology textbook for reuptake.
Catecholamines: “the name of the family”: adrenaline, noradrenaline and others (transcript “Dovermines, glutamines” [verify]). He defined them as all drugs acting on adrenergic receptors [verify] against a source.

7. Adrenal medulla: the exception

Normal sympathetic route: short preganglionic (spinal cord to chain or ganglia), long postganglionic (ganglia to effector).
Adrenal medulla: the preganglionic fibre goes directly, via the spinal nerve, to the suprarenal (adrenal) gland (“the little hat on top of the kidney”) and connects there.
The connection is not a proper synapse (a synapse is nerve to nerve): the nerve connects to a cell of the adrenal medulla, a secretory cell directly connected to the bloodstream.
Still sympathetic: cholinergic preganglionic fibre, ACh released between the axon end and the gland “just like with the synapse”. But the second element is a gland, which releases noradrenaline and adrenaline, actually more adrenaline than noradrenaline, “keep it simple”, directly into the blood.
[Slides] Preganglionic fibres enter the adrenal medulla; direct excretion of catecholamines into the bloodstream.
[Lucía] These are chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons), releasing adrenaline (80%) and noradrenaline (20%); preganglionic fibres from T5 to T9.

Why it matters: vascular tone and redistribution of blood

Link to the nasal decongestant example: activating the sympathetic system causes vasoconstriction (diameter less); vasodilation = diameter more.
We always need a vascular tone: vessels are always contracting and relaxing.
The vascular system is closed, roughly 5 litres of blood: the total is fixed, so blood must be taken from one side and sent to another (now, to the brain because you are thinking; not to the muscles, since only the lecturer is moving).
Dilating one bed and constricting another moves the cardiac output (litres leaving the heart every minute) around the body. The adrenal medulla is interesting here because it releases catecholamines directly into the blood.

8. ANS actions

Physiology is always about balance and compensation; the two systems are usually opposite: one activates, the other inhibits.
Not that simple: they are not distributed everywhere in the same proportion, and even with the same distribution (e.g. the heart), the effect of one can dominate.
[Slides] Distribution may be unequal: smooth muscle and kidney: sympathetic; genitalia: both, but differently located; heart: even distribution.
Sympathetic: “fight or flight” (strength; [Slides] strength, energy, movement). Example: something of “700 kilos” in front of you (garbled).
Parasympathetic: “rest and digest”, repair, restore, relax. Example: after lunch reading a book (anecdote: “don’t watch Netflix… you can read a book much better”).
Typical opposite pairs: saliva reduced vs stimulated; heart rate increased vs decreased; bronchoconstriction vs bronchodilation.
Sympathetic effects mentioned: increased heart rate (tachycardia), increased blood pressure (hypertension), decreased digestion (when trying to fight “there’s no need to have blood go to your problems”, last word garbled). Part of this list is garbled [verify]: see the slide.
Parasympathetic: the opposite. Full actions table: see the slide (“just memory”).

Working together: micturition
(Transcript “nutrition”; [Slides] “Neural control of micturition”.)

Bladder (detrusor):

Sympathetic: inhibits bladder contraction, so the bladder fills. High sympathetic tone: “you don’t go to the loo” (you don’t stop when running).
Parasympathetic: bladder contraction: “perfect moment to go to the toilet”.


Urethral sphincter: a sphincter is a mainly circular muscle that contracts a tube and decreases its diameter. The sphincter is contracted by the sympathetic.
To urinate: activate the parasympathetic (contract the bladder) and inhibit the sympathetic (relax the sphincter).
Filling: he then said “activation of the parasympathetic in order to contract the sphincter and activation of the sympathetic in order to fill up the bladder”. [check] This contradicts his own statement a moment earlier (sphincter contracted by the sympathetic) and FMF ANS 2 (the sympathetic closes the sphincters). See the micturition slide.
Point: opposite effects do not mean they are always opposites; often they must work together. Also in sexual function (“you cannot imagine the amount of input from one and the other”) and pupil contraction and dilation (both always present; details later from another lecturer).

9. ANS tone

Distribution even or uneven; the effect can also be even or uneven. This is ANS tone: some organs have more sympathetic, some more parasympathetic tone, always compensating ([Slides] “Some organs have uneven autonomic effect”).

Heart: parasympathetic tone

Both inputs: sympathetic gives tachycardia and hypertension; parasympathetic mainly bradycardia, via the vagus nerve.
The parasympathetic effect is greater: “parasympathetic tone in the heart”.
Clinical example, heart transplantation: the vessels are sutured and the heart works as a pump with its own automatism (explained later), but the nerves are cut and cannot be sutured. A transplanted heart beats at about 100 bpm instead of about 60 to 70, always. Reason: the parasympathetic tone is lost (vagal fibres cut); the sympathetic is cut too, but since the parasympathetic dominated, the denervated heart is “always tachycardic”. [Slides] “Automatism: 100 bpm; denervated heart!” (Transcript says “if you cut both, you get to have a heart attack. It’s always tachycardic”: “heart attack” is probably a transcription error [verify].)

Blood vessels: sympathetic tone

He first said vessels receive both, then corrected to “mainly sympathetic tone” to keep it simple. [check] [Slides]: “Only sympathetic”. The slides decide: only sympathetic. (Consistent with FMF ANS 2: the sympathetic is the only system innervating blood vessels.)
Vessels are normally contracted, by the sympathetic nerves directly and by circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla ([Slides] “circulating catecholamines + S-ANS”; “can increase contraction”).
A figure value of blood flow “roughly 200 millilitres” was mentioned [verify]: see the slide.

Experiment: stellate ganglionectomy (see the slide)





















SituationEffect on the vesselNormal sympathetic tone, test dose of norepinephrine injectedVasoconstriction (alpha-1 receptors, which create vascular tone)After stellate ganglionectomy (stellate ganglion: sympathetic, roughly in front of C7; supplies upper limb vessels)Sympathetic tone to those vessels is lost: diameter increases, blood flow increasesAfter ganglionectomy, norepinephrine (or adrenaline) given into the bloodStill vasoconstriction: the adrenergic receptors are still there; only the nerve input creating the tone was removed

“-ectomy” = surgical removal. Part of the explanation of the flow curve is garbled (“except for the first piece, afterwards it stays stable”) [verify] against the slide.

10. Cardiac output

Cardiac output = litres of blood leaving the heart per minute = blood ejected per heartbeat x beats per minute.
Normally about the same amount is ejected each beat; with bradycardia there are fewer beats, so lower cardiac output, less blood reaching the organs. The first organ to suffer: the brain.

11. Clinical case: vasovagal syncope

Typical triggers mentioned: standing too long, heat, thirst or dehydration; seeing blood in the operating theatre (“there’s always one or two every year”). Part of the definition is garbled [verify].
Mechanism: increased parasympathetic (vagal) activity → bradycardia → lower cardiac output → less cerebral perfusion (less oxygen supply to the brain) → loss of consciousness.
Treatment: a student suggested acetylcholine: no, the parasympathetic tone is already increased, so you do not give something that activates it more. Other options were mentioned but are garbled (“acetylglymesterase”, “LB and EFB” [verify]). The simple one: atropine, the vagolytic mentioned before, which stops the effect of the vagus. Other approaches: later, with the heart.
[Lucía] (ANS TBL, see FMF ANS 2 section 9): reflex bradycardia via the vagus and M2 receptors is treated with muscarinic antagonists such as atropine.

Not covered in this lecture

ANS sensory (afferent) branch, central autonomic network, hypothalamus, autonomic reflexes: in Lucía’s “Autonomic nervous system II”, not discussed here.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Physiology Smooth muscle
Sources

Smooth muscle Physiology FMF (automatic transcription, errors corrected). Starts mid-sentence (varicosities: “…where neurotransmitters are released”); the opening (single-unit vs multi-unit types, start of innervation) is not recorded. Ends with an in-class quiz, the summary and textbook recommendations, then student chatter and garbage lines.
Coverage: transcript first, filled from Lucía (“Smooth muscle” in the neuromuscular physiology section). Date not recorded.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault (see ADI). The table of neurotransmitters, receptors and second messengers is in Spanish on his slide.
Textbooks he recommended: two general physiology textbooks (names garbled), and one he considers better for muscle and neural physiology (transcript “Bernanke-Bau” [verify]).
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “Smooth muscle” and “Smooth muscle summary”. PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Biophysics Membrane potential, FMF ANS 2, FMF Embryology Spinal nerves and nervous system (origin of smooth muscle).

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Second messengers: “What you need to know”: IP3 causes contraction (calcium release from the reticulum); cyclic AMP causes relaxation. “As a general rule.” The table of neurotransmitters and receptors: “you don’t need to learn this at this moment.”
Calcium is the only common element of excitation-contraction in skeletal and smooth muscle (in-class quiz; section 2).
NO actions summarized in three: less calcium release from the reticulum, less calcium entry from outside, more phosphatase activity (section 5).
Latch-type maintenance (section 8): “don’t make too much effort to understand this”; know the idea.
Calcium sensitization/desensitization happens only in smooth muscle: “this is important” (section 6).

1. Structure and innervation

Varicosities instead of synapses: places along the axon where neurotransmitter is released; no postsynaptic specialization, no narrow cleft. The transmitter spreads to nearby areas; smooth muscle cells with receptors there respond. Not one axon to one fibre.
Single-unit smooth muscle: a varicosity per fibre is not needed; a few varicosities activate one, two or three nearby fibres which act collectively. Multi-unit: isolated fibres with fewer connections, not compact.
[Lucía] Single-unit (visceral): fibres coupled by gap junctions, acting like one long fibre. Multi-unit: each fibre contracts independently.
Disposition is very variable: compact walls (e.g. the media of arteries); digestive tract with longitudinal and circular layers (rows of cells, not one big tissue).
Nuclei and length: a skeletal fibre (up to e.g. 40 cm) needs hundreds of nuclei to stay alive; smooth muscle cells have one nucleus, are much shorter, and long distances are covered by cells placed one after another.
Receptors are concentrated in membrane areas called caveolae (transcript “capillae”), surrounded by sarcoplasmic reticulum; instead of skeletal triads, the reticulum lies near the caveolae.

2. Patterns of activity

























PatternExampleContracted most of the day, relaxed brieflySphincters (pylorus, cardia, bladder sphincter)Relaxed most of the day, contracts a few timesUrinary bladder (detrusor), gallbladder (transcript “suplectus” [verify]; contracts with meals)Rhythmic contraction-relaxationStomach / digestive tract (moving contents along)Always some tone, higher or lowerBlood vessels (blood pressure control), airways

(Skeletal muscle: type 1 fibres for sustained effort, type 2 for short efforts; most skeletal muscles are relaxed much of the time, e.g. during sleep.)
Such different patterns need a different excitation-contraction coupling.

3. Calcium acts through myosin phosphorylation

Calcium is the shared element, but it acts differently.
Skeletal (recap): calcium binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes myosin binding sites on actin.
Smooth muscle thin filaments are just actin: no troponin, no tropomyosin; binding sites are always available.
Smooth muscle myosin is a different subtype: it binds actin only when phosphorylated (on the light chain).
Calcium + calmodulin activate myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the light chain and starts contraction.
A phosphatase (myosin light chain phosphatase) removes the phosphate; if the kinase is no longer activated, contraction stops. Calcium must be maintained to sustain contraction.
Once phosphorylated, the cross-bridge cycle is the same as in skeletal muscle (ATP binding to unbind, hydrolysis to recock).
Because calcium must activate a kinase that phosphorylates myosin, contraction is much slower than in skeletal muscle.
[Lucía] Unphosphorylated smooth muscle myosin has very little affinity for actin; phosphorylation/dephosphorylation in equilibrium.

4. Sources of cytoplasmic calcium

Skeletal: only from the reticulum: action potential into the T-tubule, DHPR pushes RyR, calcium released.
Smooth muscle, several mechanisms (possibly combined in one fibre):

Reticulum release (via second messengers, e.g. IP3, from metabotropic receptors);
Extracellular calcium through receptor-operated (ligand-gated) calcium channels opened by a neurotransmitter;
Voltage-gated calcium channels: depolarization (e.g. an action potential in the fibre) opens them. (Recall: voltage-gated calcium channels also trigger transmitter release at presynaptic terminals.)
Receptors may act directly (ionotropic) or via second messengers (metabotropic).


[Lucía] Calcium entering through ligand-gated channels can depolarize and open voltage-gated channels.

5. Modulation independent of calcium: Rho and NO
Rho

Rho (activated by second messengers) activates Rho kinase, which inhibits the myosin light chain phosphatase (acting on its regulators): more phosphorylated myosin for the same calcium, i.e. more contraction.
So with the same calcium, contraction can be higher or lower. Only in smooth muscle; in skeletal muscle calcium alone decides.

Nitric oxide (NO)

Example drugs: sildenafil-type “blue pills” (Viagra, commercial name; transcript “the agra”); apart from erectile uses they treat pulmonary hypertension: they relax smooth muscle.
NO acts through cyclic GMP, leading to PKG1 (protein kinase G), with five actions:

Activates an inhibitor of the reticulum calcium channels: less release from the reticulum.
Inhibits metabotropic receptors that release calcium via IP3: less release (indirect).
Activates the myosin light chain phosphatase: less phosphorylation, less contraction.
Opens potassium channels: membrane potential more negative, voltage-gated calcium channels less likely to open: less calcium entry.
Directly inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels: less calcium entry.


Summary in three: less calcium release from the reticulum, less calcium entry from outside, phosphatase activation. A very powerful inhibitor of smooth muscle contraction, hence a good drug target.
[check] [Lucía]‘s list differs slightly: mechanism 1 inhibits IP3 activation via a G-protein receptor; 2 lowers ER calcium release; 3 phosphatase; 4 potassium channels; 5 direct block of voltage-gated calcium channels. She also writes Viagra “contains NO” (the lecturer only said these drugs act on this pathway).

6. Calcium sensitization and desensitization

Curve of calcium concentration vs myosin light chain phosphorylation can shift left or right (Rho, NO): the cell becomes more or less sensitive to calcium.
Does not happen in skeletal muscle: there the same calcium always gives the same result.
This, plus the many calcium sources, explains the very different activity patterns of section 2.
[Lucía] Active phosphatase: more calcium needed (shift right); inactive: less needed (shift left).

7. Membrane potential and force
Three patterns on his graph (membrane potential above, force below):

Action potentials (calcium via voltage-gated channels or reticulum) produce a progressive force increase, as in skeletal muscle, but always slow.
Mixed: rhythmic oscillations of membrane potential with occasional action potentials; contraction follows the rhythm (e.g. much of the lower digestive tract). Smooth muscle does not need action potentials: small changes in membrane potential change calcium entry through voltage-gated channels.
Contraction without any change in membrane potential: metabotropic receptors and second messengers release calcium from the reticulum (skeletal muscle has only nicotinic ionotropic receptors).


Second messenger rule: IP3: contraction; cAMP: relaxation.

Alpha-adrenergic receptors: contraction, via IP3. Alpha agonists raise blood pressure.
Beta-adrenergic receptors: relaxation. Beta agonists lower blood pressure or improve breathing (inhaled asthma drugs relax airway smooth muscle). [check] The transcript says beta receptors “use IP3”; by his own rule relaxation goes with cAMP.


Smooth muscle receptors are spread over the membrane, so it responds not only to varicosities but also to hormones and substances in the blood or extracellular space.

8. Long contraction with little energy

Advantages of the complex mechanism: lots of regulation (many transmitters, drugs, hormones) and sustained contraction with minimal energy.
Even type 1 skeletal fibres spend a lot of energy to stay contracted (think of the food needed after a long run).
Smooth muscle: a high initial calcium peak to start contraction, then an intermediate calcium level, just enough for a few myosin heads to bind from time to time and replace those that unbind. Smooth muscle myosin has a very slow turnover (slow ATP use).
Easy in smooth muscle because binding sites are always exposed; only the number of phosphorylated myosin heads is regulated.
Useful for sphincters.
[Lucía] Example durations: sphincters about 23 hours a day.

9. Adaptability to stretch

Skeletal muscle: sarcomeres perfectly aligned; force depends strongly on starting length.
Smooth muscle: thick and thin filaments not strictly parallel; stretching makes them more parallel. So it keeps similar force over a wide range of lengths.
Urinary bladder: can contract with little urine or when full. Limit: from fully stretched it contracts to about half its size, then the fibres readjust; so after a very long wait you may need to urinate again about half an hour later.
[Lucía] No sarcomeres; filaments dispersed.

10. Speed and force

Even the slowest skeletal muscle is about an order of magnitude faster than the fastest smooth muscle.
Skeletal: much force, fast. Smooth: less force, slower, but more adaptable, better regulated, lower energy cost.

11. In-class quiz

Common element in excitation-contraction coupling: calcium (not action potentials: some smooth muscle contracts without them; not troponin: absent in smooth muscle).
Muscles around the eye: levator palpebrae (skeletal, voluntary) and the smooth Müller’s muscle (transcript “carousel muscle of Miller”), not under voluntary control: why the eyes open more when afraid. Pupillary sphincter (constrictor) and dilator: both smooth, not voluntary. Similar pairs elsewhere: an internal smooth and an external skeletal sphincter (transcript garbled [verify] which). The pylorus is also a sphincter.

12. Growth

Smooth muscle fibres can divide (skeletal fibres usually do not, beyond some new cell generation): e.g. chronic hypertension thickens the arterial media with more smooth muscle cells.
They can also grow in size: instead of more nuclei, they increase their DNA: tetraploid or octoploid.
[Lucía] Same (hypertrophy with increased ploidy, one nucleus).

Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.title: FMF Radiology MRI
Medical-Degree/Year-1/FMF/Lectures/Lectu.content:
FMF Radiology MRI
Sources

Audio Clip 9 (automatic transcription, errors corrected): radiology lecture on MRI. Starts at the opening (“the security in MRI, that’s something that every doctor needs to know”) and ends “we’ll stop here and we’ll begin the TBL for the concepts of safety”. Looks complete. Safety was deferred to the TBL “in two weeks” with a doctor transcribed “Bucete”/“Burgette” [verify]; Clip 11 names the MRI TBL lecturer as Dr. Domínguez.
Audio Clip 12: the MRI TBL. Its physics recap (orientations, precession, T1, T2) is in FMF Biophysics MRI basics; its safety part (radiologist, with comments from the biophysics lecturer) and the TBL cases are used here (sections 7 to 10).
Coverage: transcripts first, filled from Lucía (“MRI basics”, radiology). Dates not recorded.

Resources

Slides: none in the vault; safety slides and the projectile videos are on ADI. “Regarding safety, study these slides” before the TBL.
Online: an MRI safety website for checking implants (transcript “emery safety.com”; probably mrisafety.com [verify]).
Lucía: FMF notes (FSF) (Lucía’s notes), “MRI basics” (elements, sequences, acquisition, safety, MRI safety labelling). PDF pages not in the page index.
Related notes: FMF Biophysics MRI basics.

Marking: [Lucía] = from Lucía’s FMF notes (previous year). [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. No slides or official notes in the vault for FMF.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Safety is “the most important part for you to know” (both lecturers): every doctor sends patients to MRI and may enter the room. “This is a TBL after all”: the cases at the end are “the most important” (section 10).
Both errors matter: sending a patient with an unsafe implant is a serious risk, but denying an MRI that could be done is also a real error, because often no other technique gives the same information.
“The magnet is always on”, repeated many times (sections 3 and 7).
How the device looks is “not very important for you”; T1 and T2: “the important thing is that you understand” them; sequence parameters: “you do not need to know at all”.
Ferromagnetic objects in the brain (aneurysm clip) or eye are “the worst scenario”: “under no circumstances may he enter the room without previously knowing if it’s ferromagnetic or not.”

1. What MRI is

Imaging method based on nuclear magnetic resonance. “Nuclear” is usually dropped to avoid confusion with nuclear medicine: no radioactive substance is involved, just a physical phenomenon.
The phenomenon: under a powerful magnet, atoms given a very specific radiofrequency absorb that energy and behave differently; when it stops, they release the excess energy. All MRI imaging is based on this.
History: Nobel Prizes for the phenomenon and for its application to imaging (names transcribed “Latour and North” [verify]). The first MRI was huge and needed a whole room; early brain scanners had a very narrow bore.
Device: similar to CT nowadays but longer and narrower: claustrophobia can be a problem (sedation possible). A CT takes about 10 s; an MRI keeps you in the magnet 10 to 20 minutes (exams around half an hour). Open MRI exists but usually worse image quality; most are closed bore.

2. Advantages and limitations

No ionizing radiation (it uses radiofrequency waves): it cannot alter DNA or induce cancer, as ionizing radiation can (student answer confirmed). Very safe technique.
Lots of information, not just anatomical: function, perfusion; new applications every year.
Great contrast between tissues: CT only shows density (e.g. white and grey matter have almost the same density and are hard to tell apart on CT; on MRI they look completely different).
Limitations: expensive, fewer studies per day (10 to 30 minutes per patient), less available than CT. Moving parts are difficult (each sequence takes minutes; the organ must be still): MRI started with neuro and musculoskeletal imaging; nowadays even the heart.
AI is reducing acquisition time to a half or a third.

3. The four elements
Magnet, gradients, radiofrequency, coils.
Magnet

The field strength roughly sets image quality: higher field, better quality (though even at 3 T you can get poor images if acquiring very fast).
It never turns off: computers off, lights off, 3 a.m., always on. Nothing ferromagnetic may enter.
Why: the field comes from current in a superconducting coil (kept very cold). Energy is given once; the current then circulates forever with no resistance. It cannot simply be switched off. Even with no electricity in the hospital for days, the magnet stays on.
Emergency only: make the coil stop superconducting; resistance makes the current fade and the field drops (“quench”, TBL: about 50 s, losing the helium; a problem to ramp up again; newer machines use little helium and recover it).

Hydrogen alignment and precession

Atoms with an odd number of protons have a magnetic moment. In the body the main one is hydrogen (in water): almost 99% of MRI is based on hydrogen.
Normally hydrogen atoms are randomly oriented: zero net magnetization. In a strong field they align with it, mostly parallel, some opposite, giving a net magnetic moment.
They do not point exactly along the field but rotate around an axis (precession) at a constant angular velocity that depends on the atom: a specific constant for hydrogen, the same in everyone.
Simple formula: the radiofrequency needed = the atom’s constant x the magnetic field. So a 3 T machine uses a different radiofrequency and different coils from a 1.5 T machine; coils cannot be exchanged between them.
[Lucía] This is the Larmor frequency.

Radiofrequency, T1 and T2

At the right frequency the energy is absorbed and the flip angle changes (e.g. 90° for all spins). When the radiofrequency stops, spins return to the lower-energy state, emitting energy that is detected to build images.
T1 relaxation: return to the original position; curve going up. Called spin-lattice: energy given to nearby molecules. With big molecules nearby, energy is given easily: short T1; small molecules (water): long T1.
T2 relaxation: the radiofrequency also synchronizes the spins; when it stops they desynchronize and the signal is lost (random directions = zero signal); curve going down. Called spin-spin: caused by nearby magnetization. Water (homogeneous, small molecules): long T2; bigger molecules: faster.
T1 and T2 happen at the same time. They are the only two information sources: hence T1- and T2-weighted images, no T3 or T4.
Classic: T1-weighted: fat bright; T2-weighted: water/fluid very bright. Fluid signal can be nulled (T2 with fluid attenuation: normal fluid dark, abnormal fluid still bright).
[Lucía] T1: time for the longitudinal component to reach 63%; T2: transverse component falls to 37%.

Shielding

The room must be shielded against radiofrequency in both directions (interference with equipment; outside sources would alter images): a Faraday cage; the window has a fine metal mesh, like a microwave oven.

Gradients

MRI needs a very homogeneous field. Then a small known gradient is added so that the field (and the needed and returned frequencies) is slightly different at each point (e.g. 2.999 to 3.001 T, transcript “3.111” [verify]).
This tells where the signal comes from; without gradients, a lot of signal but no image.
What the machine records is k-space (transcript “sky space” [verify]; circular wave patterns); a Fourier transform turns it into images.
Gradients produce the loud mechanical noise (TBL, section 8).

Coils

A coil must be as close as possible to the area of interest; more coils, better quality. Specific coils: head (with a mirror), neck, body, breast (patient prone), knee, finger, eye; several combined for whole-body vascular exams.
Exception: spine: the coils are inside the table, which is why the table is thin and hard.

Sequences (software)

Many parameters can be changed to weight the signal; hundreds of sequences (30 years ago essentially T1 and T2). Choose the most useful ones per patient.
Terminology: hyperintense / hypointense refer to signal intensity, always relative to something; there are no absolute values as in CT (density).
[Lucía] Tissue factors: H concentration, T1, T2, dynamic state; operational factors: TR, TE, matrix, field of view, flip angle, number of excitations (no need to know them).

4. Clinical examples

CNS: MRI far superior to CT. Spine: a tetraplegic patient’s CT showed a fracture and some stenosis, but only MRI showed a haematoma compressing the cord; for cord compression MRI is mandatory (CT cannot see the cord, especially below the shoulders). CT remains good for bone and lung.
Intravenous contrast: used less than in CT because tissue contrast is already high; used for tumours and inflammatory/infectious disease. MRI: gadolinium; CT: iodinated contrast.
Angiography without contrast (from the movement of the excited protons); also with contrast.
Heart, 3D imaging; susceptibility-weighted images now more sensitive than CT for iron and calcium (blood, calcium).
Fetal imaging: ultrasound is first line; MRI if an abnormality is suspected.
Perfusion; functional MRI (task such as finger tapping alternated with rest; a statistical analysis finds areas with more blood flow: not truly seeing function or thoughts); tractography (e.g. where a tumour has displaced the corticospinal tract, for surgical planning with neurophysiology monitoring); spectroscopy (main molecules in a tissue); diffusion; fat suppression.

5. Safety summary from the lecture

Very safe in normal conditions; very dangerous with a non-safe device or anything ferromagnetic entering the room (it flies to the magnet and can hit people).
Responsibility lies with MRI staff and radiologists, but every requesting doctor must know the basics.
Device labels: safe, conditional, unsafe. With an unsafe ferromagnetic implant (e.g. an old one from 30 years ago) the person cannot even enter the magnet room, ever, because the magnet is always on; radiofrequency is only on while acquiring.
Most medical devices nowadays are safe or conditional.

6. Labels and the Spanish “compatible” trap (TBL)

MRI safe: no limitations.
MRI unsafe: never enter the MRI room.
MRI conditional: most implants; MRI possible if specific conditions are followed (sometimes just “1.5 T but not 3 T”, sometimes many radiofrequency limits). In Spanish translated as “compatible”, which misleads people into thinking no conditions apply.
Check implants on an MRI safety website. Everyone entering the room other than the technician and radiologist (including other doctors) fills in an MRI safety questionnaire.
[Lucía] Ferromagnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt.

7. Static field: the projectile effect (TBL)

Main danger: ferromagnetic objects, pulled towards the bore very fast, with force proportional to their mass. Small objects: fast but harmless; large ones become projectiles.
Classic: a patient’s oxygen bottle (wheelchair with oxygen); a motorized wheelchair sucked into the bore; an office chair stuck to the magnet (video), easy to remove once a few centimetres away. An old, weak MRI still swings an oxygen bottle back and forth through the bore until it sticks.
Safety line: 5 gauss (transcript “0.5 micro teslas or 5 gauss”; 5 G = 0.5 mT [check]). Outside it, nothing is attracted with enough force. Inside, the force rises steeply (“exponential”): a few centimetres can multiply it by 2, 3 or 5; in one metre the field may go from 1 to 50 gauss.
Biophysics lecturer: this is a very strong gradient (how fast the field increases over a short distance). His own experiences: credit cards in a wallet completely erased; a pen with a metal part pulled from his shirt; even a small screw feels a strong force.
Equipment for the room is non-ferromagnetic, e.g. tools with green handles (mostly aluminium) are safe; a black-handled one would fly away.
Implants: ferromagnetic implants are attracted, but usually the mass is small; the real worry is a ferromagnetic object not fixed by fibrous tissue: inside the eye or inside the skull. In the brain there is gliosis, which does not anchor things: an old ferromagnetic aneurysm clip is “like the first day” decades later; the magnet would move or flip it and cause a massive subarachnoid haemorrhage, probably fatal. Aneurysm clips have been non-ferromagnetic for many years, but you must know the exact model.

8. Radiofrequency and gradients (TBL)

Radiofrequency at high field strengths is close to microwaves: it can heat tissue and damage electronic or metallic implants, like electronics in a microwave oven. Radiofrequency is only on during acquisition.
Burns: a patient wearing clothing with silver (antimicrobial lining): silver is not ferromagnetic but is metal; it acts as an antenna, absorbs radiofrequency and deposits heat in the skin (burn lines appeared later). Avoid loops (patient’s arms or feet touching each other) and contact with the bore. Tattoos (transcript: they contain iron, ferromagnetic material [verify]): not a contraindication; a wet towel over the tattoo can help dissipate heat.
The machine limits radiofrequency energy: normal mode (level 0); first level (machine asks for confirmation, risk slightly higher); second level forbidden in patients (only for research on materials).
SAR (specific absorption rate): an estimate of radiofrequency absorption; that is why you are asked your weight before an MRI. Alternative measure: B1+rms, the actual amplitude of the radiofrequency field (B1 = field created by the radiofrequency). The machine still cannot detect metal acting as an antenna.
Gradients cause loud noise during acquisition (some sequences much louder): earplugs (transcript “blocks” [verify]). Raised as a question for fetal imaging; no known danger from the noise.

9. Superconducting magnet and quench (TBL)

Emergency (e.g. a person trapped between a chair and the magnet): quench lowers the field fast (about 50 seconds) by releasing all the helium; problematic afterwards. Otherwise, removing a stuck object needs great force applied from outside the bore (transcript garbled).

10. TBL cases

Accompanying a patient with mobility problems into the scan room: which object need not be removed?

iPhone, plastic cards: not a safety risk for patient or you, but they will probably stop working.
Stethoscope: has ended up on the magnet more than once (doctor wanting to help).
Wheelchair: the worst; ferromagnetic, will fly to the magnet. Use specific non-ferromagnetic wheelchairs and beds.
Gold and silver jewellery: not a problem to enter the room (not ferromagnetic). If you are having the MRI yourself it is removed anyway (heat, burns, artefacts). If it is attracted by the magnet, it is not real gold or silver.


Relative with steel dental implants placed two days ago: as a general rule, anything screwed to the body will not fly away; most implants lack enough ferromagnetic material. Many stainless steels (usually higher quality) are non-ferromagnetic. Student: heating? Metal can absorb more radiofrequency, but in bone it is not a real issue: safe. Main consequence: artefacts (field distortion around the metal), e.g. the mouth region unreadable.
Cochlear implant: the external part (attached by a magnet) must be removed and left outside the room. The internal part (electrode into the cochlea) cannot be removed. For many years a contraindication; nowadays most are MRI conditional: know the exact model and check the conditions. Same for cardiac pacemakers: once absolute contraindication, now usually possible under conditions.
Man operated long ago for a small non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage: non-traumatic, so almost certainly an aneurysm treated with a clip. The most dangerous case: if ferromagnetic, even one or two metres from the magnet it will flip, the vessel will break and he will most probably die. Must be completely sure of the clip material before entering. Same for a ferromagnetic foreign body in the eye: contraindication if there is still vision (retina easily damaged); if vision is completely lost, MRI can usually be done.


[Lucía] Safety: no known effects of static fields on DNA, reproduction or growth; can be done in pregnancy; main risk the projectile effect; heat from radiofrequency controlled by SAR limits.
