The Placenta: Study Notes
fmf medicine
Sep 27, 2026 · @simon
1. Definition and the two components
The placenta is the ephemeral materno-fetal organ that enables nutrient and gas exchange between mother and fetus. Together with the umbilical cord it forms a transport system between the two.
The mature placenta has two parts:




















ComponentOriginWhat it isFetal: villous (bushy) chorion, chorion frondosumTrophoblast + extraembryonic mesodermThe chorionic villi at the embryonic poleMaternal: decidua basalisEndometriumThe decidua deep to the conceptus
One-line summary for the group: fetal villi float in pools of maternal blood (a hemochorial placenta); the two bloods never mix, they exchange across the placental membrane.
[image: Early chorionic sac with embryo, umbilical cord, yolk sac, chorionic vessels and villi]
Slide 4. Early chorionic sac opened: embryo attached by the umbilical cord (note intestine herniated into the cord), yolk sac, chorionic vessels, villi at the edge.
2. Development: decidua and villous chorion
The decidua (maternal side)
The decidua is the endometrium of the pregnant uterus. It has three named regions, defined by position relative to the conceptus:

























RegionPositionFateDecidua basalisDeep to the conceptus (between it and the myometrium)Becomes the maternal component of the placenta (decidual plate + septa)Decidua capsularisSuperficial, overlying the conceptusStretches and thins over the smooth chorion; by month 3 it fuses with the parietalisDecidua parietalisAll the rest of the uterine liningFuses with the amniochorionic membrane, obliterating the uterine cavity
[image: Decidua basalis, capsularis and parietalis at the end of months 2 and 3]
Slide 6. Left, end of month 2: basalis (under the bushy chorion), capsularis (over the sac), parietalis (the rest); the uterine cavity still exists. Right, end of month 3: capsularis has fused with parietalis and the cavity is gone.
Chorionic villi (fetal side)
Villi develop in three stages. The key idea: each stage adds one layer to the core.





























StageWhenCoreCoveringPrimary villusEnd of week 2Cytotrophoblast (finger-like projections pushing into the syncytiotrophoblast)SyncytiotrophoblastSecondary villusEarly week 3Extraembryonic mesoderm grows into the cytotrophoblast coreCytotrophoblast + syncytiotrophoblastTertiary villusEnd of week 3Mesenchyme differentiates into blood vessels (villous capillaries)Cytotrophoblast + syncytiotrophoblast
[image: Villus development days 4 to 17 and cross-sections of primary, secondary and tertiary villi]
Slide 12 (Carlson, 2019). Top: timeline from implantation (day 7) to anchoring and floating villi (day 17). Bottom: A primary (cytotrophoblast core), B secondary (mesoderm core), C tertiary (capillaries in the core).

Chorion = extraembryonic mesoderm (chorionic plate) + cytotrophoblast + syncytiotrophoblast.
Cytotrophoblast cell columns break through the syncytium and spread over the endometrium as the outer cytotrophoblastic shell, which anchors the chorion to the endometrium.
Anchoring villi reach and attach to the decidua basalis via the shell; floating (free) villi branch off them and hang in the intervillous space.
Intervillous space: the lacunae (from week 2) that fill with maternal blood from eroded maternal sinusoids / spiral arteries.
By the end of week 4, tertiary villi surround the entire chorionic sac.

[image: Outer cytotrophoblast shell anchoring villi to the endometrium around the intervillous space]
Slide 13. Follow a villus from the chorionic plate (bottom) up to the outer cytotrophoblast shell (top), which is glued to the endometrium. The red space between villi is the intervillous space, filled by maternal vessels.
Chorionic vessels and the first circulation

Week 3: blood islands appear first in the extraembryonic mesoderm around the yolk sac, then in the connecting stalk and chorion. They differentiate into blood cells (centre) and endothelial cells (edge): vasculogenesis.
Signals on the slide: FGF2/FGFR turns mesoderm into hemangioblasts; VEGF via VEGFR2 (Flk1) drives hemangioblasts; VEGF via VEGFR1 (Flt1) drives tube formation; later branching into arteries and veins.
Also in week 3, the embryonic (intraembryonic) mesoderm forms its own vessels.
Chorionic plate vessels join vessels in the connecting stalk (future umbilical cord), which join the embryo’s vessels.
By day 22 (start of week 4) a primordial cardiovascular system is formed and functional: heart, dorsal aortae, cardinal veins, vitelline vessels (yolk sac) and umbilical vessels (chorion).

Spiral artery remodelling and immune tolerance

Endovascular extravillous trophoblasts (eEVTs) invade maternal spiral arteries and remodel them into wide, low-resistance vessels that flood the intervillous space.
Cells at the decidual-placental interface: SCT (syncytiotrophoblast), VCT (villous cytotrophoblast), EVT, decidual NK cells (dNK, the most abundant), decidual macrophages (dM), dendritic cells, T cells, decidual stromal cells.
Why the mother does not reject the fetus: trophoblast has a unique HLA profile (HLA-C, -E, -F, -G on the slide; notably HLA-G) that binds receptors on local immune cells (KIR, NKG2, ILT families), producing tolerance (Lin et al., 2022).
Beyond the slides: trophoblast lacks classical HLA-A and HLA-B, and poor spiral artery remodelling is linked to pre-eclampsia. Good if someone asks “so what?”

From leafy sac to discoid placenta

Week 3: villi cover the whole chorionic sac (fluffy appearance).
End of month 2: villi persist and branch only at the embryonic pole (facing the decidua basalis) = villous/bushy chorion. Villi on the abembryonic side (facing the capsularis) degenerate = smooth chorion (chorion laeve).
Months 4 to 5: decidua is eroded to enlarge the intervillous space, leaving wedge-shaped placental (decidual) septa that divide the maternal surface into cotyledons. Septa do not reach the chorionic plate, so the intervillous space stays continuous.
Amnion: the amniotic cavity expands and obliterates most of the chorionic cavity. The amnion covers the umbilical cord and fuses with the smooth chorion = amniochorionic membrane, which then fuses with the decidua parietalis.

[image: Placental septa dividing the placenta into cotyledons; spiral artery jet into the intervillous space]
Slide 20. Left top: maternal surface with cotyledons. Left bottom: fetal surface with cord and chorionic vessels. Right: decidual septa hang from the decidual plate but stop short of the chorionic plate; a spiral artery jets blood into each compartment.
3. Gross anatomy of the full-term placenta
A term placenta is a disc with two very different faces. Typical figures (textbook, not on the slides): about 500 g, 15 to 25 cm across, 2 to 3 cm thick.






























FeatureFetal surfaceMaternal surfaceLookSmooth, shiny, grey-blueRough, dark red, spongyCovered byTransparent amnion (peels off) over the chorionic plateThin layer of decidua basalis that tore away at deliveryLandmarksUmbilical cord insertion; chorionic vessels radiating from it under the amnion (arteries usually cross over veins)Cotyledons (lobes) separated by grooves where the placental septa wereDerived fromChorionic plate (fetal)Decidua basalis (maternal) + villous chorion
[image: Full-term placenta: maternal surface with cotyledons, fetal surface with cord and vessels, membranes]
Slide 23 (Moore). A: maternal surface, cotyledon outlined, grooves between. B: fetal surface, vessels radiating under transparent amnion. C: amnion and smooth chorion lifted, false knot in the cord. D: fetal surface with artery and vein labelled. This is what you will hold in the lab.
At the rim, the placenta continues as the membranes: amnion (inner) + smooth chorion (outer), i.e. the amniochorionic membrane. The slide photo also shows a false knot in the cord (a vessel loop or Wharton’s jelly bulge, not a true knot).
Umbilical cord

Transverse section: 2 umbilical arteries + 1 umbilical vein, embedded in Wharton’s jelly (mucoid connective tissue), covered by amnion.
Arteries carry O2-poor blood from fetus to placenta. The vein carries O2-rich blood from placenta to fetus. (Named by direction relative to the fetal heart, not by oxygen.)
The vein has the wider lumen and thinner wall; the arteries are thick-walled, often constricted.
Single umbilical artery is a recognised variant shown on the slide; it is associated with fetal anomalies (beyond slides: roughly 1% of cords).

[image: Umbilical cord cross-section with two arteries, one vein, Wharton’s jelly; normal vs single umbilical artery]
Slide 24. Right: histology of the cord, 2 small thick-walled arteries, 1 larger vein, Wharton’s jelly, amnion on the surface. Bottom left: normal cord vs single umbilical artery.
4. The placental membrane (barrier)
The placental membrane separates maternal blood (intervillous space) from fetal blood (villous capillaries). It thins with gestation to make exchange easier.

















TimeLayers, maternal to fetal side~10 weeks: 4 layers1. Syncytiotrophoblast 2. Cytotrophoblast 3. Connective tissue (villous mesenchyme) 4. Fetal capillary endotheliumMid-gestation onward: 2 layers1. Syncytiotrophoblast 2. Endothelium
[image: Placental membrane at 10 weeks with 4 layers versus mid-gestation with 2 layers]
Slide 26. Top: villi mature from thick (left) to thin and highly branched (right). Bottom: at 10 weeks the barrier is syncytium, cytotrophoblast, connective tissue, endothelium; by mid-gestation only syncytium and endothelium.
Why it thins: the cuboidal progenitor cytotrophoblast layer becomes thin and regionally discontinuous, and fetal capillaries move up against the syncytium.
Inside a mature villus (cross-section)
Syncytiotrophoblast (outside) > scattered cytotrophoblast cells > basal lamina > fetal mesenchyme with Hofbauer cells (fetal macrophages) > fetal microvessels.
[image: Mature chorionic villus longitudinal and cross-section with transfer lists]
Slide 19. a: spiral artery and uterine vein opening through the cytotrophoblastic shell; anchoring, stem and free-floating villi in the intervillous space. b: villus cross-section with Hofbauer cells and fetal microvessels, plus what moves mother to fetus and back.
The syncytiotrophoblast (ST) is a unique epithelium

It is a syncytium: no lateral cell borders.
Its apical (maternal-facing) membrane is amplified by microvilli.
Transporters on both membranes: GLUTs (glucose), LAT and SNAT (amino acids), FATPs (fatty acids, helped by lipoprotein lipase), nucleoside transporters.
Nutrient transport is regulated by maternal hormones and nutrient supply, blood flow, fetal demand, and placental mTOR signalling.
Roles: main site of O2, nutrient and waste exchange; a selective barrier; a highly effective barrier to infection; and the main endocrine cell (section 6).

5. Placental circulation and what crosses
Two separate circuits meet at the villus surface without mixing.
Fetal circuit: fetal heart > umbilical arteries (O2-poor) > chorionic vessels in the chorionic plate > stem villi > capillaries in branch villi (exchange) > back to the umbilical vein (O2-rich) > fetus.
Maternal circuit: uterine arteries > endometrial spiral arteries (through the cytotrophoblastic shell) > jet of blood into the intervillous space toward the chorionic plate > bathes the villi > drains back through endometrial veins in the decidual plate.
[embedded content: placental circulation · fetal and maternal circuits]
Read each side top to bottom, then across the middle: exchange happens only between the two highlighted boxes, through the placental membrane.
[image: Blood circulation in a hemochorial placenta]
Slide 25 (Moore). Fetal side on top: umbilical arteries (O2-poor) and vein (O2-rich) branch into stem villi. Maternal side below: endometrial arteries spurt into the intervillous space (blue), endometrial veins drain it.
Transfer across the placental membrane

































Direction / categorySubstancesMother to fetus: O2 and nutrientsO2, water, electrolytes, carbohydrates (glucose), amino acids, lipids, hormones, vitamins, iron, trace elementsMother to fetus: antibodiesIgG (passive immunity)Mother to fetus: harmfulDrugs (e.g. alcohol), poisons, carbon monoxide, viruses (rubella, cytomegalovirus), Toxoplasma gondiiFetus to mother: wastesCO2, water, urea, uric acid, creatinine, bilirubinFetus to mother: otherHormones, RBC antigens (the basis of Rh disease)Do NOT crossBacteria, heparin, IgS (secretory IgA), IgM
[image: Schematic of transfer across the placental membrane]
Slide 27 (Moore). Red box: harmful substances that do cross. Green circle: substances that do not cross (bacteria, heparin, IgS, IgM).
Memory hook for non-transferable: large or bound molecules (IgM is a pentamer, heparin is a large charged polysaccharide) and whole bacteria. Viruses and Toxoplasma are the exceptions that do get through.
6. Functions of the placenta
The placenta does the job of five fetal organs at once.









































#FunctionActs asKey points1RespiratoryLungsO2 moves from maternal HbA to fetal HbF, which has higher O2 affinity; CO2 goes back2ExcretoryKidneysBicarbonate, H+ ions, lactic acid, urea, creatinine to the mother3NutritionGutGlucose, amino acids, lipids, micronutrients (raises maternal vitamin requirements)4ImmunityImmune systemTransfers maternal IgG (passive protection); ST barrier to infection; HLA-mediated tolerance5EndocrineEndocrine glandshCG, progesterone, estrogen, hPL, all from the syncytiotrophoblast
Endocrine timeline

hCG rises fast from implantation and peaks late in the 1st trimester (around weeks 8 to 10), then falls to a low plateau. Its job: keep the corpus luteum alive so it keeps making progesterone. It is what pregnancy tests detect.
Corpus luteum is the main progesterone source in the 1st trimester; the placenta takes over around the end of the 1st trimester (~13 weeks on the slide).
Progesterone and estrogen (mainly estriol) rise steadily until term.
hPL (human placental lactogen) appears later in the 1st trimester and rises to term; it increases maternal insulin resistance so more glucose is left for the fetus.

7. Clinical correlations: Rh disease and twins
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis)

Setting: mother Rh-negative, baby Rh-positive.
Fetal RBCs (RBC antigens) reach the mother, usually at delivery, and she makes anti-Rh antibodies (isoimmunization).
In a later Rh+ pregnancy, those antibodies are IgG, so they cross the placenta and destroy fetal RBCs. The first baby is usually spared.
Prevention: at-risk women receive anti-D immunoglobulin, which clears fetal cells before the mother can sensitise.

Multiple pregnancies

























Dizygotic (fraternal)Monozygotic (identical)Frequency~2/3 of twins~1/3 of twinsOrigin2 oocytes, 2 sperm1 zygote splits into 2 embryos within the first ~13 daysMembranesAlways 2 amnions + 2 chorions; placentas separate or fused (chorions can fuse too)Depends on when the split happens (below)
[image: Fraternal vs identical twins; mono-mono, mono-di, di-di]
Slide 32 (Osmosis). Mono-mono: share placenta and amniotic sac. Mono-di: share placenta, separate sacs. Di-di: separate placentas and sacs.
Monozygotic twins: timing of the split decides what they share. Rule: the later the split, the more they share.

































Split atApprox. dayChorionAmnionPlacenta2-cell stage / morula (A)0 to 32 (di-)2 (di-)2, separate or fusedInner cell mass of blastocyst (B), most common4 to 81 (mono-)2 (di-)1 sharedBilaminar disc (C)8 to 131 (mono-)1 (mono-)1 shared, one amniotic cavity
[image: Dizygotic twins with separate or fused placentas; monozygotic twins split at stages A, B, C]
Slide 33. Left: dizygotic twins, placentas separate (A) or fused (B), always two chorions. Right: monozygotic split at A (2-cell), B (inner cell mass: common placenta, common chorionic cavity) or C (bilaminar disc: common amniotic cavity).
The logic: the chorion forms from trophoblast (~day 4 to 5), the amnion forms around day 8. Split before a membrane forms and each twin gets its own; split after and they share it. Beyond slides: a split after ~day 13 risks conjoined twins. Days are textbook approximations; the slide only gives the 13-day limit.
[embedded content: monozygotic twins · timing of split vs shared membranes]
A membrane that already exists when the embryo splits is shared; one that forms afterwards is made twice.
8. Dissection lab: a 5-minute walkthrough
Work from outside in, and fetal side before maternal side.

Define it (1 sentence): an ephemeral materno-fetal organ made of villous chorion (fetal) + decidua basalis (maternal); hemochorial, so maternal blood bathes fetal villi.
Membranes: lift the edge. Show the amnion peeling off the smooth chorion (amniochorionic membrane). Explain that the smooth chorion is where villi degenerated (facing the decidua capsularis).
Fetal surface: smooth, shiny, amnion-covered. Point to the cord insertion and the chorionic vessels radiating out.
Umbilical cord: if cut, count the vessels: 2 arteries + 1 vein in Wharton’s jelly. Say which way each carries blood. Mention single umbilical artery and false knots.
Flip to the maternal surface: rough, dark red, lobed. Show cotyledons and the grooves left by placental septa (months 4 to 5). This surface is decidua basalis over villous chorion.
Development in 3 lines: primary (week 2) > secondary (week 3) > tertiary villi (end of week 3); villi cover the whole sac at week 4; only the embryonic pole keeps them by month 2.
Barrier: 4 layers at 10 weeks, 2 layers (syncytiotrophoblast + endothelium) by mid-gestation.
Functions: lungs, kidneys, gut, immune, endocrine (hCG, progesterone, estrogen, hPL).
Close with a question to the group: “Why does IgG cross but IgM not, and why does that matter for Rh disease?”

Likely questions from the group

Do maternal and fetal blood mix? No. They are separated by the placental membrane; only small leaks (e.g. at delivery) happen, which is how Rh sensitisation starts.
Which vessel carries oxygenated blood? The umbilical vein.
Where do the hormones come from? Syncytiotrophoblast.
What anchors the placenta? Anchoring villi via the outer cytotrophoblastic shell into the decidua basalis.
Can identical twins have two placentas? Yes, if they split in the first ~3 days.

LECTURE 7.2 MEIOSIS
Meiosis is a specialized reductive cell division that gives rise to sperm and egg cells
Diploid primordial germ cells migrate into the embryonic gonad and engage in repeated rounds of
mitosis, to generate spermatogonia in males and oogonia in females. Further growth and differentiation
produce primary spermatocytes in the testis and primary oocytes in the ovary. This process requires many
more mitotic divisions in males than in females, and likely contributes to sex differences in the mutation
rate. The diploid spermatocytes and oocytes can then undergo meiosis, the cell division process that is
designed to produce genetically unique haploid gametes. That is, each sperm cell produced by a man and each
egg cell produced by a woman is designed to have a genome sequence that is unlike that of any other sperm
or egg cell that they, or anybody else, produces.
Every diploid cell contains two chromosome sets, and so has two copies ( homologs ) of each chromosome
(except in the special case of the X and Y chromosomes in males). One homolog is paternally inherited and
the other is maternally inherited. In humans, for each of the 23 homologous pairs, the choice of which
daughter cell each homolog enters is independent. This allows 2 [23], or about 8.4 × 10 [6], different possible
combinations of parental chromosomes in the gametes that might arise from a single meiotic division
( Figure 1 ).

Meiosis is a reductive division because it involves two successive cell divisions (meiosis I and II) but
only one round of DNA replication. As a result, it gives rise to four haploid cells. In males, the two meiotic
cell divisions are each symmetrical, producing four functionally equivalent spermatozoa. Female meiosis is
different because, at each meiosis, asymmetric cell division results in unequal division of the cytoplasm.
The products of female meiosis I (the first meiotic division) are a large secondary oocyte and a small cell
( polar body ), which is discarded. During meiosis II, the secondary oocyte then gives rise to the large mature
egg cell and a second polar body, which again is discarded ( Figure 3 ).

Oogonia enter the first meiotic division early during embryogenesis. In humans, primary oocytes enter
meiosis I during fetal development but are then all arrested at prophase in a prolonged diplotene stage of
prophase I, called the dictyotene . During each menstrual cycle, one follicle (called the dominant follicle)
completes the maturation process. This oocyte completes the first meiotic division just before ovulation to
form a secondary oocyte, following which the second meiotic division is initiated only to be arrested in the
metaphase stage. The second meiotic division is completed when a sperm penetrates the oocyte during
fertilization. Because ovulation can continue up to the fifth and sometimes sixth decades, this means that
meiosis can be arrested for many decades in primary oocytes that are used in ovulation in later life.
Can you think of any potential implications of this prolonged state on the health of the embryo?
The second division of meiosis is identical to mitosis, but the first division has important differences. Its
purpose is to generate genetic diversity, creating genetic differences between the daughter cells by a process
called recombination . During meiosis I the maternal and paternal homologs of each pair of replicated
chromosomes undergo synapsis by pairing together to form a bivalent. (Although the X and Y
chromosomes have very different sequences, they too can form a bivalent in male meiosis). Because DNA
had been replicated at the beginning of meiosis, each one of the homologous chromosomes has two sister
chromatids, so each bivalent is a four-stranded structure.
[PDF p. 4]
3
Meiosis I has the same four stages of mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase), but there
are some differences (particularly in prophase I), as explained below:
Meiosis I begins with Prophase I, which is further divided into five stages ( Figure 4 ). Prophase I
begins during fetal life and, in human females, can last for decades. During this process, the
homologs within each bivalent normally exchange segments of DNA at matching locations.
Figure 4 The five stages of prophase in meiosis I. ( A ) Leptotene (shown here are
representative maternal and paternal chromosome 1 homologs, and maternal
and paternal chromosome 7 homologs). ( B ) In zygotene, duplicated maternal and
paternal homologs pair, to form bivalents comprising four chromatids. Pairing of
homologous chromosomes leads to fusion of the maternal and paternal homologs
( synapsis ). ( C ) In pachytene, chromosomes become more condensed and this
reveals the presence of recombination (crossing over) between maternal and
paternal chromosome fragments. There are two crossovers in the bivalent on the
left and one in the bivalent on the right. For simplicity, both crossovers on the left
involve the same two chromatids. In reality, more crossovers may occur, involving
three or even all four chromatids in a bivalent. ( D ) During diplotene, the
homologous chromosomes may separate slightly, except at the chiasmata. ( E )
Diakinesis is marked by contraction of the bivalents and is the transition to
metaphase I.
1. In Leptotene (leptos = thin), the duplicated chromosomes, each
with a pair of sister chromatids, begin to condense but remain unpaired.
At this stage, Double-strand breaks (DSBs, see below) begin to form, and
their repair using a homologous chromatid starts to bring together the
homologous chromosomes. The cromatin is organized into loops,
linked together at the base by some proteins called cohesins ( Figure 5 ).
2. At the Zygotene stage (zygos = join) a proteinaceous synaptonemal
complex (SC), forms between closely apposed homologous chromosomes. It is comprised by two lateral elements and a central element.
The central and lateral elements of the SC are formed by several proteins
from the SYPC family. The lateral elements bind to the axis formed by
the cohesins at the cromosome loops that were present at leptotene.
During zygotene, homologues finally pair completely, and this pairing
leads to synapsis of the parental chromosomes into bivalents comprised
of four chromatids ( Figure 5 ).
3. Completion of the synaptonemal complex marks the start of the
Pachytene stage (pachy = thick), during which recombination
(crossing-over) becomes evident. Crossing-over (or crossover) involves
the physical breakage of the DNA in one paternal and one maternal
chromatid, as explained below. Recombined homologs appear to be
physically connected at specific points. Each such connection marks the
point of a crossover and is known as a chiasma (plural chiasmata).
There are an average of 55 chiasmata per cell in human male meiosis,
and around 90 or so chiasmata per cell in female meiosis, and most of
these occur at recombination hotspots (sites of preferred recombination).
4. At the beginning of Diplotene (diplos = double), the chromatids
from the homologous chromosomes start to separate slightly as the
synaptonemal complex is degraded, but the homologs are still joined at
the points of recombination (chiasmata, plural of chiasma).

little bit, the nucleolus and the nuclear envelope dissapear, and the
spindle apparatus begins to form, in preparation for the next phase of
Meiosis I (metaphase I).

Homologous recombination at the molecular level
The molecular events that take place during recombination in the pachytene stage of prophase I have been
studied in detail. As depicted in Figure 7, homologous recombination begins with the action of specific
endonucleases that create a double-strand break (DSB) at specific sites in one of the chromatids. The
main endonuclease used in humans is SPO11 . After this, a multi-protein exonuclease complex (known as
MNR because it is made of M RE11, N BS1 and R AD50) digests the ends of the break leaving 3’ overhangs.

The next step begins when one of these 3’ overhangs searches and invades a chromatid of the
homologous chromosome, creating a Holliday structure . The 3’ ends are then extended by a polymerase
using as template the complementary strand of the other chromatid, resulting in synthesis of DNA
(segments in blue in Figure 7 ). The multi-protein complex responsible for this reactions includes
Replication protein A (REPA), RAD54 and other proteins (like BRCA1 and BRCA2, mutated in breast
cancer). Depending on the way in which the Holliday junctions are resolved, the recombination process can
result in cross-over or not between the two original chromatids, as shown in Figure 8 . At the same time,
some of the new DNA synthesized during the process might have been copied from one chromatid to its
sister ( gene conversion ). Therefore, there are four possible outcomes of homologous recombination:
crossover (that is, a recombinant chromatid) with or without gene conversion, and non-crossover (nonrecombinant chromatid) with or without gene conversion. The protein complexes involved in this last steps
in meiosis tend to favour crossovers more than non-crossovers; as we will see later, homologous
recombination can also be used for DNA repair during mitosis and in this case non-crossovers are favoured.

Mitosis involves a single turn of the cell cycle. After the DNA is replicated during S phase, the two sister

Inside each chromosome territory, chromatin is not packaged randomly, but following some rules that
establish various levels of organization. It is important to remember that such packaging must be a
dynamic and reversible process, in order to allow gene function: proteins (transcription factors) and
other molecules need access to the DNA molecule for proper gene expression and regulation.
The video that will be shown in class highlights various important concepts about chromatin
packaging, from the most basic level of organization (the “beads-on-a-string” conformation of the 10nm fiber) to the most condensed form of chromatin that we see under the microscope as
chromosomes during metaphase. The 10-nm fiber is formed by the winding of the DNA double-strand
molecule around a nucleosome, a structure formed by two tetrameric complexes (each tetramer being
formed by proteins called histones, in particular H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 ( Figure 2 ).

When we observe chromosomes during cell division, it is important to remember that there are two
copies for each chromosome (one paternal and one maternal), so that all loci (plural for the latin word
locus which designates any individual element in a genome) will be present in two different allelic forms
(or alleles ). Likewise, it must be noted that the cell has previously replicated all its DNA during the S
phase, so that each chromosome is made of two identical sister chromatids .

TADs are highly conserved across cell types and species, and appear to be fixed structural elements of
chromosomes that represent the typical 3D architecture of chromatin, but the loops inside each TAD are
more dynamic and usually change during the cell cycle. TADs are formed by a process called loop
extrusion, in which a circular molecular machine made up of proteins called cohesins threads
chromatin through the circle until it meets a dimer of CTCF molecules; at that point, extrusion will stop
and this leads to the establishment of the boundaries of a TAD, increasing the probability of interactions
between loci that are inside the same TAD.
Functionally, the genome can be partitioned into active and repressed compartments; these are
typically of the order of 5 Mb in size and contain different TADs in different cell types. Both types of
compartments cluster in the nucleus, but in general compartments located in the center of the nucleus
and on the outside of chromosome territories are generally active; compartments closer to the nuclear
lamina or within the interior of chromosome territories are generally inactive (See Figure 3, panel B at
the bottom).
This organization of chromatin folding and packaging has several advantages, the main one being that
it insulates some regions from the rest of the genome, allowing only contacts between DNA segments
located inside the same TAD (even though in the linear genome these segments would be about 1-2 Mb
apart). The loop extrusion model explained above explains such compartmentalization via the presence
of insulators, which are the DNA sequences that mark the boundaries of the TADs because they are
binding sites for the CTCF protein (together with other proteins). CTCF can dimerize when it is bound to
different DNA sequences, thus mediating long-range chromatin looping. CTCF is also involved in
positioning of nucleosomes, and in delimiting the boundaries of heterochromatin, which has a natural
tendency to spread. The binding sequence for CTCF is 5’-CCGCGNGGNGGC(G/A)(C/G)(T/C)-3’.
As mentioned above, the other main implication of this highly ordered organization of chromatin is
that it allows dynamic interactions between genomic regions inside each TAD. Figure 4 shows and
example in which different loops can be formed depending on the contacts between CTCF molecules,
thus allowing contacts between different elements (depicted as promoters and enhancers here, the
meaning of which will be explained in Lecture 8.3).

LECTURE 7.5 GENERAL FEATURES OF THE HUMAN GENOME
By adding up the lengths of the DNA molecules of our 24 different chromosomes (22 autosomes, plus X
and Y), the size of our nuclear genome is now estimated to be very close to 3.1 Gb (3100 Mb) in size, and
currently approximately 60,000 human genes are recognized, as described below. That gives a comparatively
low gene density, of roughly one gene per 50 kb, and there is a very low percentage of coding DNA (about
1% ). In comparison, the 16.6 kb mitochondrial genome is packed with genes (with one gene per 450 bp, on
average), and has a high content (66%) of coding DNA.
Haploid cells (oocytes and sperm cells) carry only one copy of the human genome (22 autosomes plus one
of the sex chromosomoses), but most somatic cells are diploid, having two copies of the nuclear genome (46
chromosomes and a total content of 6 Gb of DNA sequence).
The DNA of human chromosomes varies considerably in length, from 249.7 Mb for chromosome 1 to 46.7
Mb for chromosome 21. There is also significant variability between chromosomes in the proportions of DNA
that constitute euchromatin (true chromatin, the part that contains genes) and heterochromatin (the part of
the genome that is devoid of genes and remains condensed throughout the cell cycle). All chromosomes have
several megabases of constitutive heterochromatin at the centromere, but many chromosomes also have
significant amounts of non-centromeric heterochromatin. Thus, chromosomes 1, 9, 16, and 19 have
heterochromatic regions close to the centromeres (pericentromeric heterochromatin). The acrocentric
chromosomes (having a centromere very close to one end of the chromosome; that is, chromosomes 13, 14, 15,
21, and 22) each have two sizeable heterochromatic regions in their short arms. But the Y chromosome has by
far the largest proportion of heterochromatic DNA, with a particularly large segment of non-centromeric
heterochromatin on the long arm.
Variable G+C composition in the nuclear genome
The base composition of the nuclear genome averages out at 42% GC, but here is considerable variation
between chromosomes, from 38.3% GC for chromosome 4 to 47.9% GC for chromosome 19 and also across
the lengths of chromosomes. We can establish windows of a certain size and calculate the percentage of G
plus C in that window (the GC%). When we analyze the whole genome in this way, sliding this window from
the beginning to the end of the genome, the median GC% of those windows is 42%, as said above, but we see
a wide variability, with values as low as 30% or as high as 65% in some windows ( Figure 1) . If we plot gene
density (the number of genes per Megabase of sequence) against the GC content of the genome, we see that
regions with high GC% tend to have a higher density of genes. This reflects the fact that genes (specially one
type of genes called protein-coding genes) haver higher GC% than the average of the genome, but also
suggests that GC-rich regions are also rich in genes.

Heterochromatin and satellite DNA
The vast majority of DNA sequence is present in single-copy, because it appears only one in the whole
genome. However, some sequences are repeated many times, and these are called repeated DNA . There are
two main classes of repeated DNA in the human genome:
 - **Tandemly** repeated DNA sequences located at centromeres and other regions of

constitutive heterochromatin (which remains condensed throughout the cell cycle);
- **Interspersed** repeats that are distributed across the nuclear genome and

vary in size from hundreds of base pairs to several kilobases in length.
As we have seen in Lecture 7.4, constitutive heterochromatin is the highly condensed chromatin that is
usually located at the periphery of the nucleus, attached to the nuclear membrane. Its underlying DNA
accounts for around 200 Mb (~6.5%) of the human genome and encompasses megabase-sized regions at the
centromeres, multiple kilobases of DNA at the telomeres, and large additional regions on some
chromosomes. All these are formed by the repetition in tandem (that is, one after another) of the same
sequence. Depending on the size and the type of these repeated sequences, we can classify tandem repeats
into different classes ( Table 1 ).

The DNA underlying constitutive heterochromatin at the centromeres and other regions mostly consists of

often contain a binding site for a specific centromere protein, CENPB.

Transposon-derived interspesed repeats make up the majority of the human
genome and arose largely through retrotransposition
A significant amount of the human genome is made up of interspersed repetitive non-coding DNA
sequences derived from transposons (also called transposable elements ). Transposons are mobile
DNA sequences that can migrate to different regions of the genome. About 45% of the genome can
readily be seen to be made up of transposon repeats, but much of the remaining “unique” DNA is
likely to have been derived from ancient transposon copies that have diverged extensively over
long evolutionary timescales.
In humans and other mammals only a tiny minority of transposon repeats are actively
transposing . Both the frequency of transposition and the percentage of full-length repeats
depend on the repeat’s evolutionary age: recently evolved repeats have a comparatively high
percentage of full-length repeats and of actively transposing members, and conversely, more
ancient transposon repeats are frequently truncated copies or have inactivating mutations.
Transposons that can transpose independently are described as autonomous . Others are non-
autonomous : they can transpose only with the help of an autonomous transposon.
DNA transposons versus retrotransposons
A small minority of human transposon repeats originated from the DNA transposon class.
Transposons of this type have terminal inverted repeats and migrate directly without any
copying of the sequence using a “cut-and-paste” mechanism (they make a transposase to excise
the DNA sequence, which then reinserts elsewhere in the genome). Although these repeats were
actively transposing in the past, there is much less evidence of recent transposition; they are often
described, therefore, as transposon fossils .
The great majority of human transposon repeats belong to the retrotransposon class (also called
retroposons). They can transpose using a reverse transcriptase to convert an RNA transcript into a
cDNA copy that then integrates into the genomic DNA at a different location (a “copy-and-paste”
mechanism). There are three major types of mammalian retrotransposon repeat, as listed below
and illustrated in Figure 2 .


LINEs (long interspersed nuclear elements; over 6 kb when full length) have a
comparatively ancient evolutionary history: equivalent sequences are present in other
mammals, such as mice. Human LINEs, consisting of three distantly related families
(LINE-1, LINE-2, and LINE-3), are located primarily in euchromatic regions,
preferentially in the AT-rich regions of the genome. The LINE-1 (or L1) family is the
predominant LINE family, accounting for 17% of the genome sequence, and is detailed
below. It continues to have actively transposing members that are the only autonomous
transposon repeats in the human genome.


SINEs (short interspersed nuclear elements; full-length members are less than 400
nucleotides long) cannot transpose independently. However, SINEs and LINEs share
sequences at their 3’ end, and SINEs have been shown to be mobilized by neighboring
LINE repeats. By parasitizing on the LINE transposition machinery, SINEs can attain
high copy numbers. The primate-specific Alu repeat is the most abundant SINE in the
human genome, and is detailed below; the next most common human SINE family are
mammalian-wide interspersed repeats, known as MIR elements.

from the ORF1 region, and a protein with both endonuclease and reverse transcriptase
activities from the ORF2 region ( Figure 2 ). Full-length copies bring with them their own
promoter (located in the 5’ untranslated region) that can be used after integration in a
permissive region of the genome.

The mechanism of retrotransposition is depicted in Figure 3 . A LINE element will be
transcribed in the nucleus, and the mRNA will be processed and exported to the
cytoplam to be translated. After translation of the two encoded proteins, the LINE-1 RNA
assembles with these proteins and moves to the nucleus. To integrate into genomic
DNA, the LINE-1 endonuclease cuts a DNA duplex on one strand, leaving a free 3’ OH
group that serves as a primer for reverse transcription from the 3’ end of the LINE RNA.
The endonuclease’s preferred cleavage site is TTTT↓A A ; hence the preference for
integrating into AT-rich regions. During integration, the reverse transcription often fails
to proceed to the 5’ end, resulting in truncated, nonfunctional insertions. Accordingly,
only about 1 in 100 copies are full length, and most LINE-derived repeats are short (the
average size for all LINE-1 copies is 900 bp).
The LINE-1 machinery is responsible for reverse transcription of all retroelements in
the genome, including nonautonomous SINEs and SVA repeats, and also integrate in the
genome copies of mRNA transcripts (these are known as processed pseudogenes and
retrogenes). Of the 6000 or so full-length LINE-1 sequences in the human genome,
about 60–100 are still capable of transposing, and they occasionally cause disease as a
result of aberrant gene expression after insertion.
Alu repeats
The human Alu repeat is the most abundant sequence in the human genome. The
full-length repeat is about 280 bp long and consists of two tandem repeats, each about
120 bp in length followed by an A-rich or A n /T n sequence (see Figure 4 ). Monomers,
containing only one of the two tandem repeats, and various truncated versions of
dimers and monomers are also common, giving a genome-wide average of 230 bp. Alu
repeats are primate specific, but subfamilies of different evolutionary ages can be
identified, of which the Y and S subfamilies contain the most mobile Alu sequences.
[PDF p. 16]
6
Alu repeats have a relatively high GC content and, although dispersed mainly throughout
the euchromatic regions of the genome, are preferentially located in the GC-rich and gene-rich
light chromosome bands, in striking contrast to the preferential location of LINEs in AT-rich
DNA and dark chromosome bands. When located within genes, Alu repeats are, like LINE-1
elements, almost always confined to introns and the untranslated regions.
Like other mammalian SINEs, Alu repeats originated from cDNA copies of small RNAs
        transcribed by RNA polymerase III that reintegrated into germ-line DNA. Genes transcribed by RNA

polymerase III often have internal promoters, and so the cDNA copies of transcripts carry with
them their own promoter sequences that can activate transcription of the cDNA copy in a permissive
chromatin location. Both the Alu repeat and the mouse B1 repeat originated independently from
cDNA copies of 7SL RNA, the short RNA that is a component of the signal recognition particle, using a
retrotransposition mechanism. Some other SINEs, such as MIR elements and the mouse B2 repeat, are
known to be retrotransposed copies of tRNA sequences.

repeats are usually more than 2 kb in length and have both an Alu-like sequence and a 3′ HERV fragment (called SINE-R), separated by a VNTR
sequence. They may often be transcribed from promoters in flanking DNA sequence. VNTR, variable number of tandem repeats.

SVA repeats
SVA repeats are composite repeats, having both an Alu-like sequence and a truncated HERV
component (the 3’ end of the env gene plus an LTR) that was originally named SINE-R. These two
elements are separated by a region with a variable number of tandem copies (VNTR) of a 35–50 bp
sequence (the name SVA is short for SINE-R–VNTR–Alu). The Alu sequence is preceded by tandem
CCCTCT repeats, and the HERV component is followed by an (A/T)n tail, called a poly(A) sequence
( Figure 4 ).
The double-edged nature of transposons: both friends and foes
Transposons have been crucially important in genome evolution, and copies of transposons
have been valuable sources of novel functional sequences, including not just new regulatory
sequences, but also new exons, and, very occasionally, even new genes. Transposon repeats may also
assist gene and exon duplication (which are also important in genome evolution) by stabilizing local
mispairing of chromatids, and they can alter expression of host genes in different ways, such as by
offering new regulatory sequences or new splice sites. Retrotransposons also actively transpose during
neurogenesis, creating an additional level of genetic diversity that may be valuable in promoting
neuron plasticity.
While transposons offer many advantages, active transposons pose a threat to the genome.
Effectively, they are mutagens and potentially harmful, and excessive mobilization of transposons can
result in genomic chaos. To contain this threat, the first line of defense is epigenetic silencing: t he
transcription of active retrotransposons is down-regulated by setting epigenetic marks to alter the
chromatin state (typical epigenetic marks are DNA methylation and histone modifications).
Even so, some retrotransposons are still active in the germ-line of humans, meaning that some
people are born with a new copy in a new new location compared to the genomes of their parents.
Studies in families have revealed that 1 in 20 healthy newborns carry a novel retrotransposition of a
AluY element (the most active class of retrotransposons in humans). The second most active mobile
elements in human genomes are LINE-1 and SVA repeats, with an average activity of one new
germline insertion per 100-200 births.

LECTURE 7.6 GENES (protein-coding and non-coding)
A major motivation of the Human Genome Project (HGP) was to define a human gene catalog. But many years
after the completion of the project in 2003, we still do not know how many genes there are in the human genome!
Much of this uncertainty concerns identifying RNA genes, but even in the case of protein-coding genes, getting an
accurate number has not been straightforward.
At the time of the HGP, attempts to build a human gene catalog focused on identifying protein-coding genes,
which were widely assumed to make the overwhelming genetic contribution to dictating how our cells work. RNA
genes, by contrast, were viewed primarily as making ubiquitous accessory molecules that assisted in a general way
to guide the expression of protein-coding genes (for example, small nucleolar RNAs, tRNAs, small RNAs
responsible for splicing, etc). And although some longer noncoding RNAs had long been known to be more
specific gene regulators, they were widely regarded at the time as quirky exceptions.
Further complications stem from how we classify genes. A few genes, for example, seem to make both coding
transcripts (mRNA) and also transcripts that make a functional non-coding RNA. Additionally, genes originally
classified as making long non-coding RNAs have subsequently been found to have very short, central coding
DNA sequences that make micropeptides . The latest annotation of the human genome can be found in https://
www.gencodegenes.org/human/stats.html. Table 1 below shows the numbers of protein-coding and non-coding
genes, pseudogenes and their transcripts in the assembly called GRCh38.p14 (from 2026):
It is worth noting a few interesting things in this catalog. First, non-conding RNA genes are now more abundant
than protein-coding genes (as opposed to initial expectations). In fact, in this assembly we can see almost twice
the number of long ncRNA genes as protein-coding genes. Together with small ncRNA genes and with
pseudogenes, today we accept that our genome contains about 80,000 genes.
Another interesting fact that can be derived from this table is the much greater number of transcripts (that is,
functional RNAs) derived from these 80,000 genes. In the case of protein-coding genes, we observe an average of
ten distinct mRNAs from each gene (due to alternative splicing, as we will discuss later). Long ncRNA genes, on
the other hand, have fewer transcripts per gene, with an average of five (190,000 transcripts from 36,000 long noncoding genes).

The human genome contains about 20,000 protein-coding genes
When the first draft human genome sequences began to be studied, the initial analyses primarily focused on
looking for protein-coding genes . At least, protein-coding genes are comparatively easy to identify in a genome
sequence: there is an open reading frame, the predicted protein sequence has frequently been quite highly
conserved during evolution, and the reading frame is normally as long, or almost as long, in closely related species.
Preliminary analyses of draft human genome sequences reported in 2001 suggested about 30,000 (proteincoding) genes. Most were gene predictions made without any supportive experimental evidence and heavily reliant
on identification of sizeable open reading frames. The original gene number was recognized to be inflated when the
genome sequences of other mammals were obtained: evolutionary comparisons failed to identify counterparts of
many predicted human genes in the mouse and dog genomes. Analyses of the human genome GRChp38.p14
reference sequence suggests that there are around 20,000 human protein-coding genes.

The first and the last exon contain the UnTranslated Regions (UTR), shown in orange), which are the part of the
transcript that is not translated because it is upstream of the initiation codon (the 5’-UTR) or after the STOP codon

There are numerous different human non-coding RNAs
In the post-genome era, there has been a major re-evaluation of the importance of RNA genes. Currently, despite
decades of not seriously investigating RNA genes, the number of recognized RNA genes is already on a par with the
number of protein-coding genes. And it is now clear that RNA genes perform a wide variety of functional roles, with
many RNAs working as regulators of specific target genes.
Short and long noncoding RNA
It has become a convention to divide RNA genes into two classes, according to whether their mature RNA products are
up to 200 nucleotides in length (short noncoding RNA) or over 200 nucleotides in length, when the RNA is described as
a long noncoding RNA ( lncRNA ). This extremely arbitrary division was designed simply as a way of separating most of
the long-familiar ubiquitous RNAs (which were thought to assist in general mechanisms used to express genes) from
long RNAs that acted as regulators of specific target genes. In many ways this is a very unsatisfactory separation. First,
many important regulatory RNAs are now known to be small noncoding RNAs. Additionally, this convention would
split the ribosomal RNAs into two classes, identifying the longer ribosomal RNAs (cytoplasmic 28S and 18S rRNA;
mitochondrial 16S and 12S rRNA) as long noncoding RNAs, while classifying the cytoplasmic 5.8S and 5S rRNAs as
short noncoding RNAs. If we disregard rRNAs for the moment, the compositions of the two classes are listed below.


Short noncoding RNA. There are seven major subfamilies ( Table 2 ). Four are well-understood classes of ubiquitous RNAs;
three are recently discovered classes of tiny regulatory RNAs. MicroRNAs are often tissue-specific and/or developmental
stage-specific regulators; they work by binding to short recognition sequences in RNA transcripts produced by the target
genes. piRNAs (PiWi protein- interacting RNAs) and endogenous siRNAs (short interfering RNAs) are important in germline cells as part of genome defense mechanisms.


Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA). The interest in lncRNAs is predominantly because this non-coding RNA class contains
many important regulatory RNAs. Some lncRNAs work in the nucleus to regulate target genes, either through chromatin
modification (epigenetic regulation), or through transcriptional regulation (often as natural antisense RNA transcripts).
Many lncRNAs resemble mRNAs in having 5’ caps and 3’ poly(A) tails, but others do not.

Human genes show enormous variation in size and internal organization
Genes in simple organisms such as bacteria are comparatively similar in size and are usually very short (typically
about 1 kb long). The genes of complex eukaryotes, however, can show huge size variation. As measured by the
distance from the beginning of the first exon to the end of the last exon, the longest human protein-coding gene is
CNTNAP2, which at 2.305 Mb just pips the dystrophin gene, the previous record holder at 2.242 Mb. Using the
same definition of gene len gth, the mean length of a huma n protein-coding gene is 64.9 kb (but the median length
is 26.0 kb), but there is enormous diversity as shown in Table 3 . Although there is generally a direct correlation
between gene and product sizes, there are some striking anomalies. For example, the 2.24 Mb dystrophin gene, 50
times the length of the apolipoprotein B gene, makes a protein that is almost 900 amino acids smaller than
apolipoprotein B.
For human protein-coding genes, the mean exon size is 268 nucleotides (but median size is 129 nucleotides),
with an average of seven to nine exons per gene . As genes get larger, exon size remains fairly constant. Note,
however, that the terminal exon can occasionally be very long; if we discount the first and last exons (which quite
often are mostly untranslated sequence), the mean length of an internal exon in a human protein-coding gene
is 147 nucleotides (median length 121 nucleotides). Unlike exons, the introns of human protein-coding genes
vary enormously in size (from a few nucleotides to over 100,000 nucleotides long), and intron size generally
correlates with gene length (but there are some notable exceptions, see Table 3 ).
Human protein-coding genes generally contain introns, but a small minority lack introns and are generally
small genes (see the footnote to Table 3 for some examples). For those that do possess introns, there is an inverse
correlation between gene size and fraction of coding DNA because large genes tend to have large introns while
exons tend to be more uniform in size. Because transcribing long introns is costly in both energy and time (16
hours are needed to transcribe the 2.24 Mb dystrophin gene), very highly expressed genes often have short
introns, or no introns at all.
Size and intron content of RNA genes
Many RNA genes have been identified very recently, and statistics on RNA gene size and intron content are
being accumulated. Genes encoding lncRNAs can be tens of kilobases long and often contain introns (the
exons of these genes show a mean length of 683 nucleotides, but a median length of 129 nucleotides). At the
other end of the scale are tiny RNA genes, including those specifying miRNAs that often lack introns. However,
remember that here is some uncertainty as to how to define an RNA gene, and these numbers can change in the
future.

Different origins for duplicated genes in the human genome
Gene duplication has been an important driver in the evolution of functional complexity and the origin of
increasingly complex organisms. As a result, duplicated genes (and duplicated segments of coding sequence)
are a common feature of animal genomes, especially large vertebrate genomes. In the human genome, the
resulting multigene families have from two to many hundreds of gene copies that may be clustered together in
one subchromosomal location, or dispersed over several chromosomal locations, we consider different types of
gene-family organization below.
Segmental duplication
More than 5% of the euchromatic portion of the human genome is accounted for by 400 large blocks of
duplicated DNA where the sequence identity between the DNA copies is very high (often more than 95%
identity). The very high degree of sequence identity across such long sequences is the result of evolutionarily
recent DNA duplication, occurring within the past 40 million years of primate evolution, and this type of recent
duplication is often described as segmental duplication . It includes both intrachromosomal duplications (see
Figure 2 for an example) and also interchromosomal duplications. Segmental duplications are important
contributors to copy number variation and to chromosomal rearrangements leading to disease and rapid gene
innovation.

Functionally inactive copies of gene sequences
Gene duplication is driven by evolutionary pressure to develop specialized functions. We owe our
developed sense of smell to having a family of close to 1000 olfactory receptor genes that collectively provide a
large range of different olfactory receptor proteins. However, duplication is not always successful in producing
additional functional genes. Some duplicated genes degenerate and become non-functional gene copies called
pseudogenes (in the case of the olfactory receptor gene family, for example, the majority of the sequences are
inactive, see Box 1 for an overview of human pseudogenes).

LECTURE 7.7 GENETIC VARIATION
Genetic variation is caused by changes to the base sequence. As described below, there are different
variant classes, but all sequence changes can be classified within two broad categories.


Changes that do not affect the DNA content. Here the number of nucleotides is unchanged. Quite
often a single nucleotide is replaced by a different nucleotide. ~~More rarely, multiple nucleotides at
a time may be sent to a new location (by chromosome breakage and rejoining) without net loss or
gain of DNA content. The great majority of the latter events are balanced translocations and
inversions; they often have no effect on the phenotype, but can be harmful if the change significantly
alters the expression of a gene at, or close to, a chromosome breakpoint.


Changes in copy number of a nucleotide or DNA sequence. Simple deletion/insertion of a unique
sequence can change the haploid copy number from, respectively, 1 to 0 or 0 to 1. Or there may be
a change in copy number of a repeated DNA sequence, resulting in fewer or more copies of that
sequence. The result is a net loss or gain of a DNA sequence that may be large or small . At one
extreme are copy number changes resulting from abnormal chromosome segregation, producing
fewer or more chromosomes than normal, and therefore a change in the copy number of whole
nuclear DNA molecules. They are almost always harmful: many result in spontaneous abortion,
and some give rise to developmental syndromes. At the other end of the scale is deletion or
insertion of a single nucleotide. In between are copy number changes for sequences that range in
size from specific short oligonucleotide sequences to DNA segments hundreds of kilobases long.


DNA variants, polymorphisms, and population genomics
Alternative forms of DNA produced by mutation are generally known as DNA variants . In the past, it was
traditional to describe a common DNA variant, with a population frequency > 0.01 (1%), as a polymorphism ;
DNA variants with frequencies < 0.01 were traditionally described as rare variants . The 0.01 cut-off was an
arbitrary one, however (it was initially proposed in order to exclude recurrent mutation). In the HapMap
project, which produced detailed genetic maps based on polymorphisms in which a single nucleotide is
changed ( a single nucleotide polymorphism or SNP [pronounced “snip”]), a common SNP was defined as a
SNP where the variant had a frequency > 0.05. The general use of the term polymorphism is now declining,
partly because of the arbitrary nature of the 0.01 or 0.05 cut-offs, and partly because of ambiguity in how the
term is used. In medical disciplines, for example, polymorphism is often used to denote any sequence
variation that does not cause disease, whereas mutation is used to describe a disease-causing sequence
variant. In modern times, the term polymorphism is largely avoided in population genomics projects;
instead, DNA variants are often classified as: common (frequency > 5%); low frequency (from 1% to 5%);
and rare (< 1%) . The preference now, for example, is to describe a change to a single nucleotide as a single
nucleotide variant (SNV) .
Small-scale genetic variation and structural variation
The vast majority of DNA changes are errors of DNA replication and repair, and typically affect one or a
very small number of nucleotides (>99.9% of the DNA changes are accounted for by base substitutions and
small-scale insertions and deletions).
Because of the predominance of small-scale mutations, the study of human genetic variation was largely
focused on small-scale (<50 bp) variation until quite recently. However, additional moderate- and largescale DNA changes (that include specific types of DNA breakage and rejoining mechanisms) are also highly
significant. Such structural variation can involve very large changes, and although structural variants are
infrequent, significantly more nucleotides across the genome are altered as a result of structural variation
than as a result of small-scale mutations.
The borderline between small-scale genetic variation and structural variation is an arbitrary one. In the past,
structural variation used to be applied to sequences that were one kilobase or longer, but the modern tendency
has been to include smaller variants. In the 1000 Genomes Project, for example, changes affecting 1–50
nucleotides were classified as small-scale, and anything larger than 50 bp was classified as structural variation
(because commonly used massively parallel DNA sequencing methods used to produce quite short sequences,
and were often not suited to detecting deletions/insertions of greater than 50 nucleotides).
[PDF p. 26]
2
Although SNVs and short indels together account for more than 99.9% of the number of genetic variants, the
great majority of that variation falls outside coding DNA and other functionally important sequences, and is
thought to represent neutral mutations.
Structural variants account for just 0.05% of the variants, but some of them, notably many individual CNVs
and large deletions, are very large-scale changes. As a result they involve considerably more nucleotides in the
genome, at least nearly twice as many, than do small-scale changes ( Table 1 ). Structural variation is also more
highly correlated with functional DNA sequences than is small-scale mutation, and structural variants
contribute very significantly to altered gene expression and disease.
The overall data suggest that if we compare one haploid human genome against another, differences might be
expected, on average, at 4–5/1000 nucleotide sites (at least for the sampled DNA sequences, which are
predominantly from euchromatin: a total of ~4.9 Mb of small-scale changes plus 8.7 Mb of structural variation
superimposed on the 3000 Mb euchromatic portion of the reference genome sequence = 13.6 Mb/3000 Mb).

sequences of some variants indicate that they are related by a combination of insertion and deletion events at the
same position, such as that shown in Figure 1 .
The type of variation shown in Figure 1C has been described as an indel (or delins ) but the term indel has also
been widely used in a much broader sense to include all types of DNA change that cause a size change at a specific
position: insertions, duplications, deletions, and compound insertion/deletion. In population genome sequencing
projects, such as the 1000 Genomes Project, the term indel is reserved for small insertion/deletion events involving 1–50
nucleotides (the size restriction is sometimes emphasized by using the term short indel).
Short tandem repeat variants/polymorphisms (also known as microsatellites ) vary in size by small numbers of
nucleotides, and so although they vary in the copy number of repeats, they are classified as indels. In genome
sequencing projects, the term copy number variant ( CNV ) is often now reserved for variants that differ in copy
number of larger (>50 bp) repeat sequences (see Figure 1 ), and is included as a component of structural variation, as
described in the next section.

Single Nucleotide Variants (SNVs)
The 1000 Genomes Project data show that genetic variation in 2504 individuals from 26 different populations ranges from
approximately 4.1 million to 5.0 million variant sites, with significant variation between populations. In particular,
African populations show considerably greater genetic diversity than all other populations, consistent with the out-ofAfrica model of human origins. Because of recent population admixture, individual populations from Central and South
America also show elevated within-population genetic diversity that roughly correlates with the degree of recent African
ancestry ( Figure 2 ).

SNPs are often categorized as common (MAF>0.05), low-frequency (MAF 0.05–0.01), and rare (MAF<0.01). As
more human samples are sequenced, including less common variants, a more complete picture of variation is
emerging. The 1000 Genomes Project and other population genomics projects are providing a detailed account
of the full extent of sequence variation between and within populations. One use of these data is to construct
population-specific reference sequences.
STRUCTURAL VARIANTS AND GENOMIC DISORDERS
The variation in copy number can take different forms. One class involves large-scale insertions and
deletions so that DNA variants either lack a specific sequence (0 copies) or possess that sequence (1 copy, see
Figure 6B, part [i]). Other forms result from tandem duplication of sequences greater than 50 nucleotides in length
( Figure 6B, part [ii]) that may be complicated by subsequent insertion and/or inversion events. Variants arising in
this way are described as copy number variants ( CNVs ) and quite often have multiple alleles. In some CNVs
the DNA sequence that varies in copy number can include part of a gene sequence or regulatory sequences and
sometimes multiple genes. As a result, some CNVs are important contributors to disease, as described below,
but many common CNVs do not affect gene function and are not implicated in disease.
As we have seen above, structural variation includes large deletions, insertions and CNVs, which by definition
come in different number of copies in different individuals, and are collectively known as Structural Variants
(SVs) . These variants range in size from a few kilobases to a few megabases, so they are too small to be seen
under the microscope. In the era of rapid whole-genome sequencing it has also come to include smaller
changes, typically ones that involve more than 50 nucleotides at a time. Chromosomal abnormalities too small
to be seen under the microscope were long suspected to be the cause of a number of unexplained recurrent
syndromes and also of many individual cases in which a patient had a unique pattern of abnormalities. A
deletion or duplication of 3 Mb of DNA would be invisible under the microscope on a standard karyotype, but
could involve wrong dosage of dozens of genes. An example of these genomic disorders are microdeletion
syndromes such as DiGeorge Syndrome due to microdeletions in chromosome 22.

Structural variation: inversions, translocations, large-scale
insertions and deletions, and copy number variants
In balanced structural variation, the DNA variants have the same DNA content but differ in that some
DNA sequences are located in different positions within the genome. Here the variants are formed when DNA
molecules sustain double-strand breaks and the resulting fragments are incorrectly rejoined, but without loss
or gain of DNA. There are two significant mechanisms: in inversions, two double-strand breaks on a DNA
molecule release a central fragment that rotates through 180° before being rejoined to the end fragments;
alternatively, translocations occur when two different chromosomal DNA molecules each receive a doublestrand break and exchange fragments without any change in DNA content ( Figure 6A ). Even if there is no loss or
gain of genetic material, inversions can sometimes lead to disease, as in the case of Hemophilia A (in which 45%
of the cases are due to an inversion in the gene of Factor VIII in the X chromosome).

In population studies, SVs were also found in healthy controls . In fact, a typical “normal” genome has
around 2,000 SVs compared to the reference (that is about 20 Mb of sequence, with the average size of a SV
being 10 kb). This was unexpected: it had been commonly assumed that structural variants involving
significant loss or gain of material would normally be pathogenic. Today, we have a deep catalog of SVs in
human genomes, many of which are polymorphic (with different number of copies in different people).
These are known as Copy Number Variants (CNVs), Copy Number Polymorphisms (CNPs) or Low-Copy
number Repeats (LCRs) . In a recent study, researchers found that these variants result in about 100
protein-coding genes homozygously deleted in healthy individuals, suggesting that these genes would be
non-essential. These genes are usually members of large gene-families, and they may be redundant or they
may have late-onset phenotypic effects that do not substantially reduce the fitness of the individual.

Lecture 7.8 DNA damage and repair
In addition to the genetic variation that we inherit from our parents, DNA changes occur in the DNA of
our cells throughout life. This post-zygotic genetic variation includes changes to the DNA of both somatic
cells and germ-line cells: each of us, therefore, carries cells with different genomes. Although most postzygotic DNA changes occur in a rather random fashion, some do not. In some cells, notably maturing B
and T lymphocytes, certain DNA rearrangements occur in nonrandom, and quite defined, ways that are
functionally important.
Underlying genetic variation are changes in DNA sequences. Traditionally, the term mutation has
been used in two ways. It can describe an event or process that produces either a change in the base
sequence or in the copy number of a DNA sequence, or it can describe the outcome of that process, the
altered DNA sequence.
As events, mutations can occur at a wide variety of levels, and can have different consequences. The
altered DNA may contribute to a normal phenotype (such as height) or to a disease phenotype. Very rarely,
a mutation has some beneficial effect that produces an altered phenotype conferring a competitive
advantage over other phenotypes in the population. The great majority of mutations, however, are neutral :
they have no discernible effect on the phenotype. As a result, there has been an increasing trend toward using
the more neutral term DNA variant instead of mutation to describe, in a general way, a DNA change
produced by mutation. But DNA variants associated with an altered phenotype continue to be widely
described as mutations.
DNA variants originate as a result of changes in our DNA that have not been corrected by cellular DNA
repair systems. The DNA changes are occasionally induced by radiation and chemicals in our
environment, but the great majority arise from endogenous sources: spontaneous errors in normal
cellular mechanisms regulating chromosome segregation, recombination, DNA replication, and DNA
repair, plus spontaneous chemical damage to DNA.
Mutations are unavoidable . They may have adverse effects on individual organisms, causing aging and
underlying many human diseases. But they also provide the raw fuel for natural selection of beneficial
adaptations that allow evolutionary innovation and, ultimately, the origin of new species.
Natural errors in various processes that affect chromosome and DNA function,  chromosome segregation,
recombination, and DNA replication, are important contributors to genetic variation. That happens
because no cellular function can occur with 100% efficiency, mistakes happen. Endogenous errors in the
above processes may often not have harmful consequences, but some of them make important
contributions to disease.
Each time the DNA of a human diploid cell replicates, six billion nucleotides need to be inserted in the
correct order in the newly synthesized DNA molecules. No enzyme is 100% efficient, and DNA polymerases will
occasionally make mistakes, inserting the wrong nucleotide to produce mispaired bases (base mismatches ).
The likelihood of such an error simply reflects the relative binding energies of correctly paired bases and
mispaired bases. In the great majority of cases, the errors are quickly corrected by the DNA polymerase itself.
The major DNA polymerases engaged in replicating our DNA have an intrinsic 3’ → 5’ exonuclease activity
with a proofreading function. If, by error, the wrong base is inserted, the 3’→ 5’ exonuclease is activated and
degrades the newly synthesized DNA strand from its 3’ end, removing the wrongly inserted nucleotide and a
short stretch before it. Then the DNA polymerase resumes synthesis again. If mispaired bases are not
eliminated by the DNA polymerase, a DNA mismatch repair system is activated (as described below).
Although the vast majority of DNA changes caused by DNA replication errors are identified and
corrected, some persist. That happens because although we have many very effective DNA repair
pathways, inevitably DNA repair is also not 100% effective, and unrepaired changes in DNA sequence are an
important source of mutations. However, the great majority of the mutations introduced in this way do not
cause disease: almost 99% of the genome is noncoding DNA, many mutations in coding DNA do not change
an amino acid, and functional noncoding DNA sequences (such as those specifying non-coding RNAs) can
often tolerate many kinds of sequence change without compromising the function of the sequence.

ENDOGENOUS AND EXOGENOUS SOURCES CAN CAUSE DAMAGE
TO DNA BY ALTERING ITS CHEMICAL STRUCTURE
DNA is a comparatively stable molecule, but nevertheless there are constant threats to its integrity,
causing breakage of covalent bonds within DNA or inappropriate bonding of chemicals to DNA. Most of
the damage originates spontaneously within cells (normal cellular metabolism generates some chemicals
that are harmful to cells). A minority of the damage is induced by external sources. Figure 3 summarizes
the different types of damage, the main mechanisms used to repair them, and the cellular decisions taken
to deal with the outcome of DNA repair.

Chemical damage to DNA can involve cleavage of covalent bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA
causing single-strand or double-strand breaks ( Figure 4A ). Alternatively, bases are deleted (by cleavage of the
N -glycosidic bond connecting a base to a sugar; Figure 4B ), or they are chemically modified in some way.
Many base modifications involve replacing certain groups on bases or adding methyl or larger alkyl
groups or other large chemicals ( Figure 4C ). Sometimes covalent bonds form between two bases ( base
cross-linking ) that may be on the same strand ( Figure 4D, part [i]) or on complementary DNA strands
( Figure 4D, part [ii]). Chemically modified bases may block DNA or RNA polymerases, causing base mispairing and (if not repaired) mutations.

Endogenous chemical damage to DNA
Most of the chemical damage to our DNA arises spontaneously and is unavoidable. Every
day, under normal conditions, around 20,000–100,000 lesions are generated in the DNA of
each of our nucleated cells. Three major types of chemical change occur, as listed
below. Hydrolytic and oxidative damage are particularly significant, breaking various
covalent bonds in the nucleotides of DNA ( Figure 5 ).

Hydrolytic damage . Hydrolysis is inevitable in the aqueous environment of cells. It can disrupt
bonds that hold bases to sugars, cleaving the base from the sugar to produce an abasic site (see
Figure 4B ); loss of purine bases (depurination) is particularly common. Hydrolysis also strips
amino groups from some bases (deamination), leaving a carbonyl (C=O) group. Cytosines are
often deaminated to give uracil, which base-pairs with adenine; adenine is occasionally
deaminated to produce hypoxanthine, which effectively behaves like guanine by base-pairing
with cytosine.

Oxidative damage . Normal cellular metabolism generates some strongly elec trophilic (and,
therefore, highly reactive) molecules or ions. The most significant are reactive oxygen species
( ROS ) formed by the incomplete one-electron reduction of oxygen, including superoxide anions
(O 2− ), hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ), and hydroxyl radicals (OH·). ROS are generated in different

cellular locations and play important roles in certain intercellular and intracellular signaling
pathways, but they mostly originate in mitochondria (where electrons can prematurely reduce
oxygen). Endogenous ROS attack covalent bonds in sugars, causing damage to the sugar–
phosphate backbone of DNA. They also attack DNA bases, especially purines (see Figure 5 ), and
many derivatives are produced from each base. Some of the base derivatives are highly mutagenic,
such as 7,8-dihydro-8-oxoguanine (also called 8-oxoguanine or 8-hydroxyguanine), which basepairs with adenine; others are not mutagenic but nevertheless block DNA and RNA
polymerases (see Figure 4C, parts [i] and [ii]).

Aberrant DNA methylation. Many cytosines in our DNA are methylated by methyltransferases. Cells also use S -adenosylmethionine (SAM) as a methyl donor in a non-enzymatic
reaction to methylate different types of molecule, but sometimes SAM can inappropriately methylate
DNA to produce harmful bases. Each day about 300–600 adenosines in each nucleated cell are
converted to 3-methyladenosine, a cytotoxic base that distorts the double helix, disrupting crucial
DNA–protein interactions.
