Disease-related phenotypes in carriers
Although carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder are considered
asymptomatic, they may nevertheless express some disease-related trait
that can distinguish them from the normal population. Take sickle-cell
disease (OMIM 603903), for example. Affected individuals are homozygous
for a β -globin mutation and produce an abnormal hemoglobin, HbS, that
causes red blood cells to adopt a rigid, crescent (or sickle) shape. The sickle
cells have a shorter life span that leads to anemia, and they can block small
blood vessels, causing hypoxic tissue damage.
Carriers of the sickle-cell mutation are not quite asymptomatic. The
sickle-cell allele produces a mutant β -globin that is co-dominantly
expressed with the normal β -globin, and heterozygotes can have mild
anemia (sickle-cell trait). However, under intense, stressful conditions
such as exhaustion, hypoxia (at high altitudes), and/or severe infection,
sickling may occur in heterozygotes and result in some of the
complications associated with sickle-cell disease. Note that whereas sicklecell disease is recessively inherited, the sickle-cell trait is expressed in the
heterozygote and is therefore a dominant trait.

x-linked inheritance and x-chromosome inactivation
Before we go on to consider X-linked inheritance, we need to take account of mechanisms that compensate for the
variable number of sex chromosomes in humans (and other mammals): females have two X chromosomes but
males have one X and one Y.
Having different numbers of chromosomes usually has severe, often lethal
consequences, the loss of just one of our 46 chromosomes is lethal except for
45,X (Turner syndrome), and having an extra chromosome is usually lethal or
results in a developmental syndrome such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).
This happens because of problems with gene dosage : for some of our genes,
the amount of gene product made must be tightly controlled (having one or
three copies of these genes can be harmful because too little or too much
product is made).
The sex difference regarding the Y chromosome is minimized by the conspicuous lack of genes on the Y. Most of the very few genes on the Y
chromosome have male-specific functions, or they have an equivalent gene
copy on the X (these X–Y gene pairs are largely concentrated at the tips of the
sex chromosomes in the pseudoautosomal regions).
x-chromosome inactivation
Unlike the Y chromosome, the human X chromosome has many hun-dreds of
important genes. To compensate for having different numbers of X
chromosomes in males and females, a special mechanism is needed to
silence genes on one of the two X chromosomes in each female cell ( X-
inactivation ). That is to say, men are constitutionally hemizygous for most
genes on the X chromosome, and women are functionally hemizygous for the
same genes.
The X-inactivation mechanism is initiated after a cellular mechanism counts
the number of X chromosomes in each cell of the early embryo. If the number
of X chromosomes is two (or more), all except one of the multiple X
chromosomes is inactivated. Each such X chromosome is induced to form a
highly condensed chromosome that is mostly tran-scriptionally inactive,
known as a Barr body ( Figure 4 ). Note that some genes, including genes in
the pseudoautosomal regions, escape inactivation.

In humans the initial decision to inactivate one of the two X chromosomes is
randomly made in the preimplantation embryo, beginning at around the
eight-cell stage; some cells inactivate the paternal X and the remainder
inactivate the maternal X. Once a cell has chosen which X to inactivate in the
early embryo, that pattern of X-inactivation is continued in all descendant
cells. Thus, a female who is heterozygous at a disease locus will be a genetic
mosaic, containing cell clones in which the normal allele is expressed and
clones in which the mutant allele is expressed. As described below, this has
implications for the female phenotype in X-linked disorders.
X-linked recessive inheritance
In X-linked recessive disorders, affected individuals are mostly male, and
affected males are usually born to unaffected parents. The mother of an
affected male is quite often a carrier (and clearly so if she has affected male
relatives). A distinguishing feature is that there is no male-to-male
transmission because males pass a Y chromosome to sons ( Figure 5A ).
However, a pedigree may appear to show male-to-male transmission when an
affected man (with a condition such as hemophilia, for example) and a carrier
woman produce an affected son ( Figure 5B ). The same parents could each
potentially transmit a mutant X to produce an affected daughter.

In X-linked recessive disorders, female carriers with a single mutant allele can occasionally be quite
severely affected and are known as manifesting heterozygotes. Because of X-inactivation, female carriers of
an X-linked mutation are mosaics : some of their cells have the normal X chromosome inactivated and other
cells have the mutant X inactivated, as seen most readily in skin disorders. Manifesting heterozygotes can
occur by chance: most cells of a tissue that is critically important in disease development have an
inactivated X carrying the normal allele.
Manifesting heterozygotes can occasionally occur because of nonrandom X-inactivation . That can
happen when there is some advantage in inactivating the normal X chromosome instead of the mutant X
chromosome. For example, an X-linked disorder may manifest in a woman who has an X-autosome
translocation in which the breakpoint on the X is the cause of the disorder. If the X-autosome translocation
chromosome were to be inactivated, neighboring autosomal genes would also be silenced, causing gene
dosage problems and so the normal X is preferentially inactivated. Skewing of X-inactivation can often work
in the other direction: some female carriers are asymptomatic because of nonrandom inactivation of the
mutant X chromosome.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is one of the most common X-linked recessive disorders, affecting about
1 in 5,000 newborn males worldwide. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, that provides instructions
for making a protein called dystrophin . This protein is located primarily in skeletal and cardiac muscle,
where it helps stabilize and protect muscle fibers. Dystrophin may also play a role in chemical signaling
within cells.
Mutations in the DMD gene alter the structure or function of dystrophin or prevent any functional
dystrophin from being produced. Muscle cells without enough of this protein become damaged as muscles
repeatedly contract and relax with use. The damaged fibers weaken and die over time, leading to the
muscle weakness and heart problems characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophiy. Females who carry
a DMD gene mutation also have an increased risk of developing heart abnormalities including
cardiomyopathy.

x-linked dominant inheritance
As in autosomal dominant disorders, affected individuals with an Xlinked dominant disorder can be of either sex, and usually at least one
parent is affected. However, there are significantly more affected
females than affected males, and affected females typically have
milder (but more variable) expression than affected males.
The excess of affected females arises because there is no male-to
male transmission of the disorder. All children born to an affected
mother (and an unaffected father) have a 50% chance of being
affected, but an affected father with a single X chromosome will
consistently have unaf-fected sons (they do not inherit his X
chromosome), but his daughters will always be at risk because they
will always inherit his affected X ( Figure 6A gives an example
pedigree).
The milder phenotype seen in affected females is a result of
X-inactivation , the mutant allele is located on an inactivated X in a
proportion of their cells. For certain X-linked dominant disorders,
virtually all affected individuals are female: the phenotype is so
severe in males that they die in the prenatal period, but the
milder phenotype of affected females allows them to survive and
reproduce. We illustrate this with the example of incontinentia
pigmenti in Figure 6B .

Matrilineal inheritance for mitochondrial DNA disorders
The mitochondrial genome is a small (16.5 kb) circular genome that has 37 genes. It is much more prone to
mutation than nuclear DNA, partly because of the action of reactive oxygen species (the mitochondrion is a
major source of reactive oxygen species in the cell). As a result, mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) are
a significant cause of human genetic disease. Tissues that have a high energy requirement, such as muscle
and brain, are primarily affected in mtDNA disorders.
Individuals with a mitochondrial DNA disorder can be of either sex, but affected males do not transmit the
condition to any of their children . The sperm does contribute mtDNA to the zygote, but the paternal
mtDNA is destroyed in the very early embryo (after being tagged by ubiquitin), and a father’s mtDNA
sequence variants are not observed in his children. That is, inheritance occurs exclusively through the
mother ( matrilineal inheritance). An additional, common feature of mitochondrial DNA disorders is that the
phenotype is highly variable within families ( Figure 7 ).

Variable heteroplasmy and clinical variability
Each cell contains multiple mitochondria, and there are often several hundred to thousands of mtDNA copies per
cell. In some affected persons every mtDNA molecule carries the causative mutation ( homoplasmy ), but affected
individuals frequently have cells with a mixed population of normal and mutant mtDNAs ( heteroplasmy ). The
clinical features depend mostly on the proportion of mutant to normal mtDNA molecules in the cells of tissues with
high energy requirements.
Although a human egg cell is haploid for nuclear DNA, it contains more than 100,000 mtDNA molecules. A
heteroplasmic mother can give rise to children who differ widely from her and from each other in the ratio of
mutant to normal mtDNA molecules in their tissues ( variable heteroplasmy ). As a result, there can be very
significant clinical variability between affected members of the same family.
To explain rapid shifts in heteroplasmy that occur over only one generation, the mitochondrial genetic
bottleneck hypothesis envisages that, during early development, germ-line cells pass through a bottleneck stage in
which they contain very few mtDNA molecules. By chance, germ-line cells at this stage may have a much higher
or much lower proportion of mutant mtDNA molecules than the somatic cells. As a result, a heteroplasmic
mother could give rise ultimately to eggs with a much higher or much lower proportion of mutant mtDNA
molecules than are present in her affected tissues.
Another contributor to variable heteroplasmy is the rapid evolution of a mtDNA variant within an individual.
Mutant mtDNAs that have a large deletion or a large duplication can evolve rapidly, so that different tissues or
even the same tissue at different times may show different distributions of the mtDNA variant.

Lecture 9.3 Polygenic inheritance and multifactorial diseases
The polygenic and multifactorial nature of common diseases
It is convenient to divide genetic phenotypes into monogenic phenotypes (influenced
predominantly by a single genetic locus) and polygenic phenotypes (multiple genetic factors
determine the phenotype, each making a small contribution). Individual single-gene disorders are
rare; on the contrary, common multifactorial disorders, such as type 1 and 2 diabetes, coronary
artery disease, stroke, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer disease, and so on, are polygenic.
In reality, the division between these two categories is not quite so clear-cut. We may refer to
single-gene disorders, for example, but in virtually no case is the disease phenotype entirely
attributable to a single gene locus. We can see the effects of other loci when the phenotype in a
‘single-gene’ disorder differs between affected members of the same family (like cases of
incomplete penetrance ). The difference in phenotype can be explained if affected family
members (who would be expected to have the same disease allele or alleles) have different alleles
at one or more modifier loci . The product of a modifier gene interacts with the disease allele in
some way: it may regulate expression of the disease allele, or it may interact in the same pathway
as the product of the disease allele so as to affect its function.
What distinguishes a single-gene disorder is that, although there may be minor effects from
variants at other genetic loci, rare genetic variants at a primary gene locus have a very great effect
on the phenotype. By contrast, it is usual to think of a polygenic disorder as being one in which
the genetic susceptibility to disease risk is not dominated by a primary locus .  There may be a
predominant genetic locus in a true polygenic disease, but its effect would not normally be large:
variants at that locus would not be expected to be necessary or sufficient to cause disease.
However, as described later, there can also be a problem with heterogeneity: individual complex
diseases can be a collection of related phenotypes, and in some of these rare variants can be of
quite strong effect.
The phenotypes of polygenic diseases are also influenced by non-genetic factors, including
environmental factors (which may sometimes work though epigenetic modification) and also
chance ( stochastic ) factors. Environmental factors can sometimes have a strong influence in
certain monogenic disorders, but their effects are very important right across the spectrum of
polygenic disorders.
Because a combination of multiple genetic susceptibility loci and environmental factors is
involved, common diseases due to genetic factors have long been considered to be complex or
multifactorial diseases. Underlying polygenic theory is the idea that there is a continuous
susceptibility to the disease within the population, and that disease manifests when a certain
threshold is exceeded ( Box 1 ).
As we will see, some complex diseases can run in families. However, the tendency is much less
marked than for simple monogenic diseases. A minority of families may have multiple affected
members, and there may even be subsets of families that seem to show Mendelian or quasiMendelian transmission (such as in early-onset forms of Alzheimer disease, diabetes, Parkinson
disease, and various types of cancer). Frequently, however, there is little evidence of family history;
quite commonly an affected individual appears as a sporadic case.

BOx 1 polygenic theory and the liability threshold concept to explain dichotomous traits.
Human traits can be divided into two classes. Some,
like diseases, are dichotomous (you either have the
trait or you do not). Others, such as height or blood
pressure, are continuous (or quantitative) traits:
everybody has the trait, to differing degrees. To explain quantitative traits, polygenic theory envisages the additive contributions of variable alleles
from multiple loci. Many alleles at the underlying
quantitative trait loci ( QTL ) might have subtle
differences (causing modest changes in expression
levels of certain genes, for example); different combinations of alleles at multiple loci might then produce continuous traits (adult height, for example, is
known to be governed by genetic variants at a minimum of 180 loci ).
Polygenic theory can be extended to also explain
dichotomous traits using the concept of a liability
threshold . The idea is that there a continuous liability
(susceptibility) to disease in the population, but only
people whose susceptibility exceeds a certain threshold will develop disease. For each complex disease,
the susceptibility curve for the general population
will be a normal (bell-shaped) curve: most individuals will have a medium susceptibility, with smaller
numbers of people having low to very low susceptibility or high to very high susceptibility ( Figure 1A ).
Only a small percentage of the general population
will have a susceptibility that exceeds the threshold
so that they are affected by the disease (shown in red
in Figure 1 ).
Close relatives of a person affected by a complex disease have an increased susceptibility to that disease
( Figure 1B ). The affected person must have a combination of different high-susceptibility genes; relatives
will share a proportion of genes with the affected person and will therefore have an increased chance of
having high-susceptibility genes.
By chance, some relatives may have only a few of
the high-susceptibility genes, but others may have
many high-susceptibility genes in common with the
affected person. While disease susceptibility can
show wide variation among first-degree relatives
(parent and child, sibs), the overall effect is that the
curve, and the median susceptibility (dashed vertical
line), is displaced to higher susceptibilities to the disease ( Figure 1B ). Because the threshold remains the
same, more individuals are affected, and the relatives
that are most closely related to an affected person are
more likely to be affected.
Variability in the liability threshold for an
individual disease
Thresholds of susceptibility to a complex disease
are not absolutely fixed, they can show differences
between the two sexes, for example. For many autoimmune disorders, women have significantly more
disease risk than men. The reverse is true for some
other conditions. For example, pyloric stenosis occurs
in about 1 in 200 newborn males, but only in about
1 in 1000 newborn females. That is, a double threshold exists, one for females and one for males. The
female threshold for pyloric stenosis is farther from
the mean than that for the male. However, because
it takes more deleterious genes to create an affected
female, she has more genes to pass on to the next
generation. Her male offspring are at a relatively high
risk of being affected when compared with the population risk.
The threshold model accommodates environmental
effects by postulating that such effects can reposition
the threshold with respect to the genetic susceptibility.
Protective environmental factors move the threshold
to higher genetic susceptibilities; other environmental factors can increase the risk of disease by moving
the threshold to lower genetic susceptibilities.

Alzheimer disease (AD) is a good example of a complex or
multifactorial disease. Early-onset AD is the result of many
genetic susceptibility factors, combined with the action of
environmental risk factors. The disease is caused by the
accumulation of extracellular plaques made of aggregated
fibrils of a peptide called β -amyloid, as well as intracellular
neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) made of phosphorylated tau
protein ( Figure 1 ).
Many genes involved in the pathways leading to production
or clearance of amyloid-β can act as susceptibility genetic
factors for early-onset AD, as shown in BOX 2 : secretases that
process the initial amyloid precursor protein into several
peptides, some of which are more amyloidogenic; or proteins
involved in degradation or clearance of these toxic aggregates
from the brain. One of the main genetic risk factors identified
years ago for late-onset AD is the ApoE gene, which is present
in three different alleles in the population ( Figure 2 ).

advantageous to early humans who had a low-calorie, low-fat diet. Over

In rare dominantly inherited early-onset Alzheimer
disease, the disease usually presents between ages
30 and 60 years; disease onset in the common nonMendelian form normally occurs after age 65 years.
The early-onset and late-onset forms have the same
post-mortem brain pathology, abundant extracellular plaques, largely composed of amyloid- β (A β )
peptides of slightly different sizes, and intracellular
neurofibrillary tangles mostly made of tau protein.
The A β peptides are formed by cleavage of the 770 residue transmembrane amyloid- β precursor protein
(APP) that works as a receptor on the surface of
neurons. APP is involved in different neuronal
functions, such as neuronal adhesion and the formation and growth of axons. A β peptides are known
to be metal chelators, binding to metal ions such as
copper, zinc, and iron, and reducing them; they also
seem to have antimicrobial function. The A β peptides
are thought to be the causative agent in Alzheimer
disease, partly on the basis of the pathology and on
the observation that A β is prone to aggregation in
the same way as prions.
Genetic studies of early-onset Alzheimer
disease implicate APP and enzymes
cleaving it
Genomewide linkage studies of autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer disease have identified
three causative genes : the APP gene, which produces APP, and PSEN1 and PSEN2, which are both
involved in processing APP to make A β . The APP
processing reaction requires sequential cleavage by

The apolipoprotein E breakthrough and common pathways in early-onset and
late-onset Alzheimer disease
Early linkage studies suggested a gene for late-onset
Alzheimer disease at proximal 19q. Apolipoprotein E
(ApoE), known to be encoded by a gene at 19q13, was
identified as a component of senile plaques; differences were found between ApoE isoforms in binding
to A β in vitro, and then the APOE* ε 4 allele was found
to be quite strongly associated with Alzheimer disease (odds ratio close to 4 in many populations).
Apolipoprotein E is a key component of lipoprotein
complexes that regulate lipid metabolism (by directing the transport and delivery of lipids from one
tissue cell type to another). It is produced primarily
in the liver, and then in the brain where it works in
pathways involving A β ( Figure 2 ). APOE has also been
shown to be a modifier gene that affects the phenotype in autosomal dominant early-onset forms, for
example in families with presenilin mutations.
A β metabolism involves a balance between the
production from APP and its removal, either by enzymatic degradation (proteolysis) or receptor-mediated
transport out of the brain via the blood–brain barrier
(clearance). Pathogenesis results from an increase in
the amount of A β or the amount of A β 42 relative to
A β 40, and soluble A β oligomers may have a primary
contribution (in addition to affecting synaptic transmission, by impairing long-term potentiation). They
may exert some of their effects by regulating the production and phosphorylation of tau protein to induce
the formation of neurofibrillary tangles that can
cause neurons to die (see Figure 2). A β oligomers can
further aggregate into fibrils that may ultimately be
deposited in extracellular senile plaques. The plaques
can provoke inflammation responses that can further
contribute to pathogenesis.

Estimating the contribution made by genetic factors to the variance of complex diseases
Phenotypes are determined both by genetic factors and by nongenetic factors (that are
often described as environmental factors but include both stochastic and epigenetic
factors). The variance ( V ) of a phenotype is a statistical term defined as the square of the
standard deviation. The total variance of a phenotype, V P = V G + V E (where V G is the
genetic variance and V E is the environmental variance). V G is the sum of three
components: additive genetic effects (the combined contributions from different loci),
dominance effects (interaction of alleles at a single locus), and interaction effects
(interaction between genes at different loci; the effect of genes at several loci may not be
simply additive if they interact with each other).
Heritability ( h [2] ) is the proportion of the total variance that can be attributed to genetic
factors , that is, h [2] = V G /V P ,  and has values ranging from 0 (no genetic factors involved)
to 1 (exclusively due to genetic factors).
Heritability has been important in the prediction of disease risk, but it is not a fixed
property, and it describes a population, not an individual. More accurately, it describes the
genetic contribution to variance within a population and in a specific environment . To
estimate the heritability of a complex trait or disease, the incidence of disease is compared
in genetically related individuals. As shown in Figure 3, three types of study have been
undertaken: family studies, adoption studies, and twin studies.

Having a relative with a complex disease increases your risk of developing that disease.
The risk ratio, the disease risk to a relative of an affected person divided by the disease risk
to an unrelated person, is designated as λ, with a subscript that defines the relationship. For
example, λs represents the comparative disease risk for a sib (brother or sister) of an
affected individual. Unlike a monogenic disorder (for which the risks to family members
are fairly precisely defined, according to simple theoretical calculations), the risks for
complex diseases have quite often been empiric; that is, they have often been based on
surveys of disease incidence in families.
[PDF p. 89]
The risk ratio ( λ ) is a measure of how important genetic factors are in the
etiology of the disease. Not surprisingly, therefore, extremely high λ s
values are found in monogenic disorders. For some complex diseases, λ s
values can be quite high ( Table 1 ).
The drawback of using family studies to infer genetic factors is that family
members would normally be exposed to some common environmental
factors as a result of the shared family environment. This complicates the
interpretation of risk ratios and calls for other types of studies that can
distinguish genetic and environmental effects.
Adoption and twin studies
Adoption studies seek to separate the contributions of genetic and environmental factors. Children of affected individuals who were adopted at
birth into an unaffected family might be expected to share genetic factors
with their biological parents but be exposed to different environments.
Studies compare the incidence of disease in adopted children with that in
children raised in a family with affected relatives.
An alternative is twin studies that measure how often the twins are
concordant (both have the disease) or discordant (only one is affected).
Monozygotic twins are genetically identical but dizygotic twins, like any
pair of sibs, share 50% of their genes. Regardless of zygosity, twins should
be exposed to rather similar environment factors.  The best type of study
would be to look at monozygotic twins separated at birth and raised in
different environments, but this occurs so rarely that statistically valid
sample sizes cannot be obtained.
Table 2 lists observed concordance rates for monozygotic and dizygotic twins for various complex diseases. There are two major points to
note. First, there are significant discordance rates between monozygotic
twins , genetics is not everything! Secondly, it is clear that in certain diseases the concordance between monozygotic twins is much greater than
that between dizygotic twins. Diseases in which genetic factors have a
large role show a relatively high concordance in monozygotic twins and
a much lower concordance rate in dizygotic twins: the greater this ratio, the
greater the genetic contribution. Thus, for example, genetic factors would
seem to be much more important in schizophrenia than in Parkinson
disease (see Table 2).

Heritability can also be calculated for quantitative traits
For quantitative traits (such as blood pressure, glucose levels, etc) that
constitute the diagnosis of common diseases (hypertension or diabetes, in
these examples), heritability can be estimated using the regression line for
the average that variable in the parents (the midparent phenotypic value )
and the value in the offspring ( Figure 4 ). The slope of the regression line is
the heritability of the trait.
Figure 4 Estimation of heritability for quantitative traits. Measuring a quantitative
variable in both parents and at least one child allows estimation of heritability by
normalizing the values (making the mean = 0) and plotting the average of the parents
(X-axis) versus the value in the offspring (Y-axis). The slope of the regression line (the
coefficient of the formula) shows traits with low (left) or high (right) heritability.
Variation in the genetic contribution to common disorders
Heritability studies have indicated that genetic factors make different
contributions to different diseases. Monogenic disorders are primarily
determined by genetic factors (but in some cases environmental factors can
make very significant contributions). By contrast, infectious diseases are
primarily determined by environmental factors (exposure to the infectious
agent). Here, however, host genetic factors also make a contribution, so that
people vary in their susceptibility to an infectious disease and a small
number of individuals may be disease-resistant.
For the great bulk of other complex diseases, genetic and environmental
factors both make large contributions to the phenotype. In some complex
diseases, such as schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, Alzheimer
disease, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, and Crohn’s disease, there is a
strong genetic contribution; in others, such as Parkinson disease and type 2
diabetes, genetic factors seem to be less important. Next year we will see how
we can use the huge amount of variability in human genomes (mostly singlenucleotide variants) to identify the loci responsible for the genetic risk factors
in common diseases.

TBL 9.1 Diseases caused by expansion of trinucleotide repeats
Unrepaired expansions of trinucleotide repeats result in neurological disease
DNA replication errors are common within regions of DNA where there are sequential repeats of a
specific nucleotide or short oligonucleotide, such as a run of cytosines or multiple tandem repeats of the
CA dinucleotide. When the advancing DNA polymerase encounters a series of short tandem repeats,
there will be an increased chance that during DNA replication a mistake is made in aligning the
growing DNA strand with its template strand. The two strands can pair-up out of register, causing the
growing DNA strand to have fewer or more repeat units ( replication slippage , see Figure 1 ). When
these are not repaired successfully by the DNA mismatch repair system (MMR), we will have expansions
or contractions of trinucleotide repeats (also known as dynamic mutations). There is a group of diseases
caused by this mechanism, with some common features but also with some differences depending on
the type and location of the trinucleotide affected.

Over 20 different diseases are caused by dynamic mutations in different genes ( Table 1 ). The CAG
expansions usually involve modest expansions (dozens to a hundred or so repeat units) in coding
sequence, resulting in proteins with expanded runs of glutamines that have a tendency to aggregate.
Other expansions are usually in noncoding sequence, and can involve very large expansions
(thousands of repeat units).
The molecular cause of diseases caused by trinucleotide dynamic expansions is the same at the
DNA level, but at the cellular level the molecular pathology of these conditions varies widely. Some
expansions prevent transcription of the host gene, causing a loss of function. Others show a gain of
function due to producing altered mRNAs and/or proteins that have toxic effects ( Figure 2 ).
A characteristic of repeat expansion disorders is anticipation , that is, the symptoms tend to get more
severe or occur at earlier ages down the generations. This is a consequence of the tendency of the
repeats to expand in each successive generation.

Expansions of CAG in coding regions
Some Trinucleotide Expansion Diseases (shown in blue in Table 1 ) result from the expansion of an
unstable CAG trinucleotide in the coding region of a gene. CAG is the codon for glutamine (Q), and so the
encoded protein has a correspondingly expanded run of glutamine residues . These can be pathogenic by
several mechanisms. First, they cause the protein to form abnormal aggregates that are toxic to neurons. Also,
for ATAXIN3 (the protein with an expanded poly-glutamine in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3) it has been
shown that the expansion interferes with the normal funcion of the protein (which is to de-ubiquitinate
Beclin1 and promote autophagy ). In addition, the huntingtin protein carrying an expanded poly-glutamine
tract can sequester some transcription factors via poly-glutamine interactions, and interfere with the
transcription of genes that are important for neuron survival such as dopamine receptor D2. Whatever the
mechanism, the expansion results in a gain-of-function mutation (the deletion of the gene does not cause the
same disease as the expansion of the CAG repeat); this, in turn, implies that these diseases are usually
inherited in autosomal dominant pattern.
Looking at Table 1, it is apparent that the normal range of CAG repeats is generally below 40, whereas
expansion to more than 40 repeats usually leads to disease. In some cases (see for instance Huntington Disease
or Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1), the boundary between the normal and the pathogenic number of repeats is
just one repeat. Recent molecular studies have shown how the increase in one repeat can alter the funcion of
the protein: the structural changes caused by the extra repeat prevent the interaction between other domains
of the protein, leading to a disorganized structure that could explain some of its toxic effects ( Figure 3 ).

Expansions of non-CAG repeats in non-coding regions
All diseases shown in red in Table 1 are the result of the expansion of a non-CAG trinucleotide (or other
types of repeats) and share some important features. First, the repeat is located in the non-coding region of
the gene, so the protein is unchanged by the expansion. Second, even though the normal range of repeats is
similar to CAG expansions (with an upper limit around 40), mutated alleles have huge expansions (in the
range of hundreds or even thousands of repeats). Interestingly, normal alleles never expand directly to fullmutation; instead, the initial expansion creates a pre-mutated allele that is still non-pathogenic but has a very
high probability of undergoing the final pathogenic expansion to a full-mutation. For instance, pre-mutation
alleles would go from 38 to 55 in Myotonic Dystropy 1 (they upper limit of the normal range and the lower limit
of the mutated range, respectively), or from 55 to 200 repeats in the case of Fragile X (FRAXA). The mechanism
for this expansion to full-mutation cannot possibly be strand-slippage, and other mechanisms such as unequal
recombination have been proposed. What matters is that a full-mutation can never happen directly from a
normal allele, it must first achieve a pre-mutation status and then the probability of expansion to full-mutation
increases with the length of the repeat.
[PDF p. 94]
4
Fragile X syndrome is the best-known example of this class of diseases. Unaffected people have fewer than
55 repeats in the 5’ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene. These sequences are stable and nonpathogenic.
Alleles with 55–200 repeats are described as pre-mutations ; they do not cause the classical fragile X syndrome,
but they are unstable and have a tendency to progress to full mutations (>200 repeats) in subsequent
generations. FMR1 alleles that contain >200 CGG repeats undergo epigenetic silencing of the FMR1 promoter
at ~11 weeks of gestation. It is possible for the nascent FMR1 CGG-repeat RNA to interact with the template
strand of the unwound DNA to form a RNA•DNA duplex that is highly stabilized by its G/C content. This would
require that the CGG-repeat sequence in the RNA achieves a sufficient length to reach back and interact with
the DNA and might be the reason for the requirement of >200 CGG repeats for silencing ( Figure 4 ). The inability
of the FMR1 transcript to bind to the DNA before day 45 may relate to DNA accessibility during transcription.
The formation of the FMR1 RNA•DNA duplex coincides with the initiation of epigenetic silencing in the FMR1
gene, because R-loops are known to elicit epigenetic changes . The clinical features of fragile X syndrome are
due to the lack of FMR1 protein as a result of epigenetic silencing, but occasionally affected individuals have
conventional loss-of-function mutations in the FMR1 gene rather than expanded repeats. However, females
with pre-mutation alleles are at risk of premature ovarian failure, and premutation males often develop a
condition called FXTAS (Fragile-X related tremor and ataxia syndrome). It is believed that these premutation
phenotypes are caused by a toxic RNA gain of function .

The clinical features of Fragile X syndrome are due to lack of FMR1 protein (FMRP). This protein functions as
an RNA-binding protein thanks to an RGG domain than binds to mRNAs with G-quartets (a secondary structure
of some mRNAs caused by several regularly-spaced guanines). Therefore, FMRP protein is involved in the
biogenesis of many mRNAs critical for neuron function .
Pathogenic RNAs have been studied in another non-CAG expansion disease, Myotonic Dystrophy 1 (DM1,
OMIM #160900), and they are thought to be pathogenic because they sequester necessary RNA-binding proteins
into RNA foci inside cells. DM1 is an autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutant version of the DMPK
protein kinase gene. The mutation, an expanded run of CTG trinucleotides, is in the 3’ untranslated region of
the gene (see Figure 2B ). The protein product appears to be unaffected, either qualitatively or quantitatively, but
the (CUG)n in the mutant mRNA forms stable hairpins. These accumulate in RNA foci and sequester CUG-
binding proteins, among them the Muscleblind-like (MBNL1) protein, the insulin receptor, and cardiac
troponin T. MBNL1 is required for correct splicing of other muscle gene transcripts such as the CLCN1 muscle
chloride channel. Deficiency or incorrect splicing of these proteins explains the many features of myotonic
dystrophy (arrythmia, cataracts, myotony). Thus the pathology of the disease is indirect, and unrelated to the
function of the mutated gene.

In addition to these orthodox effects, there is also evidence of a different, unorthodox set
of gain-of-function effects. While the usual translation product may be present, and may (as
in Huntington disease) or may not (in Myotonic Dystrophy 1) be pathogenic, it appears that
the repeat RNA structure allows abnormal translation products to be formed that do not
depend on an AUG start codon. This is known as Repeat-Associated Non-ATG translation
(RAN translation).
RAN translation potentially produces homopolymeric proteins (made up of the same
aminoacid repeated many times) in all three reading frames of a mRNA. Moreover, there is
evidence that at least some of the expanded repeats are also transcribed in an antisense
direction. Therefore, RAN translation from both sense and antisense RNA in all three reading
frames has the potential to produce six different proteins ( Figure 5 ). Exactly which RAN
proteins are actually produced and where, and what role they play in the pathology of these
conditions, are still active areas of research, but there is evidence that at least some of them
are indeed produced and are toxic to a host cell.

Lecture 9.5 Ethical considerations of genetics and genomics in Medicine
Ethical and societal issues in prenatal diagnosis and genetic testing
Medical practitioners sometimes have to deal with complex issues related to genetic information in their
patients. Genetic counselling is the process of communicating such information and helping individual
patients, or their families, to make informed decisions. It is generally accepted that genetic counselling should
be non-directive, that is, the practitioner should not impose his/her own views, but help the patient/family to
make the best decision in accordance with their own views and beliefs. The definition of genetic counselling
offered by the American Society of Human Genetics in 1974 is an excellent summary of this:
“Genetic Counseling is a communication process, which deals with the human
problems associated with the occurrence, or the risk of occurrence, of a genetic disorder in a
family. This process involves an attempt by one or more appropriately trained persons to help
the individual or family (1) comprehend the medical facts, including the diagnosis, the probable
course of the disorder, and the available management; (2) appreciate the way heredity
contributes to the disorder, and the risk of recurrence in specified relatives; (3) understand the
options for dealing with risk of recurrence; (4) choose the course of action which seems
appropriate to them in view of their risk and their family goals and act in accordance with that
decision; and (5) make the best possible adjustment to the disorder in an affected family member
and/or to the risk of recurrence of that disorder.”
Screening for genetic conditions can be carried out at different times of life and may involve prenatal
screening, newborn screening, pre-conception screening of adults for carrier status, or screening adults for
susceptibility to late-onset diseases.
Prenatal screening
Pregnant women are naturally anxious that their baby should be healthy, and a number of prenatal tests for
fetal abnormalities are available. For chromosomal abnormalities, the traditional diagnostic test requires a
sample of fetal cells, obtained by chorionic villus sampling (CVS), at 10–14 weeks of gestation, or by
amniocentesis at 16–20 weeks. Both of these procedures are invasive, and carry an approximately 1-1.5% risk
of triggering a miscarriage. Therefore, they should be performed only in cases where the initial risk of having a
baby with a chromosomal abnormality is higher than that. However, it is often difficult to calculate such risk.
Figure 1 Invasive mathods of
obtaining samples for prenatal
diagnosis In CVS (A), a needle is
guided by ultrasound to obtain cells
from the placenta. Amniocentesis (B)
must be performed later, when the
amount of amniotic fluid is greater,
and obtains cells from the placenta
and from the embryo that are floating
in the amniotic fluid.
Over the years, several biomarkers in maternal serum claimed to identify pregnancies with a high risk of
Down syndrome. A non-invasive ultrasound test, the nuchal translucency test, also gives an indicative risk.
None of these would individually be useful as a screening test but combining age and several biomarkers can
give a valuable composite risk . In many programs, the threshold for offering an invasive diagnostic test would
be a composite risk of Down syndrome of 1 in 300 or greater.
[PDF p. 97]
2
After a positive diagnosis for a chromosomal disorder or a serious genetic condition, many health services
offer the option of terminating a pregnancy. However, support for abortion is far from universal and it is
important to acknowledge the significant numbers of people who are morally opposed to terminating a
pregnancy. Even for people who feel that terminating a pregnancy can be justified for serious genetic
disorders, another issue remains: where do we draw the line that divides serious disorders from non-serious
disorders? Some couples might wish to contemplate termination for what many other people might consider
mild disorders, such as congenital deafness. Diagnosis can also be compromised by the presence of placental
mosaicism, the situation where placental cells are not genetically identical; in this case, a chromosomal
abnormality could be present in some of the cells of the placenta and a test could result in a false positive if
such abnormality is not present in the embryo.
So, it should always be kept in mind that the aim of prenatal screening and diagnosis is to allow couples to
make their own fully informed decisions consistent with their own values and with the laws of their country.
This means that couples must enter into prenatal screening with informed consent and awareness of the
possible outcomes, and if the result shows an abnormality, must not be pressured in any way to terminate
the pregnancy. In addition, some disability rights campaigners and patient groups argue that offering prenatal
diagnosis for a condition, with the option of terminating the pregnancy if the fetus is affected, is equivalent to
saying that affected people are worthless and should not be alive. Any civilized society has an obligation to
look after people born with disabilities and do whatever is possible to allow them a full life.
Noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT)
More recent non-invasive methods of prenatal screening analyze cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in the blood of
pregnant women, since around 5–10% of cfDNA derives from the placenta. When the DNA is sequenced to
sufficient depth, if the fetus has an extra chromosome, sequences from that chromosome will be present in
slightly greater relative amount in the bulk cfDNA, compared to sequences from chromosomes present in
normal diploid numbers. Provided the cfDNA includes at least 4–5% of fetal DNA, NIPT has good sensitivity
from around 9 weeks of gestation onwards and is generally offered in the private sector, but most National
Health Services are reluctant to offer it due to its high cost and its relatively the high rate of false positives (see
“Non-invasive Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis: a case” in ADI).
Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD)
Assisted reproduction clinics offer the possibility of using the
DNA from one blastomere of the early embryo (before it is
implanted) to screen for genetic conditions. In addition to the
ethical problem raised by the possibility of discarding “unfit”
embryos, there are two special situations with important ethical
issues: sex selection and human leukocyte antigen (HLA)
selection . Screening for Y-linked markers allows the sex to be
identified, and cultural preferences for male children in some
societies can result in male embryos being preferentially
selected for implantation. HLA selection occurs when an
embryo is selected for implantation to produce a child that can
provide HLA-matched transplant tissue to save the life of a sick
brother or sister. In these cases, it is particularly worrying that
perfectly healthy embryos are being discarded simply for their
sex or their utility. In the latter case, it has been pointed out that
being born primarily to act as a cell donor might harm the
future psychosocial development of the unaffected child.
Genetic testing in adults
Figure 2 PGD is
performed during in
vitro fertilization Before
the embryo is implanted,
one cell (blastomere) is
extracted to perform
genetic analyses.
Genetic testing for monogenic diseases has implications for other family members, current and future. This
raises the ethical issues of consent for genetic testing, sharing of genetic information, and the confidentiality
of the test results. Genetic testing for complex multifactorial disorders is much less developed than for singlegene disorders, and it poses further ethical challenges.
[PDF p. 98]
3
In economically advanced societies, health professionals are normally required to obtain the consent of
individuals who are giving a sample or undergoing a medical intervention. The consent process is meant to
ensure that a person understands the nature and purpose of the procedure. The issue of who can give consent
for genetic testing mostly revolves around age and mental competence. The person who is being tested may
give consent if he or she is an adult and capable of understanding the implications of the test. For adults with
mental incapacity (who are judged incapable of giving consent), a genetic test can be undertaken if it is
believed to be in the best interests of the adult concerned, and a legal guardian typically provides the informed
consent.
For children below the legal age for consent, parents (or those with parental responsibility) may give consent
for genetic testing. Informed understanding of the nature of genetic testing is an important part of the
consenting process, but the complex genetic techniques used in testing are not easy to explain, and the
predictive value of the test can also be difficult to understand in many cases. For some types of genetic testing,
the process of consent is currently denied in certain societies. For example, carrier testing for β-thalassemia is
currently mandatory for couples registering for marriage in Iran, many provinces of Turkey, the Gaza Strip, and
Saudi Arabia.
Genetic testing of children raises additional consent issues. Should children at risk be tested for adult-onset
single-gene disorders? Or screened for carrier status for serious recessive disorders? The answer to both
questions is usually no; unless there is clear medical benefit, testing should be delayed until the child has the
capacity to make the choice. Two ethical principles are particularly relevant: the principle of beneficence that
considers the benefit to the child (to test for clinically relevant genetic variants), and the ‘right to an open
future’ principle (disclosure of genetic information could infringe a child’s future autonomy). This applies
especially to conditions in which adults might sometimes choose not to be tested (testing during childhood
would deny the child the right not to give consent). Current professional guidelines in many countries
therefore stipulate that children should not normally be tested unless there is clear medical benefit . Testing
for familial hypercholesterolemia is one such example: early detection of a pathogenic LDLR mutation offers
the possibility of prevention by lowering LDL-cholesterol through dietary changes and medication, and testing
is recommended from the age of 10 years.
For monogenic disorders and other conditions in which there is a high risk to unaffected family members,
genetic findings in one person may be very pertinent to those relatives at risk, and can be disclosed when
consent has been obtained to allow this (most family members wish their information to be available to help
relatives). In the absence of such consent, when is disclosing the findings to other family members justified?
What are the limits on confidentiality? Although there might be a moral obligation to contact family members
who have not sought advice (but have inherited a pathogenic mutation, for instance), individuals also have the
right not to know . Medical professionals may also be in the rather uncomfortable position of having access to
information on different family members who do not know about each other, or they might discover through
genetic testing that the biological relationships between some family members are different from the assumed
relationships. In general, a breach in confidentiality might be justified only to avoid of serious harm .
Genetic discrimination and ethical, societal, and practical issues raised by
clinical genome-wide sequencing
At the outset of the Human Genome Project there were fears about genetic discrimination in health insurance
and employment if most of the population had their genomes sequenced, and some countries passed
legislation to protect the privacy of genetic information and to prevent genetic discrimination. Until recently,
the genomes of very few people had been decoded, but that is changing because genome-wide sequencing (of
whole exomes or whole genomes) is expanding enormously. Might we soon live in a world where everyone, or
at least those living in areas with ready access to the technology,  will have their genome sequenced?
Alongside the effort to identify clinically important variants at the genome level are parallel efforts to develop
databases that link those variants to information on diseases. The ClinVar database, for example, includes all
medically important variants that have some impact on phenotypes. Looking to the future, some national
health care services are investigating the possibility of integrating clinical genome sequencing.
[PDF p. 99]
4
Some people believe that complete genome sequencing will almost certainly become part of
neonatal screening in the very near future, perhaps as part of the existing heel-prick screening of
newborns. If fetal or newborn genome sequencing were ever to be contemplated on a large scale, there
would be ethical issues relating to incidental findings and the disclosure of genetic information. Some
people are strongly opposed, arguing that analyzing a newborn’s complete genome violates the ethical
principle of respecting an individual’s autonomy. The screening would reveal all manner of variants
that are of no importance to the child’s immediate health, but also some that would be expected to
have serious consequences in later life. Proactively seeking out all genetic variants and disclosing the
genetic findings would mean that the child would be robbed of the right not to know about his or her
genome or to delay disclosure of that information until a later stage in life. And if a child were to be
burdened by the knowledge that he or she had a high risk of developing some severe condition later in
life, there could be the prospect of psychosocial harm.
This could be further complicated by the implementation of prenatal whole-genome sequencing.
Researchers recently reported sequencing a whole fetal genome from cell-free fetal DNA in a pregnant
woman’s blood, heralding the possibility of performing whole-genome sequencing as early as the first
trimester of pregnancy. With this advance, expectant parents may obtain genetic information not just
about the risk of childhood diseases but also about carrier status for autosomal recessive disorders
such as Tay– Sachs disease, the risk of complex adult-onset diseases such as diabetes, the presence of
genes causing adult-onset autosomal dominant diseases such as the hereditary breast and ovarian
cancer syndrome, and the likelihood of traits such as baldness. Such sequencing could thus blur the
boundary between diagnosis and calculating the risk of future disease. Parents could learn about the
risk of diseases that might never be manifested and about genetic variations of unclear significance.
How far would we be moving then toward an obsession with genetic perfection and eugenics ? Could
we ever contemplate going so far when we still have an imperfect knowledge about what all the
genetic variants do? Proper genetic counselling in a medical context would be very difficult to carry
out if these practices were to spread without control.
Polygenic Risks
Decades of research using Genome-Wide Association Studies have identified thousands of the
genetic variants responsible for increased risks of developing common multifactorial diseases such as
diabetes or Alzheimer’s, or even common physical and psychological traits. The genetic
predisposition for these complex traits is usually explained by dozens or hundreds of genetic variants,
each one contributing only a minor proportion of the total risk. When the effects of all these variants
are combined in Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS), then the contribution of genetic factors can be
substantial. Even so, recent studies suggest that polygenic risks will predict at most a 5-fold to 10-fold
increase in the likelihood of developing a phenotype, so using them in neonatal screening, let alone in
prenatal screening, does not seem justified. It is crucial that society is correctly informed about the
predictive power of polygenic risks and the contribution of environmental factors, particularly in the
case of cognitive and psychiatric traits.
For example, some people have requested a “personalized education” based on the genetic profiles of
children, and some assisted reproduction clinics offer embryo selection based on genetic variants that
predict “low intelligence” or “short stature”. The best way to avoid the eugenic drift resulting from
such misconceptions is to educate the public on the limited predictive power of polygenic scores, and
to highlight the importance of environmental interventions to alleviate genetic predisposition to
disease. A polygenic score should never be the only criterion to make important decisions about the
fate of embryos, children or adults.
[PDF p. 100]
4
The ethics of genetic manipulation of the germ line to prevent disease or to enhance
normal human traits
Gene therapy is now a therapeutic option for a variety of different disorders. In each case the approved
therapy is a somatic gene therapy in which the cells to be genetically modified are somatic cells. Germ-line
gene therapy, by contrast, would involve making a genetic change to germ-line cells so that genetic
modifications could be transmitted down the generations. A motivation for germ-line gene therapy is to
prevent disease, but the direct consequences would not be limited to one person; instead, they would be
extended to potentially many descendants. Germ-line gene therapy has been the subject of ethical
controversy, and genetic manipulation of the germ line is prohibited by law in many countries.
Recent research efforts have led to the advent of genetic engineering techniques that are increasingly
effective in editing the genome with great precision. The most recent is known as CRISPR/Cas9, which has
quickly established itself as the fastest and most effective technique for introducing modifications into the
genomes of plants and animals. Thanks to this technology, recent years have witnessed remarkable
advances such as the curing of hemophilia or muscular dystrophy in laboratory animals, paving the way for
clinical trials in humans.
It is important to emphasize that, in this context, the genetic modification will remain in the corrected
(somatic) cells but will not be inherited by subsequent generations because CRISPR will not have modified
the germ cells (eggs or sperm). On the other hand, this genomic correction technology could also be used in
early human embryos, in combination with assisted reproduction techniques through in vitro fertilization.
This presents a series of additional challenges since any genetic modification will spread to the vast
majority of that individual’s cells and is likely to be transmitted to future generations.
In November 2018, a researcher from a university in southern China announced that he had modified
several human embryos with CRISPR and implanted them, resulting in the birth of two twin sisters and
another child. The news stunned experts, especially when it was revealed that the genetic modification was
aimed to make them resistant to HIV infection. Several experts pointed out that this was entirely
unnecessary since we already have effective procedures to prevent virus transmission when the father is a
carrier. An analysis of the data provided by the researcher concluded that, in one of the twins, both copies
of the gene in question had been modified, although probably not all the cells of the embryo were edited; it
is unclear whether that girl is completely resistant to HIV infection. What is indisputable is that her sister is
not, as only one copy of her genome was modified. The benefits, still unconfirmed, would have been
minimal whereas the potential health risks to the girls could be significant. A particularly compelling
argument against germ-line genome editing, even for monogenic diseases, is that it is simply not necessary.
Candidate couples would most probably have dominant or recessive Mendelian disorders (recurrence risk
50% and 25%, respectively). Given a dish containing half a dozen IVF embryos from the couple, it would
seem bizarre to select the affected ones and then subject them to a risky procedure of genetic manipulation,
rather than simply select the 50% or 75% of unaffected ones for reimplantation.
Therefore, it is unlikely that genome editing of embryos will be used prevent disease; instead, its most
likely application would be to introduce advantageous modifications in genes that control normal human
traits ( genetic enhancement ). The notion of genetic enhancement means that people will use in vitro
fertilization and preimplantation diagnosis to select embryos with certain desired qualities and will most
likely lead to demands for ‘designer babies’ using genome editing. However, a single genetic modification
will not change a trait significantly, so dozens of modifications would be necessary to obtain a minor
change in the desired direction. It is hard to see how we could ever ethically get the technology of
manipulating the human germ line to a stage in which it is efficient and safe, if, on the way, unsafe
procedures must be used that could have adverse effects on future descendants. Finally, genetic editing in
humans should never endanger the person’s well-being; it should never introduce disadvantages,
discrimination, or division in society. In its present state, embryonic genome modification for genetic
enhancement does not meet any of these conditions.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/Material/FMCI--Luc.title: FMCI  Lucia Reed notes
Medical-Degree/Year-1/Material/FMCI--Luc.content:
[PDF p. 1]
FROM THE MOLECULE TO THE CELL I
Lucía Reed López
[PDF p. 2]
Lecture 1.2. Light and electron microscopy
History
The first magnification lenses were developed in the 11th century.
The invention of the microscope wasn’t done by only one person, it received many
contributions, but a name which stands out the most is the one of Robert Hooke, who in
1665 developed a microscope with 50X magnification.
Regular light microscope
Cells are very small and translucent, so to be able to see them we need a high magnification
and to create contrast.
Magnification : light microscopy can magnify samples UP TO 1500X, but no more.
Therefore, it allows us to observe mitochondria and lysosomes (using the proper
contrast), but not ribosomes.

Contrast : to produce said contrast, light microscopy uses differential staining such as
Hematoxylin-Eosin (H & E) staining, commonly used in pathology labs to differentiate
tumors in a tissue. But this method doesn’t allow us to visualize living cells. This can
only be achieved by creating contrast using special optical systems, without staining,
such as the phase contrast microscope.

Phase contrast microscope
Based on phase (wave) shifts when light passes through different objects. It alters light
pathways and produces contrast, allowing us to observe many cell processes.
Fluorescence microscope
It allows us to differentiate many different structures in
living cells, even antibodies (immunofluorescence).
Excitation light is irradiated on the sample from the light
source, passing through the excitation fiber and onto the
dichroic mirror (which reflects blue light but not green light,
so it can pass through) and the emission filter. Excitation
light (blue, 450 landa) is irradiated and green light (520
landa) is emitted.
Dichroic mirror: its function in microscopy is to reflect the
excitation wavelength, but allow the passage of the
emission wavelength.
Transmission electron microscope (TEM)
Consists not of light, but a beam of electrons passing through the sample.
There has to be a vacuum so the electrons aren’t scattered by particles in the
air. The result is observed through a computer, and samples are observed in
very thin sections. Contrast is generated using uranium citrate and lead citrate.
The differential absorption of these heavy metals gives us the contrast. Bright
areas correspond to electron lucent parts of the sample, while darker areas are
electron dense (the beam of electrons bounces off because they are repelled).
[PDF p. 3]
Images always appear in black and white. TEM allows us to see cellular organelles, such as
the cilium. It can be used to diagnose dyskinesia, a condition in which the central pair of
microtubules is missing. Proteins can’t interact and therefore function is impaired. It presents
symptoms such as infertility, deafness, bronchitis and recurrent infections.
Scanning electron microscope (SEM)
It allows us to observe three dimensional structures. It involves a gold coating, and the
electron beam scans the sample and creates a 3D image which is seen on a monitor. Once
again, the image is in black and white.
Immunodetection
Antibodies can be labelled by either using fluorochromes (immunofluorescence), enzymes
(immunohistochemistry) or gold particles (immunoelectron microscopy).
● Immunofluorescence, when used in
cancer treatment, allows us to apply
personalized medicine, by studying the
markers of malignancy and immune
response all in the same sample.
● Immunohistochemical procedures
can be used to explore the best
treatment for a particular breast
cancer.
[PDF p. 4]
TBL 1.1. Ultrastructure of the eukaryotic cells
Microscope structures
Glycogen is seen as dark accumulations found in the cytoplasm. Abundant in liver cells,
called hepatocytes.
-Differences between lysosomes and peroxisomes
Peroxisomes have a characteristic round shape and are
homogeneous inside the membrane. The round black stuff
inside the peroxisome is a crystalloid, which is a precipitation of
enzymes that are involved in oxidation and the detoxification of
cells. Lysosomes are more electron dense and have more
irregular shapes. We can differentiate darker material inside,
which corresponds to the substances that are being processed
and digested.
-Differences between microvilli and cilia
Cilia are made up of microtubules which can be observed
under the microscope, and are longer and less abundant.
We can find cilia in cells like the ones in our respiratory
tract, preventing particles and pathogens from entering our
system. Inside cilia, we find microtubules in a particular
disposition.
Microvilli can be found in many cells, like intestinal cells
called enterocytes, because their main function here is to
assist absorption. Inside microvilli, we find actin supporting
its structure.
                      - **Desmosomes**, located between

the membranes of two
neighbouring cells. Its function is
to attach these cells, allowing
them to communicate.
                      **Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER)** usually

presents as a big accumulation of round tubules,
which can sometimes be more elongated depending
on where the cut was made.
[PDF p. 5]

Centrioles, when not in cell division, are forming microtubules and controlling the
cytoskeleton

Lymphocytes
In this image, we can see a lymphocyte, with a thin ring of
cytoplasm and a few mitochondria surrounding the nucleus.
T and B lymphocytes are created inside the bone marrow. T
lymphocytes mature in the thymus, while B lymphocytes
remain and mature in the bone marrow.
-
T lymphocytes
a) Cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected or damaged cells. Cytotoxic T cells express a
protein called T-CD8 on their membrane.
b) Helper T cells, which orchestrate and regulate the immune response. Helper T cells
express T-CD4 . HIV virus attacks T-CD4 cells because it binds to that protein when
infecting a cell, giving way to the appearance of AIDS.
Morphologically, we can differentiate T and B lymphocytes by using immunofluorescence.
T-CD4 and T-CD8 are T lymphocyte markers. There are markers on B cells, most
importantly, CD20 . But they can’t be differentiated when observing them under the
microscope with differential staining.
-
B lymphocytes and their differentiation into plasma cells
B lymphocytes are produced in the bone marrow and mature there
(maturing=express CD20). After they exit the bone marrow, they enter a lymph
node. These B cells that exit are called naive B cells, because they haven’t yet
been in contact with an antigen. But once in the lymph node, there is an
encounter with different antigens. This way, they differentiate into plasma cells,
B lymphocytes which change their morphology and function to be able to
produce antibodies which correspond to the antigen they were in contact with.
Many plasma cells, after differentiating, regress to the bone marrow.
[PDF p. 6]
Plasma cells need to produce lots of antibodies, and therefore when they mature, they
develop a large RER which can allow them to produce lots of antibodies (proteins).
*Lymphatic system: Vascular system which drains the interstitial fluid between cells, and
which carries white blood cells which carry out this filtration of the blood and fluids. These
white blood cells
Granulocytes
Nucleophiles: 3 or 4 lobules
Eosinophils: 2 lobules and big granules
[PDF p. 7]
Workshop 1.2. Normal and pathological cells under the microscope
LEUKOCYTES
Granulocytes
-
Neutrophils have a size of 10-12nm. We normally find 3500-7000 cells/mm3. They
make up 60-70% of leukocytes. They have a phagocytic role. As key morphological
features, neutrophils have a multilobular nucleus (3-5 lobules) and contain
granules, but these cannot be stained with either basic nor acid dye.
- Eosinophils have a size of 10-14 nm. We can find between 150-400
eosinophils/mm3, and they make up around 1-3% of all leukocytes. Their function is
to remove parasites and destroy antibody-antigen complexes. As key morphological
features, they have a bipolar nucleus and granules which are stained with acidic
dye .
-
Basophils have a size of 8-10nm. There are normally 50-100 cells/mm3 in our blood
and they make up 0.1-1% of leukocytes. As key morphological features, their nucleus
usually has an “S” shape that is partially covered by granules which stain blue with
basic dyes . They are involved in inflammatory reactions, similarly to mastocytes.
Agranulocytes
- Monocytes have a size of 12-15nm and we can find around 200-800 cells/mm3 in
our blood. They make up 3-8% of leukocytes and, as a key morphological feature,
they have a kidney shaped nucleus . They differentiate into macrophages when
they infiltrate tissues. They also have a phagocytic role and act as antigen presenting
cells.
- Lymphocytes have a size of 7-8nm. There are 1500-2000 cells/mm3 in our
bloodstream and they make up 20-25% of leukocytes. Their nucleus occupies almost
all of the cell, and their main function is to participate in adaptive immunological
responses. They cannot be distinguished morphologically, under the microscope.
T lymphocytes are responsible for cell-mediated immunity.
B lymphocytes participate in the humoral response, throughout the release of
antibodies.
[PDF p. 8]
ERYTHROCYTES
They have a size of 7um, and there are around 3.9-5.7 million cells/mm3 in our blood. They
have a biconcave shape and lack a nucleus . The central part is thinner, explaining why
they look pale in the centre when observed under light microscope. Their main function is to
deliver oxygen to the cells via haemoglobin.
THROMBOCYTES/PLATELETS
Platelets are produced from very large bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes. As
megakaryocytes develop into giant cells, they undergo a process of fragmentation. Platelets
are made in our bone marrow. Their function is to form clots and prevent bleeding.
[PDF p. 9]
Lecture 2.2 & 2.3. Proteins I & II
Proteins have many functions, such as catalytic functions, structural, transport, defense,..
Proteins are made up of alpha-amino acids . There are 20 different types of amino acids,
which give place to thousands of proteins.
Amino acids share common characteristics:
-They have a central carbon, known as
alpha-carbon (sp3 configuration, therefore forms
tetrahedral molecules)
-Carboxyl group, or alpha-carboxyl group
-Amino group
-A hydrogen atom
-An “R” group, a side chain, which differs between
each aminoacid. The simplest amino acid is
Glycine, which only has a hydrogen atom in its
side chain.
All amino acids, except for Glycine, are chiral. But all living beings (with exceptions) are
made up of the L enantiomer, “L-amino acids”.
They can be classified in different groups depending on their ability to interact with water and
ionize. These are their structures found at physiological pH (around 7.4)
1. Nonpolar, hydrophobic
Glycine, Alanine, Proline, Valine, Leucine,
Isoleucine and Methionine
They do not like interacting with water, so
they tend to be orientated inwards in the
tridimensional structure of the protein.
2. Aromatic R groups
Phenylalanine, Tyrosine, Tryptophan
Tyrosine, because it contains an OH group, could react with
an acid, like phosphoric acid, and form phosphotyrosine
which could affect the tridimensional structure of the protein
and therefore its function.
The characteristic of these aminoacids is that they can
absorb UV light, typically light with wavelengths around
275-280nm. The ability for proteins to absorb light comes
from the presence of these three amino acids.
[PDF p. 10]
3. Polar, uncharged R groups
Serine, Threonine, Cysteine, Asparagine, Glutamine
These amino acids, due to their side chains, can form
hydrogen bonds . In the case of cysteine, it can also form
disulfide bonds .
There are enzymes which phosphorylate serines, others,
cysteines,… (serine-kinases, cysteine-kinases,…).
4. Positively charged R groups
Lysine, Arginine, Histidine
Can be found in their ionized form.
5. Negatively charged R groups
Aspartate and Glutamate
Ionization of amino acids
Amino acids can behave like acids or bases, depending on the
pH.
They can be in a Cation form, Zwitterion state (intermediate
state, called isoelectric point, known as pI, a pH value at which
the net charge of the molecule is 0, with the amino group
positively charged and a negatively charged carboxylic group), or
Anion form, when the environment has a very high pH and the
amino acid is deprotonated.
How to calculate pI when the side chain is ionizable?
-First, identify the Zwitterion, the species that carries net 0 charge
-Identify the pka value that defines the acid strength of this zwitterion
-identify the pka value that defines the base strength of this zwitterion
-Lastly, take the average of these two pKa values, and you will get the pI of the respective
amino acid.
[PDF p. 11]
Protein conformation
Proteins have specific tridimensional structures. The particular conformation will give them
their functionality. This folding state is held together by strengths and interactions, such as
hydrophobic strengths, hydrogen bonds,… They are weak, but very abundant, which
makes them important for the preservation of the structure. We can also find electrostatic
interactions (strong interactions between permanently charged groups, such as salt
bridges), Van der Waals forces (medium-range weak attraction) and disulfide bridges
(covalent).
Many neurodegenerative diseases are caused by the misfolding of one protein. In the case
of Alzheimer’s, it’s caused by the accumulation of a protein which forms aggregates,
B-amyloid, as well as aggregates formed by the accumulation of TAU protein.
In Parkinson’s disease we find the accumulation of alpha-synuclein in the neurons,…
There are 4 different levels of protein structure
1. Primary structure
It consists of the amino acid sequence which conforms the protein. The amino acids are
bound together through a peptidic bond (covalent bond) formed by C, O, N and H. It is a
partial double bond, as there is resonance between C-O and C-N. Therefore, the protein can
only rotate around the alpha-carbon (NOT in the peptidic bond).
After many peptidic bonds, we can differentiate the Amino terminal (N-terminal) and
Carboxyl terminal (C-terminal). This reaction occurs by condensation and requires energy.
This linear sequence starts to fold and form interactions in a regular form, giving way to the
secondary structure. This structure will be determined by the organization around the
peptide bond and the identity of the R groups.
2. Secondary structure
The two main arrangements are the alpha-helix and the
beta-sheets.
Alpha-helix is held together by Hydrogen bonds. Typically,
it’s formed by hydrophobic amino acids (for example,
proline disrupts the helix).
[PDF p. 12]

Beta-sheets, where the protein backbone forms a
zig-zag plain, and the R groups protuberate outwards
from the sheet. We can find two types: parallel and
antiparallel sheets, the last one being more stable.
They are held together by hydrogen bonds. Keratin,
found in nails, is formed by parallel beta-sheets.

Prion diseases are caused by misfolding of proteins, like the
case of the Cretzfiel-Jakob disease.
3. Tertiary structure
It’s the spatial arrangement adopted by the atoms in a protein.
All proteins have a tertiary structure, which is held together by those bonds mentioned
earlier.
Motifs are interactions between different segments of the protein. Each motif has a function
in the protein.
A domain is a region of the protein with a specific conformation which
allows a protein to carry out a function. For example, Troponin C,
which is a muscular calcium-binding protein involved in muscular
contraction, has 2 domains.
 - The structure of **collagen** : Collagen is an important constituent

of connective tissue (tendons, cartilage, bones,…). Each
collagen chain is rich in glycine and proline, which intertwine
to form superhelical triple helices with very high tensile
strength. Vitamin C is the cofactor which allows hydroxylation
of proline, and this 4-hydroxyproline found in collagen chains
offers more hydrogen bonds. That’s why vitC deficiency
causes scurvy.
                         - The structure of **myoglobin** : Myoglobin is an O2

storage point in the muscle. It needs a prosthetic group
to be able to bind to oxygen, a heme group like iron.
The prosthetic group needs to be located in a region
that avoids iron oxidation; because the internal part of
myoglobin is hydrophobic, the hemo group is burried
inside the tertiary structure of the protein, and so it’s
able to bind to oxygen.
4. Quaternary structure
It’s formed by the interaction of different proteins/polipeptidic chains. A classic example is
hemoglobin, a protein which transports oxygen in the blood. It needs to be able to bind to the
O2 at one place but also release it in another. It has high affinity for oxygen at the lungs but
low affinity for O2 in the blood vessels.

Types of monosaccharides
Monosaccharides are linear carbon chains with single bonds, which are bound to an alcohol
group and a main functional group, either aldehyde or ketone. The ketone is always located

TRIOSES
-Aldehyde: glyceraldehyde (important for our metabolism. Has 1 asymmetric carbon). We

group is the one that determines the D or L nomenclature.
In our metabolism, we can only process D-glyceraldehyde to

PENTOSES

D-Xylose

Monosaccharide cyclization
In aqueous solution, monosaccharides with 5 or more carbons form cycles.
In case of D-glucose, oxygen from C1 attacks C5, forming an hexagon through the
hemiacetal bond (in the case of ketones, it would be an hemicteal bond). New stereoisomers
now appear, based on the orientation of the alcohol around the carbon: beta anomer (up,
same direction as CH2OH) or alpha anomer (down, opposite direction from CH2OH).
Six-membered cyclic monosaccharides are known as pyranoses.
Five-membered cyclic monosaccharides are known as furanoses.
Monosaccharides are reducing agents . Glucose oxidase
oxidizes glucose in the presence of O2, releasing H2O2.
The amount of glucose in blood can be measured by
