Lecture 2.5. Carbohydrates II: Disaccharides and Polysaccharides
DISACCHARIDES
Disaccharides are formed by 2 monosaccharides joined together by an O-glycosidic bond .
This happens between the anomeric carbon of one monosaccharide and any OH group. The
formation of the O-glycosidic bond happens by condensation . To break the bond, we would
use hydrolysis. When the bond is formed, there is no mutarotation. It loses the capacity to
switch between alpha and beta. It’s conformation is fixed.The anomeric carbon of the 2nd
monosaccharide still mutarotates (in case of maltose for example).
Disaccharides are named by common or systematic name:
-Non-reducing monosaccharide (-yl)
-Carbon atoms that participate in the O-glycosidic bond
-Second monosaccharide (-ose)
-Maltose is formed by an alpha 1-4 bond between two
glucose monomers, and is a reducing agent because
the OH from the anomeric carbon remains out of the
O-glycosidic bond.
                   - **Sucrose** is a disaccharide formed by **glucose** and

fructose, joined together by an alpha 1-2 linkage.
Sucrose contains no free anomeric carbons, therefore, it is
a non-reducing sugar.
-Lactose is a reducing sugar formed by D-galactose
and D-glucose, joined together by beta 1-4 bonds . It’s
found in the milk of humans and other mammals, because
the natural synthesis of lactose occurs only in mammary
tissue. Lactose intolerance occurs when an individual
lacks the enzyme ( lactase ) necessary for the hydrolysis of
lactose. A more serious condition would be galactosemia,
where a person cannot convert galactose into glucose to
metabolize it.
(In the case of sucrose, the
molecule loses it’s reducing
power, as it loses the
mutarotation in both
monosaccharides. Sucrose
is a non-reducing
disaccharide. Lactose, on
the other hand, remains as a
reducing agent, because
when it opens the aldehyde
group reappears, and it’s a
reducing group)
[PDF p. 16]
POLYSACCHARIDES
It’s the most frequent way in which carbohydrates are found. Because of their nature, they
can be formed by an unlimited number of monomers. They carry out one of two functions:
energy storage or structural functions .
Classification
They can be classified in many categories, such as homopolysaccharides or
heteropolysaccharides, structural or reserve polysaccharides,…
Reserve polysaccharides
The most important reserve polysaccharides are starch in plant cells and glycogen in animal
cells. Both are found in the cytoplasm forming granules.
Glycogen is a branched polysaccharide made up of glucose monomers. The glucose is
linked by alpha 1-4 bonds . But also, glycogen has alpha 1-6 linkers in branch points .
This gives place to many non-reducing ends,
which is helpful when carrying out metabolism.
The spatial structure of glycogen is spiral-like,
which is helpful for the cell as it makes it easy to
compact. This spiral shape occurs thanks to the
alpha bond.
“Glycogen is the main storage saccharide in
animals and bacteria ”.
Starch is the equivalent of glycogen in plants. It’s a combination of two polymers: amylose
(a chain of glucose formed by alpha 1-4 bonds) and amylopectin (branched-chain
polysaccharide, identical to glycogen, but with less ramifications).
Humans possess enzymes that can degrade starch, such as alpha-amylases found in
salivary glands.
-
Structural polysaccharides
Cellulose is a linear homopolysaccharide formed by beta
1-4 bonds between glucose monomers, found in the plant
cell wall. It has a structural function, as it gives shape to
the cell. Thanks to the beta linkage, hydrogen bonds now
form between adjacent monomers forming an insoluble
fibrous structure, giving it it’s structural function. Our body
isn’t able to make use of this glucose, as we lack the
enzymes that carry out hydrolysis of this beta bond.
Chitin is present in the cell wall of fungi and the exoskeleton of arthropods. It’s a linear
homopolysaccharide of N-acetyl-glucosamine monomers linked by beta 1-4 bonds,
same as cellulose.
[PDF p. 17]
Peptidoglycan is a linear heteropolysaccharide of
N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic
acid (MurNAc) linked by beta 1→4 bonds . It’s the
main component of the bacterial wall . Lysozyme, an
enzyme present in our tears, breaks down the
glycosidic bond between the components of
peptidoglycan, and antibiotics such as Penicillin
prevent these bonds from forming, thus protecting us
from bacterial pathogens.
The extracellular matrix found surrounding our cells is rich in Glycosaminoglycans,
heteropolysaccharides that, together with fibrous proteins, provide strength and resistance
to tissues. They are linear polymers with beta 1→4 bonds of repeating disaccharides of a
uronic acid + N-acetyl-glucosamine or N-acetyl-galactosamine.
The negatively charged carboxylate and sulfate groups present in glycosaminoglycans form
hydrogen bonds with water molecules creating a hydrated gel . This raises the viscosity of
the medium and gives it an elastic consistency providing a flexible support for the
extracellular matrix.
Hyaluronic acid is a type of glycosaminoglycan, made up of
disaccharides (glucuronic acid linked to N-acetylglucosamine
via β1→3 bonds) joined by beta 1-4 bonds . It’s a characteristic
element of connective tissue (cartilage, tendons,…), where it
acts as a lubricant. Hyaluronidase is an enzyme secreted by
pathogenic bacteria which carries out hydrolysis of the
hyaluronic acid, making the tissue more susceptible to
infection.
Heparin is another type of
glycosaminoglycan,
although due to its alpha
linkage, isn’t an extracellular
structural polysaccharide. It
is stored within the secretory
granules of mast cells and is
released at sites of tissue
injury. It’s extensively used
as an anticoagulant .

Lecture 2.6. Enzymes
An enzyme is a catalyst . They increase the rate of a reaction . Usually, enzymes are
proteins, generally globular, although there are exceptions (such as ribosomes, which are
made up of RNA).
They are used as catalysts because of:


Their specificity: they catalyze a particular reaction with a particular product.


They work in mild reaction conditions. Compatible with conditions in cells


Higher catalytic power


Our body is capable of regulating the processes of the enzyme by changing its activity.


General properties of enzymes
-Generally globular proteins
-Varied sizes
-Monomeric or dimeric
-Just proteins or conjugated with other molecules
-Two main zones: active site (where binding and catalysis
happens) and regulatory site (enzymes may have one or many).
Enzyme (holoenzyme) = apoenzyme (proteic part) + cofactor (non proteic). Not all enzymes
have cofactors, but many do, such as ions. It’s a necessary part of the enzyme, it’s needed
for its catalytic activity. Without it, it doesn’t work.
Types of cofactors

Metal ions

Coenzymes (organic molecules) such as prosthetic groups or cosustrates.
Many coenzymes are vitamins. That’s why we need to ingest them, although in small
quantities, for the correct functioning of many of the enzymes in our body.
Enzyme nomenclature


Name of the substrate + -ase ( urease, lactase,…)


Substrate + enzymatic activity ending in -ase ( Triose phosphate isomerase, DNA
polymerase,…)


Given name ( Trypsin, rubisco, papain,…)


Classification of enzymes
[PDF p. 19]
How do enzymes work?
For any reaction to happen, we need to reach the activation energy .

The activation energy determines the speed of the reaction. The activation energy
tells us about the rate/speed of the reaction. How fast the reaction will transition
towards the spontaneous direction.
The difference of free energy between substrates and products will determine the
spontaneity of the reaction.

What enzymes do is reduce the activation
energy needed for a specific reaction. Therefore,
the rate will be much faster. They enhance
reaction rates by lowering activation energy. A
consequence of this is that enzymes do not
affect the equilibrium. They do not change the
direction of the reaction and its spontaneity.
Mechanisms of enzyme activity
1. Effect of proximity and
orientation : for a reaction to take
place, we need the substrates to
be able to interact with each
other. One thing that enzymes do
is put together the substrates in
a favourable position.
2. Decrease the activation energy:
There are many ways to do this, but we will focus on
effect of tension and distortion: enzymes bind
perfectly to the transition state of the substrate,
modifying it to a way that pushes it closer to such
transition state. The model considered closer to reality
is the Koshland’s induced model . Both enzyme and
substrate are modified in the process.
Example: hexokinase, when it binds to glucose, this event causes them both to
change after the catalytic reaction. But this modification is reversible.
[PDF p. 20]
Enzyme regulation
Some enzymes exhibit increased or decreased activity.
Allosteric regulators are generally
small chemicals that change the
configuration of the protein, making it
active or less active. They bind to an
area which can be very far from the
active site, although never the active
site. There are both allosteric inhibitors
and allosteric activators.
                    - **Reversible covalent modifications**, for example,

the phosphorylation of enzymes that posses an OH group.
We will have a reaction where ATP donates a phosphate to
the enzyme. This reaction is reversible, depending on the
cell’s necessities. Kinase phosphorylates, and phosphatase
produces the hydrolysis of the phospho group.
Activation by proteolysis : there are enzymes which are dangerous in the site
where they are created, so our body produces enzymes that are inactive, and are
activated when they’re in the place where needed. This happens by proteolysis: there
is a cleavage of an area of the protein, making it an active enzyme. This reaction is
irreversible.
This happens for example with the protein-degrading enzymes produced in the pancreas:
They are activated once they arrive in the small intestine.
[PDF p. 21]
Lecture 2.7. Lipids
Lipids are a heterogeneous group of biomolecules, with the common characteristic that they
have a low solubility in water .
Biological functions in lipids
-storage functions (store high amount of energy)
-structural function
-Cofactors for enzymes
-Act as signaling molecules, such as hormones
-Antioxidants (like tocopherols such as VitE)
Classification
Typically, we find two main
groups: those with fatty
acids and those without .
Lipids with fatty acids can be
further classified into storage
lipids and membrane lipids
(look at chart).
Biologically active lipids that
don’t contain fatty acids are
cholesterol, vitamin E,…
Fatty acids
Fatty acids are long carbon atom chains (hydrophobic) joined to a carboxylic head (polar
end), containing between 4 to 36 C. Most of them have an even number of carbons, and
they aren’t usually branched.
Depending on whether they have double bonds
or not, we find saturated and unsaturated
(mono or polyunsaturated/PUFA) fatty acids.
The saturation of the carbon chain changes its
direction and disposition in space: they can be
found in a CIS configuration (same direction) or
TRANS. The natural fatty acid is mostly found in
a CIS configuration.
Nomenclature: systematic (cis-9-octadecenoic acid) or common name (oleic acid). The
delta numbering of the carbon skeleton describes the position of the first carbon of the
alkene in relation to the carbonyl carbon (18:1 Δ9).The omega numbering describes the
location of the first carbon of the alkene in relation to the terminal methyl.
Examples of saturated fatty acids : palmitic acid, stearic acid,.. The higher the length, the
higher the melting point and the lower the solubility in water, due to the hydrophobic nature
of the carbon chain.
Examples of unsaturated fatty acids : oleic acid (olive oil), linoleic acid, linolenic acid,
arachidonic acid (precursor of leukotrienes, tromboxans,..).
[PDF p. 22]
Saturated fatty acids have a higher melting point because, due to their long straight carbon
chains, they can pack together better and more easily, making it more difficult to separate
them.
Essential fatty acids are those that we cannot produce endogenously, but we need them in
our diet: these are linoleic acid and linolenic acid (ALA) . ALA is an omega 3 unsaturated
fatty acid. These types of fatty acids have been linked to protection against heart disease,
that’s why they are considered healthy, although the mechanisms are unknown.
“Trans-fats” : hydrogenation of fatty acids is a process used to produce many foods, making
them taste better and giving better texture. This industrial process results in a partial
hydrogenation and in the double bonds adopting a trans configuration.
Triacylglycerols (storage lipids)
Solid triacylglycerols are known as fats, while liquid ones are known as oils.
They are the primary form of storage lipids. A triacylglycerol is made
up of Glycerol+3 fatty acid chains, linked together through
esterification of the OH groups in glycerol.
In a regular person,125,000 kcal are stored as fat and 2,000 kcal as
glycogen. This is because we can store twice the amount of energy in
1g fat than in 1g of glycogen. This is due to the carbon atoms in fat
being more reduced, and therefore, they undergo a longer oxidation
that produces more energy. In addition to this, we can obtain energy
from fats in a very fast way, which is more favorable for our body.
Biologically active lipids
- Steroid hormones
They are derivative from sterols such as cholesterol. Steroid hormones are synthesized
from cholesterol in gonads and adrenal glands. Many steroid hormones are male and female
sex hormones.
- Arachidonic acid derivatives
Enzymatic oxidation of arachidonic acid yields prostaglandins (inflammation and fever),
thromboxanes (formation of blood clots), leukotrienes (stimulates smooth muscle
contraction in lungs).
Pharmaceutical drugs such as paracetamol treat pain by blocking
the production of arachidonic acid.
- Vitamin D
VitD regulates calcium metabolism . It’s a lipid that comes from
1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol). A shortage of vitamin D
can result in osteomalacia or rickets.
[PDF p. 23]
- Vitamin A
Derived from Beta-carotene (a terpene), involved in the visual cycle .
- VItamin K
It’s a clotting cofactor with a similar structure to the previous vitamins.

Vitamin E

Acts as an antioxidant and it regulates the stress response in our body. It’s made up of the
polymerization of 3 isoprenes, resulting in a terpene. The addition of the hydrophilic head
results in an isoprenoid.
[PDF p. 24]
History
Lecture 2.8 & 2.9. Nucleotides and nucleic acids I and II
Friederich Miescher, in 1868, isolated from cells’ nuclei a substance that
contained phosphorous and that he called nuclein.
Frederick Griffith performed experiments in 1928 with virulent and nonvirulent
streptococcus pneumoniae, with the difference that one was encapsulated and
the other, not. He took the virulent, encapsulated
bacteria and killed them by heat. When they were
injected into mice, these did not die. But when he mixed the
dead lethal bacteria and nonlethal alive bacteria, and injected it
in mice, these died. He proved that there was a transforming
factor which Avory, McLeod and McCarthy identified as DNA
in 1944. They separated proteins and nucleic acids from the
dead lethal bacteria, and mixed each fraction with nonlethal
bacteria. Those which had been mixed with nucleic acids and
injected in mice produced the death of these, demonstrating it
was these nucleic acids which stored this genetic information.
In 1952 Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase performed the
definitive experiment, demonstrating that DNA is the genetic
material in living organisms. They grew a culture of bacteriophages in the presence of S35
(incorporated into proteins) and others in the presence of P32 (incorporated into nucleic
acids), for radioactive labelling. They observed that only when viruses were labeled with P32
were radioactive bacteria left behind.
Nucleic acids are linear polymers formed by nucleotides. They are made up of a
phosphate group joined to a pentose (ribose and deoxyribose) by an ester bond, and a
nitrogenous base joined by an N-glycosidic bond to the pentose.
Pentoses in nucleotides
The difference between ribose and deoxyribose is the
presence of an OH group in C2.
Nucleobases
Nitrogenous bases are aromatic molecules . We find
purines ( A and G ) and pyrimidines ( C,T,U ). The border of
the rings is characterized by their hydrophilic borders, while
the surfaces are flat and hydrophobic.
[PDF p. 25]
Nucleotides and polynucleotides
As the different components join, we
go from base, to nucleoside
(base+pentose) to nucleotide
(base+pentose+phosphate group).
Free nucleotides, such as ATP or
ADP, cAMp (cell signaling)
Polynucleotides . Depending on the
number, there are
oligonucleotides(less than 50) or
polynucleotides. The backbone is
formed by the bond between
phosphate and pentose. They are
directional molecules with a 5’ end
and 3’ end, each end being linked by
phosphodiester bridges.
The chains read from left to right, from the 5’ end to the 3’ end.
Structural levels
-Primary structure (order of bases)
-Secondary structure (3D conformation of the backbone)
-Tertiary structure (referred to the supercoiling of the chain)
RNA secondary structure : RNA molecules, which are single stranded chains of
nucleotides, can adopt very complex secondary structures. Their bases can pair with
complementary DNA and RNA bases.

DNA secondary structure : the chain forms a double helix.
DNA tertiary structure: DNA is found in the form of chromatin, more compact and
supercoiled around histones in the case of animals.

Nucleic acids stability
Under physiological conditions, the
N-glycosidic bond can undergo
spontaneous hydrolysis (every 24h)
generating apurinic residues. But there is
machinery in the cells which identifies these
sites and attempts to repair it.
In other cases, the amino group in a base can be lost in a deamination process, resulting
in the conversion, in the case of cytosine, into uracil. There is also machinery to avoid this
sort of mutation.
But why does DNA contain thymine and not uracil? A reason may be due to this
deamination process. How if not would the cell tell apart the mutated uracil bases from the
[PDF p. 26]
“original” ones? The repair mechanism would be unable to restore the original base and the
body would accumulate mutations.
Another difference between DNA and RNA is the pentose that makes up the molecule. RNA
has ribose and DNA, deoxyribose . This small difference has great consequences: under
physiological conditions, a new esther bond can be formed by the attack of an oxygen atom
(nucleophilic attack). This new bond breaks the chain. This breakage can only happen in
RNA as DNA does not possess that OH group. This has a great impact on the half life of the
molecule, making it millions of years for DNA while it’s minutes for RNA.
In addition to all of this, DNA is negatively charged, making it less prone to nucleophilic
attack and hydrolysis, and therefore more stable.
Nucleases
Nucleases are enzymes with phosphodiesterase activity, which hydrolyze the
phosphodiester bond and digest nucleic acids. There are exonucleases and
endonucleases. There is a specific group of endonucleases called restriction
endonucleases . Bacteria have learned to restrict the possibility of attack from foreign DNA
by means of these enzymes. They can identify specific regions within the DNA and generate
blunt ends or protruding ends. These are interesting for genetic engineering.
Discovery of the secondary structure of DNA
Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin were studying the
structure of DNA through X-ray diffraction, which helped to
determine its structure. The three fundamental evidences
that allowed the establishment of the secondary structure of
DNA were:
-X ray diffraction data, which suggested DNA had a double
helical linear structure, and that both strands were oriented
in an antiparallel fashion . DNA molecules exhibit 2
periodicities repeating along the length of the fiber, of 3.4 and
34 Armstrongs.
-Studies on the chemical composition of DNA, which informed
about the relative abundance of each nucleobase.
-Tautomeric forms: nucleobases were most frequently found
in their KETO and AMINO forms, info which was important for
Watson and Crick when they proposed their theory on how
nucleobases interact.
[PDF p. 27]
Additionally, we have the studies made by Chargaff :
1.The nucleobase composition of DNA varies from one species to another,
but remains the same within species.
2.DNA specimens from the same species but different tissues have the
same base composition.
3.The DNA composition of an individual does not change with age.
4.A=T and C=G in any given species.
This additional info helped Watson and Crick, who published their proposal for the DNA
double helix in 1953 .
“DNA is a helical linear molecule made up of two strands which intertwine, and are each
oriented in an antiparallel fashion. The nucleobases are oriented inwards and perpendicular
to the central axis, interacting with each other through H bonds in a very specific manner”
They proposed that this interaction involved the pairing of A and T, and C and G. They also
added that the 3.4 periodicity corresponded to the separation between bases, and the 34A
periodicity corresponded to each turn of the double helix. Major and minor grooves can be
observed on such strand. They also observed that
both strands are not the same, but
complementary.
Curiously, there are residues/functional groups on
the surface of the major grooves that inform which
base is found where, allowing for example
restriction enzymes to gain their specificity and
identify where each base is located.
Structural variations in DNA
-It’s a very flexible molecule . This is important: the genome can
measure up to 2m long, so it’s important that it can be rotated and
supercoiled to fit into the nucleus of a cell.
-The structure proposed by Watson and Crick is only one of many
that DNA can adopt. Depending on the degree of humidity ad
salinity in a solution, it can adopt different conformations, like the
so called A form, a right hand double helix in which the
nucleobases are not completely perpendicular to the axis, or the Z
form, where it adopts a left handed double helix conformation and
which is obtained in high salt concentrations.
Factors that influence the stability of DNA molecule
DNA is a very stable molecule.
-The main force of it’s stability is the interaction of stacked nucleobases within the double
helix, known as stacking interactions, like hydrophobic and van der waals forces, which
induce the helical conformations.
-The formation of H bonds between complementary bases stabilizes the double helix.
[PDF p. 28]
-But the electrostatic interactions between phosphate groups tend to destabilize the
double helix.
Denaturation and renaturation of DNA
DNA can undergo denaturation, a tensile dissociation of the two strands
which doesn’t involve any chemical change (covalent bonds). This is
important and necessary for almost all DNA processes (replication,
transcription,..). In the cell, it’s induced enzymatically . There are
enzymes called helicases which participate in the process of
denaturation. They start to separate the two strands and form what is
known as a replication bubble.
Outside the cell, heating DNA in the lab can also induce denaturation,
although it changes many of its physical properties such as the capacity
to absorb UV light. Absorption occurs in nucleic acids thanks to the
bases, which possess aromatic
groups that absorb UV light .
Denatured DNA, in single stranded conformation,
can absorb more UV light, a property known as
hyperchromicity . This is because the electrons in
this conformation can move more freely. This allows
us to determine the DNA melting point. While
increasing the temperature, we observe the UV light
absorption, which increases as the DNA becomes
denatured. A parameter can be derived from this property: the melting temperature (MT)
which corresponds to the point where half of the molecule has been denatured. Two different
DNA molecules will have different graphs and different MT. It has been observed that the
melting temperature will be determined by the proportion of C and G bases (because
they establish triple bonds). The more G and C in the molecule, the more energy will be
necessary to denature it. In the cell, helicase will have to work harder in G and C regions.
The molecule can be renatured also by reducing the temperature . This ability to denature
and renature is the base of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and many other new
technologies and techniques.
[PDF p. 29]

Knowing pH and pka values, you can know the ratio of conjugate base and conjugate acid
An example of this: (acetic acid/ acetate)

How does our body keep the pH in the right values?
Throughout a buffer solution, an acid-base equilibrium which shifts towards reactants or
products depending on the concentration of each in relation to the constant.

Blood is a buffer solution. The most
important conjugate pair in the blood is
H2CO3/HCO3-, the carbonate/bicarbonate
buffer .
The source of this carbonic acid is CO2.
But, can we control the pH in our blood? Yes! If we don’t release CO2 and retain it in our
blood, it will react with water as it is in equilibrium, giving place to a higher concentration of
H2CO3, which at the same time increases the concentration of protons and decreases pH.
This can happen when someone stops breathing.
If the body is in alkalosis, it will try to compensate this by provoking hypoventilation, to try
and decrease gas exchange and therefore decrease the pH.
If the body is in acidosis, it will try to compensate this by provoking hyperventilation, thus
extracting CO2 from the blood and shifting the equilibrium, removing H3O+.

TBL 2.2. Enzyme kinetics and inhibition
Effect of temperature : increasing temperature will increase the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
rate, but there is an optimum temperature. When we cross a line, the rate decreases
because the protein is denaturalized.
Effect of pH : there is also an optimum pH, but if it’s too low or too high, the enzyme will
change its conformation because it becomes protonated or deprotonated and the rate
decreases.
Effect of substrate concentration: it also affects the rate of the reaction as it favors the
formation of ES complex. But enzymes can be saturated with substrate and reach a point
where adding more substrate won’t affect the rate of the reaction.
Michaelis-Menten model
First, the enzyme binds to the substrate,
forming the ES complex. After this,
catalysis can occur. There are two steps:
binding and catalysis .
Michaelis menten equation: Km =Michaelis constant, which depends on the enzyme. High
Km=low affinity. Low Km=high affinity. It represents the affinity of the enzyme for the
substrate.
Interestingly, an enzyme can work with more than one substrate, but it works at different
rates depending on the affinity.
This equation (straight line) allows us to
graphically calculate in a precise way, vmax
(maximum rate) and Km, depending on
where the line intersects with the y axis and
x axis.
[PDF p. 32]
The turnover number (catalytic constant ot Kcat ) measures the number of substrate
molecules that an enzyme molecule can convert to product per unit of time . The higher
the number, the better. It’s measured in s-1.
Catalytic efficiency
To calculate the specificity constant, we divide Kcat/Km . Efficiency will be higher if the
affinity (low Km) and conversion speed are higher too.
Inhibitors
There are reversible and irreversible inhibitors. Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor.
Irreversible = permanently inactivate the enzyme
Reversible = can bind to and can dissociate from the enzyme. Often used as drugs to slow
down enzyme activity.
Types of reversible inhibition


Competitive inhibition: mechanism of action where
the inhibitor is able to bind only to the free
enzyme. This only affects the Km, because it
affects the capacity of the enzyme to bind to the
substrate. But once it’s bound to the substrate, the
inhibitor doesn’t do anything, it doesn’t affect the
catalysis.
A patient with methanol intoxication can be treated with
ethanol, because it is a competitive inhibitor of methanol.
Another example, statins, which are used to reduce cholesterol. It competes with
cholesterol for the binding site.
                  **Acompetitive:** in this situation, the inhibitor



binds to the enzyme once the substrate is bound. There
is a decrease in Km and in vmax, so the efficiency
remains constant. The inhibitor only binds to the ES
complex, not to the individual enzyme. Therefore it
doesn’t affect the affinity, and Km apparently decreases
because of the shift in equilibrium (increase in affinity),
but it inhibits catalytic function and therefore, vmax.
[PDF p. 33]

Non competitive inhibition: Substrate and

inhibitor bind to different areas . The
enzyme binds independently to each. There
is no change in Km, while there is a
decrease in vmax . The affinity remains the
same (as the binding site is independent for
substrate and inhibitor), but Vmax decreases
as catalytic function is affected.

TBL 2.3. Protein structure-function relationship
Pluricellular organisms need to distribute oxygen, but oxygen solubility in water is very low.
We need something else. For this, we use proteins, but we don’t have any aminoacids that
are able to bind to oxygen. On the other hand, transition metals do, although they are very
reactive and harmful for our cells.
Therefore, they appear bound to other organic molecules to reduce their
reactivity. This is the case of hemoglobin, in which the heme group is
bound to a protein. It has Fe2+ inside the heme group, which will be able
to bind oxygen.
This is also the case of myoglobin, mainly found in muscles as an O2
storage molecule.
MYOGLOBIN
Myoglobin is a globular protein (90% of the molecules are alpha
helices), with an ion bound in the middle. It has only one binding site
for O2, and a very high affinity for it (exponential graph), which
allows it to act as an O2 storage molecule.
Nevertheless, this tight-binding to O2
doesn’t allow myoglobin to act as an
oxygen transporter, as it will not release it when in contact with
the tissues (even when pO2 is decreased in said tissues).
Lowering its affinity for O2 could make it a better transporter, but
it would imply that not enough O2 is taken up in the lungs, and
O2 delivery would still be insufficient.
For a truly effective transport which can meet our body’s needs,
affinity must vary with pO2, as occurs during hemoglobin O2
transport thanks to its multiple binding sites and cooperativity
properties.
HEMOGLOBIN
Hemoglobin is the molecule which acts as the O2 carrier between the lungs and other
tissues.It’s a globular tetramer with a quaternary structure (a dimer of dimers, 2 alpha
chains and 2 beta chains), and therefore has different binding sites. It has 4 heme groups
found in the inner part of the molecule.
It has a homotropic regulation (the ligand is also the regulator).
An important characteristic of hemoglobin is that
it contains a histidine residue, which binds the
Fe2+ ion to the protein and retains the heme
group in position.
Fe2+ therefore appears bound to the proximal
histidine residue, heme group and O2.
[PDF p. 35]
COOPERATIVITY makes hemoglobin a good O2
transporter. Due to this property, it has different
affinities, depending on the amount of oxygen present in
the environment. Myoglobin has only one binding site with
a particular affinity; it doesn’t have this property.
But hemoglobin has more than one binding site for
oxygen.
Also, the binding sites aren’t independent, they are
connected and interact between them. When the ligand
is incorporated into one of the binding sites, it
modifies the affinity of the other binding sites.
This property (cooperativity) gives out a sigmoidal
curve.
Hemoglobin in blood
Oxygenated blood (arterial blood) has a high O2 saturation
(hemoglobin is able to bind to almost 100% of O2 in the lungs).
When in contact with tissues, it releases around 40% of the oxygen
(when pO2 is 40 mmHg in tissues and 100 mmHg in blood).
Deoxygenated blood (venous blood) has a much lower O2
saturation, and travels to the lungs to be reoxygenated thanks to
the difference in pO2 (40 mmHg in blood, 104 mmHg in lungs).
The difference between arterial and venous blood colours is due to
the light absorption spectrum of hemoglobin.
Pulse oximeters measure oxygen saturation.
T and R stages of hemoglobin
- T stage stands for tense
- R stage stands for relaxed
Hemoglobin has different quaternary structures (T
and R), each with different affinities for O2. In
the relaxed state, subunits are more able to move
and it is easier to incorporate oxygen (T stage
affinity for O2 < R stage affinity).
The main secondary structure of the chains in
hemoglobin is alpha-helix.
[PDF p. 36]
-
What happens when O2 binds to hemoglobin?
When O2 binds, it pulls the Fe2+ ion with it, which will at the same time move the
proximal histidine and therefore, the whole subunit. O2 changes the conformation
of the subunit through the pulling of the proximal histidine. This simple
movement changes everything: it changes the interaction with the other subunits .
Some of the ionic bonds will be broken, and hemoglobin goes into the R state .
So once one O2 molecule binds to hemoglobin, this will favour the binding of other
oxygen molecules until we have 4 O2 bound to heme groups in hemoglobin.
Physiological factors that regulate the affinity for O2
● pH: a certain histidine interacts with an aspartate, because
histidine (+) at physiological pH interacts with aspartate (-).
They form ionic interactions, and the hemoglobin is found
in the T stage. But pH can have an effect on this: Histidine
can be protonated or deprotonated, depending on the pH.
“When pH goes down, the affinity of hemoglobin for O2 is lower”, because the
lowering of pH causes more acid to form (histidine, +), therefore reinforcing the T
stage.
Ultimately, this favours oxygen release (as it is not in the R state) in tissues, as pH in
tissues is lower due to the generation of CO2 during catabolism. In the lungs, the
opposite effect occurs, and O2 binds to hemoglobin (pH in lungs > pH in blood). This
is known as the “Bohr effect”.

2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate: it stabilizes the T state, and is therefore a negative
heterotrophic regulator. “When 2,3-BPG is present the affinity of hemoglobin for
oxygen is lower”.
As 2,3-BPG reduces the affinity, it’s partly necessary for the correct transport of
oxygen and its release into the tissues. If it weren’t present, hemoglobin’s affinity
for oxygen wouldn’t allow it to work as an O2 carrier.
BPG concentration can be regulated, for example, by the pressure of oxygen in the
environment (altitude), which subsequently modifies the affinity of Hb for O2.
aklectures.com/lecture/myoglobin-and-hemoglobin/high-altitude-and-2-3-bgp

[PDF p. 37]
How can O2 be transported from a mother to the fetus in an efficient way during
pregnancy?
There is a specific hemoglobin in the fetus, fetal-hemoglobin, which is
different to adult hemoglobin. The affinity of fetal-hemoglobin for
oxygen is higher, and therefore, the oxygen transported by the
mother’s hemoglobin will be transported to the fetus due to this higher
affinity.
This increased affinity is due to a gamma chain in fetal hemoglobin,
which has a lower capacity to bind BPG, therefore making its affinity
for oxygen higher.
Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Clinical Case
“A child is found with reduced consciousness, hypoxic, cyanotic,… They
measure carboxyhemoglobin and it is higher than 50%; normal levels are
around 2%”
This is a case of carbon monoxide poisoning (CO). It’s responsible for
half of the deaths due to poisoning in the world. Molecularly, CO is very
similar to O2, so it binds to hemoglobin. The affinity of hemoglobin for CO is
20,000 times higher than that for O2.
To avoid CO binding due to this incredibly high affinity, we have a distal
histidine (different from the proximal histidine). Thanks to this histidine, the
affinity of hemoglobin for CO is reduced to 250 times higher, and allows us
to maintain normal CO levels in the body.
Carboxyhemoglobin is normally found in levels of 2% in the general population, except in
smokers ; they have higher levels of CO in circulation, which reduces the delivery of O2
to the tissues.
During CO poisoning, like in the case of this child, who was
having half the capacity to bind to oxygen, O2 delivery
becomes insufficient. Not only due to reduced binding sites,
but also, the binding of CO induces the R state, and causes
hemoglobin to bind more tightly to the other O2 residues; the
curve is no longer sigmoidal.
In conclusion, the capacity to bind to oxygen is lower
(lesser binding sites) and the capacity to deliver oxygen is
also lower. Only 10% of the oxygen that is taken up is
delivered to the tissues.

Lecture 3.1 and 3.2. Molecular structure of membranes I & II
Membranes are intelligent barriers that respond to extracellular stimuli if they have the
need to do so.
Functions of membranes


They limit the cell boundaries


Allow the transport of molecules


They allow compartmentalization of substances and processes within the cytoplasm. They
separate energy-producing and energy-consuming processes and keep proteolytic enzymes
away from important cellular proteins.


Common features of membranes


Membranes are made up of a bilipid layer, which can contain embedded proteins and
saccharides bound to them. It is asymmetric.


They form spontaneously in aqueous solution


Fluid mosaic model proposed by Singer and Nicholson


Types of membrane lipids
They all share the property of being amphipathic, with a polar head and a hydrophobic
tail . They differ in:
                                    - The **backbone**, which can

be Glycerol-3-phosphate or
Sphingosine (long chain
amino-alcohol).
                                    - The second difference

between the types of membrane
lipids are the polar heads .
                                    They also differ in the **fatty**

acid chains which bind to them.
Therefore, we find: Glycerophospholipids, Sphingomyelins (sphingosine and phosphate)
and Glycosphingolipids (not bound to a phosphate group, but to a mono or
oligosaccharide).
Lastly, in the membrane, we can find cholesterol .
Phospholipids = contain phosphate; Glycolipids = contain saccharides instead
GLYCEROPHOSPHOLIPIDS
They are the primary
constituents of cell
membranes .
[PDF p. 39]
They are made up of two fatty acids which form ester linkage with the 1st and 2nd hydroxyl
groups of L-glycerol-3-phosphate . The head group is charged at physiological pH.
We can find different types of molecules bound to the phosphate group, like ethanolamine,
choline, serine, inositol,…
Phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylserine are the most
abundant in plasma membranes.
We can find phosphatidylinositol, which is very important for the reactive
properties of the membrane. Some carbons of the inositol can be
phosphorylated, by kinases, to act as a recruiter for signaling molecules. It’s a
precursor of molecules with an important role in intracellular signal transduction.
It can be released from the membrane as a second messenger (IP3).
[PDF p. 40]
Lastly cardiolipins, which have a phosphatidic acid bound to a glycerol and another
phosphatidic acid. We know they play an important role in the machinery of the respiratory
processes carried out in the mitochondria. Very abundant in cardiac tissue .
Membrane phospholipids are
sources of important second
messengers after
enzyme-mediated hydrolysis.
There are a set of hydrolases
which hydrolyze specific
phospholipid bonds, like PLA1
(releases fatty acid bound at C1),
PLA2 (f.a. in C2), PLC (in the
case of inositol, it would release inositol-1,4,5-triphosphate /IP3, which is a calcium channel
opener, and diacylglycerol/DAG which activates PKC), PLD,… They could, for example,
trigger the release of arachidonic acid which is a precursor for eicosanoids.
There are glycerophospholipids containing ether
groups, like plasmalogens, which are very abundant in
mitochondrial membranes.
Another lipid with ether function is the
Platelets-Activating Factor, which contains choline and
acetyl. It’s secreted by white blood cells and stimulates
platelet aggregation.
SPHINGOLIPIDS
Instead of glycerol, we find sphingosine as the backbone, a long chain amino alcohol. A
fatty acid is linked to sphingosine via an amide linkage (NOT an ester linkage). A polar
head is connected to sphingosine by a glycosidic or phosphodiester bond (different head
group substituents).
Types of sphingolipids:

Ceramides : closely related with apoptotic
processes. When the amount of ceramides
increases in membranes, it signals apoptosis .

Sphingomyelins : formed when phosphocholine
joins the sphingosine.
Glucosylcerebroside, formed by the addition of
glucose.
Lactosylceramide (a type of globoside ),
formed by the linkage of di-,tri- or
tetrasaccharides.
Gangliosides, formed by the linkage of
complex oligosaccharides.
[PDF p. 41]
Sphingomyelins, which are highly present in the
membranes of neurons. It’s abundant in the
myelin sheaths that surround the axons . It’s
formed by sphingosine+amide-linked fatty
acid+phosphocholine attached to the alcohol.
Structurally, it is very similar to
phosphatidylcholine.
Glycosphingolipids, where we can find more simple
ones like cerebrosides (mainly present in the
membranes of neurons, where the head group is a
neutral monosaccharide such as glucose or
galactose ) or more complex ones like gangliosides
(head group composed by many sugars which are
branched and bound together. They are charged heads,
because they contain at least one acidic saccharide .
They are usually found in the extracellular side of the
membrane, because one of their main functions is to
participate in cell-to-cell recognition, and so, they are
involved in organ transplant rejection).
Glycosphingolipids determine, in part, the type of blood group . The core
antigen is present in all groups, but in addition, A groups contain A type
antigens (N-acetyl-galactose) and B groups, the B antigen (galactose). AB
groups express both antigens.
Our blood type depends on the type of glycosylation RBCs undergo, which
is determined at the level of our DNA. It encodes for specific enzymes
which will add one sugar or another, giving rise to our blood type
Turnover of membranes
Membranes are constantly flipping the lipids that make up the bilipidic layer. Defects in the
turnover of membrane lipids leads to a number of
diseases. If lipids which have been found to have errors
are not degraded, it can alter the cell functioning.
SPHINGOLIPIDOSIS comes from the lack of a certain
enzyme, which is meant to degrade these membrane
lipids. They accumulate inside of lysosomes and disrupt
their function and morphology.
Symptoms: mental retardation, blindness, liver failure,…
Examples: Gaucher’s disease, Niemann-Pick disease (lack of sphingomyelinase ),
Tay-Sachs disease (shortage of hexosaminidase- A)… Now we know that many Parkinson’s
diseases come from a reduced activity in these enzymes, a lack of glucocerebrosidase
activity (exam question).
[PDF p. 42]
Sterols and Cholesterol
Its structure is Ciclopentaneperhydrophenantrane .
Most of the molecule is hydrophobic, but it has a polar
hydrophilic head group. It fills the gaps in lipidic
membranes, so membranes with cholesterol are more
rigid . The higher the cholesterol, the lower the fluidity.
It’s a precursor of many molecules, such as Vitamin D.
Composition of membranes and asymmetry
The composition differs depending on organisms, tissues, organelles,… (tabla)
The two leaflets have different membrane compositions
Membrane rafts
There are parts of the membranes with a very specific lipidic
composition, microdomains, which contain higher amounts of
cholesterol than surrounding regions and higher amounts of
sphingolipids, which makes these regions much more rigid. These
areas contain many receptors, such as insulin receptors. These raft
areas mainly carry out endocytosis.
There are raft portions of the membrane that are bound to caveolin,
which favors invaginations and therefore allows receptor mediated
endocytosis .

Lecture 3.3. The extracellular matrix
The cellular matrix is a three dimensional network of extracellular molecules, such as
fibrous proteins and glycoconjugates, mostly synthesized by fibroblasts (fiber-producing
cells). It’s function is to provide strength, stiffness, elasticity, and physical barrier in tissues. It
largely determines the structure and function of our tissues.
Connective tissue is especially rich in extracellular matrix. Variations in the types of
molecules within the connective tissue account for the incredible diversity of tissues and
organs in our body.
FIBROUS PROTEINS
Fibrous proteins are polypeptide chains composed of repeating elements, forming linear
structures that arrange in long fibers or sheets.
Several types of fibrous proteins, including α-keratin, collagen, elastin, fibronectin and
laminin, are found within the extracellular matrix of different tissues.
Many fibrous proteins bind to integrins, transmembrane receptors that mediate cell–cell and
cell–matrix interactions.
Matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) are enzymes that catalyze the cleavage of proteins found
in the extracellular matrix. MMPs continuously remodel the extracellular matrix to control for
cell movement and responses.
Alpha-keratin
It’s a fibrous protein formed by 2 alpha helices which wrap, forming a left handed helical
structure . It’s rich in hydrophobic amino acids. These fibrils formed by keratin fibers are
what we find in hair. When together, the fibers form disulfide bonds between each other,
making the structure more stable. The shape of the hair is determined by these bonds. If we
want to break these bridges to, for example, curl your hair, you have to first reduce the S
which are bound together to SH. Once this is done, you can
reshape the hair, creating new bonds by reoxidizing the S.
Naturally curly hair and naturally straight hair difere in the
way these disulfide bonds are established.
Collagen
Scurvy is a disease which became more common in the 15th century. A Dr, Dr LInd, carried
out the first clinical trial and divided 12 sick sailors into 6 groups of 2. Daily, all patients
received the same diet together with different kinds of treatment.
After 6 days Dr Lind had to stop the trial, but amazingly two of the sailors had almost
recovered, the ones treated with citrics.
This is due to collagen : it’s an important component of connective
tissue (bones, tendons, cartilage,…). Each collagen chain is a long
left handed suprahelical structure with abundance of Glycine,
Proline and Hydroxyproline (which stabilizes the structure of
collagen and favors the interaction with other collagen fibers). 3
collagen chains intertwine and form a triple helix.
There is an enzyme responsible for hydroxylation of proline,
prolyl-hydroxylase . It’s an enzyme with a proteic part and a
cofactor, a prosthetic group: ascorbic acid / Vitamin C,
generally found in citrics. Its deficit causes teeth to fall out,
skin rashes,…
[PDF p. 44]
Elastin
Elastin is the major protein rich in hydrophobic amino
acids, such as alanine, valine, glycine and proline,
found in elastic fibers of the extracellular matrix. It
permits tissues to return to their original shape after
they have been stretched . This is of special
importance to blood vessels, which expand and
contract repeatedly in response to changes in
intravascular pressure.
Fibronectin
Fibronectin is a protein dimer, consisting of two nearly
identical polypeptide chains linked by two C-terminal
disulfide bonds. It helps position cells within the extracellular matrix. Some cells use the
fibronectin matrix to migrate, which is particularly important during embryonic development
and wound healing. Fibronectin is also necessary for cellular division .
Laminin
Laminin is a heterotrimeric protein (α, β, and γ subunits). Laminin forms sheet-like
networks that serve as the “glue” between different tissues.
GLYCOCONJUGATES
Glycoconjugates are the other main molecular components of the extracellular matrix .
Like fibrous proteins, they have structural properties and communicate cells with the
extracellular environment. There are three main types of glycoconjugates: proteoglycans,
glycoproteins and glycolipids
Proteoglycans
They are macromolecules composed of a protein core bond by glycosidic linkages to long
chains of glycosaminoglycans . All glycosaminoglycans in our body, with the exception of
hyaluronic acid and heparin, are found in proteoglycans. In contrast to fibrous proteins,
which provide resistance to stretching forces, proteoglycans provide resistance to
compressive forces . They also affect other cellular activities, such as growth and
adhesion .
There are several types of proteoglycans that differ in the glycosaminoglycan chains.
Many are free in the extracellular matrix but some are integral membrane structures.
Proteoglycans are the main components of connective tissues such as cartilage, where they
bind to each other, as well as to fibrous proteins, mainly collagen. The proteoglycan in
cartilage is rich in keratan sulfate
and chondroitin sulfate . The
complementary functions of
proteoglycan and collagen
molecules give cartilage its
resilience (cartilage can withstand a
high compressive load and then
reexpand to its previous dimensions
when that load is relieved).
[PDF p. 45]
Glycoproteins
Glycoproteins are proteins covalently linked to carbohydrates . Normally, these
carbohydrates are small, branched and structurally diverse, both in terms of monosaccharide
types and glycosidic bonds.
Oligosaccharide chains can bind to the protein by two different
linkages:

O-glycosidic bond : the anomeric carbon of the first
residue in the oligosaccharide, normally
N-acetylgalactosamine, binds to the hydroxyl group of
serine or threonine residues in the protein.
N-glycosidic bond : the anomeric carbon of the first
residue in the oligosaccharide, normally
N-acetylglucosamine, binds to the amide of an
asparagine residue.

Glycosylation of proteins occurs after their synthesis in the
endoplasmic reticulum and in transit through the Golgi
apparatus. More than half of human proteins are glycoproteins.
The oligosaccharide chain(s) in a protein exerts unique functions, such as affecting the
folding of the protein, altering polarity and solubility and establishing a recognition site
by other molecules, which allows the binding to enzymes, receptors,…
Lectins are proteins that bind carbohydrates with high specificity and affinity. Lectins serve
in a wide variety of cell-cell recognition, signaling and adhesion processes . Some lectins
bind to mannose-6-phosphate residues in newly synthesized proteins and transfer them to
the lysosomes. Secretins, a family of plasma membrane lectins, are involved in the
movement of leukocytes through the capillary wall, from blood to tissues at sites of
infection or inflammation. Several pathogens attach to their host cells through their
glycoproteins or their lectins (Influenza virus, Helicobacter pylori, Bordetella pertussis or HIV
virus, among many others).
Erythropoietin is a protein that is used to increase the production of erythrocytes
(erythropoiesis) in the bone marrow. It’s used as a treatment for anemia. It’s a
naturally-synthesized protein in our system; kidneys are the main epo producing organs in
our body. So if it’s injected, it’s difficult to recognize. But glycosylation beat Armstrong.
Erythropoietin isn’t only proteic. It is made up of aminoacid chains and sugars
(oligosaccharides). These are bound to the protein by covalent bonds (either O-glycosidic or
N-glycosidic). The pattern of glycosylation in bacteria and humans is different. When
samples from Armstrong were taken, recombinant EPO was identified due to glycosylation.
Glycolipids
Glycolipids are lipids derived from sphingosine conjugated to carbohydrates.
Cerebrosides consist of a ceramide with a single sugar residue (glucose or galactose).
In gangliosides the ceramide is bound to an oligosaccharide chain .
Glycolipids are located in the plasma membrane, where they can have cell recognition
functions.
[PDF p. 46]
Some oligosaccharide motives of gangliosides, and of some
glycoproteins, determine human ABO blood groups .
Depending on the glycosyltransferases types present in an
individual, gangliosides contain different oligosaccharides.
Blood type A and B contain an additional
N-acetylgalactosamine or galactose . The
oligosaccharides of type A and B are immunogenic,
whereas the oligosaccharide of type O is not. As a result,
antibodies to A and to B antigens occur naturally in the
blood of people whose red blood cells lack the
corresponding antigen. These antibodies may cause
intravascular destruction of red blood cells if given
inadvertently during a blood transfusion.

Lecture 3.4. Microtransport through the membrane
Microtransport occurs whenever there isn’t a deformation of the plasma membrane.
Examples: pass of ions, H2O and small molecules like glucose.
Two main types of micro transport:
-Passive transport (no energy)
-simple diffusion
-facilitated diffusion

Active transport

-primary
-secondary
PASSIVE TRANSPORT
No energy consumption. From high to low concentration
1. Simple diffusion
Affected by size, polarity, liposolubility, gradient (concentration) and charge. Molecules which
are transported by simple diffusion: gasses (O2), hydrophobic substances like benzene,
small hydrophilic uncharged polar molecules like water, ethanol, glycerol,…
2. Facilitated diffusion
Transport facilitated by proteins. Types of proteins:
-Carriers (for molecules such as glucose)
-Membrane channels (ion channels,
aquaporins,..)
This type of transport is regulated and selective
(Na+, K+,… always in specific pairs and ways)
Carrier proteins can be saturated, but membrane
channels, as long as they’re open, can allow the
pass of unlimited ions.
-
Facilitated diffusion regulation:
-Voltage gated
-Ligand gated (extracellular ligand)
-Ligand gated (intracellular ligand)
-Mechanically gated (ex: cilia in the ear, when stimulated, open the channels and allow the
stimuli to travel to the brain)
-
Types of transport in facilitated diffusion:
-Uniport (ex: glucose transporter)
-Symport (ex: glucose and Na+ transport)
-Antiport (ex: HCO3-/Cl-)
[PDF p. 48]
Passive transport through carriers
It occurs down electrochemical gradient. There is a binding to the solute which produces a
conformational change. These kinds of transporters can get saturated. They are more
efficient for when we have a low concentration of glucose, but as said, it can get saturated.
Passive transport through membrane channels. Transport of H20
H20 can be transported by simple diffusion, or by facilitated diffusion
through proteins called aquaporins . Aquaporins are very abundant in
the membrane of kidney cells, which filter 180L per day but are able to
reabsorb 178L thanks to these aquaporins. This facilitated diffusion is
much faster than simple diffusion.
Related to diabetes insipidus: it can be due to
an alteration in AQP2 (aquaporin 2) or ADH.
This person won’t have the right amount of
bodily fluids. Symptoms: polyurea (lots of urine), increased thirst,
dehydration and hypovolemia (reduce blood volume).
ACTIVE TRANSPORT
Happens against electrochemical gradient, so there will be an energy and ATP
expenditure. The protein binds to the solute, causing a conformational change. It’s selective
and regulated, and can also get saturated.
1. Direct active transport / primary active transport
Ex: Na+/K + pump: sodium ions bind to the transporter. ATP appears at
the site and is degraded into ADP+P, releasing energy. This causes a
conformational change in the protein. The 3 sodium ions are released
outside the membrane, and the new structure of the protein has a high
affinity for K+ ions, which now bind to the channel.
[PDF p. 49]
This causes the release of the P atom that had remained bound to
the protein, and this release changes the protein structure back to
its original conformation, releasing two K+ into the cell. Both sodium
and potassium ions move against concentration gradient, thanks to
the constant expenditure of ATP . It’s an example of antiport .
Ex: ABC (ATP binding cassette): They incorporate molecules into the cell and release
xenobiotics, drugs, toxic agents,… Cells which overexpress this transporter send out
more drugs than usual, which results in resistance to chemotherapy (multidrug resistance
proteins).
Ex: CFTR protein (Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator), which regulates
the expelance of Cl-.
In a normal respiratory tract, this transporter expels Cl- and it accumulates outside the cell.
In a person with CYSTIC FIBROSIS, there is a mutation in CFTR, making these
transporters unable to work. CFTR is unable to transport Cl- out of the cell, therefore H2O is
drawn in by osmosis and the mucus layer becomes thicker. This means that cilia can’t
move and function correctly, which results in infection .
There is no known cure, and life
expectancy is less than 40 years,
but treatment has improved by
preventing and controlling
infections, removing mucus from
the lungs and in extreme cases,
lung transplant.
New drug treatment has
increased life expectancy.
2. Indirect active transport / secondary active transport
ATP is broken down but used indirectly. A 1st transporter breaks down ATP to create a
gradient, and 2nd transporter makes use of this established gradient to move a
substance against the previous gradient.
A substance such as glucose is pumped from lower to higher concentration, against
gradient, through a symport protein of glucose and sodium. Na+ does go in following it’s
gradient and therefore, without ATP expenditure, because the gradient has been
previously established by the Na+/ K+ pump. Sodium-potassium pump then expels
sodium back to the exterior of the cell with the use of ATP, restarting the cycle.
[PDF p. 50]
Lecture 3.5. Macrotransport through the membrane
Macrotransport involves transportation processes which involve modifications in the
plasma membrane. It transports large molecules which can’t go in through micro transport.
-Requires energy
-Involves the plasma membrane, cytoskeletal proteins and organelles
Types of macrotransport
-
Endocytosis
Incorporation of external molecules
-
Exocytosis
Release of cell components
(Endocytic-exocytic cycle)
ENDOCYTOSIS
A. Pinocytosis
Liquid and small dissolved particles are incorporated into the cell. Seen under the
microscope, we observe small vesicles under 0.1 um diameter with a clear content,
incorporating liquid and small dissolved particles.
There are different types of pinocytosis:
- Non-receptor mediated pinocytosis : it’s a continuous and non-selective process.
Caveolin is one of the proteins which forms Caveolae, invaginations which favour
endocytosis ( 0.05 micrometers, non receptor mediated pinocytosis vesicles)
- Macropinocytosis : also continuous and non-selective
- Receptor-mediated pinocytosis : it’s a specific and selective
process. This type of pinocytosis forms vesicles with an electron
dense coating, made of clathrin.

Receptor binds to a ligand and initiates an
invagination.
Once the receptor is joined to the ligand, different
proteins will join to the receptor and assemble:
adaptins and clathrin. Together, they
form the coating.
Dynamin then joins and strangles the
vesicle, detaching it from the
membrane, with a coating which

surrounds the content.

HSP70 (ATPase activity) releases
adaptin+clathrin coating to be recycled.

[PDF p. 51]

Clathrin is the main component of the coating. It’s a
protein formed by triskelions (3 heavy chain and 3
light chain peptides). These triskelions organize in a
way that results in a structure that resembles a
honeycomb. 36 triskelions are required to form this

clathrin structure.


Endosomes are organelles which receive vesicles
from plasma membrane or Golgi apparatus.
Early endosomes receive vesicles from the plasma membrane and have
irregular shapes. They form very rapidly (1 min) and we can observe
ATPases on the membrane which decrease pH by pumping H+. They’re
necessary because enzymes such as hydrolases, which carry out digestion,
work at very low pH, hence the need for this ATPase. These endosomes can
attach to the cytoskeleton and are moved to rich areas of the cell where they


bind to other vesicles.
 - **Late endosomes** take 15 mins to form. Vesicles are incorporated coming

from the Golgi apparatus, which contain the enzymes that are going to allow
digestion. Therefore, these late endosomes differentiate into secondary
lysosomes.


Endocytosed molecules include: Hormones (such as glucagon and insulin), growth
factors, lipoproteins,…


LDL/low density lipoprotein : its incorporation is carried out to maintain correct


levels of cholesterol in the blood.

LDL is recognized by its receptor and
surrounded by clathrin coating.
After uncoating, the receptor is recycled
and returns to the plasma membrane the
vesicle fuses with an early endosome
which is then transferred to the lysosome

Lysosomes degrade cholesterol and

Abnormal levels of cholesterol can come from:
 - **Excessive intake** of cholesterol in the diet ( **hypercholesterolemia**, leads to

Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) binds to EGF. It

B. Phagocytosis
Solid substances (large particles and microorganisms) are incorporated into the cell. Seen

Protozoa uses it as a regular way of eating, while higher organisms use it as a mechanism of

First, target recognition and adhesion occurs, which happens
by opsonization : a pathogen is marked for ingestion-destruction

by a phagocyte, and antibodies bind
to them.


Secondly, target penetration
takes place by the emission of

Can happen by non-receptor (through endothelial cells
in capillaries and the pass of substances into the blood)
or receptor mediated endocytosis (maternal IgA to
newborns).

Exocytosed materials include disposable material (products of digestion and metabolism)
and cell synthesized material (cell membrane components and extracellular matrix,
enzymes, hormones,…).
Anoikis leads to programmed cell death when a cell loses its capacity to adhere to other
cells or ECM, and therefore, its capacity to communicate.
Types of exocytosis:

Constitutive : it’s a continuous process of exocytosis.

Regulated : triggered by an external signal. For example, the pancreatic acinar
cells, which release digestive enzymes when necessary. It’s also the case of cells
which release mucin in the lungs (globet cells) and endocrine cells, which carry out

Lecture 3.6 & 3.7. Organization of the cytoskeleton I and II
The cytoskeleton is not rigid, it’s really active, made up of components that are in constant
polymerization. We can find microtubules (made of tubulin, of 25 nanometers),
microfilaments (made of actin, of 7 nanometers), and thick filaments (made of myosin, of
15 nanometers), and intermediate filaments (keratin and some others, of 8-12 nanometers
of diameter).
MICROTUBULES
Microtubules are spread in the cytoplasm, and are made
of alpha and beta dimers of tubulin. They form a hollow
circle of 13 dimers of alpha and beta tubulin.
The properties of this microtubules are:
- Polarity:
A microtubule has a +end and a -end. The concentration
of alpha-beta-tubulin heterodimers for the microtubule to
start polymerizing through the -end is higher than the one
required for the polymerization to occur in the +end.
Therefore, the growth happens from the +end, which
explains the polarity of microtubules.
- Dynamic instability:
For polymerization to occur, the alpha-beta-tubulin
dimer has to be bound to GTP . When it’s incorporated
into the microtubule, beta-tubulin GTP dissociates into
GDP. When beta-tubulin is bound to GDP, it’s more
unstable than when bound to GTP.
When there is high GTP-tubulin concentration in the
medium, these dimers are quickly added to the +end of
the microtubule. But if this amount of GTP-tubulin decreases, the hydrolysis rate of GTP
(which results in GDP) will be higher than the rate of incorporation of GTP-tubulin. Therefore
the +end will become highly unstable and suffer depolymerization. In conclusion, the
amount of GTP-tubulin present in the medium is critical to determine
polymerization/depolymerization. This property is called dynamic instability.
Functions of microtubules:


Maintenance of cell shape and polarity


Cell division (spindle formation, chromatid segregation)


Transport of vesicles and organelles inside the cell


Cell movement


MAPs
The cell controls the process of polymerization and depolymerization. To control it, we have
different proteins in the cell that modify the behaviour of microtubules. They are called
microtubule associated proteins (MAPs) .
[PDF p. 55]

Non-motor MAPs: they are related to the stabilization and cross-linking of
microtubules (structural functions). For example, MAP2 (cross-links microtubules in a
parallel position) and Tau (it stabilizes microtubules and allows them to group in a
parallel disposition). In Alzheimer’s disease, there is a hyperphosphorylation of Tau,
leading it to form clusters in the neurons. These interfere with
the normal mechanisms of vesicle transport in the neurons,
which causes their death by apoptosis.

Motor MAPs: they are in charge of vesicle trafficking
throughout an ATP-dependent transport. Two examples are
kinases (move vesicles form the -end to the +end) and
dyneins (move vesicles form the +end to the-end).



Agents that block the polymerization of microtubules
- Colchicine, which is used in cytogenetics. It is also a therapeutic agent, since it treats
gout.
It’s used as an anti-inflammatory drug because it blocks leukocyte recruitment (diaperesis) in
the site of inflammation by avoiding their migration.
- Vinca alkaloids such as vincristine, vinblastine; used to treat hematologic tumors.
Agents that block depolymerization
- Taxol, used to treat solid tumors. It was first found in the Yow tree.
Complex organization of microtubules in centrioles and motile cilia
1. Centrioles: made of 9 triplets of microtubules forming a
circle, with nothing in the middle (93+0 structure) . They
form centrosomes (2 centrioles).
2. Motile cilia: found in the respiratory system, sperm,…
The stem has a 92+2 structure surrounded by a
membrane.
The basal body has a 93+0 structure (same as centrioles),
below the membrane. Microtubules are interconnected by two
proteins: nexin (it binds the doublets of microtubules in the stem)
and dynein (it is the one responsible for the movement of cilia).
Microtubule organization centres (MTOC)
Microtubules are formed in certain parts of the cell ( centrioles and
basal body of cilia are the places where microtubules are
originated). In these centres, there is another protein,
gamma-tubulin, that is needed for the polymerization (growth) of
microtubules.
[PDF p. 56]
Immotile cilia
With a 92+0 structure . They cannot move. Their function is to be involved
in sensory functions. It is one single cilium per cell, that has a lot of sensory
proteins, transmitting the conditions from the outside (whether it is too fluid,
too solid, or there is a lot of mucus,…). Some of these immotile cilia are
found in the ear, nose, and so on (neurons with these cilia, that transmit
changes of the noise wave, for example).
-
PRIMARY CILIARY DYSKINESIA (PCD)
It is a genetic defect caused by genetic mutations of dynein (90%
mutations). Therefore, cilia are disorganized. It is a rare autosomal
recessive syndrome. We have cilia that cannot move, so the patient
presents symptoms such as infections, inflammations,…
Clinical manifestations: sinusitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, otitis,
bronchiectasis, chronic infections.
Situs inversus is a reversal location of some asymmetric organs in
our bodies that 50% patients with PCD might suffer.
If there is a patient with PCD that affects the respiratory and
reproductive systems + situs inversus, it is said that he suffers
Kartagener syndrome.
Why do some people develop situs inversus? There is a hypothesis showing that the embryo
cells in the middle line (normally having motile cilia), have imotal cilia in the patients suffering
the illness.
Normally, the motile cilia translate the liquid from one side of the cell to another. The cells on
the left side sense that there is a flow and it is going to communicate to the cells on the right
that they have to differentiate into an organ. If the cilia in the embryo are inmotile, this flow is
going to stop, because the cilia cannot move, so there is no sense sent, and the formation of
