MICROFILAMENTS
They are made of actin monomers .
They are polarized (because actin always
incorporates in the +end or barbed; the -end is
the pointed end) and dynamic (present dynamic
instability ). ATP is needed for polymerization
and then it dissociates into ADP. When it
dissociates into ADP, the microfilament becomes
less stable, so depending on the concentration of
ATP-bound actin in the medium, there will be polymerization or depolymerization (same as
microtubules).
There are actin-binding proteins that control the process of polymerization (microfilament
stability and association). In the case of microvilli, we need to maintain the parallelism, and
the proteins are vibrin and fimbrin (revisar en el libro de Calvo).
[PDF p. 57]
MYOSIN
It is a motor protein (it uses ATP to move actin). There are different types:
- Myosin 1 : if we put this in a petri dish with actin, actin is going to move towards myosin. It
bends the head interacting with the actin filaments, and it moves them.
Made up of 1 head and 1 tail.
- Myosin 2: it includes two molecules of myosin. It can associate with
other myosin 2 molecules, forming a thick filament (15 nanometers)
that we are going to find in muscles .
Made up of 2 heads and 2 tails.
Actin-myosin interaction:
In muscles, we find the sarcomere, where we find cylinder filaments with actin walls, except
for the central part (where we find the myosin filaments). Contraction is the interaction of
actin and myosin.
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells is known as sarcoplasmic reticulum
and it stores calcium (because the levels of calcium in cytoplasm have to be low, and in the
reticulum and outside the cell, high).
When the nerve impulse is transmitted, a
chemical called acetylcholine is released,
making calcium exit from the endoplasmic
reticulum and appear in the cytosol.
In the actin there are filaments of troponin and
tropomyosin that block the myosin from binding
to actin active sites. When calcium is increased
in the cytosol, calcium binds to troponin, and
troponin bound to calcium separates
tropomyosin from the actin filament. Now myosin
is able to interact with actin. The breakdown of
ATP releases energy, which makes the myosin
move the actin towards the centre of the plain.
This process occurs repeatedly. Once the nerve
impulse ends, the calcium is reabsorbed.
There are also actin-myosin interactions in cells that are not muscle cells. They do not
have sarcomeres, so the mechanism is different. For example, we need cell migration in
embryogenesis, metastasis and inflammation.
- DUCHENNE’S MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
It is a genetic disorder (recessive X-linked: more frequent in males).
There is a mutation in a protein called dystrophin (bound to actin in
muscle cells), so there is a disorganization of the sarcomere. There is a
progressive muscle deterioration. As a result, throughout the years,
fat replaces the muscle .
Some clinical symptoms are weakness, motor difficulties, breathing
problems, fatigue, and cardiomyopathy (it also affects the heart).
We can treat it by symptomatic treatment and physical therapy, or with
corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and the process of infiltration of
immune cells (it is going to prevent the degeneration of muscle cells).
[PDF p. 58]
People are trying to use gene therapy to replace the mutated gene through introducing a
vector containing the Y type version of the gene in the muscle cells, although for now these
are just trials. This is very difficult, because you have to replace all the cells of the body. We
can also use cell therapy (only trials for now), which consists in taking a piece of skin and
isolating the stem cells. Then, you culture these cells, and you replace the missing gene with
a healthy gene using for example a viral vector in vitro. Then we differentiate these cells in
vitro to form muscle cells by adding different components. So we take these modified cells,
and introduce them in the body, that tend to go where they are happy (to the muscles), and
then we can have at least some of the muscle tissue made of these cells that are able to
contract.
INTERMEDIATE FILAMENTS
Their diameter is between 8 and 12 nanometers . They are polymers made of different
filamentous proteins. They don’t show polarity (they grow in both ends), nor dynamic
instability, which is why they are highly stable. They don’t require ATP for polymerization.
They are responsible for the cytoskeleton maintenance, mechanical strength and resistance
to mechanical stress (structural function, not motor). Keratin is an example of intermediate
filaments in keratinocytes.
[PDF p. 59]
CELLULAR ENDOMEMBRANE SYSTEM: ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM, GOLGI APPARATUS & LYSOSOMES
OBJECTIVES


To have a general vision of the macromolecular transport pathways in the eukaryotic cell.


To understand the structure and function of the endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi apparatus and
lysosomes.


To be capable of describing the protein biosynthetic pathways and the transport chains that take
them to their correct cellular destination.


To recognise some representative cell types that show a special development of the different
elements in the biosynthesis-secretion routes.


To be familiar with some examples of illnesses caused by alterations in the endomembrane


system compartments.
INTRODUCTION
Eukaryotic cells, unlike prokaryotic, have a series of internal membranes that delimit specific
membranous compartments with a particular morphology and function. This compartment network
requires a complex transport system that allows the movement of molecules from one compartment to
another. These membranous compartments (also called organelles), are the endoplasmic reticulum with
its rough and smooth components, the Golgi apparatus and the lysosomes. The functions of these
organelles, except for the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER), are related to the synthesis, processing,
transport and localisation of a major part of the cellular proteins. The SER, on the other hand, plays a
key role in the synthesis of lipids, and therefore it is related to providing the rest of the compartments
with membranous supplies.
ROUGH EDOPLASMIC RETICULUM
Structure and composition
The rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) consists
of an interconnecting network of membranous
flattened saccules (or cisternae) and tubules with
ribosomes attached to them (fig. 10-1). These
saccules are connected with the nuclear envelope
and with the SER. In electron microscopy cuts the
saccules appear as “profiles” (and we call its
interior “lumen”) which normally present a
thickness of 20 to 30 nm, although sometimes they
can appear dilated. (e.g. in plasma cells).
Claude, Porter and Fulham were the first, in 1945,
to describe the RER using the electron
microscope. Their work was later completed by
Sjöstrand, Palade and Porter, who in addition, they
related this organelle with protein synthesis.
The RER is present in all nucleated cells (except
for spermatozoids) and is especially well
developed in cells with a high protein synthesis
rate. In an exocrine pancreatic cell, the RER can
easily occupy 20% of the cell volume. cells with
abundant RER present a characteristic called
cytoplasmic basophilia, which consists in the
affinity of basic dyes for certain regions of the cell
cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic basophilia is seen in areas
with abundant RNA from ribosomes, either found
free in the cytosol or attached to the RER.
Depending on the position of the basophilic
component, three types of basophilia can be
differentiated (fig. 10-2):
1
[PDF p. 60]


Diffuse basophilia, which implies that
almost the whole cytoplasm is basophilic.
We can normally see a non-basophilic
region within the cell, which corresponds
to the Golgi apparatus, and is normally
called , Negative Golgi Region . An
example of diffuse basophilia can be seen
in plasma cells.


Basal basophilia: in this case, the
basophilia is seen in the basal part of the
cell. This is very common in secretory
epithelial cells which have a large amount
of RER in the basal cytoplasm. We find
this basophilia in exocrine pancreatic
epithelial cells and in the epithelial cells
of the salivary glands.


Basophilia in clumps: the basophilic
components appear in groups or clumps,
which correspond to areas were the RER
or the free ribosomes are accumulated




within the cell. This basophilia is typical
of hepatocytes and neurons (the
basophilic areas in neurons correspond to
the clumps or Nissl bodies).
Functional studies performed in the 60s of the
last century demonstrated that the RER was
involved in the synthesis and distribution of
proteins. Using radioactive amino acids and
autoradiography techniques in pancreatic acinar
cells, it was found that amino acids introduced into
a cell were incorporated into proteins, primarily in
the RER. Longer incubation periods showed that
the proteins had been transported to the Golgi
apparatus, then to the secretory vesicles and
finally secreted by the cell. Therefore, these
experiments proved the existence a pathway for
protein synthesis and secretion, which involved
passing from the RER to the Golgi apparatus then
to the cell membrane and finally to the exterior of
the cell.
The RER membrane is a trilaminar structure
typical to that seen in cell membranes, and its
thickness is of 5-6 nm, in other words, a little
thinner than the plasma membrane. Its
composition is slightly different from other cell
membranes as it it contains a higher percentage of
lipids and a series of proteins exclusive to this
organelle. Amongst these proteins, it is important
to mention those involved in the attachment of
ribosomes and the translocation of proteins
towards the lumen. Moreover, the interior of the
RER contains a series of proteins typical to this
organelle, such as enzymes involved in the
glycosylation of proteins, peptidases, disulphuric
chains isomerases and chaperones.
RER protein translation
Cellular proteins can be completely translated by
free ribosomes found in the cytosol or the
translation may start in the cytosolic ribosomes
and continue it in the RER. This difference is
related to the destination of these proteins. Those
synthesized in the RER will stay in this organelle,
or will be transported to the Golgi apparatus, the
2
[PDF p. 61]
lysosomes, the cell membrane or secreted to the
extracellular space. On the other hand, those
proteins translated by free cytosolic ribosomes can
either remain in the cytosol or be posteriorly
incorporated into the nucleus, mitochondria or
peroxisomes. As the incorporation of these latter
proteins into their target organelles takes place
once the protein has been completely translated,
this process is called post-translational
importation. However, the ribosomes that join
the RER membrane, translate the proteins at the
same time as they are incorporated to the RER,
and hence it is called co-translational
importation .
The proteins that are going to be translated
in the RER contain a signalling peptide of 16-30
residues found in the N-terminus region, as a result
of the translation of a group of signalling codons
present in the mRNA that codifies these proteins.
The existence of peptide signals in proteins,
responsible for their incorporation in specific
membranous compartments in the cell, was also
proven in the case of the cell nucleus,
mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes.
How does the translation and
simultaneous incorporation of proteins into the
RER take place? Several sequential steps can be
distinguished:
Step 1: the translation starts in the free
ribosomes. When the signalling peptide appears
at the N-terminus end of the protein in formation,
this peptide is recognized by the SRP ( signal
recognition particle ) and this indicates that the
protein must be translated in the RER. The SRP is
made up of an RNA molecule and six proteins, and
has several protein domains (for binding to the
signal peptide, for stopping translation, for joining
the ribosome and for the coupling of GTP.
Step 2: the binding of the SRP to the
ribosome stops the translation and leads to a
conformational change in the SRP which can now
be recognized and bind to its receptor in the RER
membrane . The ribosome/SRP complex and its
receptor then interact with a translocator, a
protein complex that will allow the protein that is
being synthetized to pass into the RER lumen.
Step 3: the translocator is opened the
protein synthesis continues. Then, the signal
peptide remains anchored to the internal region of
the translocator via protein interactions and hence
will not pass into the RER. The protein being
synthesized will work its way along the
translocator and then penetrate the RER. The
hydrolysis of GTP will take place resulting in
conformational changes that will lead to the SRP
release.
Step 4: a signal peptidase, bound to the
inner surface of the membrane, cuts off the signal
peptide from the protein that is being incorporated
into the RER.
Step 5: translation continues and the
protein will remain in the RER lumen.
Localization and orientation of the proteins in
the RER
This mechanism of incorporation that we
have just explained is not common to all proteins
translated in the RER. there are proteins that
remain joined to the membrane of this organelle
because they have hydrophobic signals that allow
them to stay in the lipid bilayer (fig. 10-5). Indeed,
some proteins have, in addition to the signal
peptide at the N-terminus domain, a stop-transfer
sequence in an internal region of the protein. This
sequence of 20 to 25 amino acids is hydrophobic,
which prevents the protein from continuing its
translocation towards the RER lumen. In this case,
the protein translation continues, and the sequence
that comes after the stop-transfer sequence will
remain facing the cytoplasmic side. Therefore,
once the translation finishes, we will obtain a
protein anchored to the RER membrane, with its
N-terminus end facing the RER lumen and the
carboxyl end (C-terminus) facing the cytoplasm.
(see fig. 10-5).
On the other hand, there are proteins that
are orientated within the membrane in other ways,
with the N-terminus end facing the cytosol, or with
both ends facing the same side or even there are
3
[PDF p. 62]
proteins that cross the RER membrane several
times. In order to achieve these orientations
various strategies consisting of one or more
sequences for initiating the translocation and
stop-transfer sequences are needed.
Some proteins have the start transfer sequence
located internally in the protein instead of at the
N-terminus domain. In this case, the ribosome that
translates it will only join the RER when this
signal appears, which will determine that the Nterminus end will be facing the cytoplasmic side
when its translocation through the RER membrane
begins. The translation of the protein continues in
such a way that the carboxyl end is placed facing
the RER lumen. (fig 10-6). In this case, there is no
removal of the signal sequence by the signal
peptidase, thus leaving the protein embedded in
the membrane with the hydrophobic signal
immersed in it. The internal sequences of the
protein can be arranged in such a way that they
control the translocation orientating the Nterminus end towards the cytosolic side or the
luminal side of the RER, which will in turn allow
a different conformation of the protein in the
membrane. By changing the direction of the start
and stop transfer sequences proteins can be
orientated with both N and C-terminus ends
towards the same compartment (cytosolic or
luminal side). The presence of several start and
stop transfer sequences permits the existence of
proteins that cross the RER membrane several
times (fig. 10-7).
FIGURE 10-6. Process of synthesis
and insertion in the RER membrane
of a single pass protein whose Nterminus is oriented towards the
cytoplasmic side. Source of the
image: E. Maldonado and A. Calvo
4
[PDF p. 63]
Post-translational modifications
The proteins translated in the RER must
achieve their final configuration so as to be
perfectly functional. This configuration depends
upon the correct folding of the protein as well as a
series of post-translational modifications that take
place inside the RER (glycosylation,
fragmentation and formation of disulfide bonds).
Among cellular proteins, only those that pass
through the RER will be glycosylated, which it
does not mean that all the proteins translated in the
RER will undergo the glycosylation process
(although most will). Glycosylation is a process
that starts in the RER and ends in the Golgi
apparatus. Both organelles contain enzymes
capable of transferring sugars to the proteins or
deleting some of them so as to form chains of
specific oligosaccharides for each protein. .
Glycosylation is an important process because
some proteins need to be glycosylated in order to
fold correctly in the RER. Furthermore,
glycosylation prevents protein aggregation.
All the proteins that are glycosylated in
the RER (fig.10-8) first undergo a a transference
in block of an oligosaccharide formed by 14
residues: 3 of glucose, 9 of mannose and 2 of Nacetylglucosamine, catalysed by an
oligosaccharide transferase. The oligosaccharide
has been previously synthetized on the cytosolic
side of the RER membrane by means of the
activity of several enzymes that build the sugar
chain on a lipid in the membrane called dolicholdiphosphate. Once the 14 residue oligosaccharide
has been made, a translocation of the carbohydrate
chain takes place,, from the cytosolic side to the
lumen RER. The transfer of the oligosaccharide to
the protein will take place on an asparagine amino
acid (Asn) that is found in a Asn-X-Ser/Thr
sequence (where X can correspond to any amino
acid; Ser: serine; Thr: threonine). This
oligosaccharide will be posteriorly modified in the
Golgi apparatus.
The correct formation of the three
dimensional structure (or correct folding) of the
proteins is a phenomenon of great importance.
The formation of disulfide bridges (S-S)
takes part in the process of acquisition of a correct
protein structure. In proteins located in the RER
lumen, disulfide bonds are formed by the loss of
two electrons from the SH groups found in
cysteine amino acids. This protein modification
takes place in the RER because the oxidative
5
[PDF p. 64]
environment favours the formation of S-S bonds,
unlike the reductive environment found in the
cytosol.
The folding of proteins in the RER is a
complex process which is not completely
understood. Chaperones and protein processing
enzymes act as sensors, detecting misfolded
proteins and sending them to the cytosol so that
they can be degraded.
SMOOTH ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM
The SER is formed by a system of membranous
structures, mainly tubular, without attached
ribosomes, and they differ from the RER in
morphology, composition and function (fig. 1011).
Although there are morphological and funcitonal
differences between both reticula, they are
interconnected with each other, forming a
structure or compartment with a continuous
membrane. The characteristics that differentiate
the SER from the RER are:


It does not have ribosomes.


The main membranous elements are


fundamentally tubules (not saccules).


Its membrane composition it is not the
same (different proteins and a greater
percentage of lipids).


Its functions are mainly related to the
synthesis of lipids and fat derivatives.


It is only abundant in specialized cells
such as hepatocytes, steroid hormone
secretory cells, muscular cells, etc.


The SER has numerous functions within the
cell, mainly related to the synthesis of lipids,
which are necessary for the increase and
replacement of the membranous elements of the
different organelles and the plasma membrane.
Functions
LIPID AND FAT DERIVATIVES SYNTHESIS
In every cell the synthesis of
phospholipids and cholesterol is very important
for the renewal of cellular membranes. This is
done by the SER. Moreover, there are specialised
cells in the organism in which the SER is very
abundant; in these cells the synthesis of certain
types of lipids and their derivatives takes place.
6
[PDF p. 65]
The lipid synthesis takes place in the
cytosolic hemimembrane of the endoplasmic
reticulum, therefore, the addition of lipid
molecules would only take place on this side of the
membrane. In order to redistribute the lipids in
both hemimembranes and establish the asymmetry
that characterizes them regarding their
composition, the activity of enzymes called
scramblases is required, which catalyse the
energetically unfavourable passage of the lipid
polar groups from one side of the membrane to the
other (see chapter 3).
The lipids synthesized in the SER will be
distributed by means of vesicular transport to the
different membranous compartments (RER, Golgi
apparatus, lysosomes) and to the plasma
membrane. In order for them to be transported to
mitochondria and peroxisomes cytosolic proteins
that exchange phospholipids are required
Due to its role in lipid synthesis, the SER
also contributes in a very important manner in the
formation of lipoproteins, bile acids and steroid
hormones. Enterocytes contain RER and SER that
take part in the formation of chylomicrons which
are formed by triglycerides, phosphoglycerides,
cholesterol and proteins. The liver also
synthesizes lipoproteins (LDL, VLDL, HDL and
VHDL, which are posteriorly released into the
bloodstream) and bile acids, formed from
cholesterol (and excreted into the bile canaliculi).
The steroid hormone synthesis from cholesterol,
takes place in specialized endocrine cells in
several successive steps that require the action of
mitochondrial and SER enzymes. In this way,
hormones such as testosterone, oestradiol, cortisol
and aldosterone etc. are synthetized.
DETOXIFICATION OF LIPOSOLUBLE
SUBTANCES
The SER plays an important role in the
breakdown of toxic liposoluble substances, such
as certain drugs, alcohol, pesticides and
carcinogens, as well as toxic substances produced
by the metabolism itself. All these substances are
turned into hydro soluble products, which are
more easily eliminated by the organism. In
hepatocytes, when there are high levels of such
toxic substances, the SER is highly developed and
contains detoxifying enzymes (such as the ones of
the cytochrome P450 family, which are anchored
to the cytosolic side of the SER membrane. The
activity of these enzymes include oxidation,
hydrolysis and reduction of substances which have
to be chemically modified to reduce their toxicity.
Other cytoplasmic enzymes act by conjugating
these substances to certain chemical groups
(glucuronic, sulfate, acetyl, etc), facilitating their
excretion.
PARTICIPATION IN THE GLYCOGEN
METABOLIM
In some cell types, the SER is frequently
found close to glycogen stores, especially in
hepatocytes. These cells play an important role in
the storage of glucose as glycogen. On the
cytosolic side of the SER membrane the glucose6-phosphatase is present, an enzyme that
hydrolases glucose-6-phosphate, producing free
glucose that can go to the bloodstream and then to
the tissues when their glucose levels are low.
7
[PDF p. 66]
Ca [2+ ] STORAGE
As explained in chapter 4, the SER has Ca [2+ ]
pumps, Ca2+ ATPases that introduce Ca [2+ ] into the
SER, against the concentration gradient with the
purpose of maintaining low cytoplasmic levels of
this ion. ;therefore the SER acts as an intracellular
reservoir of Ca [2+] . The increase in the cytoplasmic
Ca [2+ ] levels triggers signaling cascades that can
have different consequences, depending on the
cellular type (see chapter 13). Therefore, it acts as
a second messenger in intracellular signaling. In
skeletal muscle fibers, a special type of SER is
found, called sarcoplasmic reticulum, which
wraps the myofibrils. It constitutes a Ca2+
storage. These ions are released with the arrival of
the nervous impulse and then muscle contraction
is produced.
GOLGI APPARATUS
Structure and properties
The Golgi apparatus is formed by a group of
membranous structures, mainly flattened saccules
and stacked in a parallel fashion. Vesicles also
appear around the saccules, especially near its
ends, as well as tubular shaped membranous
elements. All these elements are grouped together
forming dictyosomes, whose number and
distribution varies according to the cell type (e.g.
hepatocytes can have up to 50 dictyosomes). The
Golgi apparatus is highly developed in cells that
produce glycoproteins and proteoglycans, such as
the pancreatic acinar cells, goblet cells,
hepatocytes, neurons, etc.
The Golgi apparatus exhibits polarity,
which means there are two areas with very
different morphology and composition, called Cis
face (or entry face) and Trans face (or exit face)
(fig. 10-14). Protein maturation takes place in the
Golgi apparatus that occurs progressively from the
Cis face to the Trans face. Hence protein
maturation is polarised towards the trans face of
the Golgi apparatus. For this,there is a clear
functional compartmentalisation within the Golgi
apparatus in such a way that it is possible to
distinguish five compartments (fig 10-14)


Cis Golgi network (CGN)


Cis cisternae


Medial cisternae


Trans cisternae


Trans Golgi network (TGN)


The two end compartments (CGN and TGN) are
not formed by cisternae but by an irregular
network of tubules and vesicles (this explains why
they are called ‘networks’). Each compartment
has a specific group of enzymes responsible for
the sequential maturation of the proteins.
Therefore, in the CGN region and in the Cis area
we can find enzymes that transfer phosphate
groups and eliminate mannose residues,
respectively. In the medial cisternae Nacetylglucosamine is added; in the Trans ones,
galactose and sialic acid, whilst in the TGN area
enzymes transfer sulphate groups to certain
proteins.
Functions
In the Golgi apparatus the proteins and the lipids
synthesized in the ER will continue their
maturation. The main changes that they will
undergo are N-glycosylation, O-glycosylation,
fragmentation and sulphation.
GLYCOSYLATION
Regarding the proteins that have been
previously glycosylated in the RER (where the N-
glycosylation took place), in the Golgi apparatus
they will lose some of their sugar radicals and have
new ones added, giving rise to glycoproteins
which contain N-oligosaccharides that can be
8
[PDF p. 67]
classified into 3 groups a) rich in mannose, b)
complex and c) hybrids, (intermediate
oligosaccharides, in between these two groups).
Apart from the modification of the
oligosaccharides of the N-glycoproteins, the Golgi
apparatus is also responsible for the O-
glycosylation (which takes place exclusively in
this organelle). In this type of glycosylation sugars
are linked to an OH group of the following amino
acids: serine, threonine and, in the case of
collagen, hydroxylysine. The O- glycosylated
proteins can be found forming mucins, which are
abundant in cells that secrete mucinous
substances; collagen also has O-ligated sugars.
MARKING OF LYSOSOMAL ENZYMES
Enzymes of the acid hydrolase type, which are
going to be responsible for the cellular digestion
that is carried out by lysosomes, are classified by
means of a special route that will direct them
towards this organelle. Primary lysosomes are
formed from clathrin-coated vesicles, that
originate in the TGN area of the Golgi apparatus.
The process begins in the CGN area, which
contains enzymes that add phosphate groups to the
6 [th] carbon of the terminal mannose on the
hydrolase proteins, that will go to lysosomes.
Mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) therefore
constitutes a way of tagging those proteins that
will go to the lysosome. All these proteins undergo
N-glycosylation as well as the addition of a
phosphate group which takes place as a result of
the enzyme activity of N-acetylglucosamine
phosphotransferase. This enzyme transfers a
phosphate group from N-acetylglucosamine-UDP
to the mannose found in lysosomal enzymes. The
labelled lysosomal hydrolases are recognized by
M6P receptors found in the TGN area. In this way,
clathrin coated vesicles are formed which leave
the TGN area and fuse with the late endosome.
Any alteration in this classifying system will
produce serious consequences for the cell, since
these enzymes are not destined for the lysosome,
but they join the secretory pathway and are
released into the extracellular space.
MEMBRANE RECYCLING
The Golgi apparatus is a very dynamic
compartment that must be in constant equilibrium,
9
[PDF p. 68]
as it continuously receiving contributions of
membranous elements that come from
endocytosis, and in turn releases vesicles or the
secretory pathway, whose membrane becomes
part of the plasma membrane. It is therefore an
organelle responsible for the correct distribution
of the different membranous components of the
cell.
PROPER DISTRIBUTION OF THE
DIFFERENT MACROMOLECULES
As we have already mentioned, the Golgi
apparatus is a classifying compartment, from
which vesicles emerge with different cell
destinations. The figure 10-15 shows the path that
several macromolecules follow form the
beginning of their synthesis in the RER to their
final destination. Proteins can be directed towards
the plasma membrane and stay there (if they are
proteins anchored to the membrane), be released
to the cell exterior, stay as Golgi resident proteins
or be destined for the lysosomes.

SUMMARY AND TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER 6, FROM THE BOOK “BIOLOGÍA CELULAR BIOMÉDICA”, PLASMA MEMBRANE SPECIALIZATIONS AND CELL INTERACTIONS WITH THE ENVIRONMENT
Authors: Elena Bodegas, Alfonso Calvo
Translation: Pedro Montero Narva

LEARNING OBJECTIVES:
•
To know the plasma membrane specializations in the different cellular domains (apical, lateral and
basal).
•
To understand the molecular structure of the different plasma membrane specializations.
•
To relate certain human pathologies with molecular and/or cellular alterations in the plasma
membrane specializations.

INTRODUCTION
Cells are usually connected to one another or to
proteins in the extracellular matrix (ECM) which
surround them. Cell interactions with its environment
are vital for functioning in a particular tissue. In fact,
most cells depend on these interactions for their
survival. Thus if they are unable to adhere to the
substrate or to other cells, they end up dying by a
process called “anoikis” (apoptosis caused by the lack
of adhesion). These types of cell-cell and cell-ECM
interactions are also key in communication and
intercellular signaling. The plasmatic membrane plays
an essential role in these processes, developing
different structures that facilitate adhesion, contact
with other cells or the interaction with the
surrounding medium. In this chapter we describe the
plasma membrane specializations and the main
extracellular molecules with which they interact.
PLASMA MEMBRANE SPECIALIZATIONS
The plasma membrane may have different
specializations (fig. 6-1) in either: a) the cells´ free
surface (whichever is not in contact with other cells),
such as microvilli, cilia and flagella (these last two
differentiations are explained in chapter 12), and b)
the contact surface with neighboring cells or the
ECM, which include interdigitations, basal infoldings
and cell-cell or cell-EMC junctions.
1
[PDF p. 70]
Figure 6.1. Representation of an idealized cell showing the
different plasma membrane differentiations studied in this
chapter.
The latter can be further classified by their function
into:


Anchoring junctions


Tight junctions


Communicating junctions


Microvilli
Microvilli are fingerlike projections in the apical
surface of epithelial cells that help increasing the
surface area of absorption (fig. 6-2, A) . These
structures are approximately 1 m in length and 0.08
m in width. Inside, they are stabilized by a bundle of
20-30 actin filaments, linked together by villin and
fimbrin . These membrane differentiations are
anchored to the terminal web, which contains
different filamentous proteins. The microvilli have a
highly developed glycocalyx, which can be seen under
the optic microscope using saccharide specific stains,
such as PAS (periodic acid Schiff) (fig. 6-2,B).
Figure 6.2. Structure of microvilli in enterocytes (Ent). EChE:
brush border; CC: Goblet cell. MB: Basal membrane. MV:
Microvilli. GC: Glycocalyx.
2
Microvilli can be scarce in some epithelial cells, but in
some others they are very abundant, as is the case
for epithelia of the intestine, proximal convoluted
tubules and choroid plexus.
In the intestinal epithelium, microvilli (fig. 6-2, C) play
an essential role in the absorption of nutrients, as
they increase the surface area of the membrane,
which contains many transporter glycoproteins.
Several enzymes, responsible for the final stages of
protein and sugar digestion, can be found on the
microvilli´ surface. These enzymes can be altered by
different causes, resulting in pathologies, either by
defect (such as lactose intolerance) or by excessive
absorption (such as hemochromatosis). Lactose
intolerance usually develops during childhood,
although its first symptoms may appear in adulthood.
In patients with this disease, among other alterations,
there is a secondary deficiency of lactases (enzymes
found in the membrane of the microvilli of
enterocytes). The function of these lactases is to split
the lactose ingested in foods into its two basic
components: glucose and galactose, which will later
be absorbed. When there is partial or complete lack
of this enzyme, lactose will not be digested, resulting
in diarrhea. Hemochromatosis is an autosomal
recessive disease characterized by an excessive iron
build-up in different organs. This disease is
characterized by gene mutations, which determines
the over-expression in the intestinal microvilli of the
DMT-1 transporter, whose function is to absorb iron.
Therefore, when an increase in this protein in the
epithelial surface occurs (as is the case in
hemochromatosis), there is an excessive iron
absorption. Because of its high concentration in the
patient´s body, iron accumulates in different organs
such as the liver heart (causing cardiomyopathy) and
hypophysis.
Microfolds: interdigitations and basal infoldings
2
[PDF p. 71]
Microfolds are narrow evaginations/invaginations of
the cellular membrane on its contact surface with
other cells or with the ECM. They can either be on
the lateral surfaces (interdigitations or lateral
infoldings), which allows to reinforce epithelial cell
junction (fig. 6-3, A) or on the epithelial cell´s basal
membrane, known as basal infoldings (fig. 6-3, B) .
These latter ones can be found in the distal
convoluted tubules of the kidney, where they are
deep and numerous. The cytoplasm within the basal
infoldings contains lots of mitochondria. This
arrangement relates to the osmotic regulation
performed by these cells via ionic transfer, which
requires a large energy source. The invaginations
increase the surface area of the basal membrane on
which the ion transporter proteins are located.
Figure 6.3. Microfoldings of the plasma membrane. A: Int:
Lateral infolding. D: Desmosome. N1: Nucleus of cell 1. N2:
Nucleus of cell 2. B: Basal infolding (PB). MT: Mitochondria.
Anchoring cell junctions
Cells adhere to one another and to the ECM through
specific membrane molecules called cell adhesion
molecules. These molecules are mostly
transmembrane proteins which, together with other
associated proteins, can be located in specific sites in
the plasma membrane. The transmembrane proteins
that participate in cell adhesion belong, mostly, to
four families: cadherins, integrins, selectins and
cellular adhesion molecules of the immunoglobulin
superfamily (IgSF-CAM, immunoglobulin superfamily
cell adhesion molecules). These transmembrane
3
proteins link to proteins of neighboring cells or the
EMC (in the case of integrins). Proteins of these
families can be monomeric (IgSF-CAM and selectins)
or appear in a dimeric form; and so, cadherins form
homodimers (dimers formed by the same type of
protein), while integrins form heterodimers (dimers
constituted by two different types of protein) (table
6-1) .
There is a large number of proteins associated to
these transmembrane proteins, usually located on the
cytoplasmic side of the membrane, participating in
the structuring and stabilization of the junction and
its anchoring to the cellular cytoskeleton. When an
adhesion protein from one cell binds to another of
the same type on a neighboring cell, we refer to this
as homophilic bonds, while if it binds to different
proteins (or other types of molecules), we refer to it
as heterophilic bonds . These junctions can also be
either of stable or temporary (v. table 6-1).
Cadherins
Cadherins constitute a family of proteins that contains
Ca2+ binding sites (fig. 6-4, A) . Cadherins form
homodimers and make Ca2+ dependent homophilic
bonds. More than 40 different proteins belong to the
cadherin family, among which we find E-cadherin
(found in epithelial cells) and N-cadherin (present in
nerve tissue cells, the lens of the eye, and skeletal
and cardiac muscle cells).
3
[PDF p. 72]
Figure 6.4. Structure of cadherins (A). Immunofluorescence
image of E-cadherin (in red) in epithelial cells in culture.
Cadherins can be grouped in specific cell locations to
form complex anchoring (or adhesion) structures.
These structures are typically found in epithelial cells,
although they may also be present in other tissues.
There are two fundamental classes of complex
anchoring structures which are cadherin dependent:


Zonula adherens or adhesion belt.


Macula adherens or desmosome.


We will now analyze the basic organization of each of
these structures and some of the pathologies that
arise when they get disorganized or undergo
alterations.
ZONULA ADHERENS OR ADHESION BELT
The zonula adherens is a 0.1-0.5 m wide cellular belt
with adhering function, normally found on the apical
surface of the lateral cell membranes, which perform
a vital role in the anchoring of epithelial cells (fig. 6-5,
A). Desmocollins and desmogleins (two types of
cadherins) are the transmembrane proteins that make
up these structures, whose cytoplasmic end joins to
an adhesion plate which contains desmoplakin,
plakophilin and plakoglobin (fig. 6-5, B). The
adhesion plate is bound to actin filaments by
intermediary proteins. The actin filaments extend
through the cytoplasm, forming an intracytoplasmic
anchoring network.
MACULA ADHERENS OR DESMOSOME
4
Macula adherens (also known as a desmosome) is
0.1-0.5 m point shaped junction usually located in
the lateral membranes of epithelial cells, providing
anchorage between them (fig. 6-5, C) . We can also
find desmosomes in intercalated disks that bind
adjacent cardiomyocytes, where they play a key role
in maintaining cardiac tissue structure. Desmosome
forming transmembrane proteins are also cadherins
( desmocollins and desmogleins ). In this sense,
desmosomes are structurally equivalent to adhesion
belts, but they have a pointed morphology (fig. 6-5,
D) . In this case, the desmosome adhesion plate is
directly attached to intermediate filaments, rather
than to actin filaments. In the skin, intermediate
filaments are keratin (tonofilaments), desmin in the
intercalated discs of cardiomyocytes and vimentin in
other tissues.
There are different types of desmogleins, which are
expressed differently depending on the tissue type.
The main desmogleins in the epidermis of the skin
(where desmosomes are abundant) are desmogleins 1
and 3. Two dermatological diseases related to
desmogleins are pemphigus vulgaris and
pemphigus foliaceus . These diseases are
characterized by the presence of blisters on the
cutaneous surface of patients. Pemphigus vulgaris
(PV) is characterized by blisters, on the surface of the
skin, which burst easily (fig. 6-6, A) . These lesions can
be found in the oral mucosa (fig 6-6, B) or extend as
far as the skin of the face, neck, extremities and torso.
Patients refer itchiness and pain in the affected areas,
and they commonly have infections due to lesion
ulceration. An anatomopathological exam of PV
shows separation between keratinocytes in the skin,
known as acantholysis (fig. 6-6, C) .
4
[PDF p. 73]
Figure 6.5. Structure of cell adhesion structures. A.
Representation of desmosomes, adhesion belts and
hemidesmosomes. Structure of an adhesion belt. C. Electron
microscopy image of a desmosome. D. Structure of a
desmosome.
These lesions are usually found above the basal layer
of the epidermis . Immunofluorescence biopsy
analysis reveals an IgG deposit on the keratinocyte
surface, due to the autoimmune nature of the
disease. Patient´s autoantibodies target desmoglein 3
(mainly expressed on the basal layer of skin and
mucosa), desmoglein 1 (found mostly in the
superficial layers of the skin and less commonly the
mucosae) or target both. Autoantibodies are
responsible for desmosome deconstruction in
keratinocytes (where they are very abundant) and for
blister appearance. This disease has a symptomatic
treatment that involves corticosteroids and
immunosuppressive drugs, as well as pain killers and
antibiotics to control infections. Pemphigus foliaceus
is also an autoimmune disease where an IgG deposit
is observed targeting desmoglein 1. Therefore, the
blisters will only be found in layers above the
epidermis and will burst easily. The prognosis for this
disease is better than that for PV, and its treatment
5
consists of the use of systemic or intralesional
corticosteroids.
Figure 6.6. Macroscopic images of blisters (A) and oral
lesions (B) in a patients with pemphigus vulgaris. C.
Histological image of acantholysis of the skin.
Integrins
Integrins are a family of proteins that participate in
the permanent or transient cell-EMC or cell-cell
adhesion. They are heterodimers made up by two
different subunits: α subunit and β subunit (fig. 6-7,
A). The -subunit has binding sites for divalent
cations (Ca2+. Mg2+). These molecules bind to both
ECM components and to intracellular cytoskeleton
proteins by means of interaction with intermediary
proteins that interact with actin filaments, but may
also bind to intermediate keratin filaments . The
extracellular domain of the -subunit can bind to
extracellular proteins ( laminin and fibronectin ).
Integrins play an important role in the migration
processes of embryonic and immune cells.
These proteins can be found as simple molecules or
in groups forming complex adhesion structures, which
constitute hemidesmosomes and focal adhesions .
Hemidesmosomes are stable adhesion structures
typically found in sessile cells, while focal adhesions
5
[PDF p. 74]
are more commonly found in cells in motion. Focal
adhesions are constantly undergoing a process of
formation and destruction.
HEMIDESMOSOMES
Hemidesmosomes (fig. 6-7, B) are structures that,
based on their morphology, would resemble half of a
desmosome located in the basal part of the cell.
These structures allow anchoring of the cell to the
extracellular basal membrane in which the cell rests.
However, the proteins that make up
hemidesmosomes are different to those found in
desmosomes, both the transmembrane anchoring
proteins (in this case integrins instead of cadherins)
and the adhesion plate proteins. The integrin that
constitutes hemidesmosomes is the  -6  -4-integrin,
and the proteins found in the plaque are known as
plakins . Another transmembrane protein found in
hemidesmosomes is BPGA2 (bullous pemphingoid
antigen-2). The plaque is connected to tonofilaments
in the cytoplasmic side (fig. 6-7, B) .
Hemidesmosomes increase the overall stability of
epithelial tissues and allow them to settle in the ECM
by binding of cytoskeletal tonofilaments to basal
membrane components.
Figure 6.7. A. Structure of integrins. B. Representation of a
hemidesmosome. C. Structure of focal adhesions.
6
FOCAL ADHESIONS
Migratory cells bind to the ECM via focal adhesions
(fig. 6-7, C), formed by clusters of integrins
interconnected with bundles of actin filaments by
means of other intermediary proteins. These
structures are very dynamic, in a process of constant
formation and destruction during the process of cell
migration, where they provide a connection at
specific points with the substrate. They are abundant
in lamellipodia (see chapter 12), which cells use to
travel through an inert substrate. Not only focal
adhesions have an adhesion function, they also
participate in intracellular signaling. Thus, integrin
interaction with the substrate in focal adhesions
results in phosphorylation of the focal adhesion
tyrosine kinase protein (FAK), a protein that
promotes the activation of proteins involved in
cellular migration and protects cells from anoikis.
Integrins act as signal transductors, keeping the cell
informed as to the conditions (mainly adhesion) of
the extracellular surroundings. FAK hyperactivation
has been associated with an increased metastatic
capacity of tumor cells.
Integrins also mediate cell-cell contacts. These
interactions are usually temporary and occur in the
adhesion processes of immune system cells. Within
these integrins we can highlight the so-called “LFA-1”,
or lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1, as well
as Mac-1 (its equivalent in macrophages). These
integrins find their receptor in ICAM and VCAM
molecules (see below) on the endothelial cell surface,
thus reinforcing the interaction produced by selectins
(see selectins, below) in the leukocyte extravasation
process.
Selectins
Selectins are Ca2+ dependent adhesion molecules,
with affinity for carbohydrates found in other cells
(fig. 6-8, A) . Rather than forming complex binding
6
[PDF p. 75]
structures, they are involved in molecular contacts
that are not visible under the microscope and are
generally temporary . They frequently participate in
the binding of leukocytes to endothelial cells,
facilitating their exit from the blood vessels to an
inflammatory site (fig. 6-8, B) .
Figure 6.8. A. Structure of selectins. B. Participation of
selections (and other adhesion molecules) in the
attachment of neutrophils to endothelial cells and
extravasation to the sites of infection.
Most leukocytes have L-selectins in their plasma
membrane (‘L’ for leukocyte), which interacts with its
receptor via heterophilic bonds in the plasma
membrane of endothelial cells that coat blood
vessels. Receptors for selectins are oligosaccharides
contained in glycoproteins (such as IgSF-CAM) or
plasma membrane glycolipids. Additionally,
endothelial cells themselves have two types of
selectins: P-selectin (‘P’ for ‘platelet’ where the
expression of this selectin is highly abundant) and E-
selectin (‘E’ for “endothelium’), which in turn interact
with oligosaccharides on the leukocyte surface.
Selectins are involved in inflammation and cancer . In
inflammatory processes, certain stimuli (such as
histamine and thrombin) stimulate the endothelial
cells to produce P-selectin on the cell surface. Some
cytokines (such as TNF-) also increase E- and P
selectin expression in the endothelium, thus favoring
the leukocyte binding. This then leads to a tighter
junction, mediated by IgSF-CAM integrins (see IgSF
7
CAM integrins below) and, finally, leukocyte migration
to the inflammatory sites.
IGSF-CAM
The adhesion molecules of the IgSF-CAM
immunoglobulin superfamily (fig. 6-9) possess bow
shaped domains, similar to those found in
immunoglobulins. They form heterophilic bonds
(interacting with integrins and selectins) or
homophilic bonds (binding to other IgSF-CAM)
(fig.6-9) . IgSF-CAMs have no Ca2+ binding sites and
regulate cell junctions, which are normally temporary .
This protein superfamily is involved in adhesions of
immune system cells. We can highlight the following
IgSF-CAMs:

Intercellular adhesion molecules (ICAM) and vascular

cell adhesion molecules (VCAM). They are present in
many cell types, especially in endothelial cells,
regulating interactions with blood cells, which have
integrins present on their membranes.

Nerve cell adhesion molecules (NCAM). These are

found in the neurons and are bound by homophilic
interaction to other NCAMs.
Figure 6.9. A. Structure of IgSF-CAM. B. Interaction
between two molecules of IgSF-CAM, or between IgSF-CAM
and selectins.
Occluding junctions (Zonula occludens or tight
junction)
Occluding junctions (or ‘tight junctions’) are belt

Communicating junctions are also called “nexus

prevents any possible damage from being transmitted
to neighboring cells.

G-proteins
They are heterotrimeric (alpha,beta and gamma subunits). When G protein is bound to GDP,

Relevance and main characteristics
Ion channels are present in every cell, but they are particularly important in electrically

-They have a very high rate of transport, no need to interact with receptors.
-Two major types of ion channel receptors:
voltage gated: the channel is regulated by changes in
membrane potential, it will open or close depending on that.
In the resting situation, membrane potential is such that there
is a negative charge in the inner membrane. A depolarization
involves a positive charge inside the membrane and negative
outside. This promotes that the protein channels open and ions
can enter the cell.
               **ligand- gated:** channels open or close depending on the

Acetylcholine and its receptors
There are many receptors for Acetylcholine . It’s a very plastic molecule, it can act through
different types of receptors and have a very different outcome, depending on the receptor
and the cell. We can differentiate two types of receptors:

Nicotinic: Called nicotinic because this channel can also be activated by nicotine.
That’s why nicotine is an agonist of Ach. Ach binds to an ion channel receptor.
Muscarinic: Ach binds to a G Protein Coupled receptor (GPCR). Called muscarinic
because it also binds to muscarine, a toxin from mushrooms.

How acetylcholine acts in neuromuscular junction:
First, there is a depolarization of the membrane. This depolarization causes the release of
calcium into the cell ( the presence of Ca2+ in a cell generally promotes exocytosis of
vesicles ), which promotes the exocytosis of vesicles with Ach into the synaptic space. It
then binds to its receptor in the muscle fiber . The channel opens and Na+ enters .
[PDF p. 85]
This propagates the stimulus in the muscle fiber: the axon potential propagates through the
membrane invaginations ( T tubules, because they are in a T shape). These tubules, at
some point, contact with the sarcoplasmic reticulum / SER in muscle fibers. The
depolarization and the close contact between membrane and reticulum opens Ca2+
channels, promoting its release into the cytosol. This will then cause muscle contraction,
as Ca2+ binds to troponin and tropomyosin, leaving the actin’s active site free for myosin
heads to bind to.
To stop contraction, Ca2+ must be
removed from the cytosol. For this
there are calcium pumps that actively
(with energy consumption) move
calcium back into the SER.
To stop the whole process, acetylcholine is either
diffused or broken down by an enzyme found in
the synaptic cleft ( acetylcholine-esterase ) into
acetic acid and choline, that is reabsorbed to
generate more acetylcholine.
(Sarcolemma=membrane of a muscle fiber)
Related pathologies. Alteration of the signaling process: MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
It’s an autoimmune disease where
antibodies are produced against
acetylcholine receptors.
They bind to the receptors and block
them, so Ach cannot bind properly to the
receptor in the channel. It isn’t a
complete blockage, otherwise the patient
would die in a few minutes. There is
some muscle contraction, but it’s impaired .
Antibodies bound to the receptors are also then incorporated through endocytosis into the
cell, because the antibodies stimulate this process. The channel and the antibody are
swallowed and destroyed by lysosomes, so as a result there is a lesser amount of receptors

[PDF p. 86]
The treatment: using immunosuppressors (corticosteroids) to block antibody production, or
the use of AchE inhibitors: it blocks the activity of
acetylcholinesterase, and keeps the signalling going for longer.
Some AchE inhibitors may be fatal, but used in small doses with this
pathology can improve movements.

Botulinic toxin: produced by clostridium botulinum . The bacteria blocks the

TBL 4.1. Signalling through tyrosine kinases
Cellular communication is possible thanks to signals that stimulate receptors. We find
intracellular receptors, and membrane receptors that we will study today.
SIGNALING THROUGH MEMBRANE RECEPTORS
Membrane receptors are amphipathic molecules that collect extracellular signals and
transmit them to the interior of the cell, activating a protein cascade that will result in gene
transcription and the production of a protein.
There are 3 types of membrane proteins:
Ligand gated ion channels
G protein coupled receptors
Enzymatic or catalytic receptors. We will focus on these last ones:
Enzymatic or catalytic membrane receptors are enzymes that once activated, due to
ligand bind, enhance the signal transmission through cytoplasm proteins.They have an
extracellular domain (where ligand binding occurs), a transmembrane domain and an
intracellular domain (which confers the catalytic activity).
This catalytic activity can be a kinase activity: kinases are
enzymes that catalyze the transfer of a phosphate group
from a donor ATP to a substrate. This process regulates
many intracellular signalling cascades.
Tyrosine-kinase receptors (RTK)
Like all membrane receptors, they possess an extracellular
domain, cross-membrane domain and intracellular domain. Once
activated by a ligand, they enhance the phosphorylation of
tyrosine residues, which will lead to a cellular response.
Tyrosine-kinase is a dimer. The ligand binds to either one or two
subunits. When in monomeric form, they are inactive . After the
binding of the signal molecule, the monomers join and form the dimer. In order to get
activated, a cross-phosphorylation has to occur by consuming ATP.
Active form = phosphorylated dimer.
An example of a tyrosine
kinase signalling is the RAS
pathway. RAS is a membrane
protein that belongs to a
small GTPase protein family,
which carries out the
RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK
pathway. At the end of the
process, ERK suppresses
upstream pathway signalling.
[PDF p. 88]
30% of human cancers are related to a hyperstimulation of this
pathway. This hyperstimulation stimulates uncontrolled growth and
tumor appearance.
Action mechanism: a ligand binds to the receptor, and the second
subunit binds to the 1st RTK. Then cross-phosphorylation occurs.
Now activated, they can recruit the intracellular proteins. RAS is
activated by GEF and stays attached to the membrane. Many RAS
proteins are activated = signal amplification. Then RAF is activated,
joining RAS and forming an inner structure. Then MEK and ERK are activated. Activated
ERK translocates to the nucleus and stimulates many processes that end in gene
transcription and a cellular response.
The medical relevance of tyrosine-kinase receptors is that many drugs developed to treat
cancer act on RTK, either targeting ATP binding sites, interfering with RKT activation or

Ovarian cancer
Known as a silent killer. It doesn’t show specific symptoms, and these appear at a late stage,
when there has already been a metastasis. Therefore it’s difficult to treat and cure. Increased
angiogenesis stimulates the formation of new blood vessels around the cell. The tumor
enhances angiogenesis by taking advantage of EGF (growth factor). Therefore angiogenesis
is targeted to stop tumor growth. Angiogenesis can be stopped by blocking EGF.
RTK-Insulin receptor
Another RTK receptor is the insulin receptor . It’s a receptor that is very abundant in cells of
the liver, adipose tissue and skeletal muscles. It’s a dimer made up of two extracellular
subunits and two intracellular subunits. When
insulin binds, intracellular tyrosine domains
become activated and there is a downstream
cascade that leads to the translocation of
GLUT4 transporters, which allows the
transport of glucose into the interior of the
cell. If glucose in the bloodstream decreases,
the GLUT4 transmembrane proteins are
stored in vesicles and removed from the

When insulin receptor does not work properly, it leads to insulin resistance (a stage where

cholesterol levels, are all factors that can lead to this disease. Molecular mechanisms that

What is DIABETES?
It’s a chronic disease where pancreas can’t produce enough insulin or the body cannot use
the insulin it produces.
Type I diabetes is an autoimmune disease where the body cannot produce enough insulin
because autoantibodies attack beta-cells in the pancreas (those in charge of insulin
production).
Type II diabetes is a metabolic disease which prevents the little insulin which the body
can produce (it’s produced, although not enough) from working properly. It can’t be taken

Factors that can impact type II diabetes: mutations in genes resulting in mutated proteins,

Lecture 5.1. Bioenergetics
Forms of obtaining carbon and energy:
Metabolic pathways are a sequence of reactions that, through the continuous modification
of a precursor, transform it into a product. These reactions are catalyzed by enzymes.
Types of chemical reactions in metabolism:
-Transfer of functional groups
-Oxidation and reduction
-Isomerization
-Hydrolysis/condensation
-Formation or cleavage of C-C bonds
Metabolic phases


Catabolism: degradative phase in which nutrients are degraded into their simpler
subunits, to obtain precursors (CO2, H2O, NH3). Two main goals: to obtain energy
and to obtain precursors . The main strategy to do this is the oxidation of the
carbon atoms, by removing electrons. This produces energy, which is stored as
ATP, and the released electrons are collected and stored in molecules called
electron carriers. They collect e- from the carbon molecules which are oxidized.


Anabolism: It’s a process in which precursors obtained from catabolism are used,
through ATP consumption, to generate macromolecules that our body needs to
function (lipids, proteins,…).


Types of metabolic pathways
The body’s interest in making the most of its resources
is reflected in the metabolic pathways. All nutrients are
converged towards a common element (normally
Acetyl-CoA ) so the same enzymes can be used at
the end of the catabolic pathway.
Catabolism is convergent, and anabolism is
divergent .
[PDF p. 91]
Catabolic stages
1st stage: big molecules are degraded into small molecules: fats into fatty acids and
glycerol, polysaccharides into glucose and other sugars, and proteins into amino
acids. This occurs by hydrolysis, which doesn’t require energy.
2nd stage: small molecules are further broken down to finally obtain
Acetyl-CoA, which is the main goal of this phase (although some energy
is released). It’s a convergent phase.
3rd stage: Acetyl-CoA undergoes a series of reactions (Krebs cycle/citric
acid cycle). Most of the ATP is generated in this phase.
Regulatory mechanisms in metabolism

Control of enzyme concentration
Control of enzyme activity: either by allosteric
control or covalent modification (such as
phosphorylation)

Compartmentalization of enzymes and
substrates (ex: cellular respiration only happens
in the mitochondria)
Pathways can be regulated by the own products of the pathway.
ATP
Adenosine triphosphate is broken down to produce ADP or AMP, by hydrolysis, which
releases a big amount of energy that is used by our body.

Lecture 5.2. Electron transport
Gibbs free energy change lets us know about the direction of a reaction. The direction in
which the free energy change is negative will be the spontaneous reaction, and
therefore, the direction in which the process will take place.
The free energy change is not a fixed number, it changes towards equilibrium.
Gibbs free energy provides NO info about the reaction rate. That depends on the activation
energy and the transition state.
How to calculate the free energy change of a reaction knowing the conditions:
(R= gas constant: 8.3 J/mol) )
Example: Glucose 6P to FRuctose 6P
It ‘s positive. How come this process occurs in our cell?
Depending on the concentration of the molecules, the free energy rate will be positive or
negative in one direction.
The direction will therefore be determined by the concentration of molecules. The free
energy change changes with the molecule concentration.
What is the ratio in the equilibrium? We equal the equation to 0. This ratio will determine if a
reaction is reversible or irreversible . If it’s too high, it’s not possible in physiological
conditions, and therefore won’t happen.
In conclusion: all processes that take place in a cell are exergonic
Degradation and synthesis follow different processes, because not all reactions are
reversible. This allows the cell to regulate the processes independently, avoiding reactions
which would be useless. It allows coordinate and reciprocal regulation.
Coupling reactions allows to establish a negative free energy change, permitting
irreversible reactions to take place. This can be done by breaking ATP bonds.
There are two main strategies to obtain ATP: Substrate
level phosphorylation (because the element we are using
has a high phosphorylation potential) and oxidative
phosphorylation.
[PDF p. 93]
Carbon oxidation releases energy
Malate to oxaloacetate = oxidation. Electrons released are collected by NAD+, which
becomes NADH (its reduced form). When there is an oxidation, there also has to be a
reduction.
Electron carriers in metabolism: NAD +, NADP +, FAD and FMN.
NAD+ and NADP+, made up of a nicotinamide ring which is the active site of the molecule.
NADP is more frequently used in anabolism.
FAD (flavin adenine diphosphate) and FMN (… mononucleotide). They typically participate in

Lecture 5.3 and 5.4. Generation of ATP from glucose and other sugars
Glucose is an excellent fuel. Nervous tissue and erythrocytes preferably use glucose and
carbohydrates as their main fuel.
-Its oxidation yields -2840 kJ/mol glucose after the full oxidation of backbone carbons. It’s
highly reduced and contains a high amount of electrons, which will allow to obtain ATP
through oxidative phosphorylation.
-It can be efficiently stored in polymeric form ( glycogen ).
-Many tissues (neurons, erythrocytes,…) can meet their energy needs on glucose only.
-It’s a versatile biochemical precursor, as it can be used to generate all amino-acids,
membrane lipids,nucleotides,…
We can use glucose to obtain energy through the oxidation of the full carbon backbone.
GLYCOLYSIS
Glycolysis is a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions where glucose (6C) is broken down
into two pyruvate molecules (3C).The most of the energy released during glycolysis remains
in the form of NADH and pyruvate . Not much energy is released during glycolysis. Pyruvate
can be further oxidized or used as a precursor for biosynthesis.
It takes place in the cytoplasm and doesn’t need O2 : it can be done with or without
oxygen. Some tissues in our body carry out glycolysis aways in anaerobic conditions, like
erythrocytes. They contain hemoglobin with O2, but they can’t use it as they lack
mitochondria and so they can’t carry out cellular respiration. When glycolysis happens
without O2, the last step is fermentation. This process also happens in skeletal muscles,
when their activity is higher than the mitochondrias possibility to reoxidize NADH.
We can differentiate two steps in glycolysis: the preparatory phase (glucose is prepared for
breakdown. ATP is consumed) and payoff phase (from which we are able to obtain energy).
-
Preparatory phase: in this phase, we need
energy, so 2 ATPs are consumed, but this will
be compensated for in the next phase. First,
glucose undergoes phosphorylation,
avoiding the possibility for it to be released out
of the cell because of the negative charge
present on the phosphate. Also this negative
charge allows the substrate to establish many
interactions with enzyme active sites.
1. Step 1: Glucose phosphorylation (usually catalyzed by kinases: they
transfer one phosphate from ATP). This step is catalyzed by hexokinase,
which can also work on fructose and
mannose.
The liver is a carbohydrate-storage organ. It
doesn’t express hexokinase, but a different
isozyme, glucokinase . The only difference
[PDF p. 95]
between them is their affinity for glucose ( hexokinase more than glucokinase ).
This is so the liver, because it stores glucose, doesn’t consume all the
glucose and fill the blood with sugars.
If not, we would always be in hypoglycemia. For the liver, the main
energy-obtaining pathway is beta-oxidation of fatty acids.
2. Step 2: Glucose-6-phosphate isomerization: it’s
isomerized into fructose-6-phosphate by
phosphohexose isomerase. This step is
reversible.
3. Step 3: 2nd priming phosphorylation :
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) phosphorylates
carbon 1. It’s a critical step in glucose degradation
regulation. It’s regulated by the increase of cAMP
and ADP (which indicate low energy). It generates
fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
4. Step 4: Aldol cleavage: fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is broken down by an
aldolase between carbon 3 and 4. Carbons1,2,3 become a ketone,
dihydroxyacetone-phosphate, and carbons 4,5,6 become
glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P).
5. Step 5: Triose phosphate isomerase then converts
dihydroxyacetone-phosphate into
glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, so we obtain 2
molecules of G3P . This isomerization will allow the
G3P molecules to undergo subsequent reactions of
glycolysis.
-
Payoff phase:
6. Step 6: Oxidation of G3P. An
inorganic phosphate is added to
G3P by an enzyme,
glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
dehydrogenase . Electrons are
released and captured by NAD+,
which converts to NADH . A high
energy molecule is produced,
1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
7. Step 7: 1st production of ATP: It
occurs by substrate level
phosphorylation. The phospho
group in C1 is transferred to ADP by
phosphoglycerate kinase.
[PDF p. 96]
The hydrolysis of this bond releases enough energy to phosphorylate ADP,
releasing ATP . 3-phosphoglycerate is produced as a product.
8. Step 8: Migration of the phosphate, which is transferred from C3 to C2.
We go from 3-phosphoglycerate to 2-phosphoglycerate, a reaction which is
catalyzed by phosphoglycerate mutase.
9. Step 9: There is a dehydration carried out by an enolase, turning it to
phosphoenolpyruvate (with a double bond). This is the second high-energy
intermediate of glycolysis, which will allow to obtain ATP through substrate
level phosphorylation in the next stage. It has a high phosphate transfer
potential.
10. Step 10: 2nd production of ATP . Phosphoenolpyruvate loses its phospho
group. It’s transferred by a pyruvate kinase to an ADP molecule, which
results in the synthesis of ATP . Finally, we obtain Pyruvate .
Glycolysis balance: 2ATPs are consumed in the preparatory phase, but out of the two G3P
molecules, each yield 2 ATPs. Therefore, the payoff phase gives us 4 ATP. The final net
balance is 2 ATPs, 2 NADH + H+ and 2 pyruvate molecules.
Regulation of glycolysis
Glycolysis is regulated through 3 enzymes: hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and
pyruvate kinase.


Hexokinase is allosterically inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate.


Phosphofructokinase is allosterically activated by low energy markers ( AMP and
ADP ) and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, and inhibited by ATP and citrate, when in
high amounts, means there is already enough energy in the mitochondria, indicating
there is no need to oxidize high amounts of glucose.


Pyruvate-kinase has two isozymes: M (skeletal muscle,…) and L (liver). They are
allosterically inhibited by ATP, Acetyl-CoA (indicates enough energy is going to be
produced) and alanin (because it’s a source of pyruvate. It can be converted to it, so
high amounts of alanin indicate the cell there is no need to produce more pyruvate).
In addition to this, the L isozyme can undergo a covalent modification by


phosphorylation and dephosphorylation. The phosphorylated form is
inactive and the non-phosphorylated form, active.
When blood glucose concentration is low, glucagon is released and binds to
receptors in the liver. This will increase intracellular cAMP production and
promote the activation of PKA (protein kinase A) which will phosphorylate and
inactivate pyruvate kinase L. (As it becomes phosphorylated, it goes into
inactive form). This PKA will increase in hypoglycemia.
In turn, if blood glucose concentrations are high, the pancreas releases insulin
which will trigger a series of reactions that activate a phosphatase which will
dephosphorylate pyruvate kinase. That way, it will become activated and will allow
the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate and the continuation of the
degradation of glucose.

Importance of the presence of phosphorylated compounds during glycolysis
The phosphate groups confer the compounds a negative charge, which prevents
them from escaping the cell during glycolysis.

The energy released from the breakage of anhydride bonds in ATP during the
preparatory phase is conserved in the form of phosphoesther bonds, which in the
pay off phase will allow the synthesis of ATP.

The interaction between phosphate groups and the active site of the enzymes will
decrease the activation energy and increase the specificity of the reaction.
Fates of pyruvate

The most part is transported to the mitochondria

and oxidized into CO2.

There are also some tissues without

mitochondria (erythrocytes) or some that work in
hypoxia, like the skeletal muscle during sport.
Therefore, the pyruvate follows a different pathway.
Fermentation will be carried out, throughout lactic
fermentation.
Lactic acid fermentation reduces
pyruvate to lactate: NADH needs
to be restored, so electrons will be
used to reduce pyruvate into lactate. By this reduction, NADH
oxidation yields NAD+ and it’s restored. This way our cells don’t
completely waste pyruvate. In skeletal muscle, lactate accumulates
in the muscle and is then transported to the liver to be reconverted
into glucose.
It yields less energy than aerobic respiration, because NADH (each NADH will
produce 2.5 ATPs) and 2 pyruvate molecules (which at the end of the cycle would
have also produced ATP) are lost, but we can restore NAD+.
Other sugars that can undergo glycolysis

Mannose: it’s phosphorylated and then

there is an isomerization. It’s converted
into fructose-6-phosphate which enters
the glycolytic pathway.

Fructose: it’s phosphorylated to
fructose-6-phosphate by an hexokinase,
and then enters the glycolytic pathway.

In the liver it’s metabolized in a different
way: the liver doesn’t have hexokinase,
but fructokinase, which phosphorylates
C1. When, further on, the aldolase breaks
the molecule into 2, it results in dihydroxyacetone-phosphate and glyceraldehyde,
which is then phosphorylated by a triose kinase and converted to G3P.

Galactose: mainly obtained from the breakdown of lactose. Galactosemias are
complicated human diseases that are based on galactose accumulation due to
galactose metabolism impairment. They come from the lack of enzymes such as
galactokinase, UDP-glucose epimerase,
UDP-glucose-galactose-1-phosphate-uridyltransferase,…
It’s mainly carried out in the liver. Galactose is phosphorylated into
galactose-1-phosphate, which then reacts with a molecule called UDP-glucose
(catalyzed by UDP-glucose-galactose-1-phosphate-uridyltransferase, which

catalyzes the attack of the phosphate to the
anhydride bonds) and binds to UDP (uracil
nucleoside diphosphate). The end products
are glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose:
there is a sugar exchange/transfer. The G1P
can be further oxidized, but the
UDP-galactose is epimerized into glucose,
into UDP-glucose. Now this UDP-glucose
can further participate in the reaction that
converts galactose into glucose-1-phosphate.
If galactose accumulates in the liver, it affects
its function and also has repercussions on the
brain. If this happens, then the patient suffers
galactosemia . Clinical symptoms: mental
retardation, liver failure,… Metabolic tests are
usually performed on babies to detect
metabolic illnesses such as galactosemia.
Glycolysis and tumors
Glycolysis occurs at elevated rates in tumors. Initially, tumors are not vascularized
(haven’t undergone angiogenesis), so they have to grow in anaerobic conditions. They are
characterized by an extreme and big growth, so they need a lot of energy, and one of the
quickest ways to do this is fermentation . It gives out less energy but by increasing the rate
of fermentation it can be compensated. Knowing that they are highly dependent on
glycolysis, we can synthesize drugs that interfere with glycolysis in tumors to treat them.
The more glycolytic enzymes, the more opportunities to obtain energy from these pathways:
hypoxia triggers the expression of HIF-1 (inducible hypoxia factor) which increases the
transcription of glucose transporters (GLUT1 and GLUT3) that allow it to take up more
glucose, and of many enzymes such as hexokinases (tumor has more ability to carry out
glycolysis).
Cancer patients usually present hypoglycemia due to all of this, even before being
diagnosed with cancer.
CT scans and PET scans allow to differentiate a normal glucose intake from an abnormal
one. Glucose is marked and given to the patient, and then its uptake is observed on the
scan.

The Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs Cycle)


The oxidation of glucose to pyruvate is a necessary step on the way to energy
production, but not a sufficient one


If you remember that process (glycolysis) you realize that the amount of ATP
generated in it is 2 molecules.


However both, the pyruvate produced in the process and the NADH that is
generated, have a high potential to generate ATP through aerobic oxidative


processes.


Now we will see how pyruvate, instead of being reduced to lactate
(fermentation), undergoes a total oxidation to CO 2


This process, as a whole, leading to the complete oxidation of the organic
fuels (glucose, fatty acids, amino acids) is known as cellular respiration


Cellular respiration takes place in three stages :


First stage : carbon skeletons of organic fuels are
oxidized to a common compound called acetyl-
coenzyme A. Depending on the starting molecule,
the route used to convert the initial carbons into
acetate units is different. As we have already seen,
in the case of glucose, we will reach pyruvate
through glycolysis, and as we will see later,
pyruvate will be converted into acetate through
an additional oxidative decarboxylation reaction
(pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction)


Second stage : in this stage, the acetate (acetylCoA) is incorporated into the citric acid cycle (or
Krebs cycle) where the two carbons are oxidized to
CO 2 . At this stage of cellular respiration, most of
the energy released during oxidations is
temporarily conserved as NADH and FADH 2 .


Third stage : the reduced cofactors (NADH and
FADH 2 ) generated both in the first and in the
second phase, are oxidized and the released
electrons will end up reducing O 2, previously
passing through a chain of electron-transport
molecules. . In this process, known as oxidative
phosphorylation, a large amount of energy is
released that allows ATP to be synthesized


As seen in the diagram, the Krebs Cycle is the central axis of cellular
metabolism


It is the gateway to the aerobic metabolism for those molecules that will allow
to produce energy


It is also a pathway that provides precursors required for biosynthesis of other
molecules, Aa, nucleotides, porphyrins, and even glucose (from oxaloacetate)


Itself, the Krebs cycle does not generate ATP; its function is to generate
electrons in the form of NADH and FADH 2
