Lecture 7.2. Meiosis
MEIOTIC CELL DIVISION
It’s a special type of cell division that occurs in germ cells that will generate 4
gametes/haploid cells with one set of genetic information. There will be 2 consecutive
divisions.
Difference between mitosis and meiosis
Consider a cell with 2 chromosomes (homologous). Cells duplicate visible chromosomes,
with 2 sister chromatids per chromosome. We now have 4 copies of the gene (2 AA, 2 aa).
At the end of mitosis, we find 2 daughter cells, each with A and a genes.
In meiosis, after DNA duplication and chromosome formation, during prophase I, the
homologous chromosomes form the bivalent structure, and recombination occurs : the
non-sister chromatids from both homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material,
resulting in chromosomes and chromatids with diverse genes. During Anaphase I, whole
chromosomes migrate towards the centrosomes. At the end of meiotic division I, we are
left with 2 haploid cells which have their genetic material duplicated, so they directly enter
the subsequent division. As a result, 4 haploid cells are generated, each with a
combination of maternal and paternal information.
[PDF p. 197]
MEIOSIS
1. Meiotic division I
-
Prophase I: we find several subphases.
a) Leptotene: chromatine starts to condensate and form chromosomes. Homologous
chromosomes begin to pair with each other.
b) Zygotene ( union ) : chromosomal pairing occurs, resulting
in the synaptonemal complex (SC). This complex is held
together by proteins. It’s important to keep them together
for recombination to occur properly. At this point, we have
bivalence .
c) Pachytene ( thick ): the chromosomes are fully visible, thick
and bound together. In this step, crossing over
(recombination) takes place: homologous chromosomes
exchange genetic material.
d) Diplotene ( diplo=double ): once recombination has taken place, chromosomes tend
to separate and decondense, but they remain bound by chiasmata . In the areas
where there has been recombination, chiasmata is produced during pachytene, but
can’t be seen due to the proximity of chromosomes. It’s in diplotene, when
chromosomes separate a bit, that chiasmata are observed.
e) Diacinesis: chiasmata disappear, the nucleolus and nucleus envelope disappear
and histones begin to form.
Meiosis takes 64 days in the testis of males. It starts
at the base and the cells suffer a morphological
change that transforms the new cells into sperms.
-
Metaphase I
Homologous chromosomes align in the equatorial plane. Bivalents are randomly oriented
and assorted, which gives place to 2^`23 options/permutations. This generates genetic
variability, along with recombination.
-
Anaphase I
Individual whole chromosomes migrate to the poles of the cell, breaking the bivalent
structure.
-
Telophase I
Nuclear membrane begins to form, but not completely, since the cells are going to undergo a
subsequent division because of the duplicated haploid genetic info.
[PDF p. 198]
- Cytokinesis
2. Meiotic division II
Prophase II goes on as a normal prophase, followed by Metaphase II, Anaphase II,
Telophase II and Cytokinesis . It results in 4 haploid daughter cells.
GAMETOGENESIS
Gametogenesis is the process by which mature germ cells are produced.


In the case of males, meiosis starts at puberty, and it’s a continuous process that takes
64 days.


In females (watch video on female gametogenesis), meiosis starts when the embryo is
developing, around the 5th month of gestation. But, these cells enter into meiosis and stop
the process at Diplotene of Prophase I, and remain halted until ovulation . Until puberty, all
the oocytes are stuck at the diplotene phase .
As a result of the release of hormones such as estrogens, these oocytes will form a follicle
that is released and completes the first meiotic division: the 2 resulting cells are haploid.
One of them gets all the cytoplasm, and becomes the viable cell or secondary oocyte
(needs a big cytoplasm area for this whole process), and the other is bound to die (known as
Polar body I ).
The secondary oocyte, which is viable, continues the process. It once again gets stopped in
Metaphase II: there is a second meiotic arrest . Only if the oocyte becomes fertilized, it
will complete meiosis .
After fertilization, the secondary oocyte will divide again to produce 2 daughter cells .
One will be removed ( Polar body II ) and the other will combine its genetic material with
that of the sperm’s to form a zygote (the pronuclei fuse).


[PDF p. 199]
Lecture 7.3. Levels of chromatin packaging
The genome is a long thread of DNA. In the nucleus, the genome is wrapped around
proteins, which creates a fiber known as chromatin . During the cell cycle, chromatin
changes its level of packaging (highest during metaphase), forming chromosomes . During
interphase, chromosomes can’t be observed under light microscope.
This packaging is not done randomly:
“Chromatin for each chromosome occupies a specific territory inside the
nucleus, with many domains for the different genes”
Levels of packaging
1. 1st level of packaging
8 different histone molecules (2H2A, 2H2B, 2H3 and 2H4) form a nucleosome when DNA
wraps around them. Histone H1 acts as a linker, giving stability between different
nucleosomes. It’s the basic level of organization of chromatin (10 nanometer); (modelo del
collar de perlas)
2. 2nd level
DNA is found wrapped around histones, forming a solenoid (solenoid model), which gives
place to the 30 nanometer fibers.
3. 3rd level
30 nanometer fiber continues to wrap and coil, giving place to the chromosomes seen
during mitosis (100 nanometers).
The human cell has 46 chromosomes.
Chromatin in interphase is seen as a random
assembly of threads, but in truth, is not so
random: the chromatin for each chromosome
occupies a specific territory inside the nucleus.
There are two pairs of chromosomes (maternal
and paternal), which are homologous.
The two homologous chromosomes don’t
necessarily occupy neighboring areas of the
nucleus.
Ex: chromosome 16 (maternal and paternal version). These homologous chromosomes
contain the same genes in the same order, but these may be different versions of said
genes ( alleles ). They may differ in a specific region of the nucleotide sequence, and each
will confer different characteristics.
Chromosome 16=MC1R, codifies for hair colour.
During DNA replication, each chromosome is copied, giving place to two sister
chromatids (each visible chromosome will be seen with two arms that contain identical
information).
[PDF p. 200]
Nucleosomes
Histones have tails, whose amino acids will undergo
modifications that will be crucial for cell replication. DNA wraps
around these histones to form nucleosomes .
The levels of packaging correlates with gene activity and
translation.
Chromosome structure
Chromosomes have a centromere, the point of attachment of microtubules . When
chromosomes are stained through G banding, it reflects the packaging levels: clearer bands
are less compact, whereas darker bands undergo higher packaging.
The short arm is known as the “p” arm, and the long arm as the “q” arm (although
chromosomes don’t always have a long and short arm, they can be found with similar
lengths).
The banding pattern allows to name the bands by number.
How chromatin undergoes packaging
1st, chromatin forms loops, giving place
to the solenoid model. These loops are
clustered into compartments . The largest
type of compartment in the hierarchy is
called TAD (topologically associating
domains), they are domains of
chromatin that associate in space.
Therefore, chromatin regions within that
domain interact with each other more
frequently than with other regions of
the genome. This has functional
consequences: everything found inside
this TAD interact among each other more
frequently. Interaction usually means
function.
The whole genome is therefore
compartmentalized into functional
domains.
Many TADs cluster and come together to form exclusive compartments.
Genes in each compartment will be active or not depending on the interactions in TAD,
within each domain.
Inactive compartments are closer to the periphery of the nucleus, closer to the nuclear
lamina.
[PDF p. 201]
Compartments come in two different
flavours: ACTIVE (A compartments),
and INACTIVE (B compartments).
Genes within each TAD: most of them
will be active, or most of them inactive.
The function of each cell is
determined by the activity and
expression of each independent
gene. This is due to cell differentiation
during embryo development. That’s
why the cells in our body, although
containing the same genome, have
different morphology and functions.
Cells differentiate into the various tissues due to differential gene expressions, different
patterns of activation.
This all occurs through the regulation of gene expression, carried out by enhancers and
promoters. The enhancer has to come into contact with the promoter to activate the
expression of the gene, and this occurs thanks to the formation of loops . That’s why genes
are found in different TADs, which contain genes and their respective enhancers.
Some proteins are responsible for the borders between TADs. A disruption in this border
can cause disease because it interferes with gene expression, by causing the formation of
bigger TADs and therefore more interactions.
In vertebrates, the boundaries are made by the protein CTCF, a protein that behaves as an
insulator. It forms a dimer that will flank compartments at the boundaries.
[PDF p. 202]
Lecture 7.4. General features of the human genome


The human genome is 3Gb long and contains thousands of genes.


The G-C content (percentage of guanine and cytosine bases) directly correlates with
functional regions of the genome.


The genome is full of repeated copies of mobile elements.


Graph about the G-C percentage
1st graph: The graph is not symmetrical. There are
regions of the genome with very low G-C percentage,
while others are very rich in Gs and Cs. The average is
below 50 ( 42%, but there are regions with G-C content
higher than 50)
2nd graph:
About relative gene density. We find a very
distinctive trend: the higher the G-C content, the
more gene-dense that region of the genome. G-C
regions associate with more genes, because
genes are G-C rich. The rest of the regions of the
genome which aren’t genes have less G-C
implications.
Repeats
There are sequences which are repeated in the genome thousands of times.
Repeats come in two flavours: tandem or dispersed .
1. Tandems
We classify tandem repeats by the size of the unit which is repeated:

Satellites are tandem repeats made up of large units
of 100 bp, which are repeated up to several
Megabases. For example, “alpha-satellite” contains
DNA that makes up the centromeres.
Minisatellites are shorter units (10-100 bp).
Microsatellites are short units made up of 1 - 9 bp,
repeated to make up the sequence. They are also
known as STRs (short tandem repeats).

[PDF p. 203]
2. Dispersed 0
They are dispersed because they are mobile elements, transposons (jump from one
region of the cell to another. Have been doing it for thousands of years). Two different types:
DNA transposons: a sequence of the genome that makes a copy of itself and
integrates it in a different region of the genome ( transposase ). They are relatively
short. We have 300 thousand copies of DNA transposons dispersed in our
genome.
RNA transposons: they work via an intermediate. The
sequence is translated into messenger RNA, which goes
into the cytoplasm, generating a protein which will then
bind to the mRNA and move back to the nucleus,
introducing it into another area of the genome through
retrotranscription (carried out by a
retrotranscriptase ).
a) LTR-retrotransposons: LTR stands for long-terminal-repeats. They are
specific sequences of retroviral genomes (ex: HIV), specifically the
sequences that make up the tail ends of these retroviral genomes, which are
flanked by target site duplications. (These regions codify for RNA which is
translated into a retrotranscriptase, which will carry out retrotranscription of
the RNA fragment (forming DNA) and reinsert it in a region of our genome).
We find many LTRs in our own genomes because we have been infected by
viruses over millions of years. 8% of our genome is made up of these
LTR-retrotransposons.
b) Non-LTR retrotransposons: They are not derived from retroviruses. We find:
- LINE (long): Quite rich in G-C (42%) and contain target site duplications.
They are very important because they are the ones that code for the
proteins that carry out retrotransposition. When LINE are transcribed to
mRNA, they codify for 2 proteins: ORF1 (protein with DNA binding ability) and
ORF2 (protein with endonuclease and retrotranscriptase activity), which are
responsible for retrotransposition. We more or less carry 850,000 LINE
retrotransposons ( 21% of our genome). LINE 1.
      - **SINE** (short): Even more rich in **G-C (56%),** also contains target site

duplications. They don’t encode for any proteins, so to carry out
retrotransposition they will have to make use of LINE/autonomous
retrotranscriptases . They are non-autonomous. We have around 1,500,000
SINE retrotransposons, which make up about 13% of our genome. ALU.
[PDF p. 204]
Lecture 7.5. DNA replication
Scientists wondered at the ability of organisms to create copies of themselves, and of cells
to produce identical copies of large molecules.
Fundamental aspects
DNA replication is a semiconservative process
Replication begins at specific replication origins, and once it has begun, it
proceeds bidirectionally

DNA synthesis progresses from 5´ to 3´end, and it’s a semi discontinuous

process.
DNA replication is semiconservative
Each daughter cell carries one original strand from the parental cell and one newly
synthesized strand (experimentally demonstrated at the end of 1950s).
Replication begins at an origin and occurs bidirectionally
(experiments made on E-Coli)
The replication origin site (Ori C) is where
replication begins, and forms replication forks,
which move bidirectionally along the DNA
strand.
Most of the observations made on bacteria can
be extrapolated to humans because DNA
replication is a highly conservative process.

Origin of replication in E. coli : characterized by having repetitive sections of
nucleotides (in tandem), which are found next to binding sites for DnaA protein.
These sites are recognized and bound to by Dna-A. This allows the recruitment of a
protein called helicase (Dna-B), which will allow the separation of the double strand.
The single strand of DNA is then bound to SSB (single stranded DNA binding
proteins), which stabilizes the strand.

Origin of replication in eukaryotes: This process is
more complex in nucleated cells due to the size of the
[PDF p. 205]
genome, number of chromosomes and the linear sequence…
In eukaryotes there are multiple origins of replication. There are no specific DNA
sequences associated with these origins of replication. Additionally, these origins of
replication are rich in A and T bases (because they form double bonds and not
triple, which makes them easier to denature), around which the origin of replication
complexes (ORC) associate. ORCs include, among other auxiliary proteins:
    An hexamer complex (similar to that formed by bacterial DnaA)

    A helicase complex formed by six subunits of the Mcm2-7 protein

    An SSB known as “replication protein A”

    Two different polymerases, DNA-pol-alpha and DNA-pol-gamma

DNA synthesis proceeds from 5´to 3´ and is semi-discontinuous
A new DNA strand is always synthesized in this direction (from 5’ to 3’). The synthesis of
the leading strand is therefore a continuous process.
But the synthesis of the opposite strand (the lagging strand ), as it is oriented in the
opposite direction, has to be done throughout fragments which begin at primers (RNA
primers) and are synthesized from 5´to 3´ in short segments. These segments are known as
Okazaki Fragments . In bacteria, they are 1000 to 2000 nucleotides long while in
eukaryotes, 150-200 nucleotides long.
Enzymes that carry out DNA replication
DNA polymerases were discovered thanks to the work of Arthur Kornberg, who discovered
DNA-polymerase I. Since then, many other elements have been discovered in bacteria,
finding that E. Coli contains at least four other distinct DNA polymerases.
There are 2 basic requirements for DNA polymerization:

All DNA polymerases require a template .
A primer with a free 3´ -OH end is needed for the reaction to begin. These primers
are RNA nucleotides, of about 5 nucleotides, synthesized by RNA polymerase
( primase ) which is also part of the replication process.

Reaction catalyzed by DNA polymerase I
This is an energy favourable
process, catalyzed by
pyrophosphatase.
DNA polymerase catalytic mechanism
[PDF p. 206]
In the catalytic site of the polymerase, there are 2 Mg2+ ions:


The presence of the upper Mg2+ ion helps in the execution of the nucleophilic attack of
the hydroxyl group


The lower Mg2+ ion helps in the displacement of the pyrophosphate.


DNA replication is a very accurate and specific process. Therefore, there are
many mechanisms and checkpoints that carry out surveillance of the process.
    - Nucleotide selection is based on its **ability to base-pair** (formation of H

bonds) and the geometry of the base pairs, specifically the catalytic sites.
Nucleobases can be found in different tautomeric forms. The selection of
bases in the incorrect tautomeric form can lead to pairing with the wrong
base.
    Active sites accommodate both A-T and G-C base pairs, as they have similar

geometries.
    The geometry of incorrectly paired bases can exclude them from the active

site of the enzyme.
DNA polymerases make mistakes, and insert one incorrect nucleotide for every 10 to the 4
correct ones, due to unusual tautomeric forms. These sorts of errors are reduced by
enzymatic mechanisms: exonuclease activity removes the mispaired nucleotide, and the
polymerase begins again. This activity is known as proofreading .
DNA polymerase I, II and III
Many other DNA polymerases were discovered, but DNA polymerase I was found in E. Coli
accounting for 90% of DNA polymerase activity. It also has the differential feature that it
has exonuclease activity.
Although it’s the most abundant polymerase, it’s not the most important. DNA pol III and
DNA pol II have higher polymerization rates.
Subsequently, another important differential feature between DNA pol I and III is the
processivity . DNA pol III has the ability to stay bound to the template, and dissociate after
many million nucleotides. DNA polymerase I dissociates after 3-20 bases.
DNA polymerase III
DNA polymerase III is much more complex than DNA pol I,
having ten types of subunits. We can distinguish different parts.
The polymerization activity resides in the alpha subunits,
and proofreading activities in the epsilon subunit.
The high processivity of DNApol-III is provided by the beta
subunits. The subunits associate in pairs and form structures
that act as clamps, preventing the dissociation from the DNA
strands.
It has 2 catalytic cores, because it needs a catalytic site for
each strand. They have to be very coordinated.
DNA replication involves many different enzymes and
cofactors
[PDF p. 207]
SSB (single stranded DNA binding proteins)
- Helicase

Primase (synthesizes the primer)

DNA polymerases
DNA ligase (binds for example Okazaki fragments between each other)
Topoisomerases (I and II) cope with the supercoiling of the DNA strands.
MECHANISM OF DNA REPLICATION in E. COLI
1. Initiation
    Proteins bind to DNA and open up the double helix

    Preparation of the DNA for complementary base

pairing takes place
At least 9 proteins participate in this initiation step, recognizing a
specific sequence and separating the strands by denaturing the
structure ( Helicase ). Then SSB (single stranded DNA binding
proteins) prevent renaturalization. Once helicase binds, the process
is considered to begin. The primer is synthesized by primase and
the replication is carried out from this point by DNA polymerase III.
2. Elongation
2 catalytic cores made up of 2 beta subunits in a doughnut-shape
carry out the process of replication, bound together by a
clamp-loading complex. Proteins connect the correct sequences
of nucleotides into a continuous new strand of DNA. Whilst DNA is
unwound by helicases, the supercoiling of the strand is relieved by
topoisomerases . From this point, the synthesis of the lagging
strand is quite different for the leading strand. It’s carried out
through the synthesis of independent segments known as Okazaki
Fragments.
For each Okazaki fragment, a new primer needs to be added. The
primase arrives and binds to the helicase, synthesizing the new
primer, while the polymerase ends the synthesis of the previous O.
fragment.
In the meantime, a new Beta-clamp is being added at the point
where the new primer has been synthesized.
The new clamp moves along the strand and is loaded onto the
catalytic core, while the other is discarded, and the synthesis of the
new fragment can begin.
Once an Okazaki fragment has been completed, its RNA primer is
removed and replaced by DNA. This process is carried out by DNA polymerase I through its
exonuclease and polymerase activity, and the remaining nick is sealed by DNA ligase .
3. Termination
[PDF p. 208]
Proteins release the replication complex when the two replication forks of the circular E.
coli chromosome encounter each other.
The two replication forks meet at a terminus region containing copies of a 20 bp sequence
known as Ter (for “terminus”). Ter sequences function as binding sites for a protein called
Tus (Terminus utilization substance).
These sequences are present in case one replication fork for some reason carries out
replication faster than the other. Even though it gets to the end first, it will remain there and
not continue replicating due to this 20 bp terminus (Ter).
MECHANISM OF DNA REPLICATION in EUKARYOTES
The essential characteristics of DNA replication are conserved between prokaryotes and
eukaryotes. But during replication, eukaryotes present many more replication origins.
These are known as “origin of replication complexes” (ORC).
Replication also occurs bidirectionally from the multiple ORC, but it’s carried out by
eukaryotic DNA polymerases:
Some catalyze DNA synthesis while others are involved in repair.
Polymerase alpha (α) lacks 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity (proofreading), but it
synthesizes the RNA primers.

Polymerase delta (δ) is the equivalent to DNA pol III in prokaryotes. Its PCNA
subunit is the equivalent to the beta clamp. It mainly performs elongation .
This protein can be analyzed in tissues by immunohistochemistry to detect tumors,
as it will appear as a marker in highly proliferating cells.

Polymerase epsilon (ϵ) is the other subunit involved in DNA synthesis and
elongation, and is thought to play a role in eliminating the primers from Okazaki
fragments.
- Polymerase gamma (γ) synthesizes mitochondrial DNA.
[PDF p. 209]

Lecture 7.6. Protein coding and non coding genes
(video that summarizes the lecture: Javier Novo)
What is a gene?
Genes come in two classes: coding and non-coding genes.
“A gene is a sequence of DNA that is used to make a messenger”
This definition was established because non-coding genes also make mRNA,
but it’s not translated into proteins. That’s the difference between coding and
non-coding genes. Enhancers don’t make messenger RNA, therefore they are
part of DNA but not considered genes.
Transcription begins where the
gene starts. It’s transcribed into a single
stranded RNA molecule, made up of both
exons and introns, called primary transcript.
The primary transcript is processed through a
mechanism called splicing: spliceosomes
cut the primary transcript at points which are
exactly the boundaries between exons and
introns. The remaining exons bind together to
create what we know as mRNA, which
contains a CAP at the 5’ end. Maturation of
the primary transcript gives mRNA.
1. PROTEIN CODING GENES

There are around 20,000 protein coding genes
Exons tend to be very short, whereas introns are very large but yet very very
variable. There are genes with one exon only, others with thousands; on average, a
human protein coding gene has 7-8 exons.
The average size of these exons is 145 nt .
The size of the average gene is 20-30 kilo bases.
Only 1.5 % of nucleotides in the genome are coding genes. The rest are destined
to regulation and many other processes.
They have a high G-C content (gene dense), of about 53%
- It has at least 4 alternative transcripts, generated by alternative splicing

They appear to have a high expression rate (generate many transcripts)
-
Low cell specificity
One gene can make many different transcripts, depending on the exons included. The
mechanism of splicing creates different alternatives of mRNA. This is known as alternative
splicing. Each of the transcripts will code for slightly different proteins.
[PDF p. 210]
Brown boxes in the picture represent gene sequences before initiation and stop codons.
Therefore, these sequences won’t transalte into proteins. They are untranslated regions
(UTRs).

Initiation codon = AUG (encodes
for methionine, proteins always
begin with methionine). The
previous part to AUG is not
translated, and is known as 5’ UTR.

Stop codons = UAA, UAG, UGA,
which indicate translation to stop.
The region of RNA that comes after
this codon isn’t translated, and is
known as 3’ UTR.
2. NON-CODING GENES

Around 15,000 genes for long and short non-coding RNAs.

IncRNA genes are shorter than protein-coding genes

IncRNA genes have fewer exons, around 2-4 exons.

They are between 10-15 Kilobases long.

In the average genome, an IncRNA has around 43% G-C content. They are less rich
in G-C content than protein coding genes, and therefore, less gene dense.
We find 2 alternative transcripts per non-coding gene

They have a lower expression than protein coding genes (weak regulators)
They have high cell specificity (mostly transcribed in specific cells)
Expression of IncRNAs is very restricted. On average, protein-coding genes tend to be
broadly expressed in all cells. But most non-protein coding genes are specific for each
cell line, being expressed sometimes in only one cell line.
[PDF p. 211]
3. PSEUDOGENES
Pseudogenes are genes which are inactive and don’t work. There are two types:
-
Non-processed, as a result of
mutations in duplication.

Processed, which have the sequence

of what mRNA would look like
(therefore, made up by exons), and are
usually silent because they lack the
promoter. These sequences are found
away from the promoter because
they’ve been relocated through LINE
retrotransposition.
HUMAN GENOME GENERAL STATISTICS
[PDF p. 212]
Lecture 7.7. Genetic variation
Mutations in the genome result in alternative forms of DNA known as DNA variants. If these
variants in a certain locus are common in the population, the variation is described as a
polymorphism.
Polymorphic genes are genes that appear in the population in the form of many different
alleles. Genomes can have two types of variation:

differ in single nucleotides

present larger structural variants.
These variants have profound implications for predisposition to disease.
SINGLE-NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM (SNP)
In the DNA of our cells, we may find polymorphisms between one individual and the next
that consist in variations in one single nucleotide.
How often do we find these
polymorphisms? Are they
common?
SNPs (pronounced “snips”) are
found every 500 letters on
average. So every 500 letters,
each individual will present a
polymorphism. Therefore, when we
compare two genomes, they will
probably differ in 3 million single
nucleotides.
-
DNA sequencing

Single peaks imply the person is homozygous for
that base, in both parental chromosomes.
Smaller, double peaks imply there are two different
nucleotides in this position in each chromosome
(maternal and paternal).

The human genome project
Took 13 years and an estimated cost of 3 billion dollars to sequence the genome of a single
individual. But technology has improved a lot, and now we can sequence one’s genome in a
single day. This has allowed us to discover more SNPs.
Genomes have constant sequences, but about 100 million letters are variants between the
different humans on the planet.
[PDF p. 213]
Typical genome vs the reference genome

A typical genome, compared to the reference genome, can present 4 to 5 million

variants.

About 10,000 (not all nucleotides in DNA are genes) of these SNPs are potentially
dangerous, as they change protein sequences.

Furthermore, in general, each of us carry 25-30 SNPs previously associated with
disease: it can set a predisposition to suffer a disease or not, depending on other
many genetic factors. By knowing the whole genome, we could predict the probability
of predisposition.
Lastly, 500,000 overlap regulatory regions . Some promoters are very strong and
make many mRNA copies; other promoters are very weak. Protein coding genes
usually have stronger promoters than non-protein coding genes. These overlapping
genes and SNPs can silence promoters and substantially affect gene regulation and
expression.
Distribution of genetic variation
Anywhere in the world, around 4 to 5 million variants are detected when comparing 2
people from anywhere around the world. Anywhere except in Africa, where we find many
more SNPs.
There is more variation inside Africa than outside Africa. Comparing two people from a same
African city, they will present more genetic variation than when comparing two genomes from
two individuals from different parts of the world.
Why is this?
African = “first humans”. From all the people in Africa, only a few of them made it to the rest
of the planet and colonized it. Therefore, only a few SNPs were present in the populations
that gave place to the many ethnicities around the world today.
[PDF p. 214]
STRUCTURAL VARIANTS and SEGMENTAL DUPLICATIONS
A lot of the genome is covered by segmental duplications.
Some of them are polymorphic in the number of times they are repeated.
In the population, there are chromosomes with one copy of segment X or
many copies of it. If you have a different number of copies for one
segment, you will therefore have repeated copies of many genes.
These segmental duplications (or structural variants) play a big role in
predisposition to disease.
A total of 68,000 SV (structural variants) have been described in
humans.
Each of us carry 20 Megabases, and around 2,000 SVs.
[PDF p. 215]
Lecture 7.8. DNA damage
Cells are able to repair the damage that DNA suffers. DNA is constantly being attacked or
destroyed by many mechanisms such as DNA replication (even with proofreading, it makes
mistakes).
There are several ways in which cells repair DNA damage:
Mismatch repair (MMR), which mostly arise from errors during DNA replication
Base Excision repair (BER), which works by removing the base, not the whole
nucleotide
Lesions that distort the double helix are repaired by Nucleotide-Excision repair
(NER)
Double strand breaks (DSBs), a type of damage created by x-rays or ionizing
agents, are repaired by a process similar to that of recombination during meiosis.
What does the cell do?
When faced with this situation, the cell tries to repair the damage. Therefore, the cell cycle
has to stop and activate cell cycle checkpoints. If the DNA is repaired, the cell continues
it’s cycle. If the damage is unrepairable, the cell will commit suicicde and proceed to
apoptosis . If these damaged cells don’t die through apoptosis, they will continue to divide
and propagate mutations, giving place to tumors and cancer.
[PDF p. 216]
A) Repair of DNA damage or altered sequence on a SINGLE STRAND
1. Repair of mismatches through mismatch repair (MMR)

Occurs mainly during DNA replication through the insertion of wrong tautomeric

forms of the nucleobases

It can also occur through strand slippage during replication (specifically during the
formation of Okazaki fragments). A bulging loop is formed due to the slippage, and at the
end of replication there is a strand with a protuberating loop.

Mechanism to repair mismatches: Carried out in eukaryotes by a protein complex, a
tetramer: a dimer made up of hMLH1 and hPMS2 can the bind, either to the
hMSH2-hMSH6 dimer or to the hMSH2-hMSH3 dimer, forming the tetrameric complex that
will repair the mismatch.
Mismatches involving abnormal nucleotides can occur by:


Hydrolytic reactions (depurination)


Deamination of non-methylated cytosines


UV light


Alkylating agents


-
Alkylating agents
Example: o6-methyl-guanine, which binds with thymine instead of cytosine. Alkylating agents
can be found in the diet or in toxic substances.
-
Benzopyrene
Molecule that intercalates in the double strand of DNA and creates a distortion. It’s found in
tobacco.
-
UV light
The incidence of UV light generates pyrimidine dimers (covalent bonds between
pyrimidines), which creates bulks and is bad for replication and transcription processes, as it
interferes with them.
[PDF p. 217]
2. Repair of abnormal bases and bulky adducts through BER and NER


Base Excision Repair or BER works by removing the incorrect base. Firstly, a DNA
glycosylase recognizes the base that needs to be changed and cleaves the
sugar-base bond to remove the base, leaving an abasic site. The remaining
sugar-phosphate backbone is removed by an endonuclease and a
phosphodiesterase, and the gap is filled by a DNA polymerase. Finally, a ligase binds
the whole strand together.


Nucleotide Excision Repair or NER: allows the repair of bulky, helix-distorting DNA
lesions. Proteins recognize the damage ( XPC, together with XPA ). They occupy the
region of the lesion and recruit a complex that opens the double helix.
RPA binds to one of the strands, and XPF and XPG make an incision and cleave the
DNA, generating an oligonucleotide around 30 nucleotides long which contains the
damaged site. The strand is removed and correctly filled in by DNA polymerases,
using the opposite strand as a template. Finally, it’s all bound together by a ligase .

XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM: Caused by a
mutation in genes that codify for XP proteins.
The NER process is interfered . If NER can’t
work, mutations accumulate and give rise to this
disease, Xeroderma Pigmentosum.



[PDF p. 218]
B) Repair of DNA lesions that affect BOTH STRANDS
Double strand breaks occur naturally in B and T lymphocytes for the rearrangement of DNA,
to maximize immunoglobulin and T cell receptor diversity.
This damage can also happen by accident, caused by external agents (ex: X Rays, which
kills cells by making these breaks), endogenous causes,…
It consists in the breakage of both strands. Cells respond to DSBs (double strand breaks)
in different ways. If DNA repair isn’t successful, the cell undergoes apoptosis.
Two repair pathways are mainly employed:
Non-homologous end joining: No template strand is needed in this repair
mechanism, because the broken ends are fused together. It rejoins the broken
strands without any type of homologous template. It just seals loose ends together
again. KU80, KU70 and DNAPKcs, bring the strands together and seal the lession
thanks to ligases .
Homologous recombination repair (HRR): this process requires a homologous
intact DNA strand to serve as a template. This mechanism uses the same
machinery that is used in meiosis for recombination : there are two strands that have
to exchange DNA, and everything starts by making a break in one of them. One is
used as a template to repair the other.
[PDF p. 219]
TBL 7.1. Apoptosis and senescence
In some occasions, cells need to die. Cell death can occur through:

Necrosis, whenever there is an acute injury or cell damage
Senescence (aging), when cells lose their ability to proliferate

Apoptosis, programmed cellular death which can occur, for
example, when there is DNA damage, pathological infection,…
APOPTOSIS
There has to be a controlled ratio between cell proliferation and
cellular death. Apoptosis consists in programmed cell death. It’s
a process that’s highly regulated, and can be induced by:
-
Genetic / biochemical changes
-
Morphological changes
Apoptosis isn’t only important for removing damaged
cells, but also for growth and neonatal development. For
example, during Syndactyly, the programmed death of
cells in the web spaces allows the formation of independent
fingers; or in the brain during embryonic development,
half of the neurons have to die through apoptosis so there
can be plenty of nutrients for neurons and microglia.
Apoptosis can be activated through two pathways, which don’t only occur independently:
the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.
a) Intrinsic pathway
Cell stress, for example caused by
DNA damage, induces specific cellular
signals that activate p53. This
transcription factor activates proteins
involved in mitochondrial membrane
destabilization (BAX and BAK) and the
organelle releases Cytochrome C,
which will activate the caspase
cascade.
[PDF p. 220]
b) Extrinsic pathway
An external ligand binds to the Death Receptor. This receptor contains a Death
Domain (FADD) which is bound to Caspase 8. Upon activation, Caspase 8 will initiate
the Caspase cascade, which ends with the activity of Caspase 3.
These two pathways are interconnected through the
protein BID. This protein, when activated by Caspase 8,
triggers the release of Cytochrome C from the
mitochondria through proapoptotic proteins (BAX and
BAK).
- BCL-2 family is a family of antiapoptotic proteins.
- BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic and destabilize the
mitochondrial membrane.
- BH3-only, released in response to chemicals, radiation
or growth factors withdrawal, inhibits anti-apoptotic
proteins (and is therefore proapoptotic).
Under the microscope
Under electron microscope, apoptotic cells present a dark, electron
dense nucleus due to the condensation of chromatin, often
presenting “blebs”. Through immunohistochemistry, apoptotic cells
can be seen more clearly as dark brown or black due to the
compacted nucleus.
p53: the guardian of the genome
p53 is a transcription factor, activated by phosphorylation when DNA damage, hypoxia,
activated oncogenes or telomeric erosion are detected. It acts by stopping the cell cycle
and allowing the entry of DNA repair proteins, to try and repair the damage. If this isn’t
achieved, it triggers apoptosis. This is why 50% of tumors harbor p53 mutations.
The main regulator of p53 is Mdm2.
Mdm2 is a p53 inhibitor, which:
Inhibits p53 gene regulation activity
Exports p53 out of the nucleus
Induces p53 degradation
[PDF p. 221]
How do T-lymphocytes induce apoptosis?
A Cytotoxic T lymphocyte binds its T cell receptor to and infected cell by:


Binding to the antigen presented to the T-lymphocyte by the cell


Binding to the Major Histocompatibility Complex I (MHC-I)


It then induces apoptosis by activating the extrinsic and intrinsic
pathways.
                        **Extrinsic pathway:** Once bound, the Cytotoxic

T-cell expresses the FAS ligand, which induces
apoptosis by binding to receptors in other
neighbouring cells.
Intrinsic pathway: the Cytotoxic T-cell releases perforin, which creates a
perforin-channel in the infected cell. Subsequently, it releases granzyme, an enzyme
which enters the infected cell through the perforin-channel and activates the
Caspase cascade, thus inducing apoptosis.
SENESCENCE
Senescence occurs when a cell loses its proliferation capacity and is permanently in a
G1 phase.
It can be induced by:
-
Oxidative stress and external damage

Genetic factors, such as telomere shortening: after each cell division, the end of
chromosomes (telomeres) shortens a little bit every time. As telomeres shorten, the
cell enters into telomere crisis after too many replications: this is a sign that the cell
is very old and has possibly accumulated mutations, so it goes into senescence.
In cancer cells and stem cells, telomerase is expressed, which allows them to
elongate telomeres and evade senescence. This enzyme is also expressed in
oocytes and spermatozoa, which are going to give rise to a new organism. This
allows the baby to be born with the telomere counter at 0.

[PDF p. 222]
PROGERIA
Progeria, also known as Hutchinson-Gilford syndrome, is caused by a mutation in
Lamin-A. It has quite a low incidence (less than 200 cases diagnosed), and conferes a life
expectancy of 13-14 years.
Lamin-A is part of the nuclear lamina : it forms an
intracellular-scaffolding for the nuclear envelope, and is in
charge of organizing nucleosomes.
In a normal LMNA gene, the sequence is transcribed and once
the primary transcript is produced, the exons are removed and
matured, forming mRNA. Exon 11 contains a sequence which
encodes for the cleavage site. This mRNA is traduced into a
protein (Lamin-A) which becomes farnesylated to allow it’s
transport into the nucleus and consequent attachment to the
inner part of the nuclear membrane. A fragment of the protein is
removed by proteolysis at the cleavage site to eliminate the
farnesyl group, which is necessary for the normal function of the
protein.
In patients with Progeria, a mutation in Exon 11 changes the
way this exon is spliced. The mutation generates a new splicing site, producing the loss of
50 amino acids. Within these 50 amino acids, the cleavage site is lost, so the farnesyl group
won’t be able to be removed, and the farnesylated protein will form aggregates and become
harmful for the cell. Chromatin suffers conformational stress and DNA becomes damaged,
which activates p53 and increases cellular senescence, thus accelerating aging. This is why
patients, at very young ages, resemble a person older than 100 years old.
Patients with this syndrome usually present tricuspid valve reflux.
Lonafarnib can be used for the treatment of Progeria, as it’s a farnesyltransferase inhibitor.
But this implies that LMNA isn’t correctly transferred into the nucleus, which can also have
side effects.
