TBL 7.2. Forensic DNA analysis
STRs (microsatellites) can be used to identify individuals. There
are many different alleles in the population for short tandem repeats
(polymorphic). Different people have different combinations of
alleles; that’s why it’s a useful method to identify suspects.
The more microsatellites you analyze, the better.
How to analyze microsatellites?
Modern DNA profiles analyze short tandem repeats (STRs), located in non-coding
regions of chromosomes.
Currently, the FBI analyzes 13 STRs, plus a sex marker. This way, they reduce the
possibility of random matches.
STRs are highly polymorphic, having nine or more different alleles
that can be detected.
To detect if a person is homozygous or heterozygous for a certain
STR, we use PCR technique, which amplifies specific regions of DNA.
PCR primers are designed to bracket the STR. In this type of PCR,
one primer of the pair is fluorescently labeled.
The same DNA region is amplified many times, although the
different alleles amplify as different sizes.
The amplified alleles fluoresce, as each has incorporated a
fluorescent primer.
Out of the 14 STRs which are analyzed, 3 or 4 different
polymorphisms are labeled with each of four fluorescent dyes.
The amplified DNA fragments are loaded onto a gel, where the smaller
pieces migrate faster than the larger ones.
Each fragment is detected when it passes by a laser when it’s near the bottom of the gel.
The laser reads all four colors and displays an output of the PCR according to the sizes and
fluorescent colors of the amplified species.
[PDF p. 224]
Each locus appears as a single peak (homozygous) or a pair
of peaks (heterozygous).
A complete DNA profile of 13 STRs+sex marker comes with a
random match probability (probability that a specific STR profile
matches that of another individual in a population). There are
ways to calculate these random match probabilities, by using the
frequencies at which different STR alleles occur in a population.
-
In homozygous individuals: (frequency of A )^2
-
In heterozygous individuals: (frequency of A) x (frequency of B) x 2
[PDF p. 225]
Lecture 8.1 and 8.2. DNA transcription I and II
Transcription will give rise to different types of RNA.
Messenger RNA (mRNA)

Transfer RNA (tRNA)
Ribosomal RNA (rRNA), essential structural and functional components of

ribosomes.
Non-coding RNA (ncRNA)
The transcriptome in a tissue is the collection of all RNAs that are being produced in said
tissue cells.
Coding and non-coding RNAs in the human genome
Nowadays, we know that less than 3% of the genome are coding genes, which are
transcribed into mRNA and then into proteins; 80% corresponds to non-coding genes,
which are only transcribed into RNA but not translated to produce proteins. These
non-coding RNAs correspond to tRNA, rRNA,… but also to Small ncRNA and Long ncRNA,
which are still being investigated but have been found to play a key role in the control of
gene expression (through regulating specific interactions with chromatin, degradation,…)
It’s also been observed that the
expression of these lncRNA and
sncRNA is varied during disease. In
relation to this, they can be targeted to
affect their expression levels, so they are
starting to be used as new
pharmacological targets.
RNA SYNTHESIS
RNA synthesis is a polymerization reaction catalyzed by RNA polymerases , a set of
enzymes which synthesize RNA from a DNA template.
It’s a reaction in which nucleotides are incorporated to form a single stranded chain, a
process during which a PPi will be released. Also it’s a directional reaction: DNA is read
from 3’ to 5’ by RNA polymerase, and the RNA strand is synthesized in 5’ to 3’ direction.
From an energetic point of view, it’s a favourable reaction: it’s going to release energy from a
breakage of an anhydride bond.
Pyrophosphatases will degrade the pyrophosphate, driving the reaction in forward manner
(shifts the equilibrium) to favour the continuation of the synthesis.
[PDF p. 226]
Catalytic mechanism of RNA polymerases
From the 3’ end of the DNA chain, RNA polymerase starts to synthesize a complementary
strand.
In the catalytic core of RNA polymerase, there are 2 Mg2+ ions:
One helps in the nucleophilic attack and the breakage of the phospho bond
The other helps in the removal of the PPi
A. TRANSCRIPTION IN PROKARYOTES
Prokaryotic RNA polymerase

It identifies specific regions in the genome where transcription begins
Unwinds the DNA double helix to expose the template ( helicase activity)
Carries out the synthesis (phosphodiester bond) from 5’ end to 3’ end.
They also identify termination sequences in the genome that mark the end
of transcription.
It interacts with activating and suppressing factors, which can modulate
its activity.

Different subunits form the prokaryotic RNA polymerase.

Alpha subunits, which have regulatory roles and interact with regulatory proteins
Beta subunits, endowed with catalytic activity and interact with the template. They
carry out the elongation of RNA.

Sigma subunits, which play a key role in the recognition of the promoter.
Mechanism of transcription in prokaryotes
[PDF p. 227]
1. Initiation step
It involves the interaction and identification of promoter regions.
First, the RNA polymerase complex binds DNA at specific regions in the
genome. These regions are known as promoter regions, and are
recognized by the sigma subunit. It binds and forms a complex (closed
complex) which undergoes structural changes that facilitate the separation of
the two strands (open complex) . From here, transcription can start.
Promoter recognition : The promoter is referred to as the
upstream/5’ region of the genome. The termination sequence is
known as downstream/3’ region.
The promoter is a part of the gene which is recognized by RNA
polymerase, marking the initiation of the transcription process.
When comparing one bacterial gene with another, we may come
across consensus sequences, which are conserved between
different genes. These consensus sequences are many promoters
with a characteristic sequence.
Another sequence greatly conserved is the -35 box.
If we continue to move upstream, we may also find similarities in the
UP element.
This consensus sequence is the one which will be recognized by RNA
polymerase, allowing it to initiate the process and carry it out in the proper
orientation. These sequences are conserved in order to help position RNA
polymerase in the right orientation.
2. Elongation
As it begins this step, the sigma subunit dissociates from the
complex. The RNA complex leaves the promoter and proceeds
with transcription, forming what is known as the transcription
bubble.
This process is accompanied by changes in the coiling of
DNA.
[PDF p. 228]
3. Termination
Two types of termination mechanisms end the process:
                   - **“rho” independent mechanisms:** some **sequences**

in the DNA template mark the end of the process. First,
sequences rich in G and C give place to the formation of
hairpin structures, which destabilize the complex between
RNA polymerase and the template.
After the G and C rich regions, there are Adenine rich
regions: because the energy required for the pairing between
As and Us is lesser than that of G and Cs, these A rich
regions will destabilize the complex.
In this mechanism, structural features will put an end to
transcription.
                   - **“rho” dependent mechanisms:** the **rho factor** is a

multimer with ATPase activity which recognizes and binds
RNA. The ATPase activity allows it to move along the RNA
strand until it comes in contact with RNA polymerase. Once in
contact, it separates and destabilizes the transcription
complex, inducing termination.
B. TRANSCRIPTION IN EUKARYOTES
Fundamental differences with prokaryotic transcription

In eukaryotes, transcription and translation take place in separate compartments .
RNAs need to travel from the nucleus to the cytoplasm to be translated, and prior to
its translocation, a maturation process needs to occur in the nucleus. This maturation
process allows the existence of many additional regulatory processes.
In prokaryotes, due to the lack of nucleus, transcription and translation can take
place almost simultaneously.

In eukaryotes, DNA is tightly associated with proteins, forming a tertiary structure
( chromatin ), which contains histones and hundreds of other proteins which aid in
DNA packaging.


In prokaryotes, there are no post transcriptional processes for RNA. The
primary transcript is directly translated.


In eukaryotes, genes are transcribed by 3 different RNA polymerases, not only


one.
Eukaryotic polymerases do not come in direct contact with DNA. They need the
help of what are known as transcription factors.
[PDF p. 229]
Eukaryotic RNA polymerases
RNA polymerase I carries out the transcription of ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
-
RNA polymerase II carries out transcription of mRNAs and most sncRNAs
-
RNA polymerase III carries out transcription of tRNAs and 5’-rRNA
RNA Polymerase II
It needs general transcription factors that are
common to all genes to carry out transcription.
There are also gene-specific transcription factors:
activators and coactivators.
In many genes we can find a region in the -30
position known as the TATA box (although it isn’t
present in all genes). If we move upstream from this
TATA box, we find that there are various regulatory sequences.
During transcription, there are also specific transcription factors which come into
contact with RNA polymerase II (thanks to cofactors) and regulatory sites (thanks to
activators), which signal the process to begin.
Not all genes have the same regulatory regions and transcription factors; therefore,
their expression will depend on hormones and signalling processes that activate
different types of factors.
Chromatin needs to be relaxed and decondensed for transcription, which is also
mediated by the binding of specific transcription factors.
[PDF p. 230]
Mechanism of transcription in eukaryotes
1. Transcription initiation phase
It’s initiated by sequential binding of general transcription
factors (GTFs) and RNA polymerase II to a promoter. During
initiation, we find many types of transcription factors which for
the preinitiation complex (PIC):

TFIID interacts with + and - regulatory proteins
TFIIF binds to RNA pol II (and TFIIB)
TFIIB binds to TBP (TATA box binding protein) and
recruits the RNA polII-TFIIF complex.
TFIIE binds and exerts a helicase activity, separating

the DNA strands

TFIIH also presents a helicase activity, as well as
kinase activity. It endowes this kinase activity on RNA
polymerase II CTD (carboxyl terminal domain): the
phosphorylation of CTD causes a conformational change
that activates the polymerase activity.

This initiation phase is the most regulated phase in the process. It’s the most important
control point.
2. Elongation phase
3. Termination phase
RNA PROCESSING
In both prokaryotes and eukaryotes,
RNAs must be chemically modified to
attain their functional forms. The
reactions involved in RNA processing
include:


Nucleotide elimination


Modification of nucleobases


Nucleotide addition


Splicing reactions
[PDF p. 231]
mRNA processing in eukaryotes
mRNA is processed in eukaryotes, which allows additional regulatory points. We find:
1. Firstly, 5’ CAP synthesis, which stabilizes the RNA strand.
The CAP synthesizing complex carries out this CAP binding to mRNA.
About this CAP structure:
    - mRNA capping **protects** the strand **from degradation** (stability)

    Participates in **mRNA transporting** from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.

2. Secondly, intron splicing takes place. Both introns and
exons are transcribed, but introns are eliminated from the
primary transcript and exons bind to form mature mRNA.
This implies a significant change in size and the existence
of many regulatory mechanisms and splicing
reactions.
This splicing is carried out by spliceosomes, sophisticated
machinery which are small nuclear ribonucleoproteins.
They perform the chemical reaction that breaks
phosphodiester bonds and forms new ones between
exons.
In most genes, there are variations in
these splicing reactions, known as
alternative splicing. As a result, different
variants coming from one same primary
transcript appear. This mechanism
expands the information contained in
the genome (as it creates protein
variants; for a single gene, we will be left
with many mRNAs) and implies the
existence of additional regulatory
possibilities.
What will happen to the introns / the exons which are eliminated through alternative splicing?
The excised portions of RNA will participate in the regulation of RNA expression by forming
circular RNA structures. They’ll do so by binding and sequestering miRNA (seen in next
lecture).
3. Thirdly, a 3’ poly-AA chain is added on the 3’ end of RNA. It is thought to protect
RNA from degradation starting in the 3’ end.
[PDF p. 232]
Lecture 8.3. Regulation of gene expression
Genes are switched on by core promoters, which are usually found upstream from the
transcription start site (TSS). But in order to regulate when that promoter is active or not,
we need further signals.
Core promoters are modulated by millions of switches in our genome, known as
enhancers (regulatory elements/developmental enhancers), in a process mediated by
changes in chromatin conformation. The level of genome packaging will allow genes to
come into contact with these enhancers/regulatory elements.
Chromatin is usually repressive, as it is packed. All these functional regions have to be
opened up and chromatin relaxed, creating regions of open chromatin known as DNAse I
Hypersensitive Sites.
These regions are opened by histone acetylases, therefore leaving promoters and
enhancers free for binding.
Initiation factor’s components and assembly
Core promoter (TATA box) + transcription start site
(TSS).
TBP (TATA box binding protein) binds to TATA box;
SP1 binds to GC boxes;
When all these factors assemble, RNA polymerase is
phosphorylated, binds and initiates transcription.
What determines the assembly of this complex?
Once chromatin is opened through specific chemical reactions, regulation can start:
100 Kb upstream from the core promoters, we find the
enhancers . Activators will bind to enhancers, creating
enhanceosomes which will trigger DNA bending, by
looping. These active enhancers (enhanceosomes)
interact with coactivators (such as HATs) to stimulate
chromatin remodeling and histone acetylation. This
creates open sites. Enhancers will then become in
contact with the promoter through the Mediator
protein, triggering the assembly of RNA polymerase
and general transcription factors at the promoter site.
[PDF p. 233]
Example: Inside each TAD, there are more probabilities of interaction. Specific TAD genes
contact each other rather frequently. But flanked TADs will not come in contact with each
other.
If there is a CTCF binding disruption, for example due to mutation, TADs aren’t correctly
flanked and this will give place to aberrant interactions. We are now left with a large TAD
which allows enhancers to activate additional genes.
There are specific enhancers for each tissue, to regulate specific gene expressions. If for
example an enhancer of one TAD in the brain can become in contact with a gene from
another TAD which should only be expressed in the liver, this will have physiological
consequences.
DHS (DNAse I Hypersensitive sites)
They are open chromatin sites and allow the activation/inactivation of genes.


There have been 3,000,000 DHS found in the past years.


DHS are very tissue specific: 50% are active in just one cell line; Around 1% (4,000) are


found in all lines.

Each of them is 100-200 Mb, so around 18.7% (⅕ of the
genome) of the genome is comprised to regulation.

[PDF p. 234]
Histone acetylation
Histone acetyl-transferases (HATs) add acetyl groups on the tails which protuberate from
histones. They can be acetylated or deacetylated.
For example, when some lysines (+), which have a positive charge and are therefore
attracted to DNA (-), are acetylated, the positive charge disappears and nucleosomes
become more relaxed, with less interactions.
Histone deacetylases (HDACs) carry out the
opposite reaction.
This acetylation creates open sites which will
allow the binding of transcription factors,
and transcription to begin.
Degradation of mRNAs
If we don’t regulate mRNA degradation, they are overtranslated and produce excessive
proteins.
Therefore, gene expression can also be regulated by the half life of its respective RNA.
-
Through miRNAs
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are genes which
are transcribed and once transcribed,
adopt a secondary structure in the form
of a hairpin. This hairpin structure is
processed through cleavage by dicer,
and we end up with a miRNA duplex
molecule. The duplex structure
dissociates, so only one of the strands
is active.
The function of these miRNA is to find
the complementary sequence within
the strand of target mRNA. Once
bound, the mRNA is degraded and
doesn’t translate into any more proteins.
RISC = “RNA-induced-silencing-complex”
RISC targets miRNA once it has found its
complementary sequence in a mRNA strand,
to form the complex which performs the
mRNA silencing.
[PDF p. 235]
-
Through long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs)
LncRNA acts as a “sponge” for miRNA (sequesters the miRNA),
therefore activating and enhancing protein translation and production.
-
Through Pseudogenes
Pseudogenes imitate the active DNA sequence, and therefore also act as a
sponge and sequester miRNA. The available miRNA strands have to
spread out to sequester both active and pseudogene mRNAs. Less miRNA
will be inhibiting the active mRNA.
-
Through circular RNA
Circular RNAs, which are differentially generated by alternative splicing of exons or from
introns, also act as sponges for miRNA.
Introns are coded by parts of the genome which can overlap with the protein-coding
regions that give rise to exons. Therefore, they can share common sequences with
these genes. If they match the complementary miRNA, this allows them to sequester
it, leaving less available for the mRNA which gives rise to proteins.
The exons excised by alternative splicing may also possess complementary
sequences to that of the miRNA.
[PDF p. 236]
Lecture 8.4. Epigenetics: DNA methylation and histone modifications
DNA methylation is a form of epigenetic regulation of gene expression. Genes can also be
regulated by specific histone modifications (acetylation or methylation). Different
combinations of chromatin marks define the functional state of chromatin regions.
Promoters and enhancers have distinctive histone modifications.
DNA METHYLATION
DNA is methylated at cytosine bases (C), but only when the C is followed by a G base (C
followed by G in the same strand / CpG dinucleotide). Methylation occurs at the 5’ carbon.
DNA methylases are the enzymes which add this methyl group to Cytosines.
CpG dinucleotides are more or less distributed randomly through the genome. But when
we look at which nucleotides are methylated or not, we notice that:
Unmethylated cytosines are concentrated around the promoter of most genes (they
themselves act as the promoter), forming “Unmethylated CpG islands” . (Not all genes are
regulated by CpG islands).
Passive and active demethylation
When methylation occurs, both strands are methylated.

Passive demethylation: When the cell divides, it does it semiconservatively, and
we are left with hemimethylated DNA strands. Methylation has to be maintained, or
else we would be left with unmethylated CpGs after many subsequent cell divisions.
There would be a delusion of methylated molecules (passive demethylation).

Active demethylation: A few years ago, an active demethylation
pathway was also discovered. Scientists discovered that it occurred
through a combination of enzymatic complexes (TET) and BER.
TET modifies methyl-cytosine, it hydroxylates it in several steps (5’
hydroxymethyl-cytosine), and continues to do so until it creates a
5’-carboxy carbamoyl methyl cytosine. BER (base excision repair)
removes all of these modifications from the DNA by removing the
modified Cytosine, and replaces it with a normal, demethylated C
nucleotide. Therefore, demethylation is carried out by modifying
methylated Cytosine until it becomes so different from an
unmethylated C, that the cell has no choice but to replace the base
through BER. There is no active demethylase , but there is an active
demethylation pathway.
[PDF p. 237]
Active methylation
There are, however, methylases which carry out an
active methylation pathway. It’s achieved through DNA
methyl-transferase 1 (DMT-1), which is in charge of
keeping DNA strands methylated even after cell division.
There are also DNA-methylases-de novo, which
methylate cytosines of CpGs which weren’t methylated
before.
They are both required to maintain correct DNA
methylation levels.
Degree of methylation
DNA methylation and cancer
One of the ways in which cells become tumor cells,
aside from mutations, can be due to changes in
methylations in CpG dinucleotides from CpG
islands.
There can be a global hypermethylation of the
promoters of CpG islands, disrupting their activity.
Tumor suppressor genes (TSG) can become
inactive due to hypermethylation, giving rise to
tumors.
[PDF p. 238]
HISTONE MODIFICATION
Nucleosomes are globular proteins with tails which protrude from the structure. They can be
modified through acetylation and methylation.
N-terminal and Histone 3 (H3)
Lysine 4, lysine 9, lysine 27 and lysine 36 are important in the amino acid sequence of
H3. Modifications in these groups will determine if a gene is active or not.
L9, L27 and L4 in inactive genes:
Lysine 4 remains unmethylated, while
Lysine 27 becomes trimethylated and
Lysine 9 can be found di- or
trimethylated. Nucleosomes around the
promoter acquire these conformations.
Active genes: We find trimethylated
Lysine 4 (L4) and trimethylated Lysine
36 (L36), while Lysine 9 and Lysine 27
become acetylated. When the promoter
becomes activated, and genes are
being actively transcribed, nucleosomes
adopt this conformation.
ENHANCERS vs PROMOTERS
Enhancers also present a series of epigenetic modifications, but they are not promoters, so
epigenetic modifications will be carried out in a different manner.
As a similarity, nucleosomes corresponding to enhancers and to promoters appear
acetylated. There is also a nucleosome depletion in both cases. There are no nucleosomes
at the centre of promoters or enhancers because transcription factors are going to bind to
this active site, and need to be free for this binding.
The difference resides in the methylation of lysine 4 from enhancer and promoter
nucleosomes: promoters present high levels of trimethylation, and low levels of di and
mono methylation. With enhancers, the opposite occurs: higher levels of
monomethylation and lesser di and trimethylation.
We can know if a promoter or an enhancer is being activated just by looking at the
methylation ratio.
[PDF p. 239]
Lecture 8.5. The genetic code
History of the genetic code
Cracking the genetic code was one of the greatest scientific developments of the 20th
century. This was thanks to the work of many people, such as Severo Ochoa, Robert Holley,
Marshall Nirenberg. They received a Nobel Prize for their contributions.
While cracking the genetic code, they reasoned that to codify 20 different amino acids, whilst
having 4 nucleotides, each amino acid must be encoded by 3 nucleotides. The first codon
identified was UUU (codifying for phenylalanine) in 1961.
Crick’s adaptor hypothesis
He suggested that in order for the cell to make proteins from
the genome sequence, we would need something to transfer
and adapt this information (what we now know as tRNA ).
Characteristics of the genetic code

There are 64 possible combinations of codons, formed by

the association of 3 different nucleotides.


The genetic code is universal (all living beings use the
same genetic code).


The information is translated in the form of codons .


The sequences are read in a continuous way: 3 letter codons are read without
spaces or overlapping. The reading frame, once established, is followed in this


fashion.
The genetic code is unambiguous : there is only 1 amino acid assigned to a
particular codon.

The genetic code is redundant: we have 64 possible combinations but only 20
amino acids. Therefore, many combinations can codify for the same amino acid.
Redundancy is usually found in the third letter.
Why is this redundancy found in this 3rd nucleotide? We know that the codon and
anticodon are complementary. The alignment between the both is done in an
antiparallel way. The specificity of the anticodon for the first two nucleotides is very
high, it will determine the specificity of the amino acid. The third is not so important:
therefore, different genes which start with the same first two codons will be able to
codify for the same amino acid.

[PDF p. 240]
Chemically similar amino acids have similar codons
(polar, non-polar, positively charged,…)


The initiation codon is always AUG . This codon codifies
methionine . Therefore all of our proteins begin with a
methionine residue. It’s helpful to find the initiation sequence
of a gene within the genome.


The termination codons are UAA, UAG, UGA, which are
“nonsense” codons: they don’t codify for any amino acid,
only signal the end of transcription.


Types of mutations and their impact on the polypeptide chain
a) Missense mutations: they change the sense/meaning of the codon, and therefore
cause one amino acid to change into another. The repercussions depend on the
difference between the previously encoded amino acid and the new one.
b) Synonymous (silent) mutations: no impact on the genome (in terms of the protein
sequence), thanks to the redundancy of the genetic code. Called silent because the
sequence of proteins remains the same, so it’s undetectable.
c) Nonsense mutations: there is a mutation which causes the codon to become a
nonsense codon (symbols termination). Generally, these mutations have a big
impact because it signals the process of transcription to stop, and we are left with an
incomplete protein.
d) Frameshift mutation: It is an insertion or deletion type of mutation, which displaces
the whole reading frame: from the point of the mutation onwards, the reading frame
will be changed. The impact is generally pretty high.
Mutations in hemoglobin gene
- Sickle cell anemia
Disease caused by a point mutation (substitution). Similarly to what
happens with mutations in glucose-6-dehydrogenase (G6DH), this
mutation is associated with resistance to malaria because it creates a
hostile environment for plasmodium falciparum in red blood cells.
There is a mutation in position 6 in the beta chain, meaning a glutamine
becomes a valine.
Glutamine is negatively charged and valine is hydrophobic, so valines
start to stick together and form fibers, modifying the structure of
hemoglobin.
[PDF p. 241]
- Hb McKees-Rock
Mutation at the very end of the protein which causes hemoglobin’s chains to be of different
sizes.
-
Hemoglobin Constant spring
There is a mutation in the stop codon, which is changed by glutamine, and therefore the
protein synthesis is continued until it encounters the next stop codon. We are left with a
hemoglobin protein which is longer than a normal hemoglobin.
Curiosities
1. Why does the genetic code seem to be unaffected by evolution?
If we change the genetic code, we change all our proteins. That would be uneventful
for any organism, as it would have such a high impact, it would not be compatible
with life.
2. Why is redundancy associated with the third nucleotide in the codon?
It avoids the impact of many mutations: a mutation in the third codon might not affect
the final amino acid if it remains with it’s first two nucleotides intact.
3. Why do chemically similar amino acids have similar codons?
It reduces the impact of mutations: a mutation could imply a change in an amino acid,
but if it has similar chemical properties, the interactions won’t be as perjudicial.
[PDF p. 242]
Lecture 8.6. Protein synthesis
Protein synthesis is a very complex and energy-expensive process. Around 90% of the
energy produced is used for protein synthesis.
It’s possibly the most complex biosynthetic process, and it’s carried out by:
messenger RNA (mRNA)
transport RNA (tRNA)
ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
ribosomal proteins

enzymes

protein factors
Messenger RNA (mRNA)
It’s a single strand of nucleotides with a 5’-CAP on the 5’ end and a 3’poly-AAA tail. Within
the messenger RNA chain we can distinguish:
- Initiation codon
-
Stop codon
- Between them, the coding sequence / open reading frame (ORF), which has the
information that will code for the respective protein.
- UTRs (untranslated regions), as not all of the RNA chain is translated into a proteins
Ribosomes
They are the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes are supramolecular structures, made up
of 2 subunits: large and small. In between them, there is a channel through which mRNA
advances while being translated.
Both subunits are composed of rRNA (65%) and ribosomal proteins (35%); They are
riboproteins : the large subunit contains up to 45 different proteins, whilst the small subunit
has approximately 30 proteins, and less RNA.
Ribosomes can be free / associated forming
polyribosomes in the cytosol, or found
bound to membranes such as the
membrane of the RER (because the
proteins they synthesize will enter the lumen
to suffer post traduction modifications).
[PDF p. 243]
Transfer RNA (tRNA)
The most important arms of tRNA are the amino acid
attachment site (on the 3’ end) and the anticodon (which will
recognize the codon).
All tRNAs end in CCA, which is the sequence to which amino
acids will bind on the 3’ end.
PROTEIN SYNTHESIS
Activation of the amino acids
It consists in the binding of the aminoacid to the tRNA. Also known as the stage of
synthesis of the aminoacyl-tRNA. We produce this aminoacyl-tRNA molecule through the
formation of a covalent bond, carried out by a synthetase, in a process by which ATP will be
consumed and form AMP (2 ATP high energy
bonds consumption).
The goal here is to activate the amino acid by
creating a high energy bond, and to create
aminoacyl-tRNAs which are correctly assigned
to each codon in mRNA.
Errors in translation occur here, because the
synthetase introduces the wrong amino acid
corresponding to the necessary anticodon.
From here, translation may begin, a polymerization process in which information from the
genome is transferred to proteins through RNAs.
Translation
1. Initiation
The initiation process consists in the formation of the complex
which will start the synthesis, by binding to AUG. Methionine will
be the first protein in the protein chain, although in
post-traductional modifications it can be removed.
In mitochondria, as they are prokaryotes, the first amino acid is
not methionine, but N-formyl-methionine (this confirms the theory
that mitochondria used to be prokaryotic cells).
Components required for initiation include: a template, many
initiation factors (eIFs), large and small ribosomal subunits,
GTP and the activated methionine-tRNA complex.
[PDF p. 244]
Within the ribosome, we differentiate different sites:

The “A” (aminoacyl) site, through which the next complementary amino acid will

arrive.

The “P” (peptide) site, where the tRNA bound to methionine is found at the
beginning of the process. In this site, the peptidyl     - transferase will form the peptidic

bond between amino acids.

The “E” (exit) site. Not a very clear site in eukaryotes, but clearly distinguished in
prokaryotes.

To carry out initiation, circularization of the mRNA occurs: The 3’-poly-A tail is the site
where the polyA binding protein will attach. PABP also interacts with other initiation factors.
The small subunit of the ribosome is going to
bind mRNA on the 5’ end, and from there it will
move trying to find the AUG sequence. Once
found, it stops and binds to the initiation codon,
while the large subunit comes to the site and
binds too.
2. Elongation
We need eEFs (eukaryotic elongation factors), energy, many
aminoacyl-tRNAs,…
            - The binding of the next incoming aminoacyl-tRNA occurs

            - Consecutively, the formation of the peptide bond takes

place within the P site, carried out by peptidyl-transferase.
When people started to investigate this enzyme, they didn’t
find it as it is not a protein: it’s a ribozyme, a non proteic
molecule with enzymatic activity.
3. Termination
The protein continues to elongate until it
reaches the termination codon, and
subsequently a termination factor (eTF)
binds, separating the complexes.
[PDF p. 245]
Polyribosomes
Polyribosomes are ribosomes found associated together, forming
ribosome clusters, which carry out protein synthesis at the same
time, using only one thread of mRNA.
“christmas trees of translation”
Inhibition of translation
There are many compounds which inhibit translation.
- Antibiotics: they inhibit translation in prokaryotes. Therefore, we use them as a
treatment for disease, as they don’t have an effect on human translation.
Examples are:
    **Tetracyclines**, which block the A site of ribosomes

    **Streptomycin**, which causes misreading and inhibits initiation

    **Cycloheximide**, which binds to the 50S subunit and blocks translocation

    **Puromycin**, which we don’t use as an antibiotic, as it’s a competitive inhibitor

of tyrosine-tRNA and can disrupt translation
- Toxins: they also block translation
-
Diphtheria toxin
- Ricin: It’s a molecule that is isolated from seeds. It’s a protein
with 2 different subunits: the B chain is a lectin (recognizes
carbohydrates) and introduces the molecule inside the cell; the
A chain is an rRNA N-glycosylase enzyme which catalyzes
the hydrolysis of an N-glycosidic formed by an adenine within
the 28S rRNA.
Barely any ricin is necessary to kill a person, as it’s not a usual inhibitor which
acts on an enzyme. Ricin IS the enzyme, and therefore one ricin molecule it
can carry out many thousands of hydrolysis reactions (murder of Georgi
Markov, through a ricin pellet).
[PDF p. 246]
Lecture 8.7. Protein maturation, folding and targeting
Protein folding
During protein translation, protein folding begins. The protein folds sequentially and
cooperatively, meaning that as some regions acquire their secondary conformations, it is
easier for other regions to do so as well. Depending on the amino acid sequences, they will
fold into alpha-helices or beta sheets.
Sometimes, proteins aren’t able to fully form by themselves. They need the help of other
cofactors and proteins. These other proteins which induce the correct conformation are
known as chaperones.
During protein folding, there are several intermediate folding states, which are generally
risky, as some hydrophobic regions become exposed and tend to cluster together and
form aggregates by establishing hydrophobic interactions.
Chaperones are involved in:
Avoiding the risk of hydrophobic regions being exposed long enough to form
aggregates
They bind to the hydrophobic regions, unfold them and allow the aberrant proteins to
become correctly folded
Lastly, some are involved in protein targeting and transport within the cell
Chaperones
HSP (heat shock proteins) (Proteins which were discovered to be present in the cell after a
heat shock, as many other proteins had been denatured) and Chaperonins.


HSP interacts with proteins during their folding
process. They can also bind poorly folded
hydrophobic regions and by hydrolyzing ATP,
favour their denaturation so they can fold
correctly.
                       **Chaperonins** are multiprotein



complexes, which are involved in the folding of
proteins that do not fold spontaneously.
One of the best known chaperonins in
eukaryotes is HSP60. They are made up of
several rings that form a chamber, inside which
the correct protein conformation is induced.
[PDF p. 247]
Protein’s final destinations
Most proteins are synthesized at RER. But, how do the ribosomes know that they have to be
bound to the RER membrane?
This is achieved due to specific signals contained within the protein, known as signalling
peptides, which c ause the protein to translocate to the RER. These signals are found in
the N (amino) terminal and are generally similar. There are some consensus sequences
for these signalling peptides.
Features:

At the C-terminal of the signal peptide (NOT of the protein), there is a short
sequence of polar amino acids with small side chains. This is the point where the
protein will cleave the signal peptide (there is an amino acid that constitutes the point
of proteolysis).

In the N terminal, we generally find positively charged amino acids.

The signal peptide core is rich in hydrophobic amino acids.

Directing proteins to the ER
The amino (N) terminal region
contains the signal peptide. The
protein begins to form and once the
N terminal emerges from the
ribosome, the sequence is
recognized by a protein, the signal
recognition particle (SRP)
ribonucleoprotein.
It attaches to the ribosome and this
stops translation, which allows the
ribosome to bind to the RER
membrane, and for the amino
terminal to enter inside the reticulum.
Once inside, the SRP hydrolyzes GTP. This is the signal which disrupts the interaction
between SRP and the signal peptide, causing them to dissociate. From here, translation is
continued within the RER lumen, until the protein is synthesized and a peptidase
proteolyzes the signal peptide.
[PDF p. 248]
Glycosylation of proteins
Many proteins undergo chemical modifications such as glycosylation, which consists in the
addition of oligosaccharides to the protein side chains. It’s an essential step in its
maturation towards the final conformation.
N-linked glycosylation begins in the RER while the protein is still being translated. The
amino acids to which oligosaccharides will bind are those with H groups (such as
asparagine).
O-linked glycosylation generally occurs further on, in the Golgi apparatus.
Although the oligosaccharides which bind differ from protein to protein, they have a
common core which is synthesized inside the reticulum, through many transferases . Once
formed, specific transferases transfer this core group to the protein, so it can bind.
Incorrect glycosylation is the
cause of many proteinopathies .
The disruption of the process
generates stress inside the
reticulum and triggers the UPR
(unfolded protein response), either
to reactivate glycosylation or
promote apoptosis.
Protein targeting for their transport into the nucleus
Proteins for the nucleus have a nuclear localization sequence (NLS). They are very short
and rich in hydrophobic regions, which are recognized by nuclear transport systems.
Targeting of nuclear proteins is mediated by importins and the
GTPase Ran.
Importins (participate as heterodimers, with 2 subunits) bind to
the specific sequences and transport the proteins close to the
nuclear pore complexes. Through the nuclear pore, proteins
translocate into the nucleus. Once in the nucleus, 2 additional
proteins (RAN, a GTPase, a small G protein; and CAS,
Cellular-apoptosis susceptibility protein) participate: Ran binds to
the importin beta subunit and separates it from the protein.
Protein-alpha importin complex binds to Ran and CAS,
causing the release of the nuclear protein.
There is a Ran reactivation process which
involves the hydrolysis of a GTP molecule.
[PDF p. 249]
Lysosomal targeting
Another well-known transport system of proteins within the cell is that of lysosomal
hydrolases. The presence of one or more mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) residues is the
structural signal that drives these enzymes to the lysosomes.
Impairments in this transport cause the accumulation of waste products inside lysosomes,
that will lead to cell dysfunction and serious diseases known as “Lysosomal storage
diseases” (sphingolipidoses, glycogenosis or mucopolysaccharidosis).
Protein degradation
2 ways to degrade proteins:
-
In the lysosomes

Through proteasome. The information for the half life of
a protein is contained within said protein.
In eukaryotes, proteins are linked to the ubiquitin
protein, through which their half life will be mediated.
The more ubiquitin present, the more likely for them to be
degraded by proteasome.
Cyclins contain a sequence that makes them more likely
to be ubiquitinated, and therefore have a shorter lifespan.

[PDF p. 250]
Lecture 8.8. Protein degradation: lysosomes
Discovery of lysosomes
They can be isolated by applying ultracentrifugation to a suspension of broken cells
containing subcellular components. After the 1st centrifugation, a pellet at the bottom of the
tube is observed, containing the cell’s nuclei. This pellet is known as the nuclei sediment. On
the top layer rests the supernatant.
If we centrifuge the supernatant at a higher speed, for 15 minutes, 2 new factions are
formed. The bottom layer corresponds to a mitochondria, peroxisomes and lysosomes
sediment. If we continued to centrifuge, we would ultimately obtain ribosomes.
Structure and components of lysosomes
The lysosomal membrane is made up of a bilipid layer that contains many elements:
    - We find **carrier proteins,** as many of the components which are hydrolyzed

in the lysosome are going to be exported out of it for their metabolic use.
For example, LDL. The lysosomal enzymes are going to degrade LDL, and
free cholesterol will be carried out of the lysosome, into the required area of
the cell, by these carrier proteins.
- The inner side of the lysosomal membrane is highly glycosylated. The
purpose is thought to be that glycosylation protects the lysosomes from
being digested by the enzymes on the inside.
    Lastly, the presence of **proton pumps** keeps the inner meidum at a low pH.

There is an ATPase enzyme which will import H+ into the lysosome to lower
the pH, down to 5.
It’s lowered so enzymes can work at their required pH.
The lysosome contains at least 40 types of acid
hydrolases (lipases, nucleases,..), which can digest
molecules. But to carry out their function they need to be
found in an acid medium.
Not every single lysosome contains every hydrolase (each
lysosome carries out the digestion of specific molecules),
but all of them posses a hydrolase that is common to all,
ACID PHOSPHATASE, which is a universal marker for
the recognition of lysosomes (as it is found in all).
How material is incorporated for digestion
                 **Primary lysosomes:** in the vesicles coming from the

Golgi apparatus, there is not such a low pH (pH=7) so
enzymes are inactive. These vesicles which aren’t active for
digestion are known as primary lysosomes.
[PDF p. 251]
Secondary lysosomes: when primary lysosomes fuse
with late endosomes, they form secondary lysosomes, in
which pH=5 and will carry out digestion.
Types of digestion
A) Intracellular digestion
1. Heterophagy: cells digest molecules coming from the outside of the cell
(pinocytosis and phagocytosis)
2. Autophagy: by this process cells are able to digest their own components for
different purposes.
What’s the use of autophagy?
    **Under normal conditions,** autophagy degrades **damaged**

components in the cell.
          - When there is a **lack of nutrients,** fasting

starves the cells and promotes them to digest some of the cell
components to obtain energy (ex: autophagy in muscles, in
prolonged starvation, causes muscle atrophy).
    **When organelles have undergone hypertrophy,**

for example due to intoxication with lipid-soluble
drugs (degraded in the SER through P450) like
phenobarbital, which will give place to an overload
of the organelle. Once it has undergone this
hypertrophy, it will be degraded.
B) Extracellular
2 types of cells able to carry out extracellular digestion.
-
Sperm: they have special lysosomes known as acrosomes.
Acrosomes are found in the heads of the sperm, and once it
contacts the oocyte, the acrosome fuses with the plasma
membrane and all the enzymes are released outside the cell to
degrade the membrane of oocyte, for fertilization.
[PDF p. 252]

Osteoclasts: bones undergo constant formation and
destruction. Two cells are in charge of this process:
osteoblasts (in charge of bone formation) and osteoclasts
(responsible for bone degradation). They have specific
lysosomes with enzymes able to digest the components

of mineral bone.
Extracellular digestion is not a common process, and is highly specialized.
Lysosomal enzymes tagging and transport
The lysosomal enzymes are tagged by Mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)
Firstly, the lysosomal enzyme is synthesized in the
Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER), where a
carbohydrate (Mannose) is also added through
N-glycosylation.
Next, the molecule travels to the Golgi Apparatus,
where Mannose is phosphorylated by the sequential
activity of two enzymes.
Within the Golgi Apparatus, Mannose-6-phosphate
binds to a receptor. This induces the release of the
enzyme, packaged in a transport vesicle.

The vesicles fuse with late endosomes to form

secondary lysosomes, where low pH causes the
dissociation between the enzyme and its receptor.
The receptor is recycled and returns to the Golgi
Apparatus.
LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASES (LSDs)
This family of diseases is characterized by:
-
Abnormal storage within lysosomes

Lack of digestion of substrates

The presence of lysosomal enzymes in the extracellular space
All of this causes cellular stress and results in cell malfunctioning.
Most are autosomal recessive disorders, such as Inclusion-cell disease/mucolipidosis
type II and Gaucher’s disease; others are X chromosome linked, like Fabry’s disease.
They are rare, but there is a high incidence of LSDs in endogamic populations. This is one of
the reasons why there are no drugs or treatments for these disorders.
[PDF p. 253]
a) INCLUSION (I) - CELL DISEASE
I-cell disease is an autosomal recessive condition, a type of LSD caused by
a mutation in the enzyme which carries out tagging, phosphotransferase .
( Molecules generally need tagging to remain within the cell or in a specific
organelle, a sort of barcode. If there is no tag, the enzymes/proteins
denature and are released outside of the cell).
As a result, endosomes are left full of undigested material.
Having endosomes full of undigested material is very stressful for the
cells, as it blocks their normal functioning, and therefore there is cell
malfunctioning.
The presence of enzymes outside the cell is another problem: they won’t be fully active
due to the pH, but they do present some activity, and are therefore able to digest some
extracellular components, giving rise to defects and mental retardation.
Patients with this disease will suffer from many defects in
development (as cells can’t use nutrients), dwarfism,… and
have a very low life expectancy.
b) GAUCHER DISEASE
Gaucher disease is caused by a glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Ga-Glu). Therefore, in
the cells there are depositions of glucosylceramide. It accumulates in cells, mainly
affecting macrophages.
Macrophages are mainly found in the bone, liver,
spleen,… which is why many of the clinical
manifestations affect bone, liver and spleen. There
are skeletal and neurological defects (as
glucocerebrosides are also found in neurons), loss of
mineral bones and also an enlargement of liver
and spleen.
It can be treated by:
Symptomatic treatment
Bone marrow transplant, by first getting rid of all the defectuous stem cells and
replacing them with transplanted healthy ones
Enzyme replacement therapy: many bacteria are covered in glycans, which are
what macrophages use to recognize and bind to them during infection. This property
can be used in enzymes, by covering glucocerebrosidase with mannose to favour its
endocitosis, tricking the macrophage into thinking it’s a pathogen
Gene therapy, which has the same goal: to replace the efficient enzyme
[PDF p. 254]
TBL 8.1. Epigenetic-related diseases
Usually, when looking at a specific gene, both alleles should be
transcribed, but some regions in the genome contain genes which
are expressed only from one of the two chromosomes. This is
achieved through IMPRINTING, a mark which tells the
chromosomes which allele is the one that will be expressed. It’s an
epigenetic mark.
Imprinting is regulated by lncRNAs, antisense genes, epigenetic
markers… When there are disruptions in these imprinting
mechanisms, diseases arise.
Only around 150 genes throughout the genome are imprinted .
Experiments done whilst investigating imprinting genes
During the experiments, a normal fertilized egg was
formed when the pronuclei from the mother and father
fused together.
But when two sets of maternal information were taken
and fused together, this gave place to a gynogenetic
embryo ( an embryo formed from eggs without genetic
contribution from penetrating sperm), which resulted in
a cyst.
When the information all proceeded from the father, an
androgenetic embryo was formed.
The embryo, to be viable, needed one set of
chromosomes from the mother and another from the father. Therefore, parental genomes
are NOT equivalent: there are regions of differential expression, which will depend on the
parental origin (IMPRINTING).
In these regions of imprinted genes, it is all done in a coordinated manner so only maternal
or only paternal genes are expressed, depending on the region in question. Each cluster is
regulated in a specific manner. This regulation is carried out by strands of lncRNA, CTCF
binding, methylation, transcription of antisense genes and many other factors.
Example of CTCF binding
CTCF only binds to CpG islands when they are unmethylated.
When the CpG islands are unmethylated, CTCF binds and creates a TAD, acting as an
insulator . Therefore, Igf2 (insulator growth factor 2) becomes inactivated .
When the island is methylated, CTCF doesn’t
bind and H19 doesn’t transcribe as its promoter
is blocked. But this allows the enhancers to act
on Igf2, permitting its transcription, as the two
regions are no longer flanked by CTCF.
[PDF p. 255]
The SNRPN domain (PWS and AS)
The CpG island is the promoter for a long ncRNA gene.
When this island promoter is methylated (in the maternal allele), the lncRNA won’t be
transcribed, allowing the expression of Ube3a but not of the other antisense genes found
on the left, which will remain untranscribed .
When the promoter is unmethylated (in the paternal allele), lncRNA will be expressed.
This lncRNA strand will overlap and cover the gene for Ube3a, making it silent, as RNA
polymerase II won’t be able to reach the promoter. In this case, the antisense genes on the
left will therefore be able to be transcribed, as Ube3a has been silenced.
Imprinting genes must be reset during gametogenesis
During gametogenesis, imprented regions must be reset and re-established depending
on the sex of the individual who is going to pass on the genes: if it is a male, both his
maternal and paternal chromosomes will have their imprented regions erased and then
remethylated according to the paternal methylation pattern. In the case of a female, the
opposite will happen, as she is going to pass on her genes as maternal.
In conclusion, after active demethylation during gametogenesis (although there are no
active demethylases, there is an active demethylation pathway), the marks corresponding
to oogenesis or spermatogenesis have to be established.
Prader-Willis and Angelman’s syndrome
- PWS: mutations and lack of genes in the
P aternal chromosome
- AS: mutations and lack of genes in the
M aternal chromosome
[PDF p. 256]
Causes of Prader-Willis syndrome (PWS) and Angelman’s syndrome (AS)
a) Microdeletion
Microdeletion, either in the paternal chromosome ( PWS, prevents genes from the paternal
chromosome from being expressed) or maternal chromosome (AS) can occur, preventing
some genes from being expressed and therefore giving rise to one syndrome or the other
(depending on which genes aren’t being expressed).
Microdeletion generally occurs because of unequal recombination during segmental
duplication (this implies that non-equivalent regions are exchanged between homologous
chromosomes during meiosis, which will lead to microdeletion).
Microdeletion can also be the result of strand slippage during replication .
Prader-Willis Angelman’s
b) UPD (uniparental disomy) affecting the SNRPN domain
During UPD, instead of having 2 chromosomes 15 marked as maternal and paternal, there
are 2 chromosomes marked both as maternal or both as paternal.
If they are both paternal, there will be an over-expression of all the antisense genes (which
isn’t really a problem), but no Ube3a; if they are both maternal, there will be Ube3a
expression, but no expression of the antisense genes (seen in red).
How does this UPD happen? It occurs by non-disjunction in meiosis I: during the first
meiotic phase, instead of each chromosome migrating to different poles of the cell, they both
go to the same gametocyte. Therefore, at the end of meiosis, this will result in cells with 2
copies of chromosome 15 (they are not haploid cells, it’s a sort of mitosis), whereas others
will have none.
When “gametocytes” fuse during fertilization, we will find trisomic zygotes on one hand ,
and monosomic zygotes on the other. Both zygotes are incompatible with life. Therefore,
the forming embryo will take different courses of action:
[PDF p. 257]
In the case of trisomics, the embryo
excludes one chromosome randomly.
Depending on which one is excluded, the
embryo may end up with chromosomes
coming from the same parent, giving place to
UPD.
In the monosomic case, the embryo
duplicates the only existing chromosome,
giving place once again to UPD.
Prader-Willi’s syndrome is caused by maternal uniparental disomy (mUPD).
Angelman’s syndrome is caused by paternal uniparental disomy (pUPD).
c) Mutations in Ube3a
Mutations in Ube3a in the maternal
chromosome (only chromosome in which it
is active) can cause Angelman’s
syndrome. But a mutation in Ube3a in the
paternal chromosome won’t be a cause
of Prader-Willi’s syndrome, as this gene is
already silenced in the said chromosome
through imprinting mechanisms.
d) Mutations in the imprinting coding region (ICR)
It accounts for less than 5% of the causes for each syndrome. As a consequence, there
cannot be demethylation and reestablishment of the corresponding imprinting patterns.
Diagnosis of each syndrome in the laboratory
The most common cause for both syndromes is microdeletion, when there is unequal
recombination due to segmental duplicates.
Once microdeletion has been discarded as the possible cause, other tests can be
performed.
PCR is performed for the diagnosis of any of the two diseases. PCR testing will recognize if
there are both methylated and unmethylated regions. Specific primers are used, one which
amplifies the methylated regions only, and the other which binds and amplifies the
unmethylated only.
[PDF p. 258]
In a person without the disease, methylated and unmethylated corresponding bands
should appear. But in case of disease, we would see only the methylated or the
unmethylated band, depending on the syndrome.
-
Diagnosing Prader-Willis Syndrome
For PWS, if the results of the PCR are normal, we can
discard the possibility of disease as it is only caused by
maternal UPD (uniparental disomy) or microdeletion in the
paternal chromosome. In the case that the person does
indeed have PWS, we would only see a methylated band
on the PCR results (due to microdeletion or to UPD).
Consequently, the next test to be performed would be a
FISH assay, to determine if the cause is microdeletion or
UPD.
If there is microdeletion, it’s detected through this FISH
assay.
If there is no microdeletion, UPD has to be confirmed by
analyzing microsatellites, to tell if the homologous
chromosomes are identical (UPD) or different.
-
Diagnosing Angelman’s syndrome
For Angelmans syndrome, if the PCR result is normal, there may be another possible
cause: a mutation in the Ube3a gene, which will not appear on the PCR and has to be
detected throughout further testing.
PWS is not caused by mutations in the Ube3a gene, as a mutation in the paternal Ube3a
gene would have no visible effect since it is silenced in said paternal chromosome. In the
paternal chromosome, what is expressed in the SNRPN region (where Ube3a is found) are
the antisense genes.
On the PCR results, in case of not being
normal, we would only see an unmethylated
band corresponding to the paternal
imprinted region. Once again, this result is
either due to microdeletion in the maternal
chromosome or due to paternal UPD.
If the bands are abnormal, we would again
carry out a FISH assay, analyze
microsatellites in case of suspecting paternal
UPD,…
[PDF p. 259]
[PDF p. 260]
Lecture 9.1. General principles of clinical genome analysis
Chromosome structure and types
Chromosomes have a “p” and a “q” arm (short and long), each with distinct bands. Light
and dark bands can be distinguished thanks to Giemsa staining (G bands).
After replication, the sister chromatids are bound by a centromere. At the terminus regions
of chromosomes, we find protective ends known as telomeres .
There are different chromosome types,
depending on the location of the centromere:
- Metacentric
- Submetacentric
- Acrocentric
- Telocentric
Human chromosome nomenclature
          - Numbers from 1-22 are assigned + X and Y chromosomes

(sex chromosomes)
           - Short arm = p; Long arm = q

           - Arms are divided into many bands and sub-bands.

Subdivision is done according to centromere proximity of said
band
How to do a Karyotype?
A Karyotype is the ordered representation of all human
chromosomes according to size and banding pattern.
Every chromosome can be recognized.
A substance known as Giemsa is used to stain the
chromosomes when they are in their most compacted
forms (during metaphase). Giemsa will produce G
bands: darker G bands correspond to more gene
dense regions, whereas lighter ones correspond to
regions where genes are less compact.
These bands reflect the active TADs: clear bands
tend to have more active genes, and darker bands
correspond to compacted and repressed genes.
Additionally, an ideogram represents the map of a single chromosome.
[PDF p. 261]
The Karyotype is a very specific array of all the chromosomes. They are organized from the
largest to the smallest (exception in chromosomes 21 and 22. Initially, chromosome 22 was
thought to be smaller), and present different centromere locations.
The typical Karyotype for a female is 46, XX
The typical Karyotype for a male is 46, XY
FISH assay
When the changes in chromosomes are small and can’t be
observed on the karyotype, FISH technique is employed
(Fluorescence in Situ Hybridization).
Double DNA strands, when separated (denatured) by heat,
bind complementarily when they are left to renature
(anheyl). This process of complementary binding is known
as hybridization.
In FISH assay, fluorescently tagged
probes are introduced in the sample,
and once DNA and the probe are
denatured, the probe anheyls to its
corresponding sequence.
If we see the probe fluoresce, the region is present. If the probe does
not fluoresce, it means it hasn’t bound due to a microdeletion in the
specific region it was sent to bind to.
It’s also very useful to detect breakpoints in translocation, as well
as fusion points.
(Example: FISH assay on chromosome 15. We can observe an
aberration in one of the copies of chromosome 15).
CHROMOSOME ABNORMALITIES
Classification of chromosomal abnormalities
-
According to which cells are affected
- Constitutional: they are present in all nucleated cells since early development.
-
Somatic/Acquired: present in certain cells or tissues, and not in all cells.
-
According to how the disease arises
- Structural abnormalities: such as duplications, inversions, deletions,…
- Numerical abnormalities: changes in the number of chromosomes in a
specific set (aneuploidy) or changes in the ploidy of the individual (polyploidy),
caused by errors in chromosomal segregation.
[PDF p. 262]
A) Structural abnormalities
These abnormalities are caused by unrepaired chromosome breaks or defects in the
recombination process (unequal crossover), due to the presence of scattered repeats.

Inversions (inv): they occur when a segment

of the chromosome is cut and inverted when
it’s rejoined. The inversion can be paracentric
(when they don’t include the centromere) or
pericentric (when the breakpoints are on
either side of the centromere, and include it.
There is a breakpoint in each arm).
Example: 46, XY, inv(11)(p11;p15)


Duplications (dup): occur when specific
segments are doubled. They will have to be
very large to be detectable on the Karyotype.
Example: dup(7)(q21;q23)


Ring chromosomes (r): consists in a fusion


between telomeres. The free ends fuse
together, and we end up with a ring structure.
Example: 46, XY, r(7)(p22;q36)
● Isochromosomes (i): an arm is lost, and the remaining arm is duplicated. We are
left with two identical arms. The total number of chromosomes is still 46, but there is
a serious modification in the genes.
Example: 46, X, i(Xq)


Deletions (del): we are left with a reduced number
of genes.
- Terminal deletions: Example: 46, XY,



del(7)(p22;pter)
- Interstitial deletions: Example: 46, XX,
del(5)(q13;q33)


Translocations (t): they consist in rearrangements
in which two non-homologous exchange segments.
In this way, derivative chromosomes are formed.
Translocations are easily detected through FISH assay.
The translocation can be reciprocal or non-reciprocal.
Reciprocal translocation: both non-homologous chromosomes exchange



segments of their genome. It can either be balanced (if it’s an even
exchange) or unbalanced (if it’s an unequal exchange which results in extra
or missing genes).
- Non-reciprocal translocation: they are one-way translocations
Example: 46, XX, t(2;5) (q31;p21). By convention, the lower number goes first. q and
p numbers symbol the bands involved.

They involve the loss or gain of complete chromosomes, and can affect only a set or the

Triploidy, which is mostly caused by dispermy (2 cells which fertilize a single

The risk of having a child with Down’s syndrome

during meiosis: instead of each homologous

Robertstonian translocation or Centric fusion
It involves acrocentric chromosomes. This type of translocation involves only chromosomes
13, 14, 15, 21 and 22, because the ends of their short arms have similar repetitive DNA
sequences that predispose to their fusion.
After the double strand break and consequent translocation, we are left with:

1 dicentric chromosome, which is stable in mitosis. The 2 centromeres where fusion

consequence.
Acrocentric chromosomes fuse together, joining two

If this translocation occurs in a potential gamete, this

translocation. There’s a possibility of passing missing

The Mendelian rules determined the laws of gene inheritance. They give a pattern for
transmission of genetic disease (depending on if an allele is dominant, recessive, X

There can only be one X active X chromosome. Therefore, whenever there are 2 (XX,

TYPES OF INHERITANCE
A) Autosomal: related to autosomes (non-sexual chromosomes). Autosomal inheritance
can be dominant or recessive, depending on which will be expressed in the phenotype
over the other.
- Autosomal recessive inheritance
In case of recessive alleles, the individual must possess two copies of it for the
character to be expressed (be homozygous for said character). Therefore, a person
can be healthy while carrying the recessive allele for a specific disease. These
people are known as carriers.
In order to work out the risks for someone to suffer from a disease, we use Punnet’s
squares, a method to calculate the outcome of different matings.
A feature of many recessive disorders, especially rare conditions, is that affected
individuals often have two identical mutant alleles because the parents are close
relatives. They are said to be consanguineous.
[PDF p. 266]
Autosomal recessive diseases
 - **CYSTIC FIBROSIS:** there are changes in the viscosity of

the mucus, so cilia cannot work properly and suffers from
recurrent infections. Also affects the pancreas. People
affected are homozygous for the same mutation.
              - **SICKLE CELL ANEMIA:** a mutation in

the beta-globin chain from hemoglobin causes
it to form rigid fibers, giving the red blood cells
a sickle-like shape and impairing their function. The sickle cells
have a shorter life span that leads to anemia, and can block small
blood vessels, causing hypoxic tissue damage.
Although carriers of an autosomal recessive disorders are considered
asymptomatic, they may nevertheless express some disease-related trait
that can distinguish them from the normal population. Take sickle-cell disease:
affected individuals are homozygous for a β-globin mutation and produce an
abnormal hemoglobin. Carriers of the sickle-cell mutation are not quite
asymptomatic. The sickle-cell allele produces a mutant β-globin that is
co-dominantly expressed with the normal β-globin, and heterozygotes can have mild
anemia (sickle-cell trait) which can worsen under intense, stressful conditions such
as exhaustion, hypoxia (at high altitudes), and/or severe infection.
- Autosomal dominant inheritance
Dominant alleles, when present, will always be expressed.
They do not need the individual to be homozygous. It’s typical to
find most of the offspring affected (at least ½ or ⅓ ). Additionally,
an heterozygous individual affected by a dominant allele could
have the possibility of not passing it on to their offspring.
Autosomal dominant diseases

Incomplete penetration: A curiosity about autosomal dominant inheritance is

Lecture 9.3. Polygenic inheritance
Multifactorial diseases have both genetic and environmental factors (cholesterol, quality
of the air, smoking, weight, diet,..). In general, most traits are the result of the interaction
between many genes and the environment.
In addition to being multifactorial, multiple genes contribute to the risk of suffering a certain
disease (polygenic inheritance) such as cancer, asthma, diabetes, heart failure,…
The genetic risk is less easy to quantify and identify than environmental factors. We all have
some sort of risk, but only when this risk goes beyond a certain thresh-hold will a person
manifest the disease. Many methods can be used to estimate the heritability of
multifactorial diseases.
How can we quantify genetic risk?
A) Firstly, we can quantify the risk by looking at the family history of the disease. There
is a small proportion of people in the general population with certain diseases, called
sporadic cases, versus familial cases, which are prevalent in successive
generations of a family tree.
    Looking at the prevalence of a disease in the general population gives a

certain probability (generally environmental factors)
    When looking at the prevalence of a selected disease in a family/group of

relatives, we obtain another probability (which involves the genetic factors
which establish predisposition to said disease) .
By calculating λ (relative ratio or relative risk) = the division of both probabilities,
we get an idea on the general risk to develop a disease (heritability), taking into
account the prevalence of disease in the general population and genetic factors
in your specific family tree.
B) Another way to quantify heritability is by using studies with twins.
Many pairs of twins are used, in which at least one has the disease being studied, to
identify the heritability of diseases.
Once we have selected the many pairs of twins, we study the concordance rate
(frequency in which, when one has the disease, the other also presents it. If they
both have the disease, they are concordant; if only one of them has it, they are
discordant).
If out of 100 diseased individuals, 80 of the twins from the pair also present the
disease, there is a concordance rate of 80%.
h = 2 x (Cmc - Cdc)
[PDF p. 270]
Heritability will only be high when the concordance rate presented by monozygotic
twins is higher than that of dizygotic twins (Cmc>>Cdc). Monozygotics share many
more genes in common: if the concordance rate is only high in monozygotic twins, it
means the disease is mainly caused by genetic factors, excluding the additional
environmental ones (more or less exclusion depending on the concordance rate
presented by dizygotic twins).
ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is caused by multiple pathogenicity,
meaning that many different disruptions lead to the same disease,
they converge into the same final result.
Two main problems lead to the disease: the accumulation of
beta-amyloid (which is prone to aggregation. It forms fibrils that
clump up together and accumulate outside the neurons, forming
amyloid plaques) and TAU protein (Associated to microtubules. If
it gets phosphorylated, it dissociates and microtubules stop working within the neurons,
forming neurofibrillary tangles inside them).
Apart from beta amyloid and TAU, there are other
factors which confer risk for Alzheimer’s. One of the
most well known risk variants is APO-E4, which
increases the risk and lowers the age at which early
onset takes place. APO-E lipoprotein is a gene
which has multiple allelic variants in the population.
Depending on your genotype for APO-E, your risk of
developing early onset Alzheimer’s varies: there are
risk APO-E variants and protective APO-E
variants.
APO-E2 is a protective variant and decreases the risk
and early onset.
APO-E4 increases the risk.
-early onset, lower than 65 years
-late onset, over 65 years old
[PDF p. 271]
Molecular characteristics of Alzheimer’s
The disease can arise by many ways:
    - The **overproduction of beta amyloid** due to **defects in cleaving enzymes**

(overly active β -secretase )
-
Faulty processing of β -amyloid
1. Accumulation of β -amyloid: In the bilipid membrane, there is a protein known as
Amyloid-precursor-protein (APP). The APP processing reaction is carried out by
secretases ( α, β 𝑎𝑛𝑑 γ), which cleave APP at certain points. The catalytic subunit of
γ -secretase is a presenilin protein ( presenilin 1 or 2).
When the first cut is done by beta-secretase, it will later
on trigger a higher the release of a 42 amino acid
isoform. If it’s done by alpha-secretase, the cut is done
in specific places which won’t produce the beta-amyloid
fragment which conferres the disease.
γ-Secretase carries out the second cut and cleaves at
alternative single locations to generate a series of Aβ
isoforms of different lengths. The Aβ42 isoform (42 residues
long) is thought to be the greatest contributor to
pathogenesis, as it is prone to form amyloid aggregates.
But under normal conditions , it’s not produced in large
quantities, unlike the predominant Aβ40 isoform.
    - The most causative **APP mutations** which give rise to Alzheimer’s are

heterozygous missense mutations distributed close to APP cleavage
sites, as they increase the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio (especially γ-secretase cleavage

- The causative mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2 ( which act as cofactors for
beta-secretase) are also heterozygous missense mutations; they, too, seem
to have the effect of increasing the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio.
[PDF p. 272]
2. Processing of beta-amyloid: On top of the effect of APP cleavage sites, there is the
influence of APO-E. Each of the alleles of APO-E is a combination of two different
SNPs. The “rs” number makes reference to the specific SNP in each allele which will
change the specific amino acid (amino acids 112 and 158).

The combination of T and T gives the allele epsilon 2, a protective variant against

Alzheimer’s

The presence of T and C in each of the SNPs gives epsilon 3 (normal allele in the

C and C give place to epsilon 4 allele, which conferres a risk for Alzheimer’s

Lecture 9.4. Cancer genetics
Concept of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes
Oncogenes are abnormal versions of protooncogenes (genes coding for cell cycle
promoting proteins such as cyclins and EGF, which stimulate the cell cycle when carrying
out their normal function). When there is a gain of function in these genes due to alterations,
it makes proteins overstimulate the cell cycle, and the cells tend to become
malignant/cancerous as they proliferate too much
and accumulate mutations.
Oncogenes are known as dominant genes,
because a point mutation in only one oncogene allele
results in an overstimulation of cell proliferation.
Tumor suppressor genes code for proteins involved in stopping or slowing down the cell
cycle (p53, Rb, p21,…). A decreased function in these genes, for example due to mutations,
makes cells divide constantly and uncontrollably, giving place to cancer.
- p21 is a TSG which blocks the activity of cdk/cyclin complexes
- Rb is found bound to E2F, and when phosphorylated, it separates and liberates E2F, which
will translocate to the nucleus as a transcription factor.
These tumor suppressor genes are known
as recessive genes, as they need the
presence of 2 mutated copies to function
abnormally, giving place to cancer.
How are oncogenes generated from protooncogenes?
1. Deletions or point mutations in the coding sequence.
For example, what occurs with the EGFR gene during cancer: there is an activating
mutation, which produces a hyperactive protein that over-stimulates the cell
(whereas normally, mutations are inactivating and cause inactivation of proteins). It
acquires more functionality than normal, so there is increased signalling.
2. Gene amplification
This happens in the case of HER-2 receptors during breast cancer: there is no
mutation, so it’s a normal version of the gene, but too many copies of the protein
are produced due to hyperstimulation of said gene.
Therefore during cancer we find more copies of the gene than normal, resulting in
overly expressed proteins on the cell membrane which promote the cell cycle.
[PDF p. 274]
3. Chromosome rearrangement
    It can occur through **fusion,** resulting in the **hyperactivation of a protein.**

    Through the **relocation of a promoter region,** causing it to be near the

gene. The nearby regulatory sequence causes a normal protein to be
overproduced (this can occur, for example, when a virus infects and
introduces its genome into the host’s DNA. The infecting virus can alter the
promoter, causing it to overproduce the protein it regulates) .
How are tumor suppressor genes inactivated?
They can be inactivated by a series of changes affecting both alleles (we usually need
dysfunctionality in both alleles for TSGs to be inactivated, although having one dysfunctional
allele makes the other more prone to suffer mutations and silencing).
We need combinations of different events which result in the inactivation of both alleles.
1. Inactivating point mutations
2. Chromosome deletion
3. Chromosome loss (of a whole
chromosome)
4. Silencing through DNA methylation:
if the promoter region is methylated,
the gene won’t be produced. Tumors
use this system to shut down tumor
suppressor genes, preventing their
expression.
All these combinations, affecting both
alleles, will result in the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes (TSGs).
[PDF p. 275]
EGFR mutations (epidermal growth factor receptor)
The oncogenic version of EGFR is very important in lung cancer.
These EGFR hyperactivating mutations are present in 10-15%
cases of lung cancers
***** (drugs ending in -ib are chemical compounds; ending in -ab are
therapeutic antibodies).
There are chemical compound drugs which can be used to treat this sort of lung cancer

Gefitinib can be injected to block kinase activity of tyrosine kinase. This will inhibit

It can be used to detect the amplification of
