TBL 9.1. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
The process used in PCR is replication, from which we produce DNA from DNA.
PCR is necessary because searching for a certain sequence on a single DNA strand is like
looking for a needle in a haystack. Before PCR, scientists had to proceed to search through
the whole genome.
In 1980, an idea arose to put an end to this problem.
PCR technique basics
To know if the sequence we are looking for is present,
we need a process which copies and amplifies that
specific DNA sequence.
It’s possible to copy a fragment repeatedly, through
replication, by using a DNA polymerase enzyme. For
replication, each strand will be used as a template.
PCR is therefore carried out to obtain millions of
copies of a specific DNA fragment.
To carry out the process in a test tube:
1. Denaturation: firstly, the double stranded DNA has to become denatured and
separate. This can be done by establishing high temperatures, at around 90
degrees celsius.
2. Primer annealing: DNA polymerases need the presence of a primer to begin
replication (a small DNA sequence which binds to the 5’ end). For it to anneal, the
temperature has to be lowered (50-70 degrees).
This step is critical for specificity: we want very specific primer fragments, which
will only bind to the sequence of interest. If it’s not specific enough, there will be
replication of other fragments and contamination of the sample.
3. Addition of DNA polymerase: The polymerase will copy and carry out the
extension on the DNA strand. For extension, a temperature of 72 degrees celsius
is required.
By repeating this process in many cycles, we increase the number of copies of the
sequence in interest.
[PDF p. 278]
By the end of the second cycle, we manage to flank a
small sequence by using 5’ and 3’ primers, which
corresponds to the fragment of interest. These small
sequences are the ones which will be repeatedly
increased after each cycle.
This is a simple procedure, but due to the different temperatures required for each cycle,
we are presented with a problem: when restarting each cycle, the DNA polymerase
enzyme will be denatured at the high
temperatures required for the denaturing of
the strand and primer annealing (90
degrees, 50-70 degrees).
Thermus-aquaticus polymerases (TAQ
polymerases) are used to solve this
problem, as they are extremophilic enzymes
which can work optimally at temperatures
even higher than 90 degrees celsius.
What do we need to carry out a PCR?

We need to know the sequence for the ends of the fragment, in order to synthesize
the primers.
- Within the tube, we need: the DNA sample, DNA primers, free available
nucleotides, TAQ polymerase enzyme, and a buffer solution (with a particular pH
and ions). This is known as the Master Mix.
- Equipment needed: a machine known as the thermal cycler, which carries out the
required fast changes in temperature.

From here, Denaturation, Primer annealing and Extension can occur in many cycles.
Typically, around 35-40 cycles are carried out, which is enough, as half a million fragments
are produced at the end.
Visualization of the result
For visualization, many techniques can be employed:
                             **Fluorescent dyes which are able to**

bind DNA: if they bind, they fluoresce, and
can be observed under UV light. The
fluorescence is present when the fragment has
been replicated. If the specific sequence which
was being searched for isn’t present, the
sample won’t fluoresce.
[PDF p. 279]
Quantitative PCR: more quantitative methods to visualize PCR results can be used.
Quantitative PCR uses a fluorescent probe, which binds to the DNA strand.
The Reporter is a fluorescent molecule, but in the presence of the Quencher, the
light is sequestered and there is no light emission.
Once PCR begins, TAQ polymerase copies the DNA strand. When it reaches and
encounters the probe, in order to continue replication, it hydrolyzes it. The Reporter
and the Quencher are separated.
Now, the liberated Reporter is capable of emitting light.
With this technique, fluorescence can be detected in
real time. We can measure the light according to
each cycle, making it a more quantitative method.
To visualize quantitative PCR/real time PCR, we use a
machine able to detect fluorescence.
PCR applications
a) Molecular identification
-
Gene expression analysis: different cells express a different set of genes.
Additionally, the amount of expression will be different depending on the tissue. This
gene expression, which leads to proteins, can be assessed through
immunohistochemistry, gene electrophoresis (for detecting the protein) or ELISA
(antibodies/antigens).
But this type of detection system has limitations:
    An antibody is required

    The sensibility of the technique is typically low, so if there is a low protein

expression, it cannot be detected.
PCR serves as an additional tool for gene expression assessment: instead of
directly measuring proteins, we amplify the RNA sequences expressed in each cell
type to detect the presence of said proteins.
Problem: TAQ polymerase only works on DNA. Therefore, we will need
retrotranscription for this detection system, by taking viral machinery which
carries out retrotranscription. mRNA is retro-transcribed into cDNA
( complementary DNA) by using an additional primer.
To measure how much DNA is present in the solution after retrotranscription, we run
a PCR, which will give different graphs depending on the initial amount of DNA.
This whole process is known as RT-PCR (retrotranscription-PCR)
[PDF p. 280]

Pathogens: pathogen identification through RT-PCR can be carried out by
introducing primers specific for the pathogenic genome.

- Forensic medicine
- Disease-risk identification
- Disease-treatment customization
b) Genetic engineering
(to obtain recombinant insulin for example, by carrying out PCR to obtain many copies of
insulin genes)
Detection of SARS-CoV2
( Document on ADI)
[PDF p. 281]
TBL 9.2. Diseases caused by expansion of trinucleotide repeats
There are a series of diseases caused by the expansion of trinucleotide repeats.
They are usually repaired by MMR (mismatch repair), but some escape, giving place to
disease.
There are two main groups of diseases caused by the expansion of trinucleotide repeats:
Caused by the expansion of CAG trinucleotide (Huntington’s disease)
Caused by expansion of other, non-CAG trinucleotides (Fragile X and myotonic
dystrophy).
These diseases are usually neuropathies, and they all show anticipation.
(Dynamic mutations, meaning they expand in subsequent generations)
1. CAG trinucleotide expansion diseases
These CAG expansions have an autosomal dominant inheritance.
They are characterized by expansions of the CAG trinucleotide, which is located in coding
regions of the mutated gene. This CAG trinucleotide codes for glutamine, so there will be an
expansion of glutamines in the polypeptide chain. This expansion seems to cause a gain of
function (the protein gains a new function and sticks together with other molecules), with
toxic effects, generally causing neuropathies.
Neuropathies caused by CAG trinucleotide repeats have a series of common features:
Anticipation: they all present anticipation, meaning that the disease appears earlier
after each subsequent generation (first generation, age 45. Second generation, age
39,… after each generation, the age of onset is earlier). This occurs because, after
each generation, the size of the expansion becomes larger. The more repeats, the
more severe the pathology, therefore symptoms appear earlier.
The expanding repeat is in a coding sequence of the gene (CAG = codes for
glutamine).
The expansion is more frequent in the paternal line. These expansions take place
mainly in spermatogenesis : during spermatogenesis, there are many more cell
[PDF p. 282]
divisions which involve replication (where trinucleotide expansion takes place). When
a father is the one who transmits the repeat, it will expand into a larger mutation in
the offspring due to spermatogenesis which occurred in the father.
The expansion results in the gain of function, not a loss of it (which would cause the
gene to be silent).
Strand slippage during replication which isn’t repaired through MMR gives place
to these expansions.
A) SPINAL CEREBRAL ATAXIA (SCA12)
SCA stands for Spinal cerebral ataxia
Ataxia is a problem with the coordination of walking, due to problems in the cerebellum.
The death of neurons in the cerebellum and spinal cord leads to ataxia. SCA12 is the only
CAG expansion disease which isn’t found in a coding region, but in 5’UTR.
B) HUNTINGTON’S DISEASE
It’s a dominant autosomal disease. It’s caused by a mutation in
the huntingtin gene: the expansion of the CAG trinucleotide in the
gene leads to a protein with additional glutamines. This has several
repercussions:

The polyglutamine mutation alters the function of
huntingtin protein: there is a lack of interaction
between the domains of the protein it codes for,
making it l ose its function and making it prone to
form aggregates and toxic deposits.

The expansion can also affect the expression of some genes which are very
important for neuronal function, such as Dopamine. Abnormal huntingtin protein
will prevent the interaction of transcription factors with the promoters of these genes.
Another important disruption is the decrease in Beclin, altering autophagy.
(Beclin is one of the molecules which regulates autophagy, and in
order to regulate the process, it has to be un-ubiquitinated by
ataxins. If ataxins are expanded due to the presence of mutated
huntingtin, they don’t function correctly. Beclin remains
ubiquitinated, and is therefore a target for proteasomes. Beclin
levels in the cell decrease (they are degraded), so autophagy isn’t
correctly regulated, leading to the death of neurons).
[PDF p. 283]
2. NON-CAG trinucleotide expansion diseases
The expansion occurs in non-coding regions of the gene. These mutations affect by
changing the expression of a coding gene (ex: expansion in promoters), and not
the amino acid sequence.


There is no gain in function, but a loss of function. There is a lack of protein
expression due to effects in regulation and promoter regions.


There is anticipation in these diseases, except in Friedreich’s disease. When
passing on the expansion mutation to children, it continues to grow (anticipation).


Additionally, the expansion is caused by hundreds of thousands of repeats which
involve a premutation state.
Premutation state: It’s a range number of premutated alleles between healthy and
pathogenic, which imply predisposition or high risk of developing full,
pathogenic mutations.
Only premutation alleles will transition to mutation, it’s a transition state that alleles go
through.


In these non-CAG expansions, the expansion is more frequent in the maternal
line.
This is because the mechanism of expansion in these diseases isn’t strand slippage
during replication. It’s thought to be due to unequal crossing over, as they are
explosive expansions. Because this unequal recombination occurs in oogenesis
and not spermatogenesis, there is maternal transmission.
A) FRIEDREICH’S ATAXIA
It is the only of these non-CAG trinucleotide expansion diseases which
doesn’t present anticipation.
[PDF p. 284]
B) FRAGILE X SYNDROME
It affects the gene FMR1, which encodes for the protein FMRP (fragile mental retardation
protein). This syndrome is caused by an expansion of CGG trinucleotides in the 5’-UTR.
The expansion shuts down the expression of the
gene due to epigenetic factors: in full mutations,
the FMR1 mRNA strand can interact with its own
DNA due to the many CGG repeats. This leads to
the formation of an RNA-DNA loop, which attracts
epigenetic repressors. As a result, there is
decreased FMRP (the protein coded by FMR1).
The absence of the protein alters the function of
neurons, as its function is to move/shuttle mRNAs
(which have structures known as TG-quartets)
that play important roles in neuronal functions.
Just one X chromosome with the expansion will
lead to Fragile X syndrome, which causes mental
retardation.
X-linked dominant inheritance. Sherman paradox
(DOMINANT inheritance, although with incomplete
penetrance , as there are premutated alleles).
Black numbers depict the number of repeats; blue
percentages depict the probability of having
offspring with the disease. The pre mutated alleles
expand until reaching >90 in the third generation.
Sherman came up with the theory that as we move
down, the probability of women having offspring
with the disease increases.
We can find normal transmitting males. They
transmitted the disease, but didn’t show incomplete penetrance, as they had a premutated
allele. The allele expands in the maternal transmission, not in the paternal
transmission. A premutated male will pass-on those premutation repeats, and not an
expanded allele. He is technically a carrier, but doesn’t suppose an expansion in repeats.
These males are healthy, but it has been seen they can develop neurological symptoms at a
very advanced age (ex: tremors).
In conclusion: The probability of passing from premutation to full mutation increases
as the size of the repeat increases as well, and expansion only occurs in the maternal
line.
[PDF p. 285]
-
TBL 9.3. Dysregulation of the cell cycle in cancer
CANCER is a genetic disease which consists in the alteration of oncogenes and tumor
suppressor genes . Inherited mutations, genetic and epigenetic changes produced by
carcinogens, viral infections or chronic inflammation cause normal cells to transform into
tumor cells, which don’t respond to regulation and start dividing uncontrollably.
There are many risk factors, such as diet, age, gender, and lifestyle choices like alcohol
and tobacco consumption.
➢ Tobacco smoke and cancer:
Tobacco components are carcinogenic . Some of these compounds bind DNA
irreversibly, causing DNA damage and producing mutations which can affect
oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes; tobacco smoke also causes chronic
inflammation: due to prolonged consumption, acute inflammation arises.
A chronic state of inflammation causes inflammatory cells to damage surrounding
tissues.
    A mechanism used by macrophages and other leukocytes in this

inflammatory process is the production of ROS, which normally kills
pathogens but in chronic inflammation, will reach our own cells and damage
them.
    Additionally, many **cytokines** are produced, to recruit more cells. Tumors can

make use of these cytokines, by expressing receptors for them, to grow and
proliferate. These receptors are in general found on immune cell’s surfaces,
but tumors can also express them. Therefore, inflammation will enhance
their growth.
Its common effects are lung and bladder cancer.
Comparison: healthy
lung and smoker’s
lung under the
microscope.
Macrophages become
full of carcinogenic
residues.
Characteristics of tumor cells
-
High proliferation potential (altered expression of GFs and continuous activation of
intracellular pathways maintain autonomous and uncontrolled growth).
-
Unlimited replication capacity (the presence of telomerase allows the tumor to
acquire unlimited replication and evade senescence).
-
Blockage of apoptosis (tumors increase the expression of antiapoptotic proteins
such as BCL-2 and block proapoptotic genes, like BAX and BAK)
-
Metastasizing capacity (by decreasing the adhesion between neighbouring cells)
-
Induction of angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels; otherwise, the tumor
will undergo necrosis)
-
Evasion of the immune system
[PDF p. 286]
We can find different types of tumors:
Benign tumors (slow growth rate, highly differentiated, don’t metastasize). Benign tumors
coming from epithelial cells are known as papillomas (stratified epithelium) or polyps
(cylindrical epithelium).
Malignant tumors (high growth rate, undifferentiated, metastasize). Malignant epithelial
tumors are known as carcinomas and non-epithelial malignant tumors are called
sarcomas.
INDUCTION OF CANCER
1. Carcinogens
They produce acquired genetic alterations. Two main types:
a) Physical carcinogens
-
Ionizing radiation, such as X-rays. These radiations produce DNA oxidation
and strand breaks. Leukemia is a malignancy that develops frequently in the
first years after exposure to ionizing radiation.
- Non-ionizing radiation, such as ultraviolet rays. UVA
rays cause indirect damage to DNA by generating free
radicals that can oxidize, while UVB rays cause direct
damage through the production of pyrimidine dimers.
These dimers, if not repaired through NER mechanism,
can generate mutations in genes involved in the cell
cycle.
Melanoma is associated with the presence of TT dimers in tumor cells.
b) Chemical carcinogens
Tobacco is an example of a chemical carcinogen. Some of its compounds damage
DNA and alter critical genes, and their continuous inhalation causes inflammation
which can become chronic, inducing the production of ROS and cytokines which
stimulate the proliferation of tumor cells.
2. Microorganisms
- Helicobacter pylori : bacterium which possesses
carcinogenic potential. Its presence in the gastric mucosa
causes chronic gastritis (inflammation) leading
inflammatory cells to produce free radicals which can
damage DNA.
-
Hepatitis C virus (HCV): its oncogenic capacity is
associated to chronic hepatocyte infection. The development
of a hepatocarcinoma is related to the virus’ capacity of surviving in the liver.
[PDF p. 287]
Papilloma virus (HPV): it’s a type of oncogenic virus. It
introduces its viral genome into host cells’ and there is
latent transcription and translation of viral proteins E6
and E7. These cause the inactivation of tumor
suppressor genes such as p53 (which is mainly in
charge of stopping cell proliferation when damage is
detected and, if not repaired, carrying out apoptosis)
and Rb (becomes permanently phosphorylated,
therefore E2F constantly promotes replication and cell
division).
3. Genetic factors
a) Alterations in DNA repair mechanisms: damage to DNA has to be repaired to
maintain the integrity of the genome, through repair mechanisms such as NER. The
alteration of NER causes a disorder with recessive autosomal origin known as
Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP), where children present erythema and in later
stages, cutaneous atrophy and telangiectasia.
b) Oncogenes: they are the altered version of protooncogenes. When mutations take
place in those genes, there is abnormal cell proliferation as protooncogenes are in
charge of stimulating cellular growth. Oncogenes are dominant genes (mutation in
one of the alleles is enough to produce an abnormal proliferative effect).
There are different types of oncogenes:
-
Growth factors, who’s overexpression causes hyperstimulation of cell
proliferation.
- Growth factor receptors, such as EGFR and HER-2 which can become
overexpressed on cell membranes and overactivate signalling cascades due
to constitutive activations or hyperactivation of the regulatory region.
-
Genes of intracellular signalling pathways. KRAS, B-RAF mutations can
alter the MAPK pathway.
Some tyrosine kinase-type proteins
implicated in intracellular signalling can
also be altered. This occurs in CHRONIC
MYELOGENOUS LEUKEMIA, where the
translocation of protooncogene Abl from
chromosome 9 to chromosome 22
produces an abnormal chromosome,
called Philadelphia chromosome. This
results in a fusion protein (Bcr-Abl) with
a constant tyrosine kinase activity that
promotes uncontrolled proliferation.
[PDF p. 288]
Genes related to apoptosis (mutations in anti-apoptotic
genes).
This type of genetic modification is produced in FOLLICULAR
LYMPHOMA. The translocation of proteins 14 and 18 causes
overexpression of BCL-2.
c) Tumor suppressor genes: they code for proteins which inhibit the cell cycle. The
loss of functionality in these genes (in both alleles) results in uncontrolled
proliferation. TSGs are recessive genes (require mutation in both alleles to affect).
There are different types of TSGs:
    - **Retinoblastoma (Rb),** which is found bound to **E2F** transcription factor to

inactivate transcription. E2F becomes active when Rb is phosphorylated. The
inactivation of Rb in both alleles makes it unable to perform its function.
- p53, which under stressful conditions halts the cell cycle
in order to repair DNA damage. It induces the expression
of p21, an inhibitor of Cyclin D/Cdk4, allowing to stop
the progression of the cell cycle. p53 is found mutated in
50% of human cancers. Individuals who inherit an altered
copy of p53 suffer from LI-FRAUMENI SYNDROME and
present a high risk of developing cancer if the other allele
becomes mutated.
d) Epigenetic alterations
-
DNA methylation, which can result in the silencing in the expression of a
gene.
- Histone modifications. In tumors, patterns of histone methylation and
acetylation are found altered, which may lead to the silencing of TSGs such
as p21.
Families of antitumoral drugs
- Alkylating agents, such as platinum derivatives, which react with DNA generating
DNA breaks and induce apoptosis.
-
Antimetabolites, structural analogues of purines and pyrimidines which generate
altered DNA sequences and result in ruptures (ex: antipyrimidine 5-fluoracyl ).

Mitotic inhibitors, such as Vinca alkaloids and taxanes (ex: taxol), which interfere
with microtubules during mitosis and cause cell death.

-
Topoisomerase inhibitors
- Antitumoral antibiotics (ex: anthracyclines )
[PDF p. 289]
Classification of inhibitors


EGFR inhibitors: Gefitinib and Osimertinib (block ATP binding site).


HER-2 inhibitors: Trastuzumab and Pertuzumab (antibodies which bind and block
different HER-2 ligand binding domains)


VEGF and VEGFR inhibitors: Bevacizumab (antibody against VEGF, inhibits
endothelial cell proliferation and angiogenesis)


Tumor angiogenesis and metastasis
Tumors requiere vascularization to survive. If not
vascularized, they undergo necrosis .
The situation of hypoxia and hypoglycemia in which the
tumor is initially found promotes angiogenesis by
stimulating expression of VEGF (HIF-1).
Angiogenesis facilitates the entry of tumor cells into
circulation, resulting in metastasis . This is also
favoured by the destruction of E cadherin and of
connections with neighbouring cells and the ECM.
Vascularization of normal cells vs vascularization of
tumors: in tumor vascularization, there is no hierarchy
(veins, arterioles, capillaries,…) because blood vessels
in tumors grow very fast and in a disorganized way.
There is a morphological and biochemical difference,
which can be used to target specific vasculature of the
tumor and not that of normal cells, by using anti-VEGF
drugs, such as Bevacizumab, which prevents the
binding of VEGF to its receptor.
Evading the immune system
Cancer cells produce tumor antigens that are not expressed on the rest of the cells. They
present some foreign antigens (proteins) which result from mutated protooncogenes/TSGs.
These antigens, together with MHC-I, can be recognized by CD8 T-lymphocytes. They will
carry out phagocytosis and present tumor antigens to T-CD4 lymphocytes.
But this mechanism isn’t always achieved, as tumors manage to evade the immune
system by decreasing the expression of MHC-I or tumor antigens.
Therefore autoantigens aren’t presented, and T cells cannot carry out surveillance.
They also express TGF-beta, a growth factor which in normal tissues stimulates proliferation
of fibroblasts, but also has a potent anti-immune effect, deactivating the killer function of T
cells. In patients without a functional immune system/immunosuppressed, tumors are
expressed at a higher frequency, as there is completely no tumor recognition.
[PDF p. 290]
Immunotherapy
The tumor types that best respond to immunotherapies are lung cancer and melanomas.
This is because they have a high load of mutations which translate into new aberrant
proteins, meaning there are more antigens for T lymphocytes to recognize.
BREAST CANCER
Incidence is very high and increasing, mainly due to exposure of new carcinogens and new
detection systems. 1 out of 8 women in Spain will develop breast cancer over the course of
their lives. Survival rate is quite high as the result of development of new treatments and
early detection methods. If detected early, there is an almost 100% chance of survival.
- Normal breast


Ductal carcinoma in situ: In DCIS, glands are enlarged,
with lots of cells invading the duct. Tumor is still only found
within the gland, although enlarged.


Invasive carcinoma: In invasive carcinoma, glands and
ducts can no longer be observed, as they are overpopulated
by tumors.


Different tumors express or repress different types of proteins. Not all tumors express
estrogen receptors; some learn how to survive without estrogens or progesterone, making
them estrogen-progesterone negative. Tamoxifen can only be used to treat
estrogen-receptors expressing tumors.
Pertuzumab is used in combination with trastuzumab, as not all tumors respond well to
each drug. They target different domains of HER-2 receptors (domains 2 and 4), making it
more effective treatment.
[PDF p. 291]
TBL 9.5. Gene mutations as therapeutic targets in cancer
CLINICAL CASE
NGS techniques can test in a very small amount of sample, thousands of genes (high
sensitivity)
A patient presents the following type of stage IV lung cancer:
The initial lung tumor was treated with Genitifib after tumor DNA sequencing (NGS) detected
a mutation in L858R, which affects the cytoplasmic domain of EGFR making it overly active.
The tumor showed significant regression until May 2015, when the patient presented tumor
growth and pleural effusion. She had developed resistance to Gefitinib (acquired resistance).
Alterations in the EGFR gene


In 40% of cases of cancers caused by point mutations, the mutation is L858R in
Exon 21 from the EGFR gene.
Hotspots are regions of oncogenes where mutations are seen frequently. They
correspond to activating mutations, very specific alterations which are going to result
in a hyperactivity of the gene.


We can also find in-frame deletions.


Either by point mutation or deletion, there is a very subtle change in the protein
associated with gain of activity.
Typically, these kinds of mutations are associated with a specific profile: adenocarcinomas,
non-smokers, asian and young females.
[PDF p. 292]
Endothelial growth factor receptors (EGFRs)
EGFR is a member of the transmembrane receptor
family. It’s part of the HER-1 family, a type of
tyrosine kinase which becomes activated by the
binding of EGF.
L858R mutation affects the cytosolic domain,
specifically an area close to the ATP binding site.
Therefore, this will affect the activity of the protein.
With the mutation, Km goes up, but Kcat increases
even more, causing efficacy to increase for ATP
and the peptide.
This causes an overactivation of the receptor. It’s so strong, it doesn’t even need the
presence of a ligand (EGF) for dimerization and activation. The process is no longer
regulated, and the cell proliferation becomes independent.
It results in the activation of the MAPK pathway, which promotes cell proliferation and
angiogenesis.
Oncogenic addiction
Once the tumor gets this mutation, it becomes addicted to it. It d epends on this pathway for
proliferation and survival. In normal cells, there are alternative pathways, but tumors
become highly dependent on this enhanced pathway. This is known as oncogenic
addiction.
Medically, oncogenic addiction is very interesting, as blocking this proliferation pathway can
have a high effect on the proliferation of the tumor. By using TKI (tyrosine kinase
inhibitors), such as Getifinib (which blocks the ATP binding site), we block the EGFR
activity.
Primary resistance vs acquired resistance
- Primary resistance: clinical situation in which a
malignant tumor does not respond to a specific
drug. It can be caused by mutations in KRAS,
Mdm2,…
KRAS mutations are mainly associated with
primary resistance, as a mutation in KRAS
implies that the pathway is always active,
independently from EGFR.
The activation is continuous even if the tyrosine
kinase has been inhibited. A patient with a
KRAS mutation can’t be treated with EGFR
TKIs, as it won’t have any effect in suppressing proliferation.
[PDF p. 293]
Secondary resistance: the most important type of mutation which causes EGFR
drugs secondary/acquired resistance is the mutation in T790M, located in the
tyrosine-kinase domain. It’s a missense somatic mutation, resulting in threonine
being interchanged by methionine. It inhibits Getinifib binding, as it doesn’t allow
the drug to enter the binding site.
Osimertinib can be prescribed in the presence of this
mutation, as it can block the ATP binding site even when
the patient presents this mutation.
To prescribe osimertinib, we must first sequence the tumor
DNA to detect the specific mutation/alteration. T790M
mutations account for 60% of secondary resistance mutations.
Additionally, osimertinib can cross the blood-brain barrier
and reach metastasis sites in the brain.
Patients can also develop resistance to osimertinib, so we would carry out another
tumor sequencing to detect any additional mutations.
In the case of our patient, an additional
activating mutation in RAF was detected. This
is a way the tumor has to evade the blockage of
EGFR, as it activates the MAPK pathway
without the need of the EGFR tyrosine kinase.
The patient was treated with dabrafenib
(B-RAF inhibitor) and trametinib (MEK
inhibitor), plus osimertinib, to block the pathway
by attacking many mutation points. The tumor
showed increased reduction.
The patient sadly died, but if there is regression, the tumor could have also continued to
develop mutations and activating pathways which we would have had to block.
All this is known as targeted therapy, a type of personalized/precision medicine to treat
particular types of cancers in particular types of patients.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/Material/FMF-notes.title: FMF notes (FSF)
Medical-Degree/Year-1/Material/FMF-notes.content:
[PDF p. 1]
FOUNDATIONS OF STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Lucía Reed López
[PDF p. 2]
Basic concepts of waves
IMAGING TECHNIQUES
1st image: normal x-ray radiograph, where we can observe the lungs
and the heart, which will provide info about the size of the heart. X-ray
radiographs are helpful but dangerous as they are ionizing. They can
cause damage to DNA. It’s the most dangerous imaging system, but
the simplest and cheapest (along with MRI).


2nd image: x-ray CT scan (computed tomography) . It has the
advantage that it provides very precise and accurate information,
regarding location and size, about the different organs of the body.


3rd image: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). It relies on a
magnetic field with a very high intensity (1.5 teslas-5 teslas, 10^4
times the magnetic field of the earth) . There is a limit to the number of
magnetic fields a person can be submitted to without suffering
consequences. In MRI we can differentiate all the different tissues,
allowing us to observe the thickness of the walls of the heart.


4th image: Ultrasound. It’s the less risky of the techniques. It also has
the advantage that it can be observed in real time.


We have to evaluate the risks and the benefits we will obtain by using each
imaging technique. The objective is to balance out the risks and the benefits.
Depending on what we want to observe, we will use one technique or another and assume
more or less risk.
We will focus on EM waves (there is an electromagnetic field being propagated) and
pressure waves (which are the base of Ultrasound) .
ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES (EM)
A wave is an oscillation of a physical magnitud that propagates in time and space,
transporting energy.
There is a source of waves, where the creation of
the wave occurs. The created wave propagates
(it will need to be characterized), and once it
reaches the target, it can go through it creating a
transmitted wave, be absorbed or be sent back
creating a reflected wave.
[PDF p. 3]
There are 2 main families of waves: X-rays and ultrasounds

X-rays (radiography or CTs): It’s based on

the transmitted wave.

Ultrasounds: It’s based on the reflected

wave
We can find 2 other families which are closely
related:


MRI: (the most complex system concerning medical physics). There is a process
which occurs, known as resonance: a person receives EM radiation (of the order of a
microwave ) and absorbs it, and after a time “t”, the amount of radiation
accumulated by the person is emitted, revealing an image. It’s a 2 step process.


PET: a drug with a specific isotope is introduced in the patient, and it emits
radioactivity depending on the amount absorbed by each organ. These isotopes
can only be absorbed by cancer cells, so it’s very useful and precise to detect


tumors.
PERIOD, WAVELENGTH AND FREQUENCY
The trajectory of a wave is a straight line. A source
radiates waves, forming a radius from the source to the
objective.
Magnitude H (positive or negative, depending on whether
it oscillates up or down) has the property of periodicity.
we move the same distance r each time, and we reach
the same H value. This distance “r” which reflects
periodicity is known as wavelength.
Period (T): For a specific point r1, we can analyze the behaviour of the wave in
relation to time: there is a periodicity in time, a time t after which the wave is found
at the same H. This periodic magnitude is known as Period. Measured in seconds.
Angular frequency (ω) is equal to 2π/T


Wavelength ( λ ): reflects the periodicity in space. Measured in meters .
Wavenumber “K” is equal to 2π λ/ .


Frequency equals 1/T. It’s the inverse value of the Period, measured in Hz or s-1.


[PDF p. 4]
HARMONIC WAVES
Physical magnitude P: P(x,t) = p0 sin (wt - kx + φ0)
This is the most simple equation that describes the oscillation of a wave.
p0= A (Amplitude)
P(x,t) = indicates it oscillates in space
and time
● How can we characterize a source?
The source generates waves, which propagate energy. The most important point
to characterize the source is how much energy is produced per second. This is
known as the Power (P) of the source.

How much of the energy arrives at each point?

The energy is distributed on the whole surface, so only a small part will reach the patient.
We need to define a magnitude which describes how much energy reaches each point in
space . In other words, how the power is distributed in space. This magnitude is known as
Intensity (I) of the wave.
In order to characterize the source, we use P.
In order to characterize a wave, we use I.
REFLECTED W., TRANSMITTED W. AND ABSORPTION
A part of the wave will be transmitted, and a part will be reflected.
The intensity is a magnitude that has to be preserved during this process. Therefore, the
intensity (energy) is split into the reflection and transmission waves. This property is
conserved in any interphase.
Each time there is an interphase, one part is transmitted and the other, reflected.
● REFLECTED INTENSITY
    - For **X-rays and MRI**, the **reflected intensity** is very very **small,** so we can

reject it.
- But in ultrasounds the intensity of the reflected wave is much bigger, it’s
important as it is the wave that will give us an image.
We can distinguish two different types of reflection:


Specular reflection: if the direction of the reflected waves are parallel
(smooth surfaces)


Diffuse reflection: if the directions of reflected waves follow different

RADIOACTIVE SOURCES
Radioactivity consists in the emission by some nuclei of energy in the form of an
electromagnetic wave or of subatomic particles, in order to obtain a more stable state. We
can find natural and artificial sources of radioactivity.

Natural sources: natural radioactivity comes from
isotopes present in nature. These isotopes have

unstable nuclei which will emit radiation.
Nuclei are not static, they are always moving. If they
move too fast, they can become unstable. These
isotopes can decay into other elements or isotopes
to become stable, through a nuclear reaction.

Artificial sources: they are created mainly by using electricity. A charged particle
is accelerated through a device with a differential voltage (dV). This potential
difference exerts a force on the electron, causing it to be accelerated. Its velocity
increases a lot, and it’s released through one of the plates, allowing it to escape. This
newly accelerated particle can now interact with matter. In this way, X-rays are
formed. Artificial sources can be switched off, stopping the x-ray emission.

WAVE-PARTICLE DUALITY
Particles and waves are different perspectives of a single entity, which sometimes
manifests itself as a particle and others as a wave. They don’t exist in an independent
manner. This is referred to as wave-particle duality.
Radioactivity can be produced from a source of waves or particles.

PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT
The energy of EM radiation waves travels in small packets of energy, particles known as
photons. The energy per photon is determined by the frequency of the radiation:
If the frequency of the incident wave is higher than a threshold value (E ion), then there
are electrons that are ejected from the metal. This phenomenon is called the
photo-electric effect . In other words, if the incident radiation has a frequency inferior to the
threshold, electrons are not emitted whatever the intensity of
the wave. However, above the threshold frequency, the
greater the intensity, the more electrons are dislodged. If,
on the other hand, we increase the frequency of the
radiation, the more kinetic energy in the ejected electrons.
Conclusion : when we increase the intensity of the wave, we modify the number of photons
which reach the target, NOT the energy of the photons (which remains unchanged). The
final kinetic energy will remain the same, but more electrons will be dislodged (Increasing the
intensity means more bonds are broken within tissue when the electrons reach the patient).
If, on the other hand, we increase the frequency and therefore the energy of the incident
photons, the kinetic energy will increase but the number of electrons will remain the same.
Radiation that can dislodge electrons, and therefore ionize atoms, is referred to as
ionizing radiation. By exclusion, all other types of radiation are non-ionizing. In the case of
the EM spectrum, the transition between ionizing and non-ionizing occurs in the UV region.

Radiation that has energy of over 10 eV per photon is considered to be ionizing
radiation. Ultraviolet light, X rays, and γ rays are ionizing.
Radiation that has energy under 10 eV: visible light, infrared, microwaves, and radio
waves are therefore non-ionizing.

TYPES OF IONIZING RADIATION
Ionizing radiation can come from the nuclei of certain chemical elements that emit it
naturally, or it can be generated artificially, by accelerating charged particles until they
acquire high energy or by generating photons with high ionizing power.
Focusing on natural sources of ionizing radiation, there are 3 types:
[PDF p. 9]

α radiation: radioactive process in which an unstable nucleus decays into a more

stable state, releasing a Helium nucleus (alpha-particle). In this process, E is
released and conserved : the initial nucleus delivers energy to the resulting nucleus
and the alpha particle (energy along with electrical charge are conserved). Most of
the E is transferred to the helium nucleus.
In all the different radioactive alpha decays, the energy delivered to each alpha
particle is the same. It’s therefore a monoenergetic process: all the particles have
the same energy. This is what is known as monoenergetic radiation (this also
occurs in a gamma process).

γ radiation: a nucleus oscillates, and during this oscillation it releases energy in the

form of photons and in a monoenergetic way. The original nuclei had “excess”
energy that has been released in the form of EM radiation (we can imagine that the
nucleons were at a level of energy higher than some baseline level, and that they
have undergone de-excitation).
The initial nucleus is said to be in a metastable situation. The different states
constitute isomers of the element.
If photons of the same energy are created in other ways , from artificial
sources ,  they are referred to as X rays.

β radiation: we refer to “beta -” radiation as beta radiation. This type of radiation is

composed of electrons deriving from the nucleus, which arise from the
disintegration of a neutron into a proton.
In this type of radiation, the emitted electrons are not found to be monoenergetic; the
electron will sometimes receive more or less energy. Their energy can have any
value between zero and a maximum value: there is a continuous spectrum of
energy, because any intermediate value can exist. Therefore, this type of radiation
is polyenergetic. The total energy released will be an average of all the energies.
[PDF p. 10]
How come the process isn’t monoenergetic?
This non-monoenergetic characteristic cannot be explained by a reaction in which an
electron is the only product. To explain it, Pauli postulated that another particle (one
with neutral charge and little mass) was created. This particle was called a neutrino,
which is now referred to as electron antineutrino.
β + radiation is a process very similar to β- radiation. But in this case, an electron
antiparticle is emitted, known as a positron. It’s identical to an electron, but with an
opposite charge (+). The positron has become important in a method of diagnosis in
medicine, the positron emission tomography (PET scan).
[PDF p. 11]

- **Beta - :** neutron decays into proton + electron + antineutrino

MONOENERGETIC AND POLYENERGETIC RADIATIONS
Alpha and gamma radiations are monoenergetic
processes. For a large set of atoms, all the
different ones will decay producing the same
amount of energy.
Beta processes on the other hand are polyenergetic
(continuous spectrum): if we have a set of n atoms and we
compare the energy of a beta particle for 2 different
radioactive decays, the energy released will be different
for beta 1 particle than for beta 2.
Alpha and gamma particle histograms present a sharp distribution.
Beta particle histogram presents a broad distribution of energies. We can determine an

A radioactive disintegration is a stochastic process, meaning that it’s impossible to predict
the behaviour of a single nuclide. We don’t know when it’s going to disintegrate. But we do
know that the probability of disintegration must be the same for all the nuclides of the
same isotope. The evolution of the number of atoms which remain follows an exponential
decay.
If we have a sample with N 0 nuclides, then the number of nuclei
that have not disintegrated N(t) after time t will be given by:
This exponential curve is determined by the decay constant λ (which
is specific to each element) or by the mean lifetime (TAU) τ0 = 1/ λ, which corresponds to
the inverse value of the decay constant.

Mean lifetime ( τ0) : The mean lifetime represents the time at which the number of
nuclides which haven’t disintegrated is N 0 /e (in other words, 37% ). It can also be
interpreted as the mean of the survival times of the nuclides of the sample. It varies

- Half-life (t ½ ): It’s NOT the same as the mean lifetime. For this big group of atoms,
we can determine the half life, which represents the time it will take for half of the

Knowing the Activity, we can know the energy released per second

CHARGED PARTICLES

When charged particles penetrate a material, they find themselves surrounded by other
particles that are also charged. Therefore, they experience Coulomb-forces.
A charged particle that interacts with matter can lose energy through 3 process:


Emitting photons: on interacting with other charged particles, the trajectory changes
(the particle is deviated) and photons are emitted. Bremsstrahlung interactions.


Collisions with electrons, knocking them out of their orbit.


Collisions with atomic nuclei.


An electron is very small and has very little mass
(light particle) , and so it is very probable that in these
interactions it will deviate appreciably from its
trajectory, while the trajectory of protons or alpha
particles (heavy particles) with which it collides will
hardly be modified.
The penetration length in the case of interaction with
charged particles is known as range. It represents the
distance that the charged particles can travel.
The result in both cases (electrons and protons) is that each of the incident particles will
generate a cascade of charged particles and photons around the trajectory that the initial
particle has followed.
[PDF p. 18]

In the case of electrons : all three types of process occur (the most likely ones
being bremsstrahlung and electron-collision). As soon as an electron enters into
matter, it is affected by other particles and will interact with them, deviating from its
trajectory and releasing part of its energy to generate photons and new electrons.
The photons and new electrons will continue interacting, deviating and in turn giving
up more energy to generate even more photons and electrons until the remaining
photons and electrons can no longer ionize more atoms. Finally, the remaining
energy will be deposited as heat. We observe a whole cascade of electrons.
The energy is deposited in a more or less droplet-shaped volume around the initial
trajectory of the electron: the energy is dispersed.

- In the case of protons: the most common interaction is Coulomb interaction with
electrons. The procedure is similar in the case of protons, but in this case the energy
is deposited along the length of the initial trajectory. Protons do not deviate from
the initial trajectory and do not disperse in the same way.

Stochastic e�ects: a stochastic effect is a random effect that appears for lower doses

of radiation, where an increase of dose brings about an increase in the probability
of the effect occurring, but not an increase in the seriousness of the effect. The
seriousness of the effect will be independent of the dose.
This is the case of a DNA mutation induced by radiation. Stochastic effects are
purely probabilistic, and have no threshold.

Deterministic e�ects: a deterministic effect is that in which the seriousness

increases with the number of incident particles. An example is erythema, which
can appear on the skin with radiotherapy treatment, or sun burns. Deterministic
effects appear for higher doses. Increasing the dose increases the seriousness of

As said, the absorbed dose considers only the physics of the process, and is measured in

Radiology is a medical specialty, which deals with generating images of the inside of the
body employing different techniques. These images are read and interpreted by radiologists,
for diagnosis and treatment of disease (although to a lesser extent)
History
X-rays were discovered by W.C. Roentgen in 1895, for which he received a
nobel prize.
On the 8th of November, 1895, his wife put her hand under the machine he
was working on, revealing the first X-ray (Bertha’s hand). It was the first
time a part of a human body was able to be seen through imaging.
Since then, radiology has hugely evolved, and we can now evaluate bone,
vasculature, organs,.. through many imaging techniques. We can see what
is going on inside a patient non-invasively.
Generation of X-rays
For conventional X-ray, we use an X-ray tube to
form the rays.

Phase 1: Generation of electrons: after generating an induced current in the X-ray
tube, we can accelerate electrons by using a differential potential.
Phase 2: Displacement of electrons: The cathode emits electrons into the vacuum
and the anode collects them, establishing a flow of electrical current through the tube
(known as beam). A high differential potential will accelerate the electrons, which

collide with the anode material.
Phase 3: Generation of photons: the photons generated by the impact of electrons
on the anode will produce the x-ray beam. They escape through a small window
(used to cause a unique direction) and impact on the area of interest, in this case, the
human body. The rest of the X-ray beam which doesn’t escape through the window is
absorbed by the metal housing surrounding the device.

Area of radiology which uses X-rays to obtain images through a

KEY CONCEPTS. kV and mAs
- kV: Kilovolts = measures the amount of differential voltage present in the x-ray tube.
Differential voltage is what will accelerate electrons going from the cathode to the
anode. Therefore: ↑kV = ↑differential potential = ↑kinetic energy (velocity) = ↑ energy
electron that are going to transmit their energy to the anode = ↑ energy photons
In conclusion, increasing kV increases the energy of the x-ray beam photons.
It also affects intensity, but the main effect we focus on for kV is the effect on energy.
It’s the only variable which will affect the energy of the beam.
-
mAs: milliampere second = measure of radiation produced (milliampere) over a set
amount of time (seconds) via an x-ray tube, at a given kV.
mA = tube current; mAs = radiation released per second.
Increasing mAs means an increase in intensity but NOT in energy
An increase in tube current (mA) results in a higher production of electrons that
are inside the x-ray tube which will, therefore, increase the quantity of x-radiation.
We release more photons, but they have the same energy as kV remains
unchanged.
↑ kV = increase in x-ray photons energy
↑ mA = increase in current = increase in the number of e- released = higher intensity beam
(more photons), but NOT higher energy
In relation to contrast and noise (image quality):
↑ kV = decrease in contrast (structures will appear darker), but more penetration
↓ kV = higher contrast (structures will appear whiter), more differential absorption
↑ mA = decrease in noise, better quality
Image 1: kV too low, too much contrast between tissues and little penetration
Image 2: kV is increased to improve penetration. But now kV is too high (high photon energy,
little absorption and much penetration. Photons with low energy are more absorbed)
Image 3: modify mAs to correct image density. Reduces amount of radiation
(milliamperes/second ↓) and corrects image quality.

Computed tomography (CT)
Radiology workshop II
Lesion in back of right lower lung:
Issues with X-ray can be resolved by using CT scans. It’s
the imaging modality of choice to detect cancer and
neoplasms, to asses cancer development,… but also
when you suspect patient with pneumonia, with abdominal
infection, to asses the heart, … 80% of CTs are used for
cancer patients but it can be used for many other purposes.
It’s a very fast imaging technique, very available and not
expensive .
The big problem with CT is the amount of radiation.
HISTORY
CT scanners were first introduced in 1971 by Godfrey N. Hounsfield . The objective was to
create a three dimensional image of an object, taking multiple measurements of it with
X-rays from different angles and using a computer to reconstruct the image from hundreds of
overlapping, intersecting planes.
Initially, to obtain 1 slice it took 7 minutes. Nowadays, 1 slice can be acquired in 0.3
seconds, and reconstructed structures in 5 seconds.
PRINCIPLES OF CT
CT is a diagnostic imaging procedure that uses X-rays to acquire cross-sectional
“slices” of the body. These cross-sections are reconstructed to recreate a 3D
image of the studied object. As it’s mainly acquired in an axial plane, it’s also known
as CAT scan.
The CT X-ray tube emits a beam of
X-rays/photons that goes through the patient
and passes through detectors which record the
intensity of attenuated radiation and convert it
into an electrical signal. This is processed on a
computer where the signal is transformed into a
grayscale image in which brightness is
proportional to the density (in UH).
As we are taking images from different angles, the tube is rotating around the patient where
beam and detector move in synchrony.
The slice is made up of small volumetric elements that represent
attenuation, called voxels (3D). When these elements are placed on
a plane (2D), they become pixels.
[PDF p. 28]
The units used to measure the density within the pixel are the Hounsfield units, which
range from values of -1000 to +3000. Each pixel is assigned a shade of grey based on its
attenuation value.
However, the human eye can distinguish only 30-40 gray values. Therefore, the target
range of HU needs to be adapted to our eye by establishing
specific windows.
In conclusion, CT allows us to detect where things are, and
characterize them according to density by using Hounsfield
units.
Grayscale:
Black structures (- dense) and white structures (+ dense).
The densities are determined within the gray scale. The 0 value corresponds to water, and
-1000 to air . Dense structures appear white (such as bone), whereas air and fat appear
black or grey.
When we look at the picture, we can ask the machine to reconstruct the image by either
using a soft tissue window or a lung window. We normally order 2 CT scans with two
centered areas of interest: lung and soft tissue. Each window allows us to differentiate
specific structures (same image acquisition, but different image reconstruction afterwards).

Soft tissue windows allow us to observe and assess soft tissue

(bone=white; muscle=gray; fat= darker gray). Soft tissues can be
observed nicely, but lungs are seen as completely black. We cannot
assess air or lung parenchyma. This reconstruction can be used to
evaluate the chest and abdomen, but not the lungs.

Lung window can be used to assess the lung parenchyma. We
can clearly observe the inside of the lungs, but we cannot

differentiate other structures. In CT we can also observe metal
density, by using iodine contrast injected through the vein, to look at
blood vessels and lung parenchyma.

moves at the same time, with 4 detectors placed
within the machine. The bid advantage is that it
allows us to acquire images faster as it covers
more surface in less time.
Spiral, helical: rotation and
movement of the patient
occur at the same time
Dual-source: 2 tubes are
found emitting radiation.
Fastest CT on the market.
Specially good for
observing and assessing

Dual source imaging, also known as spectral imaging, allows us to
differentiate the structures depending on x-ray uptake. It can be done using
contrast or not. It uses two separate x-ray photon energy spectra, allowing
the interrogation of materials that have different attenuation properties at
different energies .It allows to differentiate, for example, urinary stones
depending on energy uptake. We can tell if the stone has to be removed, or if
it can be dissolved with medication and no need for invasive surgery.

Factors that affect image quality

Radiation

Spatial resolution


Noise


Artifacts


Concepts

Kilovoltaje (kV)

Represents photon energy.
It reflects the energy in our image based on penetration capacity.


More kV = more radiation. By increasing kV, more energy is used to obtain high
quality imaging


Less kV = less radiation. Structures absorb radiation but we get image noise (grainy)


Miliampere seconds (mAs)


Represents the amount of photons released per second (intensity).
- More mAs = more radiation, but implies there is less noise
The throwback of using high Kv and mAs is the high radiation dose.
Factors affecting image quality
1. Spatial resolution
The ability to obtain small details with high contrast. It’s
influenced by system geometry, and determines image
definition.
[PDF p. 30]
Factors influencing spatial resolution:
➢ Slice thickness: the thinner the image, the
more anatomical imaging (high spatial
resolution), but higher noise. Therefore, the
thinner the slices, the better quality in terms of
anatomical detail, but this is accompanied by
increased noise.
To evaluate something small and specific = thinner slices ( 0.6 mm)
To evaluate more big and general structures = 1-2 mm slices
➢ Pitch: if a patient goes through the CT machine too fast, the detail can
decrease. Therefore, the choice of pitch affects both image quality and
radiation dose.
P = 1.0, x-ray beams are contiguous for adjacent
rotations
P>1.0, x-ray beams are not contiguous for adjacent
rotations (gaps in the x-ray helix)
P<1.0, x-ray beams overlap (a volume of tissue is
irradiated more than once per scan)
If we want detailed acquisition, the patient must go through very slowly; If we
want fast acquisition (emergency), we have to sacrifice some of the detail.
➢ Resolution : reconstruction filters / reconstruction algorithms to increase
resolution
2. Noise (ALARA principle)
Factors influencing noise
➢ Slice thickness and reconstruction filters
➢ Body size: the noise level doubles every 8cm of increase in the patient’s
diameter.
➢ kV and mAs: noise can be modified by increasing or decreasing radiation.
      - The **higher the radiation** dose, the **less noise** and better image

quality (when dose is doubled, the noise is reduced to a factor of ¼ )
- The lower the radiation dose, the higher the noise.
[PDF p. 31]
3. Artifacts: can interfere with X-ray absorption and affect image quality.
- Motion, breathing,… In this image, the data needed to
reconstruct each image has changed position due to patient
movement.
- Metals: the presence of metals such as gold produces
streak artifacts, as metals absorb radiation almost completely.
RADIATION DOSE
The radiation dose has to be carefully evaluated. The younger the patient, the more
susceptible to amounts of radiation.
We need to use the least amount of radiation possible. This is
done by following the ALARA principle, taking into account Kv
and mAs.
The effects of radiation the patient receives depend on:

Absorbed radiation (determined by kV, mAs and pitch)
The anatomical region that has been examined (effective dose): each organ has a
characteristic factor, which indicates the probability of malignant radiation effects.

Iodine properties

The basis of the molecular structure is a benzene ring, to which up to 3

iodine atoms can be attached

They make the molecule opaque = it increases the structure’s attenuation =
whiter (as a reminder: attenuation is the reduction of the intensity of an x-ray
beam as it traverses matter. The reduction is caused by absorption)

The higher the iodine, higher opacity = higher the enhancement of the tissue.

Compounds attached to C1, C3 and C5 of the contrast molecule modify its
properties such as solubility, osmolarity and viscosity
Its absorption occurs in seconds .

Then, it will be excreted. Depending on the radicals found in position R5, it will be
excreted in one way or another:
- **Organic compound** = through the **kidneys**

- **H atom** = through **bile**


Iodine can be cleared through the kidneys. If they are not working
properly, the contrast will remain within the body, and this can be
detected on the CT. If we wait some time, we can assess how the

kidneys are excreting the contrast.
Pharmacokinetics of iodinated contrast media

Injected intravenously, they bind to plasma albumin and are distributed
throughout the body following the circulatory system

They reach the peak of plasma concentration within seconds of their injection
Contrast media diffuse into the extravascular space, reaching the interstitial space
through the pores of the endothelium

They do not enter cells (except hepatocytes) and have a 2-hour half life
Elimination : as we mentioned, will occur though one secretion or another depending

on radical 5
- Unchanged via the **kidney** (by glomerular filtration). At 24 h after

administration, 90% of the administered dose has been eliminated
- To a lesser extent **biliary excretion**, which increases if there is renal failure

RADIOBIOLOGY
Ionizing radiation is a type of radiation with high enough energy to ionize matter, extracting
electrons. Can come from natural sources or be created artificially (X-rays).
Radiobiology studies the interaction of this radiation with matter and its effects.
Radiological magnitudes and units
Traditional system: röntgen, rad, rem

International system units: Coulomb/kg, Gray (Gy), Sievert (Sv). International
agreement, created with the purpose of structuring a system as universal and as
suitable as possible for the different measurements

Absorbed dose: measured in in Gray (Gy)
Equivalent dose: Sieverts (Sv)
Effective dose: measured in Sv or mSv.
Natural background radiation
It varies depending on the area we live in. We will receive more or less radiation. The
average person in the US receives an effective dose of 3 mSv per year from natural
radiation.
Artificial radiation
20% of the total radiation we receive comes from artificial radiation
(radiological examinations, nuclear escapes,…). Nowadays, the most important
source of artificial radiation (produced by humans) is medical diagnostic
equipment. Each radiological imaging technique requires more or less radiation
dose.
[PDF p. 38]
Since being discovered, it has been observed that X-rays (ionizing radiation)
can produce harmful effects on health. Ionizing radiation has many beneficial
applications, but can have harmful effects.
Biological e�ects of radiation
Biological effects derive from radiation damage to DNA. DNA contains all the information for
growth and control, and is transmitted from cell to cell during replication. Damage to it will
therefore also be transmitted.
Radiation can directly affect DNA, inciding on it and breaking it, or indirectly.
- Direct: effect on DNA molecules (target molecule)
- Indirect: effect on other molecules that form free radicals (ionization of H 2 O=HO+H)
The main action of radiation on the human body (80% composed of water) is considered
to be indirect .
Effects according to the affected cells:

Somatic

Hereditary (coming from damage to reproductive cells)
Effects according to the cause-effect relationship:


Stochastic (probabilistic)


Deterministic


Deterministic e�ects
They are produced by the death of
many cells in a tissue or organ.

The severity of the effect

increases with radiation dose.

There is a threshold dose for the

effect to occur

Deterministic effects occur after

exposure to relatively high doses
of radiation.
Acute radiation syndrome
Periods of the syndrome: prodromal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) → Latency (days-weeks)
→ Overt disease
Stochastic e�ects


Consequence of sublethal damage (chromosomal mutation) in one / few cells:

Germ cells: inherited genetic disorders
Somatic cells: development of a cancer



The probability of their occurrence, but not the severity, increases with dose


Severity doesn’t depend on the dose. Just one disruption of DNA is inherited by
dividing cells and the damage propagates. Therefore, children are more prone to
stochastic effects, as their cells are continuously proliferating and growing. Tumor
arises. Theoretically, a child with cancer who has to be diagnosed through CT and
radiological systems, after the initial cancer disappears, can then manifest cancer in
adulthood due to this stochastic effect (mutations produced and accumulated during
rutinary cancer check ups during the childhood cancer).
[PDF p. 39]

There is no threshold for stochastic effects. Can occur by just one disruption
Stochastic effects occur after exposure to moderate-low doses.
The main somatic stochastic effect induced by ionizing radiation is the increase in

Special caution should be taken in children and women at child-bearing age.

Nuclear medicine. PET I
“Nuclear medicine is a medical imaging specialty that uses small amounts of radioactive
material ( radiopharmaceutical ) to diagnose or to treat many diseases”
Radiology is destined to detect changes in size and anatomy;
Nuclear medicine focuses on metabolic changes and receptors,
etc.
It allows detection but has the disadvantage of being less
accurate. Therefore, it has to be complemented with other tests,
for example a CT scan, to observe the anatomical image.
PET and CT are fused to clearly define and precisely localize

RADIOPHARMACEUTICAL
The main difference with other techniques is that, in nuclear
medicine, we are using a drug and an isotope to create an
image. The drug determines the biological behaviour
(targets the site), and the radioisotope determines the
physical characteristics and allows the detection of the drug
(acts as a flashlight) . We detect the emission of radioactivity.

Radioisotopes: Isotopes can be stable, unstable or
radioisotopes: their nuclei emit energy in the form of ionizing radiation while
searching for a more stable configuration.

SOURCE OF RADIATION
In radiology (X-rays), radiation has its origin in the atomic shell
due to the deceleration of high velocity electrons when they collide
and interact with target material.
In nuclear medicine, the radiation comes from radioactivity, from
the disintegration of the nucleus accompanied by the emission
of radiation, as opposed to X-rays.
KINDS OF IONIZING RADIATION
Alpha radiation


Beta radiation


Gamma radiation


[PDF p. 41]
If it were necessary to detect a spinal lesion, we would select a radiopharmaceutical which
emits gamma, due to its greater penetration.
Any high amount of these radiations can be potentially dangerous for the patient, causing
irreversible DNA damage. Alpha-radiation can be stopped by paper sheets, beta by
aluminium foil and gamma by lead.
We need to use an emission strong enough to penetrate the structures of interest.
Radiopharmaceuticals are used in 2 situations: treatment and
diagnosis.
Therapy: alpha and beta
Diagnosis: gamma or positron-emission (beta +).
Gammacamera or SPECT are both gamma emitters.
We can find 3 different types of equipment in nuclear medicine:
GammaCamera (scintigraphy)
- SPECT or SPECT/CT
- PET or PET/CT
GammaCamera and SPECT/CT are both based on
gamma emission; PET is based on positron emission.
GAMMACAMERA (SCINTIGRAPHY)
We perform a planar study, which is enough to observe any
pathological uptake. To localize it better, we have to use SPECT
study, which observes the patient’s 3 axes.
Example: we see a spot on the vertebrae. But depending on the
location within the vertebrae, it will have one interpretation or
another. Metastatic or benign. To locate it, we use SPECT or
SPECT/CT (which allows the fusion of both images) to define and
localize the uptake.
Usually, first we do a planar study, and if an
abnormal uptake is observed, we perform a
SPECT/CT to further and better localize the
spot.

BONE SCINTIGRAPHY

Studies are usually performed to detect any osteo malignancies.
The radioisotopes used are Diphosphonates (MDP)+Technetium (99m) .
Diphosphonates are absorbed by the surface of the bone in proportion
to local bone vascularization and osteoblastic activity.
We know there is an association between uptake and bone vascularization and remodeling;
most pathological bone conditions (infectious, traumatic, neoplastic…) are associated
with an increase in vascularization and bone remodeling . In this way, we will be able to
detect benign or metastatic tumors.
Normal distribution
There is physiological increased uptake in
joints, sternum and spine (ex: in the
sacro-ileac joints, due to the continuous
remodeling of this area), but also in the
bladder and kidneys.
Clinical context examples:

THYROID SCINTIGRAPHY

For thyroid scintigraphy there is no need for a drug;
we only use the radioisotope, as isotopes such as iodine
incorporate naturally into the thyroid gland. This is
because iodine is involved in thyroid hormonogenesis.
Radioiodine follows normal iodine metabolism in the
thyroid gland.
It is introduced in the patient and used to detect:

size of the gland

- localization

function (example: a cold node means there is reduced uptake of iodine =
decreased function)

[PDF p. 43]
In addition, iodine has an interesting feature: it emits
both gamma and beta particles. Therefore, it can be
used for diagnosis, but also as treatment.
It can be used as Thyroid cancer Therapy. The beta
emission can destroy tumor cells in the metastatic
regions.

RENAL SCINTIGRAPHY

For renal scintigraphy, we use radiopharmaceuticals such as Technetium-MAG3 and
Technetium-DTPA. We can perform dynamic studies.
In dynamic studies, we acquire a series of images during a time of varying duration (from
seconds to mins). Acquired data are processed and give out activity-time curves, which
describe organ uptake/excretion rates.
Example of left kidney (PA view) dysfunction observed on renal scintigraphy:
We obtain images during 20-30 minutes and perform an image every 2 minutes. In the end
we are left with images which reflect the dynamic distribution of the radioisotope,
depending on its uptake/elimination rates.

MYOCARDIAL PERFUSION SCINTIGRAPHY

For this type of scintigraphy, we use radioisotope Technetium-MIBI.
With a myocardial perfusion, we can detect
blocked coronary arteries which supply blood to
the heart: in normal/resting conditions the heart
works fine; but while performing high activity,

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
MRI relies on the existence of a magnetic field, which is aligned with the orientation of the
patient (depending on the company, aligned from head to feet or feet to head). We are able
to recover 3D images of specific organs of the body, or even localize active regions of
the brain of the patient.
(TED TALK: human brain mapping and brain decoding)
WHAT IS A MAGNETIC FIELD?
We have a magnetic field (B), which consists in a manifestation of
the presence of electrical particles in movement.
1. What is its e�ect on electric particles?
The only particles that can interact with a magnetic field are moving charged particles (+ or
-), which have a velocity different than 0.
These particles will suffer from a force whose origin is the magnetic field, which will have an
effect on the particle’s trajectory. This force, known as Lorentz force, appears ONLY for
moving particles.
The behaviour of this force is quite peculiar: if we have an
electric field, the force equals the electric field times the
charge. However with magnetic fields, the Lorentz force is
proportional to the charge, but also to the velocity and to
the magnetic field. The velocity plays a role in the generation
of the field. If v= 0, it won’t be generated. Magnetic behaviour
is more complex than electric behaviour.
In the case of the magnetic field, the force will be perpendicular to the velocity and
magnetic field, and its orientation will depend on the orientation of the magnetic field,
the direction in which the particle travels (v) and the charge of the particle.
As the force is perpendicular to velocity, it will not provide energy to the particle.
Therefore it won’t modify its kinetic energy. Its only effect is to deviate the trajectory of the
particle. This is opposed to the electric field, where the force can modify Ek.
Lorentz force:
From this equation we can obtain the unit for the magnetic field, which is the Tesla (T).
1 Tesla = 10^4 Gauss (G).
[PDF p. 52]
The Earth’s magnetic field is 0.5 Gauss, quite small. There are magnetic resonance systems
of over 1-1.5 Teslas. The limit value used in medical application in the EU is 3 Teslas (for
clinical use). For research, they can be over these values, but not in clinical practice. 0.1 T is
the typical magnetic force we will find on the surface of a potent permanent magnet.
2.
How can we generate this magnetic field?
The magnetic field appears surrounding an electric charge in movement. The
appearance of any magnetic field is based on the displacement of these charged moving
particles.
In this example, a positive particle is moving along
the Y axis with a velocity “v”. As soon as it starts
moving, a magnetic field appears around the
moving particle. The field has the shape of
concentric circles which are found on a plane
perpendicular to the direction of the particle’s
velocity.
But this is in the case of a single charge.
If we take a large amount of charges and place them in a ring, each of these
single particles will generate a small magnetic field. When we combine all
of them, we obtain the second diagram (cross section): the final magnetic field
we get for a circular ring will be pointing upwards within the surface, crossing
the surface of the ring and moving outwards.
The final result is there is a region in which the magnetic field lines leave
the circle (north pole) and another in which they are entering (south
pole). This is a magnetic dipole (N and S), the most simple
configuration of a magnetic field. North and south poles cannot be
created in an isolated way. This configuration is important as at the
subatomic level, we observe this behaviour.
At a subatomic level:

in each electron orbital, the oscillating electrons are rotating,
creating a magnetic dipole.
the protons inside the nucleus aren’t stationary, but also rotating.

Both systems will generate their own magnetic field. Because of the displacement of
these charges, there will be an interaction with an external magnetic field.
Can we suppose the magnetic field has no effect on a person? NO. There is interaction
when we apply a magnetic field on a patient, due to the spin of these charged particles that
make up the molecules we are created by.
[PDF p. 53]
3.
How does the magnetic field interact with matter?
Response of the dipole to an external magnetic field: all the dipoles will be aligned with
the external magnetic field.
Green arrow: external magnetic field
Two dipoles placed within this external
magnetic field. Charges are leaving and
penetrating the screen.
What is the effect of this external
magnetic field?
In both 1st and 2nd dipole, the Lorentz
forces acting on the charges are
different directions, but same value.
Therefore, there is no displacement.
The only effect the magnetic field can have is to reorient the dipole through rotation.
There are two possibilities of reorientation:

Parallele orientaion, N pointing upwards, S pointing downwards, in a parallel
orientation in relation to the external field (more stable configuration)
Antiparallel orientation in relation to the field, which is more unstable and requires
additional energy.

Naturally, the magnetic field tries to align the north and south poles.This reorientation is
known as magnetization.
TYPES OF MAGNETIZATION
Depending on the material, there are different types of magnetization and orientations.


Ferromagnetic: if we apply an external magnetic field, we induce a global
magnetization. There is a significant degree of magnetization, which remains
when the external field is removed: the dipoles will retain magnetization and
remain oriented. Seen in materials such as iron and niquel.


Paramagnetic: in this case, magnetization is very weak. The dipoles in the
material will align, but when the external magnetic field is removed, the
magnetization disappears. The dipoles disorganize and do not remain oriented.


Seen in the case of O2 and aluminium.

Diamagnetic: When we apply a magnetic field, the system responds in a way that
acts in the opposite way. There is a resistance to being oriented. The dipoles are
found pointing in the opposite direction to the magnetic field. Observed on living

materials.
Any material interacts with magnetic fields, in one way or another. The normal interaction
seen in the human body is the diamagnetic magnetization/behaviour.
[PDF p. 54]
REAL MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
In real life, precession moment appears due to rotation: the system doesn’t follow its
original trajectory.
In the previous diagram: if the rotation of the particles is relevant, as is the case light
particles, this rotation (omega) is not “correct”, meaning that the trajectory indicated
isn’t correct.
What would be the real effect of the magnetic force when this system is rotating?
Image shows the classical point of view of the behaviour of a proton (without spin) .
Protons have a property known as spin, which is originally placed in an antiparallel way.
When submitted to a magnetic field, the proton creates a magnetic field in the sense of
the spin, found in an antiparallel fashion, which will try to obtain the more stable
orientation by transitioning to the parallel conformation.

If there were no spin, the expected result would be to follow the classical trajectory

shown.

However, due to rotation, it will orient into the parallel direction following a
helicoidal/spiral transition towards said orientation.
This spiral movement is accompanied by the emission of an EM wave, generated
because of the displacement of the protons when transitioning from antiparallel to
parallel orientation.

[PDF p. 55]
If this were the only action of the MRI device, after being introduced into the field, all the
dipoles would be oriented and nothing would happen. There is a sequence of different
processes generated by the system, whih will allow us to retrive an image.


Patient is introduced into the system, into the magnetic field. All the dipoles will
be pointing in a parallel way to the magnetic field.


Excitation . We will start applying a sequence of stimulus: first, we will send energy
in the form of an EM wave, which has an energy of the magnitude of a
radiowave/microwave (low frequency). The protons will absorb the energy and
reorient in the opposite, unstable configuration due to excitation.


We then let the system relax. When retrieving the stimulus, the system will tend to
return to its stable configuration. This is done through that spiral/helicoidal
transition mentioned earlier, which is accompanied by the emission of EM waves
that are detected by the system.
This sequence is carried out repeatedly, which is what gives out the MRI image


based on the emision.
The spiral movement generates an EM wave with a frequency that depends on the electric
dipole. This frequency is different for the different protons found in specific substances in
the body.

It depends on the type of particle. Each particle will have its own specific magnetic
dipole.
Also depends on the local value of the magnetic field. Depending on what the
surrounding molecules are, the local magnetic field will be different.

MRI mainly measures protons (hydrogen, H+) and their dipole’s emission. Therefore, the
most important echo will come from water, a very abundant molecule inside the human
body.
Other techniques can measure other nuclei, but
only those with an odd number of nucleons (for
example, O16 will not be detected by MRI as it
won’t interact with the EM field, due to lack of spin).
[PDF p. 56]
COMPONENTS OF DIPOLE BEHAVIOUR
We can split the behaviour of the dipole into 2 parts:


Longitudial magnetization : the part that is parallel to the
external magnetic field is known as the longitudinal
magnetization. Longitudinal magnetization increases in time
(asintotical increase).
T1 corresponds to the time by which 0.67 of the spin has
returned to the longitudinal magnetization value.


Transverse magnetization: the behaviour of the component perpendicular to the
external field is known as the transverse magnetization. For the transverse
movement, there is a decrease of magnetization in time.
T2 corresponds to the time you have to wait for the 0.37 transverse component to
have transitioned nto the parallel orientation.


On an MRI device, we measure T1 and T2. Depending on the
material, T1 and T2 will be different.

They can be very large, as is the case of water
(meaning it takes a long time to rearrange the dipoles).
However, in solids this reorientation is done really fast,
meaning T1 and T2 are very low.
Due to many studies, we can determine which tissue is being
detected depending on the obtained T1 and T2 for each
region, and therefore, this will allow us to classify the
structures in the image.

We have to be aware of metallic components, as this can imply mechanical and
