The key point for the device to work is that we absorb EM waves. This means that

(represents the energy absorbed by the body of the patient. Measures the ability to

MRI basics
WHAT IS MRI?
MRI is an imaging method based on the nuclear resonance phenomenon.
It obtains sectional images, in any plane, using a very strong magnetic
field, gradients and radiofrequency pulses.
The machine detector is similar to CT, but longer and more tube-like.
Advantages:

It doesn’t use ionizing radiation. Therefore, there is no cancer risk.

It can obtain anatomical, functional and other information.

It achieves very high contrast between different tissues, while in
CT, as it is based on density, when tissues with similar density are
close together they’re difficult to differentiate.

ELEMENTS

Magnet

The magnet creates a magnetic field. Its power is measured in Teslas (T, in IS) or Gauss.
1 T = 10000 G. Nowadays, the vast majority of equipment is 1.5 - 3 T.
The magnet never turns off : whenever we enter the room, we must chek we’re not wearing
ferromagnetic material.
According to quantum mechanics, each element of an atom has an angular momentum
called “spin.” For us to understand it, it is usually compared to a sphere rotating on an axis.
Every electric charge in motion (in this case spinning ) causes a magnetic field.
MRI is based on hydrogen atoms, as they interact with the magnetic field (uneven number
of protons) and there are many H atoms in our body (found in water).
Function of the magnet:


Under normal conditions, each atom is oriented randomly in parallel or antiparallel
ways and the total magnetic moment is 0.


Under a very strong magnetic field (referred as B 0 ), the
hydrogen atoms will align themselves in a parallel
or antiparallel direction to the field (this will only affect
atoms with an uneven number of protons, as they will
have an electrical charge).


There are always slightly more atoms in parallel,
making the neat magnetic moment (M) is different
from 0. This magnetic moment is what we will modify in
order to obtain a signal and create an image
[PDF p. 58]
We send a low frequency wave to induce the antiparallel state in all
of the dipoles.
Once the excitatory stimulus is removed, the particle will tend to
return to its stable state. This is done through the process of
precession (spiral/helicoidal transition). It precesses at a
constant angular velocity (omega) which is known as Larmor
frequency.
This Larmor frequency depends on the constant γ, which is specific for each atom;
and depends on B, the static magnetic field. Each material = specific Larmor frequency
Radiofrequency (B1)
When additional energy in the form of a radio wav e is added to the magnetic field, the
magnetic vector (M) is deflected.
The radio wave frequency/ radiofrequency (RF) that causes the hydrogen nuclei to resonate
is dependent on the element sought (hydrogen the case of MRI) and the strength of the
magnetic field (B = Larmor’s frequency).
Due to the phenomenon of magnetic resonance, RF is “absorbed” by the hydrogen atom,
altering its state to another of higher energy, flipping the M angle.
When the RF stops, the atoms return to their initial state, emitting that extra energy as RF
that provides us the signal for the image.
Initially, there is no magnetic moment in the transverse (Y) plane
(magnetization is purely longitudinal). After radiofrequency is
applied, we modify the spin, finding components in the Z axis and
in the transverse plane. After a certain time, the spins end up
being all oriented in the transverse plane (magnetization is
purely transverse).
But when we retrieve the radiofrequency, the atoms return their
spin to the initial orientation following a spiral transition
(precession), through the emission of a RF wave.
When we stop radiofrequency (precession), T1 relaxation and T2 relaxation both occur at
the same time
[PDF p. 59]
During precession:

T1 or longitudinal relaxation: during precession, we are gaining momentum in
the Z axis, which is measured by T1.
T1 relaxation is the process by which the net magnetization (M) grows/returns to
its initial maximum value (M0), parallel to B0.
T1 = can be viewed as the time required for the z component of M to reach 63% of its

maximum value.
During this process, there is transfer of energy from the spins to nearby molecules,
while they go back to the Z axis.

T2 or transverse relaxation: during precession, components in the transverse
plane lose momentum and decrease until reaching 0, measured by T2.
Therefore, T2 relaxation is the process by which the transverse components of
magnetization (Mxy) decay or dephase.
T2= i s defined as the time required for the transverse magnetization to fall to
approximately 37% (1/e) of its initial value.
Spins dephase and begin to desynchronize, losing overall signal.

Each tissue, depending on its composition, has different T1 and T2 relaxation times, which
have been previously studied and identified. This allows us to classify tissues and create
an image. Depending on the sequence used, a signal from the same tissue changes
radically. We can attenuate the signal of a tissue to obtain the image of interest.

Gradients

Gradients generate slight alterations in the homogeneous
magnetic field, making the magnetic field intensity at each
point slightly different. In other words, it will make the
waves/energy coming back from each point slightly
different. This will allow the machine to locate in the space
where the signal comes from, and therefore identify and
recreate the structure in the 3D space into an image.
[PDF p. 60]

Antenas or coils

For optimal image quality, the antenna/coil that receives the signal
should be as close as possible to the area to be studied. For this
reason, there are normally multiple antennas, each designed to study
a specific area. The correct use of the antennas and the positioning
of the patient in them is a determining part in the final quality of the
image.
THE SEQUENCES (“SOFTWARE”)
Each tissue behaves differently according to its composition and according to its excitation
and relaxation parameters. We can program “sequences” where we adjust different
parameters to “enhance” specific aspects of the image/tissues.
Main sequence parameters (TR, TE, TI, slice thickness, flip angle,…; no need to know them)
can be modified to obtain more signal from one tissue or another.
Each pixel is assigned a shade of gray based on the intensity of the received signal.
However, the signal intensity depends on the tissue, the equipment and the sequence
used. Therefore, ulike the HU, its value is variable : there is no absolute value for each
tissue, as the signal intensity can be modified depending on the tissue, the energy of the
incident wave and the selected sequence.
● Tissue factors:
    - H1 concentration

    - Relaxation time T1

    - Relaxation time T2

    Dynamic state

● Operational factors:
    - SEQUENCES: TR, TE,

matrix, FoV, flip angle,…
    - Number of excitations

SAFETY
Very safe technique. It does not use ionizing radiation.
Can be performed during pregnancy

It has no known effect on the tissues of the body. No cases have been described
that show that static magnetic fields produce alterations on the structure of DNA,
reproduction and/or cell growth.
The main risk is related to the presence of external metallic/electronic materials,
which can produce the projectile effect, interaction with metal components present.

MRI SAFETY LABELLING
The main risk derived from the static magnetic field is due to its interaction with
ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel and cobalt) and the consequent “projectile effect”.
This also applies to patients with ferromagnetic foreign bodies or transplants.
The production of heat due to RF absorption is also a potential risk. It can cause burns on
the patient. Levels are controlled by SAR limits. SAR levels are estimates of the amount of
energy absorbed by each region of the body, and vary significantly depending on the patient
and the equipment.

Ultrasound waves
MECHANICAL WAVES
A mechanical wave is any wave that can produce a deformation of a material through
contact forces.
The result will be a perturbation on/in the material: some of the atoms will be moved from
the previous position to a new position. In the case of material deformation, the concept of
stress is introduced.
Stress is the force that acts per unit of area on the material. It indicates how intense the
force acting on each atom will be.

When the force is applied perpendicularly, it is said to be normal stress.
When the force acts in parallel to the surface, it is said to be shear stress.
When the stress acts to shorten bonds, it’s a compressive stress.
When it acts to lengthen bonds, it’s a tensile stress.

If stresses are small, the deformation produced is proportional to the stress and is also
reversible. In this case, the process is said to be an elastic process. In contrast, if the
stresses are very large, they can end up producing permanent deformation or fracture.
TYPES OF MECHANICAL WAVES


Transverse waves: as a result of perturbations in the X or Y axis. Chemical bonds
between all the atoms are displaced and the oscillation occurs in a perpendicular
direction to the direction in which the wave propagates/advances.
Therefore, transverse mechanical waves are shear waves (transversal): the atoms
involved move in a direction that is perpendicular to wave propagation.


Longitudinal waves: as a result of a perturbation in the Z axis. The oscillation
occurs in the direction of the atom chain, one after the other. In other words, in the


same direction in which the wave advances.
Longitudinal mechanical waves are therefore waves of compression and tension
( normal): the atoms involved move in the same direction as the propagation of the
wave.
[PDF p. 64]
The state of matter affects the type of wave that can exist. In fluids it’s impossible to have
shear stress, only pressure. In solids, all range of possibilities:


In the solid state there can be longitudinal and transverse mechanical waves.


In the fluid state (liquid or gas), ONLY longitudinal waves are possible. A fluid
cannot produce a deformation to counteract the action of shear stress: the elements
of a fluid are simply displaced when subjected to shear stresses. As they are
displaced, they rub against other elements in the fluid, and thus energy that is
injected in a transverse manner is rapidly dissipated in heat. In this case, in which
only normal stresses are possible, waves are referred to as pressure waves
(act by pushing and pulling). The force that produces a pressure is always
perpendicular to the area of the system, as it’s a normal stress.

EFFECT OF ACOUSTIC IMPEDANCE
Let’s suppose that we have a flat ultrasound wave propagating through medium A, and it
arrives at a different medium B. These two mediums are separated by an interface.
Given the density and elastic properties of the medium (Z), we might find that it is very
difficult to generate a displacement of atoms, even if the incident pressure is very high. Such
reasoning suggests that if medium A is air and medium B is water, which has a density
about 1000 times greater than air, it should be difficult to transmit a sound wave from the
air into the water (This can be experienced in a swimming pool: when we put our heads
below the water, external sounds are greatly attenuated).
More rigorously: there is a series of magnitudes that are
conserved on either side of the interface. There must be continuity
in velocity and pressure, and intensity must be conserved.
From these relationships, it is found that, if a pressure wave pi is
incident from medium A to medium B, then the reflected wave p R and
the transmitted wave p T are obtained by:
Where zA and zB are the impedances of each medium.
Z is constant and specific to each material, known as Acoustic impedance . It reflects the
resistance of a material to being displaced.
The acoustic impedance depends on the number of atoms in a region (density) and the
elastic behaviour of a material (which is reflected by the velocity of sound within it).
z = density · velocity of sound in the material
From these equations, we find that the energy (the intensity) is conserved. That is, the
incident intensity is divided between the reflected wave IR and transmitted wave IT.
To sum up, we can conclude that at any interface between two materials, there will be a
reflected wave and a transmitted wave. The relation between incoming pressure wave
and reflected wave will depend on the impedances of both materials.
There are two limiting situation s:


If the impedances of the two mediums are similar (zA and zB), there is practically no
reflected wave, and 100% is transmitted.


If there are very different impedances, practically 100% of the energy is reflected,
and almost nothing is transmitted


[PDF p. 67]
When a pressure wave (constant) arrives at a material:

If the impedance is high, the velocity will be quite low.
If the impedance is low, the resulting velocity will be high.

* Remember: all these waves propagate energy. The more atoms we have to displace, the
smaller the displacement.
ULTRASOUND IMAGING
How and why is an ultrasound wave reflected? How are the different shades of grey
generated in the image?
The ultrasound is generated by a device that contains a piezoelectric crystal. This crystal,
when subjected to a voltage, oscillates and transmits its vibration to the medium around it.
This device is called a transducer and it acts both as a source and a receiver for waves.
The transducer generates and emits the US wave. This wave is generated in
air (very small impedance) and impacts on the human body (high
impedance). To avoid there being no transmission ( which would mean the
wave wouldn’t reach the rest of the tissues inside the body), the wave is
generated inside a material whose impedance is very close to the
impedance of the human body. For example, a gel.
In this way almost all of the energy is transmitted and nothing is reflected, so
the ultrasound gets into the body.
The wave propagates through the body and it will encounter different surfaces on different
organs. At each surface, part of the wave will be reflected and detected by the machine.
The intensity of the reflected part of the wave will depend on the impedance values.
At the extremes of the range of possibilities are bones and large cavities full of air. where the
impedance is very different from that of the rest of the body, and so a mechanical wave will
find it difficult to penetrate them.
The reflected wave will go back towards the
transducer, where the signal is registered.
By measuring the journey time ∆trip (from
when the wave was generated until the echo –
the reflected wave - is received), it is possible
to determine the distance at which the
surface is located.
This is the operating principle behind echography by ultrasound: by sweeping through
different directions and collecting the various echoes from each surface, it is possible to
construct an image that represents, in gray-scale, the intensity of the reflected wave .


White/bright lines are observed when there is big echo; maximum intensity


Dark/black lines are observed when there is no or almost no echo

A material that does not generate an echo is said to be an-echoic or
non-echogenic. In contrast, materials that do generate an echo are said

Inhomogeneous materials generate more echo. For this reason,

Fluids and air-filled cavities don’t generate any acho, and

ULTRASOUND - SAFETY CONCERNS
The energy which is being transported by mechanical waves is absorbed by the human
body.


Thermal index (TI): reflects that there is an energy being absorbed by the system,
and thus, increasing its temperature. If it’s being absorbed by a specific tissue, the
temperature will increase in said tissue. There is a limit temperature.
The TI reflects the power absorbed in a specific tissue compared to the power
needed to increase 1ºC the tissue of that specific organ.
This ratio has to be smaller than one. By using this limit, we
can be sure no dangerous increase in temperature will be
produced.


Mechanical index (MI): The pressure of the US will oscillate around an ambient
pressure. Is there any limit to pressure values? In the case of the maximum, we have
already seen that we can cause “damage” or heat material if the pressure is very
high. It turns out that there is also a risk of damage if the minimum pressure goes too


low.
If the oscillation minimum falls below the vapour pressure, we are going to produce
something that will locally increase the pressure (bubbles).
There will be a spontaneous transition from the vapour to the liquid phase when
the pressure falls below P vapour. This process is called cavitation, the generation of
a vapour phase in a liquid due to the fall in pressure.
The mechanical index is defined as:
It’s proportional to the peak negative pressure (p0)
and therefore, to local pressure p. MI has to be
lower than 1.9. If this MI is too large, there is a
higher possibility of producing cavitation inside the
patient (creation of vapour phase bubbles when you
try to induce a pressure on a liquid which is below
the vapour pressure of said liquid).

* Concept of vapour pressure - we introduce a small amount of a liquid in a closed
cavity. If there is no gas, the P = 0 as there is nothing exerting a force on the
material. Therefore, in principle the pressure in the liquid is equivalent to the vapour
pressure, which is 0.
However, the liquid has a temperature which is different than 0. Therefore the
molecules are vibrating. This vibration causes some of the liquid particles to switch
(jump) from the liquid to the vapour phase.
Therefore there is a region of molecules in liquid phase and a region containing more
and more molecules in vapour phase.
The pressure in the upper part will increase until there is an equilibrium between the
molecules evaporating and those recondensing.
This behaviour occurs even for temperatures below the boiling point of the liquid.
There is a point where there will be an equilibrium, so the vapour pressure will be
equilibrated with the liquid pressure. The pressure in the equilibrium depends on the
temperature of the system.

ATTENUATION IN ULTRASOUND
The amplitude and intensity of ultrasound waves decrease as they travel through tissue, a
phenomenon known as attenuation.
Given a fixed propagation distance, attenuation affects high frequency ultrasound waves
to a greater degree than lower frequency waves, as the higher the frequency, the more the
wave is absorbed and the shallower the penetration.
Amplitude and intensity of the wave therefore depend on the attenuation.
    - **Materials with low attenuation/low absorption** = **water and fluids.** They appear

black on the image, and are said to be anechoic (don’t produce an echo) . When
present as artifacts, these structures will present posterior acoustic enhancement.
    - **Materials with intermediate attenuation** = **solid tissues.** They present with

different scales of gray, depending on if they’re hypo, iso or even hyperechoic.
    - **Materials with high attenuation/high absorption** = **bones, calcium, metal,..** They

appear white on the image, and are said to be hyperechoic (produce the highest
echo). When present as artifacts, they produce posterior acoustic shadowing.
The calculi (calcium) in the kidney and gallbladder cause posterior acoustic shadowing
The hepatic cyst ( *cystic structures: closed capsule or sac-like structures, typically filled with
a liquid) demonstrates the opposite phenomenon of posterior acoustic enhancement.
[PDF p. 73]
Shadowing occurs when there is a region that does not allow
ultrasound to pass through. This is the case with bone, a gallstone,…
In each of these cases, there is a region in which there is a big
difference in impedance (bone, stone, air) that makes the wave
reflect, and consequently we cannot see what happens behind
such a region. These regions appear darkened, and are like a
shadow of the zone that has reflected the ultrasound; the zone itself

Ultrasound workshop II
1st scenario
Parkinson’s patient is treated using HIFU (high intensity focused
ultrasound). It’s an example of the applications of ultrasound to
treatment. HIFU makes it possible to destroy certain brain cells
responsible for trembling in Parkinson’s disease.
Effect of US = to increase temperature locally, in order to destroy said part of the brain.
Patient’s head is surrounded by a hemisphere where many many transducers are located.
The US waves join at the centre part of the brain.
What are the expected results when the US waves transduce?
Using a single transducer we would need a huge amount of intensity, which could potentially
damage all the crossed tissues; in addition, the intensity will decrease when it goes inside of
the patient, all along it’s path prior to reaching the centre of the brain. We would hit a whole
trajectory of tissue on the brain of the patient.
When we combine many transducers we reduce the intensity that needs to be generated
by each and can be sure that only the central part will be affected by the combination of
intensities.
Another problem: before reaching the brain, the US wave is directed onto the skull which will
absorb a large part of the energy and reflect it. Therefore, it’s temperature will increase. This
is why patients refer pain when inside the machine.
To solve this problem, the skull is recovered by a layer of water. The presence of water
serves to match the impedances, but also to refrigerate the head of the patient.
2nd scenario
We are presented with a carotid artery stenosis.
When blood vessels narrow, the blood has to circulate faster to make the same amount
of blood reach the tissues in the same amount of time as it used to (smaller diameter =
increase the velocity of erythrocytes).
In order to diagnose carotid artery stenosis, velocity of blood cells needs to be measured.
We take 2 measurements:
-
Peak systolic velocity (PSV)
-
Diastolic velocity (EDV)
If we modify the angle between the transducer and the vessel, the effect on PSV
and EDV is that their values will change. If we place the transducer in such a
way that the erythrocytes are travelling towards the transducer, we will observe
[PDF p. 78]
the Doppler shift phenomenon: it’ll be either positive (bottom) or negative (top), depending
on v ult : whether the erythrocytes are approaching or moving away from the transducer.
If the measured velocity overgoes a threshold, the patient has stenosis, which will be a
problem. Therefore, we can’t be playing with the angles of the transducer, as we will recover
different velocities which don’t correspond to the real velocity.
The velocity that we measure taking into account the Doppler effect is always smaller than
the real erythrocytr’s velocity. Therefore, if the measured value is higher than the threshold,
we can confirm that the real velocity is higher.

Dosimetry workshop
1st scenario
Man suddenly fell ill due to a polonium intoxication, which decays through alpha decay. It’s
very toxic due to its ionizing capacity, and as it’s soluble in water, can cross through
biological membranes.
How much of the energy released by the material was absorbed by this man?
Because of the size of the alpha particles, specific properties appear in the case of alpha
particles, as well as for protons. The whole amount of energy released inside the body is
absorbed, as it is found inside the body.
An external alpha source producing 5 MeV can seem to be much more dangerous as the
energy per decay is higher. However, that is not correct. An external alpha source isn’t
dangerous as this radiation has to cross a given amount of air + the outer skin. So all the
energy is absorbed before the radiation reaches the tissues, on the surface. Nothing will
penetrate.
Alpha sources are dangerous when ingested and introduced inside the body. From
here, the whole of the energy released will be absorbed.
2nd scenario

Increasing the intensity (electric current, mAmp) increases the number of
electrons released, and therefore, the number of photons.
The average energy per photon only depends on the voltage value. This
increases the probability of radiation, not the effect per photon.

What will be the effect on the absorbed dose (dose=energy per mass)?
The absorbed dose will increase, as we have more photons and the energy absorbed is
proportional to the number of photons.
3rd scenario
Lead apron = 0.25 mm of lead which attenuates approx 90% of the incoming radiation.
Mainly designed for x-ray beams of 100KeV. For this case, the lead apron is effective. Even
if it doubles the time of exposure (dose increases with time of exposure)
However, in the case of PET, 511keV photons are released. Therefore the lead apron has a
thickness of 4mm in PET scanning. This means it is not truly effective (time-thickness wise)
Therefore, we will have to use other alternatives to reduce the absorbed energy.

Factors that affect the absorbed dose

Time (try to optimize the time spent in the room. Effective personnel training)

Amount of energy

Distance to the source

Increase thickness of shielding (we can increase the shielding, in case of PET not of
the apron, but of the walls in the room)
4th scenario
PET scans release 511 keV photons; therefore, they are found in the Compton region.
In X-ray CT we try to prevent Compton scattering (as we are interested in retrieving quality
images) and therefore use energies below the 30 Kev limits.
For radiotherapy, we are interested in the radiation reaching all of the tissues with tumors.
We are interested in penetrating all the structures, therefore we will use energies in ranges
between 30 keV and 20 MeV.

Gametogenesis
What are gametes?
Gametes are highly specialized sex cells, born only for reproductive purposes . If not
fertilized, they degenerate in 24h (oocytes) or 2-3 days (sperm) after being produced. They
are haploid cells.
Where do they come from?
Gametes originate from primordial germ cells .
PGCs are diploid cells destined to perpetuate the species, giving rise to
gametes. These are the only cells that undergo meiosis.
Gametogenesis consists in the conversion of the PGCs into male or
female gametes.
Where does gametogenesis take place?
Gametogenesis occurs in the sex glands or
gonads.
During the end of the 3rd week of gestation, PGCs
originate in the wall of the yolk sac and migrate to
the gonads in the second month of gestation.
This occurs both in males and females. In males,
these PGCs remain inactive until puberty
SPERMATOGENESIS
Spermatogenesis begins at puberty in the seminiferous tubules of the testis.
- If we did a cross-section of a sex cord in a
neonate male, we would observe inactive
primordial germ cells (spermatogonia)
surrounded by sertoli cells and a basement
membrane.
- If we did a cross-section of the testis during
puberty, we would observe that these tubules
acquire a lumen. Spermatogonia begin dividing
and sperm are released and transported through
the tubules.
[PDF p. 83]
Spermatogenesis entails two events:

Genetic reduction of PGCs: from the primary spermatocyte,
there are 2 meiotic divisions which give place to 4 spermatids.
Spermiogenesis: process by which spermatids mature into 4
spermatozoa.

How does spermatogenesis occur?
Spermatogenesis is characterized by 3 specific functional phases:
1. Mitotic proliferation: from 1 first spermatogonium, there are
successive mitotic divisions. But these cells remain connected,
and we obtain a synchronic progeny (they all began dividing at
the same time and will continue to do so, synchronously).
2. Meiosis I and II, through which primary and secondary
spermatocytes give early spermatids (still joined together).
3. Differentiation / Spermiogenesis, phase in which spermatids
mature into spermatozoa . In the process of spermiogenesis:
           - Nuclear condensation occurs

           - Acrosome formation

            - Formation of neck, middle piece and tail

            - Release of cytoplasmic material

10% of ejaculated cells are grossly
abnormal. There are problems when
this percentage goes over 20%
              - This whole process takes around **64 days.**

                        - It **begins at puberty** and it’s a **continuous** process,

which continues until the death of the individual.
              - Spermatogenesis is **coordinated radially** within the

tubule cross-section. We can find spermatogonia at
different stages of development.

Blood-testis barrier
An important function of sertoli cells is the formation of the
blood-testis barrier.
They form a physical barrier that isolates meiotic and post-meiotic germ
cells from immune and lymphatic systems, protecting them.
This is done because, as they are different from the rest of the cells of the
body, they could be recognized as foreign cells and be attacked.

Sertoli cells: create the blood-testis barrier and favour

spermatogenesis (FSH)
Leydig or Interstitial cells: located in the space between the
tubules. Cells responsible for the production of testosterone (LH)
How is spermatogenesis controlled?
It’s controlled by the anterior pituitary gland, through FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone)
and LH (luteinizing hormone) . This gland is stimulated by the Hypothalamus.


FSH is going to act on sertoli cells, making them promote spermatogenesis by
activating spermatogonia.


LH acts on leydig cells, which will start producing testosterone. Testosterone will
also reinforce spermatogenesis.

OOGENESIS
Oogenesis takes place in the ovaries (which are the female gonads/sex glands).
Oogenesis vs spermatogenesis
Same as in spermatogenesis, oocytes are derived from Primordial Germ Cells (oogonia).
Oogonia, same as sperm, originates in the wall of the yolk sac. They migrate towards the
gonads in the 2nd month of gestation.
But in contrast with males, oogonia become very active and start dividing by mitosis
during the 5th month of gestation.
Many PGCs are lost during development. If
PGCs don’t reach the undifferentiated gonad,
and instead reach and accumulate in other
tissues, they give rise to bizarre tumors
known as teratomas (as they are rapidly
dividing cells).
Contrarily to spermatogenesis, from each primary oocyte (coming from oogonium), only
one secondary oocyte is obtained, and from there, only 1 mature oocyte is formed if
oogenesis is completed (formation of polar bodies).
How does oogenesis occur?
1. Before birth, oogonia proliferate and peak by mid-gestation. Some of
them will enter oogenesis and differentiate into primary oocytes which
enter meiosis I.
But they will remain arrested in diplotene of prophase I until puberty.
The rest of oogonia which don’t differentiate, degenerate before birth.
[PDF p. 86]
Primary oocytes arrested at prophase I are surrounded by
follicular cells (sustentacular cells), found forming primordial
follicles.
A primordial follicle contains the nucleus of the primary oocyte + flat
follicular cells.
Ovaries at birth only contain a given number of oocytes, arrested in
meiosis I. Only a few of them will undergo ovulation, and the rest will
die.
2. From infancy to puberty,
primary oocytes remain arrested in
diplotene of prophase I.
3. Oogenesis is resumed at
puberty. But it doesn’t continue as a
continuous process, but a cyclic one:
A few follicles start maturating, and
only 1 primary follicle will obtain
maturity. From puberty to
menopause, every 28 days , one
follicle fully matures and resumes
meiosis I, entering meiosis II where
it once again becomes arrested until
fertilization.
4. If fertilization occurs, the
secondary oocyte continues meiosis
II until it gives place to the mature
oocyte.

The zona pellucida also arises (a membrane of
glycosaminoglycans and glycoproteins which separates
the oocyte from the granulosa cell layer) .
This gives place to the primary follicle.
● Formation of secondary follicle
Under the action of FSH (pituitary g.), several changes take place in
the follicle: a cavity (Antrum) forms around granulosa cells and fills
with liquid, pushing the granulosa cells. The primary oocyte
becomes displaced and pushed onto the wall of the zona pellucida.
As the antrum evolves, it gives place to the structure of the
secondary follicle.
Theca cells are found surrounding granulosa.
● Formation of tertiary follicle or Graff follicle
The secondary follicle becomes mature at midcycle, forming the
tertiary follicle. Theca cells form a bilayer (theca-interna and
theca-externa) around the granulosa cells. Theca-interna cells produce
precursors of estrogens, which are transported to the granulosa cells
and are transformed into estrogens.
* During this whole maturation, the oocyte is still arrested at diplotene of prophase I (primary
oocyte). It enters meiosis II when released from the follicle during ovulation.
Functions of the follicle

Production of hormones (estrogens and progesterone (during luteal phase))

Enabling ovulation, as it expels the oocyte out of the ovary when the time comes
[PDF p. 88]
2. Ovulation
Ovulation takes place at mid-cycle (day 14).
The secondary oocyte which is arrested at metaphase II, is
expelled at day 14 during ovulation.
Granulosa cells and theca cells, which have been left
behind, undergo morphological changes under the influence
of LH : they are converted into secretory cells known as
luteal cells, which will now mostly secrete progesterone.
(In addition to still secreting small amounts of estrogen, they
secrete lots of progesterone).
Together, these luteal cells from the corpus luteum.

In the 1st half of the ovarian cycle: primarily estrogen
In the 2nd half of the ovarian cycle: mainly progesterone

3. Luteal phase
These luteal cells form a body known as the corpus luteum, which is
released at the same time as the secondary oocyte.
It’s made up of secretory cells whose function is to secrete
progesterone.
It finally degenerates if not fertilized, and the process is restarted.
Only if the secondary oocyte is
fertilized, it will complete meiosis II.
Characteristics of ovulation
The expulsion of the oocyte is the result of intrafollicular pressure and
possibly, the contraction of smooth muscle in the theca externa .
It’s a hormone-mediated process (this stage is regulated mainly by
LH)
The LH surge resumes meiosis I and the secondary oocyte enters
meiosis II, where it is arrested at metaphase
Ovulation consists in the release of this 2ary oocyte
[PDF p. 89]
How is oogenesis controlled?
The hypothalamus acts on the anterior pituitary gland, promoting the release of FSH and
LH.

The amount of FSH is larger in the 1st half
of the cycle.
FSH stimulates granulosa cells in the ovarian
follicles to synthesize aromatase, which
converts androgens produced by the theca
cells to estradiol, to produce estrogen.
As the levels of estrogen increase in the
blood, it has negative feedback on the
pituitary glands.
This is so until estrogens peak and acquire a
certain concentration in plasma
(200 pg/mL) around days 12-14. (This high
amount of estrogens informs the pituitary that
the oocyte is ready to be released).
From this threshold, estrogen creates a positive feedback and induces the
pituitary to increase the amount of FSH, but mainly LH.

The increased amounts of LH favour the resumption of meiosis and therefore
induce ovulation.

The amount of LH increases mainly in the 2nd part of the
cycle .
It acts on luteinized theca and granulosa cells which will
begin to secrete progesterone.
The high amounts of LH produced (LH surge) after the
estrogen threshold has been surpassed, trigger ovulation.
Ovulation normally occurs 24 to 36 hours after the LH

surge.
Estrogens and progesterone both act outside of the ovary, but not
on the ovary. They act via the vascular system. FSH and LH act on
the oocyte and structures which contain it.
[PDF p. 90]
THE MENSTRUAL CYCLE
It makes reference to the cyclic changes that take place in the endometrium, produced by
estrogens and progesterone .
Cyclic changes in the endometrium are accompanied by changes in the uterine tubes,
vagina and cervical mucus. This is controlled by estrogens and progesterone:
Estrogen promotes proliferation and cell growth (proliferative phase)
Progesterone increases secretory activity (secretory phase)
➢ Days 4-14. Proliferative phase
After the previous ovulation, from day 4 to day 14, the endometrium has to be
regenerated . This is stimulated by estrogen, which induces proliferation and renewal.
This is known as the proliferative phase:
Epithelial cells grow and proliferate
Blood vessels extend and accumulate blood in case there is implantation
Glands are formed which secrete glycogen to nurture the future embryo
Watery cervical mucus (penetrable)
➢ Days 14-21. Secretory phase
Progesterone is released, glycogen accumulates and blood vessels continue to grow
(secretory phase) :
Increases secretory activity
There is less contractility of the uterine tubes

Cervical mucus becomes thick and non elastic (non-penetrable, to protect the
oocyte)

➢ Day 25. Menstruation
If there has been no fertilization, the corpus
luteum degenerates and stops secreting
progesterone. Therefore blood vessels strat
becoming necrotic and constrict due to the lack
of progesterone, which is the hormone which
maintains the endometrium.
[PDF p. 91]
Fertilization
Fertilization marks day 1 of the life of a human being.
FERTILIZATION PROCESS
Fertilization consists in the fusion of gametes in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
PHASE 1. PENETRATION OF THE CORONA RADIATA


The secondary oocyte arrested at
metaphase II is released on day 14.


There is activity from the fimbriae in the
tube, finger-like projections which capture
the released oocyte through.


Meanwhile, after sexual intercourse,
sperm enter through the vagina and into
the uterus.

The vagina provides a very acidic environment, which is incompatible with sperm.
Therefore, sperm are released along with semen, which alkalizes the pH so sperm

can survive.
Sperm make their way to the uterine tubes. During this journey they undergo a
process known as capacitation : it consists in the removal of some glycoproteins
which, if present, don’t permit fertilization.
Only capacitated sperm will be able to fertilize the oocyte.

The few sperm which reach the oocyte penetrate the corona radiata and reach the
zona pellucida.

PHASE 2. PENETRATION OF THE ZONA PELLUCIDA
Sperms need to penetrate the strong barrier
which is the zona pellucida. This is achieved
through binding in a ligand-receptor fashion

Molecules on the surface of the sperm are
specific binding sites for the ZP3 ( zona
pellucida-3) receptors found on the zona
pellucida.

[PDF p. 92]
This ligand-receptor reaction (acrosome reaction) triggers the breakage of the
membrane which contains the acrosome and the release of enzymes such as
acrosin, which carry out extracellular digestion of the zona pellucida.
PHASE 3. FUSION OF THE SPERM AND OOCYTE MEMBRANES

After digestion of the zona pellucida, the two membranes contact one another and

fuse.

This fusion causes a weak membrane depolarization and leads to a calcium
wave that triggers resumption of meiosis II.

In the oocyte there are enzymes contained in vesicles, known as cortical granules.
The induced calcium wave also triggers a cortical reaction, the fusion of these
cortical granules with the oolemma (oocyte membrane)

The cortical granules release their content, and degrade and inhabilitate all
receptors to prevent other sperms from entering. This is known as the zona

reaction.

The zona reaction hydrolyzes ZP3 receptors, blocking the possibility of
polyspermy.

RESUMPTION OF MEIOSIS II


The entry of sperm resumes meiosis II,
which is quickly completed (giving place to
Polar body II)


Only the sperm’s nucleus enters and
fuses with the oocyte’s nucleus. This gives
place to a unicellular embryo, known as
the pronuclei stage zygote.


Female and male pronuclei duplicate their
nucleus and carry out the first mitotic
division, giving place to the two-cell stage zygote .
These are the first two cells of the future organism, known as blastomeres.


[PDF p. 93]
This whole process, from fertilization till the formation of the two-cell stage zygote, takes
around 30 hours. If there’s no fertilization, the oocyte usually degenerates after 24h .
The main outcomes of fertilization are:

The resumption of meiosis II in the oocyte

The formation of a 2 cell-stage embryo, known as zygote

Restoration of diploid number of chromosomes
Formation of a new individual with unique genetic content

Determination of the sex of the embryo (XX o XY, at the 2 cell stage)
FIRST WEEK OF DEVELOPMENT
During the first week of development, the zygote goes from the two-cell stage to the
blastocyst stage through cleavage, and begins the process of implantation .
Cleavage consists in a series of mitotic divisions which gradually reduce the size of
embryonic cells (blastomeres) until the normal size seen in somatic cells is recovered . The
zona pellucida compresses the dividing cells into a reduced space, forcing them to regain
their normal size.
FORMATION OF THE BLASTOCYST
First 30h: 2-cell stage. The zygote travels along the
tubes to the uterus for its implantation. During this
process, it undergoes cleavage and segmentation.


The zygote divides (4 cell stage, 8 cell stage,…) until
the Morula is formed on day 4.


Early blastocyst: around days 4-5, fluid enters
the morula and forms a cavity (blastocystic
cavity), which compresses the cells and forms the
early blastocyst. At this point, we find an external
layer of cells surrounding the cavity, and a
compressed inner mass.


[PDF p. 94]

Late blastocyst: the early blastocyst releases the zona pellucida, in order to
implant into the endometrium. In this way, the late blastocyst is formed. Only a
blastocyst released from the zona pellucida can achieve implantation.

At this point, the inner cell mass is known as the embryoblast (which will give place
to the embryo) and the outer layer of cells is known as the trophoblast (will be in
charge of forming structures which nurture the embryo).
BEGINNING OF IMPLANTATION
Implantation begins during day 5-6 after fertilization. In other words, between days 20-23
of the menstrual cycle. The monolayer of flat epithelial cells in the outer cell mass
(trophoblast) will differentiate upon implantation, into:
Cytotrophoblast (epithelium, seen in light green)
Syncytiotrophoblast (syncytium, seen in dark green. Formed by many dividing cells
which do not achieve complete cytokinesis; therefore, they form a mass with many
nuclei floating in one big cytoplasm) . This structure has a highly invasive power
and starts eroding the endometrium, enabling implantation.
[PDF p. 95]
Ectopic pregnancies
An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilised egg implants
itself outside of the womb . For example, in the fallopian
tubes, abdominal cavity, cervix,…
● Tubal pregnancy: the embryo begins to develop in
the ampullary region (uterine tube). It normally
ruptures during the 2nd month of development and
has to be removed.

Rectouterine pouch pregnancy: rarely, the oocyte can
escape fimbriae in the tube during its release and the
fertilized embryo implants and develops in the
rectouterine pouch, the lowest point of the abdominal
cavity (Douglas pouch).
It’s a pregnancy of risk, but it can come to term.

[PDF p. 96]
2nd week of development
The main event of the 2nd week is completion of implantation.
The 2nd week of life corresponds to days
21-28 of the endometrial cycle. This is why
each cycle has a duration of around 28
days: it allows time for implantation to
occur.
If there were no sign of implantation,
menstruation would happen.
Implantation takes place by attaching to the
endometrium at the embryonic pole: the
blastocyst leaves the uterine cavity and
penetrates into the endometrium.
8th DAY OF DEVELOPMENT. BILAMINAR DISC STAGE
In the late blastocyst which begins implantation, we can
differentiate an inner cell mass (embryoblast) and an
outer cell mass (trophoblast, which is divided into
cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast). On the 8th day
of embryonic development, the embryo enters the
bilaminar disk stage. This bilaminar structure is formed
in the embryoblast, and is composed of the Hypoblast
layer and the Epiblast . The amniotic cavity also arises
between the epiblast and the cytotrophoblast along with
amnioblasts, flat cells which are found surrounding the
amniotic cavity . Many more changes continue to take
place in the trophoblastic tissue.
The corpus luteum knows implantation has begun because
the embryo releases a hormone by day 9-10, called human
chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), the same hormone tested
for the ascertainment of pregnancy ( by the end of the 2nd
week, this hormone is found in high enough quantities as to
be detected) . This signal reaches the corpus luteum and
makes it remain active, releasing progesterone. Luteolysis
does not occur and gestation may proceed.
The corpus luteum works until the 4th month of
gestation. From there, the placenta takes over.
[PDF p. 97]
9th DAY OF DEVELOPMENT
On the 9th day, a fibrin coagulum forms to prevent the embryo from leaving the
endometrium.
Within the Syncytiotrophoblast, spaces form
and fuse together forming larger cavities,
known as trophoblastic lacunae.
In the embryoblast, cells coming from the
hypoblast begin to migrate, forming a thin
membrane which covers the inner surface of
the cytotrophoblast. This membrane is known
as the exocoelomic membrane, which lines
the blastocyst cavity. This lined cavity becomes
known as the exocoelomic cavity.
The exocoelomic membrane, together with cells of the hypoblast, form
the primitive yolk sac (which is the site of PGC formation). By day 9,
the blastocyst is completely embedded in the uterus wall.
12th DAY OF DEVELOPMENT
In relation to the trophoblast: lacunae in the
syncytiotrophoblast continue to expand and
fuse forming lacunar networks. At that
time, capillaries in the endometrium dilate,
forming maternal sinusoids.
The syncytiotrophoblast finally erodes the
wall of the endometrium, reaching
maternal sinusoids and uterine glands
and allowing maternal blood and uterine
secretions (glycogen and proteins) to flow
into the lacunar network. Through
diffusion, they will exchange gases and
metabolites with the embryo (these
lacunae are more prominent near the
embryonic pole).
This is the beginning of uteroplacental circulation or maternal circulation.
Around the same time, a new population of cells appear between the
inner surface of the cytotrophoblast and the primitive yolk sac
(exocoelomic membrane), known as the extraembryonic mesoderm .
It’s a membrane formed by loose connective tissue, found intervening
between the trophoblast and embryoblast.
As it forms, spaces/vacuoles also begin to appear within this
extraembryonic mesoderm. Spaces known as extraembryonic cavities.
[PDF p. 98]
13th DAY OF DEVELOPMENT
On the 13th day of development, extraembryonic cavities found
within the extraembryonic mesoderm gradually fuse to form one
large cavity known as the chorionic cavity or extraembryonic
cavity. Therefore, the original blastocyst cavity (blastocele) now
becomes known as coelom, surrounded by the chorionic cavity.
It divides the extraembryonic mesoderm into 2 regions: one
surrounding the trophoblast (parietal or somatic) and another
lining the yolk sac (visceral or splanchnic ) .
Around day 13, a large portion of the exocoelomic cavity is pinched,
forming a smaller remaining cavity, now known as secondary yolk
sac (smaller than the primary).
The part of the membrane found binding the
embryoblast to the cytotrophoblast is known as the
connective salk (the future umbilical cord).
Additionally, at this stage the cytotrophoblast
penetrates into the syncytiotrophoblast and forms
villi-like structures, known as primary villi. The
extraembryonic mesoderm also begins to
penetrate into the cytotrophoblast forming
finger-like projections.
DECIDUALIZATION REACTION
When the blastocyst is found borrowed into
the endometrium, the endometrial wall
becomes known as the decidua (decidua
basalis, capsularis and parietalis).
This occurs because implantation of the
blastocyst induces decidualization of the
endometrial stroma, through the decidual
reaction.
This decidual reaction (decidualization)
consists in the transformation of endometrial
cells into specialized cell types called
decidual cells, to provide nutrition and
immunological protection to the
conceptus (accumulate lipids and glycogen).
[PDF p. 99]

Why isn’t the embryo rejected and perceived as a foreign structure?

Because the syncytiotrophoblast (found surrounding and protecting the embryo) expresses
specific antigens known as human leukocyte antigen-G (HLA-G), which act as a ligand to
leukocytes and inhibit them. They downregulate the maternal immune response.
Implantation window: limited time span when blastocyst competence is at its priming point.
● Dating of pregnancy
    **Fertilization age:** date pregnancy from the time of conception/fertilization

    **Menstrual age:** dates pregnancy from the woman’s last menstrual period

A normal pregnancy would be 38 weeks after fertilization and 40 weeks after the onset of
the last normal menstrual period.
ABNORMAL SITES OF IMPLANTATION
The most frequent abnormal site of implantation is the uterine tube. Tubal pregnancies
Tubal pregnancies aren’t seen to term, and the uterine tube ruptures by the 2nd month of
gestation.
Other abnormal pregnancies can occur due to an
abnormal placenta. One example of this is
“Placenta previa”, where the placenta develops in
the lowest part of the endometrium, covering the
cervix. Bleeding often happens as the lower part of
the uterus thins during the third trimester of
pregnancy. This causes the area of the placenta over
the cervix to bleed. The risk of bleeding is higher if
a lot of the placenta covers the cervix, as is the case
of placenta previa. There is much more bleeding than
there would normally be and this leads to
hemorrhage.
● Hydatidiform moles
Hydatidiform moles are abnormal blastocysts
with no embryonic tissue. However, the
trophoblast develops and forms a placenta.
Most often, a hydatidiform mole comes from an
abnormal fertilized egg that develops into a
hydatidiform mole rather than a fetus (a
condition called molar pregnancy). However, a
hydatidiform mole can develop from cells that
remain in the uterus after a miscarriage, a
full-term pregnancy, or a mislocated pregnancy
(ectopic pregnancy).
[PDF p. 100]
Rarely, a hydatidiform mole develops when there is a living fetus. In such cases, the fetus
typically dies, and a miscarriage often occurs.
Women who have a hydatidiform mole feel as if they are pregnant. But because hydatidiform
moles grow much faster than a fetus, the abdomen becomes larger much faster than it does
in a normal pregnancy. Severe nausea and vomiting and vaginal bleeding are common. As
parts of the mole deteriorate, small amounts of tissue, which resemble a bunch of grapes,
may pass through the vagina.
The moles secrete high amounts of hCG (as this hormone comes from the
syncytiotrophoblast), which can be detected for diagnosis.
About 80% of hydatidiform moles are not cancerous, but they may become invasive and
develop into malignant tumors (choriocarcinomas) which rapidly spread into the
lymphatic system and the bloodstream.
[PDF p. 101]
3rd week of development
MAIN EVENTS
Gastrulation, which involves the formation of the 3 germ cell layers which will give
rise to all of the tissues and organs in the body.
Neurulation, which consists in the beginning of the formation of CNS (but won’t be
completed until the end of the 4th week).
GASTRULATION
In summary, gastrulation is the process by which the three primary germ layers of the
trilaminar disc are formed.
The first cells to invaginate through the primitive groove form the definitive endoderm. The
remaining cells of the epiblast are called the ectoderm. Cells that remain in the space
between ectoderm and definitive endoderm form a layer known as the mesoderm.
At the end of the 3rd week, the embryo will be known as trilaminar disc.
How does gastrulation occur?
1. Firstly, we have the formation of the primitive streak

On day 15, this new structure can be observed by
looking at the epiblast from above. It’s a groove that
initiates at the caudal end of the embryo. In the
bilaminar disc, the epiblast belongs to the dorsal
part of the embryo. As soon as the primitive streak
appears, the cranial-caudal axis is defined,
marking where the tail and head of the embryo will
be. In addition to this, we imminently know what is
left and what is right .
The embryo is now totally oriented. Thus, regions of the embryo (all 3 axes)
become identifiable by day 15.

[PDF p. 102]


The streak protuberates outwards and produces an elevation known as primitive
node (“the organizer”, it releases factors that will induce differentiation), which
possesses a hole known as the primitive pit, through which prenotochordal cells will
migrate to form the notochord.
During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate toward the midline/primitive streak,
detach from the epiblast and invaginate. They start to
pass underneath, giving rise to a new layer formed
between the epiblast and hypoblast.
Epiblast cells are epithelial cells, interconnected by
adhesion molecules. As they migrate, they lose their
adhesion molecules, change their shape and acquire
the ability to migrate, and thus become mesenchymal
cells, undifferentiated cells with proliferative capacity.
From here, epiblast cells expand as mesenchymal
cells in this new layer between epiblast and hypoblast
and form the mesoderm layer, giving place to the


trilaminar disc.
The mesenchyme corresponds to embryonic loose connective tissue.
2. Fate maps: cells in specific regions of the epiblast and entering the primitive streak will
form specific structures in the mesoderm.

Epiblastic cells which migrate and invaginate via the
primitive pit will form the axial mesoderm. This axial

mesoderm will form the notochord.
The notochord serves as the basis for the axial
skeleton.
The formation of the notochord is very complex: cells
enter via primitive pit and extend cranially. The migrated
cells fuse with the hypoblast, forming the notochordal
plate, which eventually detaches from the hypoblast
and forms the notochord.


The mesoderm expands through the space between epiblast and hypoblast except
for 2 regions:

Oropharyngeal membrane, where there is no
mesoderm. Epiblast and hypoblast are directly
in contact, tightly together. This is the region



from which the mouth is formed.
    **Cloacal plate/membrane,** Once again, there is

no mesoderm. It gives place to the anus,
urethra, urinary bladder and rectum.
At this point, we can also observe the Allantois, a region of protuberant hypoblasts
which will lead to the formation of part of the bladder.
[PDF p. 103]
The remaining mesoderm is the paraxial and lateral mesoderm.
    The cells that extend at both sides of the notochord, close to

the midline, will form the paraxial mesoderm.
    Cells closer to the caudal region form the **lateral plate**

mesoderm
    The epiblasts that enter at the caudal-most part become

continuous with the extraembryonic mesoderm, and
contribute to its formation.
3. Formation of the endoderm: mesenchymal cells also begin to replace the hypoblast
cells, forming a totally new layer known as endoderm (definitive endoderm).
As the mesoderm mesenchymal cells
migrate to replace those of the hypoblast,
they differentiate and once again become
epithelial cells.
Therefore, the initial epiblast cells will give
place to the endoderm and the mesoderm.
The epiblast that remains is known as the
ectoderm.
Cross section:

Ectoderm : skin, CNS, PNS, eyes, internal
ear, neural crest cells (in addition, bones and
connective tissue of the face and part of the
skull)
Mesoderm (+ notochord, which is part of the
mesoderm): bones, connective tissue,
urogenital system and cardiovascular
system.
Endoderm : gives rise to the gut and mucosa
of the gut + gut derivatives (liver, pancreas, lungs,…)

PATHOLOGIES
SIRENOMELIA: caudal dysgenesis. Occurs due to a lack of mesoderm in the
lumbosacral region, which results in the fusion of the limb buds, accompanied
by other defects in the organs of the body. They generally die after birth.
Tumors associated with gastrulation include SACROCOCCYGEAL
TERATOMA. After gastrulation, the primitive streak usually regresseses,
but if it doesn’t totally disappear, remnant pluripotent cells can give rise to
these teratomas.
[PDF p. 104]
GENETIC REGULATION OF LATERALITY
There is a laterality in the body that comes about due to the expression of signalling
molecules. The expression of Nodal on the left side of the body regulates left-sidedness
and leads to a cascade of events that positions the organs.
SITUS INVERSUS
There is an inversion in the positioning of organs.
It can be a partial situs inversus, seen in only one or a
few organs positioned in the wrong side of the body
(heart = dextrocardia, liver,..), or it can be a complete
situs inversus.
Complete situs inversus is more serious and involves
left-right asymmetry (all the blood vessels and
organs). “20% of people with situs inversus also present
KARTAGENER’S SYNDROME (respiratory system
problems + infertility, due to cilia malfunction in PCD)
NEURULATION
Neurulation consists in the formation of the neural tube.
During the 3rd week of development, we can observe the
initiation of neurulation.
Formation of the neural plate

The notochord forms and starts secreting molecules

that stimulate the conversion of surface ectoderm
into neural tissue .
These molecules act on the overlying ectoderm and induce the transformation of its
epithelial cells into polygonal cells. The cells change their form. As the notochord
grows, the area of influence is larger.

By the end of the 3rd week, as the embryo grows mostly cranially, the surface
ectoderm is converted into neural tissue, forming the neural plate.
Why does only the surface ectoderm undergo neurulation? Due to back inhibition. An
inhibitor is being produced laterally, so the conversion is topped and restricted to a given
area. Combination of induction and inhibition patterns.

Formation of the neural tube
Once the neural plate is formed, there is an increase in the height of cells,
forming a thickened neural plate.

The plate forms a central neural groove and two lateral neural folds

The 2 folds elevate along the groove

The two folds fuse. Once this occurs, they detach from the overlying ectoderm
surface, becoming invaginated. The ectoderm is found surrounding the neural
tube, which will give rise to the skin

[PDF p. 105]
4th week of development
At the end of the 4th week, the embryo looks like:
During the 4th week of embryonic development, neurulation
is complete and the embryo passes from being a fat
trilaminar disc to adopting a 3D structure.
NEURULATION AT MID 3rd WEEK
At mid 3rd week (18 days), the neural plate invaginates and the
folds fuse. However, this is a gradual process: the tube doesn’t
fuse and invaginate all at once. It first fuses and then
progressively invaginates during the 4th week.
NEURULATION AT THE END OF 3rd WEEK
(Day 20)
Many factors contribute to invagination, such as
somites.
Neurulation takes place while the paraxial
mesoderm becomes thick, differentiates and forms
compact segments known as somites.
Somites are independent, differentiated paraxial
mesoderm which protrude and
press against the neural tube
to favour invagination.
The formation of these structures
progresses along with
neurulation. The protruding
paraxial structures grow in
number and increase .
CLOSURE OF NEURAL TUBE DURING 4th WEEK
(days 22 - 28)
By the end of day 28, the neural tube is totally
invaginated.
[PDF p. 106]
FOLDINGS OF THE EMBRYO
At the same time, both lateral and cranial-caudal
foldings of the embryo take place. The embryo
undergoes rapid development in size and shape.
●
Lateral body foldings
The lateral folding is produced by the rapidly growing spinal cord and somites.

The ectoderm on the sides extends ventrally. The paraxial mesoderm begins to
form the somites while the neural tube continues to invaginate. The yolk sac
becomes thinner at the sides, and begins to narrow, forming what will be the gut

tube.

As the amniotic cavity and the ectoderm continue to extend ventrally, the
mesoderm differentiates into somatic mesoderm (in contact with the ectoderm) and
splanchnic mesoderm (surrounding remaining endoderm, which will form the gut).

As the amniotic cavity continues to surround and approaches the yolk sac, a new
cavity arises: the intra-embryonic body cavity. The connection between gut and
yolk sac continues to get narrower and narrower. They will remain connected by a
canal known as the vitelline duct.

Eventually, the amniotic cavity will surround the whole body of the embryo. The
body will be immersed in that cavity, floating in amniotic fluid. Within the body of the
embryo, we find the intra-embryonic body cavity / intraembryonic coelom surrounding
the gut and yolk sac. The gut remains attached to the rest of the body by a stalk
known as the dorsal mesentery (mesoderm).
Note that although not represented in all images, the ectoderm deriving from amnioblasts
still lines the inner face of the amniotic cavity, forming an epithelial layer (see picture at top of
the page)

[PDF p. 107]

Cranial-caudal folds

In the cranial-caudal folds, head and tail move ventrally, and the embryo will adopt a “C”
shape. As a result:


The primitive heart (heart mesoderm) bends ventrally and moves towards the
midline, compressing the yolk sac. The pericardial cavity and heart tube also
begin to arise within the heart mesoderm.


Neural tube also bends ventrally (anterior and posterior neuroscope)


Oropharyngeal membrane (the future mouth ) bends and ends up being located in
the head; cloacal membrane is also invaginated at the caudal end


The allantoid is also compressed anteriorly/ventrally until it presses against the
yolk sac. The upper-most part will contribute to the formation of the urinary bladder,

Upper view: the cavity extends in a “U” shape around the lateral sides of the embryo
(seen from above). The upper coelom will become known as the pericardial coelom
and the centre-most, peritoneal coelom (peritoneum = abdominal cavity lining).


Seen in the cross-section: the intraembryonic cavity initially becomes continuous with

Blood circulation in hemochorial placenta
Hemochorial placenta (human) = the blood is in contact with the chorion
Anchoring villi = no exchange
Free villi, expanding = exchange
The chorionic structure is found deep between lacunae of maternal blood, where maternal
blood vessels are draining blood. The maternal blood is released at high pressures into
these lacunae. It goes all the way down (due to high pressure) and returns slowly. Slower
rate allows the exchange of nutrients, excretion materials, CO2,.. so it slowly returns
deoxygenated.
Decidual septa doesn’t fully separate cotyledons. Blood therefore also flows laterally,
between cotyledons.

Development of the nervous system
INTRODUCTION
The nervous system is in charge of all the other systems, making it
possible for them to work in unison towards a common goal.
How is this achieved? By being aware of the external environment and
internal environment. The nervous system is able to gather information
and transmit/convey it via the nerves (PNS) to the main centre of
control (CNS, brain and spinal cord) which integrates the info and
elaborates the most appropriate response.
There are different types of responses, but we will mainly focus on motor
responses. The response is sent to effector organs.
Main parts of the Nervous System

Subdivided into:

Functional unit = the nerve cell or neuron.
Santiago Ramón y Cajal was the Spanish physician and early

-
Cell body

Induction of the neural plate. Neurulation

At the beginning of 3rd week, notochord forms from cells
migrating from the primitive streak through the primitive pit.
Ectoderm cells become polygonal, thicken and extend
rostrally, forming the neural plate.
A neural groove forms, the plate elevates forming two
neural folds which approach one another and end up
fusning and invaginating, detaching from the overlying
ectoderm, during the 4th week.

The ectoderm becomes continuous again. Therefore, the
origin of the neural tube is the ectoderm.
It’s thought that the tube invaginates first at the rostral end, and
then caudally. The structures that remain open in the final stages
are the pores, at the rostral end and caudal end (known as
anterior and posterior neuroscope ). The caudal end finally
closes by the end of the 1st month, when the neural tube
becomes fully invaginated.
Others think that the closure takes place at different places at the same time.

Neural tube defects at this stage


SPINA BIFIDA: defect caused by neural tube not closing properly, hence the
vertebral arch doesn’t correctly form. This leads to different types of pathologies.
Defect in the vertebral arch (unfused): it’s not continuous, has two tips = bifida.
- **Spina bifida occulta:** In the **mildest** case, as it’s **asymptomatic** and doesn’t



really affect. There is incomplete closure but the tips are very proximate. The

Problems come when the formation comes with lack of proper closure. The content

Spinal cord
Neuroepithelial cells form the wall of the neural tube. They derive from ectoderm cells
that invaginate and end up forming pseudostratified epithelium, known as
neuroepithelium.
From this point, cells start dividing and proliferating.
3 stages in the formation of the spinal cord:
1. Proliferation

Undifferentiated neural stem cells start dividing close to the
lumen of the tube, giving rise to immature neurons
(neuroblasts) that will eventually differentiate.

The closely packed dividing cells form the ventricular layer
(neuroepithelial layer), which is pseudostratified . Will be
found lining the cavities in the brain.
[PDF p. 122]
2. Migration
Cells in the ventricular zone stop dividing and begin to
migrate and leave the ventricular zone, forming a second
layer known as the marginal layer.


As the wall thickens, an intermediate zone forms, known
as the mantle layer.


The marginal zone is in contact with the somites (forming the meninges), which limit
the amount of space available. Intermediate zone and marginal zone will quickly fill
the neural canal and start differentiating into neurons and glial cells.


This neural canal, which becomes known as the central canal, is lined by ependymal
cells derived from the neural tube.

Once the mantle layer becomes more and more thick, axons are formed through

maturation.

Cells concentrate and mature in the mantle layer, and once matured their axons
position themselves and flow towards the marginal layers (cranially and caudally).

Therefore:
 - **mantle layer** = we mainly find **cell bodies**
 - **marginal layer** = we mainly find **axons** . The marginal layer becomes **thicker**

at midgestation due to the myelination of the axons.
Neuroepithelial cells in the mantle layer will take on different roles depending on their
position relative to the sulcus limitans:
 cells posterior to the sulcus = **alar plate** → will become sensory neurons
 - cells anterior to the sulcus = **basal plate** → will become motor neurons



During specialization and differentiation, alar plate will become known as the dorsal
sensory horn and the basal plate, as the ventral motor horn


The cells in the ventricular layer which remain lining the ventricle will give rise to
ependymal cells

The spinal cord has a specific organization.
Notochord secretes molecules (ex: SHH) and
induces differentiation in the lower part of the
spinal cord. Cells begin to express particular genes
and differentiate. It allows the cells to acquire the
particular shape and functions of neurons from that
particular region.

neurons with a sensory function (afferent). The
basal plate will originate the ventral layer, which
will have a motor function (efferent).

Sensory neurons in the dorsal horn (CNS) will receive info from sensory neurons

These neurons are spinal nerves and make up the spinal system (PNS).
We will also find interneurons that connect sensory to motor neurons, which will


allow us to have coordinated reflexes.
Many of the formed neurons enter apoptosis
and die, as to make space for the
supporting cells in the nervous tissue (glial
cells), which also arise from the
neuroepithelium

2. PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (PNS)
Neural crest cells will give rise to dorsal root ganglia and sensory
neurons.
They are a specific population of cells located above the neural tube
of the embryo. As the tube invaginates, they are found at the tips of
the neural folds. When the folds fuse, these tips join and detach,
forming the neural crest. The origin of these cells is therefore the
ectoderm (ectodermal cells).
These cells become mesenchymal (ectoderm to mesoderm
transition). As they become mesenchymal, they will give rise to many
cell types. To such an extent that they are sometimes referred to as
the 4th germ layer.
[PDF p. 124]
The most important type of cell type they give rise to are all the sensory neurons in the
body, those that receive information from the periphery.
All the soma of those sensory neurons are located within sensory ganglia (dorsal root
ganglia, containing the soma).
Sensory neurons are a special type of neuron: they have two processes, are
pseudounipolar (Why pseudounipolar? because exiting the body we see only one process,
which then splits into two). They have:

A central process (synapse region with sensory neurons in dorsal horn)

Peripheral process (going towards the periphery, join motor fibers to form spinal
nerves)
Derivatives of neural crest cells
Many other cell types are derived from neural crest cells:
Melanocytes
-
Cells from autonomous nervous system
Sensory neurons (already mentioned)

Schwann cells (form the myelin sheath in the PNS).
Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons in the CNS (1
oligodendrocyte can give rise to many internodes)
and Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PNS (1
SC per internode).

Spinal nerves
There are 2 ganglia, one on each side at every segment of the spinal cord (segments = sets
of neurons at each level of the spinal cord).
The spinal nerve comprises:
The peripheral processes of sensory neurons coming from many parts of the
body. Incoming neuron (sensory) = dorsal or posterior root

The axons of motor neurons. Exting (motor) = ventral or anterior root

Spinal nerves are mixed, containing sensory fibers (axons) and motor fibers.
As they approach the spinal cord they split, as sensory neurons have
to reach the dorsal horn and motor neurons are exiting from the
ventral horn.
The spinal cord ends at the level of L3. But we also have the sacral
cord. They have to travel long distances to reach their corresponding
foramina and exit to innervate many parts of the body. This is why
myelination will be vital. Myelination starts around the 4th month of
gestation.

INTRODUCTION
The skeletal system is composed of bones and joints. It’s dense

EMBRYONIC ORIGIN OF THE AXIAL SKELETAL SYSTEM
Metamerism or metamery: repetition of alike elements (segments)
In the embryo, the somites form structures that resemble the axial skeleton.
They look like vertebrae. The vertebrae will come from somites, which are
derived from paraxial mesoderm in the embryo.
Therefore, mesenchyme giving rise to the axial skeleton of the trunk arises mainly
from the paraxial mesoderm (somites).
Somites are metameric structures, repeated elements that are similar along the
body of the embryo. Many structures have this metameric disposition, and many
maintain this metameric, segmentary organization, such as the vertebrae and the
ribs. This is so because they originate from somites.
The number of somites increases from 3rd to 5th week, when they start to
disappear . They will give rise to:

Axial skeleton (vertebral bodies and ribs)

- Portion of striated muscle
- Portion of skin
Spinal nerves will be innervating these somitic derivatives (somatic = derivative of
somitic).
Every somite will give rise to a portion of skin, which will be innervated by the
corresponding spinal nerve.

Correspondingly, a portion of muscle will be innervated by the spinal nerve of the
corresponding segment.
(neurologists know where to explore nerve innervation, which spinal nerve they are

Somites are mesoderm which acquires a roundish structure. During the 4th week of

forming the many regions, one of them being the sclerotome
We can also find the dermatome (→skin) and the dorsal and medial muscle cells.
Sclerotome : sclero- = hard, hardened; - tome = segment. Sclerotome is the portion of
somite-derived mesenchymal cells which will give rise to bone structures.
The somite cells are mesenchymal and can therefore migrate.

They migrate and come together surrounding the notochord. They condensate
around the notochord and will form the body of the vertebrae.
These cells will also migrate and surround the neural tube, forming the vertebral

ossification centers.

(except for some portions of cartilage at the

DEVELOPMENT OF THE MUSCLES IN THE TRUNK
Striated muscle of the trunk and limbs originate from the myotome that derives from
somites. Therefore they ultimately derive from the somites.
Muscles in the trunk, at least initially, have a segmentary organization. Some
maintain that segmentary organization in adult age: for instance, intercostal
muscles, as they are found next to the ribs, which during development make it
difficult for muscles to fuse and mesh together, maintaining them separated in
their initial segmentary disposition.
Skeletal muscle and dermis originate from the dorsolateral portion of the
somites, which differentiates into myotome and dermatome.
This is why this dorsolateral portion is known as dermo-myotome, as
one part will give rise to a portion of dermis (dermatome) and
another, to a portion of muscle (myotome)
The part of the somite that will give rise to muscle are the
dorsomedial and ventrolateral regions of that embryonic
dorsolateral portion.
Dorsomedial and ventrolateral portions
We have a dorsomedial region
A ventrolateral region
Each portion expresses different genes that will give rise to different muscles:
In the dorsomedial region: myoblasts won’t migrate very
far and stay close to the vertebral column. This portion of
muscle will give rise to the intrinsic muscles of the back.
They arise from this epaxial portion / dorsomedial
portion of the myotome. Will allow to extend the back.

In the ventrolateral portion: cells will migrate and form the

muscles of the anterolateral walls of the body (hypaxial
muscle). At this level, we find muscles such as the
intercostal muscles and rectum muscles.
[PDF p. 130]
Each portion of the somite is innervated by 1 spinal nerve, very soon in
development. A functional unit is formed very early on. As myoblasts
migrate, those from the same myotome carry with them their
corresponding segmentary nerve .
To know where a muscle originated from, we can know by paying
attention to which nerve innervates it. In this way we can know from
which somite it arose/which portion of myotome.
Spinal nerves
Spinal nerves contain both motor and sensory
neurons.

Motor neurons originate from the spinal
cord (neural tube) and extend their

axons to innervate effector muscle cells

Sensory neurons arise from neural
crest cells which migrate and
concentrate in ganglia. They transmit
signals coming from the corresponding
portion of skin

The muscles will have the motor fibers, and the corresponding portion of skin which
originated from the same somite will be innervated by the sensory neuron of said spinal
nerve.
Epaxial and hypaxial muscle innervation
2 sets of muscle: Epaxial (back) Hypaxial (anterolateral).
The spinal nerve branches into 2 rami, a dorsal one and a ventral one.

Epaxial muscles (intrinsic muscles of the back) are innervated by dorsal rami of
spinal nerves

-
Hypaxial muscles ( muscles of the anterolateral walls and muscles of the limbs) are
innervated by ventral rami of spinal nerves
The dorsal ramus is thinner as it innervates many less structures than the ventral one.
Both ramus contain sensory and motor neurons.

Congenital malformations regarding the muscles of the trunk
Children with prune-belly syndrome: hypoplasia or absence (aplasia) of
abdominal musculature.
The belly is distended as the organs are not enclosed by the muscles of the
trunk.
It’s a rare disorder characterized by the following triad of anomalies:

partial or complete absence of the abdominal muscles (hypoplasia or
aplasia)
failure of both testes to descend into the scrotum (bilateral
cryptorchidism)
and/or urinary tract malformations

* What is the difference between intramembranous and endochondral ossification?
-
Intramembranous ossification is the direct deposition of bone on thin layers of
connective tissue and is characteristic of the bones on the top of the skull (flat bones)
-
In endochondral ossification, cartilage is present: endochondral ossification involves
the replacement of hyaline cartilage with bony tissue. Most of the bones of the
skeleton are formed in this manner. Involves primary and secondary ossification
centers, and allows bone growth through epiphyseal plates where cartilage remains
un-ossified.
