Development of the appendicular skeleton and limb formation
LIMB FORMATION
Limbs are formed between the 5th and 8th week of development.
Almost totally formed by the end of the 2nd month.
Limb buds however appear by the end of the 4th week (28days), at
this stage they can already be appreciated on the embryo.
What are they made of?
They are an evagination of the lateral
aspect of the embryo: therefore, they are
made up of a chore of mesenchyme
(coming from the parietal layer of lateral
mesoderm) lined by a layer of ectoderm.
Very early on, a thickening of the ectoderm forms at the tip of the
limb bud. This tip becomes known as the apical ectodermal ridge
(AER), which is the structure that induces the outgrowth of the
limb (outward, distal pull).
Molecular regulation of patterning and growth in the limb
The growth is molecularly regulated. 3 axis:
Proximodistal axis
The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) promotes limb growth in the proximodistal direction.

FGF10 secreted by lateral plate mesoderm (underneath the ectoderm layer) in the
limb forming regions leads to the formation of the AER
The ridge secretes molecules (FGF4 and FGF8) that induce
proliferation of the mesenchyme in areas proximal to the ridge ,
such that these cells proliferate and remain undifferentiated .
As the limb grows, the most proximal part, not under the action
of the ridge, starts differentiating.

It follows a proximal-distal differentiation.
[PDF p. 133]
Dorsoventral limb axis
There is also a dorsal-ventral axis. It is directed by WNT-7, which is
expressed in the dorsal ectoderm, specifying these cells as dorsal.
Anteroposterior axis
(what is the thumb, etc…), determined by SHH, with a mediolateral
differentiation (from the medial towards the lateral side, from pinky to thumb)
However it’s the HOX genes that regulate the regional patterning of the
limb. In other words, the shapes and types of bones in the limb.
Development of the limb buds


4th week: around day 28, limb buds begin to appear at the end of the 4th
week. The upper limb is slightly ahead to the lower (3 days ahead).


5 week embryo : all limb buds are clearly visible at this point


6th week: the limb develops and forms a flat end, the hand plate in the upper
limbs and foot plate in the lower limb. We see thickenings within the hand
plate, elevations known as the digital rays (future fingers). We also see a
distal constriction. (externally we first see differentiation in the distal, growing
apical area)


7th week: digital rays appear in the footplate. The fingers in hands and feet
are slightly separated and we can begin to see the elbow and the knee.


Also during this 7th week, the upper and lower limbs rotate in opposite
directions.
Initially, thumb and toe are pointing upwards.
➢ The upper limb will rotate laterally 90 degrees (supine anatomical view),
implying:
    - The **elbow will be facing dorsally**
    - The **extensor muscles** will be located **posteriorly**

➢ The lower limb rotates medially almost 90 degrees.
    - The **knee** is **facing anteriorly**
    - **Extensor muscle** s lie **anteriorly**

○ 8th week: in the 8-week embryo, we see the rotated limbs, and separate
digits in hands and feet
How do the fingers separate?
Due to induced apoptosis . Programmed
cell death causes the destruction of
the interdigital spaces, and fingers
become fully separated.
[PDF p. 134]
Maximum point of vulnerability in relation to limb formation:
Between the 3rd and 8th week, during their period of formation. The defect will be more
severe during the 4th-5th week as damage here will cause the limb to maybe not form at
all. Defects further along in development will have more mild consequences.

Children born with limb abnormalities between 1957 a 1962 in

DEVELOPMENT OF THE APPENDICULAR SKELETON
The appendicular skeleton originates from mesenchymal cells arising
from the parietal layer of the lateral mesoderm


During the 5th week, mesenchymal bones arise in the limbs


During the 6th week, mesenchymal bone models in the limbs
undergo chondrification to form hyaline cartilage bone
models. Bones will become cartilaginous.


○ During the 7th week, bones continue to develop as
cartilaginous structures

At the 8th week, ossification begins in the long bones in primary ossification
centers, and initially occurs in the diaphyses of the bones.

In a 12-week fetus, primary ossification centers are present in nearly all
bones of the limbs.
Secondary ossification centers appear after birth.
Skeletal malformations
In a 3 month fetus, there are primary ossification centers (black) in all bones
of the body. Secondary ossification centers appear afterwards, in the
epiphysis, from where bones will grow.
Disruptions during these ossification processes lead to malformations:
● ACHONDROPLASIA is caused by a dominant autosomal mutation in the
receptor fibroblast growth factor 3 (FGFR3).
Consists in a disturbance of endochondral ossification during fetal
life at the epiphyseal cartilage plates, particularly of long bones.
● OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA: autosomal mutation,
dominant or recessive, for the gen of type I collagen. It
results in extreme bone fragility with spontaneous
fractures.

SKELETAL MUSCLES IN THE LIMB
Skeletal muscles in the limbs originate from the somites,
specifically from the ventrolateral myotome.
These cells, which migrate for the original dermo-myotome,
also expand into the growing limb buds and extend with
them (hypaxial muscle) . Give rise to flexor and extensor
muscles in the limb.
However, as they enter into the limb, the muscles fuse together
forming muscle bands and lose their segmentary
organization.
As this is hypaxial muscle, the muscles in the limbs will be innervated by ventral rami. The
nerves also extend with the migrating cells and combine, forming plexuses .
We will find networks / plexuses of ventral rami that have fused to finally form terminal
nerves in the limbs.

Brachial plexus: made up of ventral rami of spinal nerves C5-T1
- Lumbosacral plexus: made up of ventral rami of spinal nerves L2-S2

Dermatome in the limbs
In contrast to the skeletal muscle in the limbs, the dermatome cells in the limb maintain
their segmentary pattern. Although regions are slightly overlapped, they are well
differentiated.
Therefore, sensory innervation to the limb maintains a segmental pattern, reflecting the
embryological origin of each dermatome and its innervation.
Forelimbs with their sensory innervation to the
dermatomes represented:
There is also a cutaneous distribution of the
dorsal rami (towards the intrinsic muscles in the
back+dermatome) of the spinal nerves.
VASCULARIZATION
Blood vessels follow the same trajectory and
accompany the spinal nerves in extension
during muscle cell migration.
Blood vessels receive sympathetic innervation:
                           - Skeletal muscle bv = Ach

                           - Rest of bv = adrenaline and noradrenaline

Autonomous nervous system
Aside from the somatic nervous system, found innervating structures derived from somites,
we will also have an autonomous nervous system (visceral plexuses) . It innervates
smooth muscle in glands and viscera . It’s not a voluntary muscle. (Gray’s anatomy book.
Final part)
Somatic plexuses = striated muscle; visceral plexuses = muscles in viscera and glands
The Autonomous nervous system is further divided into Sympathetic (S) and
parasympathetic (PS) nervous systems.
Where does smooth muscle come from?
It originates from the splanchnic layer of the lateral
mesoderm. The parietal/somatic mesoderm lines the
body walls and this other layer surrounds the
endoderm of the gut, the forming endocardium, and
other viscera.

The endoderm will give rise to the mucosa
of the GI tract, whereas
The smooth muscle that forms the walls of the gut originates from the splanchnic
layer of the lateral mesoderm.

Di�erences between somatic and autonomous system

Somatic or spinal nerves innervate striated muscle via one

motor neuron.

Autonomic nerves innervate smooth muscle via two

neurons.
Autonomic nerves have second neurons:

The 2nd neuron of the SNA is always located in ganglia, and
is therefore found originating outside the CNS. We therefore
call it postganglionic neuron. The nerve (accumulation of
fibers) will be referred to as postganglionic fiber. It makes
reference to the trajectory followed by the axons.
The 1st neuron is located in the CNS (spinal cord or brain
stem) and activates the 2nd neuron, located in ganglion. It’s
known as preganglionic neuron, and its fiber, preganglionic
fiber, as its synapse occurs in the ganglion.

Where do those ganglionic neurons come from?
They come from the neural crest cells. NCCs give rise
to the ganglion of sympathetic trunk where the
somas of these neurons will be found, and from which
their processes will extend. Axons of the CNS finally
target and penetrate them to be in connection.
Neural crest cells will give rise to both Sympathetic
and Parasympathetic ganglionic neurons.
[PDF p. 138]
The autonomic nervous system is made up of afferent branches (sensory) and efferent
branches (motor).
VISCEROMOTOR FIBERS
These efferent visceromotor branches belong either to the Sympathetic
or Parasympathetic SNA. They are both characterized by having
autonomic nerves, made up of 2 neurons (pre and post ganglionic). It is a
two neuron motor system:
preganglionic neuron in the brainstem or spinal cord
postganglionic neuron in a ganglion. The postganglionic axon
synapses with its target.
Sympathetic and parasympathetic systems

Sympathetic system : fight and flight response. It prepares
the body for this situation, by activating organs in order to
respond to a danger/challenge.
Involves the activation of muscles, change to far sight rather
than near site (dilates pupils), increased heart rate, inhibits
digestion…

Parasympathetic: “rest and digest” response
It involves stimulation of digestion, slow contraction, reduces
blood flow to skeletal muscle,… Near sight is also facilitated
by the activation of the parasympathetic system (pupil
constriction).
Each of these two systems are complementary, but have different effects.
Location of preganglionic neurons
Preganglionic axons exit the spinal cord through the ventral root with other
motor axons. Where are they found? In the CNS .
Parasympathetic system: preganglionic cells originating from the
brainstem which innervate the visceral wall (through the vagus nerve
mainly), and preganglionic cells located at the sacral level (S2-S4).
We will see more about them later.

Sympathetic system: whole column of preganglionic cells along the
spinal cord (originate from T1 to L2 ).

a) SYMPATHETIC SYSTEM
Sympathetic ganglia
We find 2 sets of sympathetic ganglia:
1- Sympathetic trunk or chain: a series of paired ganglia at each side/level of the
spinal cord, found forming a chain. Also known as paravertebral.
2 - Preaortic single ganglia: located ventral to the aorta (= preaortic). They are located in
the abdominal and pelvic cavities. Also known as prevertebral. These ganglia are located
beneath the diaphragm, in the mentioned cavities.
[PDF p. 139]
Preganglionic sympathetic axons will synapse either in sympathetic chain ganglia
(paravertebral ganglia) or preaortic/prevertebral ganglia.
The Postganglionic sympathetic axons will then go and synapse with blood vessels, glands
and other tissues throughout the body.
Preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Preganglionic sympathetic neurons originate in the intermediolateral cell
column (lateral horn) in thoracic and upper lumbar spinal
cord (spinal segments T1 to L2 ). Only these portions have
said intermediate horn. Therefore, in order for upper and
lower postganglionic neurons to be innervated, preganglionic
neurons will have to originate in the intermediate horns at
T1-L2 levels, and travel through the sympathetic trunk to
reach their corresponding ganglion.
Therefore, we will see that preganglionic axons can ascend
or descend in the sympathetic chain on the sides of the
vertebrae, depending on which ganglion they are targeting.
What viscera will they innervate?

Dermal smooth muscle: there are other viscera that are only innervated by the
sympathetic nervous system: the dermis, such as the dermis in sweat glands,
arrector pili muscle (hair follicles) and blood vessels (endothelium). The
postganglionic neuron originates at the sympathetic trunk ganglia .
Thoracic viscera: the synapse between pre and postganglionic neurons won’t
occur in preaortic single ganglia. Therefore their 2nd effector neurons will be
located in the sympathetic chain. The postganglionic fibers form cardiac nerves.
Abdominal viscera : They will have their motor neurons located in preaortic single
ganglia. The long preganglionic fibers will form splanchnic nerves (thoracic and
lumbar)

arrector pili → sympathetic
trunk
Thoracic viscera →
sympathetic trunk. Cardiac
nerves = postganglionic
Abdominal and pelvic viscera
→ preaortic single ganglia.

preganglionic
[PDF p. 140]
As the distance between the trunk and preaortic ganglia is small in the SNS (both are very
close to the spinal cord):
- preganglionic fibers are quite short
postganglionic fibers will be very long and extended.
The preganglionic fiber is myelinated, so it has a whitish color.
These myelinated preganglionic fibers join together to form a cord,
known as the white communicating ramus = all the nervous cords
that are connecting the sympathetic ganglia to the spinal cord.
The second, visceromotor neurons, the postganglionic neurons
whose soma originates in the ganglion are unmyelinated. When
they exit the ganglion they form another cord known as the gray
communicating ramus = unmyelinated, so they have a Gray-ish
color.
Sympathetic fibers from T1-L2. Dermal smooth muscle
Innervation of dermal smooth muscle . It’s innervated exclusively by Sympathetic fibers.
Bodies of the preganglionic neurons originate in a special horn in the spinal cord: the
intermediate horn / lateral horn. This horn is found only from T1 to L2. It contains
sympathetic preganglionic visceromotor neurons.
As it is a motor, it will take the ventral root to exit and extend towards the neuron it has to
connect with, which is in the ganglion. Therefore it exits the nerve and enters the
ganglionic chain through the white communicating ramus.
Here, the postganglionic fiber exits and overlaps:

If it goes towards the back, it will take the dorsal ramus.
These glands in the dorsal portion (back) also have a
segmentary distribution as they are in every portion of
skin. Therefore, these postganglionic nerves follow the
same route as spinal nerves, taking the easiest route, in
order to reach sweat glands, hair follicles and blood
vessels of that part of the dermis.
If it goes towards the front, it will take the ventral ramus.
These visceromotor sympathetic neurons exit along with
many other motor neurons, going to innervate other bodily

structures.
Dermal sympathetic fibers beyond T1-L2
What happens above T1 or below L2? We don’t have
preganglionic fibers entering the corresponding ganglion of the
sympathetic chain, as at these levels of the spinal cord, we
don’t find an intermediate horn. Therefore, no
preganglionic fiber.
Who innervates the postganglionic fiber then? For this
purpose, preganglionic neurons originating at T1 go into their
corresponding ganglion; but instead of innervating the
postganglionic neurons at that level, they go up to innervate
these others that are at levels that lack intermediate horn. If it
were at a lumbar level, it would go down from L2 level to
connect with the lower sacral ganglia.
[PDF p. 141]
They enter the ganglionic chain and either go up or down to innervate postganglionic
nerves which are at a level in which there is no intermediate horn.
Sympathetic innervation of thoracic viscera
The thoracic viscera are innervated through both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic
divisions of the autonomic nervous system. The sympathetic nerves in question arise from
the cervical and thoracic sympathetic trunk ganglia.
At the thoracic level we have an intermediate horn. The postganglionic
fiber/axon directly exits the ganglion. It won’t follow the route taken by
spinal nerves ***** as it is not going to innervate muscles of the back,…etc, but
rather thoracic viscera (such as the heart, esophagus,… ). All together, the
postganglionic nerves which arise from the sympathetic trunk are called
cardiac sympathetic nerves, which join to form the cardiac sympathetic
plexus.
***** Postganglionic fibers which go to innervate smooth muscle in peripheral dermis and body
walls do follow the same route as spinal nerves = exit through dorsal and ventral rami
Sympathetic innervation of abdominal and pelvic viscera
They do have single preaortic ganglia. The preganglionic nerve will enter the
sympathetic trunk but exit the ganglion to directly enter the preaortic single ganglion,
where the postganglionic neuron is found. There, they will synapse.
These preganglionic neurons which exit the sympathetic trunk and meet up in preaortic
ganglia are known as splanchnic nerves, (greater splanchnic, lesser splanchnic and least
splanchnic plexuses). We find both thoracic splanchnic (innervating abdomen) and lumbar
splanchnic.
All these are splanchnic nerves = preganglionic fibers.
Sympathetic nerves generally enter the viscera together with the blood vessels. This is
so because all the arteries that also go to the kidneys, to the gut,… are exclusively
innervated by sympathetic nerves. These are visceromotor neurons.
[PDF p. 142]
b) PARASYMPATHETIC SYSTEM
Parasympathetic ganglia
Parasympathetic ganglia are generally only seen microscopically . They’re located very
close to the viscera or even in the wall of the viscera itself. Therefore, in the PS:

Axons of preganglionic neurons are very long
Postganglionic fibers will be quite short

Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons
The preganglionic neurons will be located in:


The brainstem


In the spinal cord from S2 to S4.
The postganglionic neurons, as they’re very close to the viscera, have very short axons.


Innervation from the brainstem
We have one nerve, the vagus nerve, which exits via the
jugular foramen, passess through the neck and provides
parasympathetic innervation for abdominal viscera and
thoracic viscera.
It slows down the heart rate, contracts the bronchi,… and
stimulates the GI tract.
It innervates all the way down to the distal third of the colon,
and is therefore “in charge” of ⅔ of the transverse colon
(AC, TC, DC).
Therefore, it innervates thoracic and abdominal viscera all
the way to the Transverse Colon (TC).
(There are also other clusters of neurons innervating facial
structures, which as well as the vagus, also arise in the brain
stem. But we will focus on the vagus nerve).
Innervation from S2-24
Preganglionic fibers arising from S2-S4 are known as pelvic nerves. They innervate the
rest of the GI tract (remaining abdominal viscera: AC and DC + ⅓ of TC) and pelvic
viscera, the remaining structures.
We call these nerves pelvic splanchnic nerves
(don’t mix with thoracic and lumbar splanchnic,
from the sympathetic). These pelvic splanchnic
nerves are preganglionic fibers which reach the
bladder, rectum, prostate in males, clitoris in
females,… they are involved in erection,
therefore also known as erogenous nerves.
These nerves form the inf. hypogastric plexus.
                     - PS innervation of the abdominal viscera: There is a

whole network of tiny ganglia containing postganglionic
neurons and fibers which stimulate peristaltism .
[PDF p. 143]
PS innervation of pelvic viscera: there is no intermediolateral horn in S2-S4, but we
do have motor neurons. They exit from the motor horn, go through the ventral root
and exit it. They follow the route towards the midline and innervate for example, the
bladder, to trigger and regulate micturition.
VISCEROSENSORY FIBERS
Sympathetic and parasympathetic systems stimulate smooth muscle. But viscera also have
sensory innervation (stomach pain, menstrual pain,…). We will also find sensory fibers
conveying information about pain or how full the viscera are (distention in the stomach,
rectum,..)
2 modalities of sensory innervation:
- Pain
- Distention
[PDF p. 144]
Trajectory of these viscerosensory fibers

Pain: as a general rule, pain information travels
with motor sympathetic fibers (although in the
opposite direction ). They generally accompany
the sympathetic system in the opposite direction,
except for pelvic pain which will accompany the

PS.
Therefore, they will convey pain information and
reach the CNS, first through white communicating
rami and then through the dorsal root.

Distention: distention information accompanies
Parasympathetic fibers ( vagus nerve and other
cranial nerves) in the opposite direction. They

enter the CNS at the brainstem and sacral level.
Distension information
Therefore, distension sensory info from thoracic
viscera, abdominal viscera, till the distal third of TC
will travel following the vagus nerve.
Distension information of the pelvic viscera travels with the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
Pain in pelvic viscera will also follow this trajectory, accompanying the pelvic splanchnic
nerve.
Pain information
Pain information is conveyed by sensory neurons accompanying
Sympathetic nervous system. It will accompany either cardiac
nerves, thoracic splanchnic or lumbar splanchnic nerves, in the
opposite direction. They reach the spinal nerve via the white
communicating ramus.
As said, this is so except for pelvic pain, which follows the same route as pelvic
splanchnic nerves in the PS.
Where are their sensory neurons located?
Sensory neurons are ALWAYS located in sensory ganglia, in this case, in the ganglia
prior to entering the jugular nerve which contains all the bodies of the sensory neurons. In
the brain stem, it makes synapse in an area similar to the dorsal horn.
Chroma�n cells
Some neural crest cells enter adrenal structure and stay there (chromaffin
cells). These cells release norepinephrine and epinephrine to the
bloodstream upon stimulation, as if it were a sympathetic ganglion
located in the adrenal gland. When activated, the adrenal medulla
releases epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood, which potentiates
sympathetic activity throughout the body. Needed to coordinate the bodily
“fight-or-flight” response to fear, stress, exercise, or conflict.
[PDF p. 145]
NEUROTRANSMITTERS
All preganglionic fibers release Acetylcholine (Ach) neurotransmitter (cholinergic).
The neurotransmitters vary between the postganglionic fibers of the Sympathetic and
Parasympathetic nervous systems:
Sympathetic neurotransmitters
As said, the preganglionic fiber will release Ach
- The second neurotransmitter will generally be Norepinephrine and Epinephrine
(adrenergic), as is the case of arrector pili muscles, blood vessels of the skin,…

However there are exceptions: postganglionic sympathetic fibers innervating sweat
glands and blood vessels in skeletal muscle will release Ach

Adrenal medulla
Adrenal glands are innervated by preganglionic sympathetic neurons. They receive
stimulation through the release of Ach, and they themselves release Norepinephrine and
Epinephrine into the bloodstream. They are not postganglionic neurons, but are
considered as such as they fulfill the same function, with the exception that instead of
innervating smooth muscle, they release their neurotransmitters into the blood.
Adrenal glands are adrenergic .
Parasympathetic neurotransmitters
The preganglionic fiber will release Ach.
Here in the PS, the postganglionic fiber will also
release Ach to innervate smooth muscle (cholinergic)

Heart rate, 98 beats per minute.

epidural = space between the vertebral arch. Anesthesia is administered there to

What complication has appeared as a result of the anesthesia?
Arterial hypotension as a direct consequence. Anesthesia has the intention of blocking
sensory information, but has had other effects.
The consequence that the anesthesia has brought this patient is:
Arterial hypotension (low bp)
Tachycardia: heart rate increases to compensate the hypotension, to maintain blood
supply to all the organs
Why is the woman suffering from hypotension?
Because the anesthesia has reached the sympathetic system, which is found innervating
smooth muscle in the walls of the vessels.
The vascular smooth muscle is innervated only by the sympathetic system which is
normally activated at a basal level. This small muscle contraction is needed to maintain a
constant pressure in the vessels, by keeping them constricted. Inhibition of the sympathetic
nerves after the epidural anesthesia decreases the stimulation of alpha1 receptors in
the arterioles, increasing the diameter of arterioles and leading to arterial hypotension.
By trying to block the afferent sensory system, we somehow block the motor sympathetic
nerves. The vascular smooth muscle is normally activated, to induce a basal sympathetic
tone. If inhibited, it induces ↓ in neurotransmitter release (alpha1 receptors) = smooth
muscle in the vessels relaxes = increase in arterial diameter = ↓ bp = hypotension

Key ideas:

Organs and systems such as the vascular system are exclusively innervated by
the sympathetic nerves. Other examples would be the kidney and the system
regulating glucemia.
There is a basal sympathetic tone in the sympathetic system and the regulation of
function under that control depends on the increase or decrease of that basal tone.
That is why our patient responded to the treatment with alpha-1 receptor (like

Other organs have both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation and their
regulation depends on the basal sympathetic and the parasympathetic tones .
An example of this is the heart. That is why if our patient experiences bradycardia

CHARACTERISTICS


It’s an avascular tissue; in general connective tissue is highly vascularized, except in
the case of cartilage. This is why this tissue is compact and forms thin layers, as to
easily obtain nutrients through diffusion from surrounding tissues, drawn in
through osmosis.
They proliferate very slowly as they have a scarce supply of nutrients which they
have to store. As an adaptation to this, chondrocytes have developed a way to store
energy, in the form of glycogen. Therefore, cartilage is very rich in glycogen.
(chondrocytes replicate very slowly that’s why it is difficult to recover from lesions
affecting cartilage).


It serves as a precursor/model for embryonic development and subsequent
growth of many long bones. Cartilage is replaced by bone tissue in adult life,
except for the surfaces that articulate with other bones.

The cartilaginous ECM allows the surrounding tissues to bear mechanical stresses

Serves as a framework to give support to other tissues


It’s shock-absorbing and acts as a gliding area for joints


It facilitates bone movements


It’s responsible for development and formation of long bones

TYPES OF CARTILAGE

Hyaline cartilage (type II collagen)   - It’s the most abundant cartilage in the body. It’s

found on articular surfaces (articular cartilage = specialized form
of hyaline cartilage, has NO perichondrium) , forming the nasal
septum and the tracheal rings, sternal end of ribs, … It also

Hyaline cartilage forms the temporary skeleton in the fetus, until

Elastic cartilage (type II collagen)   - found in pinna of the ear,

ear). Abundant elastic fibres.

Fibrocartilage (large amount of type I and type II collagen)   - found

CARTILAGE ECM
Some areas of the matrix stain more blue than other areas; these darker areas represent
regions with more fibers, specifically type II collagen. In the lighter areas of the matrix, we
find more proteoglycans and therefore, water.
The matrix is not homogeneous (not the same amount of substances in each
of the regions) because we need areas which draw in water and therefore,
nutrients and oxygen through diffusion, and others which provide protection.


The darker matrix (more basophilic = seen in blue/dark red in this case)
which is adjacent to the chondrocytes is known as the territorial matrix . Richer in
proteoglycans, stains darker.


The lighter matrix ( eosinophilic areas = clearer), found between isogenous
groups is the interterritorial matrix . Less proteoglycans, stains darker. All
the O2 and nutrients can easily flow and diffuse into the different cells.


CARTILAGE FORMATION / GROWTH
Cartilage begins to form from embryonic mesenchymal
cells. It can either originate from fibroblasts and
chondroblasts found in the perichondrium layer, or
from interstitial growth through the mitotic division of
chondrocytes, which results in the formation of
isogenous groups that accumulate in lacunae.
[PDF p. 154]
Appositional growth: consists in the deposition of new cartilage on the surface of
existing cartilage: it grows from the outside, originating from the perichondrium. This
occurs through the differentiation of fibroblasts, a layer of cells with proliferative
capacity. Each layer contains more and more differentiated cells until they finally
derive to chondrocytes (fibroblasts-chondroblasts-chondrocytes). This
differentiation by layers is known as appositional growth.
Interstitial growth: formation of new cartilage within existing cartilage: this is
another way in which cartilage can grow (which is really slow) and is known as
interstitial growth (through the middle). It occurs through the division of
chondrocytes. All the daughter cells will be a clone of the mother cells, which will
give place to clonal groups found within the lacunae, known as isogenous groups.
Interstitial growth is not an efficient kind of growth, as it is a slow
process that takes a long time to happen. This is why it takes lots
of time to recover from a cartilage injury; the cells will divide very
slowly. These cells can be stimulated to grow through
physiotherapy: throughout movement and exercising, we are
inducing these cells to proliferate.

PERIOSTEUM

Periosteum is a layer of noncalcified connective tissue, found covering bone on its
external surfaces (except at synovial articulations and muscle attachments).
It presents an outer dense, fibrous collagenous layer and an inner cellular
osteoprogenitor ( osteogenic ) layer.
Sharpey fibers (type I collagen) attach the periosteum to the bone surface. It serves as

Its function is to provide cells, fibroblasts, that will differentiate into osteoblasts which will
later on differentiate into osteocytes . This type of growth (one layer on top of the other) is
known as appositional growth.

ENDOSTEUM

Endosteum consists of thin, specialized connective

osteoblasts, which begin to secrete collagen type I.
Therefore, its function is to supply osteoprogenitor cells
(fibroblasts) and osteoblasts for bone growth and repair.

➢ What is the main difference between trabeculae and cortex bone?
The organization .

In trabecular bone (immature bone), we don’t find osteons, just bone tissue and
osteocytes. Collagen isn’t being deposited in concentric lamellae, but in lines. There
are no central vessels (no Harvesian canal) , so they are therefore not concentric.
In addition to this, in immature bone, we can find different ranges of calcification.
Woven bone/osteoid will start to become calcified in certain areas, and remain

unmineralized in others.

In cortical bone (mature bone), we can observe these concentric structures
known as osteons. In this mature bone, the matrix is all calcified.

➢ What do we mean by lamellar and non-lamellar bone?

Lamellar bone = calcified bone. It can be concentric on non-concentric.

Cortical bone (concentric calcified) and trabecular bone (non-concentric calcified)

Non-lamellar = unmineralized (non-concentric decalcified) . Also
known as “woven” bone, unmineralized spongy bone.

In trabecular bone, the linear deposition of collagen becomes calcified and
therefore matured (woven → lamellar). Therefore, it becomes lamellar bone.
It’s still, however, a non-concentric structure. Spongy bone tissue does not
contain the osteons that constitute compact bone tissue. Instead, it consists of
trabeculae, which are lamellae that are arranged as rods or plates.

REMODELING PROCESS
Bone mass is maintained by a balance between formation ad destruction, controlled by
the activity of osteoblasts, which form bone, and osteoclasts, which break it down. Bone
remodeling has to go through several phases
OSTEOCLASTS
Osteoclasts are in charge of bone degradation, and secrete acid, collagenases and
proteases that demineralize the bone matrix and degrade matricellular proteins such as type
I collagen. Hydroxyacetate = calcium phosphate. Main component of bone, which is liberated
upon demineralization.
They are derived from myeloid lineage cells (monocytes). Signalling molecules (growth
factors such as M-CSF and RANKL , mainly released by osteoblasts), which support
osteoclastogenesis, cause the transformation of monocytes into osteoclasts,
characteristic due to their polynucleated features.
Osteoprotegerin is an endogenous receptor of RANKL that inhibits
osteoclastogenesis.
Parts and characteristics
Osteoclasts are highly polarized (EM image) . Invaginations of the
membrane on the basal face, found forming the ruffled border,
increase the area of the membrane, and therefore increase the
surface area for bone reabsorption. This zone is known as the
sealing zone, where reabsorption process takes place. Enzymes are
released from this zone onto mineralized bone, and as the osteoclast
advances, the bone becomes demineralized and all the minerals
are freed, becoming readily available for the body through
circulation.
* Excessive bone loss = osteoporosis
OSTEOBLASTS
Osteoblasts are in charge of bone formation, which originate from mesenchymal stem
cells coming from within the bone marrow .
Osteoclasts resorb bone, thus allowing the release of factors usually stored in the bone
matrix that recruit osteoblasts in the resorbed area. Once recruited, osteoblasts produce
the new bone matrix and promote its mineralization, thus completing the bone
remodeling process.

Functional classification of neurons
Neurons are spatially organized in chains and networks. We have 3 different

Sensory neurons: receive information from the internal and external environment.
They conduct impulses to the CNS for processing and analysis.


Interneurons: conduct information and connect different neurons in a chain of


information. They generally connect sensory and motor neurons. In charge of
regulating signals transmitted to neurons. Most abundant type of neurons we have.

Motor neurons: transmit the information from the CNS to the motor cell/effector

cell in order to exert the response (muscles and glands), or to other neurons.

Multipolar neurons: a single axon and
more than one dendrite, with different


branching degrees. These are the most
abundant type in vertebrates.

- Microtubules (24 nm): in the soma
-
Microfilaments (actin filaments, 6 nm):
associated with the plasma membrane.
[PDF p. 166]
Dendrites
Receive stimuli (signals) from sensory cells, axons, or other neurons and convert these
signals into small electrical impulses (NOT action potentials yet) transmitted toward the
soma.
Generally branched (arborized structures) (except in bipolar neurons) , allowing neurons to
obtain stimuli from very different neurons .
Besides this, within the branches they contain very different spines which play a very
important role in transmission as they increase the area available for synapse formation.
These spines decrease with age and poor nutrition.

Its cytoplasm is similar to that of the soma
With reduced number of organelles as they are not necessary,
with the exception of mitochondria
Abundant mitochondria (necessary)

Axons
Axons conduct impulses away from the soma to the axon terminals without any diminution
in their strength.
Axon hillock
Axons originate from the axon hillock, which is continuous with the soma
(can be considered as a specialized region of the soma) ; however, in this
axon hillock:

There are no Nissl bodies, which are characteristic of the soma.
They also have a very abundant network of microtubules and
neurofilaments which will allow the passage of mitochondria and

vesicles into the axons.
It is the region where the electrical impulse is generated.
Axon

The proper axon has a surrounding plasma membrane, known as axolemma

Cytoplasm known as axoplasm:
    **No RER or Golgi** as it won’t be in charge of any synthesis

    However, it contains **abundant cytoskeleton**
    - Also contains **SER and elongated mitochondria.**

It derives into many small branches = axon terminals, regions
where synapsis will take place. Impulses are passed to another
neuron or other types of cells.
-
Protected by glial cells, in general because the axon is a very
thin, long structure and if it gets damaged, we risk losing many
connections. They can be up to 1m long, so they have to be
protected, and this is done by glial cells.
[PDF p. 167]
Axonal transport systems
In the axons, mostly in the membrane, we have to transport molecules. This is a bidirectional
mechanism:
Anterograde transport: from the cell body to axon terminals (periphery), where
there is regeneration of proteins and vesicles. MAPs, such as kinesin, plays an
important role in anterograde transport.
Retrograde transport: from axon terminal to body. It’s the way of recycling
material. Dynein plays important role in this retrograde transport.
Recognizing neurons under microscope:
Clear, pale nucleus, clearly well-centered
Dark, condensed and developed nucleolus
Basophilic clumps, Nissl bodies, found
within the cytoplasm of the soma
Large size with a characteristic shape
NEUROGLIAL CELLS
Found both in CNS and PNS. The neuroglia is a web of tissue composed of modified
ectodermal elements.
Main function of neuroglial cells is to support and protect neurons . But they’re also
involved in synapse.
They don’t conduct neurological impulse, but are involved in synapsis by providing some
regulation of neurons in the process of neural transmissions through:
Actively monitoring synapses
Removing neurotransmitters from synapses
Delivering molecules known as gliotransmitter substances into the synaptic space
From an imaging point of view, we can’t really differentiate the different neuroglial cells
under conventional staining. We have to use specific staining, gold and silver stains.
- IN THE CNS:
Astrocytes
They are very branched, with long extended processes. Astrocytes are the largest of
neuroglial cells, characterized by having many processes, with different functions:
Surrounding blood vessels through expanded pedicles (vascular feet). They
participate in reinforcing the blood-brain barrier: it tightly regulates exchange and
passage of substances from blood to brain stroma.

Surrounding neurons, scavenging for ions involved in synapses after they have
completed their function, and supplying energy for metabolism

In contact with meninges (pia mater), also creating a protective barrier. They form a
protective sealed barrier between the pia mater and the nervous tissue.

In the brain, astrocytes form scar tissue (glial scar) after injury to the CNS.

[PDF p. 168]
Different types of astrocytes :


Protoplasmic astrocytes: .
Mainly found in **gray matter**
- Have **short processes but very arborized**, which have the mentioned



functions (enveloping blood vessels, neurons, and synaptic areas) .
- In these cells, we can find some intermediate filaments composed of glial
fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP).
- Mainly involved in the formation of blood brain barrier and its maintenance


Fibrous astrocytes:
- Mainly found in **white matter**
- **long, slender processes** with **little arborization,**



carrying out characteristic functions.
- Many intermediate filaments composed of GFAP
Blood-brain barrier
In CNS there is very tight regulation of the diffusion of molecules from blood into nerve
tissue. This is mainly controlled by the blood-brain barrier, composed of tight junctions
formed between adjacent endothelial cells in the capillary walls surrounding nerve tissue.
Tight junctions exert a very restricted regulation:

02, H20, C02 and certain liposoluble molecules can pass via diffusion

Some Ions can pass through active transport
Macromolecules and drugs have to go through receptor
mediated transport.
This barrier is supported by the feet of astrocytes. These
astrocytes don’t form occluding junctions, they reinforce those
formed between endothelial cells by connecting through
anchoring junctions. They themselves don’t create the tight
junctions but reinforce them.
Oligodendrocytes
Oligodendrocytes live symbiotically with neurons. They are essential in the survival of
neurons in the CNS. They protect the axons of neurons in the CNS. Can be found both in
grey and white matter.
Characteristics
They have a small, condensed centered nucleus
They contain an electron dense cytoplasm.
    - Ribosomes

    - Numerous microtubules

    - Mitochondria

    - RER

    Large Golgi complex

[PDF p. 169]

Have a few short processes.
The short processes surround the axon and create concentric layers of myelin,
myelin sheaths, which will play an important role in the electrical transmission.
Oligodendrocytes form several processes, and each process produces myelin for a
single internode. Therefore, each oligodendrocyte can myelinate several axons.

Microglial cells
Very similar to astrocytes under the microscope.
They are small, phagocytic neuroglial cells derived from the mononuclear phagocytic cell
population in the bone marrow.
Characteristics
Present a condensed, elongated nucleus


Many short, branching processes. Very arborized


They are sort of the immune cells of the CNS.
When activated, they change their shape, loose branching and
become more similar to macrophages. They start to secrete
cytokines which recruit other immune cells (T cells); they act as


APCs.
Ependymal cells

Derived from the neuroepithelium

Located in very particular places: they are the epithelial cells
that line the neural tube and ventricles of the brain


In certain regions of the brain, they contain cilia (responsible
for moving the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF))


Modified ependymal cells contribute to the formation of the
choroids plexus (It is a highly organized tissue that lines all
the ventricles of the brain. Resides in the innermost layer of the
meninges (pia mater) which is in close contact with the cerebral
cortex and spinal cord).


[PDF p. 170]
- IN THE PNS:
Schwann cells
Their function is similar to that of oligodendrocytes . They protect and isolate the
neurons, same as oligodendrocytes in the CNS. But they exert their functions in cells of
the PNS.
Oligodendrocytes are flat cells ( with basement membrane) with only a few mitochondria
and a small Golgi region.
They can form:
myelinated covers, surrounding the axons
unmyelinated covers : in this situation, Schwann cells are just found surrounding the
axon.
A single Schwann cell can only insulate a single axon in a myelinated fiber, whereas a
single oligodendrocyte may insulate several axons.
Neuroglial cells. Origin and functions
SYNAPSES
Synapse consists in the signal transmission from one neuron to another or to another
cell type (e.g., muscle cell) . Classified according to the site of synaptic contact and the
method of signal transmission:
Classification according to site

Axodendritic synapses: most common type,

between axon and dendrite


Axosomatic synapses: between axon and soma


Axoaxonic synapses: between 2 axons, much less


common
[PDF p. 171]
Classification according to signal transmission


Chemical synapses. Unidirectional
- **Most common** type of **neuron-neuron synapse,** and the **only** type of



muscle-neuron synapse (neuromuscular junction).
- Occurs by the release of neurotransmitters from the
presynaptic cell which reach and act on the
postsynaptic cell.
    - The **transmission will be slower** than the electrical

synapse as it is a longer process. Delayed by about 0.5
ms, time required for secretion and diffusion of
neurotransmitter from the presynaptic membrane into
the synaptic cleft and then to the postsynaptic
membrane.
    - Also important: **neurotransmitters themselves don’t**

effect the change; they only activate a response in
the receptor cell.


Electrical synapses. Bidirectional
- Much **less numerous** than chemical synapses

- Consists in the **movement of ions** from one neuron to



another via gap junctions.
    They **transmit the action potential** of the presynaptic cell

directly to the postsynaptic cell
- It’s much faster than the chemical synapse. Signal
transmission across these synapses is nearly
instantaneous
Synaptic morphology (chemical synapse)
Axon terminal:

Axon terminals can have different shapes. They vary
morphologically, depending on the site of contact.

They contain synaptic vesicles (distinguishable
morphological features)

Contain voltage-gated calcium channels which will play
important role in the process of synapse (regulate the entry
of Ca2+ into the axon terminal)
The region of the presynaptic membrane in “contact” with
the postsynaptic has a thicker membrane in the area of

synapses.
Synaptic vesicles fuse with vesicles and release the containing neurotransmitters
into the synaptic space.
The postsynaptic membrane:
The membrane of the neuron or other target cell that is receiving the impulse is also
thickened.
[PDF p. 172]
Synaptic cleft:
It’s the narrow space (20-30 nm wide) between presynaptic - postsynaptic membranes.
Space neurotransmitters have to diffuse across to reach the next neuron.
Astrocytes:
Astrocytes protect the synaptic region. They aren’t actively involved in
synapsis, but participate by:
removing neurotransmitters from the synaptic space (glutamate)

secrete molecules that will play a role in regulating synapse
(gliotransmitters)

Synaptic vesicles and neurotransmitters:
Synaptic vesicles: small, membrane-bound structures
in the axoplasm of the transmitting neuron. Synaptic
vesicles discharge neurotransmitters into the
synaptic cleft by exocytosis. Can be seen through EM
like small vesicles with a membrane, found in the
cytoplasm of the transmitting neuron.

Neurotransmitters : Produced, stored (vesicles),
and released by presynaptic neurons.
Released by exocytosis : they diffuse through
the synaptic cleft and bind different receptors in
the postsynaptic neuron, facilitating the
transmission of the electrical impulse. They
generate an action potential:

-
Transmitter-gated channels
-
G-protein–coupled receptors

Neuromuscular junction
Particular type of synapses: Neuromuscular junction / Motor end plate (muscle
innervation). It’s a type of chemical synapse.
1 Axon can innervate several muscle cells, and therefore:

Motor unit refers to the group of muscle cells innervated
by the same motor neurons
Motor end plate is the large area where the different
synapses take place. We can see that the axons branch

into several axon terminals.
[PDF p. 173]
Focusing on one motor end plate, we focus on a neuromuscular junction:
The general structure is the one already seen in chemical synapses. The special feature is
that in the postsynaptic membrane, there are junctional folds. These are deep
invaginations of the muscle cell plasma membrane ( sarcolemma ) which increase the
surface area for the neurotransmitter (ACh) to interact.
NERVE FIBERS
1 axon = 1 nerve fiber.
Motor neurons:
The axon leaves CNS, and in the PNS the nerve fibers (individual axons)
group, forming bundles which give place to nerves.

In the CNS, enveloped by Oligodendrocytes, with myelin sheath
In PNS, enveloped by Schwann cells, myelinated or
unmyelinated sheaths

Myelin sheath
Axon recovered by concentric myelin layers

Produced by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and by Schwann cells in the PNS

Deposited in concentric layers forming an insulating sheet. Seen as several spiral
layers of the plasma membrane of an oligodendrocyte or Schwann cell wrapping
around the axon

However this layer is not continuous. It has the length that a single Schwann
cell/oligodendrocyte can cover. These gaps left between adjacent glial cells are

known as nodes of Ranvier.

The thickness of these layers is usually constant along the length of an axon;
however, thickness usually increases as the axonal diameter increases.

Process of formation:
Schwann cell/oligodendrocyte starts to wrap around a portion of an axon;
their cytoplasm and plasma membrane begin to form consecutive spiral layers
around the axon
Overlapping inner layers of the Schwann
cell/oligodendrocyte plasma membrane form the myelin
sheath.

The nucleus gets pushed to the periphery of the cell.

[PDF p. 174]
Image 1: nucleus of the Schwann cell (SC) + axon (A) embedded in its cytoplasm and
recovered by myelin sheath (M); inside said axon, we see microtubules (MT) and
neurofilaments (NF); on the top right, we see another SC surrounding an axon and a forming
myelin sheath (FM); on the bottom right, another axon-surrounding SC, but in this case the
recovering is unmyelinated (UM).
Image 2: axon, with microtubules (MT) and NF. We can find organelles (mitochondria, Mit) +
a surrounding myelin sheath (M). The surrounding cytoplasm corresponds to that of a
schwann cell. Extracellular granules (C) correspond to collagen fibers, transversal cut.
Schmidt-Lanterman clefts
The Schwann cell or oligodendrocyte’s cytoplasm is found surrounding
the myelin sheath, but also in between the myelin sheath and the
axon. There has to be communication between the inner and outer
cytoplasm of the recovering cells. This is done through incisions in
myelin, known as Schmidt-Lanterman clefts.
They are oblique discontinuities of the myelin sheath due to the
presence of Schwann cell (or oligodendrocyte) cytoplasm within the
myelin.
Nodes of Ranvier
Nodes of Ranvier are periodic gaps in the insulating sheath between Schwann cells or
oligodendrocytes. It facilitates the rapid conduction of nerve impulses.
Differences between PNS and CNS:

In PNS, the small unprotected area (node) is covered
by interdigitated cytoplasmic processes of the
adjacent Schwann cells, which protect the axon.
In CNS, the myelin free surface at the node is
covered by a foot plate of an astrocyte, protecting
those unmyelinated regions.

In these regions there are abundant Na+ voltage gated
channels to facilitate “saltatory” conduction.
[PDF p. 175]
Internodes
Length between adjacent Nodes of Ranvier (extension of the recovering cells which will
give place to the myelin sheets).
Vary in length from 0.08 to 1 mm, depending on the size of the Schwann cells or
oligodendrocytes associated with the fiber.
Myelinated nerve fibers
Cross section and longitudinal view of a peripheral nerve. We can see the axons and
epineurium on the left image. We can also distinguish Schmidt-Lanterman clefts and Nodes
and Ranvier.
Unmyelinated nerve fibers
Surrounded by a large number of Schwann cells.
In the case of SC unmyelinated fibers, a single SC is seen to recover
many axons at a time. Many axons embedded within its cytoplasm.
Remember: only SC give rise to unmyelinated fibers.
[PDF p. 176]
Myelinated vs Unmyelinated

In CNS, oligodendrocytes only produce
myelinated fibers. In PNS they can be myelinated
or unmyelinated (SCs)

Since impulses in myelinated axons jump from one
node of Ranvier to another, propagation of the
impulse is much faster in myelinated axons. For
unmyelinated fibers, it has to be continuously
regenerated so as not to lose action potential.
-
Myelinated SC → 1 axon; Unmyelinated SC → several axons
Myelinated-related diseases
Multiple sclerosis, (MS), the typical disease related to unmyelinated fibers which should be
myelinated.
NERVES
Nerves are cordlike bundles made up of nerve fibers,
surrounded by connective tissue sheaths. Within each
nerve bundle it is difficult to distinguish any other cells.
Whitish surrounding structure (light microscopy): myelin
Connective tissue components: we can differentiate three
layers:


Epineurium: the outermost . It consists of dense fibrous connective tissue
(fascia), found surrounding nerve bundles. Often embedded in adipose tissue.


Perineurium: surrounds each bundle of nerve fibers (fascicle) .
Made up of specialized connective tissue cells, which block and regulate the
transmission of specific molecules by binding through tight junctions. Form the
blood-nerve barrier, preventing the transmission of toxic components.


Endoneurium: connective tissue layer that surrounds each individual nerve fiber.
Made up of a thin layer of reticular fibers and collagen, containing some


fibroblasts.
[PDF p. 177]
GANGLIA
Encapsulated aggregations of neuronal cell bodies (soma) outside the CNS + abundant
small glial cells (satellite cells). Found containing the neuronal bodies.
Neurons surrounded by satellite cells (glial cells marked by blue arrow heads)
WHITE MATTER & GRAY MATTER
Both present in the CNS. We will differentiate them by identifying the different parts of the
neuron.
Gray matter


Neuronal cell bodies (soma)


Dendrites


Some axons: mostly unmyelinated fibers +
some myelinated fibers
Neuroglial cells
White matter

Neural axons: mostly myelinated nerve fibers



some unmyelinated
Neuroglial cells


There are 2 very clear regions in the CNS:
In the spinal cord:

Grey matter located in the center of the spinal

cord

Outer white matter

In the cerebellum:

Grey matter in the outer layer
White matter in the inner layer

MENINGES
Membranous coverings of brain and spinal cord, formed by connective
tissue. Found protecting the inner nerve tissue. 3 layers:
- Dura Mater: Outermost, lining the bony skull and close to vertebrae.
- Arachnoid Mater: Intermediate, abutting the dura
- Pia Mater: Innermost, highly vascular. Lying directly on the surface

Muscle histology I. Skeletal muscle
Muscle cells are specialized elongated cells with the primary roles of contraction.
OVERVIEW
Muscle can be classified into 2 major groups:

Striated muscle (cells present striations)

- skeletal muscle
- cardiac muscle
● Smooth muscle (no striations)
Muscle cells are contractile filaments, whose major components are actin and myosin
filaments.
Regarding contraction, we find:
-
Voluntary contraction (skeletal muscle)
Involuntary contraction (in cardiac and smooth muscle)
Skeletal muscle is found attached to bones and / or skin;
cardiac muscle is located in the walls of the heart; smooth
muscle located in almost all the visceral organs of the body:
arteries, airways,… The appearance of the different types varies
greatly.
CONNECTIVE TISSUE IN MUSCLE
Found surrounding and giving structure to the muscles. Connective tissue conveys neural
and vascular elements to muscle cells and provides a vehicle that harnesses the forces
of muscle contraction.
Organization:

Epimysium : surrounds the entire muscle and forms a connection between skeletal
muscle to other muscles and tendons, which at the same time connect to bone . It

will be important in conveying the contraction to tendons = pull on bones.


Perimysium : layer of connective tissue surrounding each muscle bundle. Also
mostly found in skeletal muscle.


Endomysium : surrounding each individual muscle cell. It’s composed of collagen
fibers, reticular fibers and some fibroblasts. In skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.


[PDF p. 180]
SKELETAL MUSCLE
Skeletal muscle in longitudinal view:

Multinucleated cells (fibers)
Nuclei are located at the periphery of the cell
Long, large cells , cylindrical in shape
The cytoplasm presents striations which
corresponds to the myofibrils and thin filaments

Skeletal muscle in cross-section:
In the cross sectional views, we can also see these cylindrical
structures
- Multinucleated

Peripheral location
Surrounded by connective tissue layers and many blood
vessels (BV), as it is highly vascularized.

Types of skeletal muscle
We can distinguish 3 types:
-
Red fibers (type I)
-
White fibers (type IIb)
-
Intermediate fibers (type IIa)
Different coloring patterns. Specific staining for metabolic components also reveals that the
metabolic components for each of these cells are different .
These muscle types differ in:
Contractile speed
Metabolic profile

Size

RED FIBERS = slow fibers (type I)
Slow contraction, but don’t fatigue
easily (due to high ox. activity)


Abundant myoglobin: O2 storage point,
contains iron → gives red fibers their color


Abundant mitochondria


Strong oxidative capacity
Smaller, thinner fibers

More vascularized

In muscles that contract frequently
(diaphragm, lower extremities,..)
WHITE FIBERS = fast fibers (type IIb)
-
Fast contraction but fatigue easily
Low myoglobin

Few mitochondria, as they have a fast
anaerobic glycolysis metabolism

Larger, more myofibrils


Less vascularized


Found in muscles that contract less


frequently (eyeball muscles)
[PDF p. 181]
Skeletal muscle cell characteristics


1 cell = 1 fiber.


Multinucleated and peripheral location


Long, cylindrical nuclei
Enveloped by an external lamina (basement membrane) and reticular fibers
Has a plasma membrane known as sarcolemma; The sarcolemma forms deep
invagination known as T tubules → together with terminal cisternae, form triads
The cytoplasm is known as sarcoplasm, where the most abundant component are
cylindrical collections: myofibrils
In the cytoplasm we will also find the sarcoplasmic
reticulum, surrounding the myofibrils. It’s specialized
SER which stores Ca2+

Small abundant Golgi, surrounding the nucleus

- Mitochondria
-
Glycogen
Myofibrils
The abundant myofibrils are 1-2 micrometers in diameter and
extend the whole length of the cell.
They’re formed by bundles of thick and thin fibers, aligned in
a specific pattern that gives place to striations (Banding
pattern visible in light microscopy: dark bands = A bands, light
bands = I bands, which are bisected by Z discs).
This repeated pattern forms the contractile unit of the muscle
cell: the sarcomere .
➢ Sarcomere: formed by portion between two Z discs.
Green arrows: mitochondria
Yellow: sort of vesicles, surrounding the myofibrils =
sarcoplasmic reticulum + T tubules
Try to identify the banding pattern and the different lines
Structure of the sarcomere
Contractile unit of striated muscle.
Basic components:

In the middle, darker A band
Lighter I band, cut through the middle by Z discs (each I band
on the sides of the sarcomere is bisected by the Z discs = we
have two halves of different I bands)

In the middle of the A band, paler region = H zone,

In the middle of the H zone we can find darker lines

corresponding to M lines
Each sarcomere = A band + 2 halves of 2 different I bands
[PDF p. 182]
Structural components:
Myofilaments:
Thick filaments = mostly myosin

Thin filaments = mostly actin
In between, many proteins stabilize them and maintain

the structure:

Titin (myosin associated), an elastic protein that

binds thick filaments to Z disc

alpha-Actinin (at Z disc), bound to actin
Desmin (at Z disc), which binds Z discs to the
plasma membrane to transmit the force of the
contraction to the whole cell)

-
Dystrophin (binding actin to cell membrane)
Myofilaments. Thick and thin
They lie parallel to the long axis of the myofibril in a precise arrangement that is
responsible for the sarcomere banding pattern.
Thick filaments
Diameter and length: 15nm diameter, 1.5 micrometers long

Each thick filament consists of many myosin molecules, whose heads protrude at
opposite ends of the filament
Each myosin molecule (= myosin II): composed of 2 heads (at each end) and 2 tails
The heavy chains which form the tail constitute the central bare zone. Central part
of myosin molecules lack myosin heads
Light chains form the myosin heads, with bipolar location (heads at the two
terminal regions of the thick filament) Located at the interaction sites with actin.

Accessory proteins:

Titin : bound to titin, elastic protein which acts as a spring and anchors thick
filaments (myosin) to the Z disc.
Myomesin : located at the central region (M line), to maintain thick filament
cross-linking

Thin filaments

7 nm in diameter (half the thickness) and 1.0 μm long
Thin filament (F-actin) consists of 2 strands of actin
subunits (G-monomers) twisted into a helix

In addition, 2 regulatory proteins are bound: troponin and
tropomyosin, covering the actin active sites
- F-actin: a polymer of G-actin monomers arranged in a double
helix, which posses an active site that will interact with myosin
[PDF p. 183]
Accessory proteins:
Tropomyosin: two-stranded alpha-helical coiled protein, located in the grooves of
the F-actin helix (bound to its active sites )


Troponin : binds to calcium and reveals active sites
Troponin T (TnT): binds troponin complex to tropomyosin
Troponin I (TnI): binds to actin and troponin T

Troponin C (TnC): binds Ca2+



-
Alpha-actinin and CapZ
Tropomodulin and nebulin: other associated proteins that help in stabilization
They are organized in a parallel disposition which gives muscle its characteristic striations.
Sarcomere bands and striations
How structure corresponds to the images:

A bands: overlapping between thick and thin filaments. 6 thin

filaments surround each thick filament. It stains and is seen as a dark
band.
When muscle contracts, the A band doesn’t change size.


I bands: The band corresponds to a region where there are only thin filaments.
Appears as a lightly stained band. Bisected by the Z discs.


H bands: light zone in the middle of the A band.
Corresponds to the bare region of thick filaments, where there
are no myosin heads, only myosin tails.


M lines: narrow, dark lines in the middle of the H zone.
Correspond to cross-connections (M bridges) between
adjacent thick filaments. They are crosslinked by myomesin
(accessory protein of myosin) located on the M line.


Z discs: sarcomere stabilization


Z discs are found bisecting the I bands. Their function is to
stabilize the sarcomere. They have many different proteins,
highlighting:
    - Titin, for the stabilization of **thick filaments**
    - alpha-actinin and Cap Z, which bind **thin filaments to the Z**

discs to stabilize them with the assistance of nebulin
Also important to have the different sarcomeres bound among
them + to other components of the cell:
    - Desmin: In this regard desmin plays a major role:

   - Connecting sarcomeres between them by

anchoring Z discs
   - **Binds myofibrils to other components** of the cell,

like cytoskeleton and cytoplasm = distributes
contraction force throughout the cell
[PDF p. 184]

Costameres: Peripherally located Z disks are anchored to the sarcolemma
through costameres. They are important to transmit contraction to the

whole cell and external environment.
Connection to adjacent cells or fibres also occurs through costameres.
- Dystrophin: binds the cytoskeleton of the cell to the ECM through the
sarcolemma. Important to transmit contraction force to the extracellular
region .
Alterations in dystrophin cause effects on muscular movement that lead to
muscular dystrophies.

T-Tubule system
Deep invaginations of the sarcolemma, very important for regulating the contraction of the
muscle cell. Responsible for conducting the depolarization deep into the muscle fiber,
thus propagating the signal and triggering release of Ca2+
T (transverse) tubules:

Run perpendicular (transverse) to the myofibrils

Conduct membrane depolarization deep into fibers
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
Found surrounding the myofibrils.

It’s specialized SER, found forming a meshwork surrounding each of the myofibrils.

Very important in contraction as it regulates calcium content inside the cells:
- Sequestering Ca2+ ions – **Relaxation**

- Releasing Ca2+ ions – **Contraction**


There are dilations in the SER in the areas proximate to
the T tubules, known as terminal cisternae.
This structure formed by the T tubule + the terminal

cisternae at both sides are known as triads. In
mammals, these triads are in the intersection between I
and A bands. Important structures as they help to
provide uniform contraction throughout the muscle cell.
[PDF p. 185]
Longitudinal cross section: we can observe the triads; but there
is something abnormal, their location, as this section
corresponds to an amphibian and not mammalian cell. The
triads are located on the Z discs, not between the A-I bands.
Muscle motor innervation. Neuromuscular junction
Bunch of muscle fibers innervated by the same neuron =
motor end plate (several neuromuscular junctions). However, each fiber is innervated by 1
and only 1 neuron.
Synapse :

Action potential in the motor neuron stimulates release
of acetylcholine from axon terminal into synaptic cleft
Junctional folds → grooves of the sarcolemma to
increase surface area, where Ach-receptors are located.

Acetylcholine in synaptic cleft binds Na+ ligand-gated
channel receptors and initiates sarcolemma AP
Signal propagation:


In the process of transmitting action potential, T
tubules play a very important role.
They conduct membrane depolarization
deep into the cell


The terminal cisternae of the SER


(sarcoplasmic ret.), closely located to T tubules,
detects this depolarization through
voltage-gated channels, which releases
calcium in response.
After contraction, Ca2+ pumps put calcium
back into the SER to stop the process
Contraction. Sliding filament theory
Changes in the amount of overlap between thick and thin filaments within the sarcomeres
allows for contraction and relaxation of muscle fibers.

Sliding theory → Sliding of the thick filaments over the thin filaments = contraction

Makes the sarcomere become shorter, and the cell contracts.
Relaxes when sarcomere goes back to its original position.


Many sarcomeres contracting at the same time results in muscle contraction .


It’s a calcium and ATP (energy) dependent process
During contraction:


Z discs move closer together

Basic concepts
INTRODUCTION
Key ideas about electric properties


Electric forces are conservative forces. The work that is done by an electric force
only depends on the initial and final point, but is independent from the trajectory. If
we do a circular trajectory, W=0.


An electric field is a real quantity. It’s a vector, not a scalar quantity: depending on
the direction of the field, we will obtain different results.


The electric current in the human body is caused due to the displacement of ions.
This displacement is the source of electric current. In electric circuits, it’s caused by
the displacement of electrons.


As this is a conservative system, mechanical energy remains constant. It
consists in the balance of kinetic and potential energy. If one increases, the other
decreases, as to maintain a constant Em.


Electric field lines and isopotential lines are perpendicular.
Electricity comes in 2 flavours: positive and negative charges, whose charge
corresponds to 1.6 · 10^ -19 C, either with + or - sign.

There are repulsive forces (interaction between particles with same electric charge)
or attractive forces (particles with different electric charge). Different to gravity,
where we only find attractive forces.

Charged particle interactions
Situation: we place a + charge and place a “probe” charge. If the probe is also +, the force
exerted will be a repulsive force.
This can be explained either by the appearance of an interaction between the particles, or
because this charge interacts with another magnitude known as electric field, in such a way
that the force will be equal to the charge of the affected particle (probe) times the electric
field created by our positive particle.
This last version is correct: the interaction appears
between the charge and the electric field.
[PDF p. 196]

When we have a positive charge, we say we have a source of electric field lines,
found pointing outwards.

When we have a negative charge, we have a sink of electric field lines, found
pointing inwards.



(convention: we establish this supposing that we will be using a + charge. Therefore, when
the field is created by a + charge = repels, outwards lines. Source; when it’s created by a -
charged = attracts, pointing inwards. Sink)
In the human body it’s rare to find isolated charges. We usually find many charges. To
analyze their behaviour, we must know, what is the global behaviour of the electric field?
To analyze it and answer this question, we can apply the superposition principle . We will
be able to recover a total value.
Example: a sodium ion perceives the existence of an electric field formed by another ion.
There will be an electric force created on the system (formula) due to the field : if we
suppose there is no friction, the result will be that the ion will begin to move in the direction
of the field lines. There will be an acceleration, and the kinetic energy will increase.
As previously mentioned, because this is a conservative system, the kinetic energy has to
be in balance with the potential energy. If one increases, the other will decrease. Here
we can introduce a new magnitude, known as electric potential voltage (V):
POTENTIAL ENERGY
For a + charge:
Potential energy decreases from point 1 to point 2 when we move along an electric
field line in the same direction as the field (away from a + charge creating the field,
or towards the - charge creating it, as Ek increases) .
If we are moving in the opposite direction, the potential energy of the system will
increase (towards a + or away from a -, as Ek decreases)
For a - charge:

Potential energy (Ep) increases when we move in the same direction
Ep decreases when we move in the opposite direction

ELECTRIC POTENTIAL
When we move along a field line, the electric potential changes, independent of the charge:

If we move in the opposite direction, potential (V) will increase
If we move in the same direction as the field lines, V will decrease

FOR ANY CHARGED PARTICLE, + or -

ELECTRIC BEHAVIOUR OF A CELL
Impermeable membrane
We will focus on the membrane: when considering a cell, we have a small volume of fluid
enclosed inside a membrane.
In principle, this membrane is impermeable (closed barrier), permeability = 0. Inside this
cavity we find water but also other components, ions or small charged proteins.
What is the interaction between these particles and
other ions found on the outer part of the cell?
We introduce a few sodium ions. What will happen? Due to the presence of all the other
particles, on each of them there will be a repulsive force. The expected result is that these
ions will try to separate, and will finally be placed on the inner side of the membrane. This is
what would be expected if we only have sodium ions.
However, in a real system we find many other charged particles, + and -, placed randomly
inside this volume. There is a huge amount of positive and negative ions present.
Therefore, one may ask, what is the total force experienced by one single particular ion?
This total force will be 0 if the total number of positive and negative charges is balanced .
In other words, we can reach an
equilibrium of that system if the total
charge (Q) is 0.
In order to have an equilibrium
situation, we need to fulfill this
condition (Qt = 0)
This is the situation found in a resting
cell: balance between + and - . There
is charge neutrality.
Membrane permeability for single ion
Now let’s consider the real situation, in which the
permeability of the membrane isn’t 0, although selective.
This selective permeability of the membrane means that
only one of the single ions (+ or -) will be able to cross
the barrier, in this situation.
We are in a situation in which Qt inside = 0 and Qt
outside = 0 (normal situation) . However, the concentration
of a positive ion A is greater inside than outside; the same
happens with the concentrations of negative ion B.
[PDF p. 198]
Will this situation persist?
In the human body the temperature is NOT = 0; it’s 37ºC. This is important as temperature
means vibration. These ions aren’t stationary, but slightly vibrating, so there will be a
small random displacement of all these ions.
This random displacement is the mechanism that will create the resting potential in the
cells of the human body.
If the temp were = 0, there would be no change in the equilibrium of the system. However,
this is not the case. There is a small amount of kinetic energy, so each one of these
molecules will follow a random trajectory and will eventually arrive at the membrane:

If the membrane is impermeable for the specific ion, they will collide and come back if
(membrane doesn’t allow their trespass).
But if there is permeability (in this situation, there is, only for ion A) : if one of the
incoming moving ions hits one of the pores, it can cross the membrane. It’s an
event that may occur for the positive charge (ion A), but not for the negative charge
as the membrane is not permeable for it. If this ion B hits one of the holes, the result
will be to change its direction.

Due to the selective permeability, only one of the ions will be able to cross the barrier. This
ion transports charge. Therefore, the ion that has crossed causes the Qt outside to be +
and the Qt inside to become negative.
In order to see if this is a stable situation, we have to check if this diffusion
from left to right can continue in time.
What is the probability to cross from left to right? Can we go back to the
initial situation?
The probability will depend on the number of ions we
have on each side. The probability of crossing will be
higher when the concentration of ions on the other side is
greater. Therefore, we will create a flux of ions, all going
from left to right.
The result: the total charge inside is smaller than 0,
and the total charge outside is larger than 0.
[PDF p. 199]
As we said, the system tends to transition to its stable state, when Qt = 0. Therefore, the
inner volume will divide into 2 parts, as to maximize the distance between the excess of
particles (due to repulsive forces, they press against the membrane):

The negative charges from the inside will be placed on the inner face of the

membrane

The positive charges which have exited the cell will place themselves on the outer

face of the membrane
There will be an excess of + on the outer
face of the membrane and an excess of -
on the inside (talking about A and B) . Only if
there is an excess of particles on the inner
and outer side of the membrane will there be
Qt different than 0. When we move away
from the membrane and separate, having a
more global view, Qt REMAINS being 0 (we
are talking in relation to proximity of the
membrane)
Therefore, Qt is greater and smaller than 0 only in the regions that are proximate to
the membrane.
Coming back to our question: is this going to continue forever, or will there be a mechanism
to stop this diffusion process?
Because of diffusion, positive charges will continue to try
and cross the membrane from left to right.
However, now there is the presence of positive charges all
around the outer face, exerting a force pointing in the
opposite direction. Diffusion will have to fight against the
repulsive forces created by the + charges located on the
outer membrane.
In other words, due to the generation of an electric field, a
voltage is created between the inner and outer part.
Voltage = difference of Potential energy (E p ) between 2
points
When is equilibrium reached, putting an end to the pass of molecules?
Equilibrium appears when the energy due to the electric force (created by repulsive
forces on the outside of the membrane) is equivalent to the energy available because of
the vibration.
[PDF p. 200]
(Ep elect =Energy that you can obtain from the
electric field. Potential energy obtained by the
electric forces)
The voltage potential on a membrane in an
equilibrium situation will be:

MEMBRANE RESTING POTENTIAL.

both sides? the log=0. The nernst potential is 0.

Cl- and K+
How would we define the membrane resting potential / Nernst potential for each individual
ion? It’s the potential at which ion X stops flowing from in → out, as we have reached
equilibrium between the force driving it and the force stopping it. For each particular ion, this
equilibrium is reached at specific concentrations, which will determine the potential at which
the process stops and the situation is sustained.
SUMMARY:
The concentration of each ions inside and outside are different (starting situation), but
there is charge neutrality. Our membrane becomes permeable to ion A only. Some of the
ions will be able to cross the barrier instead of bouncing off. There is a displacement of
ions because of diffusion . As soon as a small amount of charges are placed on the outer
membrane, there is an electric force pointing in the other direction.
The process stops when diffusion is balanced by the electric field created by the outer
charges. There is a voltage for which there is equilibrium between diffusion and electric
potential (membrane resting potential).
KEY POINTS

Inner and outer concentrations remain CONSTANT, even if there is a small
amount of particles crossing. It’s a very tiny amount compared to the total amount of
ions. Therefore, no modification in concentration.

Total charge inside and outside the cell is ALWAYS 0 in a global view, when we
are far from the membrane.

Membrane & action potentials
Introduction
At a basal (resting) state:
We are at the resting potential (-70 mV), for which potassium is mainly responsible.
How is it reached?
There are different concentrations in and out of the cell, for each ion. Therefore,
diffusion will tend to move these ions in favour of the concentration gradient
As they are charged particles, while this movement proceeds, an electric force will
appear due to the excess accumulation of charges on the opposite face of the
membrane
Diffusion will have to fight this electric force. The flow of ions will stabilize when the
chemical force driven by diffusion is in equilibrium with the electric force exerted in
the opposite direction
At this point, the resting membrane potential is established
The resting membrane potential is negative. Why?
At resting potential, the few resting-Na channels are open, carrying out this
mentioned process. Na+ voltage-gated channels are closed. The K+ resting channels
are much more abundant than the Na+ ones. Therefore, the resting membrane
potential is very close to that of K+ Nernst potential (although not quite the same,
as the resting Na channels play a role. PNa+ = 0.02 PK+ )
At rest, the inner side of the membrane is negative and the outer, positive.
    If the membrane were only permeable to Na+, the membrane potential would

be positive (as sodium is found at higher concentration out of the cell and it
would tend to enter, increasing the n of + charges inside the cell)
    If it were only permeable for K+, V would be even more negative than it is.

The inner side of the cell would become negative as + charges would tend to
exit the cell.
