ACTION POTENTIAL
The action potential is necessary to transmit information through the axons of neurons. It’s a
sequence of opening and closing of voltage-gated channels.
It appears due to a sequence of opening and closure of voltage-gated sodium and
potassium channels. This sequence begins when the cell is depolarized to a certain
threshold
It is an all-or-nothing process
It allows the propagation of an electrical current without decrement despite the
distance
It supports electrical transmission through axons (neurons) and muscle fibers
VG sodium channels
This action potential is reached thanks to a specific type of subchannels: voltage-gated
sodium channels.
It has 2 different gates: Fast gate (involved in activation) and a Slow gate (involved in
deactivation). They are proteins that change their conformation when a specific voltage is
reached. Ther activity is opposite.


Rest : at normal potential, the fast gate is closed and the slow gate is open.


Activation: when we reach the threshold (-60 mV), the fast gate opens and the
slow gate closes after a while. There is a 1ms time difference between the
opening of the fast and the closing of the slow. During this brief period, the channel
remains open (both gates are open) and sodium can enter the cell. Membrane
potential will increase, becoming much less negative and reaching positive


values.
This explains why the action potential is always the same: the gates are always or
always closed the same amount of time.

Deactivation: After a while, the channel is deactivated as the slow gate finally
closes. Sodium stops flowing into the cell and the process decreases.

VG potassium channels
To go back to a normal voltage, the sodium potassium pump
actively transfers Na+ ions back out. But this is a very slow
process.
To reinstate the potential, there are two main events that
contribute:

The closing of the voltage-gated Na+ channel
occurs (slow and fast gate)

Voltage-gated K+ channels open. Why now?
because their activation is slower than that of Na
voltage-gated channels.

Neuronal refractory period

Absolute refractory period = Period between the moment the threshold is reached
during depolarization, until it’s reached again during repolarization (in other words,
from the opening of the fast gate to the closing of the slow ). In this period of
time, it’s impossible to fire up an action potential. It corresponds to values higher

than -60 mV.
Relative refractory period = Corresponds to the period in which Na+ gates are
closed and K+ gates are open ( hyperpolarization ). If we want to depolarize again
from this point, we would have to fight against the open potassium channels. It is
harder than normal to fire up an action potential, but it is possible.
The absolute refractory period is the main factor that limits the maximal firing rate of a
neuron (the number of action potentials a neuron can fire up in a period of time). There are
also other limiting factors, such as energy (it’s a very energy demanding process).
In order to reach the threshold we need to slightly depolarize the membrane (PPE), needed
to trigger the opening of sodium channels.
But before we begin the action potential, we need to go from the deactivated Na+ channel
to the resting state of said channel (fast gate closed, slow gate open).

NERVE CONDUCTION
We need action potentials to transmit information.
The amplitude of the voltage in an electric field decreases exponentially with distance.
So if we wanted to send a message to our big toe from the spinal cord, there would be no
way to do it using normal electrical transmission.
This is why we use action potentials. At each neuron, a new action potential is
generated every few micrometers. In this way, the signal is not lost during the journey. We
can transmit the same signal over a long distance.
This is what occurs in unmyelinated fibers. This type of conduction has one problem: it’s
an extremely slow process as generating an action potential requires time (3-4 ms). The
final conduction velocity is half a meter per second. Very slow.
This means if we touch something burning, we would burn before executing a response.
[PDF p. 219]
To improve that conduction velocity, we use myelin.
It allows saltatory conduction.
Myelin and conduction
Myelin insulates the axons of neurons. It’s different
in the CNS and PNS:

In the CNS = oligodendrocytes, which cover

the axons. Each one covers several axons. It’s
a lipid recovery.

In the PNS = Schwann cells. 1 SC per axon.
Axons with no myelin in the PNS are also
surrounded by Schwann cells (provides
protection), but unmyelinated, so there is no

isolation.
Insulation improves conduction. The length constant becomes higher if we recover the
axon, and instead of having to place voltage gated channels all over the axon, we do it only
in a few regions. It allows us to be able to regenerate the action potential every few
millimeters and not every few microns. We get an action velocity of 80 m/s. Much faster.
Those places in which we find the channels are the Nodes of Ranvier, where there is no
myelin. Points where the action potential is regenerated .
There is alternating action potential generation ( nodes ) and
electrical conduction (myelinated regions).
We lose time every time we regenerate the action
potential, but in between nodes (myelin regions,
where there is electrical conduction) the
conduction is immediate.
Action potential will only be regenerated in the nodes.
Therefore, the lower the number of nodes, the
higher the conduction capacity (faster impulse
transmission)

Presynaptic bouton

We have an action potential traveling through the neuron.
In the last part of the axon,this action potential is regenerated one last time to be transmitted.
Therefore, we find many sodium-potassium voltage-gated channels for this purpose.
We also find many calcium voltage gated-channels in this region. When the potential
reaches the presynaptic bouton, these Ca2+ channels will open and calcium will enter into
the cell (Ca2+ out >> in).
This calcium will trigger the fusion of the neurotransmitter vesicles with the membrane
and exocytosis.

ii. Calcium enters (Ca2+ channels)

One it enters, the accumulated calcium has to be expelled out of the cell, through an

Introduction to neuromuscular junction disorders
The disorders of the neuromuscular junction are classified according to the portion of the
synapse that is affected: presynaptic and postsynaptic disorders. The differentiation is
important because the clinical course, the diagnostic process and the treatment vary.
1. Presynaptic disorders
In this group of disorders, the affected portion is the terminal bouton of the motor neuron.
The common effect in all of them is a reduced acetylcholine release despite a normal arrival
of action potentials. Two disorders will be discussed in more detail: botulism and
Lambert-Eaton syndrome
A) BOTULISM
Botulinum toxin is one of the most powerful poisons found in nature. The toxin is generated
by a bacterium named Clostridium botulinum . The characteristics of the bacteria and the
clinical course of the disease will be seen in detail in other courses. In short, this bacterium
does not usually directly infect our organism. When it grows in an adequate manner (like
improperly processed preserves) it can produce the toxin, and it is the intake of the toxin
(with the food) that generates the clinical consequences.
Botulinum toxin has a heavy and a light chain (with several subtypes of the latter; only
subtypes A, B and E are related to human disease). The heavy chain allows the toxin to
enter cholinergic neurons (giving the neuronal specificity), while the light chain is an
endopeptidase that cleaves proteins involved in neurotransmitter vesicle release.
How does botulinum toxin block the release of acetylcholine in the presynaptic terminal? As
seen in the previous session (and shown in the image), there are several proteins involved in
the fusion of neurotransmitter vesicles with the presynaptic membrane. Some of these
proteins are located in the membrane of the vesicle (v-SNAREs) while others are located in
the membrane of the neuron (t-SNAREs). Synaptotagmin is the calcium sensor that begins
the fusion process. The different subtypes of botulinum toxin cleave v-SNAREs or t-SNAREs
due to their endopeptidase action, making the fusion process impossible.
Although the fusion mechanism of neurotransmitter vesicles is common to all neurons (and
other vesicle fusion processes), botulinum toxin only acts in some types of cholinergic
neurons due to the selectivity of entry mechanism provided by the heavy chain, as
mentioned above. In fact, the light chain of the tetanus toxin (produced by another bacteria
of the same genre, Clostridium tetani ) has the same mechanism of action as the light chain
of the botulinum toxin, but the clinical effect is apparently opposite (in the tetanus, there is
[PDF p. 232]
involuntary contraction of several muscles groups). How can this be possible? Because
instead of inhibiting the neurotransmitter release in motor neurons, the tetanus toxin inhibits
the release of neurotransmitter in inhibitory motor neurons (its heavy chain takes the toxin
into these interneurons). The final effect of a loss of inhibition in motor circuits is an excess
of contraction.
Botulinum toxin can affect other subtypes of cholinergic neurons apart from motor neurons.
Thus, autonomic symptoms and signs (which will be studied later) may be part of the clinical
course of the disease.
B) LAMBERT-EATON SYNDROME
This is an autoimmune syndrome usually observed in the context of certain neoplasms. The
appearance of antibodies against the voltage-gated calcium channels of the presynaptic
terminal leads to a decreased release of acetylcholine, despite the presence of normal
action potentials in the motor axon. As in botulism, other subtypes of cholinergic neurons
can be affected, causing autonomic dysfunction.
2. Postsynaptic disorders: MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
In this group of disorders, the postsynaptic portion of the synapse (and particularly, the
nicotinic receptors) is affected.
The prototypical postsynaptic disorder is myasthenia gravis, a disease you have already
heard of.
In summary, it is an autoimmune disease in which there are antibodies against the nicotinic
receptors of the muscle that lead to their elimination. As the antibodies are specific against
this subtype of receptor, there is no autonomic involvement (unless there are other
antibodies produced in the context of the autoimmune dysfunction).
3. Relevance of knowing both types of disorders
There are diagnostic tests that can differentiate both types of disorders depending on the
response to brief or prolonged exercise, or to repetitive stimulation. It is beyond the scope of
this course to enter in more detail about this. But, as a simple rule, a presynaptic defect can
be compensated (in the short term) with an increase in the firing rate of action potentials in
the motor neuron (leading to an increase in acetylcholine release). However, in postsynaptic
defects the problem is not in the ACh release, but in the limited number of receptors
available. An increased firing rate of action potentials may lead to neurotransmitter depletion
without achieving any significant effect. Instead, in myasthenia gravis the patient can benefit
from acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, used as symptomatic treatment. These inhibitors
prolong the union of ACh to the receptors, maximizing the effect of the remaining nicotinic
channels.
[PDF p. 233]
4. Drugs that block the neuromuscular junction
In patients under general anesthesia, muscle relaxation may be convenient after intubation
to avoid fighting against the respirator, and to facilitate the work of the surgeon. There are
two main types of neuromuscular blockers: analogues of curare (a natural poison) that block
the union of ACh to the nicotinic receptors, and depolarizing blockers, that keep permanently
open the nicotinic channels, generating a sustained depolarization of the muscle fiber
membrane. This mechanism is similar to the primary afferent depolarization mechanism
studied in presynaptic inhibition. If the membrane is kept depolarized at a level beyond the
activation threshold of the sodium voltage-gated channels, these channels remain blocked
and there cannot initiate any new action potential.
[PDF p. 234]
SKELETAL MUSCLE
Muscle contraction
The nerve branches and reaches several muscle fibers, forming
the terminal motor plaque.
Each muscle fiber receives innervation from 1 motor neuron.
The motor neuron can innervate many motor fibers. All
those muscle fibers get depolarized and generate action
potentials at the same time: it’s like a functional unit, which is
why it’s all grouped together into the so-called motor plaque.
Sequence of events in the postsynaptic terminal
The release of Ach neurotransmitters occurs. These reach their respective
receptors in the motor end plate, causing the opening of ligand-gated Na
channels, which leads to Na influx and K efflux = depolarization. These
nicotinic receptors have 2 binding
sites for the Ach ligand.
The depolarization extends along the
cell and reaches voltage-gated Na
channels, which also open. All
contributes to generating muscle
action potential.
Sarcoplasmic reticulum and T tubules
This series of events will lead to a Ca2+ increase in the cytoplasm of the muscle fiber.
But the mechanism is somehow different than to what happens in neurons:
The action potential is generated in the center of the fiber and it propagates
in both directions (fastest way to propagate).
We want it to generate an increase in the muscle’s intracellular Ca2+ levels.
For this purpose: the sarcolemma is invaginated every short distance, to
increase the surface area .
These invaginations, called T tubules, allow the membrane to be in very
close contact to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SER).

In those invaginations the reticulum is adjacent to the membrane. This

area constitutes what is known as a triad.
This interaction between membranes will
cause the increase of intracellular
calcium. However it doesn’t come from
outside (as in the case of neurons), but from
inside . In neurons for ex, it comes from the
extracellular space and enters the cell. But
not in this case.
This is the case for skeletal muscle. In cardiac muscle, Ca2+ additionally comes from
outside as well as inside.
[PDF p. 235]
DHP and RYR proteins - Ca2+ release
2 very important proteins allow this depolarization transmission and
Ca2+ release:

DHPR, located on the T tubule (sarcolemma)
And RYR, located on the SER membrane.
DHPR changes its conformation upon stimulation and acts on RYR,
which opens by changing its conformation and allows Ca2+ release

inside the cell. 4 molecules of DHPR interact with 1 molecule of
RYR to trigger calcium release.
DHPR will also act as a calcium channel in cardiac cells to allow
calcium entry, but in this case, it’s only role is to interact with RYR.
How do we get Ca2+ inside the SER?
Various proteins:

SERCA: it acts as a calcium pump, constantly pumping calcium
into the reticulum. After each action potential, there is a short
lasting calcium release, as this protein will quickly pump Ca2+
back into the SER. Therefore, a single action potential generates
a short transient contraction, stopped by the retrieving of Ca.

Process of contraction in skeletal muscle
Calcium is the trigger for the beginning of contraction

In the muscle at rest, the binding site for myosin is covered by tropomyosin.

Muscle is relaxed .


In the muscle during contraction
**Ca binds troponin (troponin C),** making it change conformation. It **pulls**



tropomyosin from the binding site, leaving it exposed. Immediately, myosin
(very high affinity for actin in skeletal muscle fibers ) binds it. Calcium allows
myosin to bind to actin.
    From here there is an automated process: myosin binds, and the **binding**

triggers a change in conformation in myosin (turn).
    Up till now, there has been no energy consumption. But **energy is needed to**

release the myosin head from the actin and recover the original position. At
rest, myosin has an ADP bound to it. The turn causes ADP to be released,
and this site is free for ATP binding. When ATP is bound to myosin, it is
converted to ADP and P is released, causing the detachment of myosin
from actin.

Types of smooth muscle
There are 2 main types of smooth muscle:

Multiunit smooth muscle: made up of individual
fibers (each cell is a unit). Each fiber will contract and
relax independently.

Single unit or visceral smooth muscle: they are all
bound by gap junctions, as if they were a single very
long fiber. Calcium increase will be transmitted through
the different fibers through gap junctions. They can
contract coordinately.
Varicosities
In smooth muscle we don’t usually talk about synapses, but Varicosities . The
neurotransmitters are released and diffuse to many nearby areas. Not restricted to a
synaptic cleft. There can be many varicosity regions per axon.
In the case of visceral smooth muscle, we don’t need many varicosities per fiber, as the
cells are interconnected by gap junctions that will transmit the calcium release triggered by
1 varicosity. These muscle fibers can also be activated by circulating hormones released
from the blood, not only by neurotransmitters.
Calcium release in smooth muscle can be triggered by:

Neurotransmitters released at varicosity
regions
Hormones coming in from the bloodstream

When calcium increases, affinity increases as myosin is

The contraction process and dynamics, its movement

In smooth muscle, the actin binding site is always

At the same time there is a phosphatase dephosphorylating myosin, removing

Long lasting contractions
Smooth muscle has different roles than those of skeletal muscle. It’s designed to be much
more flexible and be contracted for a very long time (ex: sphincters, 23h per day; soleus =
many h per day, whenever we are standing).
It is optimized to have the minimum energy consumption during that time.
In smooth muscle, to generate a long lasting
contraction, the key is to increase calcium
concentration which then stays at an intermediate
concentration for a long time. This is only possible in

Smooth muscle structure. Adaptability
Myofibrils are very rigid and strictly parallel in skeletal muscle.
But in smooth muscle they’re not strictly parallele. This allows the muscle fiber to change

contract when needed. It can adapt to different tensions depending on the volume. Skeletal
muscle is much more rigid and is not so adaptable. Smooth muscle keeps the ability to
contract even when it is stretched . It’s more adaptable.

In smooth muscle we only have one nuclei per cell. To grow, the cell may
increase the genetic material (ploidy) inside the cell, but without
increasing the number of nuclei (in skeletal muscle, we do find growing

Skeletal muscle metabolism
[PDF p. 243]
i. In the muscle, when we begin to contract, we use the available ATP in the
cytoplasm.
ii. To obtain more, the phosphocreatine system will convert ADPs to ATP s for about
8-10 seconds.
iii. If we still need energy, glucose metabolism begins.
    If we need fast energy, we carry out many successive **glycolysis**

(anaerobic) . It generates lactic acid, which will then be reused. But this only
gives 2ATPs per glucose. It’s fast but all the glycogen would finally be
consumed.
    - **To keep the muscle contraction,** we need to carry out **aerobic metabolism**

(yields 32 APs per glucose). However, it is slower. To carry out aerobic
metabolism we have to lower energy consumption, which explains the
presence of type I fibers: they maintain the muscle contracted but with lower
energy consumption as the contraction is slower.

Low distances, fast sprints = anaerobic metabolism
Resistance, long distance = aerobic metabolism

Why do we hyperventilate?
If we do anaerobic metabolism for prolonged time, we will need to compensate at some
point. We need to recover. Lactic acid needs to be turned into pyruvate and through the
Krebs system, to be turned back to glucose or consumed. This can
only be done through aerobic metabolism.
This is what is known as oxygen debt: the O2 needed to carry out
aerobic metabolism which compensates for that anaerobic metabolism
which we’ve done to quickly perform a task. This is why we
hyperventilate.

by the generation of lactic acid crystals. But this is
false. This soreness is probably caused by
microtears in the muscle and inflammation.
[PDF p. 244]
Accessory proteins and disorders
Myofibrils contract due to the displacement of thin filaments (actin) over thick filaments
(myosin), shortening the sarcomeres. But myofibrils must be attached to the
sarcolemma, and the sarcolemma must be linked to the connective tissue around it, in
order to transmit the force generated by the contraction. Moreover, if the myofibrils are
not properly attached to the sarcolemma, and the sarcolemma is not anchored to the
connective tissue around, the muscle fibers will suffer damage.
Let’s go step by step. Muscles usually exert their force through tendons that insert into
a bone (although there are exceptions, like the tongue). Muscle fibers (muscle cells) do
not extend up to this insertion. Tendons are formed by connective tissue (they are
acellular); in fact they are formed by the fusion of the different connective layers that
surround the fibers (endomysium), the muscle fascicles (perimysium) and the whole
muscle (epimysium) (see the image below).
Thus, muscle fibers must be firmly attached (through the sarcolemma) to the
connective tissue that surrounds them in order to transmit their contractile force to the
tendon (or any other insertion). But inside the fiber, myofibrils must be attached to other
myofibrils, to the cytoskeleton and to the sarcolemma in order to generate and transmit
force adequately. Force transmission should therefore be both longitudinal (along the
main axis of the fiber, to the tendon) and lateral (circumferential, through the minor
axis, linking myofibrils, cytoskeleton, sarcolemma and connective tissue).
Thin filaments are attached to the Z bands by means of alpha-actinin. Thick filaments
are also attached to the Z bands, by means of an “elastic” protein, titin. Titin needs to
be elastic because the distance between the end of the thick filaments and the Z band
[PDF p. 245]
depends on the overlap between thin and thick filaments (if the sarcomere is relaxed,
the distance is longer than if the sarcomere is contracted). Myomesin links thick
filaments in the M line (see figure).
Myofibrils are attached to the cytoskeleton (that includes a different subtype of actin
fibers) by desmin (from Z lines) and dystrophin. Desmin links the different myofibrils,
and through the cytoskeleton, attaches them to the nuclei and mitochondria. It also
attaches the myofibrils to the membrane (integrins). Dystrophin is the main responsible
of attaching the cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber to the sarcolemma and the
extracellular connective tissue.
The different protein complexes that attach the membrane both to the extracellular
tissue and to the intracellular structures are named costameres. In the skeletal muscle,
the most relevant costameres are the integrin complex (that interacts with desmin) and
the complex that includes dystroglycan/sarcoglycan/dystrobrevin/sarcospan and other
proteins, where dystrophin binds. The costameres bind to the extracellular collagen by
means of laminin alpha 2.
[PDF p. 246]
It is clinically relevant to know these attachment systems because many muscular
dystrophies are due to defects in some of these proteins. Other forms of muscular
dystrophy are due to damage in other structural proteins or in intracellular signaling
pathways related to them. A defective attachment of the myofibrils to the sarcolemma
and the surrounding connective tissue (that will form the tendon), besides impeding an
adequate force transmission, also damages the muscle fibers due to an excess of
movement. Alterations in desmin usually associated with cardiac muscle disorders;
cardiac muscle (as you will learn later) shares many structural similarities. Absence of
dystrophin causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a severe disorder, while its
dysfunction causes a milder form of muscular dystrophy named Becker muscular
dystrophy. Alterations in the genes that encode the different sarcoglycans cause a
different type of muscular dystrophy, globally known as “limb-girdle” muscular
dystrophies (LGMD), as the muscles affected initially are located around the pelvic and
scapular areas. Defects in alpha 2 laminin, extracellular collagen VI, titin, or the
complex dysferlin/caveolin 3 (related to sarcolemmal repair; the sarcolemma may suffer
damage during normal contraction) also cause muscular dystrophies.
[PDF p. 247]
AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYSTEM
[PDF p. 248]
Autonomic nervous system II
INTRODUCTION
Division of the nervous system that controls bodily functions in a largely unconscious
manner, supplying innervation to smooth muscle, glands and internal organs.
General functions
                             Heart and respiratory rates

                             Digestion

                             Pupillary response

                             - Urination

                             - Sexual arousal

                             Body temperature

                             - Nutrition

Classified into the afferent branch (sensory)
and efferent branch (motor, further subdivided
into Sympathetic and Parasympathetic SNA)
EFFERENT BRANCH
Efferent branch organization
Preganglionic fiber: stems from the CNS and ends in an autonomic ganglion
Postganglionic fiber: stems from the autonomic ganglion and ends in its target
effector
A. SYMPATHETIC SYSTEM
“Fight-flight” response
Characteristics

CNS: sympathetic motor neurons arise at the intermediate cell columns, which are
found from T1-L2 along the spinal cord.

Autonomic ganglion: from where the postganglionic neuron will originate. These
neurons extend their processes either to:
- **Sympathetic trunk ganglia** (cervical ganglia and ganglia which give rise to

the cardiac nerves)
- **Preaortic single ganglia** (thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves)

As the preganglionic fibers extend either to sympathetic trunk or
preaortic single ganglia (further, but still pretty close to the spinal
cord), we find that:
- Preganglionic fibers are quite short
-
Postganglionic neurons have very long fibers, extending
all the way to effectors
[PDF p. 249]
Levels of innervation
The sympathetic trunk extends from T1-L2 / L3
Cervical ganglia: at this level, there is no intermediolateral horn in the spinal cord to give
rise to sympathetic motor neurons. Therefore, preganglionic neurons from lower levels
where there is this horn, extend their processes up to cervical ganglia, from where the
postganglionic neuron will arise.
Provided by T1-T2 short preganglionic fibers, which extend their processes up to:
Superior cervical ganglion (C1-C4 levels)
Middle cervical ganglion (C5-C6 levels)
Inferior cervical ganglion (C7-C8 levels)
Cardiac plexus : arise from T3-T6. Long postganglionic fibers.
-
Thoracic and lumbar plexus Prevertebral ganglia
These nerves, which innervate abdominal viscera, arise at preaortic single ganglia:
Celiac ganglion & Superior mesenteric ganglion (T7-T11 preganglionic fibers)
Inferior mesenteric ganglion (T12-L3 preganglionic fibers)
Dermal smooth muscle innervation
In parallel, along the whole of the spinal cord, we will have sympathetic motor
neurons which will innervate blood vessels and dermal smooth muscle (ex:
sweat glands) all over the body. These portions aren’t just restricted to areas in the
abdomen, but are found all over. Therefore, the preganglionic neurons arising from
the intermediolateral horn will extend up or down along the sympathetic trunk.
When they reach the level they are ought to innervate, they connect with their
corresponding postganglionic neuron in the sympathetic trunk ganglia.
This postganglionic neuron will then accompany somatic neurons which go to
innervate skeletal muscle found at the same portion as the dermis (remember:
each portion of muscle arises from the same somite as its corresponding portion of
skin. In the somites we find myotome and dermatome) .
Depending on where it is located, it will accompany the ones taking the dorsal ramus (to the
back) or ventral ramus (to the hypaxial skeleton: muscles and dermis in the abdomen and
limbs).
Adrenal medulla - Chroma�n cells
Adrenal Medulla: provided by T5-T9 preganglionic
fibers
The adrenal medulla cells are modified
postganglionic sympathetic neurons, known as
chromaffin cells.
These cells release adrenaline (also known as
epinephrine) into the blood mainstream.
Adrenaline synthesis requires large
concentrations of cortisol, which is provided
by venous supply from the adrenal cortex
[PDF p. 250]
B. PARASYMPATHETIC SYSTEM
Characteristics

CNS: Brainstem and lumbosacral spinal cord (S2-S4)

Autonomic ganglion: Next to the target effector. Postganglionic PS neurons originate
very close to their target organ
As a consequence, we will find that in the Parasympathetic system:
Preganglionic fibers are very long, extend all the way to the target organ
- Postganglionic fibers are short
Levels of innervation
Brain Stem (Face ⇒ splenic colic flexure)
Long Preganglionic fibers
- Edinger-Westphal Nuclei, part of the oculomotor nucleus

(III)

flexure (X)

Different pelvic nerves innervating abdominal and pelvic organs
from the splenic colic flexure downwards

SYMPATHETIC

[PDF p. 251]
AUTONOMIC SYSTEM SYNAPSE
Synaptic terminals
Both sympathetic and parasympathetic have axonal varicosities instead of regular
synaptic terminals, which are found in the neuromuscular junction of somatic synapses.
Varicosities
Axonal enlargement
Neurotransmitters are released and diffuse, along a big synaptic cleft
Allows for neurotransmitter action on up to 10 µm of distance
Neurotransmitters
Preganglionic terminals (both S and PS)
Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter released both by Sympathetic and Parasympathetic
preganglionic neurons. They are cholinergic fibers.
Other neurotransmitters: Enkephalin, Substance P, Neurotensin. They have a modulatory
effect. Detected by Nicotinic receptors (N2) in postganglionic neurons.
Postganglionic sympathetic terminals
Release Adrenaline and Noradrenaline. They are adrenergic fibers.
This is one of the reasons why the adrenal medulla is considered to be part of the
sympathetic system. Chromaffin cells, upon Ach release by the preganglionic fiber, release
Adrenaline (80%) and Noradrenaline (20%) ( also known as epinephrine and
norepinephrine). Detected by metabotropic receptors (𝛼1, 𝛼2,..) in effector organs.
However, there are exceptions: sweat glands and piloerector muscles. Rather than
releasing adrenaline, upon stimulation, the postganglionic neurons innervating these
structures release Ach . Once again, we fin cholinergic fibers (in the case of sweat glands:
muscarinic cholinergic receptors in effector muscle; M3)
Postganglionic parasympathetic terminals
In the case of PS, the neurotransmitter released continues to be Acetylcholine. They are
postganglionic parasympathetic cholinergic fibers. Ach detected by muscarinic receptors in
effector organs (M1, M2, M3,…)
Receptors
Cholinergic receptors


Nicotinic: ligand gated channels, which upon binding, effectuate by allowing ion
transport. They turn into ionic channels.
Location: sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia. Located on postganglionic
neurons, receiving the Ach stimulation from preganglionic


Muscarinic: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs). Act through second
messengers, triggering either the opening of ionic channels along the cell (not
restricted to the area of binding) or other mechanisms (protein synthesis,
transcription,…).
Location: Parasympathetic target effectors, Sweat glands and piloerector


muscles
[PDF p. 252]
Types of Muscarinic cholinergic receptors:
    M1: CNS, stomach secretion

    - M2: heart

    - M3: smooth muscle

    M4: pancreas, lungs

    M5: salivary glands, pupil sphincter

Adrenergic receptors
Location: Sympathetic target effectors
● Alpha receptors:
- 𝛼 1 receptors: postsynaptic.
Smooth muscle contraction ⇒ G protein coupled mechanism of
phosphatidylinositol degeneration = IP3 = Ca2+ release and muscle
contraction
- 𝛼 2 receptors: Pre & Postsynaptic (autoreceptor)
Smooth muscle relaxation ⇒ G protein coupled mechanism of adenylate
cyclase inhibition. Inhibit release of NA from adrenergic neurons.
● Beta receptors
- 𝜷 1, 𝜷 2 and 𝜷 3: postsynaptic
Activating receptors, act through adenylate cyclase (AC) stimulation = ↑cAMP
AFFERENT BRANCH
Sensory branch of the autonomic nervous system

Medical-Degree/Year-1/POM/Lectures/Lectu.content:
POM Being a doctor reflection cards
Sources

Audio Clip 3(2) (automatic transcription, errors corrected). An identical copy is in the FMF transcripts folder (misfiled there). Starts mid-sentence (“…the lives of your patients”) and ends in a group discussion; the end of the session (written reflection) is not recorded.
Structure: short introduction by the lecturer (about 10 minutes), then a recorded group discussion of the cards (students, partly in Spanish). The group discussion is summarized as the students’ interpretations, not the lecturer’s.
The scheduled teacher was Dr. Rocío (palliative care); the lecturer was covering (“I wasn’t going to have to lead this”).
Coverage: transcript only. No slides or other material in the vault.

Resources

The cards: titled “Ser médico” (To be a doctor), in Spanish, developed by a palliative care doctor (as far as the lecturer remembered).
Slides: none.

Marking: [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it.
Exam flags / tasks

No exam statements. Task: discuss 10 to 20 cards in groups, then write a reflection and submit it before leaving (last half hour).
Message: “Don’t hold it in.”

1. Introduction: medicine enters people’s lives

As doctors you enter your patients’ lives, families and problems; medical and personal problems may shock you. We don’t just treat a blood pressure; if that patient is dying of cancer, we enter their whole life.
The first death you see will affect you. She remembers the first, not the second, third or fourth, “because it hurt”.
As a student you are “the watcher”, on the sidelines, “watching somebody’s movie, but the movie was real”.
Few students have seen someone die; a hundred years ago, everyone in the room would have, because death happened at home. Now it is “tucked away in the hospital”, which is where you will be.
You need to process those feelings to keep going: journaling, talking, writing, reflecting on what bothered you and why.
We all carry our own “baggage” (upbringing, imperfect parents, our past). A patient whose problem “hits home” may make you a worse doctor for them: reflect, and sometimes let someone else take over.

2. Her story: the first death

First rotation as a student: emergency medicine, after a major storm left much of the US east coast without electricity for about a day (many chainsaw injuries).
A large man came in with a heart attack; CPR; they “called it”: stopped resuscitation and stated the time of death (e.g. 11:44). The family was screaming in the hallway amid the chaos. Her first death.
“You’re going to see a lot of stuff… take care of yourself and talk to somebody about it, and don’t hold it inside.”
She dislikes the ER (surprises, trauma).

3. Seeing patients disrespected

A third-year student told her about a woman whose migraine medication change caused depression; her calls to the clinic went unanswered until her husband brought her in. The student felt the patient was not respected but was part of the team.
You will feel this often: burned-out doctors can become rough and cold. You cannot tell the attending what to do, but acknowledge it to yourself and talk to someone; it is not normal.
Dr. Rocío’s story: as a student, an attending told a dying patient’s family to leave the room, then had the students stand and watch the man die. “My heart almost broke in half.” Such things would not happen today.

4. The cards: group discussion (students’ interpretations)
Each group picked cards, read them aloud and discussed. Example card read by the lecturer: “Habrá momentos muy bajos. No los pasas solo.” (There will be very low moments. You don’t go through them alone.)





























Card (as read)Students’ discussionDon’t become an advertising board (drawing of pens and highlighters with drug brand names)Don’t be used as publicity by the pharmaceutical industry; stay impartial and independent of companies; gifts or paid events create influence. Example: the old Lucky Strike adverts claiming doctors said they were “less irritating”, which people read as a doctor recommending smoking; the US opioid crisis. One student: having a preference for a good drug is fine, being an advert is not. Also: don’t become a machine for profit or patient volume; you are there to heal”Your professional development, free of industry” [verify] wordingDon’t let brands manipulate what you say or recommend”Cambia de bata con frecuencia” (change your white coat often)Literally keep it clean; deeper: adapt, stay open to new ideas, other doctors’ opinions, other specialties, teamwork, even wellness practices such as meditationBe careful on social media (picture of a doctor)Patient confidentiality first (by law and by the Hippocratic oath); never post patients; educational content about yourself is acceptable”Libra las guardias”Interpreted as “get through / survive your on-call shifts”: take care of yourself (water, food, sleep, comfortable clothes), don’t rely on stimulants, protect yourself because a bad state means worse care; take breaks

[verify] Exact card texts: the transcript gives English paraphrases or partial Spanish; check against the cards if available.

Medical-Degree/Year-1/POM/Lectures/Lectu.content:
POM Clinical interview social and family history
Sources

Medical (automatic transcription, errors corrected): the whole workshop in one file. Starts cleanly with the objectives and ends cleanly with the exam information.
Structure: three simulated scenarios with an actor patient. Each is played by one or more student volunteers, followed by a group debrief led by the lecturer.
Gaps: the student-patient encounters are largely inaudible or garbled in the transcript (long runs of repeated filler, side conversations in Spanish). They are summarized only where the debrief confirms what was said. The debriefs are well transcribed.
The previous session (history of present illness, past medical history, the pain mnemonic SOCRATES) has no transcript or note; this session builds on it.
Coverage: transcript only. No slides, POM material or other notes in the vault or Drive.

Resources

Slides: “Jen will upload the slide” (harmful effects of smoking, standard drinking unit tables, extended social history items). None in the vault yet.
Textbook: an American book on the clinical interview is mentioned by students (hand-holding example, asking about suicidal thoughts); title not given.
Related: POM Goals of medicine and CanMEDS roles (communicator role).

Marking: [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. There are no slides, official notes or Lucía notes for POM in the vault, so there are no [Slides], [Notes], [Lucía] or [check] items.
Exam flags from the lecturer

Patient encounter exam in November (an actor as patient, 6 minutes): “much more straightforward”; “we just want to know if you know how to ask”. “Know your SOCRATES really well”, past medical history, social history, “the basics that we talked about”. The topics of today were “just to introduce” them. Further wording garbled (“it will start asking about leisure and economic status”) [verify].
There is also a separate multiple choice theory exam.
Harmful effects of smoking: “we want you to know for the exam what are the main harmful effects of smoking”; “not perfectly by far”, a general idea (section 4).
Pack years: “it’s for the exam, knowing how to calculate the pack years” (section 4).
Standard drinking units and the risk tables: “This will enter in the exam” (section 5).
Harmful effects of alcohol: “please for the exam know” them; study at home (“go to books or ask AI”); “it’s not going to be very specific, the question, but have an idea” (section 5).
Past medical history: “You have to know it really, really well”, “especially those four” (which four is not clear) [verify] (section 2).
Social history: she expects you to practise asking a core set of items every time (she says “all these five”; which five is not clear from the transcript) [verify] (section 3).
Not to learn: the details of the lung cancer screening guideline (“I don’t want you to learn it. I just want you to understand why”) and the nicotine dependence questionnaire (“you don’t have to learn it”).

1. Objectives of the session

Continue to perfect the interview, building on last session (history of present illness, past medical history; past medical history was covered quickly at the end, so it is practised again).
New items: social history and family history.
Keep working on active listening and empathy.
Within social history: the sensitive topics, alcohol and drugs in general.

2. Scenario 1: pneumothorax follow-up (pulmonology office)
Case

Medical student in the pulmonology office. Patient comes for a checkup two months after being admitted for a pneumothorax (treated for four days, then home). This is the “official discharge”: checking everything is fine so the patient can go back to normal life.
She calls this a very standard procedure: patients often keep taking a medication they should not, or still have pain and must be seen again.
In real life the past medical history would be in the digital record (the patient was hospitalized); here you ask everything for practice.
Actor patient: young woman, sad that she must stay home while friends go out and school has started; hospital stay painful (chest tube) and lonely. Daily smoker since 16, about 10 cigarettes a day, did not stop during recovery, does not want to stop.

History of present illness at a follow-up: what to ask





































ItemLecturer’s pointPainOne of the main symptoms of pneumothoraxTrouble breathingOne of the cardinal symptoms; respiratory distress: “have you had any more trouble breathing?”Other symptoms”Any other problems” is fine, since it is not only about painEmotional impactIt was a traumatic, “pretty violent” episodeEffect on daily lifeE.g. told to rest, not going to school: relevant to deciding when she can go backMedicationHas she continued or discontinued anythingWound healingShe had a chest tube: healing, scarring

“These are basic questions, there’s not much more than that.”
Praise for the first student: did not interrupt the patient. The tendency is to cut patients off when they talk a lot; sometimes necessary if far too long, but here letting her talk was good.

Medication adherence

Patients may keep taking medication “forever” because they did not hear well or the doctor was too quick; others discontinue. So ask whether she has been taking any.
Painkillers are usually taken for the few days after the intervention, not two months.
Anecdote (poverty and medication): a student asked what to do when patients cannot afford drugs. “There’s nothing you can really do” in general; “a very frustrating and difficult reality for a doctor”. In her four years in primary care in very poor neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires, patients had no money for drugs; they had a set of basic drugs covered by the World Health Organization (wording garbled) [verify], but sometimes even those were missing. Some medication is secondary (e.g. cough medicine in a viral infection; painkillers are often for comfort), others are really important: then you try to get it for the patient through a social worker, or (in her clinic) donated medication kept for that situation. “It’s really context specific.”

Not going blank

A student went blank in the past medical history after the patient said “no” to surgery. Answer: learn the structure really well; “that’s what’s going to give you freedom to really interact with the patient and not be stressed out”.

Past medical history items









































ItemLecturer’s pointsMedical conditions (past and current)Ask first: more important than surgeries (a surgery may happen once; diabetes or asthma matter throughout). In five years of teaching, students “always forget about medical conditions”SurgeriesAllergiesImportant “because you might medicate your patient and you don’t want to kill your patient”. Ask specifically about drug allergies, then food and environmental allergiesMedicationNot the medication linked to the history of present illness (already asked there): “are you on any current medication?” Broad: prescribed, over the counter, supplements, herbal remedies, things not for an illness such as a contraceptive. Phrase it so the patient understands you mean medication in generalVaccinesRaised by a student; not top priority at this checkupTransfusionsTrips abroadNot relevant at a checkup; can be very relevant when you suspect an infectionObstetric historyChildren, C-section, miscarriages: important and often forgotten; “I would put it here” (context garbled) [verify]

Childhood illnesses were asked by a student; not discussed further.
Students’ laptops: “What I don’t really like are laptops” in the encounter; garbled [verify].

Family history

Ask an open, general question first (“any disease running in the family”): going straight to directed questions misses most of it.
But open questions can miss relevant illnesses: e.g. many patients do not consider hypertension a disease, especially if a parent’s is controlled with pills.
So ask in a directed way about the most prevalent diseases: diabetes, heart disease, cancer.
Then also diseases related to the case (here: any lung disease in the family).
Asking “what led up to the episode” belongs to the history of present illness (the fundamental question from last class: “do you relate it to anything?”), not to past medical or family history.

Introducing sensitive topics (social history)

Avoid “would you consider yourself a drinker?”: “we always try not to associate the identity of the person with a habit or a disease”.
First introduce the topic so it is not abrupt: e.g. “I’m going to ask you a few things about your lifestyle, and there might be a few sensitive questions, so I can help you.”
Then a simple, neutral question: “Do you drink alcohol?”
Social history is not only alcohol.

3. Social history: the items

In Spanish: “hábitos de vida y hábitos tóxicos”.
Items raised in class: diet, exercise, sleep, stress, occupation (profession, student, daily activity), smoking, alcohol, other drugs, leisure / entertainment, economic situation, sexual activity.
She separates items to ask always in practice from items to ask when relevant (economic situation “could be very relevant… but it could also not be”; sexual activity discussed here). The split is garbled in the transcript [verify].
Real practice: in the emergency department with abdominal pain you probably would not ask about alcohol unless relevant; experience tells you. For now, always ask the core items so you practise them.
The slides add further aspects of social history: spirituality, social support system (“could be very relevant, but not all of it”).

4. Tobacco
Harmful effects of smoking (class brainstorm; slides to follow)









































AreaPoints from the classPneumothoraxSmoking is a risk factor (“I did not tell you”; she will add it to the scenario next time)Emphysema (transcribed “impicillin”)Loss of functional lung tissue from inflammation, trapped air, poor oxygenation. Part of COPD, which includes it and chronic bronchitis. Heavy smokers at the end of life with oxygen tanks: lungs so destroyed they desaturate when walkingLung cancer”That’s what everybody has in their head”Other cancersAnything in contact with smoke and its toxic metabolites: throat, mouth, tongue, oesophagus; bladder cancer is “a very known one” (contact with the metabolites)Lung fibrosisCould be a final stage of any inflammatory lung condition, “but it’s not a disease in itself” (passage partly garbled) [verify]Cardiovascular disease”The number one killer of our society”: heart disease, stroke, heart attack, peripheral arterial pathology (arteries clogged by cholesterol); smoking is one of the main risk factorsPregnancyDefects in pregnancy; after birth, breastfeeding (passage garbled) [verify]Passive exposure at homeHouse air is contaminated even if the parent smokes outside (residues on clothes); small children have more respiratory infections and more otitis. Counsel the parents to limit or stop

A student asked whether nicotine is a “gateway” like alcohol or marijuana. Lecturer: the literature describes an association between substance use in general, so if one is positive, ask about the others (alcohol, marijuana, other drugs).

What to ask a smoker





































QuestionWhySince whenExposure (with amount)How much (cigarettes per day)ExposureHas she ever considered quittingReadiness; ask before offering helpHas she tried before, what therapy (e.g. nicotine patches or pouches)Previous attemptsMoments when she smokes more (stress, social)“Getting to know your patients so that you can tailor your counselling”How dependent she isDetermines whether medication is used and what type of therapyOther substancesAssociation between substance use

Dependence indicators: amount per day; frequency (back to back); whether it is hard to be in a closed place without being able to get out (e.g. cinema); smoking first thing in the morning (“their body asks for it”; same in alcohol abuse).
A primary care questionnaire for nicotine dependence (name garbled as “Yaki”) [verify]; “you don’t have to learn it”. Items she read: how soon after waking you smoke; difficulty refraining where forbidden (church, library, cinema); which cigarette you would hate to give up (the first in the morning indicates severe dependence); cigarettes per day; smoking more frequently at certain times; smoking when ill (“it’s not natural for the body to want a cigarette when you’re ill”).

Pack years

Merges duration and amount into one measure of exposure:

pack years = years smoked x cigarettes per day / 20 (20 = cigarettes in a pack)


Class example: 8 years (since 16) x 10 cigarettes per day / 20; the class answer is transcribed “four or five years” [verify].
It is not packs per year or per week: “it’s just a measure… to compare patients”. Second example: 30 years of 5 cigarettes a day gives 7.5.
Variable consumption (e.g. 5 years at 20 a day, then less): fraction it and calculate each period.
Why compare exposures: science needs it for evidence-based guidelines, to know the risk at 1, 10, 20 pack years and decide whom to screen (e.g. a yearly scan for lung cancer), rather than improvising by intuition. “It’s a strong decision”; there is radiation.
Guideline she quoted: a patient with 20 pack years, aged 50 to 80 (the range where lung cancer usually develops), and an active smoker should be told to have a yearly CT scan (transcribed “HHS scan”). A following fragment, “because it’s not useful. It doesn’t diminish mortality”, has lost its context [verify]. Not to learn: “I just want you to understand why you’re doing the things you’re doing.”

Counselling by stage

Scenario 1 lesson: the student said “I’m going to talk to my attending and see how we can help you” before asking whether she wanted to quit; the patient said she did not want to. Be slower: first ask if she has ever considered quitting.
Precontemplation (not considering it): give a little information, “see if it grows into a plant”, without spending too much time; insisting makes the patient defensive. A few sentences: it is harmful, it is a risk factor for the pneumothorax and its recurrence, we are here to help if you give it some thought. A student’s point accepted: since she is recovering, at least advise her to limit smoking.
Contemplation (“I’m considering it, but not now”): give more information, tell her how you can help, plan a “when” for the next consultation.
“These are all stages that have been studied” in smoking.
General message: smoking is harmful in general, not only now; advise reducing if the patient cannot quit; explain cumulative effects.
Your role as a medical student: take notes and pass it on to the attending, not counsel as the doctor.

5. Scenario 2: sadness and trouble sleeping (outpatient clinic)
Case

Patient has just arrived; you do not know why. Find out why, and do the full introduction, identification, chief complaint, fundamental questions, plus social and personal history.
Actor patient: trouble sleeping, sad mood, studying for a public position. Over three attempts: a motorbike accident about a year ago, then her best friend died of cancer; sadness for about one to two months (time frames differed between attempts). Drinks every day: a beer in the morning, a beer while studying in the afternoon, two glasses of wine with a friend.

Reading and naming the emotion

Student noticed the sadness from body language: no eye contact, looking down, long time to answer, even to give her name and date of birth.
He said “I see you’re sad”: praised as honest and “a very intelligent move”. Otherwise you do the whole consultation without naming it, “an elephant in the room”.
He also said this was a confidential space (setting the stage) and asked softly whether there was a specific reason; she answered “life”.
Why she does not say more: it is hard to share with a stranger after three minutes; in a depressed mood “you don’t feel like connecting with anyone. That’s a characteristic of depression.” Adapt your rhythm and make space.

Strategies to get the story out (from the debriefs)













































StrategyExample or pointRephrase and insist once more”Has anything else happened that you would like to share?”Short, directed questions”Is it a family issue?”Explore the feeling”Are you sad all the time?”, “Have you been feeling depressed?” (name it)Encourage continuationIf you interrupted her: stop and say “please continue”EchoRepeat her “and also…”Silence and waitingDepressed patients need “even more space, even more slow”; silence “actually shows that you’re a professional”. Do not move on in the interview when you know something is unsaidRespect a refusalAt some point “I’m not going to insist anymore”; “a delicate balance”Use her nameHelps create the connectionAsk why nowShe has felt this way for a while: what led her to consult now

The student who waited through the silence got the information (“If I interrupted… she would have lost her”).

Physical touch

Students saw hand-holding in “an American book” and were unsure. Class discussion on cultural differences (Latin countries felt to be more physical).
Lecturer: possibly not in a first encounter in an outpatient clinic; you do not know the person (she may dislike physical contact). With a bond, e.g. when someone dies, a hug is “totally normal and natural if you feel like it”. It depends on your own style: “know who you are and do what you feel is natural”; not touching does not make you a bad doctor.

Showing empathy





























ChannelPointsVerbal”I’m very sorry to hear that”Non-verbalPosture (leaning forward shows engagement; a remark on distance and crossed arms is garbled)Tone and paceMatch the patient’s level of voice and pace; “mirror” body language subtly (used in psychology), not acting depressed. Mismatch example: a slow, soft, sad patient and a loud, fast “so now I’m going to ask you about your diet”Offer help”Would you be interested in talking to someone?”, the same kind of question as “would you be interested in quitting smoking?”SupportAsk whether she has told friends or family; is anybody there to listen. Tells you how much help she needs
Normal grief or depression?

“Grieving can last up to two years” and still be normal (to give an idea).
Not normal: lost interest in everything, nothing brings pleasure, not meeting friends.
A student cited the textbook: ask about suicidal thoughts. Lecturer: “have it in your mind to ask if you feel that could be a concern”; be careful but it is important.

Severity adapted to other complaints

The 0 to 10 severity scale is for pain; adapt the idea of intensity. For sleep: how rested she feels on waking, how sleepy during the day, hours slept now versus before (sleeping two hours = very sleep deprived).

Alcohol: asking and documenting

Patients first say “the usual”: alcohol carries stigma, patients fear judgement and get defensive. Be subtle, respectful and neutral, but never settle for “the usual” or something superficial: you need the information to know if she is at risk.
Do not suggest numbers (“like four? like one?“): ask an open question. If you feel she is not telling you, ask “do you drink anything else other than beer?”
Never write “she drinks a lot”: “what’s a lot?”
Document:


























ItemWhyAmountAs for smokingType of drinkDifferent alcohol concentrationTime of dayDrinking first thing in the morning suggests dependencePatternDaily, social, or nothing during the week and very drunk at the weekend (a known pattern, still harmful)
Why alcohol matters in this patient

Alcohol and sadness form a vicious circle (sadder, drink more), with risk of dangerous situations if there are suicidal thoughts (student’s answer, accepted).
She consulted for trouble sleeping: possibly rumination over the tragedy; possibly seeking a sleeping pill prescription; alcohol abuse may relate to the sleep problem.
Alcohol plus sleeping pills: “not a good idea”. Point of a complete history: “Just like the allergies, we could kill our patient… because of these interactions.”

Standard drinking unit (SDU, unidad de bebida estándar)

“The new way that we assess the risk”; before it was grams. 1 SDU = 10 g of alcohol.
Concentrations given in class (approximate, garbled): beer about 5 to 12 (“depends on the beer”), wine about 13, whiskey/liquor transcribed as “47 and above” and then “25 and above” [verify].
Equivalences given: a small glass of wine = 1 SDU = 200 ml of beer = 50 ml of liquor [verify against slides].
Grams of alcohol: stated as “milliliters of alcohol multiplied by the density of alcohol divided by 100”. In the worked example the volume, the concentration (5) and a density factor (transcribed “zero”) were multiplied [verify the exact formula on the slides].
Worked example (simplified, not the patient’s real intake): 3 beers a day, about 1 litre at 5: 40 g per day = 4 SDU per day. The risk classification is per week, so multiply by 7; the class answer is transcribed “twenty” [verify].
Classification: for a woman this level is dangerous (“Para una mujer…”), and it would be dangerous for a man too (thresholds not stated; see slide) [verify].
Mixed drinks: calculate SDUs for each drink and add them, or add the grams and convert.
Why tables: “to help us not improvise”, to know the risk based on evidence.

6. Scenario 3: abdominal pain (emergency department)
Case

Medical student in the emergency department; patient with abdominal pain: use the history of present illness with the mnemonics from last class, then the complete clinical history: chief complaint, history of present illness, past medical history, social history, family history.
Actor patient: 24 years old; pain for two days, started in the centre and moved to the right lower quadrant, constant, worse standing and better sitting; had taken something that morning without relief (garbled) [verify]; allergy to nuts; vaccines up to date; drinks sporadically at weekends; had not gone to the bathroom for two days. The script was appendicitis; the actor forgot to mention fever and nausea.
Peers’ feedback: good non-verbal attitude (posture, clear speech, tone, pace), organized and complete. Suggested extra question: has she ingested anything lately that could be related.

Structure of the clinical note

Identifying information first, then a headline summarizing the chief complaint: a quick idea of what happened that day, for you or a colleague reading it months later.
Headline options from class: “three-day abdominal pain” (the case says two days [verify]); “acute abdominal pain” (gives a sense of onset and time frame); “abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant”.
Praised: it said what she said and did not give a diagnosis.
In the clinical note you do not write the SOCRATES letters; you write a paragraph. Not everything in the note is structured.
Do not use shorthand such as “allergy: -” in a clinical note (she uses it on the board only to save time).

SOCRATES applied









































LetterIn this caseS SiteRight lower quadrant (right iliac region)O OnsetTwo days ago; onset also means sudden or gradual. Last class: brain haemorrhage = very sudden onset. Here not asked; it would be gradual, which fits appendicitis (gets worse and worse)C CharacterNot clearly obtainedR RadiationNot radiation: it started periumbilical and moved to the right lower quadrant (typical appendicitis presentation). Radiation = pain in both places at once, e.g. chest pain in a heart attack also felt in the armA Associated symptomsForgotten in the script: nausea and fever (“also very typical”). Not going to the bathroom for two days: do not write “constipation”, which is a diagnosis with criteria (she may normally go every three days); write that she has not gone for two daysT TimingConstant (“there’s no timing because it’s constant”). In other mnemonics “constant” goes with character; depends on the mnemonicE Exacerbating / relievingWorse standing, better sitting (patient’s words; the debrief wording is confused)S SeverityNot asked; the script was 7 to 8 out of 10

Could also ask about previous consultations.

Past medical history in this case

Order: medical conditions first, then surgery, allergies (nuts), medication (in general, not only the painkiller for this pain; it “shouldn’t be that she only answers paracetamol”), vaccines, transfusions, trips.
Vaccines relevant here: an infection she would not get if vaccinated could cause abdominal pain; and she may go to surgery if it is appendicitis, so everything must be in order.
Trips could be relevant: parasites in some countries, endemic illnesses; e.g. dengue is more and more common and can present with severe abdominal pain and fever. “You can’t rule out dengue.”
Family history was asked too early: put it after the personal history (first you are more interested in the patient than her family).
Social history covered diet, exercise, alcohol, smoking, other drugs: “90% of what you ask for”.

Signposting

Advice to everybody: say where you are going: “I’m going to ask you a few questions about your past medical history”, “…about your family history”. It helps you be organized and helps the patient know where she stands; otherwise the patient can get disoriented.

POM Goals of medicine and CanMEDS roles
Sources

CANMED ROLES (automatic transcription, errors corrected): first half of the workshop. Starts mid-sentence in the introductions and ends at the 10-minute break.
Audio Clip 2: second half, after the break: Hastings Institute goals (led by Dr. Jennifer), euthanasia debate, videos, history, today’s challenges, the final reflection. Ends in a conversation with students after the reflection.
One workshop in two files; nothing obvious is missing between them except the end of the break.
Personal experiences shared by students in the final conversation are not included in this note.
Coverage: transcripts only. No slides, POM material or other notes in the vault.

Resources

Slides: will be on ADI (“you’ll have all the slides from all the professors”). None in the vault.
Reading: a paper on dignity by a friend of his, Harvey (surname transcribed “Chachanov” [verify]), “the ABCD of dignity”, to be shared as a PDF: “at some point in the next six years, read this paper.”
Film: title transcribed “Quixote” [verify] (a literature professor, expert in Shakespeare, with advanced ovarian cancer), shown in clips; used in his optional six-day course on decision making (“Optativa”).
Video by ChenMed on physician burnout; clip from Patch Adams.

Marking: [check] = sources conflict (named). [verify] = looks wrong or garbled, and no vault source settles it. There are no slides, official notes or Lucía notes for POM in the vault.
Exam flags from the lecturers

“I want you to remember those seven roles, because I’m going to ask those in the test”: “what are the seven roles of being a doctor, as described by CanMEDS, or something like that” (section 2). “This is important.”
But: “This class is not about writing exams. This class is about becoming a good doctor.”
Link everything you learn in the degree (theory, practicals, workshops) to the seven CanMEDS roles.
The quadruple aim slide: “these are not in the exams, by the way” (section 9).
Reflection at the end: upload a photo to ADI the same day; it counts for attendance, which is part of the grade (section 10).

1. Why did you choose medicine? / What does a firefighter do?

Opening private reflection: why did you choose medicine (not shared).
Group brainstorm: what does a firefighter (bombero) do? Beyond putting out fires: rescuing people and animals, help in natural disasters (floods, storms, earthquakes, fallen trees), clearing chemical spills, first aid, prevention (presence at events, clearing land in summer), education in schools and villages, risking their lives (commitment to society), and their mere presence gives a sense of security; fire stations are a place of refuge (e.g. for pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago).
Point: a firefighter does much more than the obvious role; so does a doctor.

2. The CanMEDS roles

CanMEDS (“Canadian Medical”): used internationally by many medical schools to define the roles of a doctor and the competencies required. Seven roles.
Built from the class brainstorm (“what do doctors do?“):






































RoleWhat he describedMedical expert (at the centre)The whole clinical process: prepare for the patient, observe (limp, grimace, jaundice, pallor), history, physical examination, investigations if needed, differential diagnosis, diagnosis, care plan (pharmacological or not), treatment. Includes prevention and health promotionCommunicatorWith patients, families and colleagues, with respect and dignity; tone and non-verbal communication matter; breaking bad newsCollaboratorWith other specialties (e.g. referring for radiotherapy for bone pain) and other professions (nurses, social workers, therapists), all with equal roles; increasingly with engineers, AI and data expertsAdvocateFrom writing to authorities for a family’s home care, to policy and leadershipScholar (“scholarship”)Research, teaching, quality improvementProfessionalCaring for persons; commitment to the patient, to society, to the profession (to be developed in the professionalism class)Seventh roleNot named clearly in the transcript. He mentions managers and leaders of teams, services and hospitals within advocacy. [verify] against the slide

At the centre of all the roles: being human: empathy, compassion, respect, dignity. Empathy = putting yourself in the other person’s shoes (e.g. a very active person after a stroke; a 29-year-old with advanced cancer). Compassion vs empathy will be covered in later workshops.

Examples he gave for the roles

Medical expert: a 78-year-old with diabetes and long-standing kidney disease, short of breath, swollen feet: think of heart failure, look for signs (e.g. jugular venous distension), order an echocardiogram.
Humanizing: not “a 63-year-old diabetic” but “José, 63, with diabetes, widowed two years ago, lives in a flat without a lift, a retired artist”.
Cure, control, comfort: sometimes we can cure; sometimes not, but we can control (e.g. immunotherapies for cancers and autoimmune diseases); when we cannot control, we can always comfort. He gets upset when doctors say “there’s nothing more we can do”. About 5 to 10% of people die suddenly; 85 to 90% after an illness of weeks, months or years. Chronic illness and multimorbidity are increasing.
Research (scholar): not only diseases and treatments, also communication and the health system:

Palliative care unit in Ottawa: patients felt doctors spent little time with them. A paper showed that doctors who sat down were perceived as spending more time than those who stood, for the same measured time. They bought folding chairs; within months patients felt doctors spent much more time.
Nova Scotia: a protocol sent end-of-life patients by ambulance to the emergency room; most wanted to be at home. After training paramedics in basic palliative care (pain crisis, breathlessness, conversations), transfers fell by more than 60% in 18 months; paramedics found more meaning in their work.


Primary care is “the foundation, the bastion of any healthcare system”; countries that underinvest have overcrowded emergency rooms. Do not think of it as second class.
Prevention in every specialty (e.g. obstetrics detecting a placenta in the wrong position; endocrinology controlling diabetes to prevent complications); public health (first called in the COVID pandemic, with infectious disease, respiratory and immunology specialists).
Advocacy (his story): as a fifth-year student in South Africa, a Portuguese patient with advanced prostate cancer died in uncontrolled pain, treated only with pethidine (a weak opioid with toxic metabolites causing opioid neurotoxicity: hallucinations, confusion, agitation, twitching), because morphine was feared as addictive. In Canada (1993-94) he refused to increase a patient’s very low morphine dose for fear of addiction; the patient left in tears (“I hope one day doctors like you can look after people like me”). He did a short course in Toronto, called the patient back, apologized, and cared for him comfortably in his last three months. He then specialized (Edmonton) and founded Pallium Canada (2000), training health professionals across Canada in basic palliative care (number garbled, “mighty thousand” [verify]).

Opioids: “like a car”: safe if used properly, dangerous if not; appropriate doses depend on the patient (lower in severe kidney or lung disease, or neuromuscular disease affecting breathing).
Portugal has had a law since 2012 giving every citizen the right to palliative care, but it is not fully implemented: leaders are needed to make laws real.
“No matter what specialty you go into, you will be caring for patients with serious illnesses; don’t run away from them.”


Communicator: “I’m really busy, I’ll come back later” vs “Are you okay? I’ve got a very big priority and then I’ll come back to you”: same content, different tone; the patient feels it. Breaking bad news (e.g. worse lung function in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis): “I wish I were giving you good news… I’m worried about what I’m seeing” gives a warning shot, then the news, keeping realistic hope. Avoid false hope: it takes away time to prepare.
Collaborator: his son, a biomedical engineer, designed a cheap laparoscopy simulator (a blue box) now used here, working with gastroenterologists.

3. The Hastings Institute goals of medicine

Founded in 1969 in the USA by a psychiatrist and a philosopher, at a time of change (civil rights movement, Vietnam War, advances in mental health care and technology), to deal with the ethical challenges of a medicine that could now prolong life. Still exists today.
The goals of medicine:

Prevention of disease and injury, and promotion and maintenance of health.
Relief of pain and suffering.
Care and cure of those with a malady, and care of those who cannot be cured.
Avoidance of premature death and pursuit of a peaceful death.


Group examples:

Prevention: sport and strength training for bone density (osteoporosis), hygiene and hand washing, awareness campaigns (smoking), screening, universal health care / access (in the USA, undiagnosed diabetes in people who cannot afford care).
Relief of suffering: treating pain in incurable cancer; even just talking with and comforting the patient.
Peaceful death: a friend of Dr. Jennifer’s, in her 30s with breast cancer, kept being sent to the emergency room and died in hospital; doctors should advocate for a peaceful death.



4. Euthanasia and assisted suicide (the lecturer’s position)

A student raised euthanasia under “peaceful death”. He stated it is controversial and gave his own view, saying there are other viewpoints and pros and cons.
Terms: assisted suicide = the doctor prescribes a lethal substance and the person takes it themselves (e.g. Oregon, Netherlands, Belgium); euthanasia = the doctor administers it. In Canada both fall under MAID (medical assistance in dying), a euphemism he finds troubling (compared with “apartheid” as a euphemism for racism).
His position: it should not be part of a doctor’s role; our role is to maintain life, but also to let go when it is time, not to end life. “This medical school believes it’s not part of being a doctor.”
His arguments (he testified for the Canadian government in 2013-2014, received threats and needed a police escort):

No real choice without palliative care: if the only way to relieve suffering is to end your life, society has failed.
Social slippery slope: first only for the very end of life, then dementia, children… In Canada the end-of-life requirement was later removed. Cases: about 13,500 in 2023, 16,000 to 18,000 per year by 2024-2025 (as given). In 2023, loneliness was listed as a reason in about 1,300 cases.
Autonomy has become imbalanced: autonomy has limits in society (you cannot drive at 200 km/h). Even an individual request has ripple effects: thresholds drop; people with disabilities and elderly people feel less valued (disability associations sued).
Depression is not allowed as the main reason in Canada, but he has seen cases recorded under other diagnoses.
The UK recently voted against legalization because of gaps in palliative care; Spain has legalized it; Portugal has not.


The doctor’s role regardless: know how to respond to “I cannot live like this”, “my life is not worth living”: often a call for help, not a request for euthanasia. Sit down, explore the source of the suffering with compassion and without judgment.
Palliative sedation: for patients in the last days or weeks with a refractory symptom (e.g. pain, severe breathlessness in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) despite all treatments: intentionally lowering consciousness with the lowest effective dose of a sedative, usually midazolam (short-acting benzodiazepine, adjustable). Needed in about 5% of dying patients.
Four pillars of ethics: autonomy, beneficence (doing good), non-maleficence (not doing harm), justice (and equity). They must stay balanced.

5. Videos and lessons on the doctor-patient relationship

Burnout video (ChenMed): doctors’ goals are prevention, cure and easing suffering; documentation and lack of control over schedules lead to burnout; remember why you went into medicine.
Patch Adams clip: a professor presenting a diabetic patient’s ulcers to students without addressing her; a student asks her name (“Marjorie”) and greets her. The palliative care lecturer said this happened when he was training, and to his own family (next point).
His sister’s story: as a final-year student he saw a tumour in her acetabulum on an X-ray. The orthopaedic surgeon (his admired professor) never greeted them, held the X-ray to the window and said “I’ve got to send you to a cancer doctor”. Surgery showed a benign tumour, but she was traumatized for years by how it was told.
Dr. Jennifer’s stories: an infectious disease doctor who listened and did a one-minute magic trick for her son; a doctor who put a hand on hers and said “we’re going to find out what’s wrong with you”. “Take the things you like and put them in your pocket; throw out the things you don’t.”

6. Film clip: code status and informed consent

Clip: a nurse sits with the patient, shares a popsicle, admits the cancer is not being killed, and explains code status: full code (resuscitation, ICU) vs DNR (do not resuscitate). The patient chooses DNR.
Lesson on autonomy vs informed consent: in very advanced disease (last weeks or months, advanced heart disease or cancer), CPR succeeds in less than about 4%; on TV and in films it succeeds in about 75%, which is what people believe. CPR is very effective in sudden events (heart attack, trauma, lightning).
How he discusses it: we are here to look after you, there is still a lot of living to do; at the very end, when treatments have not worked (not because you gave up), compressions and shocks work in about 4%, survivors are usually on machines, ribs are broken. With this information most choose not to be resuscitated; some still choose everything, and that must be respected.
Asking “do you want us to resuscitate you?” without this context gives autonomy without informed consent.

7. History of the profession

Hippocrates: the Hippocratic oath (help patients and society, do no harm); scientific thinking about causes and treatments.
Asclepius: mythological figure whose staff with a snake became a symbol of medicine (he calls it the caduceus [verify]). His school: you can only be a healer when you have healed yourself, are aware of yourself and your biases; seeing the patient as a whole person.
Life expectancy around 1900: about 50 to 60; pneumonia a common cause of death at all ages.
Penicillin changed this, but also contributed to a death-denying society; large hospitals (early to mid 1900s) moved death from the community to hospitals. Few students have seen someone die; a century ago everyone had.
“To cure sometimes, to relieve often, to comfort always.”
ICU picture: a great advance, but balance cure and control with quality of life; sometimes say “these treatments won’t help you; let’s talk about other possibilities”.

8. Medicine in your generation

Personalized medicine: targeting cancers by their receptors instead of the same chemotherapy for all.
Artificial intelligence, digital health.
Antimicrobial resistance (“superbugs”): e.g. tuberculosis now resistant to treatments he used in South Africa. Stewardship: antibiotics for sore throats (mostly viral) breed resistance; examine, test, and if viral, no antibiotic (“come back in two or three days if worse”).
Self-awareness: notice your nerves as a student; it is fine to tell your supervisor or friends.
Lifelong learning, teamwork, quality improvement.

9. Quadruple aim (not in the exam)

Improve the patient experience, health outcomes, lower costs, and improve the care providers’ experience.

10. Conclusion and reflection

Remember the CanMEDS roles: being a doctor is much more than treating disease; behind all roles is the relationship.
Closing quote by “an Indian philosopher” (name not given): “I slept and dreamt that life was joy. I awoke and saw that life was service. I acted and learned that service was joy.”
Reflection (15 minutes, upload to ADI the same day; part of attendance and grade): Why did you decide to become a doctor? What type of doctor would you like to be? How has this workshop impacted you?
